It was founded in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") in 1946 by [Herb Abramson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Abramson "Herb Abramson"). His partner was [Jerry Blaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Blaine "Jerry Blaine"). Blaine bought Abramson's half of the company in 1947, when Abramson went on to co-found [Atlantic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Records "Atlantic Records") with [Ahmet Ertegun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmet_Ertegun "Ahmet Ertegun").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jubilee_Records#cite_note-blaine-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jubilee_Records#cite_note-Inc.1959-2) The company name was Jay-Gee Recording Company, a subsidiary of the Cosnat Corporation. Cosnat was a wholesale record distributor. ## History \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jubilee_Records&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: History")\] Jubilee was the first [independent record label](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_record_label "Independent record label") to reach the white market with a black vocal group, when [the Orioles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Orioles "The Orioles")' recording of " [Crying in the Chapel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crying_in_the_Chapel "Crying in the Chapel")" reached the Top Twenty on the [Pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_music "Popular music") chart in 1953.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jubilee_Records#cite_note-gillett-3) [The Four Tunes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Four_Tunes "The Four Tunes") started recording for Jubilee in 1953. The biggest early hit for Jubilee was "Crying in the Chapel" by [the Orioles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Orioles "The Orioles"). A subsidiary label, [Josie Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josie_Records "Josie Records"), was formed in 1954 and issued more uptempo material. Hits on Josie included " [Speedoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speedoo "Speedoo")" by the [Cadillacs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Cadillacs "The Cadillacs") (number 3 R&B, number 17 pop) and " [Do You Want to Dance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Do_You_Want_to_Dance "Do You Want to Dance")" by [Bobby Freeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Freeman "Bobby Freeman") (number 2 R&B, number 5 pop). The biggest success was the million-seller " [Last Kiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Kiss "Last Kiss")", by J. Frank Wilson and the Cavaliers, which reached number 2 on the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100") in 1964. In the late 1960s, [The Meters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Meters "The Meters"), a group of New Orleans session musicians, released a series of R&B instrumental hits, including " [Cissy Strut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cissy_Strut "Cissy Strut")", which reached number 4 R&B and number 23 pop. The label's last [rock-and-roll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_roll "Rock and roll") hit was the [rhythm-and-blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues") instrumental "Poor Boy"/"Wail!" by the Royaltones (number 17, 1957).[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jubilee_Records#cite_note-gillett-3) Of the label's novelty recordings, releases by the [blooper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blooper "Blooper") compiler [Kermit Schaefer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kermit_Schaefer "Kermit Schaefer"), and the comedian [Rusty Warren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rusty_Warren "Rusty Warren") were successful. Jubilee/Josie also had a custom label, Gross Records, whose only artist was [Doug Clark and the Hot Nuts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doug_Clark_and_the_Hot_Nuts "Doug Clark and the Hot Nuts"); their material was so off-color that the Jubilee and Josie names appeared nowhere on their albums.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jubilee_Records#cite_note-4) In 1970, Jubilee/Josie, in financial difficulties, was sold to Viewlex, which owned [Buddah Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddah_Records "Buddah Records"), and Blaine left the company.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jubilee_Records#cite_note-5) The catalog was eventually taken over by [Roulette Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roulette_Records "Roulette Records").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jubilee_Records#cite_note-blaine-1) The label was declared bankrupt in 1971.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jubilee_Records#cite_note-6) In the late 1980s, Roulette was sold jointly to [Rhino Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhino_Records "Rhino Records") and [EMI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EMI "EMI"), and in the 1990s, Rhino was sold to [Time Warner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_Warner "Time Warner"). The rights to the Jubilee Records archives in North America are now owned by Warner Music, with EMI holding the rights in the rest of the world until 2013. [Warner Music Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Music_Group "Warner Music Group") now has worldwide rights to the Roulette/Jubilee catalogue as a result of acquiring [Parlophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parlophone "Parlophone") in 2013. ## Roster \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jubilee_Records&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Roster")\] This is a list of [recording artists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_artists "Recording artists") who have had at least one [recording](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gramophone_record "Gramophone record") released on the Jubilee Records label. | | | | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | - [The Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Association "The Association")

(1970) | | _**Bitches Brew**_ is a studio album by the American [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") trumpeter, composer, and bandleader [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis"). It was recorded from August 19 to 21, 1969, at [Columbia's Studio B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS_Studio_Building "CBS Studio Building") in New York City and released on March 30, 1970, by [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records"). It marked Davis's continuing experimentation with electric instruments that he had featured on his previous record, the critically acclaimed _[In a Silent Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way "In a Silent Way")_ (1969). With these instruments, such as the [electric piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_piano "Electric piano") and [guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_guitar "Electric guitar"), Davis departed from traditional jazz rhythms in favor of loose, rock-influenced arrangements based on improvisation. The final tracks were edited and pieced together by producer [Teo Macero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teo_Macero "Teo Macero"). The album initially received a mixed critical and commercial response, but it gained momentum and became Davis's highest-charting album on the U.S. [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200"), peaking at No. 35. In [1971](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/13th_Annual_Grammy_Awards "13th Annual Grammy Awards"), it won the [Grammy Award for Best Large Jazz Ensemble Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Large_Jazz_Ensemble_Album "Grammy Award for Best Large Jazz Ensemble Album").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-7) In 1976, it became Davis's first album to be certified [Gold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_(RIAA_certification) "Gold (RIAA certification)") by the [Recording Industry Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America "Recording Industry Association of America") (RIAA).[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-9) In subsequent years, _Bitches Brew_ gained recognition as one of jazz's greatest albums and a progenitor of the [jazz rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_rock "Jazz rock") genre, as well as a major influence on rock and '70s crossover musicians.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-Jurek-4) In 1998, Columbia released _[The Complete Bitches Brew Sessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Complete_Bitches_Brew_Sessions "The Complete Bitches Brew Sessions")_,[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-10) a four-disc box set that includes the original album and previously unreleased material. In 2003, the album was certified [Platinum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platinum_(RIAA_certification) "Platinum (RIAA certification)") by the RIAA, reflecting shipments of one million copies in the United States. In 2025, the album was deemed "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant" by the [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress") and selected for preservation in the [National Recording Registry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Recording_Registry "National Recording Registry").[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-11) ## Background and recording [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a3/Cbs-studio.jpg/330px-Cbs-studio.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cbs-studio.jpg) Current CBS Studio Building By 1969, Davis's core working band consisted of [Wayne Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter "Wayne Shorter") on soprano saxophone, [Dave Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Holland_(bassist) "Dave Holland (bassist)") on bass, [Chick Corea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chick_Corea "Chick Corea") on electric piano, and [Jack DeJohnette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_DeJohnette "Jack DeJohnette") on drums.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1990295-12) The group, minus DeJohnette, recorded _[In a Silent Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way "In a Silent Way")_ (1969), which also featured [Joe Zawinul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Zawinul "Joe Zawinul"), [John McLaughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McLaughlin_(musician) "John McLaughlin (musician)"), [Tony Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer) "Tony Williams (drummer)"), and [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"). The album marked the beginning of Davis's "electric period", incorporating instruments such as the [electric piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_piano "Electric piano"), guitar, and [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") styles.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1990295-12) For his next studio album, Davis wished to explore his electronic and fusion style even further. While touring with his five-piece from the spring to August 1969, he introduced new pieces for his band to play, including early versions of what became "Miles Runs the Voodoo Down", "Sanctuary", and "Spanish Key".[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-1999CD-13) At this point in his career Davis was influenced by contemporary rock and funk music, Zawinul's playing with [Cannonball Adderley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannonball_Adderley "Cannonball Adderley"), and the work of English composer [Paul Buckmaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Buckmaster "Paul Buckmaster").[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1990298-14) In August 1969, Davis gathered his band for a rehearsal, one week prior to the booked recording sessions. As well as his five-piece, they were joined by Zawinul, McLaughlin, [Larry Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Young_(jazz) "Larry Young (jazz)"), [Lenny White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenny_White "Lenny White"), [Don Alias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Alias "Don Alias"), [Juma Santos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juma_Santos "Juma Santos"), and [Bennie Maupin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bennie_Maupin "Bennie Maupin").[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-1999CD-13) Davis had written simple chord lines, at first for three pianos, which he expanded into a sketch of a larger scale composition. He presented the group with some "musical sketches" and told them they could play anything that came to mind as long as they used his chosen chords.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1990299-15) Davis had not arranged each piece because he was unsure of the direction the album was to take; he wanted whatever was produced to come from an improvisational process, "not some prearranged shit."[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1990301-16) Davis booked [Columbia's Studio B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS_Studio_Building "CBS Studio Building") in New York City from August 19–21, 1969.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-1999CD-13) The session on August 19 began at 10 a.m., with the band playing "Bitches Brew" first. Everyone was set up in a half-circle with Davis and Shorter in the middle. Lenny White explained: > It was like an orchestra, and Miles was our conductor. We wore headphones. We had to be able to hear each other. There were no guests at that session. No photos allowed. But there was one guest that nobody talked about, [Max Roach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Roach "Max Roach"). All live recording, no overdubs. 10 a.m. to 1 p.m., for three days.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-17) As usual with Davis's recording sessions during this period, tracks were recorded in sections.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-1999CD-13) Davis gave a few instructions: a tempo count, a few chords or a hint of melody, and suggestions as to mood or tone. Davis liked to work this way; he thought it forced musicians to pay close attention to one another, to their own performances, or to Davis's cues, which could change from moment to moment. On the quieter passages of "Bitches Brew", for example, Davis's voice is audible giving instructions to the musicians, snapping his fingers to indicate tempo, telling the musicians to "Keep it tight" in his distinctive voice, or even directing individuals when to solo, such as when he says "John" during the title track.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-18) "John McLaughlin" and "Sanctuary" were also recorded during the August 19 session. Towards the end, the group rehearsed "Pharaoh's Dance".[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-1999CD-13) Despite his reputation as a " [cool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cool_jazz "Cool jazz")", melodic improviser, much of Davis's playing on this album is aggressive and explosive, often playing fast runs and venturing into the upper [register](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Register_(music) "Register (music)") of the trumpet. His closing solo on "Miles Runs the Voodoo Down" is particularly noteworthy in this regard. Davis did not perform on the short piece "John McLaughlin". Electric bassist [Harvey Brooks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_Brooks_(bassist) "Harvey Brooks (bassist)") was unusual among the musicians in having virtually no jazz experience, though he had worked extensively in rock and pop.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-Grella_2015-19) ## Album title It is not known where the album title came from, and there are various theories about it.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-Tingen-20) Some believe it was a reference to women in Davis's life who were introducing him to cultural changes in the 1960s.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-Tingen-20)[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-21)[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-22) Other explanations\[ _[which?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Avoid_weasel_words "Wikipedia:Avoid weasel words")_\] have been given.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-Tingen-20) ## Post-production Significant editing was made to the recorded music. Short sections were [spliced](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reel-to-reel_audio_tape_recording "Reel-to-reel audio tape recording") together to create longer pieces, brief fragments were looped or repeated, and various effects were applied to the recordings. "Miles Runs the Voodoo Down" is the only track without any editing, presented exactly as it was recorded in the studio.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-Grella_2015-19) [Paul Tingen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tingen "Paul Tingen") reports:[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-23) > _Bitches Brew_ also pioneered the application of the studio as a musical instrument, featuring stacks of edits and studio effects that were an integral part of the music. Miles and his producer, [Teo Macero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teo_Macero "Teo Macero"), used the recording studio in radical new ways, especially in the title track and the opening track, "Pharaoh's Dance". There were many special effects, like tape loops, tape delays, reverb chambers and echo effects. Through intensive tape editing, Macero concocted many totally new musical structures that were later imitated by the band in live concerts. Macero, who has a classical education and was most likely inspired by '50s and '60s French [musique concrète](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musique_concr%C3%A8te "Musique concrète") experiments, used tape editing as a form of arranging and composition. > "Pharaoh's Dance" contains 19 edits – its famous stop-start opening is entirely constructed in the studio, using repeat loops of certain sections. Later on in the track there are several micro-edits: for example, a one-second-long fragment that first appears at 8:39 is repeated five times between 8:54 and 8:59. The title track contains 15 edits, again with several short tape loops of, in this case, five seconds (at 3:01, 3:07 and 3:12). Therefore, _Bitches Brew_ not only became a controversial classic of musical innovation, it also became renowned for its pioneering use of studio technology. Though _Bitches Brew_ was in many ways revolutionary, perhaps its most important innovation was [rhythmic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm "Rhythm"). The [rhythm section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_section "Rhythm section") for this recording consists of two bassists (one playing [bass guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_guitar "Bass guitar"), the other [double bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_bass "Double bass")), two to three [drummers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drummer "Drummer"), two to three [electric piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_piano "Electric piano") players, and a [percussionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percussion_instrument "Percussion instrument"), all playing at the same time.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-tanner-24) As [Paul Tanner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tanner "Paul Tanner"), Maurice Gerow, and David Megill explain, "like rock groups, Davis gives the rhythm section a central role in the ensemble's activities. His use of such a large rhythm section offers the soloists wide but active expanses for their solos."[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-tanner-24) Tanner, Gerow and Megill further explain that > "the harmonies used in this recording move very slowly and function modally rather than in a more tonal fashion typical of [mainstream jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainstream_jazz "Mainstream jazz").... The static harmonies and rhythm section's collective embellishment create a very open arena for improvisation. The musical result flows from basic rock patterns to hard bop textures, and at times, even passages that are more characteristic of [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz")."[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-tanner-24) The solo voices heard most prominently on this album are the trumpet and the [soprano saxophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soprano_saxophone "Soprano saxophone"), respectively of Miles and [Wayne Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter "Wayne Shorter"). Notable also is [Bennie Maupin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bennie_Maupin "Bennie Maupin")'s [bass clarinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_clarinet "Bass clarinet") present on five tracks. The technology of recording, analog tape, disc mastering, and inherent recording time constraints had, by the late 1960s, expanded beyond previous limitations and sonic range for the stereo vinyl album, and _Bitches Brew_ reflects this. Its long-form performances include improvised suites with [rubato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubato "Rubato") sections, [tempo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tempo "Tempo") changes or the long, slow crescendo more common to a symphonic orchestral piece or [Indian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India") [raga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raga "Raga") form than the three-minute rock song. Starting in 1969, Davis's concerts included some of the material that would become _Bitches Brew_.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-25) ## Release _Bitches Brew_ was released in March 1970. It gained commercial momentum for the next four months and peaked at No. 35 on the U.S. [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") for the week of July 4, 1970. This remains Davis's second best performance on the chart behind _[Kind of Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue "Kind of Blue")_, which has peaked at number 3 on Vinyl and number 12 in 2020.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-26) On September 22, 2003, the album was certified platinum by the [RIAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RIAA "RIAA") for selling one million copies in the U.S. In addition to the standard [stereo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereo "Stereo") version, the album was also mixed for [quadraphonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadraphonic "Quadraphonic") sound. Columbia released a quad LP version, using the [SQ matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereo_Quadraphonic "Stereo Quadraphonic") system, in 1971. Sony reissued the album in Japan in 2018 on the [Super Audio CD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Audio_CD "Super Audio CD") format containing both the complete stereo and quadraphonic | Retrospective professional reviews Reviewing for _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ in 1970, [Langdon Winner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langdon_Winner "Langdon Winner") said _Bitches Brew_ shows Davis's music expanding in "beauty, subtlety and sheer magnificence", finding it "so rich in its form and substance that it permits and even encourages soaring flights of imagination by anyone who listens". He concluded that the album would "reward in direct proportion to the depth of your own involvement".[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-36) _[Village Voice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Village_Voice "Village Voice")_ critic [Robert Christgau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Christgau "Robert Christgau") deemed it "good music that's very much like jazz and something like rock",[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-37) naming it the year's best jazz album and Davis "jazzman of the year" in his ballot for _Jazz & Pop_ magazine.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-38) Years later, he had lost some enthusiasm about the album; in _[Christgau's Record Guide: Rock Albums of the Seventies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christgau's_Record_Guide:_Rock_Albums_of_the_Seventies "Christgau's Record Guide: Rock Albums of the Seventies")_ (1981), he called _Bitches Brew_ "a brilliant wash of ideas, so many ideas that it leaves an unfocused impression", with [Tony Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer) "Tony Williams (drummer)")' steadier rock rhythms from _In a Silent Way_ replaced by "subtle shades of Latin and funk polyrhythm that never gather the requisite fervor". He concluded that the music sounded "enormously suggestive, and never less than enjoyable, but not quite compelling. Which is what rock is supposed to be."[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-CG-28) Selling more than one million copies since it was released, _Bitches Brew_ was viewed by some writers in the 1970s as the album that spurred jazz's renewed popularity with mainstream audiences that decade. As Michael Segell wrote in 1978, jazz was "considered commercially dead" by the 1960s until the album's success "opened the eyes of music-industry executives to the sales potential of jazz-oriented music". This led to other fusion records that "refined" Davis's new style of jazz and sold millions of copies, including _[Head Hunters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_Hunters "Head Hunters")_ (1973) by [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock") and [George Benson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Benson "George Benson")'s 1976 album _[Breezin'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breezin' "Breezin'")_.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-39) [Tom Hull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Hull_(critic) "Tom Hull (critic)"), who would later become a jazz critic, has said, "Back in the early '70s we used to listen to _Bitches Brew_ as late night [chill-out music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chill-out_music "Chill-out music") – about the only jazz I ran into at the time."[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-40) According to [independent scholar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_scholar "Independent scholar") Jane Garry, _Bitches Brew_ defined and popularized the [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") genre, also known as jazz-rock, but it was hated by a number of [purists](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/purist "wikt:purist").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-Garry-2) Jazz critic and producer [Bob Rusch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Rusch "Bob Rusch") recalled, "This to me was not _great Black music_, but I cynically saw it as part and parcel of the commercial crap that was beginning to choke and bastardize the catalogs of such dependable companies as [Blue Note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records") and [Prestige](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_Records "Prestige Records").... I hear it 'better' today because there is now so much music that is worse."[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-rusch-41) Despite the controversy the album stirred among the jazz community, it nonetheless topped _[DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat")_'s annual critics' poll in 1970.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-42) _[The Penguin Guide to Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Penguin_Guide_to_Jazz "The Penguin Guide to Jazz")_ called _Bitches Brew_ "one of the most remarkable creative statements of the last half-century, in any artistic form. It is also profoundly flawed, a gigantic torso of burstingly noisy music that absolutely refuses to [resolve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resolution_(music) "Resolution (music)") itself under any recognized guise."[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-penguin-33) In 2003, the album was ranked number 94 on _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ magazine's list of [the 500 greatest albums of all time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone's_500_Greatest_Albums_of_All_Time "Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Albums of All Time"). In the 2020 list, it climbed to number 87.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-43) Along with this accolade, the album has been ranked at or near the top of several other magazines' "best albums" lists in disparate genres.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] The album was also included in the book _[1001 Albums You Must Hear Before You Die](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1001_Albums_You_Must_Hear_Before_You_Die "1001 Albums You Must Hear Before You Die")_.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-44) In 2024, _[Paste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paste_(magazine) "Paste (magazine)")_ ranked _Bitches Brew_ number 12 on its list of the greatest albums of all-time.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-45) Experimental jazz drummer [Bobby Previte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Previte "Bobby Previte") considered _Bitches Brew_ to be "groundbreaking": "How much groundbreaking music do you hear now? It was music that you had that feeling you never heard quite before. It came from another place. How much music do you hear now like that?"[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-snyder-46) [Thom Yorke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thom_Yorke "Thom Yorke"), singer of the English rock band [Radiohead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiohead "Radiohead"), cited it as an influence on their 1997 album _[OK Computer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OK_Computer "OK Computer")_: "It was building something up and watching it fall apart, that's the beauty of it. It was at the core of what we were trying to do."[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-Sutcliffe1999-47) The singer [Bilal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bilal_(American_singer) "Bilal (American singer)") names it among his 25 favorite albums, citing Davis's stylistic reinvention.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-48) The album has also left a mark on ambient and electronic music: [Brian Eno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Eno "Brian Eno"), along with [Aphex Twin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aphex_Twin "Aphex Twin"), [Tricky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tricky_(musician) "Tricky (musician)"), [Can](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Can_(band) "Can (band)"), [Portishead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portishead_(band) "Portishead (band)"), and [Flying Lotus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_Lotus "Flying Lotus"), have all cited it as an influence.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-49) Rock and jazz musician [Donald Fagen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Fagen "Donald Fagen") criticized the album as "essentially just a big trash-out for Miles ... To me it was just silly, and out of tune, and bad. I couldn't listen to it. It sounded like \[Davis\] was trying for a funk record, and just picked the wrong guys. They didn't understand how to play funk. (1969) | | _**In a Silent Way**_ is a studio album by the American [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") trumpeter, composer, and bandleader [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis"), released on July 30, 1969, on [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records"). Produced by [Teo Macero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teo_Macero "Teo Macero"), the album was recorded in one session date on February 18, 1969, at [CBS 30th Street Studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS_30th_Street_Studio "CBS 30th Street Studio") in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"). Macero edited and arranged Davis's recordings from the session to produce the album. Marking the beginning of his ["electric" period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#1968%E2%80%931975:_The_electric_period "Miles Davis"), _In a Silent Way_ has been regarded by music writers as Davis's first [fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") recording, following a stylistic shift toward the genre in his previous records and live performances. Upon its release, the album was met by controversy among music critics, particularly those of jazz and [rock music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music"), who were divided in their reaction to its experimental musical structure and Davis's electric approach. It was nominated for the 1970 [Grammy Award for Best Jazz Instrumental Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Jazz_Instrumental_Album "Grammy Award for Best Jazz Instrumental Album"). Since its initial reception, it has been regarded by fans and critics as one of Davis's greatest and most influential works. In 2001, Columbia Legacy and [Sony Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_Music_Entertainment "Sony Music Entertainment") released the three-disc box set _[The Complete In a Silent Way Sessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Complete_In_a_Silent_Way_Sessions "The Complete In a Silent Way Sessions")_, which includes additional tracks.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-complete-4) ## Background and recording By January 1969, Davis' core working band had stabilised around [Wayne Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter "Wayne Shorter") on soprano saxophone, [Dave Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Holland_(bassist) "Dave Holland (bassist)") on bass, [Chick Corea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chick_Corea "Chick Corea") on electric piano, and [Jack DeJohnette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_DeJohnette "Jack DeJohnette") on drums.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1990295-5) For his next studio album, Davis also brought in drummer [Tony Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer) "Tony Williams (drummer)") and keyboardist [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"), previously members of his [Second Great Quintet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_great_quintet "Second great quintet").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1990295-5) In the following month, the six were joined by Austrian keyboardist [Josef Zawinul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josef_Zawinul "Josef Zawinul")[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1990296-6) and English guitarist [John McLaughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McLaughlin_(musician) "John McLaughlin (musician)"), who had been in the United States for less than two weeks to join [The Tony Williams Lifetime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tony_Williams_Lifetime "The Tony Williams Lifetime") before Davis asked him to attend the recording session. McLaughlin had been a longtime fan of Davis, and spoke with Davis of his nervousness at the prospect of recording with his idol.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1990296-6) Among the compositions by Zawinul that Davis took a liking to was "In a Silent Way", an atmospheric piece that was titled at the suggestion of [Nat Adderley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nat_Adderley "Nat Adderley") while Zawinul was in the [Cannonball Adderley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannonball_Adderley "Cannonball Adderley") band. Adderley wished to use the piece for his band, but Zawinul turned him down, informing him that he had already promised it to Davis.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-tingen2001-7) Although Davis' live performances and recent albums _[Miles in the Sky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_in_the_Sky "Miles in the Sky")_ and _[Filles de Kilimanjaro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filles_de_Kilimanjaro "Filles de Kilimanjaro")_ (both 1968) had indicated his stylistic shift towards [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") and increasing incorporation of electric instrumentation, _In a Silent Way_ marked a complete transition into the style, marking the beginning of his ["electric" period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#1968%E2%80%931975:_The_electric_period "Miles Davis").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-Considine-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-Southall-9)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-O'Brien-10)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-11) It was also his first recording to be constructed largely by the editing and arrangement of Davis and producer [Teo Macero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teo_Macero "Teo Macero"),[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-O'Brien-10) whose editing techniques on _In a Silent Way_ were informed by classical [sonata form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonata_form "Sonata form").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-tingen2001-7) Both tracks on the album consist of three distinct parts that could be thought of as an [exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonata_form#Exposition "Sonata form"), [development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonata_form#Development "Sonata form"), and [recapitulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonata_form#Recapitulation "Sonata form"), with the first and third section of each track being the same piece.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-tingen2001-7) _In a Silent Way_ was assembled from various takes from a three-hour session on February 18, 1969, at [CBS 30th Street Studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS_30th_Street_Studio "CBS 30th Street Studio")'s Studio B in [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-FOOTNOTESvorinich201547-12)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1990296-6) "Shhh/Peaceful" was composed solely by Davis, while the opening and closing section to "In a Silent Way/It's About That Time" is based on Zawinul's "In a Silent Way", which he would record in its original form in 1970 for his third solo album, _[Zawinul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zawinul_(album) "Zawinul (album)")_ (1971).[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-tingen2001-7) After Zawinul presented the tune to the group, it was rehearsed as it was originally written, but Davis wished for it to sound more rock-oriented and stripped the various chord changes to leave a more basic melody built around a [pedal point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedal_point "Pedal point").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-FOOTNOTESvorinich201547-12) McLaughlin had some difficulty playing in the manner Davis wished of him, but found his way after the trumpeter suggested he play the guitar as if he were a novice.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-tingen2001-7) Davis believed that Zawinul was never happy with his adaptation of "In a Silent Way", but felt that the album would have been less successful had its original arrangement been kept.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1990297-13) Zawinul had expressed some dislike of Davis' arrangement, in particular of two chords that he believed that Davis was wrong to remove.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-tingen2001-7) Zawinul claimed that he was responsible for the melodic bass line and descending melody of "It's About That Time" but was not credited; he blamed Macero for this, as he "always put things together so that it came out as if Miles had written it."[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-tingen2001-7) Two days after the February 18 session, Davis returned to the studio and recorded "Ghetto Walk" with drummer [Joe Chambers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Chambers "Joe Chambers"). "Ghetto Walk" was intended to be included on _In a Silent Way_ with "Shhh/Peaceful", but it was later swapped for "In a Silent Way/It's About That Time".[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-FOOTNOTESvorinich201547-12) The group also played through "Early Minor", another Zawinul piece, on February 20, but it too was scrapped.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-FOOTNOTESvorinich201547-12) ## Release _In a Silent Way_ was originally released on July 30, | Retrospective professional reviews Peaking at number 134 on the U.S. [_Billboard_ Top LPs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") chart, _In a Silent Way_ became Davis's first album since _[My Funny Valentine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_Funny_Valentine_(Miles_Davis_album) "My Funny Valentine (Miles Davis album)")_ in 1965 to reach the chart.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-22) While it performed better commercially than most of his previous work,[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-Freeman-23) critics were divided in their reaction to the album upon its release. The album's incorporation of electric instrumentation and tape editing became sources of controversy among jazz critics.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-Taruskin-24) According to _[The Rolling Stone Album Guide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rolling_Stone_Album_Guide "The Rolling Stone Album Guide")_ (1992), Davis' recording process and producer Teo Macero's studio editing of individual recordings into separate tracks for the album "seemed near heretical by jazz standards".[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-Considine-8) In his book _Running the Voodoo Down: The Electric Music of Miles Davis_, Phil Freeman writes of critical response to the album: "Rock critics thought _In a Silent Way_ sounded like rock, or at least thought Miles was nodding in their direction, and practically wet themselves with joy. Jazz critics, especially ones who didn't listen to much rock, thought it sounded like rock too, and they reacted less favorably".[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-Freeman-23) Freeman continues by expressing that both reactions were "rooted, at least partly, in the critic's paranoia about his place in the world", writing that rock criticism was in its early stage of existence and such critics found "reassurance" in viewing the album as having [psychedelic rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelic_rock "Psychedelic rock") elements, while jazz critics felt "betrayed" amid the genre's decreasing popularity at the time.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-Freeman-23) > "It didn't swing, the solos weren't even a little bit heroic, and it had _electric guitars_... But though _In a Silent Way_ wasn't exactly jazz, it certainly wasn't rock. It was the sound of Miles Davis and Teo Macero feeling their way down an unlit hall at three in the morning. It was the soundtrack to all the whispered conversations every creative artist has, all the time, with that doubting, taunting voice that lives in the back of your head, the one asking all the unanswerable questions." —Phil Freeman[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-Freeman-23) In a rave review, _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ rock critic [Lester Bangs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lester_Bangs "Lester Bangs") described _In a Silent Way_ as "the kind of album that gives you faith in the future of music. It is not rock and roll, but it's nothing stereotyped as jazz either. All at once, it owes almost as much to the techniques developed by rock improvisors in the last four years as to Davis' jazz background. It is part of a transcendental new music which flushes categories away and, while using musical devices from all styles and cultures, is defined mainly by its deep emotion and unaffected originality".[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-Bangs-25) Davis' next fusion album, _[Bitches Brew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew "Bitches Brew")_, showed him moving even further into the area that lay between the genres of rock and jazz. The dark, fractured dissonance of _Bitches Brew_ ultimately proved to be instrumental in its success; it far outsold _In a Silent Way_.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-Freeman-23) _In a Silent Way_ has been retrospectively regarded by fans and critics as one of Davis' best albums. In a retrospective review, _[Blender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blender_(magazine) "Blender (magazine)")_ writer K. Leander Williams called it "a proto- [ambient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambient_music "Ambient music") masterpiece". Citing it as "one of Davis's greatest achievements", Chip O'Brien of _[PopMatters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PopMatters "PopMatters")_ viewed that producer Teo Macero's studio editing on the album helped Davis "embrace the marriage of music and technology".[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-O'Brien-10) In regards to its musical significance, O'Brien wrote that _In a Silent Way_ "transcends labels",[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-O'Brien-10) writing "It is neither jazz nor rock. It isn't what will eventually become known as fusion, either. It is something altogether different, something universal. There is a beautiful resignation in the sounds of this album, as if Davis is willingly letting go of what has come before, of his early years with [Charlie Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Parker "Charlie Parker"), with [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane") and Cannonball Adderley, of his early '60s work, and is embracing the future, not only of jazz, but of music itself".[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-O'Brien-10) _[Stylus Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stylus_Magazine "Stylus Magazine")_ writer Nick Southall called the album "timeless" and wrote of its influence on music, stating "The fresh modes of constructing music that it presented revolutionised the jazz community, and the shifting, ethereal beauty of the actual music contained within has remained beautiful and wonderful, its echoes heard through the last 30 years, touching [dance music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_dance_music "Electronic dance music"), [electronica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronica "Electronica"), rock, [pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music "Pop music"), all music".[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-Southall-9) _[The Penguin Guide to Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Penguin_Guide_to_Jazz "The Penguin Guide to Jazz")_ has included _In a Silent Way_ in its suggested "Core Collection".[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-CookMorton-18) The album was also included in the 2005 book _[1001 Albums You Must Hear Before You Die](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1001_Albums_You_Must_Hear_Before_You_Die "1001 Albums You Must Hear Before You Die")_.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-26) ## Track listing | No. | Title | Writer(s) | Length | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 1. | "Shhh"/"Peaceful" | [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis") | 18:16 | Side one - Released: 1974 | | | _**Head Hunters**_ is the twelfth [studio album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio_album "Studio album") by American pianist, keyboardist and composer [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"), released October 26, 1973, on [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records"). Recording sessions for the album took place in the evening at [Wally Heider Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wally_Heider_Studios "Wally Heider Studios") and [Different Fur Trading Co.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Different_Fur "Different Fur") in [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"). Hancock is featured with woodwind player [Bennie Maupin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bennie_Maupin "Bennie Maupin") from his previous "Mwandishi" sextet and three new collaborators – bassist [Paul Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Jackson_(bassist) "Paul Jackson (bassist)"), percussionist [Bill Summers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Summers_(musician) "Bill Summers (musician)"), and drummer [Harvey Mason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_Mason "Harvey Mason"). The latter group of collaborators, which would go on to be known as [the Headhunters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Headhunters "The Headhunters"), also played on Hancock's subsequent studio album _[Thrust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrust_(album) "Thrust (album)")_ (1974). All of the musicians (with the exception of Mason) play multiple instruments on the album. The album was a commercial and artistic breakthrough for Hancock, crossing over to [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk") and [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music") audiences and bringing [jazz-funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk "Jazz-funk") and [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") to mainstream attention, peaking at number 13 on the [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200"). Today the album is regarded as a landmark of fusion and has influenced artists in numerous other genres. In 2008, the [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress") inducted it into the [National Recording Registry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Recording_Registry "National Recording Registry") for being "culturally, historically or aesthetically important".[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_Hunters#cite_note-3) ## Background and recording _Head Hunters_ followed three experimental albums by Hancock's "Mwandishi" sextet: _[Mwandishi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mwandishi "Mwandishi")_, _[Crossings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossings_(Herbie_Hancock_album) "Crossings (Herbie Hancock album)")_, and _[Sextant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sextant_(album) "Sextant (album)")_, released between 1971 and 1973. He later reflected on moving away from this style: > I began to feel that I had been spending so much time exploring the upper atmosphere of music and the more ethereal kind of far-out spacey stuff. Now there was this need to take some more of the earth and to feel a little more tethered; a connection to the earth. ... I was beginning to feel that we (the sextet) were playing this heavy kind of music, and I was tired of everything being heavy. I wanted to play something lighter. —Hancock's sleeve notes: 1997 CD reissue For the new album, Hancock assembled a new band, [the Headhunters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Headhunters "The Headhunters"), of whom only woodwind player [Bennie Maupin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bennie_Maupin "Bennie Maupin") had been a member of the "Mwandishi" sextet. Hancock handled all synthesizer parts himself, having shared these duties with [Patrick Gleeson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Gleeson "Patrick Gleeson") on _Crossings_ and _Sextant,_ and decided against the use of guitar altogether in favor of the Hohner [Clavinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clavinet "Clavinet"), one of the defining sounds on the album. The new band featured a tight [rhythm section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_section "Rhythm section") composed of [Paul Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Jackson_(bassist) "Paul Jackson (bassist)") (bass guitar) and [Harvey Mason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_Mason "Harvey Mason") (drums), creating a relaxed [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk") sensibility that gave it an appeal to a wider audience. Of the four tracks on the album, " [Watermelon Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watermelon_Man_(composition) "Watermelon Man (composition)")" was the only one not written for the album. A hit from Hancock's [hard bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop "Hard bop") days, originally appearing on his debut _[Takin' Off](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takin'_Off "Takin' Off")_ (1962) and later covered by [Mongo Santamaría](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongo_Santamar%C3%ADa "Mongo Santamaría"), it was reworked by Hancock and Mason for this album, featuring Bill Summers blowing into a beer bottle in imitation of the [hindewho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pygmy_music "Pygmy music") flute used by the Mbuti [Pygmies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pygmy_peoples "Pygmy peoples") of [Zaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zaire "Zaire"). The track features heavy use of African percussion. "Sly" was dedicated to [Sly Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sly_Stone "Sly Stone") of [Sly and the Family Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sly_and_the_Family_Stone "Sly and the Family Stone"). "Chameleon" features a famous bassline played by Hancock on an [ARP Odyssey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARP_Odyssey "ARP Odyssey") synthesizer. Closing track "Vein Melter" is a slow-burner, predominantly featuring Hancock on [Rhodes piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodes_piano "Rhodes piano") and Maupin on [bass clarinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_clarinet "Bass clarinet"). Heavily edited versions of "Chameleon" and "Vein Melter" were released as two sides of a 45 RPM single. The Headhunters band, with [Mike Clark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Clark_(drummer) "Mike Clark (drummer)") replacing Mason, worked with Hancock on a number of other albums, including _[Thrust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrust_(album) "Thrust (album)")_ (1974), _[Man-Child](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man-Child "Man-Child")_ (1975), and _[Flood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flood_(Herbie_Hancock_album) "Flood (Herbie Hancock album)")_ (1975). The subsequent albums _[_Secrets_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secrets_(Herbie_Hancock_album) "Secrets (Herbie Hancock album)")_ (1976) and _[Sunlight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunlight_(jazz_album) "Sunlight (jazz album)")_ (1977), had widely diverging personnel. The Headhunters, with Hancock featured as a guest soloist, produced the albums _[Survival of the Fittest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Survival_of_the_Fittest_(album) "Survival of the Fittest (album)")_ (1975) and _Straight from the Gate_ (1978), the first of which was produced by Hancock and included the hit "God Make Me Funky". ## Album cover The album cover, designed by [Victor Moscoso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso "Victor Moscoso"), features Hancock wearing a mask based on the _[kple kple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goli_(dance) "Goli (dance)")_ mask of the [Baoulé people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baoul%C3%A9_people "Baoulé people") of [Ivory Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivory_Coast "Ivory Coast"). Positioned clockwise around Hancock from lower left are Mason, Jackson, Maupin, and Summers. ## Release and reception The album was released on October 26th, 1973. The album was remixed for [quadraphonic sound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadraphonic_sound "Quadraphonic sound") in 1974. Columbia released this mix on [LP record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LP_record "LP record") in the [Stereo Quadraphonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereo_Quadraphonic "Stereo Quadraphonic") matrix format and [8-track tape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/8-track_cartridge "8-track cartridge"). The quadraphonic mixes feature elements not heard in the stereo version, including an additional keyboard melody at the beginning of "Sly". Surround sound versions of the album have been released a number of times on the [Super Audio CD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Audio_CD "Super Audio CD") format, using a digital transfer of the original four-channel quad mix re-purposed into [5.1 surround sound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5.1_surround_sound "5.1 surround sound"). ### Commercial performance _Head Hunters_ was a commercial success, peaking at No. 13 on the [Billboard 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") and at No. 2 on the [Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Top_R&B/Hip-Hop_Albums "Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums") chart. The album remained in the top 30 and top 5 respectively for each chart into the end of the next year. Ultimately, _Head Hunters_ became the biggest-selling jazz album of all time until surpassed by [George Benson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Benson "George Benson")'s _[Breezin'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breezin' "Breezin'")_ in 1976.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] ## Reception and | Professional ratings The album received contemporary critical acclaim and continues to receive acclaim. Writing for [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic"), Stephen Thomas Erlewine would say, "Head Hunters was a pivotal point in Herbie Hancock's career, bringing him into the vanguard of jazz fusion. Hancock had pushed avant-garde boundaries on his own albums and with Miles Davis, but he had never devoted himself to the groove as he did on Head Hunters," concluding, "Jazz purists, of course, decried the experiments at the time, but Head Hunters still sounds fresh and vital decades after its initial release, and its genre-bending proved vastly influential on not only jazz, but funk, soul, and hip-hop." Writing for [Pitchfork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitchfork_(website) "Pitchfork (website)"), Jeremy Larson would say, "Head Hunters is the bond that connects unnamable forces at the center of jazz and of funk, divine aspirations and base desires, head and body. It’s foolish to try to name the spark of music like this, a parlor game better left to the comedown of an acid trip or a street preacher on his last leg. Head Hunters isn’t the god, it’s just five consummate pros jamming, with a light amount of editing and production." In 2005, the album was ranked number 498 in the book version of _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ magazine's list of [the 500 Greatest Albums of All Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone's_500_Greatest_Albums_of_All_Time "Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Albums of All Time"). While it was not included in _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")'_ s original 2003 online version of the list, nor its 2012 revision, it was ranked at number 254 in the 2020 revision.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_Hunters#cite_note-11) _Head Hunters_ was a key release in Hancock's career and a defining moment in the genre of [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), and has been an inspiration not only for jazz musicians, but also to [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk"), [soul music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_music "Soul music"), [jazz funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_funk "Jazz funk") and [hip hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip_hop_music "Hip hop music") artists.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_Hunters#cite_note-Erlewine-2) The [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress") added it to the [National Recording Registry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Recording_Registry "National Recording Registry"), which collects "culturally, historically or aesthetically important" sound recordings from the 20th century.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_Hunters#cite_note-12) It was included in the book [1001 Albums You Must Hear Before You Die](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1001_Albums_You_Must_Hear_Before_You_Die "1001 Albums You Must Hear Before You Die"). ##
