- [Dave MacRae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_MacRae "Dave MacRae") | | | | Website | [softmachine.org](http://softmachine.org/) | **Soft Machine** are an English [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music") band from [Canterbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury "Canterbury"), Kent. The band were formed in 1966 by [Mike Ratledge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Ratledge "Mike Ratledge"), [Robert Wyatt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Wyatt "Robert Wyatt"), [Kevin Ayers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Ayers "Kevin Ayers"), [Daevid Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daevid_Allen "Daevid Allen") and Larry Nowlin. Soft Machine were central in the [Canterbury scene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_scene "Canterbury scene"); they became one of the first British [psychedelic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelic_music "Psychedelic music") acts, and later helped pioneer [progressive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock "Progressive rock")[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-6)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-7) and [jazz rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_rock "Jazz rock") and are widely regarded as the first progressive rock band. Soft Machine's lineup has undergone many changes, and has included [Andy Summers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Summers "Andy Summers"), [Hugh Hopper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Hopper "Hugh Hopper"), [Elton Dean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elton_Dean "Elton Dean"),[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-:0-8) [John Marshall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Stanley_Marshall "John Stanley Marshall"), [Karl Jenkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Jenkins "Karl Jenkins"), [Roy Babbington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Babbington "Roy Babbington") and [Allan Holdsworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allan_Holdsworth "Allan Holdsworth"). As of 2025[\[update\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Soft_Machine&action=edit), the current lineup consists of [John Etheridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Etheridge "John Etheridge"), [Theo Travis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theo_Travis "Theo Travis"), [Fred Thelonious Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Thelonious_Baker "Fred Thelonious Baker") and [Asaf Sirkis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asaf_Sirkis "Asaf Sirkis"). The band's name originates from [William S. Burroughs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_S._Burroughs "William S. Burroughs")'s novel _[The Soft Machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Soft_Machine "The Soft Machine")_. Originating from the band [The Wilde Flowers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wilde_Flowers "The Wilde Flowers"), Soft Machine began as a [psychedelic rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelic_rock "Psychedelic rock") band, releasing their [self-titled debut album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Soft_Machine_(Soft_Machine_album) "The Soft Machine (Soft Machine album)") in 1968. Their second album, [_Volume Two_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volume_Two_(The_Soft_Machine_album) "Volume Two (The Soft Machine album)") (1969), marked their move towards progressive rock and jazz rock, which was fully realised with the subsequent two albums, [_Third_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_(Soft_Machine_album) "Third (Soft Machine album)") (1970) and [_Fourth_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_(album) "Fourth (album)") (1971). By 1971, Soft Machine became a purely instrumental jazz rock band,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-Lynch22-9) continuing this direction across their subsequent albums, [_Fifth_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifth_(Soft_Machine_album) "Fifth (Soft Machine album)") (1972), [_Six_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Six_(Soft_Machine_album) "Six (Soft Machine album)"), [_Seven_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_(Soft_Machine_album) "Seven (Soft Machine album)") (both 1973), [_Bundles_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bundles_(album) "Bundles (album)") (1975), [_Softs_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Softs_(album) "Softs (album)") (1976), and [_Alive & Well_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alive_&_Well:_Recorded_in_Paris "Alive & Well: Recorded in Paris") (1978). The band split in 1978, though two brief reunions occurred during the 1980s, first for the recording of the album [_Land of Cockayne_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_of_Cockayne_(album) "Land of Cockayne (album)") (1981), and then for a few live shows in 1984. The group Soft Machine Legacy was formed in 2004, and released three studio albums, including their self-titled debut (2006), [_Steam_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steam_(Soft_Machine_Legacy_album) "Steam (Soft Machine Legacy album)") (2007), and [_Burden of Proof_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burden_of_Proof_(Soft_Machine_Legacy_album) "Burden of Proof (Soft Machine Legacy album)") (2013). The "Legacy" suffix was dropped in 2015, and they have since released three studio albums, _[Hidden Details](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hidden_Details "Hidden Details")_ (2018), _Other Doors_ (2023) and _[Thirteen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirteen_(Soft_Machine_album)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Thirteen (Soft Machine album)")_ (2026). Though the band has achieved little commercial success, critics consider Soft Machine to have been influential in rock music.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-Jones-10)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-Keepnews-11)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-Lynch-12) Dave Lynch at [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") called them "one of the most influential underground bands of their era".[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-Lynch2-13) ## History ### Original run (1966–78) #### Early releases and _The Soft Machine_ (1966–1968) In mid-1966, [Mike Ratledge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Ratledge "Mike Ratledge") (keyboards), [Robert Wyatt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Wyatt "Robert Wyatt") (drums, vocals), [Kevin Ayers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Ayers "Kevin Ayers") (bass, vocals), [Daevid Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daevid_Allen "Daevid Allen") (guitar) and Larry Nowlin (guitar) formed Soft Machine, who were billed as The Soft Machine up to 1969 or 1970.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-14) Allen and Wyatt first played together in 1963 as part of the Daevid Allen Trio, and were occasionally accompanied by Ratledge. In 1964, Wyatt and Ayers were founder members of [The Wilde Flowers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wilde_Flowers "The Wilde Flowers"); by 1966, they had both left that band and rejoined Allen to form the short-lived band Mister Head, which also included Nowlin.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-15) The four members soon joined with Ratledge to form the Soft Machine.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-16) Ayers suggested the band's name, which comes from [William S. Burroughs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_S._Burroughs "William S. Burroughs")'s novel _[The Soft Machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Soft_Machine "The Soft Machine")_ (1961),[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-17) after the group performed under several other names including _the Four Skins_.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-18) The band became a quartet when Nowlin departed in September 1966.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-19) During late 1966 and early 1967, the Soft Machine became involved in the early [UK underground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_underground "UK underground") scene. Along with [Pink Floyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pink_Floyd "Pink Floyd"), they became one of the major resident bands at the [UFO Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UFO_Club "UFO Club"), and played other London clubs like the [Speakeasy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speakeasy_Club "Speakeasy Club") and [Middle Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Earth_(club) "Middle Earth (club)"). According to Wyatt, the Soft Machine received negative reactions when playing at venues other than these underground clubs; this led to their penchant for long tracks and segued tunes because continuously playing deprived their audiences chances to boo them.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-StumpHistDuf-20) In February 1967, the band released their first single " [Love Makes Sweet Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love_Makes_Sweet_Music "Love Makes Sweet Music")" on [Polydor Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polydor_Records "Polydor Records").[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-StumpHistDuf-20) In April 1967, the Soft Machine recorded nine demo songs with producer [Giorgio Gomelsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giorgio_Gomelsky "Giorgio Gomelsky") in [De Lane Lea Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Lane_Lea_Studios "De Lane Lea Studios"); due to a dispute over studio costs, these tracks were unreleased for several years.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-21) Polydor later released these demos in 1972 as _Jet Propelled Photographs_.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-22) Later in 1967, the band began touring in mainland Europe, becoming especially popular in France.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-23) When returning from a tour of France in August, Allen, an Australian, was denied re-entry to the UK,[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-StumpHistDuf-20) so the group continued as a trio while Allen returned to Paris to form [Gong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gong_(band) "Gong (band)").[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-24) The Soft Machine, who shared the same management as [the Jimi Hendrix Experience](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Jimi_Hendrix_Experience "The Jimi Hendrix Experience"), supported them on two North American tours during 1968.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-calyx-chronology-25) The band signed to [Probe Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probe_Records "Probe Records") and recorded their eponymous [first album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Soft_Machine_(Soft_Machine_album) "The Soft Machine (Soft Machine album)") in New York City in April at the end of the first tour, though it was not released until December. In London, guitarist [Andy Summers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Summers "Andy Summers"), later of [the Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Police "The Police"), joined the Soft Machine. The band's new line-up began a US tour with some headlining shows before supporting Hendrix in August and September 1968. By the time the Hendrix tour began, Summers had been fired at Ayers' insistence.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-26) Ayers himself departed amicably after the final tour date at the Hollywood Bowl in September, and the Soft Machine disbanded. Wyatt stayed in the US to record solo demos while Ratledge returned to London and began composing.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-27) #### Transition into jazz; _Volume Two_, _Third_, and _Fourth_ (1969–1971) In December 1968, to fulfil contractual obligations, Wyatt and Ratledge re-formed the Soft Machine with their former road manager [Hugh Hopper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Hopper "Hugh Hopper") replacing Ayers on bass. Hopper, like Ayers and Wyatt, was a founding member of The Wilde Flowers. In 1969, the Soft Machine recorded their second album _[Volume Two](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volume_Two_(The_Soft_Machine_album) "Volume Two (The Soft Machine album)")_, which started a change to [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion"). The album fulfilled the band's contract with Probe and they signed with [CBS Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS_Records_International "CBS Records International") by the beginning of 1970. In May 1969, the Soft Machine played as the uncredited backing band on two tracks of _[The Madcap Laughs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Madcap_Laughs "The Madcap Laughs")_, the debut solo album of Pink Floyd's [Syd Barrett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syd_Barrett "Syd Barrett"). Shortly after the Barrett recording, Hopper's brother [Brian Hopper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Hopper "Brian Hopper"), another Wilde Flowers co-founder, joined the Soft Machine on saxophone. Around this time, the band recorded the soundtrack for a multimedia show called _Spaced_, which ran in London for five days in mid 1969. The soundtrack was commercially released in 1996 by Cuneiform Records. In October 1969, following Brian Hopper's departure, the Soft Machine expanded to a septet; Wyatt, Ratledge and Hugh Hopper added a four-piece horn section composed of the saxophonists [Elton Dean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elton_Dean "Elton Dean") and [Lyn Dobson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyn_Dobson "Lyn Dobson"), cornet player [Mark Charig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Charig "Mark Charig") and trombonist [Nick Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Evans_(trombonist) "Nick Evans (trombonist)"). After two months, Charig and Evans departed the band.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-28) The quintet continued until March 1970, when Dobson departed. The remaining quartet recorded the double album _[Third](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_(Soft_Machine_album) "Third (Soft Machine album)")_ (1970) and its single-album follow-up _[Fourth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_(album) "Fourth (album)")_ (1971). _Third_ was mostly instrumental save for Wyatt's song "Moon in June", the last Soft Machine song to have lyrics. _Third_ is unusual for its time in having each of the four sides feature one suite.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-:0-8) _Third_ has since become Soft Machine's biggest-selling album. From _Fourth_ onwards, the band became completely instrumental on record, and then on stage following Wyatt's departure soon after the album's release. During this period, the band received unprecedented acclaim across Europe, and they became the first rock band to be invited to play in August 1970 at London's [Proms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Proms "The Proms") concert, and the show was broadcast live on UK national television.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-29) #### _Fifth_ to _Softs_ and breakup (1972–1978) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dc/Konzert_mit_Soft_Machine%2C_Family%2C_Yes%2C_Man._Deutschlandhalle%2C_M%C3%A4rz_1971.jpg/500px-Konzert_mit_Soft_Machine%2C_Family%2C_Yes%2C_Man._Deutschlandhalle%2C_M%C3%A4rz_1971.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Konzert_mit_Soft_Machine,_Family,_Yes,_Man._Deutschlandhalle,_M%C3%A4rz_1971.jpg) Ticket for a 1971 Soft Machine concert in the [Deutschlandhalle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deutschlandhalle "Deutschlandhalle"), West Berlin, supported by [Family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_(British_band) "Family (British band)"), [Yes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band) "Yes (band)") and [Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_(band) "Man (band)"). After differences over the group's musical direction, Wyatt was fired[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-unterberger-30) in August 1971 and formed [Matching Mole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matching_Mole "Matching Mole") (a pun on "machine molle", French for "soft machine"; also said at the time to have been taken from stage lighting equipment "Matching Mole").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-:0-8) He was briefly replaced by Australian drummer [Phil Howard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Howard_(musician) "Phil Howard (musician)"). This line-up toured extensively in Europe during late 1971 and began the recording of their next album _[Fifth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifth_(Soft_Machine_album) "Fifth (Soft Machine album)")_, but further musical disagreements led to Howard's dismissal at the beginning of 1972, with the album being completed with his replacement, [John Marshall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Stanley_Marshall "John Stanley Marshall"). _Fifth_ was released in 1972, with side one comprising tracks recorded with Howard and side two comprising tracks recorded with Marshall. Later that year, Dean left the band[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-:0-8) and was replaced by [Karl Jenkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Jenkins "Karl Jenkins"), who also played keyboards in addition to saxophone. Both Marshall and Jenkins were former members of [Ian Carr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Carr "Ian Carr")'s [Nucleus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nucleus_(band) "Nucleus (band)"). The band's next album was a half-live half-studio double album _[Six](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Six_(Soft_Machine_album) "Six (Soft Machine album)")_, released in early 1973. After the release of _Six_, Hopper left the band[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-:0-8) and was replaced by [Roy Babbington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Babbington "Roy Babbington"), another former Nucleus member. During this period, Jenkins began to take over as bandleader and main composer. After they released _[Seven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_(Soft_Machine_album) "Seven (Soft Machine album)")_ in late 1973, Soft Machine again switched record labels from CBS to [Harvest Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvest_Records "Harvest Records"), a sub-label of [EMI Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EMI_Records "EMI Records"). At the end of 1973, another former Nucleus member [Allan Holdsworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allan_Holdsworth "Allan Holdsworth") was added to the band, becoming their first guitarist since Andy Summers' brief tenure in 1968. Holdsworth played on the next album _[Bundles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bundles_(album) "Bundles (album)")_ (1975) before leaving in early 1975. Holdsworth's replacement was [John Etheridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Etheridge "John Etheridge"), and the saxophonist [Alan Wakeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Wakeman "Alan Wakeman"), a cousin of [Yes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band) "Yes (band)") keyboardist [Rick Wakeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Wakeman "Rick Wakeman"), also joined at the beginning of 1976.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-:0-8) The next album, _[Softs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Softs_(album) "Softs (album)")_ (1976), was the first without Ratledge, the last-remaining original member of the band, who left in March 1976. Other members of Soft Machine during the late 1970s were the saxophonist [Ray Warleigh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Warleigh "Ray Warleigh"), the violinist [Ric Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ric_Sanders "Ric Sanders"), and the bassists [Percy Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percy_Jones_(musician) "Percy Jones (musician)") of [Brand X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brand_X "Brand X") and Steve Cook.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-31) During 1977, Soft Machine recorded the live album _[Alive & Well: Recorded in Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alive_&_Well:_Recorded_in_Paris "Alive & Well: Recorded in Paris")_, which was released early the following year. In 1978, Soft Machine gave only one live performance, which was at the Sound & Musik Festival in [Dortmund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dortmund "Dortmund"), [West Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Germany "West Germany"), on 8 December, with a line-up of Marshall, Jenkins, Cook and Holdsworth.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-calyx.perso.neuf.fr_Soft_Machine_chronology_2-32)[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-Bennett-33) After this show, Soft Machine disbanded. ### Occasional reunions (1980–81; 1984) The name Soft Machine was resurrected for the 1981 album _[Land of Cockayne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_of_Cockayne_(album) "Land of Cockayne (album)")_. Soft Machine also briefly reformed for a series of concerts at London's [Ronnie Scott's Jazz Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronnie_Scott's_Jazz_Club "Ronnie Scott's Jazz Club") in mid 1984[\[f\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-34) that featured John Marshall, Karl Jenkins, Ray Warleigh, John Etheridge, bassist [Paul Carmichael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Carmichael "Paul Carmichael") and pianist [Dave MacRae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_MacRae "Dave MacRae"). ### Alternative bands (1978–2015) #### Soft Heap / Soft Head (1978–88) [Soft Heap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Heap_(band) "Soft Heap (band)") was formed in January 1978 by [Hugh Hopper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Hopper "Hugh Hopper") and [Elton Dean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elton_Dean "Elton Dean") from Soft Machine, and [Alan Gowen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Gowen "Alan Gowen") and [Pip Pyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pip_Pyle "Pip Pyle") from [National Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Health "National Health"). _Heap_ is an acronym that is composed of the initials of the members' first names. The band toured in the early-to-mid 1978 as [Soft Head](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Heap_(band) "Soft Heap (band)") because Dave Sheen replaced Pip Pyle due to Pyle's commitments to National Health.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-calyx-canterbury.fr_Elton_Dean_chronology-35) The live album _Rogue Element_ was recorded on that tour and was released in 1978. The original Soft Heap line-up reformed in October 1978 to record their eponymous studio album, which was released in 1979.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] After two line-up changes from 1979 to 1981, the new line-up intermittently toured throughout the 1980s; they performed four tours during the decade in 25 European concerts, culminating on 11 May 1988 at the festival "Jazz sous les pommiers" in [Coutances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coutances "Coutances"), France.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-calyx-canterbury.fr_Elton_Dean_chronology-35) #### Soft Ware (1999), Soft Works (2002–04), Soft Mountain (2003) and Soft Bounds (2004) Soft Ware (sometimes SoftWhere), which was formed in September 1999, was composed of Elton Dean, Hugh Hopper, [John Marshall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Marshall_(drummer) "John Marshall (drummer)") on drums and Marshall's long-time friend [Keith Tippett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett "Keith Tippett"). This short-lived line-up played one performance at ( [Augustusburg Hunting Lodge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustusburg_Hunting_Lodge "Augustusburg Hunting Lodge"), Germany, on 4 September 1999. In 2002, with Tippett unavailable, another former Soft Machine member [Allan Holdsworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allan_Holdsworth "Allan Holdsworth") (on guitar) joined the other three members of Soft Ware, who in June 2002 renamed themselves Soft Works[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-calyx.perso.neuf.fr_Soft_Machine_chronology_2-32) to avoid confusion with Peter Mergener's band [Software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_(band) "Software (band)"). Soft Works made their live debut on 17 August 2002 at the [Progman Cometh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progman_Cometh "Progman Cometh") Festival at Moore Theater in [Seattle, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle,_Washington "Seattle, Washington"); and a live album of the performance was released on 29 July 2003.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-allmusic_Soft_Works_Abracadabra-36) Their only studio album _Abracadabra_, consisting of new material and recorded at Eastcote Studios, London, on 5–7 June 2002. The album was toured in Japan in August 2003, Italy in January and February 2004, and Mexico in March 2004.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-calyx.perso.neuf.fr_Soft_Machine_chronology_2-32) During a Japanese Soft Works tour in August 2003, Elton Dean on saxophone and Hugh Hopper on bass formed the band Soft Mountain along with Japanese musicians [Hoppy Kamiyama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoppy_Kamiyama "Hoppy Kamiyama") on keyboards, whom Hopper had met two years earlier, and [Yoshida Tatsuya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoshida_Tatsuya "Yoshida Tatsuya") from the band [Ruins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruins_(Japanese_band) "Ruins (Japanese band)") on drums. Soft Mountain named themselves after Hoppy Kamiyama, whose name translates as "God Mountain".[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-huxrecords.com_Soft_Mountain-37) Looking for a break from relatively fixed set lists and song forms, Hugh Hopper had contacted Kamiyama with the idea of using a studio for one day to see what might happen. Kamiyama brought in Tatsuya, and, with no discussion, the quartet played two 45-minute improvisations. In 2007, a year after Elton Dean died aged 60, Soft Mountain released the eponymous album they had recorded on 10 August 2003 in Tokyo, Japan.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-huxrecords.com_Soft_Mountain-37) The two-part "Soft Mountain Suite" extracts the best thirty minutes from each improvisation.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-AllAboutJazz.com_Soft_Mountain-38) In June 2004, Elton Dean and Hugh Hopper formed the band Soft Bounds with [Sophia Domancich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophia_Domancich "Sophia Domancich") on keyboards and Simon Goubert on drums); they played at the Festival "Les Tritonales" in [Les Lilas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_Lilas "Les Lilas"), Paris, France.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-calyx-canterbury.fr_Elton_Dean_chronology-35) This concert was partially released in 2005 as the Soft Bounds' album _Live at Le Triton_. #### Soft Machine Legacy (2004–15) In October 2004, the members of Soft Works, with John Etheridge permanently replacing Holdsworth, took the name "Soft Machine Legacy" and performed two festival shows; one on 9 October in Turkey and the other on 15 October in the Czech Republic. [Liam Genockey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liam_Genockey "Liam Genockey") temporarily replaced John Marshall who had ligament problems. The new band's line-up was Elton Dean, John Etheridge, Hugh Hopper and Liam Genockey.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-calyx.perso.neuf.fr_Soft_Machine_chronology_2-32) Soft Machine Legacy released three albums: _Live in Zaandam_ (2005),[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-zaan-39) the studio album _Soft Machine Legacy_ (2006),[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-zaan-39) which was recorded in September 2005 and features fresh material, and _Live at the New Morning_ (2006).[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-40) After Elton Dean died in February 2006, the band continued with the British saxophonist and flautist [Theo Travis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theo_Travis "Theo Travis"), formerly of Gong and [The Tangent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tangent "The Tangent"). In December 2006, the new Legacy line-up recorded the album _Steam_[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-lynchsteamreview-41)[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-astaritasteamreview-42)[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-jonessteamreview-43) in [Jon Hiseman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Hiseman "Jon Hiseman")'s studio. _Steam_ was released in August 2007 by [Moonjune Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moonjune_Records "Moonjune Records") before a European tour. Hopper left the band in 2008 because he was suffering from [leukaemia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leukaemia "Leukaemia"), so for live performances [Fred Thelonious Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Thelonious_Baker "Fred Thelonious Baker") deputising for Hopper. Following Hopper's death in 2009, the band announced they would continue with Roy Babbington again replacing Hopper on bass.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-44) Soft Machine Legacy released their fifth album in October 2010; the 58-minute record _Live Adventures_ was recorded live in October 2009 in Austria and Germany during a European tour.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-allmusic.com_Soft_Machine_Legacy_Live_Adventures-45) Founding Soft Machine bassist Kevin Ayers died in February 2013 at aged 68,[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-46)[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-consequenceofsound-47) and 77-year-old Daevid Allen died in March 2015 from cancer.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-48)[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-49) On 18 March 2013, the Legacy band released a new studio album titled _[Burden of Proof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burden_of_Proof_(Soft_Machine_Legacy_album) "Burden of Proof (Soft Machine Legacy album)")_.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-50) Travis stated: "legally we could actually be called Soft Machine but for various reasons it was decided to be one step removed".[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-51) ### A return to the name "Soft Machine" (2015–present) #### Reformation and _Hidden Details_ (2015–2018) In September and October 2015, it was announced Soft Machine Legacy, which was composed of drummer John Marshall, guitarist John Etheridge, bassist Roy Babbington, and sax, flute and keyboard player Theo Travis, would be performing under the name Soft Machine in late 2015 and early 2016: they would perform two shows in the Netherlands and Belgium in early December 2015,[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-songkick.com_Soft_Machine_6_October_2015-52)[\[g\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-54) and seven UK shows in March and April 2016.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-songkick.com_Soft_Machine_6_October_2015-52)[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-teamrock.com_Soft_Machine_1_December_2015-55)[\[h\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-58) In December 2015, it was confirmed the band were dropping the word "Legacy" from their name, becoming known as Soft Machine for the first time since 1984.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-teamrock.com_Soft_Machine_1_December_2015-55) The former Soft Machine member Allan Holdsworth, aged 70, died from heart failure on 15 April 2017 at his home in [Vista, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vista,_California "Vista, California").[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-sandiegouniontribune-59)[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-GPmag20170629-60)[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-61) On 7 September 2018, Soft Machine released _[Hidden Details](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hidden_Details "Hidden Details")_ on Dyad Records in the UK and Tonefloat Records in the US, their first new studio album since _Land of Cockayne_ (1981). In late 2018 and until February 2019, they toured the world to mark their 50th anniversary and to support the new album.[\[i\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-64) #### Further tours, _Other Doors_ and _Thirteen_ (2019–present) On 20 March 2020, Soft Machine released _Live at The Baked Potato_, their first original live album since _Alive & Well_ (1978). It was recorded live on 1 February 2019 at [The Baked Potato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Baked_Potato "The Baked Potato"), Los Angeles, and was initially only available as a twelve-track limited-edition double vinyl LP of 200 copies but it has since been released on Compact Disc (CD). The album documents their extensive 2018–2019 world tour.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-tonefloat.com_Soft_Machine_Live_at_The_Baked_Potato-65)[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-theotravis.com_Soft_Machine_Live_at_The_Baked_Potato-66) On 7 December 2021, Soft Machine announced Babbington was retiring from the band and would be replaced by Fred Thelonious Baker.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-67) In June 2023, Soft Machine released the new studio album _Other Doors_, which was recorded with John Marshall before he retired from music. Marshall died on 16 September 2023.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-68)As of January 2023[\[update\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Soft_Machine&action=edit), the line-up of Soft Machine was Etheridge, Travis, Baker and drummer [Asaf Sirkis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asaf_Sirkis "Asaf Sirkis").[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-mobile.twitter.com_Soft_Machine_new_drummer_Asaf_Sirkis-69)[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-www.jazzmusicarchives.com_Soft_Machine_new_drummer_Asaf_Sirkis-70) They embarked on a seven-date UK tour beginning on 3 February 2023 at the [New Cross Inn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Cross_Inn "New Cross Inn") in London and ending on 26 May 2023 at [City Varieties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leeds_City_Varieties "Leeds City Varieties") in [Leeds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leeds "Leeds").[\[j\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-71) The band began touring again in November 2023 with dates booked until November 2024.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-softmachine.org_Past_Gigs-72) Co-founding member [Mike Ratledge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Ratledge "Mike Ratledge") died on 5 February 2025. On 4 March 2025 in Manchester (at Band On The Wall), the band embarked on an 8-date UK Spring tour which concluded on 4 April in London (at The Vortex Jazz Club), celebrating on that occasion John Etheridge's 50 years with the band (since 12 April 1975).[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine#cite_note-softmachine.org_Past_Gigs-72) Soft Machine toured Europe from 9 May in London (at Signature Brew) to 25 May 2025 in Zoetermeer, The Netherlands (at De Boerderij): the 10-date Spring tour also included Sweden (four dates), Norway (one date), Finland (two dates) and Germany (one date). After a special show dedicated to Mike Ratledge on 1 September 2025 in London (at the Pizza Express jazz club), Soft Machine embarked on 2 November 2025 in [Cardiff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiff "Cardiff") (at Acapela Studio) on an 8-date UK Fall tour which concluded on 30 November 2025 in [Southampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southampton "Southampton") (at 1865) (with [Colosseum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colosseum_(band) "Colosseum (band)")), also visiting [Market Harborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_Harborough "Market Harborough"), [Barnard Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barnard_Castle "Barnard Castle"), [Hull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_upon_Hull "Kingston upon Hull"), [Bristol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol "Bristol") and London again (2 dates at Sound Lounge and at Cadogan Hall, again with Colosseum). - (see [Personnel section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#Personnel) for others) | | | | Website | [santana.com](http://santana.com/) | **Santana** is an American [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_Music "Rock Music") band formed in [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco"), California in 1966 by Mexican-American guitarist [Carlos Santana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Santana "Carlos Santana").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-10) The band has had various recording and performing line-ups in its history, with Santana being the only consistent member. After signing with [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records"), the band's appearance at the [Woodstock Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodstock_Festival "Woodstock Festival") in 1969 increased their profile and they went on to record the critically acclaimed and commercially successful albums _[Santana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(1969_album) "Santana (1969 album)")_ (1969), _[Abraxas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraxas_(album) "Abraxas (album)")_ (1970) and _[Santana III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(1971_album) "Santana (1971 album)")_ (1971). These were recorded by the group's "classic" line-up, comprising organist and lead vocalist [Gregg Rolie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregg_Rolie "Gregg Rolie"), percussionists [José "Chepito" Areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Areas "José Areas") and [Michael Carabello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Carabello "Michael Carabello"), drummer [Michael Shrieve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Shrieve "Michael Shrieve") and bassist [David Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Brown_(American_musician) "David Brown (American musician)"). Hit songs of this period include " [Evil Ways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evil_Ways_(Santana_song) "Evil Ways (Santana song)")" (1970), " [Black Magic Woman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Magic_Woman "Black Magic Woman")" (1970), " [Oye Como Va](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oye_Como_Va "Oye Como Va")" (1971) and the instrumental " [Samba Pa Ti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samba_Pa_Ti_(instrumental) "Samba Pa Ti (instrumental)")" (1970). Following a change in line-up and musical direction in 1972, the band experimented with elements of [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") on _[Caravanserai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caravanserai_(album) "Caravanserai (album)")_ (1972), _[Welcome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welcome_(Santana_album) "Welcome (Santana album)")_ (1973) and _[Borboletta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borboletta "Borboletta")_ (1974). The band reached a new peak of critical and commercial success with their eighteenth album, _[Supernatural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supernatural_(Santana_album) "Supernatural (Santana album)")_ (1999), which included the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100")-number one singles " [Smooth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_(Santana_song) "Smooth (Santana song)")" (featuring [Rob Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rob_Thomas_(musician) "Rob Thomas (musician)")) and " [Maria Maria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Maria "Maria Maria")" (featuring [The Product G&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Product_G&B "The Product G&B")). The album peaked atop the charts in eleven countries and sold 12million copies domestically. It won eight [Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Awards "Grammy Awards") at the [42nd Annual Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/42nd_Annual_Grammy_Awards "42nd Annual Grammy Awards"), a record tied with [Michael Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Jackson "Michael Jackson"), and three [Latin Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_Grammy_Awards "Latin Grammy Awards").[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-11) In 2014, the "classic" line-up—with the exception of Brown, who died in 2000, and Areas, who was not invited to participate[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-12)—reunited for the _[Santana IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_IV "Santana IV")_ album (2016) and tour. Santana is one of the [best-selling groups of all time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_best-selling_music_artists "List of best-selling music artists"), with over 47million certified records sold in the US and an estimated 100million sold worldwide.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-RIAAsales-13)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-14) Its [discography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_discography "Santana discography") includes 25 studio albums, 14 of which reached the US Top 10. In 1998, the line-up of Santana, Rolie, Carabello, Shrieve, Brown and Areas was inducted into the [Rock and Roll Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_Roll_Hall_of_Fame "Rock and Roll Hall of Fame").[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-RRHOF-15) ## History ### 1966–1972: Formation and breakthrough In 1966, Mexican-born American musician [Carlos Santana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Santana "Carlos Santana") discovered San Francisco's [hippie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippie "Hippie") and [counterculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterculture "Counterculture") movement and found himself "wanting to be part of this new wave."[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-RS72-16) Later that year, he began to assemble his own band, the first line-up of which included Sergio "Gus" Rodriguez on bass, Danny Haro on drums, and [Michael Carabello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Carabello "Michael Carabello") on percussion. In January 1967, the four were granted an audition spot for concert promoter [Bill Graham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Graham_(promoter) "Bill Graham (promoter)") at the [Fillmore Auditorium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fillmore "The Fillmore") on a bill with the [Paul Butterfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Butterfield "Paul Butterfield") Blues Band and the [Charles Lloyd Quartet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Lloyd_(jazz_musician) "Charles Lloyd (jazz musician)"), and named themselves the Santana Blues Band.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-17) Within a month, the group expanded with the addition of Tom Fraser on guitar and vocals, who also brought in [Gregg Rolie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregg_Rolie "Gregg Rolie") on organ and vocals.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-RS72-16) The band stalled for several weeks, however, after Carlos was hospitalised with [tuberculosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuberculosis "Tuberculosis"). In June 1967, Graham fired the group from performing at the Fillmore after some members turned up late for a gig supporting [The Who](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Who "The Who") and [Loading Zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loading_Zone "Loading Zone"). The incident drove Carlos to bring in new and committed musicians, keeping Rolie with him.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-RS72-16) By the year's end, the band adopted the shorter name of Santana. Until early 1969, the band were joined by [Marcus Malone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Malone "Marcus Malone") on percussion, who left the group after being convicted of manslaughter.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-RS72-16) In late 1968, the group secured a record deal with [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records"), following a successful audition opening for the [Grateful Dead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grateful_Dead "Grateful Dead"). The band had caught the interest of Columbia and [Atlantic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Records "Atlantic Records"), and an audition was organised for both labels, but Carlos refused to perform for Atlantic as he wanted to be on the same label as [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis") and [Bob Dylan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Dylan "Bob Dylan").[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeng200040-18) In December, Santana performed a series of concerts at the Fillmore that were recorded for a proposed live album. Biographer Simon Leng said it marked Santana moving away from its blues and R&B roots towards the "Santana sound" with the addition of Afro-Cuban and jazz numbers into their sets.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeng200042-19) After several line-up changes, the group finally stabilised in May 1969 with Santana, Rolie, Carabello, [David Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Brown_(American_musician) "David Brown (American musician)") on bass, [Michael Shrieve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Shrieve "Michael Shrieve") on drums, and [Jose "Chepito" Areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jose_Areas "Jose Areas") on percussion, which became known as the "classic" line-up.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-TGG83-20) [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/Woodstock_redmond_stage.JPG/500px-Woodstock_redmond_stage.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Woodstock_redmond_stage.JPG) Santana rose to prominence following their appearance at Woodstock The band recorded their debut album, _[Santana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(1969_album) "Santana (1969 album)")_, in San Francisco in May 1969. It was their third go at recording an album, after previous attempts failed to produce results they wanted. The sessions featured Alberto Gianquinto on piano, who also helped with the arrangements of the tracks. He quickly noticed the group's main problem: the solo spots were too long.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeng200046-21) Graham agreed, and advised that the band needed to cut the lengthy jams and begin constructing songs. He also got the band to listen to [Willie Bobo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Bobo "Willie Bobo")'s version of " [Evil Ways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evil_Ways_(Santana_song) "Evil Ways (Santana song)")", and suggested they record their own version.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeng200046-21) With the album recorded, Graham arranged for Santana to tour the Midwest as openers for [Crosby, Stills and Nash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crosby,_Stills_and_Nash "Crosby, Stills and Nash"), which expanded the group's profile outside the West Coast.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeng200048-22) Around this time, Graham had been asked to help organise the upcoming [Woodstock Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodstock_Festival "Woodstock Festival") and agreed to promote it on the condition that Santana would be added to the bill. Graham persisted, and the band were assigned a 45-minute set in the afternoon of August 16, the second day, for $2,500.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeng200049-23) The performance launched the group to international fame, and _Santana_, released on August 30, peaked at No. 4 on the US [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200"). The first single, " [Jingo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jin-go-lo-ba "Jin-go-lo-ba")", was followed by "Evil Ways", which peaked at No. 9 on the _Billboard_ [Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100"). In October 1969, Graham had Santana perform at the [Gold Rush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_Rush_(music_festival) "Gold Rush (music festival)") rock music festival and on _[The Ed Sullivan Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ed_Sullivan_Show "The Ed Sullivan Show")_, further increasing the group's nationwide exposure.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeng200048-22)[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-24) In November 1969, Santana performed at New Providence High School in New Providence, NJ. In April 1970, Santana returned to the studio to record its second album, _[Abraxas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraxas_(album) "Abraxas (album)")_.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-25) The album, highlighted by a reworking of " [Black Magic Woman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Magic_Woman "Black Magic Woman")" by [Fleetwood Mac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fleetwood_Mac "Fleetwood Mac") that peaked at No. 4 in the US [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100"), was released in September 1970 and rose to No. 1 on the US [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200"). By 1971, the group were still struggling to maintain a strong musical direction.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-TGG83-20) From January to July they recorded _[Santana III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(1971_album) "Santana (1971 album)")_. Released in September 1971, the album also reached No. 1 on the US _Billboard_ 200\. At the peak of the band's popularity, the album was the last to feature its classic Woodstock era line-up. Santana explained that there was a lot of unnecessary internal resentment and that managerial problems contributed to the problem, leading to Graham's dismissal.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-TGG83-20) That year, they performed at a concert in [Accra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accra "Accra") to commemorate [Ghana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghana "Ghana")'s 14th [Independence Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independence_Day_(Ghana) "Independence Day (Ghana)"). The concert was filmed and released in theaters as _[Soul to Soul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_to_Soul_(film) "Soul to Soul (film)")_.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-26) Matters came to a head shortly before the _Santana III_ tour in September 1971 began, when Carlos wanted Carabello to leave the group, otherwise Carlos himself would quit. The band started the tour without Carlos, performing amidst shouts from the audience for the guitarist. After several gigs, Carlos reunited with the band to find Carabello, Areas, and manager/promoter Stan Marcum had quit, leaving the band to perform without percussionists. [James "Mingo" Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mingo_Lewis "Mingo Lewis") was quickly brought in as a temporary replacement after he saw the band live and offered his services.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeng200064%E2%80%9365-27) Santana's gig in [Lima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lima "Lima"), Peru in December 1971 brought further trouble, as the outbreak of violence resulted in their equipment being confiscated and the band deported from the country. The incident was a wake-up call for Carlos, who was determined to "bring the madness to an end."[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeng200064%E2%80%9365-27) In 1972, Santana had been increasingly influenced by the music of [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis"), [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane"), and [Joe Zawinul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Zawinul "Joe Zawinul"), who had explored jazz fusion by this time.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-TGG83-20) The fourth album, _[Caravanserai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caravanserai_(album) "Caravanserai (album)")_ (1972), marked a number of line-up changes; bassist David Brown left in 1971 before recording started and was replaced by Doug Rauch and Tom Rutley. Carabello was replaced with two percussionists, Armando Peraza and Mingo Lewis. Rolie was replaced by [Tom Coster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Coster "Tom Coster") on a few songs. _Caravanserai_ debuted at No. 8 in the US. ### 1973–1979: Experimentation and consolidation [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/71/Santana_1973_%28cropped%29.jpg/500px-Santana_1973_%28cropped%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Santana_1973_(cropped).jpg) Carlos Santana in 1973 Thirteen months after _Caravanserai_, Santana released _[Welcome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welcome_(Santana_album) "Welcome (Santana album)")_. _Welcome_ was the first of four consecutive albums to achieve gold certification, as opposed to the previous four, which all at least reached platinum status. The album peaked at No. 25 on the _Billboard_ 200, the lowest of the band's career so far. The next few albums contained a more experimental style than their previous work, beginning with _[Borboletta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borboletta "Borboletta")_, which fared arguably worse than its predecessor, despite climbing five spots higher on the Billboard album charts in the US. The group's 1976 release, _[Amigos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amigos_(Santana_album) "Amigos (Santana album)")_, was far more successful. Reaching No. 10 on the US charts and also hitting the Top 10 in France, Australia, New Zealand, Austria, and the Netherlands, it was a return to the success of their early albums. _[Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Festival_(Santana_album) "Festival (Santana album)")_ did not obtain the same newfound success, but it was followed by another successful album, _[Moonflower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moonflower_(album) "Moonflower (album)")_, released in 1977. The album was possibly the most successful since _Santana III_, achieving 2× platinum in the US, and being the first album since 1974's _Borboletta_ to break the Top 10 in the UK. It was characterized by a stylistic shift for the band, as it contained heavier influences from the more conventional sound of the group's early work, while still maintaining the experimental sound of their last few albums. Their next two releases, _[Inner Secrets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_Secrets "Inner Secrets")_ and _[Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon_(Santana_album) "Marathon (Santana album)")_, released in 1978 and '79, respectively, were a further musical shift for the band, moving away from the Latin-fused rock music that had characterized their work in the late 1960s and the majority of the '70s, to move toward a more album-oriented, conventional rock sound. These albums, however, fared poorly commercially, although both achieved gold status in the U.S. [_Marathon_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon_(Santana_album) "Marathon (Santana album)") featured the debut of lead singer [Alex Ligertwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Ligertwood "Alex Ligertwood"), who would remain with the band off and on until 1994. ### 1980–1997: Commercial decline and seven-year hiatus The 1980s started relatively brightly for Santana, with 1981's platinum-selling _[Zebop!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zebop! "Zebop!")_, which also reached the Top 20 in several countries, and continued the more conventional rock sound. The following year, _[Shangó](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shang%C3%B3_(Santana_album) "Shangó (Santana album)")_ was released; this album marked a steep decline in the band's commercial fortunes, although it still achieved gold status. The group waited another three years to release the follow-up, the longest break for them so far. 1985's _[Beyond Appearances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beyond_Appearances "Beyond Appearances")_ was a commercial failure and their first album not to achieve gold certification. Their following three releases all continued this commercial decline, with the last of these failing to break the _Billboard_ Top 100. In the midst of this commercial pitfall, the band stopped recording material for an unprecedented seven years but continued to tour. ### 1998–2001: _Supernatural_ and the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame In 1998, Santana was inducted into the [Rock and Roll Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_Roll_Hall_of_Fame "Rock and Roll Hall of Fame"). The following year, their album _[Supernatural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supernatural_(Santana_album) "Supernatural (Santana album)")_ (1999) debuted at No. 19 on the _Billboard_ 200 and reached No. 1 after eighteen weeks. Also reaching No. 1 were two singles: " [Smooth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_(Santana_song) "Smooth (Santana song)")", recorded with [Rob Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rob_Thomas_(musician) "Rob Thomas (musician)"), and " [Maria Maria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Maria "Maria Maria")" featuring [The Product G&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Product_G&B "The Product G&B"). The album was certified platinum 15 times by the [RIAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RIAA "RIAA") and sold 30million copies worldwide.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-28)[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-29) Santana's previous No. 1 album had been _[Santana III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(1971_album) "Santana (1971 album)")_ in 1971. According to _[Guinness World Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guinness_World_Records "Guinness World Records")_, this is the longest gap between No. 1 albums.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-30)[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-31) _Supernatural_ won eight Grammy Awards, including the award for [Album of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Album_of_the_Year "Grammy Award for Album of the Year"),[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-32) and also won three [Latin Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_Grammy_Awards "Latin Grammy Awards").[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-33) ### 2002–2012: Dealing with newfound success [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6a/Santana_Acer_Arena_%285558204467%29.jpg/960px-Santana_Acer_Arena_%285558204467%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Santana_Acer_Arena_(5558204467).jpg) Santana performing in 2011 The follow-up to _Supernatural_ came three years later and was highly anticipated by international media and fans alike. On October 22, 2002, _[Shaman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaman_(album) "Shaman (album)")_ was released worldwide. Although it initially sold briskly (298,973 copies in the US in its first week) and debuted at number 1 on the _Billboard_ 200, the album's appeal quickly wore off and it soon slid down the charts. Despite this, it went on to sell 2× platinum in the US, and achieved platinum status in several other countries including Australia. The first single released from the album, " [The Game of Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Game_of_Love_(Santana_song) "The Game of Love (Santana song)")", which featured vocals from [Michelle Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Branch "Michelle Branch"), debuted at number 5 on the Hot 100. The album's next four singles failed to chart in most countries, but the final single, " [Why Don't You & I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Why_Don't_You_&_I "Why Don't You & I")", featuring the vocals of [Alex Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Band "Alex Band"), reached number 8 on the Hot 100. Musically, the album was a return to a more conventional sound for the group, with a mainly Latin rock-based sound. With their renewed appeal worn off, another three-year wait saw the release of 2005's _[All That I Am](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_That_I_Am_(Santana_album) "All That I Am (Santana album)")_. The album debuted at number 2 on the _Billboard_ 200 but fared worse internationally, and quickly lost appeal. The album, a continuation of the Latin-rock influenced sound of _Shaman_, achieved gold certification in the US. A five-year break from recording saw the release of another studio album, _[Guitar Heaven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar_Heaven "Guitar Heaven")_ (2010). Musically it was a drastic change for the band, with a far heavier sound at its core and strong [heavy metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_metal_music "Heavy metal music") influences. It debuted at number 5 on the _Billboard_ 200 but marked another decline for the band, failing to achieve gold status. In 2012 the group released _[Shape Shifter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shape_Shifter_(album) "Shape Shifter (album)")_, which returned to the conventional Latin rock sound and was completely album-oriented, as no singles were released from it. It debuted at number 16 on the [Billboard 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200"). ### 2013–2020: Reunion of the classic line-up, _Corazón_, _Santana IV_, and _Africa Speaks_ In February 2013, Carlos Santana confirmed that he would reunite his classic line-up, most of whom played Woodstock with him in 1969. Santana stated that he was reuniting the group with the intention of recording new music. Confirmed for the reunion were Neal Schon, who was in the band in the early 1970s where he traded lead guitar work with Santana before leaving with founding Santana singer-organist Gregg Rolie in 1973 to form [Journey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journey_(band) "Journey (band)"); drummer Mike Shrieve and percussionist Mike Carabello. Santana said of Rolie, who played with Ringo Starr's All-Starr Band for the last two years, "I'm pretty sure Gregg's going to do it." In February 2013, Rolie told Radio.com, "it's (the reunion) just a matter of putting it together and going and doing it. I would do it. I think it's a great idea. People would love it. It could be great!"[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-34) Before the reunion album was released, on May 6, 2014, the then-current lineup of Santana released a new studio album titled _[Corazón](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coraz%C3%B3n_(Santana_album) "Corazón (Santana album)")_. On September 9, 2014, this was followed by the release of _Corazón – Live from Mexico: Live It to Believe It_, a live album (on CD, DVD and Blu-ray) of their December 14, 2013 concert in Guadalajara, Mexico.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-35) On April 15, 2016, Santana released _[Santana IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_IV "Santana IV")_, the wildly anticipated studio album that reunited the late 1960s and early 1970s classic lineup of Carlos Santana (guitar, vocals), Gregg Rolie (keyboards, lead vocals), Neal Schon (guitar, vocals), Michael Carabello (percussion) and Michael Shrieve (drums). The album marked the first time in 45 years – since 1971's multi-platinum classic _[Santana III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(1971_album) "Santana (1971 album)")_ – that the quintet had recorded together.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-facebook.com_carlossantana_post_25_January_2016-36) The first single from _Santana IV_, titled "Anywhere You Want to Go", had been previously released on February 5, 2016.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-news.iheart.com_Anywhere_You_Want_To_Go-37) The origins of the reunion went back several years, when Schon suggested that he and Carlos Santana record together. Santana liked the idea but proposed that they recruit Rolie, Shrieve, and Carabello for what would be called "Santana IV". After initial writing sessions and rehearsals in 2013, the group recorded throughout 2014 and 2015, amassing 16 new tracks that combined all their signature elements – Afro-Latin rhythms, soaring vocals, electrifying blues-psychedelic guitar solos, and irrepressible jubilant percussion work. About the "Santana IV" team, Santana stated: "It was magical, we didn't have to try to force the vibe – it was immense. From there, we then needed to come up with a balance of songs and jams that people would immediately identify as Santana."[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-santana.hifi247.com_Santana_IV-38) _Santana IV_ features 16 all-new tracks written and produced by the band. Joining the core "Santana IV" band in the studio are current Santana members Karl Perazzo (percussion) and Benny Rietveld (bass), with vocalist [Ronald Isley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Isley "Ronald Isley") guesting on two cuts. On October 21, 2016, Santana released _Santana IV: Live at the House of Blues Las Vegas_ on Eagle Rock Entertainment, a live album (on DVD/Blu-ray/2CD) of their concert on March 21, 2016 at [House of Blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Blues "House of Blues") in [Mandalay Bay Resort and Casino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandalay_Bay_Resort_and_Casino "Mandalay Bay Resort and Casino") on the [Las Vegas Strip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Las_Vegas_Strip "Las Vegas Strip") in [Nevada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevada "Nevada"). In early January 2019, Santana signed with [Concord Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concord_Records "Concord Records");[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-concord.com_Carlos_Santana_signs_with_Concord_Records-39) in late January, they released _[In Search of Mona Lisa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_Search_of_Mona_Lisa "In Search of Mona Lisa")_, a new five-track EP.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-AllMusic-40) The day before, they also released a video for new single, "Do You Remember Me."[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-41) In March 2019, the band announced plans to release on _[Africa Speaks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa_Speaks_(Santana_album) "Africa Speaks (Santana album)")_, their new full-length album produced by [Rick Rubin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Rubin "Rick Rubin"), on June 7.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-42) 2019 marked the 20th anniversary of Carlos Santana's album _Supernatural_ and the 50th anniversary of his performance at Woodstock. Santana headlined a multi-year residency at House of Blues. The band was expected to headline at both [Woodstock 50](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodstock_50 "Woodstock 50") (which was cancelled)[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-43) and Bethel Woods' half-centennial celebration in Bethel, NY, in August 2019.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-44) The band toured in support of the latest album, from April to November 2019.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-45) ### 2021–2024: _Blessings and Miracles_ On 18 and 20 August 2021, "Move" and "She's Fire", the first and second singles taken from Santana's (then) forthcoming new album _[Blessings and Miracles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blessings_and_Miracles "Blessings and Miracles")_, were released; it was announced that the album would be released on 15 October 2021 via [BMG Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BMG_Rights_Management "BMG Rights Management"). ### 2025–present: _Sentient_ On 21 February 2025, it was announced the upcoming release via [Candid Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candid_Records "Candid Records") of _Sentient_, Santana's new studio album, a retrospective of 11 tracks featuring collaborations with other artists including [Michael Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Jackson "Michael Jackson"), [Smokey Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smokey_Robinson "Smokey Robinson"), [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis"), [Paolo Rustichelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paolo_Rustichelli "Paolo Rustichelli"), [Darryl "DMC" McDaniels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darryl_%22DMC%22_McDaniels "Darryl \"DMC\" McDaniels") and [Cindy Blackman Santana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cindy_Blackman_Santana "Cindy Blackman Santana").[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-santana.com_Sentient-46) The album includes "Whatever Happens", a track from Michael Jackson's last album, _[Invincible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invincible_(Michael_Jackson_album) "Invincible (Michael Jackson album)");_ remastered tracks such as "Let the Guitar Play", a re-work of "Song for Cindy" from _Blessings and Miracles_ featuring Darryl "DMC" McDaniels; Grammy Awards winner "Blues for Salvador"; and three new tracks: Smokey Robinson's "Please Don't Take Your Love", "Coherence", and a track featuring Cindy Blackman Santana. It also includes an instrumental live version of Michael Jackson's " [Stranger in Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stranger_in_Moscow "Stranger in Moscow")" recorded in 2012 with Carlos as guest of [Narada Michael Walden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narada_Michael_Walden "Narada Michael Walden")'s band.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-news.theurbanmusicscene.com_Sentient-47) The album was released on 28 March 2025.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-sentient-48) On 16 April 2025 in [Highland, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highland,_California "Highland, California") at the Yaamava’ Resort & Casino at San Manuel, Santana embarked on the eight-date Oneness North American tour, which ended on 29 April 2025 in [Nashville, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville,_Tennessee "Nashville, Tennessee") at The Pinnacle.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-Oneness_Tour_2025_US_&_Europe-49) On 9 June 2025 in [Łódź](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C5%81%C3%B3d%C5%BA "Łódź"), Poland at the [Atlas Arena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Arena "Atlas Arena"), Santana embarked on the 29-date Oneness Europe and UK tour. The tour included a show on 21 June 2025 in London, England, at [The O2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_O2 "The O2") and a seven-date leg in Spain from 26 July to 4 August 2025; it was due to end on 11 August 2025 in [Copenhagen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copenhagen "Copenhagen"), Denmark.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-Oneness_Tour_2025_US_&_Europe-49) ## Personnel Main article: [List of Santana band members](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Santana_band_members "List of Santana band members") Santana has had various recording and performing lineups in its history, with Santana being the only consistent member. ### Current members The current[\[update\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santana_(band)&action=edit) members of Santana are: | Image | Name | Years active | Instruments | Release contributions | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/Santana_Acer_Arena_%285558151833%29_%28cropped%29.jpg/960px-Santana_Acer_Arena_%285558151833%29_%28cropped%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Santana_Acer_Arena_(5558151833)_(cropped).jpg) | [Carlos Santana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Santana "Carlos Santana") | 1966–present | - lead guitar
