- [Universal Classics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Music_Group "Universal Music Group") | | | | Website | [keith-jarrett.de/en](https://keith-jarrett.de/en) | Musical artist **Keith Jarrett** (born May 8, 1945) is an American pianist and [composer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composer "Composer").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-Larkin-1) Jarrett started his career with [Art Blakey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Blakey "Art Blakey") and later moved on to play with [Charles Lloyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Lloyd_(jazz_musician) "Charles Lloyd (jazz musician)") and [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis"). Since the early 1970s, he has also been a group leader and solo performer in [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion"), and [classical music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_music "Classical music"). His improvisations draw from the traditions of jazz and other genres, including Western classical music, [gospel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_music "Gospel music"), [blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues "Blues"), and ethnic [folk music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music "Folk music"). His album _[The Köln Concert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert "The Köln Concert")_, released in 1975, is the best-selling piano recording in history.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-3) In 2008, he was inducted into the _[DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat")_ Jazz Hall of Fame in the magazine's 73rd Annual Readers' Poll.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-4) In 2003, Jarrett received the [Polar Music Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polar_Music_Prize "Polar Music Prize") and was the first recipient to be recognized with the prizes for both contemporary and classical music.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-5) In 2004, he received the [Léonie Sonning Music Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A9onie_Sonning_Music_Prize "Léonie Sonning Music Prize"). In February 2018, Jarrett suffered a [stroke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stroke "Stroke") and has been unable to perform since. A second stroke in May 2018 left him partially paralyzed and unable to play with his left hand.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-:0-6) ## Early life and education \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Keith_Jarrett&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")\] Jarrett was born on May 8, 1945, in [Allentown, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allentown,_Pennsylvania "Allentown, Pennsylvania"),[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-Larkin-1) to a mother of [Slovenian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovenes "Slovenes") descent. Jarrett's grandmother was born in [Segovci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Segovci "Segovci"), near [Apače](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apa%C4%8De "Apače") in [Slovenia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovenia "Slovenia").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-7) Jarrett's father was of mostly [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germans "Germans") descent.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-8) He grew up in suburban Allentown with significant early exposure to music.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-9) Jarrett possesses [absolute pitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_pitch "Absolute pitch") and displayed prodigious musical talents as a young child. He began piano lessons before his third birthday. At age five, he appeared on a television talent program hosted by swing bandleader [Paul Whiteman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Whiteman "Paul Whiteman").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-10) He performed in his first formal piano recital at the age of seven, playing works by composers such as [Bach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Sebastian_Bach "Johann Sebastian Bach"), [Beethoven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_van_Beethoven "Ludwig van Beethoven"), [Mozart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfgang_Amadeus_Mozart "Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart"), and [Saint-Saëns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camille_Saint-Sa%C3%ABns "Camille Saint-Saëns"), and ending with two of his own compositions.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-11) Encouraged by his mother, he took classical piano lessons with a series of teachers, including [Eleanor Sokoloff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eleanor_Sokoloff "Eleanor Sokoloff") of the [Curtis Institute of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curtis_Institute_of_Music "Curtis Institute of Music") in [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia"). Jarrett attended [Emmaus High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmaus_High_School "Emmaus High School") in [Emmaus, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmaus,_Pennsylvania "Emmaus, Pennsylvania"), where he learned [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") and became proficient in it. He developed a strong interest in [contemporary jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") and was inspired by a [Dave Brubeck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Brubeck "Dave Brubeck") performance he attended in [New Hope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Hope,_Pennsylvania "New Hope, Pennsylvania").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-12) He was invited to study classical composition in Paris with [Nadia Boulanger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadia_Boulanger "Nadia Boulanger"), but he was already leaning toward jazz and turned it down.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-13) After his graduation from Emmaus High School in 1963, Jarrett moved to [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston") to attend [Berklee College of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berklee_College_of_Music "Berklee College of Music") and play [cocktail piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_bar "Piano bar") in local Boston clubs. ## Career \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Keith_Jarrett&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Career")\] ### The Jazz Messengers \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Keith_Jarrett&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: The Jazz Messengers")\] Main article: [The Jazz Messengers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Jazz_Messengers "The Jazz Messengers") In 1964, Jarrett moved to [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), where he played at the [Village Vanguard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Village_Vanguard "Village Vanguard") in [Greenwich Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenwich_Village "Greenwich Village").[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-Jurek-14) [Art Blakey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Blakey "Art Blakey") hired Jarrett to play with [The Jazz Messengers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Jazz_Messengers "The Jazz Messengers"). Jarrett's appearance on the Messengers' live album _[Buttercorn Lady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buttercorn_Lady "Buttercorn Lady")_ (1966) marked his commercial recording debut.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-15) However, there was friction between Blakey and Jarrett, and Jarrett left after four months of touring.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-16) ### Charles Lloyd Quartet \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Keith_Jarrett&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: Charles Lloyd Quartet")\] During a show, he was noticed by [Jack DeJohnette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_DeJohnette "Jack DeJohnette"), who recommended Jarrett to his band leader [Charles Lloyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Lloyd_(jazz_musician) "Charles Lloyd (jazz musician)").[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-17) The Charles Lloyd Quartet had formed not long before and was exploring open, improvised forms while building supple grooves, and it was moving into terrain that was also being explored, although from another stylistic background, by some of the [psychedelic rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelic_rock "Psychedelic rock") bands of the West Coast.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-carr_32-18) Their 1966 album _[Forest Flower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_Flower "Forest Flower")_ was one of the most successful jazz recordings of the mid-1960s.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-19) They were invited to play [The Fillmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fillmore "The Fillmore") in San Francisco, and won over the local [hippie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippie "Hippie") audience.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-carr_33-20) The quartet toured across the U.S. and Europe, including appearances in Leningrad and Moscow.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-carr_33-20) Their concert at London's [Royal Albert Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Albert_Hall "Royal Albert Hall") was attended by [The Beatles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beatles "The Beatles").[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-21) The band was profiled in _[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")_ and _[Harper's Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harper's_Magazine "Harper's Magazine")_,[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-carr_33-20) which made Jarrett a popular musician in rock and jazz. The tour also laid the foundation for a lasting musical bond with DeJohnette.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-carr_32-18) Jarrett began to record his own tracks as a leader of small groups, at first in a trio with [Charlie Haden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Haden "Charlie Haden") and [Paul Motian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Motian "Paul Motian"). _[Life Between the Exit Signs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_Between_the_Exit_Signs "Life Between the Exit Signs")_ (1967), his first album as a band leader, was released by [Vortex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vortex_Records "Vortex Records") and was followed by _[Restoration Ruin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Restoration_Ruin "Restoration Ruin")_ (1968), which Thom Jurek of [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") later wrote was "a curiosity in his catalog".[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-Jurek-14) Not only does Jarrett barely touch the piano, but he plays all the other instruments on what is essentially a [folk-rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_rock "Folk rock") album; he also sings.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-Jurek-14) _[Somewhere Before](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somewhere_Before "Somewhere Before")_, another trio album with Haden and Motian, was released in 1968 on [Atlantic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Records "Atlantic Records"). ### Miles Davis \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Keith_Jarrett&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: Miles Davis")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/57/Keith_Jarrett-140908-0009WP.jpg/250px-Keith_Jarrett-140908-0009WP.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Keith_Jarrett-140908-0009WP.jpg) Jarrett performing as part of [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")'s septet in November 1971 The Charles Lloyd Quartet with Jarrett, [Ron McClure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_McClure "Ron McClure"), and DeJohnette came to an end in 1968 after their recording of _[Soundtrack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soundtrack_(Charles_Lloyd_album) "Soundtrack (Charles Lloyd album)")_ because of money disputes and artistic differences.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-22) Jarrett was asked to join the [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis") group after the trumpeter heard him in a New York City club.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-23) During his tenure with Davis, Jarrett played both [electronic organ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_organ "Electric organ") and [Rhodes piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodes_piano "Rhodes piano"), alternating with [Chick Corea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chick_Corea "Chick Corea"). The two appear side by side on some 1970 recordings, including the [Isle of Wight Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isle_of_Wight_Festival "Isle of Wight Festival") performance of August 1970 in the film _[Miles Electric: A Different Kind of Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Electric:_A_Different_Kind_of_Blue "Miles Electric: A Different Kind of Blue")_ and on _[Bitches Brew Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew_Live "Bitches Brew Live")_. After Corea left in 1970, Jarrett often played electric piano and organ simultaneously.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-24) Despite his growing dislike of amplified music and electric instruments within jazz, Jarrett continued with the group out of respect for Davis and because of his desire to work with DeJohnette. Jarrett has often cited Davis as a vital musical and personal influence on his own thinking about music and improvisation.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-25) Jarrett performs on several Davis albums, including _[Miles Davis at Fillmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis_at_Fillmore "Miles Davis at Fillmore")_, recorded June 17–20, 1970, at [Fillmore East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fillmore_East "Fillmore East") in New York City, and _[The Cellar Door Sessions 1970](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Cellar_Door_Sessions_1970 "The Cellar Door Sessions 1970")_, recorded December 16–19, 1970, at [The Cellar Door](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Cellar_Door "The Cellar Door") club in Washington, D.C.. His keyboard playing features prominently on _[Live-Evil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live-Evil_(Miles_Davis_album) "Live-Evil (Miles Davis album)")_ and he plays electric organ on _[Get Up with It](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Get_Up_with_It "Get Up with It")_. Some other tracks from this period were released much later.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-26) DeJohnette left Davis's band in the middle of 1971, and Jarrett followed in December.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-carr_52-27) Jarrett later reflected: "When Jack left I knew I was going to have to leave ... Nobody knew what Jack knew and could do what he could do simultaneously. That was the end of the flexibility of the band."[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-carr_52-27) ### 1970s quartets and Manfred Eicher \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Keith_Jarrett&action=edit§ion=6 "Edit section: 1970s quartets and Manfred Eicher")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/Miles_Davis-140916-0018-105WP.jpg/250px-Miles_Davis-140916-0018-105WP.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Miles_Davis-140916-0018-105WP.jpg) Jarrett playing with [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis") in November 1971 In 1971, Jarrett, Haden, and Motian participated in a four-day session for [Atlantic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Records "Atlantic Records") during which they recorded the trio album _[The Mourning of a Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mourning_of_a_Star "The Mourning of a Star")_ and two albums, _[El Juicio (The Judgement)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Juicio_(The_Judgement) "El Juicio (The Judgement)")_ and _[Birth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_(album) "Birth (album)")_, on which the trio was augmented by saxophonist [Dewey Redman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dewey_Redman "Dewey Redman").[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-carr_56-28) Redman became an official member of the group, which later became referred to as Jarrett's "American quartet". They would go on to record over a dozen albums over five years.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-carr_56-28) The group was often supplemented by an extra percussionist, such as Danny Johnson, [Guilherme Franco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guilherme_Franco "Guilherme Franco"), or [Airto Moreira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airto_Moreira "Airto Moreira"), and occasionally by guitarist [Sam Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Brown_(guitarist) "Sam Brown (guitarist)"). Later in 1971, the quartet, with Brown and Moreira, recorded _[Expectations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expectations_(Keith_Jarrett_album) "Expectations (Keith Jarrett album)")_ for [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records"), with string and brass arrangements by Jarrett.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-carr_56-28) However, Columbia suddenly dropped Jarrett in favor of [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"),[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-29) and Jarrett's manager negotiated a contract with [Impulse! Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records "Impulse! Records"),[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-Carr,_Ian_p._61-30) for whom the group would record eight albums. The quartet members played various instruments. Jarrett played soprano saxophone, recorder, banjo, percussion, and piano. Redman played [musette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suona "Suona"), a Chinese double-reed instrument, and percussion, and Motian and Haden played a variety of percussion. Haden also produced a variety of unusual plucked and percussive sounds with his acoustic bass, running it through a [wah-wah pedal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wah-wah_pedal "Wah-wah pedal") for one track ("Mortgage on My Soul" on the album _Birth_).[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-31) _[Byablue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byablue "Byablue")_ and _[Bop-Be](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bop-Be "Bop-Be")_, albums recorded for Impulse!, feature the compositions of Haden, Motian, and Redman, as opposed to Jarrett's own, which dominated the previous albums. Jarrett's compositions and the musical identities of the group members gave this ensemble a distinctive sound. The quartet's music is an amalgam of free jazz, straight-ahead post-bop, gospel music, and exotic, Middle-Eastern-sounding improvisations. During this time, Jarrett received a letter from producer [Manfred Eicher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manfred_Eicher "Manfred Eicher") asking if he would like to record for the relatively new [ECM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records "ECM Records") label.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-32) Jarrett was impressed by the fact that Eicher was primarily concerned with musical quality, as opposed to financial gain.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-carr_59-33) Jarrett's American quartet released two albums, _[The Survivors' Suite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Survivors'_Suite "The Survivors' Suite")_ and _[Eyes of the Heart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eyes_of_the_Heart_(album) "Eyes of the Heart (album)")_, on ECM, and the label also issued _[Ruta and Daitya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruta_and_Daitya "Ruta and Daitya")_, consisting of duo tracks featuring Jarrett and DeJohnette recorded in early 1971 and tracks with Miles Davis after Jarrett gave tapes of the session to Eicher.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-Carr,_Ian_p._61-30) In 1972, Eicher proposed that Jarrett work with Norwegian saxophonist [Jan Garbarek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Garbarek "Jan Garbarek"), whom Jarrett had met while in Europe with Charles Lloyd during the late 1960s.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-34) Their initial collaborations laid the groundwork for what would become referred to as Jarrett's "European quartet", which also featured [Palle Danielsson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palle_Danielsson "Palle Danielsson") on bass and [Jon Christensen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Christensen_(musician) "Jon Christensen (musician)") on drums.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-35) The group recorded five albums for ECM, each played in a style similar to that of the American quartet but with many of the avant-garde and Americana elements replaced by the European folk and classical music influences that characterized the work of ECM artists at the time. ### Solo piano \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Keith_Jarrett&action=edit§ion=7 "Edit section: Solo piano")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2e/Keith_Jarrett-commons.jpg/250px-Keith_Jarrett-commons.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Keith_Jarrett-commons.jpg) Jarrett performing in [Antibes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antibes "Antibes"), France, in July 2003 Jarrett recorded a few solo pieces live under the guidance of [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis") at [the Cellar Door](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Cellar_Door "The Cellar Door") in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), in December 1970. These were done on electric pianos ( [Rhodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodes_piano "Rhodes piano") and [Contempo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fender_Contempo_Organ "Fender Contempo Organ")).[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-36) Most parts of these recorded sets were released in 2007 on _[The Cellar Door Sessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Cellar_Door_Sessions_1970 "The Cellar Door Sessions 1970")_, featuring four improvisations by Jarrett. Jarrett's first album for ECM, _[Facing You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facing_You "Facing You")_, was released in 1971. He has continued to record solo studio piano albums intermittently throughout his career, including _[Staircase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staircase_(album) "Staircase (album)")_ (1976), _[Invocations / The Moth and the Flame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invocations_/_The_Moth_and_the_Flame "Invocations / The Moth and the Flame")_ (1981), and _[The Melody at Night, with You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Melody_at_Night,_with_You "The Melody at Night, with You")_ (1999). _[Book of Ways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Ways "Book of Ways")_ (1986) is a studio recording of [clavichord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clavichord "Clavichord") solos. In 1973, Jarrett began playing totally [improvised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation "Free improvisation") solo concerts, and it is the popularity of these concert recordings that made him one of the best-selling jazz artists in history. Albums released from these concerts were _[Solo Concerts: Bremen/Lausanne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solo_Concerts:_Bremen/Lausanne "Solo Concerts: Bremen/Lausanne")_ (1973), which _Time_ magazine named "Jazz Album of the Year", _[The Köln Concert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert "The Köln Concert")_ (1975), which became the best-selling piano recording in history, and _[Sun Bear Concerts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Bear_Concerts "Sun Bear Concerts")_ (1976), a 10-LP (and later 6-CD) box set. Another of Jarrett's solo concerts, _[Dark Intervals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_Intervals "Dark Intervals")_, was released in 1987. After a hiatus, Jarrett returned to extended solo improvised concert format with _[Paris Concert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Concert_(Keith_Jarrett_album) "Paris Concert (Keith Jarrett album)")_ (1990), _[Vienna Concert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna_Concert "Vienna Concert")_ (1991), _Live at the Royal Festival Hall_ (1991), and _[La Scala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Scala_(album) "La Scala (album)")_ (1995). These later concerts tended to be more influenced by classical music than the earlier ones, reflecting his interest in composers such as [Bach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Sebastian_Bach "Johann Sebastian Bach") and [Shostakovich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dmitri_Shostakovich "Dmitri Shostakovich"). In the [liner notes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liner_notes "Liner notes") to _Vienna Concert_, Jarrett named the performance his greatest achievement and the fulfillment of everything he was aiming to accomplish; "I have courted the fire for a very long time, and many sparks have flown in the past, but the music on this recording speaks, finally, the language of the flame itself", he wrote.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-37) Jarrett has commented that his best performances have been when he has had only the slightest notion of what he was going to play at the next moment. He also said that most people don't know "what he does" which relates to what Miles Davis said to him expressing bewilderment as to how Jarrett could "play from nothing".[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-38) Jarrett's 100th solo performance in Japan was captured on video at [Suntory Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suntory_Hall "Suntory Hall"), Tokyo, in April 1987, and released the same year as _Solo Tribute_. This is a set of almost all standard songs. Another video recording, _Last Solo_, was released in 1987 from a solo concert at Kan-i Hoken Hall in Tokyo in January 1984. In the late 1990s, Jarrett was diagnosed with [chronic fatigue syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myalgic_encephalomyelitis/chronic_fatigue_syndrome "Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome")[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-Jurek-14) and was unable to leave his home for long periods of time. During this period, he recorded _[The Melody at Night, with You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Melody_at_Night,_with_You "The Melody at Night, with You")_, a solo piano effort consisting of [jazz standards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_standard "Jazz standard"). The album had originally been a Christmas gift to his second wife, Rose Anne.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-Gross-39) By 2000, Jarrett had returned to touring, both solo and with the Standards Trio. Two 2002 solo concerts in Japan, Jarrett's first solo piano concerts following his illness, were released on the 2005 CD _[Radiance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiance_(Keith_Jarrett_album) "Radiance (Keith Jarrett album)")_ (a complete concert in [Osaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osaka "Osaka") and excerpts from one in Tokyo) and the 2006 DVD _Tokyo Solo_ (the entire Tokyo performance). In contrast with previous concerts (which were generally a pair of continuous improvisations 30–40 minutes long), the 2002 concerts consist of a linked series of shorter improvisations (some as short as a minute and a half). In September 2005, at [Carnegie Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Hall "Carnegie Hall"), Jarrett performed his first solo concert in North America in more than ten years, released a year later as a double-CD set, _[The Carnegie Hall Concert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Carnegie_Hall_Concert_(Keith_Jarrett_album) "The Carnegie Hall Concert (Keith Jarrett album)")_. In late 2008, he performed solo at the [Salle Pleyel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salle_Pleyel "Salle Pleyel") in Paris and at London's [Royal Festival Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Festival_Hall "Royal Festival Hall"), marking the first time Jarrett played solo in London in 17 years. Recordings of these concerts were released in October 2009 on the album _[Paris / London: Testament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_/_London:_Testament "Paris / London: Testament")_. The 2005 documentary _The Art of Improvisation_, broadcast on [BBC Two](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Two "BBC Two") on November 12, 2021, concluded with his trio performing a recognizable version of " [Basin Street Blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basin_Street_Blues "Basin Street Blues")".[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-art-40) ### The Standards Trio \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Keith_Jarrett&action=edit§ion=8 "Edit section: The Standards Trio")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a8/Keith_Jarrett_Trio_-_Montreal_Concert_July_1_2007_03.jpg/250px-Keith_Jarrett_Trio_-_Montreal_Concert_July_1_2007_03.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Keith_Jarrett_Trio_-_Montreal_Concert_July_1_2007_03.jpg) Keith Jarrett Trio, Montreal Concert, 2007 In 1983, at the suggestion of ECM head [Manfred Eicher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manfred_Eicher "Manfred Eicher"),[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-test-41) Jarrett asked bassist [Gary Peacock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Peacock "Gary Peacock") and drummer [Jack DeJohnette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_DeJohnette "Jack DeJohnette"), with whom he had worked on Peacock's 1977 album _[Tales of Another](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tales_of_Another "Tales of Another")_, to record an album of [jazz standards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_standard "Jazz standard"), simply titled _[Standards, Vol. 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standards,_Vol._1 "Standards, Vol. 1")_. Two more albums, _[Standards, Vol. 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standards,_Vol._2 "Standards, Vol. 2")_ and _[Changes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Changes_(Keith_Jarrett_album) "Changes (Keith Jarrett album)")_, both recorded at the same session, followed soon after. The success of these albums and the group's ensuing tour, which came as traditional acoustic post-bop was enjoying an upswing in the early 1980s, led to this new standards trio becoming one of the premier working groups in jazz, and certainly one of the most enduring, continuing to record and tour for more than 25 years. The Trio went on to record numerous live and studio albums consisting primarily of jazz repertory material. The Jarrett–Peacock–DeJohnette trio also produced recordings that consist largely of challenging original material, including 1987's _[Changeless](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Changeless_(album) "Changeless (album)")_. Several of the standards albums contain an original track or two, some attributed to Jarrett, but most are improvisations on jazz standards. The live recordings _[Inside Out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inside_Out_(Keith_Jarrett_album) "Inside Out (Keith Jarrett album)")_ and _[Always Let Me Go](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Always_Let_Me_Go "Always Let Me Go")_ (released in 2001 and 2002, respectively) marked a renewed interest by the trio in wholly improvised [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz"). By this point in their history, the musical communication among these three men had become nothing short of telepathic, and their group improvisations frequently take on a complexity that sounds almost composed.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-42) The standards trio undertook frequent world tours of recital halls (the only venues Jarrett, a notorious stickler for acoustics, will play) and was one of the few truly successful jazz groups to play both straight-ahead (as opposed to [smooth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_jazz "Smooth jazz")) and free jazz.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-43) A related recording, _[At the Deer Head Inn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/At_the_Deer_Head_Inn "At the Deer Head Inn")_ (1992), is a live album of standards recorded with [Paul Motian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Motian "Paul Motian") replacing DeJohnette, at the venue in [Delaware Water Gap, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware_Water_Gap,_Pennsylvania "Delaware Water Gap, Pennsylvania"), 40 miles from Jarrett's hometown, where he had his first job as a jazz pianist. It was the first time Jarrett and Motian had played together since the demise of the American quartet sixteen years earlier. The Standard Trio disbanded in 2014 after more than 30 years.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-44) The final concert of Keith Jarrett's trio was on November 30, 2014 at the [New Jersey Performing Arts Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey_Performing_Arts_Center "New Jersey Performing Arts Center"), Newark, New Jersey. The last encore was [Thelonious Monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thelonious_Monk "Thelonious Monk")'s composition " [Straight, No Chaser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_compositions_by_Thelonious_Monk#Straight,_No_Chaser "List of compositions by Thelonious Monk")". Peacock died in September 2020. ### Classical music \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Keith_Jarrett&action=edit§ion=9 "Edit section: Classical music")\] Since the early 1970s, Jarrett's success as a jazz musician has enabled him to maintain a parallel career as a classical composer and pianist, recording almost exclusively for ECM Records. _[In the Light](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_the_Light_(Keith_Jarrett_album) "In the Light (Keith Jarrett album)")_, an album made in 1973, consists of short pieces for solo piano, strings, and various chamber ensembles, including a string quartet and a brass quintet, and a piece for cellos and trombones. This collection demonstrates a young composer's affinity for a variety of classical styles.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-45) _[Luminessence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luminessence "Luminessence")_ (1974) and _[Arbour Zena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arbour_Zena "Arbour Zena")_ (1975) both combine composed pieces for strings with improvising jazz musicians, including [Jan Garbarek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Garbarek "Jan Garbarek") and [Charlie Haden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Haden "Charlie Haden"). The strings here have a moody, contemplative feel that is characteristic of the "ECM sound" of the 1970s and is also particularly well suited to Garbarek's keening saxophone improvisations. From an academic standpoint, these compositions are dismissed by many classical music aficionados as lightweight, but Jarrett appeared to be working more towards a synthesis between composed and improvised music at this time, rather than the production of formal classical works.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-46) From this point on, however, his classical work would adhere to more conventional disciplines. _[Ritual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ritual_(Keith_Jarrett_album) "Ritual (Keith Jarrett album)")_ (1977) is a composed solo piano piece recorded by [Dennis Russell Davies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennis_Russell_Davies "Dennis Russell Davies") that is somewhat reminiscent of Jarrett's own solo piano recordings. _[The Celestial Hawk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Celestial_Hawk "The Celestial Hawk")_ (1980) is a piece for orchestra, percussion, and piano that Jarrett performed and recorded with the [Syracuse Symphony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syracuse_Symphony_Orchestra "Syracuse Symphony Orchestra") under [Christopher Keene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Keene "Christopher Keene"). This piece is the largest and longest of Jarrett's efforts as a classical composer. _[Bridge of Light](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridge_of_Light_(album) "Bridge of Light (album)")_ (1993) is the last recording of classical compositions to appear under Jarrett's name. The album contains three pieces written for a soloist with orchestra, and one for violin and piano. The pieces date from 1984 and 1990. In 1988, [New World Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_World_Records "New World Records") released the CD _Lou Harrison: Piano Concerto and Suite for Violin, Piano and Small Orchestra_, featuring Jarrett on piano, with Naoto Otomo conducting the piano concerto with the [New Japan Philharmonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Japan_Philharmonic "New Japan Philharmonic"). [Robert Hughes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Hughes_(American_composer) "Robert Hughes (American composer)") conducted the Suite for Violin, Piano, and Small Orchestra. In 1992 came the release of Jarrett's performance of [Peggy Glanville-Hicks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peggy_Glanville-Hicks "Peggy Glanville-Hicks")'s _Etruscan Concerto_, with Dennis Russell Davies conducting the [Brooklyn Philharmonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Philharmonic "Brooklyn Philharmonic"). This was released on [MusicMasters Classics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MusicMasters_Records "MusicMasters Records"), with pieces by [Lou Harrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou_Harrison "Lou Harrison") and [Terry Riley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terry_Riley "Terry Riley"). In 1995, MusicMasters Jazz released a CD on which one track featured Jarrett performing the solo piano part in _[Lousadzak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lousadzak "Lousadzak")_, a 17-minute piano concerto by American composer [Alan Hovhaness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Hovhaness "Alan Hovhaness"). The conductor again was Davies. Most of Jarrett's classical recordings are of older repertoire, but he may have been introduced to this modern work by his one-time manager [George Avakian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Avakian "George Avakian"), who was a friend of the composer. Jarrett has also recorded classical works for ECM by composers such as [Bach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Sebastian_Bach "Johann Sebastian Bach"), [Handel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Frideric_Handel "George Frideric Handel"), [Shostakovich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dmitri_Shostakovich "Dmitri Shostakovich"), and [Arvo Pärt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arvo_P%C3%A4rt "Arvo Pärt"). In 2004, Jarrett was awarded the [Léonie Sonning Music Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A9onie_Sonning_Music_Prize "Léonie Sonning Music Prize").[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-47) Usually associated with classical musicians and composers, [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis") is the only other jazz performer to have won it. ### Other works \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Keith_Jarrett&action=edit§ion=10 "Edit section: Other works")\] Jarrett has also played [harpsichord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harpsichord "Harpsichord"), [clavichord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clavichord "Clavichord"), organ, [soprano saxophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soprano_saxophone "Soprano saxophone"), and drums. He often played saxophone and various forms of percussion in the American quartet, though his recordings since the breakup of that group have rarely featured these instruments. On the majority of his recordings in the last 20 years, he has played acoustic piano only. He has spoken with some regret of his decision to give up playing the saxophone, in particular.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-48) On April 15, 1978, Jarrett was the musical guest on _[Saturday Night Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturday_Night_Live "Saturday Night Live")_. The 2001 German film _[Mostly Martha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mostly_Martha_(film) "Mostly Martha (film)")_, whose music consultant was [ECM Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records "ECM Records") founder [Manfred Eicher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manfred_Eicher "Manfred Eicher"), features Jarrett's "Country" from the European quartet album _My Song_ and "U Dance" from the Standards Trio album _Tribute_, as well as excerpts from Jarrett's solo concerts. ## Lawsuit against Steely Dan \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Keith_Jarrett&action=edit§ion=11 "Edit section: Lawsuit against Steely Dan")\] Following the release of the album _[Gaucho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaucho_(album) "Gaucho (album)")_ in 1980 by the U.S. rock band [Steely Dan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steely_Dan "Steely Dan"), Jarrett sued the band for copyright infringement. _Gaucho_'s title track, credited to [Donald Fagen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Fagen "Donald Fagen") and [Walter Becker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Becker "Walter Becker"), bore a resemblance to Jarrett's "Long As You Know You're Living Yours" from Jarrett's 1974 album _[Belonging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belonging_(Keith_Jarrett_album) "Belonging (Keith Jarrett album)")_. In an interview with _[Musician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musician_(magazine) "Musician (magazine)")_ magazine, Becker and Fagen were asked about the similarity between the two pieces of music, and Becker told _Musician_ that he loved the Jarrett composition, while Fagen said they had been influenced by it. After their comments were published, Jarrett sued, and Becker and Fagen were legally obliged to add his name to the credits and provide Jarrett with publishing royalties.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-49) ## Idiosyncrasies \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Keith_Jarrett&action=edit§ion=12 "Edit section: Idiosyncrasies")\] Jarrett frequently emits loud vocalizations, sometimes characterized as moaning, during his playing.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-50) Jarrett is also physically active while playing jazz and improvised solo performances, but the vocalizations are generally absent whenever he plays classical repertoire. Jarrett has noted his vocalizations are based on involvement, not content, and are more of an interaction than a reaction.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-51)[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-popmatters-52) Interviewed in 2015, Jarrett explained the involuntary vocalizations made during his performances: "It's potential limitlessness that I'm feeling at that moment. If you think about it, it's often in a space between phrases, \[when I'm thinking,\] 'How did I get to this point where I feel so full?' And if you felt full of some sort of emotion you would have to make a sound. So that's actually what it is – with the trio, without the trio, solo. Luckily for me, I don't do it with classical music".[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-53) Jarrett is highly intolerant of audience noise, especially during solo improvised performances. He feels extraneous noise affects his inspiration and distracts from the purity of the sound. Cough drops are routinely supplied to Jarrett's audiences in cold weather, and he has been known to stop playing and lead the crowd in a group cough.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-play-jazz-54) He has also complained onstage about audience members taking photographs,[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-idolator-55) and has performed in the dark to prevent this.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-jazz-times-56) Jarrett is opposed to electronic instruments and equipment, which he has described as "toys".[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-art-40) His [liner notes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liner_notes "Liner notes") for the 1973 album _Solo Concerts: Bremen/Lausanne_ states, "I am, and have been, carrying on an anti-electric-music crusade of which this is an exhibit for the prosecution. Electricity goes through all of us and is not to be relegated to wires."[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-57) He has largely eschewed electric or electronic instruments since his time with Miles Davis. However, in October 1972, he played electric piano and piano on [Freddie Hubbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Hubbard "Freddie Hubbard")'s _[Sky Dive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sky_Dive "Sky Dive")._[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-58) ## Cultural references \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Keith_Jarrett&action=edit§ion=13 "Edit section: Cultural references")\] A 2025 feature film, _[Köln 75](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ln_75 "Köln 75")_, tells the story of Jarrett's 1975 concert at the Köln Opera House.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-59) Jarrett was referred to in Season 5, Episode 6, of [HBO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HBO "HBO")'s _[The Sopranos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sopranos "The Sopranos")_ in 2004, titled " [Sentimental Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentimental_Education_(The_Sopranos) "Sentimental Education (The Sopranos)")"; in the episode, [Tony Blundetto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Sopranos_characters#Tony_Blundetto "List of The Sopranos characters") mentions "piping in a little Keith Jarrett" among his plans for the massage studio he is building.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-60)\[ _[importance?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:What_Wikipedia_is_not#Encyclopedic_content "Wikipedia:What Wikipedia is not")_\] ## Personal life \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Keith_Jarrett&action=edit§ion=14 "Edit section: Personal life")\] Jarrett lives in an 18th-century farmhouse in [Oxford Township, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford_Township,_New_Jersey "Oxford Township, New Jersey"), in rural [Warren County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_County,_New_Jersey "Warren County, New Jersey"), where he used an adjacent barn as a recording and practice studio.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-61) Jarrett was a follower of the teachings of mystic [George Gurdjieff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Gurdjieff "George Gurdjieff") for many years,[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-Chase_2010_e310-62) and in 1980 recorded an album of Gurdjieff's compositions, called _[Sacred Hymns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacred_Hymns "Sacred Hymns")_, for ECM. His forebears were [Christian Scientists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Science "Christian Science"), and though he endorses the core of the faith, he does not follow all its precepts, and also identifies with the [Sufi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sufi "Sufi") tradition and mystical [Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam "Islam").[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-63) In 1964, Jarrett married Margot Erney, his girlfriend from [Emmaus High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmaus_High_School "Emmaus High School") with whom he reconnected in [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston"). The couple had two sons, Gabriel and Noah, and divorced in 1979.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-64) He and his second wife Rose Anne (née Colavito) divorced in 2010 after a 30-year marriage. Jarrett has four younger brothers, two of whom are involved in music. Chris Jarrett is also a pianist and Scott Jarrett is a producer and songwriter. Of the two sons from his first marriage, Noah Jarrett is a bassist and composer, and Gabriel Jarrett is a drummer based in [Vermont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vermont "Vermont"). Keith Jarrett is currently married to Akiko Jarrett.[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-Beato_interview-65) Jarrett's race has been a source of commentary by media and activists throughout his career,[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-66)[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-67) as he has reported being recurrently mistaken as a [black person](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_people "Black people"). In a 2000 interview with [Terry Gross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terry_Gross "Terry Gross"), Jarrett relates an incident at the Heidelberg Jazz Festival in the [Rhine-Neckar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhine-Neckar "Rhine-Neckar") region of Germany when he was protested by black musicians for something akin to [cultural appropriation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_appropriation "Cultural appropriation"). He also tells of a separate moment in his career when black jazz musician [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman") approached him backstage, and "said something like 'Man, you've got to be Black. You just have to be black.'" Jarrett replied, "I know. I know. I'm working on it."[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-Gross-39)[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-68) In a September 11, 2000, interview with Terry Gross, Jarrett revealed that [chronic fatigue syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myalgic_encephalomyelitis/chronic_fatigue_syndrome "Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome") required him to radically overhaul his piano to have less breakaway keypress resistance in order for him to keep playing.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-Gross-39) Jarrett suffered two [strokes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stroke "Stroke") in February and May 2018. After the second, he was paralyzed and spent nearly two years in a rehabilitation facility. Although he has regained a limited ability to walk with a cane and can play piano with his right hand, he remains partly paralyzed on his left side and is not expected to perform again. "I don't know what my future is supposed to be. I don't feel right now like I'm a pianist", Jarrett told _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")_ in October 2020.[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-69) ## Discography \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Keith_Jarrett&action=edit§ion=15 "Edit section: Discography")\] Main article: [Keith Jarrett discography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett_discography "Keith Jarrett discography") ## References \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Keith_Jarrett&action=edit§ion=16 "Edit section: References")\] 01. - gamelan | Musical artist **Donald Eugene Cherry** (November 18, 1936 – October 19, 1995)[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-1) was an American jazz trumpeter, bandleader, and multi-instrumentalist. Beginning in the late 1950s, he had a long tenure performing in the bands of saxophonist [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman"), including on the pioneering [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") albums _[The Shape of Jazz to Come](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shape_of_Jazz_to_Come "The Shape of Jazz to Come")_ (1959) and _[Free Jazz: A Collective Improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Jazz:_A_Collective_Improvisation "Free Jazz: A Collective Improvisation")_ (1961). Cherry also collaborated separately with musicians including [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane"), [Charlie Haden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Haden "Charlie Haden"), [Sun Ra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Ra "Sun Ra"), [Ed Blackwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Blackwell "Ed Blackwell"), the [New York Contemporary Five](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Contemporary_Five "New York Contemporary Five"), and [Albert Ayler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler "Albert Ayler"). Cherry released his debut album as bandleader, _[Complete Communion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complete_Communion "Complete Communion")_, in 1966. In the 1970s, he became a pioneer in [world fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_music "World music"), with his work drawing on African, Middle Eastern, and [Hindustani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindustani_classical_music "Hindustani classical music") music, as heard on the 1975 release _[Brown Rice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_Rice_(album) "Brown Rice (album)")_. He was a member of the [ECM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records "ECM Records") group [Codona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona "Codona"), along with percussionist [Naná Vasconcelos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nan%C3%A1_Vasconcelos "Naná Vasconcelos") and sitar and tabla player [Collin Walcott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collin_Walcott "Collin Walcott").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-2) Chris Kelsey of [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") called Cherry "one of the most influential jazz musicians of the late 20th century."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-3) ## Early life \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Early life")\] Cherry was born in [Oklahoma City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma_City "Oklahoma City"), [Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma "Oklahoma"), to a mother of [Choctaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choctaw "Choctaw") descent and an [African-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Americans "African Americans") father.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-4) His mother and grandmother played piano and his father played trumpet.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-atc1995-5) His father owned Oklahoma City's Cherry Blossom Club, which hosted performances by jazz musicians [Charlie Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Christian "Charlie Christian") and [Fletcher Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fletcher_Henderson "Fletcher Henderson").[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-biojazz-6) In 1940, Cherry moved with his family to the [Watts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watts,_Los_Angeles "Watts, Los Angeles") neighborhood of [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"), where his father tended bar at the Plantation Club on [Central Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Avenue_(Los_Angeles) "Central Avenue (Los Angeles)"), at the time the center of a vibrant jazz scene.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-biojazz-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-cadence-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-carr-8) Cherry recalled skipping school at [Fremont High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_C._Fremont_High_School "John C. Fremont High School") in order to play with the [swing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing_music "Swing music") band at [Jefferson High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_High_School_(Los_Angeles) "Jefferson High School (Los Angeles)").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-cadence-7) This resulted in his transfer to Jacob Riis High School, a [reform school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_school "Reform school"),[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-cadence-7) where he met drummer [Billy Higgins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Higgins "Billy Higgins").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-voce1995-9)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-crouch-10) ## Career \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Career")\] By the early 1950s Cherry was playing with jazz musicians in Los Angeles, sometimes acting as pianist in [Art Farmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Farmer "Art Farmer")'s group.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-jost-11):134 While trumpeter [Clifford Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_Brown "Clifford Brown") was in Los Angeles with [Max Roach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Roach "Max Roach"), Cherry attended a jam session with Brown and [Larance Marable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larance_Marable "Larance Marable") at [Eric Dolphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy "Eric Dolphy")'s house, and Brown informally mentored Cherry.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-cadence-7) He also toured with saxophonist [James Clay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Clay_(musician) "James Clay (musician)").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-litweiler-12):45 Cherry became well known in 1958 when he performed and recorded with [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman"), first in a quintet with pianist [Paul Bley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Bley "Paul Bley") and later in the quartet which recorded for [Atlantic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Records "Atlantic Records"). During this period, "his lines ... gathered much of their freedom of motion from the free harmonic structures."[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-litweiler-12):289 Cherry co-led _[The Avant-Garde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Avant-Garde_(album) "The Avant-Garde (album)")_ session which saw [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane") replacing Coleman in the quartet, recorded and toured with [Sonny Rollins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Rollins "Sonny Rollins"), was a member of the [New York Contemporary Five](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Contemporary_Five "New York Contemporary Five") with [Archie Shepp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Shepp "Archie Shepp") and [John Tchicai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Tchicai "John Tchicai"), and recorded and toured with both [Albert Ayler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler "Albert Ayler") and [George Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Russell_(composer) "George Russell (composer)"). His first recording as a leader was _[Complete Communion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complete_Communion "Complete Communion")_ for [Blue Note Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records") in 1965. The band included Coleman's drummer [Ed Blackwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Blackwell "Ed Blackwell") as well as saxophonist [Gato Barbieri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gato_Barbieri "Gato Barbieri"), whom he had met while touring Europe with Ayler, and bassist [Henry Grimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Grimes "Henry Grimes").[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-13) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/Firenze_DonCherry_1975.jpg/250px-Firenze_DonCherry_1975.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Firenze_DonCherry_1975.jpg) Cherry at Park Le Cascine, [Florence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence "Florence"), Italy, September 1975 After leaving Coleman's quartet, Cherry often played in small groups and duets, many with ex-Coleman drummer [Ed Blackwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Blackwell "Ed Blackwell"), during a long sojourn in [Scandinavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scandinavia "Scandinavia") and other locations. He traveled through Europe, India, Morocco, South Africa, and elsewhere to explore and play with a variety of musicians. In the late 1960s he settled in [Tågarp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C3%A5garp "Tågarp"), Sweden with his wife, Swedish designer and textile artist Moki Cherry. In 1968, Don Cherry taught music classes with guest lecturers, performance collaborators, and workshop leaders from around the world at Arbetarnas bildningsförbund (ABF) House, a Swedish labor movement-run education center. For ten years, Don and Moki Cherry lived and worked collaboratively in an abandoned schoolhouse in Tågarp, holding classes and performances, hosting guests and collaborators, and exploring their concept of Organic Music Society. In 1969, Cherry played trumpet and other instruments for poet [Allen Ginsberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allen_Ginsberg "Allen Ginsberg")'s 1970 LP _[Songs of Innocence and Experience](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Songs_of_Innocence_and_Experience_(Allen_Ginsberg_album) "Songs of Innocence and Experience (Allen Ginsberg album)")_, a musical adaptation of [William Blake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Blake "William Blake")'s [poetry collection of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Songs_of_Innocence_and_of_Experience "Songs of Innocence and of Experience").[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-Jurek-14) He appeared on Coleman's 1971 LP _[Science Fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_Fiction_(Ornette_Coleman_album) "Science Fiction (Ornette Coleman album)")_, and from 1976 to 1987 reunited with Blackwell and fellow Coleman alumni [Dewey Redman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dewey_Redman "Dewey Redman") and [Charlie Haden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Haden "Charlie Haden") as [Old and New Dreams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_and_New_Dreams "Old and New Dreams").[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-15) Old and New Dreams recorded four albums (two for [ECM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_(record_label) "ECM (record label)") and two for [Black Saint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Saint/Soul_Note "Black Saint/Soul Note")) where Cherry's "subtlety of rhythmic expansion and contraction" was noted.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-litweiler-12):290 [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/06/Don_Cherry_1989.jpg/250px-Don_Cherry_1989.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Don_Cherry_1989.jpg) Don Cherry in 1989 In the 1970s, Cherry ventured into the developing genre of world fusion music. Cherry incorporated influences of Middle Eastern, African, and Indian music into his playing. He studied Indian music with [Vasant Rai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasant_Rai "Vasant Rai") in the early seventies. From 1978 to 1982, he recorded three albums for ECM with "world jazz" group [Codona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona "Codona"), consisting of Cherry, percussionist [Naná Vasconcelos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nan%C3%A1_Vasconcelos "Naná Vasconcelos") and [sitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sitar "Sitar") and [tabla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabla "Tabla") player [Collin Walcott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collin_Walcott "Collin Walcott").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-voce1995-9) Cherry also collaborated with classical composer [Krzysztof Penderecki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krzysztof_Penderecki "Krzysztof Penderecki") on the 1971 album _[Actions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Actions_(album) "Actions (album)")_. In 1973, he co-composed the score for [Alejandro Jodorowsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alejandro_Jodorowsky "Alejandro Jodorowsky")'s film _[The Holy Mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Holy_Mountain_(1973_film) "The Holy Mountain (1973 film)")_, together with Jodorowsky and Ronald Frangipane. At the end of the 1970s, the trio Organic Music Theater (with Gian Piero Pramaggiore and [Naná Vasconcelos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nan%C3%A1_Vasconcelos "Naná Vasconcelos")) had an intense live activity in Italy and France. In 1982, Cherry released the duet album _[El Corazon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Coraz%C3%B3n_(Don_Cherry_and_Ed_Blackwell_album) "El Corazón (Don Cherry and Ed Blackwell album)")_ with Ed Blackwell. He also released two albums as a bandleader in the 1980s: _[Home Boy (Sister Out)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_Boy_(Sister_Out) "Home Boy (Sister Out)")_ in 1985 and _[Art Deco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Deco_(album) "Art Deco (album)")_ in 1988. He recorded again with the original Ornette Coleman Quartet on the first disc of Coleman's 1987 album _[In All Languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_All_Languages "In All Languages")_. Other playing opportunities in his career came with [Carla Bley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carla_Bley "Carla Bley")'s 1971 opera _[Escalator over the Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escalator_over_the_Hill "Escalator over the Hill")_ and as a sideman on recordings by [Lou Reed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou_Reed "Lou Reed"), [Ian Dury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Dury "Ian Dury"), [Rip Rig + Panic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rip_Rig_+_Panic "Rip Rig + Panic"), and [Sun Ra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Ra "Sun Ra"). Cherry played with Ian Dury and the Blockheads on their 1980 tour, including the final gig on Christmas Eve, which was broadcast live by the BBC, from the [Dominion Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominion_Theatre "Dominion Theatre") in London, on _[The Old Grey Whistle Test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Old_Grey_Whistle_Test "The Old Grey Whistle Test")_. He also toured UK and Europe with the band in 1981.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-16) In 1992, Don Cherry was invited by renowned Indian violinist [L. Shankar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L._Shankar "L. Shankar") to perform in Mumbai, India. This interaction was captured in a documentary film titled "Rhythms of the World: Bombay and all the Jazz". In 1994, Cherry appeared on the [Red Hot Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Hot_Organization "Red Hot Organization")'s compilation _[Stolen Moments: Red Hot + Cool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stolen_Moments:_Red_Hot_+_Cool "Stolen Moments: Red Hot + Cool")_, on a track titled "Apprehension", alongside [the Watts Prophets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Watts_Prophets "The Watts Prophets").[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-17) This album, meant to raise awareness of the [HIV/AIDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV/AIDS "HIV/AIDS") epidemic among African-Americans, was named "Album of the Year" by _[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")_. ## Death and legacy \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Death and legacy")\] Cherry died of liver cancer in [Málaga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%A1laga "Málaga"), Spain, on October 19, 1995, at the age of 58.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-atc1995-5) Cherry was inducted into the [Oklahoma Jazz Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma_Jazz_Hall_of_Fame "Oklahoma Jazz Hall of Fame") in 2011.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-18) ## Family and personal life \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: Family and personal life")\] Cherry was married to Monika Karlsson ( [Moki Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moki_Cherry "Moki Cherry")), a Swedish painter and textile artist, who also occasionally played [tanpura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanpura "Tanpura") with him.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-johnson-19) His stepdaughter [Neneh Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neneh_Cherry "Neneh Cherry"),[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-johnson-19) his step-granddaughters [Mabel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mabel_(singer) "Mabel (singer)") and Tyson, and his sons David Ornette Cherry, Christian Cherry, and [Eagle-Eye Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eagle-Eye_Cherry "Eagle-Eye Cherry"), are also musicians. David Ornette Cherry died from an asthma attack at the age of 64 on November 20, 2022.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-20) Don Cherry practiced [Vajrayana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vajrayana "Vajrayana") Buddhism.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-21)[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-22) ## Instruments \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: Instruments")\] Cherry learned to play various brass instruments in high school.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-jost-11):134 Throughout his career, he played an F. [Besson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Besson_(music_company) "Besson (music company)") (Paris) MEHA pocket cornet[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-23) (though he identified this as a [pocket trumpet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pocket_trumpet "Pocket trumpet")), trumpet, [cornet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornet "Cornet"), [flugelhorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flugelhorn "Flugelhorn"), and [bugle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bugle "Bugle").[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-wynn-24)[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-pocketcornets-25) Cherry began his career as a pianist, and continued playing piano and organ as secondary instruments throughout his career.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-wynn-24) After returning from a musical and cultural journey through Africa, he often played the _donso ngoni_, a harp-lute with a gourd body originating from West Africa (see _[ngoni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ngoni_(instrument) "Ngoni (instrument)")_). During his international journeys, Cherry also collected a variety of non-Western instruments, which he mastered and often played in performances and on recordings. Among these instruments were [berimbau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berimbau "Berimbau"), [bamboo flutes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bamboo_flute "Bamboo flute") and assorted percussion instruments.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-wynn-24) ## Technique and style \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)&action=edit§ion=6 "Edit section: Technique and style")\] Cherry's trumpet influences included [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis"), [Fats Navarro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fats_Navarro "Fats Navarro"), [Clifford Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_Brown "Clifford Brown"), and [Harry Edison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweets_Edison "Sweets Edison").[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-wynn-24) Journalist Howard Mandel suggests [Henry "Red" Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Allen "Red Allen") as a precedent (given Allen's "blustery rather than Armstrong-brazen brass sound, jauntily unpredictable melodic streams, squeezed-off and/or half-valve effects and repertoire including novelty vocals")[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-mandel1995-26) while Ekkehard Jost cites [Wild Bill Davison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Davison "Bill Davison").[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-jost-11):138 Some critics have noted shortcomings in Cherry's technique.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-voce1995-9)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-jost-11):137[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-wynn-24) [Ron Wynn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Wynn "Ron Wynn") writes that "\[Cherry's\] technique isn't always the most efficient; frequently, his rapid-fired solos contain numerous missed or muffed notes. But he's a master at exploring the trumpet and cornet's expressive, voice-like properties; he bends notes and adds slurs and smears, and his twisting solos are tightly constructed and executed regardless of their flaws."[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-wynn-24) Jost notes the tendency for writers to focus on Cherry's "technical insecurity", but asserts that "the problem lies elsewhere. Perfect technical control in extremely fast tempos was more or less risk-free as long as the improviser had to deal with standard changes that were familiar to him from years of working with them.... In the music of the Ornette Coleman Quartet—a 'new-found-land' where the laws and habits of functional harmony do not apply—there is no use for patterns that had been worked out on that basis."[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-jost-11):137 Miles Davis was initially dismissive of Cherry's playing, claiming that "anyone can tell that guy's not a trumpet player—it's just notes that come out, and every note he plays he looks serious about, and people will go for that, especially white people."[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-mandel1995-26) According to Cherry, however, when Davis attended an Ornette Coleman performance at the [Five Spot Café](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Spot_Caf%C3%A9 "Five Spot Café") in [Greenwich Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenwich_Village "Greenwich Village"), he was impressed with Cherry's playing and sat in with the group using Cherry's pocket trumpet.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-mandel1995-26) Later, in a 1964 _[DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat")_ blindfold test, Davis indicated that he liked Cherry's playing.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-blindfold-27) ## Discography \[
