[Frank Sinatra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Sinatra "Frank Sinatra") has been referred to as a vocalist whose style blended jazz influences with [traditional pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditional_pop "Traditional pop") and [crooning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crooner "Crooner").[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-39) A more recent example of a vocalist described as jazz-pop is [Laufey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laufey_(singer) "Laufey (singer)").[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-nprtradpop-40)[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-nytpop-41) ## Smooth jazz \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jazz_fusion&action=edit§ion=8 "Edit section: Smooth jazz")\] Main article: [Smooth jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_jazz "Smooth jazz") [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/62/Spyro_Gyra_-_jazz_band.JPG/250px-Spyro_Gyra_-_jazz_band.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Spyro_Gyra_-_jazz_band.JPG) [Spyro Gyra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spyro_Gyra "Spyro Gyra") combines jazz with R&B, funk and pop. By the early 1980s, much of the original fusion genre was subsumed into other branches of jazz and rock, especially [smooth jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_jazz "Smooth jazz"), a radio-friendly subgenre of fusion which is influenced by R&B, funk, and pop music.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-WhatIsSmoothJazz-42) Smooth jazz can be traced to at least the late 1960s, when producer [Creed Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creed_Taylor "Creed Taylor") worked with guitarist [Wes Montgomery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wes_Montgomery "Wes Montgomery") on three popular music-oriented albums. Taylor founded [CTI Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CTI_Records "CTI Records") and many established jazz performers recorded for CTI, including [Freddie Hubbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Hubbard "Freddie Hubbard"), [Chet Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chet_Baker "Chet Baker"), George Benson, and [Stanley Turrentine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Turrentine "Stanley Turrentine"). Albums under Taylor's guidance were aimed at both pop and jazz fans.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] The merging of jazz and pop/rock music took a more commercial direction in the late 1970s and early 1980s, in the form of compositions with a softer sound palette that could fit comfortably in a [soft rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_rock "Soft rock") radio playlist. The AllMusic guide's article on fusion states that "unfortunately, as it became a money-maker and as rock declined artistically from the mid-'70s on, much of what was labeled fusion was actually a combination of jazz with easy-listening pop music and lightweight R&B."[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-Fusion_overview-5) [Michael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Brecker "Michael Brecker") and [Randy Brecker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Brecker "Randy Brecker") produced funk-influenced jazz with soloists.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-Lawn-43) David Sanborn was considered a "soulful" and "influential" voice.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-Lawn-43) However, Kenny G was criticized by both fusion and jazz fans, and some musicians, while having become a huge commercial success. Music reviewer George Graham argues that the "so-called 'smooth jazz' sound of people like Kenny G has none of the fire and creativity that marked the best of the fusion scene during its heyday in the 1970s."[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-44) ## Other styles \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jazz_fusion&action=edit§ion=9 "Edit section: Other styles")\] ### Punk jazz \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jazz_fusion&action=edit§ion=10 "Edit section: Punk jazz")\] Main article: [Punk jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punk_jazz "Punk jazz") In the 1990s, another kind of fusion took a more hardcore approach. [Bill Laswell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Laswell "Bill Laswell") produced many albums in this movement, such as _Ask the Ages_ by avant-garde guitarist Sonny Sharrock and _[Arc of the Testimony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arc_of_the_Testimony "Arc of the Testimony")_ with Laswell's band [Arcana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arcana_(American_band) "Arcana (American band)"). [Niacin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niacin_(band) "Niacin (band)") was formed by rock bassist Billy Sheehan, drummer Dennis Chambers, and organist John Novello.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-OxMilkowski-7) In London, [The Pop Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pop_Group "The Pop Group") began to mix free jazz and reggae into their form of punk rock.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-Lang-45) In New York City, [no wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_wave "No wave") was inspired by free jazz and punk. Examples of this style include [Lydia Lunch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydia_Lunch "Lydia Lunch")'s _Queen of Siam_,[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-Bangs-46) [James Chance and the Contortions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Chance_and_the_Contortions "James Chance and the Contortions"), who mixed soul music with free jazz and punk rock, and the [Lounge Lizards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lounge_Lizards "Lounge Lizards"),[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-Bangs-46) the first group to call themselves [punk jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punk_jazz "Punk jazz").[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-Bangs-46) [John Zorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Zorn "John Zorn") took note of the emphasis on speed and dissonance that was becoming prevalent in punk rock and incorporated them into free jazz with the release of the _[Spy vs Spy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spy_vs_Spy_(album) "Spy vs Spy (album)")_ album in 1986. The album was a collection of [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman") tunes played in the [thrashcore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrashcore "Thrashcore") style.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-47) In the same year, [Sonny Sharrock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Sharrock "Sonny Sharrock"), [Peter Brötzmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Br%C3%B6tzmann "Peter Brötzmann"), Bill Laswell, and [Ronald Shannon Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Shannon_Jackson "Ronald Shannon Jackson") recorded the first album under the name [Last Exit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Exit_(free_jazz_band) "Last Exit (free jazz band)"), a blend of thrash and free jazz.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-48) ### Jazz-funk \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jazz_fusion&action=edit§ion=11 "Edit section: Jazz-funk")\] Main article: [Jazz-funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk "Jazz-funk") Jazz-funk is characterized by a strong [back beat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music) "Beat (music)") ( [groove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groove_(music) "Groove (music)")), electrified sounds,[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-49) and an early prevalence of [analog synthesizers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analog_synthesizers "Analog synthesizers"). The integration of [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk"), [soul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_music "Soul music"), and [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues") music and styles into jazz resulted in the creation of a genre whose spectrum is quite wide and ranges from strong [jazz improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_improvisation#Jazz_improvisation "Musical improvisation") to soul, funk or [disco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disco "Disco") with jazz arrangements, jazz [riffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riff "Riff"), jazz solos, and sometimes soul vocals.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-allmusic-50) Jazz-funk is primarily an American genre, where it was popular throughout the 1970s and the early 1980s, but it also achieved noted appeal on the club-circuit in England during the mid-1970s. Jazz-funk retains a stronger feel of groove and R&B versus some of the jazz fusion production, and is more arranged and features more improvisation than [soul jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz "Soul jazz"). ### M-Base \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jazz_fusion&action=edit§ion=12 "Edit section: M-Base")\] Main article: [M-Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base "M-Base") [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/60/Steve_Coleman_1611.JPG/250px-Steve_Coleman_1611.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Steve_Coleman_1611.JPG) Steve Coleman in Paris, July 2004 M-Base ("macro-basic array of structured extemporization") centers on a movement started in the 1980s. It started as a group of young African-American musicians in New York which included [Steve Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Coleman "Steve Coleman"), [Greg Osby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greg_Osby "Greg Osby"), and [Gary Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Thomas_(musician) "Gary Thomas (musician)") developing a complex but grooving sound.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-Jost-51) In the 1990s most M-Base participants turned to more conventional music, but Coleman, the most active participant, continued developing his music in accordance with the M-Base concept.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-Blumenfeld-52)[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-Undead-53) M-Base changed from a loose collective to an informal "school".[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-54) ### Afro-Cuban jazz \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jazz_fusion&action=edit§ion=13 "Edit section: Afro-Cuban jazz")\] Main article: [Afro-Cuban jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afro-Cuban_jazz "Afro-Cuban jazz") Afro-Cuban jazz, one of the earliest forms of [Latin jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz "Latin jazz"), is a fusion of Afro-Cuban clave-based rhythms with jazz harmonies and techniques of improvisation. Afro-Cuban jazz emerged in the early 1940s with the Cuban musicians [Mario Bauza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Bauza "Mario Bauza") and [Frank Grillo "Machito"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machito "Machito") in the band Machito and his Afro-Cubans in New York City. In 1947 the collaborations of bebop innovator Dizzy Gillespie with Cuban percussionist [Chano Pozo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chano_Pozo "Chano Pozo") brought Afro-Cuban rhythms and instruments, most notably the congas and the bongos, into the East Coast jazz scene. Early combinations of jazz with Cuban music, such as Gillespie's and Pozo's "Manteca" and Charlie Parker's and Machito's "Mangó Mangüé", were commonly referred to as "Cubop", short for Cuban bebop.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-Fernandez2006-55) During its first decades, the Afro-Cuban jazz movement was stronger in the United States than in Cuba.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-Acosta-56) ## Influence on rock music \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jazz_fusion&action=edit§ion=14 "Edit section: Influence on rock music")\] See also: [Progressive rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock "Progressive rock"), [art rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_rock "Art rock"), and [progressive metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_metal "Progressive metal") According to bassist [Randy Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Jackson "Randy Jackson"), jazz fusion is a difficult genre to play. "\[I\] picked jazz fusion because I was trying to become the ultimate technical musician—able to play anything. Jazz fusion to me is the hardest music to play. You have to be so proficient on your instrument. Playing five tempos at the same time, for instance. I wanted to try the toughest music because I knew if I could do that, I could do anything."[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-JacksonBaker2004-57) [Progressive rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock "Progressive rock"), with its affinity for long solos, diverse influences, non-standard time signatures, and complex music had very similar musical values as jazz fusion. Some prominent examples of progressive rock mixed with elements of fusion is the music of [Gong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gong_(band) "Gong (band)"), [King Crimson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Crimson "King Crimson"), [Ozric Tentacles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozric_Tentacles "Ozric Tentacles"), and [Emerson, Lake & Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerson,_Lake_&_Palmer "Emerson, Lake & Palmer"). Jazz rock fusion's technically challenging guitar solos, bass solos, and odd-metered, syncopated drumming started to be incorporated in the technically focused [progressive metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_metal "Progressive metal") genre by the late 1980s. [Watchtower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watchtower_(band) "Watchtower (band)")'s 1989 album _[Control and Resistance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Control_and_Resistance "Control and Resistance")_ is one of the earliest progressive/ [thrash metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrash_metal "Thrash metal") albums to experiment with a jazz fusion-influenced sound.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-58) The [death metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_metal "Death metal") band [Atheist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atheist_(band) "Atheist (band)") produced albums _[Unquestionable Presence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unquestionable_Presence "Unquestionable Presence")_ in 1991 and _[Elements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elements_(Atheist_album) "Elements (Atheist album)")_ in 1993 containing heavily syncopated drumming, changing time signatures, instrumental parts, acoustic interludes, and Latin rhythms. [Meshuggah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meshuggah "Meshuggah") first attracted international attention with the 1995 release _[Destroy Erase Improve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Destroy_Erase_Improve "Destroy Erase Improve")_ for its fusion of fast-tempo death metal, thrash metal, and progressive metal with jazz fusion elements. [Cynic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cynic_(band) "Cynic (band)") recorded a complex, unorthodox form of jazz fusion influenced experimental death metal with their 1993 album _[Focus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Focus_(Cynic_album) "Focus (Cynic album)")_. In 1997, Guitar Institute of Technology guitarist [Jennifer Batten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jennifer_Batten "Jennifer Batten") under the name of [Jennifer Batten's Tribal Rage: Momentum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jennifer_Batten's_Tribal_Rage:_Momentum "Jennifer Batten's Tribal Rage: Momentum") released _Momentum_—an instrumental hybrid of rock, fusion, and exotic sounds. [Mudvayne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mudvayne "Mudvayne") is heavily influenced by jazz, especially in bassist [Ryan Martinie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryan_Martinie "Ryan Martinie")'s playing.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-Ratliff-59)[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-Rvr-60) [Puya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puya_(band) "Puya (band)") frequently incorporates influences from American and [Latin jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz "Latin jazz") music.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-Mateus-61) Another, more cerebral, all-instrumental progressive jazz fusion-metal band [Planet X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planet_X_(band) "Planet X (band)") released _[Universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universe_(Planet_X_album) "Universe (Planet X album)")_ in 2000 with [Tony MacAlpine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_MacAlpine "Tony MacAlpine"), [Derek Sherinian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Sherinian "Derek Sherinian") (ex- [Dream Theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dream_Theater "Dream Theater")), and [Virgil Donati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgil_Donati "Virgil Donati") (who has played with [Scott Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Henderson "Scott Henderson") from [Tribal Tech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tribal_Tech "Tribal Tech")). The band blends fusion-style guitar solos and syncopated odd-metered drumming with the heaviness of metal. Tech-prog-fusion metal band [Aghora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aghora_(band) "Aghora (band)") formed in 1995 and released their first album, self-titled _[Aghora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aghora_(album) "Aghora (album)")_, recorded in 1999 with [Sean Malone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Malone "Sean Malone") and [Sean Reinert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Reinert "Sean Reinert"), both former members of Cynic. [Gordian Knot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gordian_Knot_(band) "Gordian Knot (band)"), another Cynic-linked experimental progressive metal band, released its debut album in 1999 which explored a range of styles from jazz fusion to metal. [The Mars Volta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mars_Volta "The Mars Volta") is extremely influenced by jazz fusion, using progressive, unexpected turns in the drum patterns and instrumental lines. ## See also \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jazz_fusion&action=edit§ion=15 "Edit section: See also")\] - [![icon](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/Saxo_Boca1.JPG/40px-Saxo_Boca1.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Saxo_Boca1.JPG)[Jazz portal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portal:Jazz "Portal:Jazz") - [List of jazz fusion musicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_jazz_fusion_musicians "List of jazz fusion musicians") - [Jazz fusion ensembles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Jazz_fusion_ensembles "Category:Jazz fusion ensembles") - [Progressive soul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_soul "Progressive soul") ## References \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jazz_fusion&action=edit§ion=16 "Edit section: References")\] 01. - [saxophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxophone "Saxophone")
- [trumpet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trumpet "Trumpet")
- [trombone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trombone "Trombone")
- [piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano "Piano")
- [double bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_bass "Double bass")

- [acoustic guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acoustic_guitar "Acoustic guitar") | **Modal jazz** is [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") that makes use of [musical modes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mode_(music) "Mode (music)"), often [modulating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulation_(music) "Modulation (music)") among them to accompany the [chords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chord_(music) "Chord (music)") instead of relying on one [tonal center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonic_(music) "Tonic (music)") used across the piece. Though exerting influence to the present, modal jazz was most popular in the 1950s and 1960s, as evidenced by the success of [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")'s 1958 composition " [Milestones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milestones_(composition) "Milestones (composition)")" and 1959 album _[Kind of Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue "Kind of Blue")_, and [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane")'s quartet from 1960 to 1965. Other performers of modal jazz include [Chick Corea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chick_Corea "Chick Corea"), [Bill Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans "Bill Evans"), [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"), [Joe Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Henderson "Joe Henderson"), [Bobby Hutcherson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Hutcherson "Bobby Hutcherson"), [Pharoah Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharoah_Sanders "Pharoah Sanders"), [Woody Shaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woody_Shaw "Woody Shaw"), [Wayne Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter "Wayne Shorter"), [McCoy Tyner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner "McCoy Tyner"), and [Larry Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Young_(musician) "Larry Young (musician)").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-Essential-1) ## History In [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop") as well as in [hard bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop "Hard bop"), musicians use chords to provide the background for solos. A piece starts out with a theme that introduces a series of chords for the solos. These chords repeat throughout the whole piece, while the soloists play new, improvised themes over the repeated [chord progression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chord_progression "Chord progression"). By the 1950s, improvising over chords had become such a dominant part of jazz that sidemen at recording dates were sometimes given nothing more than a list of chords to play from.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-2) [Mercer Ellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercer_Ellington "Mercer Ellington") has stated that [Juan Tizol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Tizol "Juan Tizol") conceived the melody to " [Caravan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caravan_(1937_song) "Caravan (1937 song)")" in 1936 as a result of his days studying music in Puerto Rico, where they could not afford much sheet music so the teacher would turn the music upside down after they had learned to play it right-side up.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-mercer1994-3) This "inversion" technique led to a modal sound throughout Tizol's work.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-mercer1994-3) [Sun Ra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Ra "Sun Ra") reportedly rehearsed a small group consisting of [Harold Ousley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Ousley "Harold Ousley"), [Vernel Fournier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernel_Fournier "Vernel Fournier"), and [Wilbur Ware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilbur_Ware "Wilbur Ware") in 1950 that played original songs that were modal in which the melody was based on a single chord or [vamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostinato#Vamp "Ostinato") – ten years before this approach became popular in jazz.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-4) Saxophonist [Wayne Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter "Wayne Shorter") has noted that the 1953 composition " [Glass Enclosure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass_Enclosure "Glass Enclosure")" by pianist Bud Powell was one of the earliest jazz compositions to make use of [Lydian chords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_chord "Lydian chord"), based on the [Lydian mode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_mode "Lydian mode") that was not widely used in jazz until about a decade later.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-5) Powell's 1951 [Un Poco Loco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Un_Poco_Loco "Un Poco Loco") uses the Lydian chords and even uses Lydian chords stacked on top of each implying a [polytonality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polytonality "Polytonality") (D [major 7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_seventh_chord "Major seventh chord") over C major 7: CEGBDF#AC#) with the improvisation based on alternating Lydian-ish polytonality and an [altered dominant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altered_dominant "Altered dominant") chord.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-6) Towards the end of the 1950s, spurred by the experiments of composer and bandleader George Russell, musicians began using a modal approach. They chose not to write their pieces using conventional chord changes, but instead using modes. Musicians employing this technique include Miles Davis, [Freddie Hubbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Hubbard "Freddie Hubbard"), Bill Evans, [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"), and Wayne Shorter. [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/Minor_eleventh_chord_Herbie_Hancock_Maiden_Voyage.png/500px-Minor_eleventh_chord_Herbie_Hancock_Maiden_Voyage.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Minor_eleventh_chord_Herbie_Hancock_Maiden_Voyage.png) Opening chord to " [Maiden Voyage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maiden_Voyage_(composition) "Maiden Voyage (composition)")": minor [eleventh chord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eleventh_chord "Eleventh chord") (Am9/D).[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-What-7)[Play](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/9/9e/Minor_eleventh_chord_Herbie_Hancock_Maiden_Voyage.mid/Minor_eleventh_chord_Herbie_Hancock_Maiden_Voyage.mid.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Minor_eleventh_chord_Herbie_Hancock_Maiden_Voyage.mid "File:Minor eleventh chord Herbie Hancock Maiden Voyage.mid") Using D [Dorian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorian_mode#Modern_Dorian_mode "Dorian mode").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-8) Among the significant compositions of modal jazz were " [So What](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/So_What_(composition) "So What (composition)")" by Miles Davis and " [Impressions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impressions_(composition) "Impressions (composition)")" by John Coltrane.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-Dummies-9) "So What" and "Impressions" follow the same AABA structure and were in D Dorian for the A sections and modulated a half step up to E-flat Dorian for the B section. The [Dorian mode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorian_mode "Dorian mode") is the [natural minor scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minor_scale#Natural_minor "Minor scale") with a raised sixth. Other compositions include Davis's " [Flamenco Sketches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flamenco_Sketches "Flamenco Sketches")", Bill Evans's " [Peace Piece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_Piece "Peace Piece")", and Shorter's " [Footprints](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footprints_(composition) "Footprints (composition)")".[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-Dummies-9) Davis recorded one of the best-selling jazz albums of all time in this modal framework. _Kind of Blue_ is an exploration of the possibilities of modal jazz.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-Complete-10)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-Dummies-9) Although his explorations of modal jazz were sporadic throughout the 1960s, he included several of the tunes from _Kind of Blue_ in the repertoire of his second quintet. Coltrane took the lead in extensively exploring the limits of modal improvisation and composition with his quartet, featuring [Elvin Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elvin_Jones "Elvin Jones") (drums), [McCoy Tyner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner "McCoy Tyner") (piano), and [Reggie Workman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggie_Workman "Reggie Workman") and [Jimmy Garrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Garrison "Jimmy Garrison") (bass). Several of Coltrane's albums from the period are recognized as examples of modal jazz: _[Africa/Brass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa/Brass "Africa/Brass")_ (1961),[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-Dummies-9) _[Live! at the Village Vanguard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live!_at_the_Village_Vanguard "Live! at the Village Vanguard")_ (1962), _[Crescent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crescent_(John_Coltrane) "Crescent (John Coltrane)")_ (1964), _[A Love Supreme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme "A Love Supreme")_ (1964),[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-Dummies-9) and _[Meditations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meditations_(John_Coltrane_album) "Meditations (John Coltrane album)")_ (1965). Coltrane's compositions from this period such as "India", "Chasin' the Trane", "Crescent", and "Impressions" have entered the jazz repertoire, along with his interpretations of standards like Richard Rodgers's " [My Favorite Things](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_Favorite_Things_(song) "My Favorite Things (song)")", and the traditional " [Greensleeves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greensleeves "Greensleeves")". ## References 01. - [psychedelia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelic_music "Psychedelic music") | **Free improvisation** (also known as **free-form music**) is a form of [improvised music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_improvisation "Musical improvisation") centered on a commitment to non- [idiomatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idiomatic_(music) "Idiomatic (music)") musical expression.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation#cite_note-1) It developed through [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz"), [serialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serialism "Serialism") and [indeterminacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indeterminacy_(music) "Indeterminacy (music)"), and is characterized by a general rejection of formal [music theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_theory "Music theory") and [tonality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonality "Tonality"), instead following the intuition of its performers and the exploration of dynamic, timbre and texture. The term can refer to both a technique—employed by any musician in any genre—and as a recognizable genre of [experimental music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experimental_music "Experimental music") in its own right. Free improvisation, as a genre of music, developed primarily in the U.K. as well as the U.S. and Europe in the mid to late 1960s, largely as an outgrowth of [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") and [contemporary classical music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_classical_music "Contemporary classical music"). Exponents of free improvised music include the improvising groups [AMM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AMM_(group) "AMM (group)") and [Spontaneous Music Ensemble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spontaneous_Music_Ensemble "Spontaneous Music Ensemble"), as well as solo instrumentalists such as saxophonists [Evan Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evan_Parker "Evan Parker"), [Anthony Braxton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Braxton "Anthony Braxton"), [Peter Brötzmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Br%C3%B6tzmann "Peter Brötzmann") and [John Zorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Zorn "John Zorn"), trombonist [George E. Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_E._Lewis "George E. Lewis"), guitarists [Derek Bailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Bailey_(guitarist) "Derek Bailey (guitarist)"), [Henry Kaiser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Kaiser_(musician) "Henry Kaiser (musician)"), [Fred Frith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Frith "Fred Frith"), [Taku Sugimoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taku_Sugimoto "Taku Sugimoto") and [Toshimaru Nakamura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toshimaru_Nakamura "Toshimaru Nakamura"), bassists [Damon Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damon_Smith "Damon Smith") and [Jair-Rohm Parker Wells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jair-Rohm_Parker_Wells "Jair-Rohm Parker Wells"), and composer [Pauline Oliveros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pauline_Oliveros "Pauline Oliveros"). ## Characteristics \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Free_improvisation&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Characteristics")\] In the context of [music theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_theory "Music theory"), free improvisation denotes the shift from a focus on [harmony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmony "Harmony") and structure to other dimensions of music, such as [timbre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbre "Timbre"), [texture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texture_(music) "Texture (music)"), melodic intervals, [rhythm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm "Rhythm") and spontaneous musical interactions between performers. This can give free improvised music abstract and nondescript qualities.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation#cite_note-2) Although individual performers may choose to play in a certain style or [key](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Key_signature "Key signature"), or at certain [tempos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tempo "Tempo"), conventions such as song structures are highly uncommon; more emphasis is generally placed on the [mood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mood_(psychology) "Mood (psychology)") of the music, or on performative gestures, than on preset forms of [melody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melody "Melody"), harmony or [rhythm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm "Rhythm"). These elements are improvised at will as the music progresses, and performers will often intuitively react to each other based on the elements of their performance. English guitarist [Derek Bailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Bailey_(guitarist) "Derek Bailey (guitarist)") described free improvisation as "playing without memory".[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation#cite_note-3) In his book _Improvisation_, Bailey wrote that free improvisation "has no stylistic or idiomatic commitment. It has no prescribed idiomatic sound. The characteristics of freely improvised music are established only by the sonic musical identity of the person or persons playing it."[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation#cite_note-4) Free music performers from disparate backgrounds often engage musically with other [genres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_genres_of_music "List of genres of music"). For example, Italian composer [Ennio Morricone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ennio_Morricone "Ennio Morricone") was a member of the free improvisation group Nuova Consonanza. [Anthony Braxton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Braxton "Anthony Braxton") has written [opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opera "Opera"), and [John Zorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Zorn "John Zorn") has written acclaimed orchestral pieces. ## History \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Free_improvisation&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: History")\] Though there are many important precedents and developments, free improvisation developed gradually, making it difficult to pinpoint a single moment when the style was born. Free improvisation primarily descends from the [Indeterminacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indeterminacy_(music) "Indeterminacy (music)") movement and [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz"). Guitarist [Derek Bailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Bailey_(guitarist) "Derek Bailey (guitarist)") contends that free improvisation must have been the earliest musical style, because "mankind's first musical performance couldn't have been anything other than a free improvisation." Similarly, [Keith Rowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Rowe "Keith Rowe") stated, "Other players got into playing freely, way before [AMM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AMM_(group) "AMM (group)"), way before Derek \[Bailey\]! Who knows when free playing started? You can imagine [lute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lute "Lute") players in the 1500s getting drunk and doing improvisations for people in front of a log fire.. the noise, the clatter must have been enormous. You read absolutely incredible descriptions of that. I cannot believe that musicians back then didn't float off into free playing. The [melisma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melisma "Melisma") in [Monteverdi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claudio_Monteverdi "Claudio Monteverdi")\[ _[sic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sic "Sic")_\] must derive from that. But it was all in the context of a repertoire."[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation#cite_note-5) The London-based independent radio station [Resonance 104.4FM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resonance_FM "Resonance FM"), founded by the [London Musicians Collective](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Musicians_Collective "London Musicians Collective"), frequently broadcasts experimental and free improvised performance works. [WNUR 89.3 FM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WNUR_89.3_FM "WNUR 89.3 FM") ("Chicago's Sound Experiment") is another source for free improvised music on the radio. Taran's Free Jazz Hour broadcast on Radio-G 101.5 FM, Angers and [Euradio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euradio?action=edit&redlink=1 "Euradio (page does not exist)")\[ [fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euradio "fr:Euradio")\] 101.3 FM, [Nantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nantes "Nantes") is entirely dedicated to free jazz and other freely improvised music. A l'improviste.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation#cite_note-6)\[ _[incomprehensible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Cleanup "Wikipedia:Cleanup")_\] ### Classical precedents \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Free_improvisation&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Classical precedents")\] By the middle decades of the 20th century, composers such as [Henry Cowell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Cowell "Henry Cowell"), [Earle Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earle_Brown "Earle Brown"), [David Tudor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Tudor "David Tudor"), [La Monte Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Monte_Young "La Monte Young"), [Jackson Mac Low](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_Mac_Low "Jackson Mac Low"), [Morton Feldman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morton_Feldman "Morton Feldman"), [Sylvano Bussotti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvano_Bussotti "Sylvano Bussotti"), [Karlheinz Stockhausen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karlheinz_Stockhausen "Karlheinz Stockhausen"), and [George Crumb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Crumb "George Crumb"), re-introduced improvisation to European art music, with compositions that allowed or even required musicians to improvise. One notable example of this is [Cornelius Cardew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_Cardew "Cornelius Cardew")'s _[Treatise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treatise_(music) "Treatise (music)")_: a [graphic score](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphic_notation_(music) "Graphic notation (music)") with no conventional notation whatsoever, which musicians were invited to interpret. Improvisation is still commonly practised by some organists at concerts or church services, and courses in improvisation (including free improvisation) are part of many higher education programmes for church musicians.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation#cite_note-7) ### International free improvisation \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Free_improvisation&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: International free improvisation")\] Since 2002 [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand "New Zealand") collective Vitamin S has hosted weekly improvisations based around randomly drawn trios. Vitamin S takes the form beyond music and includes improvisers from other forms such as dance, theatre and puppetry.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation#cite_note-8) Since 2006, improvisational music in many forms has been supported and promoted by ISIM, the International Society for Improvised Music. ISIM comprises some 300 performing artists and scholars worldwide, including [Pauline Oliveros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pauline_Oliveros "Pauline Oliveros"), [Robert Dick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Dick_(flautist) "Robert Dick (flautist)"), [Jane Ira Bloom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Ira_Bloom "Jane Ira Bloom"), [Roman Stolyar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Stolyar "Roman Stolyar"), [Mark Dresser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Dresser "Mark Dresser"), and many others. Founded in Manchester, England, in 2007, _the Noise Upstairs_ has been an institution dedicated to the practice of improvised music,[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation#cite_note-9) hosting regular concerts and creative workshops where they have promoted international and UK-based artists such as [Ken Vandermark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Vandermark "Ken Vandermark"),[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation#cite_note-10) [Lê Quan Ninh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%AA_Quan_Ninh "Lê Quan Ninh"), [Ingrid Laubrock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingrid_Laubrock "Ingrid Laubrock"), and [Yuri Landman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuri_Landman "Yuri Landman"). On top of these events, the Noise Upstairs runs monthly jam nights.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation#cite_note-11) In Berlin, Germany, from the 1990s onwards, a school of free improvisation emerged known as _echtzeitmusik_ (‘real-time music’ or ‘immediate music’). This has been sustained by supportive venues such as [ausland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ausland_(Berlin) "Ausland (Berlin)"), Anorak Club, Labor Sonor, and others.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation#cite_note-:1-12) ### The downtown scene \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Free_improvisation&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: The downtown scene")\] In late 1970s New York a group of musicians came together who shared an interest in free improvisation as well as rock, jazz, contemporary classical, world music and pop. They performed at lofts, apartments, basements and venues located predominantly in [downtown New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Manhattan "Lower Manhattan") ( [8BC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/8BC "8BC"), [Pyramid Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyramid_Club_(New_York) "Pyramid Club (New York)"), Environ, [Roulette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roulette "Roulette"), [The Knitting Factory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Knitting_Factory "The Knitting Factory") and [Tonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonic_(music_venue) "Tonic (music venue)")) and held regular concerts of free improvisation which featured many of the prominent figures in the scene, including [John Zorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Zorn "John Zorn"), [Bill Laswell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Laswell "Bill Laswell"), [George E. Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_E._Lewis "George E. Lewis"), [Fred Frith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Frith "Fred Frith"), [Tom Cora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cora "Tom Cora"), [Toshinori Kondo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toshinori_Kondo "Toshinori Kondo"), [Wayne Horvitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Horvitz "Wayne Horvitz"), [Eugene Chadbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugene_Chadbourne "Eugene Chadbourne"), [Zeena Parkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeena_Parkins "Zeena Parkins"), [Anthony Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Coleman "Anthony Coleman"), [Polly Bradfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polly_Bradfield "Polly Bradfield"), [Ikue Mori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ikue_Mori "Ikue Mori"), [Robert Dick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Dick_(flautist) "Robert Dick (flautist)"), [Ned Rothenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ned_Rothenberg "Ned Rothenberg"), [Bob Ostertag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Ostertag "Bob Ostertag"), [Christian Marclay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Marclay "Christian Marclay"), [David Moss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Moss_(musician) "David Moss (musician)"), [Kramer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kramer_(musician) "Kramer (musician)") and many others. They worked with each other, independently and with many of the leading European improvisers of the time, including [Derek Bailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Bailey_(guitarist) "Derek Bailey (guitarist)"), [Evan Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evan_Parker "Evan Parker"), [Han Bennink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_Bennink "Han Bennink"), [Misha Mengelberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Misha_Mengelberg "Misha Mengelberg"), [Peter Brötzmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Br%C3%B6tzmann "Peter Brötzmann") and others. Many of these musicians continue to use improvisation in one form or another in their work. ### Electronic free improvisation \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Free_improvisation&action=edit§ion=6 "Edit section: Electronic free improvisation")\] Electronic devices such as oscillators, echoes, filters and alarm clocks were an integral part of free improvisation performances by groups such as [Kluster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kluster "Kluster") at the underground scene at Zodiac Club in [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin") in the late 1960s.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation#cite_note-13) For the 1975 [jazz-rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-rock "Jazz-rock") concert recording _[Agharta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album) "Agharta (album)")_, [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis") and his band employed free improvisation and electronics,[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation#cite_note-14) particularly guitarist [Pete Cosey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Cosey "Pete Cosey") who improvised sounds by running his guitar through a [ring modulator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_modulator "Ring modulator") and an [EMS Synthi A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EMS_Synthi_A "EMS Synthi A").[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation#cite_note-15) But it was only later that traditional instruments were disbanded altogether in favour of pure electronic free improvisation. In 1984, the Swiss improvisation duo [Voice Crack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voice_Crack "Voice Crack") started making use of strictly "cracked everyday electronics".[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation#cite_note-16) ### Electroacoustic improvisation \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Free_improvisation&action=edit§ion=7 "Edit section: Electroacoustic improvisation")\] Main article: [Electroacoustic Improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electroacoustic_Improvisation "Electroacoustic Improvisation") A recent branch of improvised music is characterized by quiet, slow moving, minimalistic textures and often utilizing laptop computers or unorthodox forms of electronics. Developing worldwide in the mid-to-late 1990s, with centers in New York, Tokyo and Austria, this style has been called _[lowercase music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lowercase_music "Lowercase music")_ or EAI ( [electroacoustic improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electroacoustic_improvisation "Electroacoustic improvisation")), and is represented, for instance, by the American record label [Erstwhile Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erstwhile_Records "Erstwhile Records") and the Austrian label [Mego](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mego_Records "Mego Records"). EAI is often radically different even from established free improvisation. Eyles writes, "One of the problems of describing this music is that it requires a new vocabulary and ways of conveying its sound and impact; such vocabulary does not yet exist – how do you describe the subtle differences between different types of [controlled feedback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_feedback "Audio feedback")? I've yet to see anyone do it convincingly – hence the use of words like 'shape' and 'texture'!"[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation#cite_note-17) ## Legacy \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Free_improvisation&action=edit§ion=8 "Edit section: Legacy")\] [Paul McCartney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_McCartney "Paul McCartney") is anecdotally noted as having been an audience member for an AMM performance in 1967, and said that "they went on too long", although he did feel inspired by them.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation#cite_note-18) Additionally, [Syd Barrett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syd_Barrett "Syd Barrett") of [Pink Floyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pink_Floyd "Pink Floyd") also sat in at early AMM performances, with Barrett later drawing influences from Keith Rowe's [prepared guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prepared_guitar "Prepared guitar") technique in his own psychedelic free-form playing on _[The Piper at the Gates of Dawn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Piper_at_the_Gates_of_Dawn "The Piper at the Gates of Dawn")_ through the use of a [zippo lighter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zippo_lighter "Zippo lighter") as a [guitar slide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar_slide "Guitar slide").[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation#cite_note-19) Free improvised music maintained a partial influence on the [first wave of post-rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-rock#1990s:_first_wave "Post-rock") in the 1990s.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation#cite_note-20) ## See also \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Free_improvisation&action=edit§ion=9 "Edit section: See also")\] - - [math rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Math_rock "Math rock") | | Local scenes | | [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") | **Loft jazz** (also known as the **loft scene** or **loft era**) was a cultural music phenomenon that occurred in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") during the mid-1970s. ## Description [Gary Giddins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Giddins "Gary Giddins") described it as follows: "\[A\] new coterie of avant-garde musicians took much of the jazz world by surprise... \[T\]hey interpreted the idea of freedom as the capacity to choose between all the realms of jazz, mixing and matching them not only with each other, but with old and new pop, R&B and rock, classical music and world music... \[S\]eemingly overnight new venues - in many instances, apartments or lofts (hence the phrase 'loft jazz') - opened shop to present their wares."[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loft_jazz#cite_note-1) According to Michael Heller, "lofts were not an organization, nor a movement, nor an ideology, nor a genre, nor a neighborhood, nor a lineage of individuals. They were, instead, a meeting point, a locus for interaction."[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loft_jazz#cite_note-2) Heller stated that "loft practices came to be defined by a number of key characteristics, including (1) low admission charges or suggested donations, (2) casual atmospheres that blurred the distinction between performer and audience, (3) ownership / administration by musicians, and (4) mixed-use spaces that combined both private living areas and public presentation space."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loft_jazz#cite_note-3) Regarding the music played in these venues, Michael J. Agovino wrote: "This was community music. Part of the point was that, free of the strictures of clubs, the music could be anything, go anywhere, go on for as long as it wanted."[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loft_jazz#cite_note-4) David Such stated that "the cutting contests, personality cults, and vices that characterized the jazz scene of the 1940s and 1950s were mostly missing."[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loft_jazz#cite_note-5) The scene was reviewed and documented by Giddins, Peter Occhiogrosso[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loft_jazz#cite_note-6) of the [SoHo Weekly News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SoHo_Weekly_News "SoHo Weekly News"), [Leroi Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amiri_Baraka "Amiri Baraka"),[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loft_jazz#cite_note-7) [Robert Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Palmer_(author/producer) "Robert Palmer (author/producer)"),[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loft_jazz#cite_note-8) and [Stanley Crouch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Crouch "Stanley Crouch").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loft_jazz#cite_note-9) Coinciding with this activity was an influx of musicians from outside New York. Newcomers from Chicago included a group associated with the [AACM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians "Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians"); these included [Muhal Richard Abrams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhal_Richard_Abrams "Muhal Richard Abrams"), [Anthony Braxton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Braxton "Anthony Braxton"), [Kalaparusha Maurice McIntyre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalaparusha_Maurice_McIntyre "Kalaparusha Maurice McIntyre"), [Lester Bowie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lester_Bowie "Lester Bowie"), [Amina Claudine Myers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amina_Claudine_Myers "Amina Claudine Myers"), [Henry Threadgill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Threadgill "Henry Threadgill"), [Steve McCall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_McCall_(drummer) "Steve McCall (drummer)"), [Fred Hopkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Hopkins "Fred Hopkins"), [Chico Freeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chico_Freeman "Chico Freeman"), [Malachi Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malachi_Thompson "Malachi Thompson"), and [George E. Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_E._Lewis "George E. Lewis"). Various members of the [Black Artists Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group "Black Artists Group") came from St. Louis, including [Charles "Bobo" Shaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_%22Bobo%22_Shaw "Charles \"Bobo\" Shaw"), [Baikida Carroll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baikida_Carroll "Baikida Carroll"), [Oliver Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Lake "Oliver Lake"), [Julius Hemphill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Hemphill "Julius Hemphill"), [Hamiet Bluiett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamiet_Bluiett "Hamiet Bluiett"), [J. D. Parran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._D._Parran "J. D. Parran"), and [Joseph Bowie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Bowie "Joseph Bowie"). Members of [Horace Tapscott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott "Horace Tapscott")'s [UGMAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_of_God's_Musicians_and_Artists_Ascension "Union of God's Musicians and Artists Ascension"), such as [Arthur Blythe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Blythe "Arthur Blythe"), [David Murray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Murray_(saxophonist) "David Murray (saxophonist)"), and [Butch Morris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butch_Morris "Butch Morris"), arrived from California. All of these, plus many local musicians, participated in the loft scene to some degree.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loft_jazz#cite_note-10) Immediate predecessors to the loft scene were the establishment in the late 1960s of [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman")'s _Artist House_, where he hosted musicians and dancers, and James DuBoise's _Studio We_.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loft_jazz#cite_note-11) However, the scene did not begin to flourish until 1972, when, in reaction to the relocation of the [Newport Jazz Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport_Jazz_Festival "Newport Jazz Festival") to New York, locally based musicians established a counter-festival called the New York Musicians' Jazz Festival (NYMJF), with music presented in parks, community centers, and lofts.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loft_jazz#cite_note-12) One of the most influential lofts during this time was _Studio Rivbea_, run by [Sam Rivers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Rivers_(jazz_musician) "Sam Rivers (jazz musician)") and his wife Bea.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loft_jazz#cite_note-13) Other lofts included [Rashied Ali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rashied_Ali "Rashied Ali")'s _Studio 77_, which became _Ali's Alley_, _Studio Infinity_, run by [Stanley Crouch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Crouch "Stanley Crouch") and [David Murray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Murray_(saxophonist) "David Murray (saxophonist)"), _[Environ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environ_(Loft) "Environ (Loft)")_, run by [John Fischer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Fischer_(pianist) "John Fischer (pianist)"), the _Ladies' Fort_, _Studio WIS_, _Firehouse Theater_, and _Sunrise Studios_.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loft_jazz#cite_note-14) Musically, loft jazz was in many ways a continuation of the [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") and [avant-garde jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz") traditions inaugurated by [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane"), [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman"), [Albert Ayler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler "Albert Ayler"), [Pharoah Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharoah_Sanders "Pharoah Sanders"), [Archie Shepp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Shepp "Archie Shepp"), and [Sun Ra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Ra "Sun Ra"). However, it didn't follow any one particular style or idiom. According to Scott Deveaux and [Gary Giddins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Giddins "Gary Giddins"), "A critical byword of the Loft Era was 'eclecticism,' used to signal an enlightened approach to all styles of music."[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loft_jazz#cite_note-15) Few loft jazz musicians played continuously atonal or arhythmic music in the style of Coltrane's legendary albums [_Ascension_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album) "Ascension (John Coltrane album)") and [_Om_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album) "Om (John Coltrane album)"). They often combined conventional melodic elements with free jazz; used instruments less familiar to jazz, such as the bass saxophone, oboe and cello; and combined instruments in nontraditional formats, like the [World Saxophone Quartet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Saxophone_Quartet "World Saxophone Quartet"), whose changing members used a variety of saxophones and flutes, usually without any rhythm section.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loft_jazz#cite_note-16)[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loft_jazz#cite_note-17) Not surprisingly, most of the musicians rejected the term "loft jazz" as too confining and not representative of their diversity.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loft_jazz#cite_note-18) The loft scene began to decline in the late 1970s and early 1980s, mainly due to a steady rise in rents.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loft_jazz#cite_note-19) ## Recordings A series of five LPs known as _[Wildflowers: The New York Loft Jazz Sessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wildflowers:_The_New_York_Loft_Jazz_Sessions "Wildflowers: The New York Loft Jazz Sessions")_ was released on [Casablanca Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casablanca_Records "Casablanca Records") in 1976, documenting sessions hosted by [Sam Rivers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Rivers_(jazz_musician) "Sam Rivers (jazz musician)") at Studio Rivbea.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loft_jazz#cite_note-20) The recordings were reissued on CD in 1999.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loft_jazz#cite_note-21) ## References 01. - [Phil Cohran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Cohran "Phil Cohran") | | Type | Non-profit organization | | Location | - Chicago, Illinois | | Region served | U.S. | | Official language | English | | Key people | - [Henry Threadgill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Threadgill "Henry Threadgill")

- [Roscoe Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roscoe_Mitchell "Roscoe Mitchell") | | Affiliations | [Black Artists Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group "Black Artists Group") | | [Endowment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_endowment "Financial endowment") | [MacArthur Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacArthur_Foundation "MacArthur Foundation") | | Website | [aacmchicago.org](http://aacmchicago.org/) | Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians The **Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians** ( **AACM**) is an American [nonprofit organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonprofit_organization "Nonprofit organization"), founded in 1965 in Chicago by pianist [Muhal Richard Abrams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhal_Richard_Abrams "Muhal Richard Abrams"), pianist [Jodie Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jodie_Christian "Jodie Christian"), drummer [Steve McCall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_McCall_(drummer) "Steve McCall (drummer)"), and composer [Phil Cohran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Cohran "Phil Cohran").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians#cite_note-RCJE-1) The AACM is devoted "to nurturing, performing, and recording serious, original music," according to its charter. It supports and encourages [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") performers, composers and educators. Although founded in the jazz tradition, the group's outreach and influence has, according to Larry Blumenfeld, "touched nearly all corners of modern music."[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians#cite_note-2) Per the AACM, it "pays homage to the diverse styles of expression within the body of Black Music in the USA, Africa and throughout the world."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians#cite_note-AACMaboutPage-2022-3) ## Background \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Background")\] By the 1960s, jazz music was losing ground to rock music, and the founders of the AACM felt that a proactive group of musicians would add creativity and outlet for new music.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians#cite_note-Reich-4) The AACM was formed in May 1965 by a group of African-American musicians in Chicago centered on [pianist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pianist "Pianist") [Muhal Richard Abrams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhal_Richard_Abrams "Muhal Richard Abrams"), who had organized the Experimental Band since 1961.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians#cite_note-LarkinGE-5) The musicians were generally steadfast in their commitment to their music, despite a lack of performance venues and sometimes indifferent audiences. From 1969 the AACM organised a music education program for inner-city youths.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians#cite_note-6) In the 1960s and 1970s AACM members were among the most important and innovative in all of jazz, though the AACM's contemporary influence has waned some in recent years. Many AACM members have recorded widely: in the early days on the [Delmark Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delmark_Records "Delmark Records") Avant Garde Jazz series and later on the [Black Saint/Soul Note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Saint/Soul_Note "Black Saint/Soul Note") and [India Navigation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India_Navigation "India Navigation") labels, and to a lesser extent on the [Arista Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arista_Records "Arista Records") and [ECM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_(record_label) "ECM (record label)") labels.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians#cite_note-7) The musical endeavors of members of the AACM often include an adventurous mixing of avant-garde jazz, classical, and world music. The AACM also ran a school, The AACM School of Music, with classes in all areas taught by members of the AACM. The AACM also had a strong relationship with an influential sister organization, the [Black Artists Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group "Black Artists Group") (BAG) of [St. Louis, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis,_Missouri "St. Louis, Missouri").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians#cite_note-LarkinJazz-8) The AACM has received aid from the [MacArthur Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacArthur_Foundation "MacArthur Foundation") and has a strong relationship with [Columbia College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_College_Chicago "Columbia College Chicago"). _A Power Stronger Than Itself: The AACM and American Experimental Music_ by AACM member [George E. Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_E._Lewis "George E. Lewis"), which documents the AACM's history, has been published by the University of Chicago Press (May 2008).[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians#cite_note-nyt_2008-9) In 2015, a 50-year retrospective exhibition of art, music and group-related artifacts, entitled, "Free at First", was held at the [DuSable Museum of African American History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DuSable_Museum_of_African_American_History "DuSable Museum of African American History").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians#cite_note-Reich-4) ## Music \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Music")\] The AACM has been on the forefront of the [avant-garde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde "Avant-garde") since its inception in 1965. [Anthony Braxton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Braxton "Anthony Braxton"), [Henry Threadgill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Threadgill "Henry Threadgill"), and the [Art Ensemble of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Ensemble_of_Chicago "Art Ensemble of Chicago") pushed the boundaries of jazz and challenged the avant-garde classical movement led by [John Cage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cage "John Cage"). Concerts were heavily improvised, and many AACM members created scores that blended music, geometry, painting, and ciphers to be interpreted by the performers live. The AACM was part of an artistic movement on the South Side of Chicago that included AFRICobra (African Commune of Bad Relevant Artists) and other collectives.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians#cite_note-10) In the third decade of the 21st century, AACM members continue to produce vibrant avant-garde jazz and jazz-influenced music in Chicago and elsewhere.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] ## Members \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Members")\] (some deceased; largely complete through at least early 2026) [\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians#cite_note-AACM-TShirt-2025-11)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians#cite_note-12) - [Muhal Richard Abrams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhal_Richard_Abrams "Muhal Richard Abrams")[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians#cite_note-LarkinGE-5) - [Peggy Abrams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peggy_Abrams?action=edit&redlink=1 "Peggy Abrams (page does not exist)") - [Soji Adebayo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soji_Adebayo?action=edit&redlink=1 "Soji Adebayo (page does not exist)") - [Willel Afi-Fi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willel_Afi-Fi?action=edit&redlink=1 "Willel Afi-Fi (page does not exist)") - [Ajaramu Joseph Shelton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajaramu_Joseph_Shelton?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ajaramu Joseph Shelton (page does not exist)") - [Dee Alexander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dee_Alexander "Dee Alexander") - [Martin Alexander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Alexander?action=edit&redlink=1 "Martin Alexander (page does not exist)") - [Leon Q. - What is jazz-rock music?







Jazz-rock is a popular music style blending modern jazz improvisation with rock music's bass lines, drumming, and instrumentation. It emphasizes electronic instruments and dance rhythms.



Since the 1920s, fusions of jazz and popular music existed, contrasting jazz's qualities with popular music. In the 1960s, jazz tunes started incorporating rock rhythms. By 1969, artists like Miles Davis, Tony Williams, and John McLaughlin created distinctive fusion music contrasting jazz and rock elements.



In the early 1970s, bands such as Mahavishnu Orchestra, Headhunters, and Weather Report further explored this style. This music gained a large audience and was known as crossover, appealing to both jazz and popular music fans.

- When did jazz-rock become popular?







Jazz-rock, a fusion of modern jazz improvisation with rock music elements, gained popularity by the early 1970s. This musical form incorporates the bass lines, drumming styles, and instrumentation of rock, with a strong emphasis on electronic instruments and dance rhythms.



Figures like Miles Davis, along with associates such as John McLaughlin, Wayne Shorter, and Herbie Hancock, pioneered this distinctive fusion. Davis's 1969 album, _In a Silent Way_, is often regarded as the seminal album of the jazz fusion movement, and his subsequent work, _Bitches Brew_, further embraced rock elements, influencing groups like Weather Report and Chick Corea’s Return to Forever.



Although some critics dismissed Davis's post- _Bitches Brew_ music, his efforts helped maintain jazz's popularity with mainstream audiences. The style became known as crossover because sales of the music crossed over from the jazz market to the popular music market.

- How has jazz-rock influenced other types of music?







Jazz-rock, a fusion of modern jazz improvisation with rock music's bass lines, drumming, and electronic instruments, has significantly impacted other musical genres.



Funk, with its aggressive urban dance music driven by syncopated rhythms, owes its development to jazz improvisation and was further explored by jazz artists like [Miles Davis](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Miles-Davis) and [Herbie Hancock](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Herbie-Hancock). The blues, sharing close ties with jazz, have also seen jazzmen like [Jelly Roll Morton](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Jelly-Roll-Morton) and [Louis Armstrong](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Louis-Armstrong) incorporate blues elements in their music.

**jazz-rock**, popular [musical form](https://www.britannica.com/art/musical-form) in which modern [jazz](https://www.britannica.com/art/jazz) improvisation is accompanied by the bass lines, drumming styles, and instrumentation of rock music, with a strong emphasis on electronic instruments and dance rhythms.

Since the recordings of 1920s bands, notably [Paul Whiteman](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Paul-Whiteman)’s, there have been fusions of jazz and [popular music](https://www.britannica.com/art/popular-music), usually presenting jazz’s “hot,” swinging, staccato qualities in contrast to “sweet,” legato popular music characteristics. With the slow development of a unique identity in [rock](https://www.britannica.com/art/rock-music) [music](https://www.britannica.com/art/music), occasional jazz tunes also began including rock rhythms in the 1960s. Beginning in 1969, trumpeter [Miles Davis](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Miles-Davis) and associates such as drummer Tony Williams, guitarist [John McLaughlin](https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-McLaughlin), saxophonist [Wayne Shorter](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Wayne-Shorter), and electric keyboardists [Joe Zawinul](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Joe-Zawinul), [Herbie Hancock](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Herbie-Hancock), Larry Young, and [Chick Corea](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Chick-Corea) broke through to distinctive fusion musics. Jazz and rock elements contrasted, even competed with or [enhanced](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/enhanced) each other, in bands of the early 1970s such as Davis’s increasingly African-music-oriented groups, Williams’s Lifetime quartet, McLaughlin’s fiercely loud and energetic Mahavishnu Orchestra, the light, danceable music of Hancock’s Headhunters and Corea’s Return to Forever, and the mobile sound and rhythmic colours of Zawinul’s and Shorter’s [Weather Report](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Weather-Report).

The most important work by these musicians dates from the early 1970s; since then, most have alternated between periods of playing fusion music and playing mainstream jazz. The jazz-rock [idiom](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/idiom) gained one of the largest jazz audiences since the [swing](https://www.britannica.com/art/swing-music) era ended in the mid-1940s. The style was also known as crossover because sales of the music crossed over from the jazz market to the popular music market. Guitarist [Larry Coryell](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Larry-Coryell) was popular in the early years of jazz-rock fusion; guitarist [Pat Metheny](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Pat-Metheny), with his pastoral harmonies, has been a star since the late 1970s.

Meanwhile, two other kinds of fusion music were also current. The most popular jazz-rock strain grew out of hard bop: the funky 1960s jazz of musicians such as flutist [Herbie Mann](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Herbie-Mann), alto saxophonist Hank Crawford, and the Crusaders. Their [repertoires](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/repertoires) included original and standard rock tunes over which they improvised jazz. In the 1970s the CTI record label in particular offered this kind of fusion music on albums by Stanley Turrentine, Freddie Hubbard, and others. Less commercially successful was the [free jazz](https://www.britannica.com/art/free-jazz) fusion of [Ornette Coleman](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ornette-Coleman)’s [Prime Time](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Deion-Sanders) group (beginning in 1973) and his associates, guitarist James Blood Ulmer, bassist Jamaaladeen Tacuma, and drummer Ronald Shannon Jackson, though all led valuable bands in the 1980s. One problem was that the recurring rhythmic-harmonic patterns of rock tended to dominate, reducing jazz improvisation to mere decoration.

A later development of jazz-rock—contemporary jazz, or light jazz—appeared on the radio in the 1980s and ’90s. The most popular kind of fusion music, it abandoned jazz elements almost completely and frequently used a minimum of improvisation. Stars of [contemporary](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/contemporary) jazz included saxophonist Kenny G and the group Spyro Gyra. Two jazz-rock fashions of the 1990s were acid jazz, a catchall term for [bop](https://www.britannica.com/art/bebop) and free jazz improvising over [funk](https://www.britannica.com/art/funk) and [hip-hop](https://www.britannica.com/art/hip-hop) rhythms; and neo-swing, which revived the shuffle rhythms of small 1940s swing (“jump”) bands.

### What was Miles Davis known for?

Miles Davis was an American [trumpeter](https://www.britannica.com/art/trumpet), bandleader, and composer known for his tremendous influence on [jazz](https://www.britannica.com/art/jazz) and [popular music](https://www.britannica.com/art/popular-music) from the late 1940s to the end of the 20th century. He was widely admired for his cool, intimate playing style without vibrato (deliberate, rapid variations in [pitch](https://www.britannica.com/art/pitch-music)). As a visionary bandleader and composer, Davis changed the direction of jazz multiple times throughout his career, introducing cool jazz, modal jazz, and jazz fusion. His albums, such as _Birth of the Cool_ (1957), _Kind of Blue_ (1959), and _Bitches Brew_ (1970), were pivotal in these transformations. Along with [Louis Armstrong](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Louis-Armstrong), [Duke Ellington](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Duke-Ellington), and [Charlie Parker](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Charlie-Parker), he is regarded as one of the four most important and influential musicians in jazz history.

### How did Miles Davis die?

Miles Davis died on September 28, 1991, in [Santa Monica](https://www.britannica.com/place/Santa-Monica), [California](https://www.britannica.com/place/California-state), of [pneumonia](https://www.britannica.com/science/pneumonia), respiratory failure, and [stroke](https://www.britannica.com/science/stroke-medical-condition). He was 65 years old.

### What was Miles Davis’s personality like?

[Jazz](https://www.britannica.com/art/jazz) great Miles Davis was known for being aloof onstage, especially in his later years, when he would often turn his back to the audience or leave the stage while other musicians were performing their solos. Earlier in his career, when he was playing with [Dizzy Gillespie](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Dizzy-Gillespie) and [Charlie Parker](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Charlie-Parker) in the 1940s, he began cultivating this cool, tough, even antagonistic persona. Gillespie, however, dismissed Davis’s aloofness and toughness as a mask for shyness.

Davis was extremely individualistic as an artist, having been advised by his father to develop his own sound and style and not become an imitation of others. Davis once stated of his craft, “I pay no attention to what the critics say about me. The toughest critic I got, and the only one I worry about, is myself. The music has to get past _me_.”

**Miles Davis** was an American [jazz](https://www.britannica.com/art/jazz) musician and one of the major influences on the art from the late 1940s to the end of the 20th century. A titan of modern jazz [music](https://www.britannica.com/art/music), Davis was an outstanding [trumpeter](https://www.britannica.com/art/trumpet) known for his cool, [intimate](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/intimate), luminous playing and a visionary bandleader and composer who changed the direction of jazz several times throughout his career. He recorded best-selling albums, such as the [seminal](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/seminal) _Kind of Blue_ (1959) and the controversial _Bitches Brew_ (1970), that were also testimonies to his individualistic spirit. In the liner notes of one of his albums, Davis stated, “I pay no attention to what the critics say about me. The toughest critic I got, and the only one I worry about, is myself. The music has to get past _me_.”
