## Starting out

Davis grew up in [East St. Louis](https://www.britannica.com/place/East-Saint-Louis), Illinois, where his father, Miles Davis II, was a prosperous dental surgeon. (In later years he often spoke of his comfortable upbringing, sometimes to [rebuke](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/rebuke) critics who assumed that a background of poverty and suffering was common to all great jazz artists.) His first music lessons began at age 10, when he was encouraged to learn the [violin](https://www.britannica.com/art/violin) by his mother, Cleota Henry Davis, an accomplished musician. He began studying [trumpet](https://www.britannica.com/art/trumpet) in his early teens. Fortuitously, in light of his later stylistic development, his first teacher advised him to play without vibrato (deliberate, rapid variations in [pitch](https://www.britannica.com/art/pitch-music)), telling Davis, “You’re gonna get old anyway and start shaking.” Years later Davis would recount his teacher’s advice to _Time_ magazine, [explaining](https://time.com/archive/6805793/music-post-bopper/), “That’s how I tried to play—fast and light and no vibrato.”

Davis played with jazz bands in the [St. Louis](https://www.britannica.com/place/Saint-Louis-Missouri) area before moving to [New York City](https://www.britannica.com/place/New-York-City) in 1944 to study at the Institute of Musical Art (now the [Juilliard School](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Juilliard-School))—although he skipped many classes and instead was schooled through jam sessions with masters such as [Dizzy Gillespie](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Dizzy-Gillespie) and [Charlie Parker](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Charlie-Parker). With his father’s blessing, Davis dropped out of school in 1945 to focus entirely on jazz; his father urged him to avoid imitation and develop his own sound. Davis and Parker recorded together often during the years 1945–48, before Davis decided to quit Parker’s [band](https://www.britannica.com/art/band-music). Already a budding [maverick](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/maverick), Davis began to [cultivate](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/cultivate) a tough, cool, even antagonistic public image. His mentor Gillespie dismissed this as a mask for shyness, but soon Davis’s [mercurial](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/mercurial) temperament and onstage aloofness would become as much a part of his fame as his musical brilliance.

Davis’s early playing was sometimes tentative and not always fully in tune, but his unique, intimate tone and his fertile musical imagination outweighed his technical shortcomings. By the early 1950s Davis had turned his limitations into considerable assets. Rather than emulate the busy, wailing style of such [bebop](https://www.britannica.com/art/bebop) pioneers as Gillespie, Davis explored the trumpet’s middle register, experimenting with [harmonies](https://www.britannica.com/art/harmony-music) and [rhythms](https://www.britannica.com/art/rhythm-music) and varying the phrasing of his [improvisations](https://www.britannica.com/art/improvisation-music). With the occasional exception of multinote flurries, his melodic style was direct and unornamented, based on quarter [notes](https://www.britannica.com/art/note-staff-notation) and rich with [inflections](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/inflections). The deliberation, pacing, and lyricism in his improvisations are striking.

## [Cool jazz](https://www.britannica.com/art/cool-jazz) and [modal jazz](https://www.britannica.com/art/modal-jazz)

In the summer of 1948, Davis formed a nonet that included the renowned jazz artists [Gerry Mulligan](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Gerry-Mulligan), [J.J. Johnson](https://www.britannica.com/biography/J-J-Johnson), [Kenny Clarke](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Kenny-Clarke), and [Lee Konitz](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Lee-Konitz), as well as players on [French horn](https://www.britannica.com/art/horn-musical-instrument) and [tuba](https://www.britannica.com/art/tuba), instruments rarely heard in a jazz [context](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/context). Mulligan, [Gil Evans](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Gil-Evans), and pianist [John Lewis](https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-Lewis-American-musician) did most of the band’s arrangements, which [juxtaposed](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/juxtaposed) the flexible, improvisatory nature of bebop with a thickly textured orchestral sound. The group was short-lived but during its brief history recorded a dozen tracks that were originally released as singles (1949–50). These recordings changed the course of modern jazz and paved the way for the West Coast styles of the 1950s. The tracks were later collected in the album _[Birth of the Cool](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Birth-of-the-Cool)_ (1957).

During the early 1950s Davis struggled with a [heroin](https://www.britannica.com/science/heroin) addiction—he described this time as “a four-year horror show”—that affected his playing. Yet he still managed to record albums that rank among his best, including several with such jazz notables as [Sonny Rollins](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Sonny-Rollins), [Milt Jackson](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Milt-Jackson), and [Thelonious Monk](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Thelonious-Monk). In 1954, having overcome the addiction, Davis embarked on a two-decade period during which he was considered the most innovative musician in jazz. He formed classic small groups in the 1950s that featured [saxophone](https://www.britannica.com/art/saxophone) [legends](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/legends) [John Coltrane](https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-Coltrane) and [Cannonball Adderley](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Cannonball-Adderley), pianists Red Garland and [Bill Evans](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Bill-Evans), bassist Paul Chambers, and drummers “Philly” Joe Jones and Jimmy Cobb. Davis’s albums recorded during this era, including _’Round About Midnight_ (1957), _Milestones_ (1958), _Relaxin’_ (1958), _Workin’_ (1959), and _Steamin’_ (1961), affected the work of numerous other artists. He capped this period of his career with _[Kind of Blue](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Kind-of-Blue)_ (1959), perhaps the most celebrated album in the history of jazz. A mellow, relaxed collection, the album includes the finest recorded examples of modal jazz, a style in which improvisations are based upon sparse [chords](https://www.britannica.com/art/chord-music) and nonstandard [scales](https://www.britannica.com/art/scale-music) rather than on complex, frequently changing chords. The modal style lends itself to solos that are focused on [melody](https://www.britannica.com/art/melody); this accessible quality ensured _Kind of Blue_’s popularity with jazz fans.

Released concurrently with the small-group recordings, Davis’s albums with pieces arranged and conducted by [Gil Evans](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Gil-Evans)— _[Miles Ahead](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Miles-Ahead)_ (1957), _[Porgy and Bess](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Porgy-and-Bess-album-by-Davis)_ (1959), and _[Sketches of Spain](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Sketches-of-Spain)_ (1960)—were also monuments of the [genre](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/genre). The Davis-Evans collaborations were marked by complex arrangements, a near-equal emphasis on orchestra and soloist, and some of Davis’s most soulful and emotionally powerful playing. Davis and Evans occasionally [collaborated](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/collaborated) in later years but never again so memorably as on these three masterful albums.

## [Free jazz](https://www.britannica.com/art/free-jazz) and fusion

[![Miles Davis](https://cdn.britannica.com/90/215290-050-9D95001B/American-musician-jazz-trumpeter-Miles-Davis.jpg?w=300)](https://cdn.britannica.com/90/215290-050-9D95001B/American-musician-jazz-trumpeter-Miles-Davis.jpg)

[Miles Davis](https://cdn.britannica.com/90/215290-050-9D95001B/American-musician-jazz-trumpeter-Miles-Davis.jpg) Jazz trumpeter Miles Davis approached his art according to his philosophy, “Don't play what's there, play what's not there.”(more)

The early 1960s were transitional, less-innovative years for Davis, although his music and his playing remained top-caliber. He began forming another soon-to-be-classic small group in late 1962 with bassist [Ron Carter](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ron-Carter), pianist [Herbie Hancock](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Herbie-Hancock), and teenage drummer Tony Williams; tenor saxophonist [Wayne Shorter](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Wayne-Shorter) joined the lineup in 1964. Davis’s new quintet was characterized by a light, free sound and a [repertoire](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/repertoire) that extended from the [blues](https://www.britannica.com/art/blues-music) to avant-garde and [free jazz](https://www.britannica.com/art/free-jazz). Compared with the [innovations](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/innovations) of other modern jazz groups of the 1960s, the Davis quintet’s experimentations in [polyrhythm](https://www.britannica.com/art/polyrhythm) and [polytonality](https://www.britannica.com/art/polytonality) were more subtle but equally daring. _Live at the Plugged Nickel_ (1965), _E.S.P._ (1965), _Miles Smiles_ (1966), and _Nefertiti_ (1968) were among the quintet’s timeless, influential recordings.

About the time of _Miles in the Sky_ (1968) and _Filles de Kilimanjaro_ (1969), Davis began experimenting with [electronic instruments](https://www.britannica.com/art/electronic-instrument). With other musicians, including keyboardists [Chick Corea](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Chick-Corea) and [Joe Zawinul](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Joe-Zawinul) and guitarist [John McLaughlin](https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-McLaughlin), Davis cut _[In a Silent Way](https://www.britannica.com/topic/In-a-Silent-Way)_ (1969), regarded as the seminal album of the jazz [fusion](https://www.britannica.com/art/jazz-rock) movement. It was considered by purists to be Davis’s last true jazz album.

“Miles just called and said he wants this album to be titled: ‘BITCHES BREW.’ Please advise.”

— [Columbia Records](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Columbia-Records) internal memo dated November 14, 1969

Davis won new fans and [alienated](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/alienated) old ones with the release of _[Bitches Brew](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Bitches-Brew)_ (1970), an album on which he fully embraced the rhythms, electronic instrumentation, and studio effects of [rock music](https://www.britannica.com/art/rock-music). (Davis’s brief marriage to the model and singer-songwriter [Betty Mabry](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Betty-Davis) in 1968 had opened up new vistas for him; she inspired him to adopt a more youthful fashion sense and introduced him to such musicians as [Jimi Hendrix](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Jimi-Hendrix), [James Brown](https://www.britannica.com/biography/James-Brown-American-singer), and [Sly Stone](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Sly-and-the-Family-Stone).) A cacophonous kaleidoscope of layered sounds, rhythms, and textures, the album’s influence was heard in such 1970s fusion groups as Weather Report and Chick Corea’s Return to Forever. Davis continued in this style for a few years, with the album _Live-Evil_ (1971) and the film soundtrack _A Tribute to Jack Johnson_ (1971) being particular highlights.

## Later years and legacy

Personal Life

Davis was married three times: to dancer Frances Taylor (1960–68), model and singer-songwriter [Betty Mabry](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Betty-Davis) (1968–69), and actress [Cicely Tyson](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Cicely-Tyson) (1981–88). All his marriages ended in divorce. He had four children: Cheryl, Gregory, and Miles IV (with his former high-school sweetheart Irene Cawthon), and Erin (with his then-girlfriend Marguerite Eskridge). Another significant relationship was his love affair with French actress and singer Juliette Greco, whom he met while playing at a jazz festival in [Paris](https://www.britannica.com/place/Paris) in 1949, his first time traveling outside the [United States](https://www.britannica.com/place/United-States) and his first time experiencing a more racially tolerant [culture](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/culture).

Davis was injured in an auto accident in 1972, curtailing his activities, and then retired from 1975 through 1980. When he returned to public notice with _The Man with the Horn_ (1981), critics felt that Davis’s erratic playing showed the effects of his five-year layoff, but he steadily regained his powers during the next few years. He dabbled in a variety of musical styles throughout the 1980s, concentrating mostly on jazz-rock dance music, but there were also notable experiments in other styles, such as a return to his [blues](https://www.britannica.com/art/blues-music) roots ( _Star People_, 1983) and a set of Gil Evans-influenced orchestral numbers ( _Music from Siesta_, 1987).

Davis won several [Grammy Awards](https://www.britannica.com/art/Grammy-Award) during this period for such albums as _We Want Miles_ (1982), _Tutu_ (1986), and _Aura_ (1989). One of the most memorable events of Davis’s later years occurred at the [Montreux Jazz Festival](https://www.britannica.com/art/Montreux-Jazz-Festival) in July 1991, when he joined with an orchestra conducted by [Quincy Jones](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Quincy-Jones) to perform some of the classic Gil Evans arrangements of the late 1950s. Davis died less than three months later of [pneumonia](https://www.britannica.com/science/pneumonia), respiratory failure, and [stroke](https://www.britannica.com/science/stroke-medical-condition). His final album, _Doo-Bop_ (1992), was released posthumously.

Although critics dismissed much of the music Davis released after _Bitches Brew_, his excursions helped keep jazz popular with mainstream audiences. In later years he ignored the critics, and he defied convention by wandering around the stage, often playing with his back to the audience. In his much-praised and revealing autobiography, _Miles_ (1989; with Quincy Troupe), he wrote frankly of his hedonistic past and of the [racism](https://www.britannica.com/topic/racism) he saw in the music industry, as well as his experiences with police harassment and brutality. Along with [Louis Armstrong](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Louis-Armstrong), [Duke Ellington](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Duke-Ellington), and [Charlie Parker](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Charlie-Parker), Davis is regarded as one of the four most important and influential musicians in jazz history, as well as the music’s most [eclectic](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/eclectic) practitioner.

In 2002 the U.S. [Library of Congress](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Library-of-Congress) added _Kind of Blue_ to the [National Recording Registry](https://www.britannica.com/topic/National-Recording-Registry), a list of audio recordings deemed “culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant.” _Bitches Brew_ was added to the registry in 2025. Davis was awarded an honorary doctorate from the [New England Conservatory of Music](https://www.britannica.com/topic/New-England-Conservatory-of-Music) in 1986, received a Grammy for lifetime achievement in 1990, and was posthumously inducted into the [Rock and Roll Hall of Fame](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Rock-and-Roll-Hall-of-Fame-and-Museum) in 2006.

(m.1954;div.1964)​ | Musical artist **Randolph Denard Ornette Coleman** (March 9, 1930 – June 11, 2015)[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Ratliff-1) was an American [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") saxophonist, trumpeter, violinist, and composer. He is best known as a principal founder of the [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") genre, a term derived from his 1960 album _[Free Jazz: A Collective Improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Jazz:_A_Collective_Improvisation "Free Jazz: A Collective Improvisation")_. His pioneering works often abandoned the [harmony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmony "Harmony")-based composition, [tonality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonality "Tonality"), chord changes, and fixed rhythm found in earlier jazz idioms;[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-2) instead, Coleman emphasized an experimental approach to [improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Improvisation "Improvisation") rooted in ensemble playing and [blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues "Blues") phrasing.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-allmusicbio-3) Thom Jurek of [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") called him "one of the most beloved and polarizing figures in jazz history", noting that while "now celebrated as a fearless innovator and a genius, he was initially regarded by peers and critics as rebellious, disruptive, and even a fraud."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-allmusicbio-3) Born and raised in [Fort Worth, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Worth,_Texas "Fort Worth, Texas"), Coleman taught himself to play the saxophone when he was a teenager.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Ratliff-1) He began his musical career playing in local [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues") and [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop") groups and eventually formed his own jazz group in [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"), featuring members such as [Ed Blackwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Blackwell "Ed Blackwell"), [Don Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter) "Don Cherry (trumpeter)"), [Charlie Haden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Haden "Charlie Haden"), and [Billy Higgins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Higgins "Billy Higgins"). In November 1959, his quartet began a controversial residency at the [Five Spot Café](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Spot_Caf%C3%A9 "Five Spot Café") in New York City and he released the influential album _[The Shape of Jazz to Come](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shape_of_Jazz_to_Come "The Shape of Jazz to Come")_ on [Atlantic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Records "Atlantic Records"). Coleman's subsequent Atlantic releases in the early 1960s would profoundly impact the direction of jazz in that decade, and his compositions " [Lonely Woman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lonely_Woman_(composition) "Lonely Woman (composition)")" and " [Broadway Blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_Blues_(Coleman) "Broadway Blues (Coleman)")" became [standards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_standard "Jazz standard") cited as important early works in free jazz.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-HellmerLawn2005-4) In the mid 1960s, Coleman left Atlantic for other labels, including [Blue Note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records") and [Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records"), and began performing with his young son [Denardo Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denardo_Coleman "Denardo Coleman") on drums. He explored symphonic composition with his 1972 album _[Skies of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skies_of_America "Skies of America")_, featuring the [London Symphony Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Symphony_Orchestra "London Symphony Orchestra"). In the mid-1970s, he formed the group [Prime Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Time_(band) "Prime Time (band)"), which performed electric [jazz-funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk "Jazz-funk") and elaborated on his theory of [harmolodics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmolodics "Harmolodics").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-allmusicbio-3) In 1995, he and Denardo founded the [Harmolodic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmolodics#Record_label "Harmolodics") record label. Coleman's 2006 album _[Sound Grammar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_Grammar "Sound Grammar")_ received the 2007 [Pulitzer Prize for Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize_for_Music "Pulitzer Prize for Music"), making him the second jazz musician ever to receive the honor.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-5) ## Biography \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ornette_Coleman&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Biography")\] ### Early life \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ornette_Coleman&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Early life")\] Coleman was born Randolph Denard Ornette Coleman on March 9, 1930, in [Fort Worth, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Worth,_Texas "Fort Worth, Texas"),[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Fordham-6) where he was raised.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Atlantic1972-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-EGP-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Litweiler-9) He attended [I.M. Terrell High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I.M._Terrell_High_School "I.M. Terrell High School") in Fort Worth, where he participated in the band program until he was dismissed for improvising during [John Philip Sousa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Philip_Sousa "John Philip Sousa")'s march " [The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Washington_Post_(march) "The Washington Post (march)")". He began performing [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues") and [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop") on tenor saxophone, and formed The Jam Jivers with [Prince Lasha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Lasha "Prince Lasha") and [Charles Moffett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Moffett "Charles Moffett").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Litweiler-9) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/Ornette_Coleman-140911-0002-96WP.jpg/250px-Ornette_Coleman-140911-0002-96WP.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ornette_Coleman-140911-0002-96WP.jpg) Coleman playing his signature alto saxophone in 1971 Eager to leave town, he accepted a job in 1949 with a [Silas Green from New Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silas_Green_from_New_Orleans "Silas Green from New Orleans") traveling show and then with touring rhythm and blues shows. After a show in [Baton Rouge, Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baton_Rouge,_Louisiana "Baton Rouge, Louisiana"), he was assaulted and his saxophone was destroyed.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Spellman-10) Coleman subsequently switched to alto saxophone, first playing it in New Orleans after the Baton Rouge incident; the alto would remain his primary instrument for the rest of his life. He then joined the band of [Pee Wee Crayton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pee_Wee_Crayton "Pee Wee Crayton") and traveled with them to Los Angeles. He worked at various jobs in Los Angeles, including as an elevator operator, while pursuing his music career.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-11) Coleman found like-minded musicians in Los Angeles, such as [Ed Blackwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Blackwell "Ed Blackwell"), [Bobby Bradford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Bradford "Bobby Bradford"), [Don Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter) "Don Cherry (trumpeter)"), [Charlie Haden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Haden "Charlie Haden"), [Billy Higgins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Higgins "Billy Higgins"), and [Charles Moffett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Moffett "Charles Moffett").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-allmusicbio-3)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-EJN-12) Thanks to the intercession of friends and a successful audition, Ornette signed his first recording contract with Los Angeles-based [Contemporary Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_Records "Contemporary Records"),[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-13) which allowed him to sell the tracks from his debut album, _[Something Else!!!!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Something_Else!!!! "Something Else!!!!")_ (1958), with Cherry, Higgins, [Walter Norris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Norris "Walter Norris"), and [Don Payne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Payne_(musician) "Don Payne (musician)").[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Jurek-14) During the same year, he briefly belonged to a quintet led by [Paul Bley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Bley "Paul Bley") that performed at a club in Los Angeles. (That band is recorded on _[Live at the Hilcrest Club 1958](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_at_the_Hilcrest_Club_1958 "Live at the Hilcrest Club 1958")._)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-allmusicbio-3) By the time _[Tomorrow Is the Question!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomorrow_Is_the_Question! "Tomorrow Is the Question!")_ was recorded soon after with Cherry, bassists [Percy Heath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percy_Heath "Percy Heath") and [Red Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Mitchell "Red Mitchell"), and drummer [Shelly Manne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelly_Manne "Shelly Manne"), the jazz world had been shaken up by Coleman's music. Some jazz musicians called him a fraud, while conductor and composer [Leonard Bernstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein "Leonard Bernstein") praised him.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-EJN-12) ### 1959: _The Shape of Jazz to Come_ \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ornette_Coleman&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: 1959: The Shape of Jazz to Come")\] In 1959, [Atlantic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Records "Atlantic Records") released Coleman's third studio album, _[The Shape of Jazz to Come](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shape_of_Jazz_to_Come "The Shape of Jazz to Come")_. According to music critic Steve Huey, the album "was a watershed event in the genesis of avant-garde jazz, profoundly steering its future course and throwing down a gauntlet that some still haven't come to grips with".[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Huey-15) _[Jazzwise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazzwise "Jazzwise")_ magazine listed it at number three on their list of the 100 best jazz albums of all time in 2017.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Flynn-16) Coleman's quartet received a long and sometimes controversial engagement at the [Five Spot Café](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Spot_Caf%C3%A9 "Five Spot Café") in [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan"), New York City. Leonard Bernstein, [Lionel Hampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionel_Hampton "Lionel Hampton"), and the [Modern Jazz Quartet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_Jazz_Quartet "Modern Jazz Quartet") were impressed and offered encouragement. Hampton asked to perform with the quartet, while Bernstein helped Haden obtain a [Guggenheim Fellowship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guggenheim_Fellowship "Guggenheim Fellowship") grant. A young [Lou Reed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou_Reed "Lou Reed") followed Coleman's quartet around New York City.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-:0-17) Among detractors, [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis") said that Coleman was "all screwed up inside",[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-18)[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Roberts-19) although he later became a proponent of Coleman's innovations;[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Kahn-20) [Dizzy Gillespie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie "Dizzy Gillespie") remarked of Coleman that "I don't know what he's playing, but it's not jazz."[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-:0-17) Coleman's early sound was due in part to his use of a plastic [Grafton saxophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grafton_saxophone "Grafton saxophone"), which he had purchased in Los Angeles in 1954 because he was unable to afford a metal saxophone at the time.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Litweiler-9) On his Atlantic recordings, Coleman's sidemen were Cherry on cornet or [pocket trumpet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pocket_trumpet "Pocket trumpet"); Charlie Haden, [Scott LaFaro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_LaFaro "Scott LaFaro"), and then [Jimmy Garrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Garrison "Jimmy Garrison") on bass; and Higgins or [Ed Blackwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Blackwell "Ed Blackwell") on drums. Coleman's complete recordings for the label were collected on the box set _[Beauty Is a Rare Thing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_Is_a_Rare_Thing "Beauty Is a Rare Thing")_ in 1993.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Yanow-21) ### 1960s: _Free Jazz_ and Blue Note \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ornette_Coleman&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: 1960s: Free Jazz and Blue Note")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Ornette_Coleman_trumpet.jpg/250px-Ornette_Coleman_trumpet.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ornette_Coleman_trumpet.jpg) Coleman playing the trumpet at the [Great American Music Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_American_Music_Hall "Great American Music Hall"), [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco"), in 1981 In 1960, Coleman recorded _[Free Jazz: A Collective Improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Jazz:_A_Collective_Improvisation "Free Jazz: A Collective Improvisation")_, which featured a "double quartet" including Cherry and [Freddie Hubbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Hubbard "Freddie Hubbard") on trumpet, [Eric Dolphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy "Eric Dolphy") on bass clarinet, Haden and LaFaro on bass, and Higgins and Blackwell on drums.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-rhino-22) The album was recorded in stereo, with one woodwind/trumpet/bass/drums quartet in each channel. _Free Jazz_ was, at 37 minutes, the longest recorded continuous jazz performance at the time[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-23) and was one of Coleman's most controversial albums.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-24) The January 18, 1962, issue of _[DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat")_ magazine presented an article entitled "Double View of a Double Quartet" in which Pete Welding gave the album five stars while John A. Tynan rated it zero stars.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Welding-25) While Coleman had intended "free jazz" as simply an album title, [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") was soon considered a new genre; Coleman expressed discomfort with the term.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Reich2010-26) After he left Atlantic, Coleman's music became more angular and engaged with the [avant-garde jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz") which had developed in part around his innovations.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Yanow-21) He formed a trio with bassist [David Izenzon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Izenzon "David Izenzon") and drummer [Charles Moffett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Moffett "Charles Moffett") and began playing trumpet and violin in addition to the saxophone. His friendship with free jazz saxophonist [Albert Ayler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler "Albert Ayler") influenced his unorthodox self-taught style on the trumpet and violin. Charlie Haden sometimes joined this trio to form a two-bass quartet. In 1966, Coleman signed with [Blue Note Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records") and released the two-volume live album _[At the "Golden Circle" Stockholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/At_the_%22Golden_Circle%22_Stockholm "At the \"Golden Circle\" Stockholm")_ featuring Izenzon and Moffett, recorded in Sweden the previous December.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Freeman-27) Later that year, he recorded _[The Empty Foxhole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Empty_Foxhole "The Empty Foxhole")_ with Haden on bass and his ten year-old son [Denardo Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denardo_Coleman "Denardo Coleman") on drums;[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_2015-28) [Freddie Hubbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Hubbard "Freddie Hubbard") and [Shelly Manne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelly_Manne "Shelly Manne") regarded Denardo's appearance on the album as an ill-advised publicity stunt.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Gabel-29)[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Spencer-30) Denardo later became his father's primary drummer in the late 1970s. Coleman formed another quartet with Haden, Garrison, and [Elvin Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elvin_Jones "Elvin Jones"), and [Dewey Redman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dewey_Redman "Dewey Redman") joined the group, usually on tenor saxophone. On February 29, 1968, Coleman's quartet (with Haden, Izenzon, and Ed Blackwell) performed live with [Yoko Ono](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoko_Ono "Yoko Ono") at the [Royal Albert Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Albert_Hall "Royal Albert Hall"), and a recording from their rehearsal was subsequently included on Ono's 1970 album _[Yoko Ono/Plastic Ono Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoko_Ono/Plastic_Ono_Band "Yoko Ono/Plastic Ono Band")_ as the track "AOS".[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Chrispell-31) He explored his interest in string textures on _[Town Hall, 1962](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Town_Hall,_1962 "Town Hall, 1962")_, culminating in the 1972 album _[Skies of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skies_of_America "Skies of America")_ with the [London Symphony Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Symphony_Orchestra "London Symphony Orchestra"). ### 1970s–1990s: Harmolodic funk and Prime Time \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ornette_Coleman&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: 1970s–1990s: Harmolodic funk and Prime Time")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/63/Ellerbie_Coleman_Nix.jpg/250px-Ellerbie_Coleman_Nix.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ellerbie_Coleman_Nix.jpg) Coleman playing the violin with Prime Time in 1978, flanked by guitarists Charlie Ellerbee (left) and [Bern Nix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bern_Nix "Bern Nix") (right) Coleman, like Miles Davis before him, soon took to playing with electric instruments and incorporating [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") and [jazz-funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk "Jazz-funk") influences. The 1976 album _[Dancing in Your Head](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dancing_in_Your_Head "Dancing in Your Head")_, Coleman's first recording with the group which later became known as [Prime Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Time_(band) "Prime Time (band)"), prominently featured bass guitarist [Jamaaladeen Tacuma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamaaladeen_Tacuma "Jamaaladeen Tacuma") and electric guitarists [Bern Nix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bern_Nix "Bern Nix") and Charlie Ellerbee. While this marked a stylistic departure for Coleman, the music retained aspects of what he called [harmolodics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmolodics "Harmolodics") _._ Coleman's subsequent albums with Prime Time, such as _[Virgin Beauty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_Beauty "Virgin Beauty")_ and _[Of Human Feelings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Of_Human_Feelings "Of Human Feelings")_, continued to use rock and funk rhythms in a style sometimes called [free funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_funk "Free funk").[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-32)[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-33) [Jerry Garcia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Garcia "Jerry Garcia") of the [Grateful Dead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grateful_Dead "Grateful Dead") played guitar on three tracks on _Virgin Beauty_: "Three Wishes", "Singing in the Shower", and "Desert Players". Coleman later joined the Grateful Dead on stage at a 1993 performance in [Oakland, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oakland,_California "Oakland, California").[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Deadbase-34)[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-35) In December 1985, Coleman and guitarist [Pat Metheny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pat_Metheny "Pat Metheny") recorded _[Song X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Song_X "Song X")_ with Haden, Denardo Coleman, and second drummer [Jack DeJohnette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_DeJohnette "Jack DeJohnette"). [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/11/Ornette_at_The_Forum_1982.jpg/250px-Ornette_at_The_Forum_1982.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ornette_at_The_Forum_1982.jpg) Coleman performing in [Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto "Toronto") in 1982 In 1990, [Reggio Emilia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggio_Emilia "Reggio Emilia"), Italy, held a three-day "Portrait of the Artist" festival in Coleman's honor, in which he performed with Cherry, Haden, and Higgins. The festival also presented performances of his chamber music and _Skies of America_.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-36) In 1991, Coleman played on the soundtrack of [David Cronenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Cronenberg "David Cronenberg")'s film _[Naked Lunch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naked_Lunch_(film) "Naked Lunch (film)")_; the orchestra was conducted by [Howard Shore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Shore "Howard Shore").[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-37)[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-38) Coleman released four records in 1995 and 1996, and for the first time in many years worked regularly with piano players ( [Geri Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geri_Allen "Geri Allen") and [Joachim Kühn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joachim_K%C3%BChn "Joachim Kühn")). ### 2000s \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ornette_Coleman&action=edit§ion=6 "Edit section: 2000s")\] Two 1972 Coleman recordings, "Happy House" and "Foreigner in a Free Land", were used in [Gus Van Sant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gus_Van_Sant "Gus Van Sant")'s 2000 _[Finding Forrester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finding_Forrester "Finding Forrester")_.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-39) In September 2006, Coleman released the album _[Sound Grammar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_Grammar "Sound Grammar")_. Recorded live in [Ludwigshafen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwigshafen "Ludwigshafen"), Germany, in 2005, it was his first album of new material in ten years. It won the 2007 [Pulitzer Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize "Pulitzer Prize") for music, making Coleman only the second jazz musician (after [Wynton Marsalis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wynton_Marsalis "Wynton Marsalis")) to win the prize.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Pulitzer-40) ## Personal life \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ornette_Coleman&action=edit§ion=7 "Edit section: Personal life")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/Ornette_Coleman.jpg/250px-Ornette_Coleman.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ornette_Coleman.jpg) Coleman playing his [Selmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Selmer_Paris "Henri Selmer Paris") alto saxophone in [The Hague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hague "The Hague") in 1994 Jazz pianist [Joanne Brackeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joanne_Brackeen "Joanne Brackeen") stated in an interview with [Marian McPartland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marian_McPartland "Marian McPartland") that Coleman mentored her and gave her music lessons.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Lyon-41) Coleman married poet [Jayne Cortez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jayne_Cortez "Jayne Cortez") in 1954. The couple divorced in 1964.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-42) They had one son, [Denardo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denardo_Coleman "Denardo Coleman"), born in 1956.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Fox-43) Coleman died of [cardiac arrest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiac_arrest "Cardiac arrest") in Manhattan on June 11, 2015, aged 85.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Ratliff-1) His funeral was a three-hour event with performances and speeches by several of his collaborators and contemporaries, including [Pharoah Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharoah_Sanders "Pharoah Sanders") and [Cecil Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor "Cecil Taylor").[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Remnick-44) ## Awards and honors \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ornette_Coleman&action=edit§ion=8 "Edit section: Awards and honors")\] - [Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn "Brooklyn"), New York, U.S. | | Genres | [Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), [avant-garde jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz"), [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz"), [free improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation "Free improvisation") | | Occupations | Musician, bandleader, composer, improviser, poet | | Instrument | Piano | | Years active | 1956–2018 | | Labels | [Transition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transition_Records "Transition Records"), [Blue Note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records"), [Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_Records "Freedom Records"), [Hathut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hathut_Records "Hathut Records"), [Enja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enja_Records "Enja Records"), [FMP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FMP/Free_Music_Production "FMP/Free Music Production") | Musical artist **Cecil Percival Taylor** (March 25, 1929–April 5, 2018)[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-Such-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-Feather-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-Seisdedos-3) was an American pianist and poet.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-FOOTNOTESuch199361-4)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-Yanow-5) Taylor was [classically trained](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classically_trained "Classically trained") and was one of the pioneers of [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz"). His music is characterized by an energetic, physical approach, resulting in complex [improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_improvisation "Musical improvisation") often involving [tone clusters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tone_clusters "Tone clusters") and intricate [polyrhythms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyrhythms "Polyrhythms"). His technique has been compared to [percussion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percussion_instrument "Percussion instrument"). Referring to the number of keys on a standard piano, [Val Wilmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Val_Wilmer "Val Wilmer") used the phrase "eighty-eight tuned drums" to describe Taylor's style.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-6) He has been referred to as " [Art Tatum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Tatum "Art Tatum") with contemporary-classical leanings".[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-Tatum-7) ## Early life and education \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cecil_Taylor&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")\] Cecil Percival Taylor was born on March 25, 1929, in [Long Island City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Island_City "Long Island City"), [Queens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queens "Queens"),[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-nytobit-8) and raised in [Corona, Queens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corona,_Queens "Corona, Queens").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-NYT2012-9) As an only child in a middle-class family, Taylor was encouraged by his mother, Almeda Ragland Taylor, to play music at an early age. He began playing piano at age six and went on to study at the [New York College of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_College_of_Music "New York College of Music") and [New England Conservatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England_Conservatory "New England Conservatory") in [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston"). At the New England Conservatory, Taylor majored in popular music arrangement. During his time there, he also became familiar with contemporary European [art music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_music "Art music"). [Bela Bartók](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9la_Bart%C3%B3k "Béla Bartók") and [Karlheinz Stockhausen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karlheinz_Stockhausen "Karlheinz Stockhausen") notably influenced his music.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-:0-10) In 1955, Taylor moved back to New York City from Boston. He formed a quartet with soprano saxophonist [Steve Lacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Lacy_(saxophonist) "Steve Lacy (saxophonist)"), bassist [Buell Neidlinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buell_Neidlinger "Buell Neidlinger"), and drummer [Dennis Charles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denis_Charles "Denis Charles").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-:0-10) Taylor's first recording, _[Jazz Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Advance "Jazz Advance")_, featured Lacy and was released in 1956.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-11) The recording is described by [Richard Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Cook_(journalist) "Richard Cook (journalist)") and [Brian Morton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Morton_(Scottish_writer) "Brian Morton (Scottish writer)") in the _[Penguin Guide to Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penguin_Guide_to_Jazz "Penguin Guide to Jazz")_: "While there are still many nods to conventional [post-bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-bop "Post-bop") form in this set, it already points to the freedoms in which the pianist would later immerse himself."[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-12) Taylor's quartet featuring Lacy also appeared at the 1957 [Newport Jazz Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport_Jazz_Festival "Newport Jazz Festival"), which was made into the album _[At Newport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/At_Newport_(Cecil_Taylor_and_Gigi_Gryce_album) "At Newport (Cecil Taylor and Gigi Gryce album)")_.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-13) Taylor collaborated with saxophonist [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane") in 1958 on _[Stereo Drive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereo_Drive "Stereo Drive")_, now available as _Coltrane Time_.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-14) ## 1950s and early 1960s \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cecil_Taylor&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: 1950s and early 1960s")\] Throughout the 1950s and 1960s, Taylor's music grew more complex and moved away from existing jazz styles. Gigs were often hard to come by, and club owners found that Taylor's approach of playing long pieces tended to impede business.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-15) His 1959 [LP record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LP_record "LP record") _[Looking Ahead!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Looking_Ahead! "Looking Ahead!")_ showcased his innovation as a creator as compared to the jazz mainstream. Unlike others at the time, Taylor utilized virtuosic techniques and made swift stylistic shifts from phrase to phrase. These qualities, among others, still remained notable distinctions of his music for the rest of his life.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-16) Landmark recordings, such as _[Unit Structures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_Structures "Unit Structures")_ (1966), also appeared. Within the [Cecil Taylor Unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor_Unit "Cecil Taylor Unit") (a distinction that was often used at performances and recordings between 1962 and 2006 for a shifting group of sidemen), musicians were able to develop new forms of conversational interplay. In the early 1960s, an uncredited [Albert Ayler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler "Albert Ayler") worked with Taylor, jamming and appearing on at least one recording, _Four_, which was unreleased until appearing on the 2004 Ayler [box set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_set "Box set") _[Holy Ghost: Rare & Unissued Recordings (1962–70)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Ghost:_Rare_&_Unissued_Recordings_(1962%E2%80%9370) "Holy Ghost: Rare & Unissued Recordings (1962–70)")_.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-17) By 1961, Taylor was working regularly with alto saxophonist [Jimmy Lyons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Lyons_(saxophonist) "Jimmy Lyons (saxophonist)"), who would become one of his most important and consistent collaborators. Taylor, Lyons, and drummer [Sunny Murray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunny_Murray "Sunny Murray") (and later [Andrew Cyrille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Cyrille "Andrew Cyrille")) formed the core personnel of the [Cecil Taylor Unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor_Unit "Cecil Taylor Unit"), Taylor's primary ensemble until Lyons' death in 1986. Lyons' playing, strongly influenced by jazz icon [Charlie Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Parker "Charlie Parker"), retained a strong [blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues "Blues") sensibility and helped keep Taylor's increasingly [avant garde music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_music "Avant-garde music") tethered to the jazz tradition.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-Kelsey-18) ## Late 1960s and 1970s \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cecil_Taylor&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Late 1960s and 1970s")\] Taylor began to perform solo concerts in the latter half of the 1960s. The first known recorded solo performance was "Carmen With Rings" (59 minutes) in [De Doelen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Doelen "De Doelen") concert hall in [Rotterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotterdam "Rotterdam") on July 1, 1967. Two days earlier, Taylor had played the same composition in the [Amsterdam Concertgebouw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam_Concertgebouw "Amsterdam Concertgebouw"). Many of his later concerts were released on album and include _[Indent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indent_(album) "Indent (album)")_ (1973), side one of _[Spring of Two Blue-J's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spring_of_Two_Blue_J's "Spring of Two Blue J's")_ (1973), _[Silent Tongues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silent_Tongues "Silent Tongues")_ (1974), _[Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garden_(album) "Garden (album)")_ (1982), _[For Olim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/For_Olim "For Olim")_ (1987), _[Erzulie Maketh Scent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erzulie_Maketh_Scent "Erzulie Maketh Scent")_ (1989), and _[The Tree of Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tree_of_Life_(Cecil_Taylor_album) "The Tree of Life (Cecil Taylor album)")_ (1998).[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-19) He began to garner critical and popular acclaim, playing for [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter "Jimmy Carter") on the [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House") Lawn,[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-20) lecturing as an [artist-in-residence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artist-in-residence "Artist-in-residence") at universities, and eventually being awarded a [Guggenheim Fellowship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guggenheim_Fellowship "Guggenheim Fellowship") in 1973.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-21) In 1976, Taylor directed a production of [Adrienne Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrienne_Kennedy "Adrienne Kennedy")'s _[A Rat's Mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Rat's_Mass "A Rat's Mass")_ at [La MaMa Experimental Theatre Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_MaMa_Experimental_Theatre_Club "La MaMa Experimental Theatre Club") in the [East Village of Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Village,_Manhattan "East Village, Manhattan"). His production combined the original script with a chorus of orchestrated voices used as instruments. [Jimmy Lyons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Lyons_(saxophonist) "Jimmy Lyons (saxophonist)"), [Rashid Bakr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rashid_Bakr_(musician) "Rashid Bakr (musician)"), [Andy Bey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Bey "Andy Bey"), [Karen Borca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karen_Borca "Karen Borca"), [David S. Ware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_S._Ware "David S. Ware") and [Raphe Malik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raphe_Malik "Raphe Malik") performed in the production as the Cecil Taylor Unit, among other musicians and actors.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-22) ## 1980s, 1990s, and the Feel Trio \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cecil_Taylor&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: 1980s, 1990s, and the Feel Trio")\] Following Lyons' death in 1986, Taylor formed the Feel Trio in the late 1980s with [William Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Parker_(musician) "William Parker (musician)") on bass and [Tony Oxley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Oxley "Tony Oxley") on drums. The group can be heard on _[Celebrated Blazons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrated_Blazons "Celebrated Blazons")_, _[Looking (Berlin Version) The Feel Trio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Looking_(Berlin_Version)_The_Feel_Trio "Looking (Berlin Version) The Feel Trio")_ and the 10-disc set _[2 Ts for a Lovely T](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2_Ts_for_a_Lovely_T "2 Ts for a Lovely T")_.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-23)[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-24)[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-25) Compared to his prior groups with Lyons, the Feel Trio had a more abstract approach, tethered less to jazz tradition and more aligned with the ethos of European [free improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation "Free improvisation"). He also performed with larger ensembles and [big band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_band "Big band") projects. Taylor's extended residence in [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin") in 1988 was documented by the German label [FMP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FMP_(Free_Music_Production) "FMP (Free Music Production)"), resulting in a [box set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_set "Box set") of performances in duet and trio with a large number of European free improvisors, including Oxley, [Derek Bailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Bailey_(guitarist) "Derek Bailey (guitarist)"), [Evan Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evan_Parker "Evan Parker"), [Han Bennink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_Bennink "Han Bennink"), [Tristan Honsinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tristan_Honsinger "Tristan Honsinger"), [Louis Moholo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Moholo "Louis Moholo"), and [Paul Lovens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Lovens "Paul Lovens"). Most of his later recordings have been released on European labels, with the exception of _[Momentum Space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Momentum_Space_(album) "Momentum Space (album)")_ (a meeting with [Dewey Redman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dewey_Redman "Dewey Redman") and [Elvin Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elvin_Jones "Elvin Jones")) on [Verve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verve_Records "Verve Records")/Gitanes. The classical label [Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridge_Records "Bridge Records") released his 1998 [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress") performance _Algonquin_, a duet with violinist [Mat Maneri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mat_Maneri "Mat Maneri").[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-26) Taylor continued to perform for capacity audiences around the world with live concerts, usually playing his favored instrument, a [Bösendorfer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%B6sendorfer "Bösendorfer") piano featuring nine extra lower-register keys. In 1987, he toured England with Australian pianist [Roger Woodward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Woodward "Roger Woodward"), presenting recitals on which Woodward played solo works by [Xenakis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iannis_Xenakis "Iannis Xenakis"), [Takemitsu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toru_Takemitsu "Toru Takemitsu"), and [Feldman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morton_Feldman "Morton Feldman"), followed by Taylor, also playing solo.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-27) A [documentary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Documentary_film "Documentary film") on Taylor, entitled [_All the Notes_](https://web.archive.org/web/20080924143425/http://www.chrisfelver.com/films/taylor.html), was released on [DVD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DVD "DVD") in 2006 by director [Chris Felver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Felver "Chris Felver"). Taylor was also featured in a 1981 documentary film entitled _[Imagine the Sound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imagine_the_Sound "Imagine the Sound")_, in which he discusses and performs his music, poetry, and dance.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-28) In 1993, he was awarded a [MacArthur Fellowship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacArthur_Fellows_Program "MacArthur Fellows Program").[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-29)[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-30) ## 2000s \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cecil_Taylor&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: 2000s")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f3/Cecil_Taylor_DSC0029.jpg/250px-Cecil_Taylor_DSC0029.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cecil_Taylor_DSC0029.jpg) Cecil Taylor, Buffalo, New York Taylor recorded sparingly in the 2000s, but continued to perform with his own ensembles (the Cecil Taylor Ensemble and the Cecil Taylor Big Band) and with other musicians such as [Joe Locke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Locke_(musician) "Joe Locke (musician)"), [Max Roach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Roach "Max Roach"), and [Amiri Baraka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amiri_Baraka "Amiri Baraka").[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-31) In 2004, the Cecil Taylor Big Band at the [Iridium Jazz Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iridium_Jazz_Club "Iridium Jazz Club") was nominated a best performance of 2004 by [All About Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_About_Jazz "All About Jazz").[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-AAJ-32) The Cecil Taylor Trio was nominated for the same at the [Highline Ballroom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highline_Ballroom "Highline Ballroom") in 2009.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-AAJ09-33) The trio consisted of Taylor, Albey Balgochian, and [Jackson Krall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_Krall "Jackson Krall"). In 2010, Triple Point Records released a deluxe [limited-edition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limited-edition "Limited-edition") double [LP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LP_record "LP record") titled _[Ailanthus/Altissima: Bilateral Dimensions of 2 Root Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ailanthus/Altissima:_Bilateral_Dimensions_of_2_Root_Songs "Ailanthus/Altissima: Bilateral Dimensions of 2 Root Songs")_, a set of duos with Taylor's longtime collaborator [Tony Oxley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Oxley "Tony Oxley") that was recorded live at the [Village Vanguard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Village_Vanguard "Village Vanguard").[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-34) In 2013, he was awarded the [Kyoto Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyoto_Prize_in_Arts_and_Philosophy "Kyoto Prize in Arts and Philosophy") for Music.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-Guardian_obit-35) He was described as "An Innovative Jazz Musician Who Has Fully Explored the Possibilities of Piano Improvisation".[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-Kyoto-36) In 2014, his career and 85th birthday were honored at the [Painted Bride Art Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Painted_Bride_Art_Center "Painted Bride Art Center") in [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia") with the tribute concert event "Celebrating Cecil".[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-37) In 2016, Taylor received a retrospective at the [Whitney Museum of American Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitney_Museum_of_American_Art "Whitney Museum of American Art") entitled "Open Plan: Cecil Taylor".[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-38) In 2008, Taylor performed with [Pauline Oliveros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pauline_Oliveros "Pauline Oliveros") at the [Curtis R Priem Experimental Media and Performing Arts Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experimental_Media_and_Performing_Arts_Center "Experimental Media and Performing Arts Center") at [Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rensselaer_Polytechnic_Institute "Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute"). The concert was recorded and is available on a DVD which also features a 75-minute video of a Taylor poetry recital entitled _Floating Gardens: The Poetry Of Cecil Taylor_.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-39)[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-40) Taylor, along with dancer [Min Tanaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Min_Tanaka "Min Tanaka"), was the subject of [Amiel Courtin-Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amiel_Courtin-Wilson "Amiel Courtin-Wilson")'s 2016 documentary film _The Silent Eye_.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-41) ## Ballet and dance \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cecil_Taylor&action=edit§ion=6 "Edit section: Ballet and dance")\] In addition to piano, Taylor was always interested in ballet and dance. His mother, who died while he was young, was a dancer and played the piano and violin. Taylor once said: "I try to imitate on the piano the leaps in space a dancer makes."[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-42) He collaborated with dancer [Dianne McIntyre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dianne_McIntyre "Dianne McIntyre") from the mid 1970s to the early 1980s.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-43) In 1979, he composed and played the music for a 12-minute ballet, "Tetra Stomp: Eatin' Rain in Space", featuring [Mikhail Baryshnikov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikhail_Baryshnikov "Mikhail Baryshnikov") and [Heather Watts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heather_Watts "Heather Watts").[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-44) ## Poetry \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cecil_Taylor&action=edit§ion=7 "Edit section: Poetry")\] Taylor was a poet, and cited [Robert Duncan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Duncan_(poet) "Robert Duncan (poet)"), [Charles Olson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Olson "Charles Olson"), and [Amiri Baraka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amiri_Baraka "Amiri Baraka") as major influences.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-45) He often integrated his poems into his musical performances, and they frequently appear in the [liner notes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liner_notes "Liner notes") of his albums. The album _[Chinampas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinampas_(album) "Chinampas (album)")_, released by [Leo Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Records "Leo Records") in 1987, is a recording of Taylor reciting several of his poems while accompanying himself on percussion.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-46) His poetry was likened to his music primarily by the ways in which Taylor alters and transforms material both linguistic and musical.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-47) ## Musical style and legacy \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cecil_Taylor&action=edit§ion=8 "Edit section: Musical style and legacy")\] According to Steven Block, [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") originated with Taylor's performances at the [Five Spot Cafe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Spot_Caf%C3%A9 "Five Spot Café") in 1957 and with [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman") in 1959.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-48) In 1964, Taylor co-founded the [Jazz Composers Guild](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Composers_Guild "Jazz Composers Guild") to enhance opportunities for [avant-garde jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz") musicians.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-Walden-49) Taylor's style and methods have been described as " [constructivist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constructivism_(art) "Constructivism (art)")".[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-50) Despite [Scott Yanow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Yanow "Scott Yanow")'s warning regarding Taylor's "forbidding music" ("Suffice it to say that Cecil Taylor's music is not for everyone"), he praises Taylor's "remarkable technique and endurance", and his "advanced", "radical", "original", and uncompromising "musical vision".[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-Yanow-5) This musical vision is a large part of Taylor's legacy: > Playing with Taylor I began to be liberated from thinking about chords. I'd been imitating John Coltrane unsuccessfully and because of that I was really chord conscious. — [Archie Shepp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Shepp "Archie Shepp"), quoted in [LeRoi Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amiri_Baraka "Amiri Baraka"), album liner notes for _Four for Trane_ (Impulse A-71, 1964) Scott Yanow of [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") wrote: "Taylor's high-energy atonalism fit in well with the free jazz of the period but he was actually leading the way rather than being part of a movement. \[...\] In fact, it could be safely argued that no jazz music of the era approached the ferocity and intensity of Cecil Taylor's."[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-51) ## Personal life and death \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cecil_Taylor&action=edit§ion=9 "Edit section: Personal life and death")\] Taylor moved to [Fort Greene, Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Greene,_Brooklyn "Fort Greene, Brooklyn"), in 1983.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-NYT2012-9) He died at his Brooklyn residence on April 5, 2018, at the age of 89.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-52)[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-53) At the time of his death, Taylor was working on an autobiography and future concerts, among other projects.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-Cecil_Taylor_Website-54) ## Discography \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cecil_Taylor&action=edit§ion=10 "Edit section: Discography")\] Main article: [Cecil Taylor discography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor_discography "Cecil Taylor discography") ## References \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cecil_Taylor&action=edit§ion=11 "Edit section: References")\] 01.
