Rollins was replaced by [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane"), completing the membership of the first quintet. To fulfill Davis's contract with Prestige, this new group worked through [two marathon sessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Legendary_Prestige_Quintet_Sessions "The Legendary Prestige Quintet Sessions") in May and October 1956 that were released by the label as four [LPs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LPs "LPs"): _[Cookin' with the Miles Davis Quintet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cookin'_with_the_Miles_Davis_Quintet "Cookin' with the Miles Davis Quintet")_ (1957), _[Relaxin' with the Miles Davis Quintet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relaxin'_with_the_Miles_Davis_Quintet "Relaxin' with the Miles Davis Quintet")_ (1958), _[Workin' with the Miles Davis Quintet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Workin'_with_the_Miles_Davis_Quintet "Workin' with the Miles Davis Quintet")_ (1960) and _[Steamin' with the Miles Davis Quintet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steamin'_with_the_Miles_Davis_Quintet "Steamin' with the Miles Davis Quintet")_ (1961). Each album was critically acclaimed and helped establish Davis's quintet as one of the best.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChambers1998223-76)[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook200745-77)[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarr199899-78) The style of the group was an extension of their experience playing with Davis. He played long, legato, melodic lines, while Coltrane contrasted with energetic solos. Their live repertoire was a mix of bebop, standards from the [Great American Songbook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_American_Songbook "Great American Songbook") and pre-bop eras, and traditional tunes. They appeared on _['Round About Midnight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/'Round_About_Midnight "'Round About Midnight")_, Davis's first album for Columbia.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-79) In 1956, he left his quintet temporarily to tour Europe as part of the Birdland All-Stars, which included the [Modern Jazz Quartet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_Jazz_Quartet "Modern Jazz Quartet") and French and German musicians. In Paris, he reunited with Gréco and they "were lovers for many years".[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989186-80)[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEarly2001215-81) He then returned home, reunited his quintet and toured the U.S. for two months. Conflict arose on tour when he grew impatient with the drug habits of Jones and Coltrane. Davis was trying to live a healthier life by exercising and reducing his use of alcohol, though he continued to use cocaine.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989209-82) At the end of the tour, he fired Jones and Coltrane and replaced them with Sonny Rollins and [Art Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Taylor "Art Taylor").[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989214-83) In November 1957, Davis went to Paris and recorded [the soundtrack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascenseur_pour_l'%C3%A9chafaud_(soundtrack) "Ascenseur pour l'échafaud (soundtrack)") to _[Ascenseur pour l'échafaud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_to_the_Gallows "Elevator to the Gallows"),_[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-New_Grove-42) directed by [Louis Malle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Malle "Louis Malle") and starring [Jeanne Moreau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeanne_Moreau "Jeanne Moreau"). Consisting of French jazz musicians [Barney Wilen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barney_Wilen "Barney Wilen"), [Pierre Michelot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Michelot "Pierre Michelot") and [René Urtreger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Urtreger "René Urtreger"), and American drummer [Kenny Clarke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Clarke "Kenny Clarke"), the group avoided a written score and instead improvised while they watched the film in a recording studio.[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-84) After returning to New York, Davis revived his quintet with alto saxophonist [Julian "Cannonball" Adderley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_%22Cannonball%22_Adderley "Julian \"Cannonball\" Adderley")[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-New_Grove-42) and Coltrane, who was clean from his drug habit. Now a sextet, the group recorded material in early 1958 that was released on _[Milestones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milestones_(Miles_Davis_album) "Milestones (Miles Davis album)")_, an album on which [the title track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milestones_(instrumental_composition) "Milestones (instrumental composition)") demonstrated Davis's interest in [modal jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz "Modal jazz"). A performance by [Les Ballets Africains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_Ballets_Africains "Les Ballets Africains") drew him to slower, deliberate music that allowed the creation of solos from static harmony rather than constant changing chords.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Complete_Illustrated_History''200797-85) By May 1958, he had replaced Jones with drummer [Jimmy Cobb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Cobb "Jimmy Cobb"), and Garland left the group, leaving Davis to play piano on "Sid's Ahead" for _Milestones_.[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989224-86) He wanted someone who could play modal jazz, so he hired [Bill Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans "Bill Evans"), a young pianist with a background in classical music. This new edition of the sextet made their recording debut on _[Jazz Track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Track "Jazz Track")_ (1958).[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989229-87) Evans had an [impressionistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impressionism_in_music "Impressionism in music") approach to piano. His ideas greatly influenced Davis. But after eight months of touring, a tired Evans left. [Wynton Kelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wynton_Kelly "Wynton Kelly"), his replacement, brought to the group a swinging style that contrasted with Evans's delicacy.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] ### 1957–1963: Collaborations with Gil Evans and _Kind of Blue_ \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Miles_Davis&action=edit§ion=7 "Edit section: 1957–1963: Collaborations with Gil Evans and Kind of Blue")\] By early 1957, Davis was exhausted from recording and touring and wished to pursue new projects. In March, the 30-year-old Davis told journalists of his intention to retire soon and revealed offers he had received to teach at [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University") and be a musical director at a record label.[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTESzwed2004139-88)[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarr1998107-89) Avakian agreed that it was time for Davis to explore something different, but Davis rejected his suggestion of returning to his nonet as he considered that a step backward.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarr1998107-89) Avakian then suggested that he work with a bigger ensemble, similar to _Music for Brass_ (1957), an album of orchestral and brass-arranged music led by [Gunther Schuller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunther_Schuller "Gunther Schuller") featuring Davis as a guest soloist.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] Davis accepted and worked with Gil Evans in what became a five-album collaboration from 1957 to 1962.[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTESzwed2004140-90) _[Miles Ahead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Ahead_(album) "Miles Ahead (album)")_ (1957) showcased Davis on [flugelhorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flugelhorn "Flugelhorn") and included a rendition of "The Maids of Cadiz" by [Léo Delibes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A9o_Delibes "Léo Delibes"), the first piece of classical music that Davis recorded. Evans devised orchestral passages as transitions, thus turning the album into one long piece of music.[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTESzwed2004141-91)[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-92) _[Porgy and Bess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porgy_and_Bess_(Miles_Davis_album) "Porgy and Bess (Miles Davis album)")_ (1959) includes arrangements of pieces from [George Gershwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Gershwin "George Gershwin")'s [opera of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porgy_and_Bess "Porgy and Bess"). _[Sketches of Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sketches_of_Spain "Sketches of Spain")_ (1960) contained music by [Joaquín Rodrigo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joaqu%C3%ADn_Rodrigo "Joaquín Rodrigo") and [Manuel de Falla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_de_Falla "Manuel de Falla") as well as originals by Evans. The classical musicians had trouble improvising, while the jazz musicians could not handle the difficult arrangements, but the album was a critical success, selling more than 120,000 copies in the U.S.[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Complete_Illustrated_History''2007108-93) Davis performed with an orchestra conducted by Evans at [Carnegie Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Hall "Carnegie Hall") in May 1961 to raise money for charity.[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Complete_Illustrated_History''2007109-94) The pair's final album was _[Quiet Nights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quiet_Nights_(Miles_Davis_album) "Quiet Nights (Miles Davis album)")_ (1963), a collection of [bossa nova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bossa_nova "Bossa nova") songs, released against their wishes. Evans stated it was only half an album and blamed the record company; Davis blamed producer [Teo Macero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teo_Macero "Teo Macero") and refused to speak to him for over two years.[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarr1998192%E2%80%93193-95) The box set _[Miles Davis & Gil Evans: The Complete Columbia Studio Recordings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis_&_Gil_Evans:_The_Complete_Columbia_Studio_Recordings "Miles Davis & Gil Evans: The Complete Columbia Studio Recordings")_ (1996) won the [Grammy Award for Best Historical Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Historical_Album "Grammy Award for Best Historical Album") and [Best Album Notes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Best_Album_Notes "Best Album Notes") in 1997.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] In March and April 1959, Davis recorded what some consider his greatest album, _[Kind of Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue "Kind of Blue")_. He named the album for its mood.[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Complete_Illustrated_History''2007106-96) He called back Bill Evans, as the music had been planned around Evans's piano style.[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKahn2001a95-97) Both Davis and Evans were familiar with [George Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Russell_(composer) "George Russell (composer)")'s ideas about modal jazz.[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKahn2001a29%E2%80%9330,_74-98) But Davis neglected to tell pianist Wynton Kelly that Evans was returning, so Kelly appeared on only one song, " [Freddie Freeloader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Freeloader "Freddie Freeloader")".[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKahn2001a95-97) The sextet had played " [So What](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/So_What_(Miles_Davis_composition) "So What (Miles Davis composition)")" and " [All Blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Blues "All Blues")" at performances, but the remaining three compositions they saw for the first time in the studio.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] Released in August 1959, _Kind of Blue_ was an instant success, with widespread radio airplay and rave reviews from critics.[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Complete_Illustrated_History''2007106-96) It has remained a strong seller over the years. In 2019, the album achieved [5× platinum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RIAA_certification "RIAA certification") certification from the [Recording Industry Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America "Recording Industry Association of America") for sales of more than five million copies in the U.S., making it one of the most successful jazz albums in history.[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-riaa-99) In 2009, the [U.S. House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._House_of_Representatives "U.S. House of Representatives") passed a resolution that honored it as a national treasure.[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-100)[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-101) In August 1959, during a break in a recording session at the [Birdland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birdland_(New_York_jazz_club) "Birdland (New York jazz club)") nightclub in New York City, Davis was escorting a blonde-haired woman to a taxi outside the club when policeman Gerald Kilduff told him to "move on".[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThe_Complete_Illustrated_History2007100-102)[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-arrest-103) Davis said that he was working at the club, and he refused to move.[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-104) Kilduff arrested and grabbed Davis as he tried to protect himself. Witnesses said the policeman hit Davis in the stomach with a nightstick without provocation. Two detectives held the crowd back, while a third approached Davis from behind and beat him over the head. Davis was taken to jail, charged with assaulting an officer, then taken to the hospital where he received five stitches.[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-arrest-103) By January 1960, he was acquitted of disorderly conduct and third-degree assault. He later stated that the incident "changed my whole life and whole attitude again, made me feel bitter and cynical again when I was starting to feel good about the things that had changed in this country".[\[104\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEarly200189-105) Davis and his sextet toured to support _Kind of Blue_.[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Complete_Illustrated_History''2007106-96) [Cannonball Adderley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannonball_Adderley "Cannonball Adderley") left the group September of that year reducing the band back to a quintet. Coltrane was ready to leave as well, but Davis persuaded him to play with the group on one final European tour in the spring of 1960. Coltrane then departed to form his quartet, though he returned for a couple tracks on Davis's album _[Someday My Prince Will Come](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Someday_My_Prince_Will_Come_(Miles_Davis_album) "Someday My Prince Will Come (Miles Davis album)")_ (1961). Its front cover shows a photograph of Davis's wife, [Frances Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frances_Taylor_Davis "Frances Taylor Davis"), after Davis demanded that Columbia depict black women on his album covers.[\[105\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989252-106) ### 1963–1968: Second quintet \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Miles_Davis&action=edit§ion=8 "Edit section: 1963–1968: Second quintet")\] [![Davis, in a white blazer, standing center on stage and playing trumpet; behind him are Ron Cater on bass and Tony Williams at the drum set](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/93/Miles_Davis_%28Antibes_Juan-les-Pins_1963%29.jpg/250px-Miles_Davis_%28Antibes_Juan-les-Pins_1963%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Miles_Davis_(Antibes_Juan-les-Pins_1963).jpg) Davis performing in [Antibes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antibes "Antibes"), France, in July 1963. Behind him are bassist [Ron Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Carter "Ron Carter") and drummer [Tony Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer) "Tony Williams (drummer)"). In December 1962, Davis, Rollins, Kelly, Chambers and Cobb played together for the last time, as the latter three wanted to leave and play as a trio. Rollins left them soon after, leaving Davis to pay more than $25,000 (equivalent to $266,100in 2025[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-inflation-US-34)) to cancel upcoming gigs and quickly assemble a new group. Following auditions, he found his new band in tenor saxophonist [George Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Coleman "George Coleman"), bassist [Ron Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Carter "Ron Carter"), pianist [Victor Feldman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Feldman "Victor Feldman") and drummer [Frank Butler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Butler_(musician) "Frank Butler (musician)").[\[106\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989260%E2%80%93262-107) By May 1963, Feldman and Butler were replaced by 23-year-old pianist [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock") and 17-year-old drummer [Tony Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer) "Tony Williams (drummer)"), who made Davis "excited all over again".[\[107\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989262-108) With this group, Davis completed the rest of what became _[Seven Steps to Heaven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Steps_to_Heaven "Seven Steps to Heaven")_ (1963) and recorded the live albums _[Miles Davis in Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis_in_Europe "Miles Davis in Europe")_ (1964), _[My Funny Valentine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_Funny_Valentine:_Miles_Davis_in_Concert "My Funny Valentine: Miles Davis in Concert")_ (1965) and _[Four & More](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_&_More "Four & More")_ (1966). The quintet played essentially the same bebop tunes and standards that Davis's previous bands had played, but they approached them with structural and rhythmic freedom and occasionally breakneck speed.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] In 1964, Coleman was briefly replaced by saxophonist [Sam Rivers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Rivers_(jazz_musician) "Sam Rivers (jazz musician)") (who recorded with Davis on _[Miles in Tokyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_in_Tokyo "Miles in Tokyo")_) until [Wayne Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter "Wayne Shorter") was persuaded to leave [the Jazz Messengers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Jazz_Messengers "The Jazz Messengers"). The quintet with Shorter lasted through 1968, with Shorter becoming the group's principal composer. The album _[E.S.P.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E.S.P._(Miles_Davis_album) "E.S.P. (Miles Davis album)")_ (1965) was named after one of his compositions. While touring Europe, the group made its first album, _[Miles in Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_in_Berlin "Miles in Berlin")_ (1965).[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEinarson200556%E2%80%9357-109) [![Davis, standing on stage; he holds his trumpet beside him in his left hand and rests his head on his right hand](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/12/Miles-Davis-1964-Helsinki.jpg/250px-Miles-Davis-1964-Helsinki.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Miles-Davis-1964-Helsinki.jpg) Davis performing at [Töölö Sports Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C3%B6%C3%B6l%C3%B6_Sports_Hall "Töölö Sports Hall") (Messuhalli) in [Helsinki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helsinki "Helsinki"), Finland, October 1964 Davis needed medical attention for hip pain, which had worsened since his Japanese tour during the previous year.[\[109\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarr1998202-110) He underwent [hip replacement surgery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip_replacement_surgery "Hip replacement surgery") in April 1965, with bone taken from his shin, but it failed. After his third month in the hospital, he discharged himself due to boredom and went home. He returned to the hospital in August after a fall required the insertion of a plastic hip joint.[\[110\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarr1998203-111) In November 1965, he had recovered enough to return to performing with his quintet, which included [gigs at the Plugged Nickel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Complete_Live_at_the_Plugged_Nickel_1965 "The Complete Live at the Plugged Nickel 1965") in Chicago. Teo Macero returned as his record producer after their rift over _Quiet Nights_ had healed.[\[111\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989282%E2%80%93283-112)[\[112\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarr1998204-113) In January 1966, Davis spent three months in the hospital with a liver infection. When he resumed touring, he performed more at colleges because he had grown tired of the typical jazz venues.[\[113\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989283-114) Columbia president [Clive Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_Davis "Clive Davis") reported in 1966 that Davis's sales had declined to around 40,000–50,000 per album, compared to as many as 100,000 per release a few years before. Matters were not helped by the press reporting his apparent financial troubles and imminent demise.[\[114\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarr1998209%E2%80%93210-115) After his appearance at the 1966 Newport Jazz Festival, he returned to the studio with his quintet for a series of sessions. He started a relationship with actress [Cicely Tyson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cicely_Tyson "Cicely Tyson"), who helped him reduce his alcohol consumption.[\[115\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989284-116) Material from the 1966–1968 sessions was released on _[Miles Smiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Smiles "Miles Smiles")_ (1966), _[Sorcerer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sorcerer_(Miles_Davis_album) "Sorcerer (Miles Davis album)")_ (1967), _[Nefertiti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nefertiti_(Miles_Davis_album) "Nefertiti (Miles Davis album)")_ (1967), _[Miles in the Sky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_in_the_Sky "Miles in the Sky")_ (1968) and _[Filles de Kilimanjaro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filles_de_Kilimanjaro "Filles de Kilimanjaro")_ (1968). The quintet's approach to the new music became known as "time no changes"—which referred to Davis's decision to depart from chordal sequences and adopt a more open approach, with the rhythm section responding to the soloists' melodies.[\[116\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorton200549-117) Through _Nefertiti_, the studio recordings consisted primarily of originals composed by Shorter, with occasional compositions by the other sidemen. In 1967, the group began to play their concerts in continuous sets, each tune flowing into the next, with only the melody indicating any sort of change. His bands performed this way until his hiatus in 1975.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] _Miles in the Sky_ and _Filles de Kilimanjaro_—which tentatively introduced electric bass, electric piano and electric guitar on some tracks—pointed the way to the [fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") phase in Davis's career.[\[117\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-118) He also began experimenting with more rock-oriented rhythms on these records. By the time the second half of _Filles de Kilimanjaro_ was recorded, bassist [Dave Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Holland_(bassist) "Dave Holland (bassist)") and pianist [Chick Corea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chick_Corea "Chick Corea") had replaced Carter and Hancock. Davis soon took over the compositional duties of his sidemen.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] ### 1968–1975: The electric period \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Miles_Davis&action=edit§ion=9 "Edit section: 1968–1975: The electric period")\] _[In a Silent Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way "In a Silent Way")_ was recorded in a single studio session in February 1969, with Shorter, Hancock, Holland and Williams alongside keyboardists [Chick Corea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chick_Corea "Chick Corea") and [Joe Zawinul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Zawinul "Joe Zawinul") and guitarist [John McLaughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McLaughlin_(musician) "John McLaughlin (musician)"). The album contains two side-long tracks that Macero pieced together from different takes recorded at the session. When the album was released later that year, some critics accused him of "selling out" to the [rock and roll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_roll "Rock and roll") audience. Nevertheless, it reached No. 134 on the U.S. [_Billboard_ Top LPs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") chart, his first album since _My Funny Valentine_ to reach the chart. _In a Silent Way_ was his entry into [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion"). The touring band of 1969–1970—with Shorter, Corea, Holland and [Jack DeJohnette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_DeJohnette "Jack DeJohnette")—never completed a studio recording together, and became known as Davis's "lost quintet", though radio broadcasts from the band's European tour have been extensively [bootlegged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bootleg_recording "Bootleg recording").[\[118\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-119)[\[119\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-120) [![Davis playing trumpet, holding it close in to his chest and tilting his head down. He is wearing sunglasses, a white band on his left wrist and a sweater.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b2/Miles_Davis-140916-0016-103WPA.jpg/250px-Miles_Davis-140916-0016-103WPA.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Miles_Davis-140916-0016-103WPA.jpg) Davis performing in 1971 For the double album _[Bitches Brew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew "Bitches Brew")_ (1970), he hired Jack DeJohnette, [Harvey Brooks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_Brooks_(bassist) "Harvey Brooks (bassist)") and [Bennie Maupin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bennie_Maupin "Bennie Maupin"). The album contained long compositions, some exceeding twenty minutes, which more often than not, were constructed from several takes by Macero and Davis via splicing and [tape loops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tape_loop "Tape loop") amid epochal advances in multitrack recording technologies.[\[120\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreeman200583%E2%80%9384-121) _Bitches Brew_ peaked at No. 35 on the [_Billboard_ Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") chart.[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Bitches-122) In 1976, it was [certified gold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Certified_gold "Certified gold") for selling more than 500,000 records. By 2003, it had sold one million copies.[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-riaa-99) In March 1970, Davis began to perform as the opening act for rock bands, allowing Columbia to market _Bitches Brew_ to a larger audience. He shared a [Fillmore East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fillmore_East "Fillmore East") bill with the [Steve Miller Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Miller_Band "Steve Miller Band") and [Neil Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young "Neil Young") with [Crazy Horse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crazy_Horse_(band) "Crazy Horse (band)") on March 6 and 7.[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Complete_Illustrated_History''2007150-123) Biographer [Paul Tingen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tingen "Paul Tingen") wrote, "Miles' newcomer status in this environment" led to "mixed audience reactions, often having to play for dramatically reduced fees, and enduring the 'sell-out' accusations from the jazz world", as well as being "attacked by sections of the black press for supposedly genuflecting to white culture".[\[123\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTETingen2001114-124) The 1970 tours included the [Isle of Wight Festival 1970](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isle_of_Wight_Festival_1970 "Isle of Wight Festival 1970") on August 29 when he performed to an estimated 600,000 people, the largest of his career.[\[124\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Complete_Illustrated_History''2007153-125) Plans to record with [Jimi Hendrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimi_Hendrix "Jimi Hendrix") ended after the guitarist's death; his funeral was the last one that Davis attended.[\[125\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989318%E2%80%93319-126) Several live albums with a transitional sextet/septet including Corea, DeJohnette, Holland, [Airto Moreira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airto_Moreira "Airto Moreira"), saxophonist [Steve Grossman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Grossman_(saxophonist) "Steve Grossman (saxophonist)") and keyboardist [Keith Jarrett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett "Keith Jarrett") were recorded during this period, including _[Miles Davis at Fillmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis_at_Fillmore "Miles Davis at Fillmore")_ (1970) and _[Black Beauty: Miles Davis at Fillmore West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Beauty:_Miles_Davis_at_Fillmore_West "Black Beauty: Miles Davis at Fillmore West")_ (1973).[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Miles_Davis-11) By 1971, Davis had signed a contract with Columbia that paid him $100,000 a year (equivalent to $794,990in 2025[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-inflation-US-34)) for three years in addition to royalties.[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarr1998302-127) He recorded a soundtrack album ( _[Jack Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Johnson_(album) "Jack Johnson (album)")_) for [the 1970 documentary film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Johnson_(film) "Jack Johnson (film)") about heavyweight boxer [Jack Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Johnson "Jack Johnson"), containing two long pieces 25 and 26 minutes in length, with Hancock, McLaughlin, [Sonny Sharrock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Sharrock "Sonny Sharrock") and [Billy Cobham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Cobham "Billy Cobham"). He was committed to making music for African-Americans who liked more commercial, pop, groove-oriented music. By November 1971, DeJohnette and Moreira had been replaced in the touring ensemble by drummer [Leon "Ndugu" Chancler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leon_%22Ndugu%22_Chancler "Leon \"Ndugu\" Chancler") and percussionists [James Mtume](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Mtume "James Mtume") and [Don Alias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Alias "Don Alias").[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-128) _[Live-Evil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live-Evil_(Miles_Davis_album) "Live-Evil (Miles Davis album)")_ was released in the same month. Showcasing bassist [Michael Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Henderson "Michael Henderson"), who had replaced Holland in 1970, the album demonstrated that Davis's ensemble had transformed into a [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk")-oriented group while retaining the exploratory imperative of _Bitches Brew_.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] [![Performing on-stage with his septet, Davis is playing trumpet, leaning over. The members of his band, with their instruments, surround him.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/Miles_Davis-140916-0018-105WPa.jpg/250px-Miles_Davis-140916-0018-105WPa.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Miles_Davis-140916-0018-105WPa.jpg) Davis's septet in November 1971; _from left_: [Gary Bartz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Bartz "Gary Bartz"), Davis, [Keith Jarrett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett "Keith Jarrett"), [Michael Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Henderson "Michael Henderson"), [Leon "Ndugu" Chancler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leon_%22Ndugu%22_Chancler "Leon \"Ndugu\" Chancler"), [James Mtume](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Mtume "James Mtume") and [Don Alias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Alias "Don Alias") In 1972, composer-arranger [Paul Buckmaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Buckmaster "Paul Buckmaster") introduced Davis to the music of the avant-garde composer [Karlheinz Stockhausen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karlheinz_Stockhausen "Karlheinz Stockhausen"), leading to a period of creative exploration. Biographer J. K. Chambers wrote, "The effect of Davis' study of Stockhausen could not be repressed for long... Davis' own 'space music' shows Stockhausen's influence compositionally."[\[128\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChambers1998246-129) His recordings and performances during this period were described as "space music" by fans, Feather, and Buckmaster, who described it as "a lot of mood changes—heavy, dark, intense—definitely space music".[\[129\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarr1998-130)[\[130\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-131) The studio album _[On the Corner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner "On the Corner")_ (1972) blended the influence of Stockhausen and Buckmaster with funk elements. Davis invited Buckmaster to New York City to oversee the writing and recording of the album with Macero.[\[131\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorton200572%E2%80%9373-132) The album reached No. 1 on the _Billboard_ jazz chart but peaked at No. 156 on the more heterogeneous [Top 200 Albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Top_200_Albums "Top 200 Albums") chart. Davis felt that Columbia marketed it to the wrong audience: "The music was meant to be heard by young black people, but they just treated it like any other jazz album and advertised it that way, pushed it on the jazz radio stations. Young black kids don't listen to those stations; they listen to R&B stations and some rock stations."[\[132\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989328-133) In October 1972, he broke his ankles in a car crash. He took painkillers and cocaine to cope with the pain.[\[133\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECole200528-134) Looking back at his career after the incident, he wrote, "Everything started to blur."[\[134\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Complete_Illustrated_History''2007154-135) After recording _On the Corner_, he assembled a group with Henderson, Mtume, [Carlos Garnett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Garnett "Carlos Garnett"), guitarist [Reggie Lucas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggie_Lucas "Reggie Lucas"), organist [Lonnie Liston Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lonnie_Liston_Smith "Lonnie Liston Smith"), [tabla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabla "Tabla") player [Badal Roy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Badal_Roy "Badal Roy"), sitarist [Khalil Balakrishna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khalil_Balakrishna "Khalil Balakrishna") and drummer [Al Foster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Foster "Al Foster"). In striking contrast to that of his previous lineups, the music emphasized rhythmic density and shifting textures instead of solos. This group was recorded live in 1972 for _[In Concert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_Concert_(Miles_Davis_album) "In Concert (Miles Davis album)")_, but Davis found it unsatisfactory, leading him to drop the tabla and sitar and play organ himself. He also added guitarist [Pete Cosey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Cosey "Pete Cosey"). The compilation studio album _[Big Fun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Fun_(Miles_Davis_album) "Big Fun (Miles Davis album)")_ contains four long improvisations recorded between 1969 and 1972.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] > This was music that polarized audiences, provoking boos and walk-outs amid the ecstasy of others. The length, density, and unforgiving nature of it mocked those who said that Miles was interested only in being trendy and popular. Some have heard in this music the feel and shape of a musician's late work, an egoless music that precedes its creator's death. As [Theodor Adorno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodor_Adorno "Theodor Adorno") said of the late [Beethoven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beethoven "Beethoven"), the disappearance of the musician into the work is a bow to mortality. It was as if Miles were testifying to all that he had been witness to for the past thirty years, both terrifying and joyful. — [John Szwed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Szwed "John Szwed") on _[Agharta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album) "Agharta (album)")_ (1975) and _[Pangaea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pangaea_(album) "Pangaea (album)")_ (1976)[\[135\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTESzwed2004343-136) Studio sessions throughout 1973 and 1974 led to _[Get Up with It](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Get_Up_with_It "Get Up with It")_, an album that included four long pieces alongside four shorter recordings from 1970 and 1972. The track "He Loved Him Madly", a 30-minute tribute to the then-recently deceased [Duke Ellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Ellington "Duke Ellington"), influenced [Brian Eno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Eno "Brian Eno")'s [ambient music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambient_music "Ambient music").[\[136\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-137) In the United States, it performed comparably to _On the Corner_, reaching No. 8 on the jazz chart and No. 141 on the pop chart. He then concentrated on live performance with a series of concerts that Columbia released on the double live albums _[Agharta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album) "Agharta (album)")_ (1975), _[Pangaea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pangaea_(album) "Pangaea (album)")_ (1976) and _[Dark Magus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_Magus "Dark Magus")_ (1977). The first two are recordings of two sets from February 1, 1975, in [Osaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osaka "Osaka"), by which time Davis was troubled by several physical ailments; he relied on alcohol, codeine and morphine to get through the engagements. His shows were routinely panned by critics who mentioned his habit of performing with his back to the audience.[\[137\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Complete_Illustrated_History''2007177-138) Cosey later asserted that "the band really advanced after the Japanese tour",[\[138\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTETingen2001167-139) but Davis was again hospitalized, for his ulcers and a [hernia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hernia "Hernia"), during a tour of the U.S. while opening for Herbie Hancock.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] After appearances at the 1975 Newport Jazz Festival in July and the [Schaefer Music Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schaefer_Music_Festival "Schaefer Music Festival") in New York in September, Davis dropped out of music.[\[137\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Complete_Illustrated_History''2007177-138)[\[139\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-140) ### 1975–1980: Hiatus \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Miles_Davis&action=edit§ion=10 "Edit section: 1975–1980: Hiatus")\] In his autobiography, Davis wrote frankly about his life during his hiatus from music. He called his [Upper West Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_West_Side "Upper West Side") brownstone a wreck and chronicled his heavy use of alcohol and cocaine, in addition to sexual encounters with many women.[\[140\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarr1998330-141) He also stated that "Sex and drugs took the place music had occupied in my life." Drummer Tony Williams recalled that by noon (on average) Davis would be sick from the previous night's intake.[\[141\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Byrnes-2005-142) In December 1975, he had regained enough strength to undergo a much-needed hip replacement operation.[\[142\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorton200576-143) In December 1976, Columbia was reluctant to renew his contract and pay his usual large advances. But after his lawyer started negotiating with [United Artists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Artists_Records "United Artists Records"), Columbia matched its offer, establishing the Miles Davis Fund to pay him regularly. Pianist [Vladimir Horowitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Horowitz "Vladimir Horowitz") was the only other musician with CBS Records who had similar status.[\[143\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarr1998329-144) In 1978, Davis asked [fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") guitarist [Larry Coryell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Coryell "Larry Coryell") to participate in sessions with keyboardists [Masabumi Kikuchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masabumi_Kikuchi "Masabumi Kikuchi") and George Pavlis, bassist [T. M. Stevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._M._Stevens "T. M. Stevens") and drummer [Al Foster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Foster "Al Foster").[\[144\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECole200536-145) Davis played the arranged piece uptempo, abandoned his trumpet for the organ, and had Macero record the session without the band's knowledge. After Coryell declined a spot in a band that Davis was beginning to put together, Davis returned to his reclusive lifestyle in New York City.[\[145\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTESzwed2004347-146)[\[146\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorton200577,_78-147) Soon after, Marguerite Eskridge had Davis jailed for failing to pay child support for their son Erin, which cost him $10,000 (equivalent to $49,360in 2025[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-inflation-US-34)) for release on bail.[\[142\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorton200576-143)[\[144\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECole200536-145) A recording session that involved Buckmaster and Gil Evans was halted,[\[147\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECole200538-148) with Evans leaving after failing to receive the payment he was promised. In August 1978, Davis hired a new manager, Mark Rothbaum, who had worked with him since 1972.[\[148\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTESzwed2004358-149) ### 1980–1985: Comeback \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Miles_Davis&action=edit§ion=11 "Edit section: 1980–1985: Comeback")\] Having played the trumpet little throughout the previous three years, Davis found it difficult to reclaim his [embouchure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embouchure "Embouchure"). His first post-hiatus studio appearance took place in May 1980.[\[149\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorton200579-150) A day later, Davis was hospitalized due to a leg infection.[\[150\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarr1998349-151) He recorded _[The Man with the Horn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Man_with_the_Horn "The Man with the Horn")_ from June 1980 to May 1981 with Macero producing. A large band was abandoned in favor of a combo with saxophonist [Bill Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans_(saxophonist) "Bill Evans (saxophonist)") and bassist [Marcus Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Miller "Marcus Miller"). Both would collaborate with him during the next decade.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] _The Man with the Horn_ received a poor critical reception despite selling well. In June 1981, Davis returned to the stage for the first time since 1975 in a ten-minute guest solo as part of [Mel Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel_Lewis "Mel Lewis")'s band at the [Village Vanguard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Village_Vanguard "Village Vanguard").[\[151\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECole200592-152) This was followed by appearances with a new band.[\[152\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarr1998363-153)[\[153\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorton200577-154) Recordings from a mixture of dates from 1981, including from the Kix in Boston and [Avery Fisher Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avery_Fisher_Hall "Avery Fisher Hall"), were released on _[We Want Miles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/We_Want_Miles "We Want Miles")_,[\[154\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorton200578-155) which earned him a [Grammy Award for Best Jazz Instrumental Performance by a Soloist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Jazz_Instrumental_Album "Grammy Award for Best Jazz Instrumental Album").[\[155\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Complete_Illustrated_History''2007180-156) [![Davis, leaning over, playing trumpet. He has on sunglasses and two pendant necklaces and is wearing a reflective set of textured blazer and striped pants.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/92/Miles_Davis_23.jpg/250px-Miles_Davis_23.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Miles_Davis_23.jpg) Davis performing in 1985 In January 1982, while Tyson was working in Africa, Davis "went a little wild" with alcohol and suffered a stroke that temporarily paralyzed his right hand.[\[156\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989348%E2%80%93350-157)[\[157\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEarly2001222-158) Tyson returned home and cared for him. After three months of treatment with a Chinese acupuncturist, he was able to play the trumpet again. He listened to his doctor's warnings and gave up alcohol and drugs. He credited Tyson with helping his recovery, which involved exercise, piano playing and visits to spas. She encouraged him to draw, which he pursued for the rest of his life.[\[156\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1989348%E2%80%93350-157) [Takao Ogawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takao_Ogawa "Takao Ogawa"), a Japanese jazz journalist who befriended Davis during this period, took pictures of his drawings and put them in his book along with the interviews of Davis at his apartment in New York. Davis told Ogawa, "I'm interested in line and color, line is like phrase and coating colors is like code. When I see good paintings, I hear good music. That is why my paintings are the same as my music. They are different than any paintings."[\[158\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-159) Davis resumed touring in May 1982 with a lineup that included percussionist [Mino Cinélu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mino_Cin%C3%A9lu "Mino Cinélu") and guitarist [John Scofield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Scofield "John Scofield"), with whom he worked closely on the album _[Star People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_People "Star People")_ (1983). In mid-1983, he worked on the tracks for _[Decoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decoy_(album) "Decoy (album)")_, an album mixing soul music and [electronica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronica "Electronica") that was released in 1984. He brought in producer, composer and keyboardist [Robert Irving III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Irving_III "Robert Irving III"), who had collaborated with him on _The Man with the Horn_. With a seven-piece band that included Scofield, Evans, Irving, Foster and [Darryl Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darryl_Jones "Darryl Jones"), he played a series of European performances that were positively received. In December 1984, while in Denmark, he was awarded the [Léonie Sonning Music Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A9onie_Sonning_Music_Prize "Léonie Sonning Music Prize"). Trumpeter [Palle Mikkelborg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palle_Mikkelborg "Palle Mikkelborg") had written "Aura", a contemporary classical piece, for the event, which impressed Davis to the point of returning to Denmark in early 1985 to record his next studio album, _[Aura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aura_(Miles_Davis_album) "Aura (Miles Davis album)")_.[\[159\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Complete_Illustrated_History''2007183-160) Columbia was dissatisfied with the recording and delayed its release.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] In May 1985, one month into a tour, Davis signed a contract with [Warner Bros.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Records "Warner Records") that required him to give up his publishing rights.[\[160\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECole2005352-161)[\[161\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Complete_Illustrated_History''2007194-162) _[You're Under Arrest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You're_Under_Arrest_(Miles_Davis_album) "You're Under Arrest (Miles Davis album)")_, his final album for Columbia, was released in September. It included cover versions of two pop songs: " [Time After Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_After_Time_(Cyndi_Lauper_song) "Time After Time (Cyndi Lauper song)")" by [Cyndi Lauper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyndi_Lauper "Cyndi Lauper") and [Michael Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Jackson "Michael Jackson")'s " [Human Nature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Nature_(Michael_Jackson_song) "Human Nature (Michael Jackson song)")". He considered releasing an album of pop songs, and he recorded dozens of them, but the idea was rejected. He said that many of today's jazz standards had been pop songs in [Broadway theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_theatre "Broadway theatre") and that he was simply updating the standards repertoire.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] Davis collaborated with a number of figures from the British [post-punk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-punk "Post-punk") and [new wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_wave "New wave") movements during this period, including [Scritti Politti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scritti_Politti "Scritti Politti").[\[162\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-163) This period also saw Davis move from his funk-inspired sound of the early 1970s to a more melodic style.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Cook-1985-35) ### 1986–1991: Final years \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Miles_Davis&action=edit§ion=12 "Edit section: 1986–1991: Final years")\] [![Davis, looking out to the crowd, from on stage. He is holding his trumpet in front of him and is wearing sunglasses, a white cuff bracelet and a reflective blazer.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ac/Miles_Davis_Strasbourg_face_2.jpg/250px-Miles_Davis_Strasbourg_face_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Miles_Davis_Strasbourg_face_2.jpg) Davis performing in [Strasbourg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strasbourg "Strasbourg"), 1987 After taking part in the recording of the 1985 protest song " [Sun City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_City_(song) "Sun City (song)")" as a member of [Artists United Against Apartheid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artists_United_Against_Apartheid "Artists United Against Apartheid"), Davis appeared on the instrumental "Don't Stop Me Now" by [Toto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toto_(band) "Toto (band)") on its album _[Fahrenheit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fahrenheit_(Toto_album) "Fahrenheit (Toto album)")_ (1986). Davis collaborated with [Prince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_(musician) "Prince (musician)") on a song titled "Can I Play With U", which went unreleased until 2020.[\[163\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-164) Davis also collaborated with Zane Giles and [Randy Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Hall "Randy Hall") on the _[Rubberband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubberband_(Miles_Davis_album) "Rubberband (Miles Davis album)")_ sessions in 1985, but those would remain unreleased until 2019.[\[164\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-announce-165) Instead, he worked with Marcus Miller, and _[Tutu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tutu_(album) "Tutu (album)")_ (1986) became the first time he used modern studio tools such as programmed synthesizers, [sampling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sampling_(music) "Sampling (music)") and [drum loops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drum_loops "Drum loops"). Released in September 1986, its front cover is a photographic portrait of Davis by [Irving Penn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irving_Penn "Irving Penn").[\[161\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Complete_Illustrated_History''2007194-162) In 1987, he won a Grammy Award for [Best Jazz Instrumental Performance, Soloist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Best_Jazz_Instrumental_Performance,_Soloist "Best Jazz Instrumental Performance, Soloist"). In 1987, Davis contacted American journalist [Quincy Troupe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quincy_Troupe "Quincy Troupe") to work with him on his autobiography.[\[165\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Broeske-2006-166) The two men had met the previous year when Troupe conducted a two-day-long interview, which was published by _[Spin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin_(magazine) "Spin (magazine)")_ as a 45-page article.[\[165\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-Broeske-2006-166) In 1988, Davis had a small part as a street musician in the Christmas comedy film _[Scrooged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scrooged "Scrooged")_ starring [Bill Murray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Murray "Bill Murray"). He also collaborated with the Italian blues musician [Zucchero Fornaciari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zucchero_Fornaciari "Zucchero Fornaciari") in a version of "Dune Mosse" ( _[Blue's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue's "Blue's")_), published in 2004 in the compilation _[Zu & Co.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zu_&_Co. "Zu & Co.")_ In November 1988, he was inducted into the [Sovereign Military Order of Malta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereign_Military_Order_of_Malta "Sovereign Military Order of Malta") at a ceremony at the [Alhambra Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alhambra_Palace "Alhambra Palace") in Spain.[\[166\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTETroupe2002388-167)[\[167\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarr1998496-168)[\[168\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGelbard201273%E2%80%9374-169) Later that month, Davis cut his European tour short after he collapsed and fainted after a two-hour show in Madrid, and he flew home.[\[169\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-170) There were rumors of more poor health reported by the American magazine _[Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_(magazine) "Star (magazine)")_ in its February 21, 1989, edition, which published a claim that Davis had contracted [AIDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIDS "AIDS"), prompting his manager Peter Shukat to issue a statement the following day. Shukat said Davis had been in the hospital for a mild case of pneumonia and the removal of a benign polyp on his vocal cords and was resting comfortably in preparation for his 1989 tours.[\[170\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-latimes1989-171) Davis later blamed one of his former wives or girlfriends for starting the rumor and decided against taking legal action.[\[171\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTETingen2001263-172) He was interviewed on _[60 Minutes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/60_Minutes "60 Minutes")_ by [Harry Reasoner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Reasoner "Harry Reasoner"). In October 1989, he received a [Grande Medaille de Vermeil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_the_City_of_Paris "Medal of the City of Paris") from Paris mayor [Jacques Chirac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Chirac "Jacques Chirac").[\[172\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChambers1998Introduction,_xv-173) In 1990, he received a [Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Lifetime_Achievement_Award "Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award").[\[173\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTECole2005443-174) In early 1991, he appeared in the [Rolf de Heer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolf_de_Heer "Rolf de Heer") film _[Dingo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dingo_(film) "Dingo (film)")_ as a jazz musician.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] [![A close-up of Davis playing trumpet with only his right hand, facing downward.
