- gamelan | Musical artist **Donald Eugene Cherry** (November 18, 1936 – October 19, 1995)[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-1) was an American jazz trumpeter, bandleader, and multi-instrumentalist. Beginning in the late 1950s, he had a long tenure performing in the bands of saxophonist [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman"), including on the pioneering [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") albums _[The Shape of Jazz to Come](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shape_of_Jazz_to_Come "The Shape of Jazz to Come")_ (1959) and _[Free Jazz: A Collective Improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Jazz:_A_Collective_Improvisation "Free Jazz: A Collective Improvisation")_ (1961). Cherry also collaborated separately with musicians including [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane"), [Charlie Haden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Haden "Charlie Haden"), [Sun Ra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Ra "Sun Ra"), [Ed Blackwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Blackwell "Ed Blackwell"), the [New York Contemporary Five](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Contemporary_Five "New York Contemporary Five"), and [Albert Ayler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler "Albert Ayler"). Cherry released his debut album as bandleader, _[Complete Communion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complete_Communion "Complete Communion")_, in 1966. In the 1970s, he became a pioneer in [world fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_music "World music"), with his work drawing on African, Middle Eastern, and [Hindustani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindustani_classical_music "Hindustani classical music") music, as heard on the 1975 release _[Brown Rice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_Rice_(album) "Brown Rice (album)")_. He was a member of the [ECM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records "ECM Records") group [Codona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona "Codona"), along with percussionist [Naná Vasconcelos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nan%C3%A1_Vasconcelos "Naná Vasconcelos") and sitar and tabla player [Collin Walcott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collin_Walcott "Collin Walcott").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-2) Chris Kelsey of [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") called Cherry "one of the most influential jazz musicians of the late 20th century."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-3) ## Early life Cherry was born in [Oklahoma City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma_City "Oklahoma City"), [Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma "Oklahoma"), to a mother of [Choctaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choctaw "Choctaw") descent and an [African-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Americans "African Americans") father.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-4) His mother and grandmother played piano and his father played trumpet.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-atc1995-5) His father owned Oklahoma City's Cherry Blossom Club, which hosted performances by jazz musicians [Charlie Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Christian "Charlie Christian") and [Fletcher Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fletcher_Henderson "Fletcher Henderson").[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-biojazz-6) In 1940, Cherry moved with his family to the [Watts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watts,_Los_Angeles "Watts, Los Angeles") neighborhood of [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"), where his father tended bar at the Plantation Club on [Central Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Avenue_(Los_Angeles) "Central Avenue (Los Angeles)"), at the time the center of a vibrant jazz scene.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-biojazz-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-cadence-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-carr-8) Cherry recalled skipping school at [Fremont High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_C._Fremont_High_School "John C. Fremont High School") in order to play with the [swing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing_music "Swing music") band at [Jefferson High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_High_School_(Los_Angeles) "Jefferson High School (Los Angeles)").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-cadence-7) This resulted in his transfer to Jacob Riis High School, a [reform school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_school "Reform school"),[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-cadence-7) where he met drummer [Billy Higgins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Higgins "Billy Higgins").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-voce1995-9)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-crouch-10) ## Career By the early 1950s Cherry was playing with jazz musicians in Los Angeles, sometimes acting as pianist in [Art Farmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Farmer "Art Farmer")'s group.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-jost-11):134 While trumpeter [Clifford Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_Brown "Clifford Brown") was in Los Angeles with [Max Roach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Roach "Max Roach"), Cherry attended a jam session with Brown and [Larance Marable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larance_Marable "Larance Marable") at [Eric Dolphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy "Eric Dolphy")'s house, and Brown informally mentored Cherry.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-cadence-7) He also toured with saxophonist [James Clay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Clay_(musician) "James Clay (musician)").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-litweiler-12):45 Cherry became well known in 1958 when he performed and recorded with [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman"), first in a quintet with pianist [Paul Bley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Bley "Paul Bley") and later in the quartet which recorded for [Atlantic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Records "Atlantic Records"). During this period, "his lines ... gathered much of their freedom of motion from the free harmonic structures."[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-litweiler-12):289 Cherry co-led _[The Avant-Garde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Avant-Garde_(album) "The Avant-Garde (album)")_ session which saw [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane") replacing Coleman in the quartet, recorded and toured with [Sonny Rollins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Rollins "Sonny Rollins"), was a member of the [New York Contemporary Five](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Contemporary_Five "New York Contemporary Five") with [Archie Shepp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Shepp "Archie Shepp") and [John Tchicai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Tchicai "John Tchicai"), and recorded and toured with both [Albert Ayler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler "Albert Ayler") and [George Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Russell_(composer) "George Russell (composer)"). His first recording as a leader was _[Complete Communion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complete_Communion "Complete Communion")_ for [Blue Note Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records") in 1965. The band included Coleman's drummer [Ed Blackwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Blackwell "Ed Blackwell") as well as saxophonist [Gato Barbieri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gato_Barbieri "Gato Barbieri"), whom he had met while touring Europe with Ayler, and bassist [Henry Grimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Grimes "Henry Grimes").[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-13) [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/Firenze_DonCherry_1975.jpg/500px-Firenze_DonCherry_1975.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Firenze_DonCherry_1975.jpg) Cherry at Park Le Cascine, [Florence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence "Florence"), Italy, September 1975 After leaving Coleman's quartet, Cherry often played in small groups and duets, many with ex-Coleman drummer [Ed Blackwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Blackwell "Ed Blackwell"), during a long sojourn in [Scandinavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scandinavia "Scandinavia") and other locations. He traveled through Europe, India, Morocco, South Africa, and elsewhere to explore and play with a variety of musicians. In the late 1960s he settled in [Tågarp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C3%A5garp "Tågarp"), Sweden with his wife, Swedish designer and textile artist Moki Cherry. In 1968, Don Cherry taught music classes with guest lecturers, performance collaborators, and workshop leaders from around the world at Arbetarnas bildningsförbund (ABF) House, a Swedish labor movement-run education center. For ten years, Don and Moki Cherry lived and worked collaboratively in an abandoned schoolhouse in Tågarp, holding classes and performances, hosting guests and collaborators, and exploring their concept of Organic Music Society. In 1969, Cherry played trumpet and other instruments for poet [Allen Ginsberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allen_Ginsberg "Allen Ginsberg")'s 1970 LP _[Songs of Innocence and Experience](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Songs_of_Innocence_and_Experience_(Allen_Ginsberg_album) "Songs of Innocence and Experience (Allen Ginsberg album)")_, a musical adaptation of [William Blake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Blake "William Blake")'s [poetry collection of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Songs_of_Innocence_and_of_Experience "Songs of Innocence and of Experience").[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-Jurek-14) He appeared on Coleman's 1971 LP _[Science Fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_Fiction_(Ornette_Coleman_album) "Science Fiction (Ornette Coleman album)")_, and from 1976 to 1987 reunited with Blackwell and fellow Coleman alumni [Dewey Redman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dewey_Redman "Dewey Redman") and [Charlie Haden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Haden "Charlie Haden") as [Old and New Dreams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_and_New_Dreams "Old and New Dreams").[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-15) Old and New Dreams recorded four albums (two for [ECM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_(record_label) "ECM (record label)") and two for [Black Saint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Saint/Soul_Note "Black Saint/Soul Note")) where Cherry's "subtlety of rhythmic expansion and contraction" was noted.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-litweiler-12):290 [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/06/Don_Cherry_1989.jpg/500px-Don_Cherry_1989.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Don_Cherry_1989.jpg) Don Cherry in 1989 In the 1970s, Cherry ventured into the developing genre of world fusion music. Cherry incorporated influences of Middle Eastern, African, and Indian music into his playing. He studied Indian music with [Vasant Rai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasant_Rai "Vasant Rai") in the early seventies. From 1978 to 1982, he recorded three albums for ECM with "world jazz" group [Codona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona "Codona"), consisting of Cherry, percussionist [Naná Vasconcelos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nan%C3%A1_Vasconcelos "Naná Vasconcelos") and [sitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sitar "Sitar") and [tabla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabla "Tabla") player [Collin Walcott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collin_Walcott "Collin Walcott").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-voce1995-9) Cherry also collaborated with classical composer [Krzysztof Penderecki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krzysztof_Penderecki "Krzysztof Penderecki") on the 1971 album _[Actions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Actions_(album) "Actions (album)")_. In 1973, he co-composed the score for [Alejandro Jodorowsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alejandro_Jodorowsky "Alejandro Jodorowsky")'s film _[The Holy Mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Holy_Mountain_(1973_film) "The Holy Mountain (1973 film)")_, together with Jodorowsky and Ronald Frangipane. At the end of the 1970s, the trio Organic Music Theater (with Gian Piero Pramaggiore and [Naná Vasconcelos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nan%C3%A1_Vasconcelos "Naná Vasconcelos")) had an intense live activity in Italy and France. In 1982, Cherry released the duet album _[El Corazon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Coraz%C3%B3n_(Don_Cherry_and_Ed_Blackwell_album) "El Corazón (Don Cherry and Ed Blackwell album)")_ with Ed Blackwell. He also released two albums as a bandleader in the 1980s: _[Home Boy (Sister Out)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_Boy_(Sister_Out) "Home Boy (Sister Out)")_ in 1985 and _[Art Deco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Deco_(album) "Art Deco (album)")_ in 1988. He recorded again with the original Ornette Coleman Quartet on the first disc of Coleman's 1987 album _[In All Languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_All_Languages "In All Languages")_. Other playing opportunities in his career came with [Carla Bley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carla_Bley "Carla Bley")'s 1971 opera _[Escalator over the Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escalator_over_the_Hill "Escalator over the Hill")_ and as a sideman on recordings by [Lou Reed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou_Reed "Lou Reed"), [Ian Dury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Dury "Ian Dury"), [Rip Rig + Panic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rip_Rig_+_Panic "Rip Rig + Panic"), and [Sun Ra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Ra "Sun Ra"). Cherry played with Ian Dury and the Blockheads on their 1980 tour, including the final gig on Christmas Eve, which was broadcast live by the BBC, from the [Dominion Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominion_Theatre "Dominion Theatre") in London, on _[The Old Grey Whistle Test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Old_Grey_Whistle_Test "The Old Grey Whistle Test")_. He also toured UK and Europe with the band in 1981.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-16) In 1992, Don Cherry was invited by renowned Indian violinist [L. Shankar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L._Shankar "L. Shankar") to perform in Mumbai, India. This interaction was captured in a documentary film titled "Rhythms of the World: Bombay and all the Jazz". In 1994, Cherry appeared on the [Red Hot Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Hot_Organization "Red Hot Organization")'s compilation _[Stolen Moments: Red Hot + Cool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stolen_Moments:_Red_Hot_+_Cool "Stolen Moments: Red Hot + Cool")_, on a track titled "Apprehension", alongside [the Watts Prophets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Watts_Prophets "The Watts Prophets").[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-17) This album, meant to raise awareness of the [HIV/AIDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV/AIDS "HIV/AIDS") epidemic among African-Americans, was named "Album of the Year" by _[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")_. ## Death and legacy Cherry died of liver cancer in [Málaga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%A1laga "Málaga"), Spain, on October 19, 1995, at the age of 58.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-atc1995-5) Cherry was inducted into the [Oklahoma Jazz Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma_Jazz_Hall_of_Fame "Oklahoma Jazz Hall of Fame") in 2011.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-18) ## Family and personal life Cherry was married to Monika Karlsson ( [Moki Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moki_Cherry "Moki Cherry")), a Swedish painter and textile artist, who also occasionally played [tanpura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanpura "Tanpura") with him.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-johnson-19) His stepdaughter [Neneh Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neneh_Cherry "Neneh Cherry"),[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-johnson-19) his step-granddaughters [Mabel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mabel_(singer) "Mabel (singer)") and Tyson, and his sons David Ornette Cherry, Christian Cherry, and [Eagle-Eye Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eagle-Eye_Cherry "Eagle-Eye Cherry"), are also musicians. David Ornette Cherry died from an asthma attack at the age of 64 on November 20, 2022.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-20) Don Cherry practiced [Vajrayana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vajrayana "Vajrayana") Buddhism.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-21)[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-22) ## Instruments Cherry learned to play various brass instruments in high school.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-jost-11):134 Throughout his career, he played an F. [Besson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Besson_(music_company) "Besson (music company)") (Paris) MEHA pocket cornet[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-23) (though he identified this as a [pocket trumpet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pocket_trumpet "Pocket trumpet")), trumpet, [cornet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornet "Cornet"), [flugelhorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flugelhorn "Flugelhorn"), and [bugle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bugle "Bugle").[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-wynn-24)[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-pocketcornets-25) Cherry began his career as a pianist, and continued playing piano and organ as secondary instruments throughout his career.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-wynn-24) After returning from a musical and cultural journey through Africa, he often played the _donso ngoni_, a harp-lute with a gourd body originating from West Africa (see _[ngoni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ngoni_(instrument) "Ngoni (instrument)")_). During his international journeys, Cherry also collected a variety of non-Western instruments, which he mastered and often played in performances and on recordings. Among these instruments were [berimbau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berimbau "Berimbau"), [bamboo flutes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bamboo_flute "Bamboo flute") and assorted percussion instruments.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-wynn-24) ## Technique and style Cherry's trumpet influences included [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis"), [Fats Navarro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fats_Navarro "Fats Navarro"), [Clifford Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_Brown "Clifford Brown"), and [Harry Edison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweets_Edison "Sweets Edison").[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-wynn-24) Journalist Howard Mandel suggests [Henry "Red" Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Allen "Red Allen") as a precedent (given Allen's "blustery rather than Armstrong-brazen brass sound, jauntily unpredictable melodic streams, squeezed-off and/or half-valve effects and repertoire including novelty vocals")[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-mandel1995-26) while Ekkehard Jost cites [Wild Bill Davison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Davison "Bill Davison").[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-jost-11):138 Some critics have noted shortcomings in Cherry's technique.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-voce1995-9)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-jost-11):137[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-wynn-24) [Ron Wynn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Wynn "Ron Wynn") writes that "\[Cherry's\] technique isn't always the most efficient; frequently, his rapid-fired solos contain numerous missed or muffed notes. But he's a master at exploring the trumpet and cornet's expressive, voice-like properties; he bends notes and adds slurs and smears, and his twisting solos are tightly constructed and executed regardless of their flaws."[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-wynn-24) Jost notes the tendency for writers to focus on Cherry's "technical insecurity", but asserts that "the problem lies elsewhere. Perfect technical control in extremely fast tempos was more or less risk-free as long as the improviser had to deal with standard changes that were familiar to him from years of working with them.... In the music of the Ornette Coleman Quartet—a 'new-found-land' where the laws and habits of functional harmony do not apply—there is no use for patterns that had been worked out on that basis."[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-jost-11):137 Miles Davis was initially dismissive of Cherry's playing, claiming that "anyone can tell that guy's not a trumpet player—it's just notes that come out, and every note he plays he looks serious about, and people will go for that, especially white people."[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-mandel1995-26) According to Cherry, however, when Davis attended an Ornette Coleman performance at the [Five Spot Café](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Spot_Caf%C3%A9 "Five Spot Café") in [Greenwich Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenwich_Village "Greenwich Village"), he was impressed with Cherry's playing and sat in with the group using Cherry's pocket trumpet.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-mandel1995-26) Later, in a 1964 _[DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat")_ blindfold test, Davis indicated that he liked Cherry's # Codona Codona Free jazz and world fusion ensemble | Codona | | --- | | Genres | [Free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz")
[World fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_fusion "World fusion") | | Years active | 1978(1978)–1982(1982) | | Labels | [ECM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_(record_label) "ECM (record label)") | | | | Past members | [Don Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(jazz) "Don Cherry (jazz)")
[Nana Vasconcelos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Vasconcelos "Nana Vasconcelos")
[Collin Walcott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collin_Walcott "Collin Walcott") | **Codona** was a [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") and [world fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_fusion "World fusion") group which released three self-titled albums on the [ECM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_(record_label) "ECM (record label)") label in 1979, 1981 and 1983. The trio consisted of [multi-instrumentalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-instrumentalist "Multi-instrumentalist") [Don Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(jazz) "Don Cherry (jazz)"), [Collin Walcott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collin_Walcott "Collin Walcott"), and [Nana Vasconcelos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Vasconcelos "Nana Vasconcelos"). The name of the group was derived from the first two letters of the musicians' first names (COllin, DOn, NAna).[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-1) The members of the group declared that their goal was "to be open and incorporate all we know, without turning the whole world into milk toast - still encouraging the survival of the traditions".[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-2) Critic [Robert Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Palmer_(American_writer) "Robert Palmer (American writer)") stated that the group's "self-appointed mission is to fuse African, Indian and other music traditions in the heat of improvisation".[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-3) The authors of [The Penguin Guide to Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Penguin_Guide_to_Jazz "The Penguin Guide to Jazz") on CD called the group's debut album "one of the iconic episodes in so-called (but never better called) 'world music'", and stated: "Any tendency to regard Codona's music... as floating impressionism is sheer prejudice, for all these performances are deeply rooted in modern jazz (Coltrane's harmonies and rhythms, Ornette Coleman's melodic and rhythmic primitivism) and in another great and related improvisational tradition from Brazil."[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-4) ## Background The musicians had crossed paths on a number of occasions prior to the formation of the group in 1977.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-5) Vasconcelos appeared on Cherry's album _[Organic Music Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organic_Music_Society "Organic Music Society")_, recorded and released in 1972,[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-6) while Walcott played on Cherry's _[Hear & Now](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hear_&_Now_(Don_Cherry_album) "Hear & Now (Don Cherry album)")_, recorded in 1976 and released in 1977.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-7) Cherry also appeared on Walcott's _[Grazing Dreams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grazing_Dreams "Grazing Dreams")_, recorded and released in 1977,[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-8) while both Walcott and Vasconcelos played on [Egberto Gismonti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egberto_Gismonti "Egberto Gismonti")'s _[Sol do Meio Dia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sol_do_Meio_Dia "Sol do Meio Dia")_, recorded in 1977 and released in 1978.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-9) The members' involvement with Codona overlapped with their participation in other projects, Cherry with [Old and New Dreams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_and_New_Dreams "Old and New Dreams"), Walcott with [Oregon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oregon_(band) "Oregon (band)"), and Vasconcelos with [Pat Metheny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pat_Metheny "Pat Metheny"), [Milton Nascimento](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton_Nascimento "Milton Nascimento"), [Jan Garbarek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Garbarek "Jan Garbarek"), [Jon Hassell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Hassell "Jon Hassell"), and others. Although the group was conceived as a leaderless trio, Walcott was the organizer and primary composer.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-10)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-11) Codona was noted for its use of a broad range of instrumentation.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-kelman-12) While Cherry was primarily known as a trumpet and cornet player, he also performed on various [flutes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flute "Flute"), [organ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organ_(music) "Organ (music)"), [melodica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melodica "Melodica"), and the [Malian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mali "Mali") doussn’gouni.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-grillo-13) Walcott played [sitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sitar "Sitar"), [tabla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabla "Tabla"), [hammered dulcimer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hammered_dulcimer "Hammered dulcimer"), [sanza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mbira "Mbira"), and [timpani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timpani "Timpani"), while Vasconcelos performed on [berimbau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berimbau "Berimbau"), [cuica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuica "Cuica"), [talking drum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talking_drum "Talking drum"), and a variety of [percussion instruments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percussion_instrument "Percussion instrument").[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-grillo-13) In addition, all three musicians sang.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-grillo-13) The group was also known for its unusual arrangements, an example being "Colemanwonder", a medley of two [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman") tunes combined with [Stevie Wonder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stevie_Wonder "Stevie Wonder")'s " [Sir Duke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Duke "Sir Duke")", performed on trumpet, sitar, cuica, and percussion, and appearing on the group's [debut album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona_(album) "Codona (album)").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona#cite_note-kelman-12) The group disbanded following Walcott's death in a traffic accident in [East | Professional ratings _**Mwandishi**_ is the ninth studio album by American [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") pianist [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"), released in March 1971. It is the first album to officially feature Hancock’s ‘Mwandishi’ sextet, consisting of reed player [Bennie Maupin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bennie_Maupin "Bennie Maupin"), trumpeter [Eddie Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Henderson_(musician) "Eddie Henderson (musician)"), trombonist [Julian Priester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_Priester "Julian Priester"), bassist [Buster Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buster_Williams "Buster Williams"), and drummer [Billy Hart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Hart "Billy Hart"). ## Background \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mwandishi&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Background")\] This album is one of Hancock's first departures from the traditional idioms of jazz, as well as the beginning of an original and creative style which eventually appealed to a wider audience. In addition, _Mwandishi_ was Hancock's attempt at continuing the musical principles and styles he explored in his previous experiences with [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis") (on the album _[In A Silent Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_A_Silent_Way "In A Silent Way")_, for instance). Hancock's previous explorations of [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") included _[Fat Albert Rotunda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fat_Albert_Rotunda "Fat Albert Rotunda")_, an album related to the TV special ‘’ [Hey, Hey, Hey, It's Fat Albert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Hey,_Hey,_It's_Fat_Albert "Hey, Hey, Hey, It's Fat Albert")’’. _Mwandishi_ was recorded at [Wally Heider Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wally_Heider_Studios "Wally Heider Studios") Studio C, San Francisco, in January 1971. The recording incorporated progressive notions of funk, jazz, and rock. The tracks on _Mwandishi_ include "Ostinato," the [time signature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_signature "Time signature") of which is **15** **8**, "You'll Know When You Get There," and "Wandering Spirit Song." "Wandering Spirit Song" features Hancock's extensive use of tension and release, in which he builds the tension of the song by crescendos and an increasing number of musical voices, and then releases the tension with long held chords on his [synthesizer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthesizer "Synthesizer"). _[Mwandishi](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/mwandishi#Swahili "wikt:mwandishi")_ ("composer") is the [Swahili](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swahili "Swahili") name Hancock adopted during the late 1960s and early 1970s. The members of the Sextet each adopted a Swahili name: _[Mchezaji](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/mchezaji#Swahili "wikt:mchezaji")_ ("player," someone who plays a game) for [Buster Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buster_Williams "Buster Williams"), _[Jabali](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/jabali#Swahili "wikt:jabali")_ ("strong as a rock") for [Billy Hart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Hart "Billy Hart"), _[Mganga](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/mganga#Swahili "wikt:mganga")_ ("doctor," whose traditional functions include exorcism, prophecy, and the removal of spells) for [Eddie Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Henderson_(musician) "Eddie Henderson (musician)"), Mwile ("body", from Swahili _[mwili](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/mwili#Swahili "wikt:mwili")_) for [Bennie Maupin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bennie_Maupin "Bennie Maupin"), _[Pepo](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/pepo#Swahili "wikt:pepo")_ _[Mtoto](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/mtoto#Swahili "wikt:mtoto")_ ("demon baby") for [Julian Priester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_Priester "Julian Priester"), and _[Ndugu](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/ndugu#Swahili "wikt:ndugu")_ ("brother") for [Leon Chancler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leon_%22Ndugu%22_Chancler "Leon \"Ndugu\" Chancler"). ## Release history \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mwandishi&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Release history")\] _Mwandishi_, along with _[Fat Albert Rotunda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fat_Albert_Rotunda "Fat Albert Rotunda")_ and _[Crossings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossings_(Herbie_Hancock_album) "Crossings (Herbie Hancock album)")_, was reissued in one set as _Mwandishi: The Complete Warner Bros. Recordings_ in 1994 [\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mwandishi#cite_note-5)\[ _[deprecated source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Deprecated_sources "Wikipedia:Deprecated sources")_\] and as _The Warner Bros. Years (1969-1972)_ in 2014.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mwandishi#cite_note-6)\[ _[deprecated source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Deprecated_sources "Wikipedia:Deprecated sources")_\] ## Track listing \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mwandishi&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Track listing")\] All songs composed by [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock") except where noted. | No. | Title | Length | | --- | --- | --- | | 1. | "Ostinato (Suite for [Angela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angela_Davis "Angela Davis"))" | 13:10 | | 2. | "You'll Know When You Get There" | 10:22 | | Total length: | 23:32 | Side A | No. | Title | Writer(s) | Length | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 3. | "Wandering Spirit Song" | [Julian Priester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_Priester "Julian Priester") | 21:26 | | Total length: | 21:26 | Side B ## Personnel \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mwandishi&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: Personnel")\] - - [space rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_rock "Space rock") | **Progressive rock** (shortened to **prog rock** or simply **prog**) is a broad [genre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_genre "Music genre") of [rock music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music")[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin199871%E2%80%9375-9) that primarily developed in the United States and United Kingdom through the mid- to late 1960s. Initially termed " [progressive pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_pop "Progressive pop")", the style emerged from [psychedelic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelic_music "Psychedelic music") bands who abandoned standard [pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music "Pop music") or [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music") traditions in favour of [instrumental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instrumentation_(music) "Instrumentation (music)") and [compositional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composition_(music) "Composition (music)") techniques more commonly associated with [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), [folk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music "Folk music"), or [classical music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_music "Classical music"), while retaining the instrumentation typical of rock music. Additional elements contributed to its " [progressive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_music "Progressive music")" label: lyrics were more poetic, technology was harnessed for new sounds, music approached the condition of " [art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_music "Art music")", and the studio, rather than the stage, [became the focus of musical activity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_studio_as_an_instrument "Recording studio as an instrument"), which often involved creating music for listening rather than dancing. Progressive rock includes a fusion of styles, approaches and genres, and tends to be diverse and [eclectic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eclecticism_in_music "Eclecticism in music"). Progressive rock is often associated with long solos, extended pieces, fantastic lyrics, grandiose stage sets and costumes, and an obsessive dedication to technical skill and [virtuosity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtuoso "Virtuoso"). While the genre is often cited for its merging of [high culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_culture "High culture") and [low culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_culture "Low culture"), few artists incorporated Western classical themes in their work to a significant degree, with only a minority of groups ( [Emerson, Lake & Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerson,_Lake_&_Palmer "Emerson, Lake & Palmer"), [Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance_(band) "Renaissance (band)"), [Ekseption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ekseption "Ekseption"), etc.) directly emulating or referencing classical music. In the early to mid-1970s, progressive rock groups such as [Pink Floyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pink_Floyd "Pink Floyd") and [Yes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band) "Yes (band)") experienced great worldwide success; in the late 1970s, it declined in popularity, and has never fully recovered.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell20111-10) [Conventional wisdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conventional_wisdom "Conventional wisdom") holds that the rise of [punk rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punk_rock "Punk rock") caused this, but several more factors contributed to the decline.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell20111-10) Music critics, who often labelled the style of progressive rock as "pretentious" and the sounds as "pompous" and "overblown", tended to be hostile towards the genre or to completely ignore it.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTELucky20007-11) After the late 1970s, progressive rock fragmented into numerous forms. Some bands achieved commercial success well into the 1980s (albeit with changed lineups and more compact song structures) or crossed into [symphonic pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphonic_pop "Symphonic pop"), [arena rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arena_rock "Arena rock"), or [new wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_wave_music "New wave music"). Early groups who exhibited progressive features are retroactively described as " [proto-prog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-prog "Proto-prog")". The [Canterbury scene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_scene "Canterbury scene"), originating in the late 1960s, denotes a subset of progressive rock bands who emphasised the use of [wind instruments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind_instrument "Wind instrument"), complex chord changes and long improvisations. [Rock in Opposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_in_Opposition "Rock in Opposition"), from the late 1970s, was more [avant-garde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde "Avant-garde"), and when combined with the Canterbury style, created [avant-prog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-prog "Avant-prog"). In the 1980s, a new subgenre, [neo-prog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-prog "Neo-prog"), enjoyed some commercial success, although it was also accused of being derivative and lacking in innovation. [Post-progressive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-progressive "Post-progressive") draws upon newer developments in popular music and the avant-garde since the mid-1970s. ## Definition and characteristics Further information: [Progressive music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_music "Progressive music") ### Scope and related terms ![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg/120px-Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail) [The Fourth Colour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Fourth_Colour.mp3 "File:The Fourth Colour.mp3") _[The Fourth Colour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fourth_Colour "The Fourth Colour")_, a progressive rock song by [King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Gizzard_and_the_Lizard_Wizard "King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard"). * * * _Problems playing this file? See [media help](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Media "Help:Media")._ See also: [Progressive pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_pop "Progressive pop") and [Art rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_rock "Art rock") The term "progressive rock" is related to and sometimes considered [synonymous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synonym "Synonym") with " [art rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_rock "Art rock")", "classical rock" (not to be confused with [classic rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classic_rock "Classic rock")), and "symphonic rock".[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECovach19975-12) Historically, "art rock" has been used to describe at least two related, but distinct, types of rock music.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBannister200737-13) The first is progressive rock as it is generally understood, while the second usage refers to [experimental rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experimental_rock "Experimental rock") groups who rejected [psychedelia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelia "Psychedelia") and the [hippie counterculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterculture_of_the_1960s "Counterculture of the 1960s") in favour of a [modernist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernist "Modernist"), [avant-garde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde "Avant-garde") approach.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBannister200737-13)[\[nb 1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-15)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-16) Similarities between the two terms are that they both describe a mostly British attempt to elevate rock music to new levels of artistic credibility. However, art rock is more likely to have experimental or avant-garde influences.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-AMProg-17) "Prog" was devised in the 1990s[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTERobinson2017223-18) as a shorthand term, but later became a transferable adjective, also suggesting a wider palette than that drawn on by the most popular 1970s bands.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell20119-19) Progressive rock is varied and is based on fusions of styles, approaches, and genres, tapping into broader cultural resonances that connect to avant-garde art, [classical music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_music "Classical music") and [folk music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music "Folk music"), performance and the moving image.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell201113-20) Although a unidirectional English "progressive" style emerged in the late 1960s, by 1967, progressive rock had come to constitute a diversity of loosely associated style codes.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECotner200090-21) When the "progressive" label arrived, the music was dubbed " [progressive pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_pop "Progressive pop")" before it was called "progressive rock",[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoore200422-22)[\[nb 2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-24) with the term "progressive" referring to the wide range of attempts to break with standard pop music formula.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHaworthSmith1975126-25) A number of additional factors contributed to the acquired "progressive" label: lyrics were more poetic; technology was harnessed for new sounds; music approached the condition of "art"; some harmonic language was imported from jazz and [19th-century classical music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romantic_music "Romantic music"); [the album format overtook singles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album_Era "Album Era"); and the studio, rather than the stage, became the focus of musical activity, which often involved creating music for listening, not dancing.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoore2016201%E2%80%93202-26) > One of the best ways to define progressive rock is that it is a heterogeneous and troublesome genre – a formulation that becomes clear the moment we leave behind characterizations based only on the most visible bands of the early to mid-1970s — [Paul Hegarty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Hegarty_(musician) "Paul Hegarty (musician)") and Martin Halliwell[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell201113-20) Critics of the genre often limit its scope to a stereotype of long solos, overlong albums, fantasy lyrics, grandiose stage sets and costumes, and an obsessive dedication to technical skill.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell20112-27) While progressive rock is often cited for its merging of high culture and low culture, few artists incorporated literal classical themes in their work to any great degree,[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHolm-Hudson201316,_85%E2%80%9387-28) and only a handful of groups purposely emulated or referenced classical music.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell201113-20) Writer Emily Robinson says that the narrowed definition of "progressive rock" was a measure against the term's loose application in the late 1960s, when it was "applied to everyone from [Bob Dylan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Dylan "Bob Dylan") to [the Rolling Stones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rolling_Stones "The Rolling Stones")". Debate over the genre's criterion continued to the 2010s, particularly on [Internet forums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_forum "Internet forum") dedicated to prog.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTERobinson2017223-18) According to musicologists [Paul Hegarty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Hegarty_(musician) "Paul Hegarty (musician)") and Martin Halliwell, [Bill Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Martin_(philosophy) "Bill Martin (philosophy)") and Edward Macan authored major books about progressive rock while "effectively accept\[ing\] the characterization of progressive rock offered by its critics. ... they each do so largely unconsciously."[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell20112-27) Academic John S. Cotner contests Macan's view that progressive rock cannot exist without the continuous and overt assimilation of classical music into rock.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECotner200090-21) Author Kevin Holm-Hudson agrees that "progressive rock is a style far more diverse than what is heard from its mainstream groups and what is implied by unsympathetic critics."[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHolm-Hudson201316-29) ### Relation to art and social The song contained an eclectic array of exotic instruments and several disjunctive key and modal shifts.[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBooneCovach199741%E2%80%9346-61) Scott Interrante of _[Popmatters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popmatters "Popmatters")_ wrote that its influence on progressive rock and the psychedelic movement "can't be overstated".[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-62) Martin likened the song to the Beatles' " [A Day in the Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Day_in_the_Life "A Day in the Life")" from _Sgt. Pepper_, in that they showcase "the same reasons why much progressive rock is difficult to dance to".[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin199840-63) Although _Sgt. Pepper_ was preceded by several albums that had begun to bridge the line between "disposable" pop and "serious" rock, it successfully gave an established "commercial" voice to an alternative youth culture[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHolm-Hudson200810-64) and marked the point at which the [LP record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LP_record "LP record") emerged as a creative format whose importance was equal to or greater than that of the single.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-pirenne1-65)[\[nb 5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-67) [Bill Bruford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Bruford "Bill Bruford"), a veteran of several progressive rock bands, said that _Sgt. Pepper_ transformed both musicians' ideas of what was possible and audiences' ideas of what was acceptable in music.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeigel2012b-68) He believed that: "Without the Beatles, or someone else who had done what the Beatles did, it is fair to assume that there would have been no progressive rock."[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBruford2012159-69) In the aftermath of _Sgt. Pepper_, magazines such as [Melody Maker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melody_Maker "Melody Maker") drew a sharp line between "pop" and "rock". Americans increasingly used the adjective "progressive" for groups like [Jethro Tull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jethro_Tull_(band) "Jethro Tull (band)"), [Family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_(British_band) "Family (British band)"), [East of Eden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_of_Eden_(British_band) "East of Eden (British band)"), [Van der Graaf Generator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_der_Graaf_Generator "Van der Graaf Generator") and [King Crimson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Crimson "King Crimson").[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZoppo2014[[Category:Wikipedia_articles_needing_page_number_citations_from_December_2016]]%3Csup_class=%22noprint_Inline-Template_%22_style=%22white-space:nowrap;%22%3E[%3Ci%3E[[Wikipedia:Citing_sources|%3Cspan_title=%22This_citation_requires_a_reference_to_the_specific_page_or_range_of_pages_in_which_the_material_appears. Pink Floyd and [Soft Machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine "Soft Machine") functioned as [house bands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_band "House band") at all-night events at locations such as [Middle Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Earth_(club) "Middle Earth (club)") and the [UFO Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UFO_Club "UFO Club"), where they experimented with sound textures and long-form songs.[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTESweers2004114%E2%80%9315-71)[\[nb 6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-74) Many psychedelic, folk rock and early progressive bands were aided by exposure from [BBC Radio 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Radio_1 "BBC Radio 1") DJ [John Peel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Peel "John Peel").[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTESweers2004119-75) [Jimi Hendrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimi_Hendrix "Jimi Hendrix"), who rose to prominence in the London scene and recorded with a band of English musicians, initiated the trend towards guitar virtuosity and eccentricity in rock music.[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin1998164%E2%80%9365-76) The Scottish band 1-2-3, later renamed [Clouds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clouds_(60s_rock_band) "Clouds (60s rock band)"), were formed in 1966 and began performing at London clubs a year later. According to _Mojo_'s George Knemeyer: "some claim \[that they\] had a vital influence on prog-rockers such as Yes, The Nice and Family."[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHogg1994-77) Symphonic rock artists in the late 1960s had some chart success, including the singles " [Nights in White Satin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nights_in_White_Satin "Nights in White Satin")" (the Moody Blues, 1967) and " [A Whiter Shade of Pale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Whiter_Shade_of_Pale "A Whiter Shade of Pale")" (Procol Harum, 1967).[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FowlesWade2012-78) The Moody Blues established the popularity of symphonic rock when they recorded _Days of Future Passed_ together with the [London Festival Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Festival_Orchestra "London Festival Orchestra").[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan199721%E2%80%9322-79) Classical influences sometimes took the form of pieces adapted from or inspired by classical works, such as [Jeff Beck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Beck "Jeff Beck")'s _[Beck's Bolero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beck's_Bolero "Beck's Bolero")_, [Love Sculpture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love_Sculpture "Love Sculpture")'s[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-80) [_Farandole (Arlésienne Suite No 2. Movement 4)_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L'Arl%C3%A9sienne_(Bizet) "L'Arlésienne (Bizet)") and parts of the Nice's _[Ars Longa Vita Brevis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ars_Longa_Vita_Brevis_(album) "Ars Longa Vita Brevis (album)")_. The latter, along with such tracks as " [Rondo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Rondo_%C3%A0_la_Turk "Blue Rondo à la Turk")" and " [America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/America_(West_Side_Story_song) "America (West Side Story song)")", reflect a greater interest in music that is entirely instrumental. _Sgt. Pepper's_ and _Days_ both represent a growing tendency towards [song cycles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Song_cycle "Song cycle") and suites made up of multiple [movements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movement_(music) "Movement (music)").[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan199721%E2%80%9322-79) [Focus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Focus_(band) "Focus (band)") incorporated and articulated jazz-style chords, and irregular off-beat drumming into their later rock-based riffs, and several bands that included jazz-style [horn sections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horn_section "Horn section") appeared, including [Blood, Sweat & Tears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood,_Sweat_&_Tears "Blood, Sweat & Tears") and [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_(band) "Chicago (band)"). Of these, Martin highlights Chicago in particular for their experimentation with suites and extended compositions, such as the " [Ballet for a Girl in Buchannon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballet_for_a_Girl_in_Buchannon "Ballet for a Girl in Buchannon")" on _[Chicago II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_(album) "Chicago (album)")_.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin1998163%E2%80%93164-81) Jazz influences appeared in the music of British bands such as [Traffic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traffic_(band) "Traffic (band)"), [Colosseum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colosseum_(band) "Colosseum (band)") and [If](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_(band) "If (band)"), together with [Canterbury scene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_scene "Canterbury scene") bands such as [Soft Machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine "Soft Machine") and [Caravan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caravan_(band) "Caravan (band)"). Canterbury scene bands emphasised the use of wind instruments, complex chord changes and long improvisations.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan199720-82) Martin writes that in 1968, "full-blown progressive rock" was not yet in existence; however, albums were released by three bands who would later come to the forefront of the music: Jethro Tull, Caravan and Soft Machine.[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin1998168-83) ![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg/120px-Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail) ["The Court of the Crimson King" (1969)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:King_Crimson_-_The_Court_of_the_Crimson_King.ogg "File:King Crimson - The Court of the Crimson King.ogg") Macan writes that King Crimson's album "displays every element of the mature progressive rock genre... \[and\] exerted a powerful extramusical influence on later progressive rock bands".[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan199723-84) * * * _Problems playing this file? See [media help](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Media "Help:Media")._ The term "progressive rock", which appeared in the liner notes of Caravan's 1968 [self-titled debut LP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caravan_(Caravan_album) "Caravan (Caravan album)"), came to be applied to bands that used classical music techniques to expand the styles and concepts available to rock music.[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan199726-85)[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBowman2001184-86) The Nice, the Moody Blues, Procol Harum and Pink Floyd all contained elements of what is now called progressive rock, but none represented as complete an example of the genre as several bands that formed soon after.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan199722%E2%80%9323-87) Almost all of the genre's major bands, including Jethro Tull, King Crimson, Yes, [Genesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genesis_(band) "Genesis (band)"), [Van der Graaf Generator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_der_Graaf_Generator "Van der Graaf Generator"), [ELP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerson,_Lake_&_Palmer "Emerson, Lake & Palmer"), [Gentle Giant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentle_Giant "Gentle Giant"), [Barclay James Harvest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barclay_James_Harvest "Barclay James Harvest") and [Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance_(band) "Renaissance (band)"), released their debut albums during the years 1968–1970. Most of these were folk-rock albums that gave little indication of what the bands' mature sound would become, but King Crimson's _[In the Court of the Crimson King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_the_Court_of_the_Crimson_King "In the Court of the Crimson King")_ (1969) and Yes' [self-titled debut album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(Yes_album) "Yes (Yes album)") (1969) were early, fully formed examples of the genre.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan199723-84)[\[nb 7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-88) ### 1970s–1980s #### Peak years (1971–1976) See also: [Krautrock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krautrock "Krautrock") [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8f/DarkSideOfTheMoon1973.jpg/500px-DarkSideOfTheMoon1973.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:DarkSideOfTheMoon1973.jpg) [Pink Floyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pink_Floyd "Pink Floyd") performing _[The Dark Side of the Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dark_Side_of_the_Moon "The Dark Side of the Moon")_ (1973), the best-selling album of the entire progressive rock period[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPriore200579-89) Most of the genre's major bands released their most critically acclaimed albums during the years 1971–1976.[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan199727-90) The genre experienced a high degree of commercial success during the early 1970s. Between them, the bands Jethro Tull, [ELP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerson,_Lake_&_Palmer "Emerson, Lake & Palmer"), [the Moody Blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Moody_Blues "The Moody Blues"), Yes, and Pink Floyd had five albums that reached number one in the US charts, and sixteen that reached the top ten.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan199728-91)[\[nb 8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-96) [Mike Oldfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Oldfield "Mike Oldfield")'s _[Tubular Bells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tubular_Bells "Tubular Bells")_ (1973), an excerpt of which was used as the theme for the film _[The Exorcist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Exorcist "The Exorcist")_, sold 16 million copies.[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-97) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b5/Emerson%2C_Lake_%26_Palmer_01.jpg/500px-Emerson%2C_Lake_%26_Palmer_01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Emerson,_Lake_&_Palmer_01.jpg) [Emerson, Lake & Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerson,_Lake_&_Palmer "Emerson, Lake & Palmer") were one of the most commercially successful progressive rock bands of the 1970s. They are seen here performing in 1992. Progressive rock came to be appreciated overseas, but it mostly remained a European, and especially British, phenomenon. Many of these groups were very influential even among bands that had little enthusiasm for the symphonic variety of progressive rock.[\[113\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin200282-124) ##### Avant-prog See also: [Zeuhl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeuhl "Zeuhl") **Avant-prog** (originally known as **avant-garde progressive rock** or **experimental prog**) is a subgenre of progressive rock that emerged in the 1970s. Originally pioneered by artists such as [Frank Zappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa "Frank Zappa") and [Captain Beefheart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_Beefheart "Captain Beefheart"), the genre was further developed by the London [Canterbury scene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_scene "Canterbury scene") and later [Rock in Opposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_in_Opposition "Rock in Opposition") movement. The style drew influences from [avant-garde music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_music "Avant-garde music"), [modern classical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_classical "Modern classical"), [avant-garde jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz"), [experimental rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experimental_rock "Experimental rock"), [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") and [psychedelic rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelic_rock "Psychedelic rock"). This led to a progressive-soul movement in the 1970s that inspired a newfound sophisticated musicality and ambitious lyricism in black Times")_ calls Wonder's mid-1970s albums "prog soul of the highest order, pushing the form yet always heartfelt, ambitious and listenable".[\[118\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-129) #### Decline and fragmentation See also: [Punk rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punk_rock "Punk rock") and [Symphonic pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphonic_pop "Symphonic pop") Political and social trends of the late 1970s shifted away from the early 1970s [hippie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippie "Hippie") attitudes that had led to the genre's development and popularity. The rise in [punk cynicism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punk_ideologies "Punk ideologies") made the utopian ideals expressed in progressive rock lyrics unfashionable.[\[119\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin200278-130) Virtuosity was rejected, as the expense of purchasing quality instruments and the time investment of learning to play them were seen as barriers to rock's energy and immediacy.[\[120\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin2002115-131) There were also changes in the music industry, as record companies disappeared and merged into large [media conglomerates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Media_conglomerates "Media conglomerates"). Promoting and developing experimental music was not part of the [marketing strategy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marketing_strategy "Marketing strategy") for these large corporations, who focused their attention on identifying and targeting profitable [market niches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niche_market "Niche market").[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin2002108%E2%80%93110-132) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/Robert_Fripp_2.jpg/500px-Robert_Fripp_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Robert_Fripp_2.jpg) King Crimson's [Robert Fripp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Fripp "Robert Fripp") believed that the prog movement had gone "tragically off course".[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011177-133) Four of progressive rock's most successful bands – King Crimson, Yes, ELP and Genesis – went on hiatus or experienced major personnel changes during the mid-1970s.[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011177-133) Macan notes the September 1974 breakup of King Crimson as particularly significant, noting that Fripp (much later) referred to 1974 as the point when "all English bands in the genre should have ceased to exist".[\[123\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997179-134) More of the major bands, including Van der Graaf Generator, Gentle Giant and [U.K.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.K._(band) "U.K. (band)"), dissolved between 1978 and 1980.[\[124\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997187%E2%80%93188-135) Many bands had by the mid-1970s reached the limit of how far they could experiment in a rock context, and fans had wearied of the extended, epic compositions. The sounds of the [Hammond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hammond_organ "Hammond organ"), [Minimoog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimoog "Minimoog") and [Mellotron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mellotron "Mellotron") had been thoroughly explored, and their use became clichéd. Those bands who continued to record often simplified their sound, and the genre fragmented from the late 1970s onwards.[\[125\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997181%E2%80%93183-136) In [Robert Fripp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Fripp "Robert Fripp")'s opinion, once "progressive rock" ceased to cover new ground – becoming a set of conventions to be repeated and imitated – the genre's premise had ceased to be "progressive".[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997206-137) The era of record labels investing in their artists, giving them freedom to experiment and limited control over their content and marketing ended with the late 1970s.[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoore2016202-138) Corporate [artists and repertoire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artists_and_repertoire "Artists and repertoire") staff exerted an increasing amount of control over the creative process that had previously belonged to the artists,[\[128\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin1996188-139) and established acts were pressured to create music with simpler harmony and song structures and fewer changes in meter. A number of symphonic pop bands, such as [Supertramp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supertramp "Supertramp"), [10cc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10cc "10cc"), [the Alan Parsons Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Alan_Parsons_Project "The Alan Parsons Project") and the [Electric Light Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_Light_Orchestra "Electric Light Orchestra"), brought the orchestral-style arrangements into a context that emphasised pop singles while allowing for occasional instances of exploration. Jethro Tull, Gentle Giant and Pink Floyd opted for a harder sound in the style of [arena rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arena_rock "Arena rock").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997187-5) Few new progressive rock bands formed during this era, and those who did found that record labels were not interested in signing them.[\[129\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-derogatis98-140) The short-lived supergroup U.K. was a notable exception since its members had established reputations; they produced two albums that were stylistically similar to previous artists and did little to advance the genre.[\[130\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997183-141) Part of the genre's legacy in this period was its influence on other styles, as several European guitarists brought a progressive rock approach to [heavy metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_metal_music "Heavy metal music") and laid the groundwork for [progressive metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_metal "Progressive metal"). [Michael Schenker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Schenker "Michael Schenker"), of [UFO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UFO_(band) "UFO (band)"); and [Uli Jon Roth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uli_Jon_Roth "Uli Jon Roth"), who replaced Schenker in [Scorpions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scorpions_(band) "Scorpions (band)"), expanded the modal vocabulary available to guitarists.[\[131\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlackett2001-142)\[ _[further explanation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_\] Roth studied classical music with the intent of using the guitar in the way that classical composers used the violin.[\[132\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGress2007-143) Finally, the Dutch-born and classically trained [Alex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Van_Halen "Alex Van Halen") and [Eddie Van Halen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Van_Halen "Eddie Van Halen") formed [Van Halen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Halen "Van Halen"), featuring ground-breaking whammy-bar, tapping and cross-picking guitar performances[\[133\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGress1993-144) that influenced " [shred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shred_guitar "Shred guitar")" music in the 1980s.[\[134\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-145) ##### Commercialisation > By the early 1980s, progressive rock was thought to be all but dead as a style, an idea reinforced by the fact that some of the principal progressive groups had developed a more commercial sound. ... What went out of the music of these now ex-progressive groups ... was any significant evocation of art music. —John Covach[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECovach19975-12) Some established artists moved towards music that was simpler and more commercially viable.[\[135\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011182-146)\[ _[verification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_\][\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECovach19975-12) Arena rock bands like [Journey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journey_(band) "Journey (band)"), [Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_(band) "Kansas (band)"), [Styx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Styx_(band) "Styx (band)"), [GTR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GTR_(band) "GTR (band)"), [ELO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_Light_Orchestra "Electric Light Orchestra") and [Foreigner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreigner_(band) "Foreigner (band)") either had begun as progressive rock bands or included members with strong ties to the genre. These groups retained some of the song complexity and orchestral-style arrangements, but they moved away from lyrical mysticism in favour of more conventional themes such as relationships.[\[136\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011181%E2%80%93182-147) These radio-friendly groups have been called "prog lite".[\[137\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECateforis2011154%E2%80%93159-148) Genesis transformed into a successful pop act, the prog supergroup [Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia_(band) "Asia (band)") (consisting of members of Yes, King Crimson, and ELP) scored a number-one album in 1982,[\[138\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-149) and a re-formed Yes released the relatively mainstream _[90125](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/90125_(album) "90125 (album)")_ (1983), which yielded their only US number-one single, " [Owner of a Lonely Heart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owner_of_a_Lonely_Heart "Owner of a Lonely Heart")". One band who remained successful into the 1980s while maintaining a progressive approach was Pink Floyd, who released _[The Wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wall "The Wall")_ late in 1979. The album, which brought punk anger into progressive rock,[\[139\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011174-150) was a huge success and was later filmed as _[Pink Floyd – The Wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pink_Floyd_%E2%80%93_The_Wall "Pink Floyd – The Wall")_.[\[nb 12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-158) #### Post-punk and post-progressive Main articles: [Post-punk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-punk "Post-punk") and [Post-progressive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-progressive "Post-progressive") See also: [New wave music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_wave_music "New wave music") Punk and progressive rock were not necessarily as opposed as is commonly believed.
