See [media help](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Media "Help:Media")._ Progressive rock and [heavy metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_metal_music "Heavy metal music") have similar timelines. Both emerged from late-1960s psychedelia to achieve great early-1970s success despite a lack of radio airplay and support from critics, then faded in the mid-to-late 1970s and experienced revivals in the early 1980s. Each genre experienced a fragmentation of styles at this time, and many metal bands from the [new wave of British heavy metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_wave_of_British_heavy_metal "New wave of British heavy metal") – most notably [Iron Maiden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Maiden "Iron Maiden") – onwards displayed progressive rock influences.[\[187\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011259%E2%80%93260-201) [Progressive metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_metal "Progressive metal") reached a point of maturity with [Queensrÿche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queensr%C3%BFche "Queensrÿche")'s 1988 concept album _[Operation: Mindcrime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation:_Mindcrime "Operation: Mindcrime"),_ [Voivod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voivod_(band) "Voivod (band)")'s 1989 _[Nothingface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nothingface_(Voivod_album) "Nothingface (Voivod album)")_, which featured abstract lyrics and a King Crimson-like texture, and [Dream Theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dream_Theater "Dream Theater")'s 1992 _[Images and Words](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Images_and_Words "Images and Words")_.[\[188\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011260%E2%80%93262-202) Progressive rock elements appear in other metal subgenres. [Death metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_metal "Death metal")'s [guttural vocals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_growl "Death growl") are sometimes used by bands who can be classified as progressive, such as [Mastodon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mastodon_(band) "Mastodon (band)"), [Mudvayne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mudvayne "Mudvayne") and [Opeth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opeth "Opeth").[\[189\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011264,_266-203) [Symphonic metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphonic_metal "Symphonic metal") is an extension of the tendency towards orchestral passages in early progressive rock.[\[190\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011266%E2%80%93267-204) Progressive rock has also served as a key inspiration for genres such as [post-rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-rock "Post-rock"),[\[191\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-allen-205) [post-metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-metal "Post-metal") and [avant-garde metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_metal "Avant-garde metal"),[\[192\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-caramanica-206) [math rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Math_rock "Math rock"),[\[193\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-tudor-207) [power metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_metal "Power metal") and [neo-classical metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-classical_metal "Neo-classical metal").[\[194\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-miers-208) #### New prog Not to be confused with [Neo-prog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-prog "Neo-prog"). **New prog** describes the wave of progressive rock bands in the 2000s who revived the genre. According to _[Entertainment Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment_Weekly "Entertainment Weekly")_'s Evan Serpick, "success stories like [System of a Down](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/System_of_a_Down "System of a Down") and up-and-comers like the [Dillinger Escape Plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dillinger_Escape_Plan "Dillinger Escape Plan"), [Lightning Bolt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lightning_Bolt_(band) "Lightning Bolt (band)"), [Coheed and Cambria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coheed_and_Cambria "Coheed and Cambria"), and [the Mars Volta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mars_Volta "The Mars Volta") create incredibly complex and inventive music that sounds like a heavier, more aggressive version of '70s behemoths such as Led Zeppelin and King Crimson."[\[195\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-209) #### Wider influence The turn of the millennium also saw the rise of a number of bands to mainstream success who, whilst not explicitly identifying as progressive rock, have incorporated influences from it and embraced an experimentalism and complexity in their music which has been regarded as being in keeping with the genre's traditions. [Radiohead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiohead "Radiohead") have been embraced by some progressive rock fans and musicians, with Rush's [Geddy Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geddy_Lee "Geddy Lee") declaring _[OK Computer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OK_Computer "OK Computer")_ as one of his favourite albums and arguing that they carried on the torch from bands like Yes and Genesis. Radiohead's drummer [Philip Selway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Selway "Philip Selway") has cited King Crimson and Pink Floyd as influences, and the band's eclectic and experimental style has drawn on a range of sources, including jazz, electronic music, art rock, krautrock, post-rock and the work of [Captain Beefheart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_Beefheart "Captain Beefheart").[\[196\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-210) [Tool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tool_(band) "Tool (band)") and King Crimson have acknowledged each other as influences and toured Thorgerson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storm_Thorgerson "Storm Thorgerson")-designed cover art.[\[204\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-218) ### 2010s–2020s The Progressive Music Awards were launched in 2012 by the British magazine _[Prog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prog_(magazine) "Prog (magazine)")_ to honour the genre's established acts and to promote its newer bands. In 2019, the Prog Report named [Mike Portnoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Portnoy "Mike Portnoy") and [Neal Morse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neal_Morse "Neal Morse") artists of the decade for 2010–2019. During this time, Portnoy released 40 albums, 24 of them with Morse, while Morse released an additional 5 albums of his own.[\[205\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-219) During the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic") in 2020, the Prog Report launched a virtual concert, _Prog From Home_, bringing together many of the biggest artists active in the genre.[\[206\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-220) On April 3, 2022, "The Alien" won a [Grammy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Awards "Grammy Awards") for [Best Metal Performance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Metal_Performance "Grammy Award for Best Metal Performance"), giving [Dream Theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dream_Theater "Dream Theater") their first Grammy.[\[207\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-221) ## Festivals Many prominent progressive rock bands got their initial exposure at large [rock festivals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_festival "Rock festival") that were held in Britain during the late 1960s and early 1970s. King Crimson made their first major appearance at the [1969 Hyde Park free concert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stones_in_the_Park "Stones in the Park"), before a crowd estimated to be as large as 650,000, in support of [the Rolling Stones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rolling_Stones "The Rolling Stones").[\[208\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFripp1975-222) Emerson, Lake & Palmer debuted at the [1970 Isle of Wight Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isle_of_Wight_Festival_1970 "Isle of Wight Festival 1970"), at which [Supertramp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supertramp "Supertramp"), [Family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_(British_band) "Family (British band)") and Jethro Tull also appeared.[\[209\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell201150%E2%80%9351-223) Jethro Tull were also present at the 1969 [Newport Jazz Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport_Jazz_Festival "Newport Jazz Festival"), the first year in which that festival invited rock bands to perform. [Hawkwind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawkwind "Hawkwind") appeared at many British festivals throughout the 1970s, although they sometimes showed up uninvited, set up a stage on the periphery of the event, and played for free.[\[210\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell201150-224) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/Supertramp0062.jpg/500px-Supertramp0062.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Supertramp0062.jpg) Supertramp performing in 1979[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/da/King_Crimson_-_Dour_Festival_2003_%2801%29.jpg/500px-King_Crimson_-_Dour_Festival_2003_%2801%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:King_Crimson_-_Dour_Festival_2003_(01).jpg) [King Crimson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Crimson "King Crimson") performing at the Dour Festival, 2003 Renewed interest in the genre in the 1990s led to the development of progressive rock festivals.[\[182\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGill1995-196) ProgFest, organised by Greg Walker and David Overstreet in 1993, was first held in [UCLA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UCLA "UCLA")'s Royce Hall,[\[211\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECovach2000-225) and featured Sweden's Änglagård, the UK's IQ, Quill and Citadel. CalProg was held annually in Whittier, California during the early 2000s.[\[212\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-226) The North East Art Rock Festival, or [NEARfest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NEARfest "NEARfest"),[\[184\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKarnick2003-198) held its first event in 1999 in [Bethlehem, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethlehem,_Pennsylvania "Bethlehem, Pennsylvania") and held annual sold-out concerts until 2012's NEARfest Apocalypse, which featured headliners [U.K.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.K._(band) "U.K. (band)") and Renaissance.[\[213\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeigel2012e-227) Other festivals include the annual ProgDay (the longest-running and only outdoor progressive music festival) in [Chapel Hill, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_Hill,_North_Carolina "Chapel Hill, North Carolina"); the annual Rites of Spring Festival (RoSfest) in [Sarasota, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarasota,_Florida "Sarasota, Florida"); [The Rogue Independent Music Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rogue_Independent_Music_Festival "The Rogue Independent Music Festival") in Atlanta, Georgia; [Baja Prog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baja_Prog "Baja Prog") in [Mexicali, Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexicali "Mexicali"); [ProgPower USA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ProgPower_USA "ProgPower USA") in Atlanta, Georgia; [ProgPower Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ProgPower_Europe "ProgPower Europe") in [Baarlo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baarlo "Baarlo"), Netherlands; and ProgStock in Rahway, NJ, which held its first event in 2017.[\[214\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-228) Another popular prog festival is Cruise to the Edge; 2026's line-up included [Marillion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marillion "Marillion"), [Steven Hackett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Hackett "Steve Hackett"), and [Big Big Train](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Big_Train "Big Big Train").[\[215\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-229) ## Reception The genre has received both critical acclaim and criticism throughout the years. Progressive rock has been described as parallel to the classical music of [Igor Stravinsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Igor_Stravinsky "Igor Stravinsky") and [Béla Bartók](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9la_Bart%C3%B3k "Béla Bartók").[\[211\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECovach2000-225) This desire to expand the boundaries of rock, combined with some musicians' dismissiveness toward mainstream rock and pop, dismayed critics and led to accusations of elitism. Its intellectual, fantastic and apolitical lyrics, and shunning of rock's blues roots, were abandonments of the very things that many critics valued in rock music.[\[216\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997168%E2%80%9373-230) Progressive rock also represented the maturation of rock as a genre, but there was an opinion among critics that rock was and should remain fundamentally tied to adolescence, so rock and maturity were mutually exclusive.[\[217\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin2002107-231) Criticisms over the complexity of their music provoked some bands to create music that was even more complex.[\[nb 15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-235) BBC radio DJ [John Peel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Peel "John Peel"), who was one of the first people to play progressive rock on British radio, later said "the one distinguishing feature about early-70s progressive rock was that it didn't progress".[\[221\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-236) Most of the musicians involved were male, as was the case for most rock of the time,[\[222\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011204-237) although [Annie Haslam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annie_Haslam "Annie Haslam") of [Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance_(band) "Renaissance (band)") was a notable exception. Female singers were better represented in [progressive folk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_folk "Progressive folk") bands,[\[223\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997135-238) who displayed a broader range of vocal styles than the progressive rock bands[\[224\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTESweers2004204-239) with whom they frequently toured and shared band members.[\[225\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTESweers2004131-240) British and European audiences typically followed concert hall behaviour protocols associated with classical music performances and were more reserved in their behaviour than audiences for other forms of rock. This confused musicians during US tours, as they found American audiences less attentive and more prone to outbursts during quiet passages.[\[226\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997263-241) These aspirations towards [high culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_culture "High culture") reflect progressive rock's origins as a music created largely by [upper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_class "Upper class")\- and [middle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_class "Middle class")-class, [white-collar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White-collar_workers "White-collar workers"), college-educated males from [Southern England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_England "Southern England"). The music never reflected the concerns of or was embraced by working-class listeners,[\[227\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997144%E2%80%9348-242) except in the US, where listeners appreciated the musicians' virtuosity.[\[228\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997156-243) Progressive rock's exotic, literary topics were considered particularly irrelevant to British youth during the late 1970s, when the nation suffered from a poor economy and frequent strikes and shortages.[\[229\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011163%E2%80%93164-244) Even King Crimson leader Robert Fripp dismissed progressive rock lyrics as "the philosophical meanderings of some English half-wit who is circumnavigating some inessential point of experience in his life".[\[230\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTETamm1990-245) Bands whose darker lyrics avoided utopianism, such as King Crimson, Pink Floyd and Van der Graaf Generator, experienced less critical disfavour.[\[231\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan199778-246) In 2002, Pink Floyd guitarist [David Gilmour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Gilmour "David Gilmour") said, "I wasn't a big fan of most of what you'd call progressive rock. I'm like [Groucho Marx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groucho_Marx "Groucho Marx"): I don't want to belong to any club that would have me for a member."[\[232\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-247) In 2014, [Peter Gabriel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel "Peter Gabriel") remarked, "Despite prog probably being the most derided musical genre of all time there were—as today—a lot of extraordinary musicians trying to break down the barriers to reject the rules of music. It was genuinely pioneering at the time. We didn't always get it right, but when it did work we could move people and get some magic happening. I see it all as a very healthy part of growing up."[\[233\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-248) [Ian Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Anderson "Ian Anderson"), the frontman of Jethro Tull, commented: > I still like the original term that comes from 1969: progressive rock – but that was with a small "p" and a small "r". Prog Rock, on the other hand, has different connotations – of grandeur and pomposity \[...\] I think looking back on it that most of it was a pretty good experience for musicians and listeners alike. Some of it was a little bit overblown, but in the case of much of the music, it was absolutely spot on.[\[234\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-249) While music fans for years have declared progressive rock to be dead,[\[235\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-250) the scene is still active with many sub-genres.[\[236\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-251) ## List of progressive rock artists Main article: [List of progressive rock artists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_progressive_rock_artists "List of progressive rock artists") ## See also [![Wiktionary logo](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/99/Wiktionary-logo-en-v2.svg/120px-Wiktionary-logo-en-v2.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wiktionary-logo-en-v2.svg) Look up _**[progressive rock](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/progressive%20rock "wiktionary:progressive rock")**_ in Wiktionary, the free dictionary. - [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_ref-32)Formalism refers to a preoccupation with established external compositional systems, structural unity, and the autonomy of individual art works. Examples include [the Beatles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beatles "The Beatles")' " [Within You Without You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Within_You_Without_You "Within You Without You")" (1967) and [Jimi Hendrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimi_Hendrix "Jimi Hendrix")'s 1969 version of " [The Star-Spangled Banner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Star-Spangled_Banner "The Star-Spangled Banner")".[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECotner200093-31) 04. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_ref-96)Tull alone scored 11 [gold albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_album "Gold album") and 5 [platinum albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platinum_album "Platinum album").[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECleveland2005-92) Pink Floyd's 1970 album _[Atom Heart Mother](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atom_Heart_Mother "Atom Heart Mother")_ reached the top spot on the UK charts. Their 1973 album _[The Dark Side of the Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dark_Side_of_the_Moon "The Dark Side of the Moon")_, which united their extended compositions with the more structured kind of composing employed when [Syd Barrett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syd_Barrett "Syd Barrett") was their songwriter,[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhiteley199234%E2%80%9335-93) spent more than two years at the top of the charts[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhiteley19924,_38-94) and remained on the [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") album chart for fifteen years.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFriedlander1998245-95) 09. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_ref-101)Radio airplay was less important in the UK, where popular music recordings had limited air-time on official radio stations (as opposed to on [pirate radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pirate_radio_in_the_United_Kingdom "Pirate radio in the United Kingdom")) until the 1967 launch of [BBC Radio 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Radio_1 "BBC Radio 1").[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-pirenne1-65) UK audiences were accustomed to hearing bands in clubs, and British bands could support themselves through touring. US audiences were first exposed to new music on the radio, and bands in the US required radio airplay for success.[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurtis1987296-7-99) Radio stations were averse to progressive rock's longer-form compositions, which hampered [advertising sales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_advertisement "Radio advertisement").[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-100) 10. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_ref-113)Van der Graaf Generator were much more popular there than in their own country. Genesis were hugely successful in Continental Europe at a time when they were still limited to a [cult following](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cult_following "Cult following") in Britain and the US.[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-spicer-112)\[ _[importance of example(s)?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Template:Refexample#Self-sourcing "Template:Refexample")_\] 11. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_ref-120)This can be heard in [Triumvirat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triumvirat "Triumvirat"), an organ trio in the style of ELP; [Ange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ange_(band) "Ange (band)") and [Celeste](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celeste%20(gruppo%20musicale) "it:Celeste (gruppo musicale)") who have had a strong King Crimson influence.[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997267-118) Others brought national elements to their style: Spain's [Triana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triana_(band) "Triana (band)") introduced [flamenco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flamenco "Flamenco") elements, groups such as the Swedish [Samla Mammas Manna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samla_Mammas_Manna "Samla Mammas Manna") drew from the folk music styles of their respective nations, and Italian bands such as [Il Balletto di Bronzo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Il_Balletto_di_Bronzo "Il Balletto di Bronzo"), Rustichelli & Bordini, leaned towards an approach that was more overtly emotional than that of their British counterparts.[\[109\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997184-119) 12. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_ref-158)Pink Floyd were unable to repeat that combination of commercial and critical success, as their sole follow-up, _[The Final Cut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Final_Cut_(album) "The Final Cut (album)")_, was several years in coming[\[140\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997188-151) and was essentially a [Roger Waters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Waters "Roger Waters") solo project[\[141\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-merc-152) that consisted largely of material that had been rejected for _The Wall_.[\[142\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-tsmith-153) The band later reunited without Waters and restored many of the progressive elements that had been downplayed in the band's late-1970s work.[\[143\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997195-154) This version of the band was very popular,[\[144\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-harrington87-155) but critical opinion of their later albums is less favourable.[\[145\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-graves-156)[\[146\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-wyman-157) 13. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_ref-164)[Sex Pistols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_Pistols "Sex Pistols") frontman [Johnny Rotten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lydon "John Lydon") famously wore a T-shirt that read "I hate Pink Floyd",[\[129\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-derogatis98-140) but he expressed admiration for Van der Graaf Generator,[\[148\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-boros-160) Can,[\[149\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-lydon-161) and many years later, Pink Floyd themselves.[\[150\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-162) [Brian Eno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Eno "Brian Eno") expressed a preference for the approach of the punk and new wave bands in New York, as he found them to be more experimental and less personality-based than the English bands.[\[151\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTETamm199530-163) 14. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_ref-171)[Julian Cope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_Cope "Julian Cope") of [the Teardrop Explodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Teardrop_Explodes "The Teardrop Explodes") wrote a history of the krautrock genre, _[Krautrocksampler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krautrocksampler "Krautrocksampler")_.[\[157\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-170)\[ _[importance of example(s)?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Template:Refexample#Self-sourcing "Template:Refexample")_\] 15. ​
(m.1970)​ | Musical artist **Keith Graham Tippetts** (25 August 1947 – 14 June 2020),[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-guardian-1) known professionally as **Keith Tippett**, was a British [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") pianist and composer. According to [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic"), Tippett's career "...spanned jazz-rock, [progressive rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock "Progressive rock"), improvised and contemporary music, as well as modern jazz for more than half-a-century". He held "an unparallelled place in British contemporary music,"[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-Eder-2) and was known for "his unique approach to improvisation".[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-guardian-1) Tippett appeared and recorded in many settings, including a duet with [Stan Tracey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Tracey "Stan Tracey"), duets with his wife [Julie Tippetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julie_Tippetts "Julie Tippetts") (née Driscoll), solo performances, and as a bandleader.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-guy-3) ## Early life Born in [Southmead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southmead "Southmead"), [Bristol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol "Bristol"), England,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-LarkinJazz-4) Tippett was the son of an English father who was a policeman and an Irish mother named Kitty. He wrote music dedicated to her after she died. He was the oldest of three siblings and went to Greenway Secondary Modern school in Southmead. As a child he played piano, church organ, cornet, and tenor horn.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-Eder-2) At fourteen he formed his first band, KT Trad Lads, with school friends Richard Murch, Mike Milton, Terry Pratt, and Bob Chard, and Eric Condell performing traditional jazz. He formed a modern jazz trio in Bristol and played regularly at the Dugout Club in Park Row, Bristol. ## Music career In 1967, Tippett moved to London to pursue a career in music, taking menial jobs while performing in jazz clubs.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-Eder-2) With a scholarship he attended the Barry Summer School Jazz Course in Wales, where he met [Elton Dean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elton_Dean "Elton Dean"), [Nick Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Evans_(trombonist) "Nick Evans (trombonist)"), and [Marc Charig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Charig "Marc Charig") and with them started a band.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-Eder-2) The Keith Tippett Sextet was hired for a residency at the [100 Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/100_Club "100 Club") in Oxford Street,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-LarkinJazz-4) leading to a contract with Polydor, which released their first two albums, _You Are There... I Am Here_ (1970) and _Dedicated to You, but You Weren't Listening_ (1971).[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-Eder-2) After leaving Vertigo, Tippett formed [Centipede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centipede_(band) "Centipede (band)"), a 50-piece band that included his wife [Julie Driscoll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julie_Driscoll "Julie Driscoll"), and brought together much of a generation of young British jazz and rock musicians.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-Eder-2) As well as performing some concerts (limited economically by the size of the band), they recorded one double-album, _[Septober Energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Septober_Energy "Septober Energy")_, a Tippett composition, which was released on the [RCA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Records "RCA Records") label in 1971. Despite substantial publicity, the album failed to sell in sufficient numbers to justify the expense of maintaining the project.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-Eder-2) In early 1970, Tippett was part of a temporary [King Crimson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Crimson "King Crimson") line-up for the recording of their second album _[In the Wake of Poseidon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_the_Wake_of_Poseidon "In the Wake of Poseidon")_.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-5)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-7) He also contributed as a session musician to the band's subsequent two albums _[Lizard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lizard_(album) "Lizard (album)")_ later in 1970 and _[Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islands_(King_Crimson_album) "Islands (King Crimson album)")_ in 1971. For his next album as a leader, _Blueprint_ (1972),[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-LarkinJazz-4) he used a smaller group comprising himself and Julie Tippetts with bassist [Roy Babbington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Babbington "Roy Babbington") and drummer Frank Perry. The band then expanded slightly to become Ovary Lodge,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-LarkinJazz-4) who recorded two albums, one for RCA and a second for the Ogun label. Tippett and his band also recorded in the 1970s for [Giorgio Gomelsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giorgio_Gomelsky "Giorgio Gomelsky")'s label, Utopia, releasing the Julie Tippetts album, _Sunset Glow_. Tippett continued to play with various combinations of musicians through the 1970s, playing improvisational jazz and [jazz-rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-rock "Jazz-rock") with such musicians as [Stan Tracey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Tracey "Stan Tracey"), [Robert Wyatt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Wyatt "Robert Wyatt"), [Dudu Pukwana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dudu_Pukwana "Dudu Pukwana"), [Harry Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Miller_(jazz_bassist) "Harry Miller (jazz bassist)"), Elton Dean, [Hugh Hopper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Hopper "Hugh Hopper"), and [Louis Moholo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Moholo "Louis Moholo").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-guardian-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-Eder-2) From 1979, he also started to release many live albums of solo piano performances, beginning with _The Unlonely Raindancer_. In the late 1980s, he, along with [Paul Dunmall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Dunmall "Paul Dunmall") saxes, Paul Rogers bass, and [Tony Levin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Levin_(drummer) "Tony Levin (drummer)") drums, formed the quartet Mujician, playing purely improvised jazz.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-LarkinJazz-4) Mujician released six albums between 1990 and 2002. He also formed a trio with Julie Tippetts and Willi Kellers, and wrote film and television scores. He also wrote music for [string quartets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_quartet "String quartet") and piano, and taught at summer schools. Tippett also continued to record and to tour in Britain and Europe with various ensembles. He also worked with musicians [Andy Sheppard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Sheppard "Andy Sheppard"), as well as with his frequent collaborators Elton Dean, Louis Moholo, and Howard Riley.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-Eder-2) In Bristol, starting in 1989 and continuing through the 1990s, he started the Seedbed Orchestra, which performed at venues including the [Thekla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Thekla "The Thekla"), the [Arnolfini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnolfini,_Bristol "Arnolfini, Bristol") and [Bristol Old Vic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Old_Vic "Bristol Old Vic").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-SO_1-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-SO_2-9) This enabled beginners, amateurs and professional musicians to play in a large ensemble and was "emblematic of his quest to unite music of all types in a non-elitist, open to all, friendly environment free of establishment restrictions."[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-SO_3-10) He became a "musician's musician when he first set up the Seedbed Orchestra where many Bristol musicians could benefit from his guidance."[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-SO_4-11) ## Personal life and death He married singer [Julie Driscoll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julie_Driscoll "Julie Driscoll") in 1970. In 2018, he had a [heart attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_attack "Heart attack") and [pneumonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pneumonia "Pneumonia") but returned to performing in 2019.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-guardian-1) He died on 14 June 2020 at the age of 72.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Tippett#cite_note-guardian-1) In 2026, the Authorised biography, “ Keith Tippett: Mujician”, written by Martin Phillips with a Foreword by Richard Williams, was published by Jazz In Britain. ## Discography ### As leader - _You Are Here... (1977) | | | | _**The _Köln_ Concert**_ is a live solo double album by pianist [Keith Jarrett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett "Keith Jarrett") recorded at the [Opera House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cologne_Opera#The_opera_house "Cologne Opera") in [Köln (Cologne)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cologne "Cologne"), [West Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Germany "West Germany"), on 24 January 1975 and released on [ECM Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records "ECM Records") later that year.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-ECM-1) It is the best-selling solo album in jazz history and the best-selling piano album. In 2025, the album was deemed "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant" by the [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress") and selected for preservation in the [National Recording Registry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Recording_Registry "National Recording Registry").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-3) ## Concert and recording The concert was organized by 18-year-old [Vera Brandes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vera_Brandes "Vera Brandes"),[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-Krueger_2015-4) then Germany's youngest concert promoter.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-BBC_2011-5) The concert took place on a Friday at the late hour of 11:30 pm, following an earlier opera performance. The late time was the only one the administration would make available to Brandes for a jazz concert—the first at the Köln Opera House. The show was sold out, filled to capacity at over 1,400 people at a ticket price of 4 [DM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deutsche_Mark "Deutsche Mark"). At Jarrett's request, Brandes had selected a [Bösendorfer 290 Imperial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%B6sendorfer_290_Imperial "Bösendorfer 290 Imperial") concert grand piano for the performance. However, there was some confusion by the opera house staff and instead they found another Bösendorfer piano backstage—a much smaller [baby grand piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baby_grand_piano "Baby grand piano")—and, assuming it was the one requested, placed it on the stage. The error was discovered too late for the correct Bösendorfer to be delivered to the venue in time for the evening's concert. The piano they had was intended for rehearsals only and was in poor condition and required several hours of [tuning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_tuning "Piano tuning") and adjustment to make it playable.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-B%C3%B6sendorfer_2010-6)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-Krueger_2015-4) The instrument was tinny and thin in the upper registers and weak in the bass register, and the pedals did not work properly.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-Krueger_2015-4) While Brandes made an attempt and procured another grand piano up to Jarrett's standards to be delivered as an emergency, the piano tuner who had meanwhile arrived to fix the baby grand warned her that transporting a grand piano without the proper equipment at low temperatures in the middle of a rainstorm would irreparably damage the instrument, forcing Brandes to stick to the small one.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-BBC_2011_Witness-7)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-Krueger_2015-4) Jarrett had performed a few days earlier in [Lausanne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solo_Concerts:_Bremen/Lausanne "Solo Concerts: Bremen/Lausanne"), Switzerland and although Brandes had sent him a ticket for a flight to Cologne on the record company's request, he exchanged the ticket for cash and joined ECM Records producer [Manfred Eicher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manfred_Eicher "Manfred Eicher") travelling to Cologne by car in Eicher's old [Renault 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renault_4 "Renault 4"), so they arrived at the opera house late in the afternoon tired after the exhaustingly long drive.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-Krueger_2015-4) Jarrett had not slept well in several nights and was in pain from back problems, having to wear a [brace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back_brace "Back brace") as a result. After trying out the substandard piano and learning a replacement instrument was not available, Jarrett nearly refused to play and was about to leave, but Brandes was able to convince him to perform anyway as the concert was scheduled to begin in just a few hours.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-online.wsj.com-8)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-Krueger_2015-4) Brandes had booked a table at a restaurant in advance of the performance, but delays meant Jarrett was able to eat very little of the meal before leaving.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-BBC_2011_Witness-7)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-Krueger_2015-4) Ultimately, Jarrett decided to play largely because the recording equipment was already set up.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-grammy-9) Jarrett used [ostinatos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostinato "Ostinato") and rolling left-hand rhythmic figures during his performance to give the effect of stronger bass notes, and concentrated his playing in the middle portion of the keyboard. Eicher later said: "Probably \[Jarrett\] played it the way he did because it was not a good piano. Because he could not fall in love with the sound of it, he found another way to get the most out of it."[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-online.wsj.com-8) A notable aspect of the concert was Jarrett's ability to produce very extensive improvised material over a [vamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vamp_(music) "Vamp (music)") of one or two chords for prolonged periods of time. In Part I, he spends almost 12 minutes vamping over the chords Am7 (A minor 7) to G major, sometimes in a slow, [rubato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubato "Rubato") feel, and other times in a bluesy, gospel [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music") feel. For about the last 6 minutes of Part I, he vamps over an A major theme. Roughly the first 8 minutes of Part II A is a vamp over a D major groove with a repeated bass vamp in the left hand, and in Part IIb, Jarrett improvises over an F♯ minor vamp for about the first 6 minutes. The performance was recorded by ECM Records engineer Martin Wieland using a pair of [Neumann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georg_Neumann "Georg Neumann") U67 vacuum-tube powered condenser microphones and a [Telefunken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telefunken "Telefunken") M-5 portable tape machine. The recording is in three parts, lasting about 26 minutes, 34 minutes, and 7 minutes respectively. As it was originally programmed for vinyl [LP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LP_album "LP album"), the second part was split into sections labelled "IIa" and "IIb". The third part, labelled "IIc", was actually the final piece, a separate encore. "IIc" is a reinterpretation of a composition by Keith Jarrett, "Memories of Tomorrow", which can be heard during a trio concert with [Gus Nemeth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gus_Nemeth?action=edit&redlink=1 "Gus Nemeth") (double bass) and [Paul Motian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Motian "Paul Motian") (percussion) given in [Oslo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo "Oslo") in December 1969 and broadcast in 1972 on the Norwegian public television channel [NRK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NRK "NRK").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-10) [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/Keith_Jarrett.jpg/500px-Keith_Jarrett.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Keith_Jarrett.jpg) Jarrett in 1975 Subtle laughter may be heard from the audience at the very beginning of "Part I" in response to Jarrett's quoting of the melody of the signal bell which announces the beginning of an opera or concert to patrons at the Köln Opera House, the notes of which are G D C G A D.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-online.wsj.com-8) An article from the German newspaper _[Die Welt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Die_Welt "Die Welt")_ disputed this theory in stating that this pattern has never been used by the Köln Opera House and that it might rather be the very end of the melody of the song " [The Faithful Hussar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Faithful_Hussar "The Faithful Hussar")" played by the chiming clock of the house 4711 located close to the opera house, a tune Keith Jarrett might have heard just before going on stage.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-11) Jarrett himself noted that while he does not remember doing it consciously, he credits it for putting the audience in a good mood that helped him through a difficult concert experience.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-grammy-9) ## Transcription Subsequent to the release of _The Köln Concert_, Jarrett was asked by pianists, [musicologists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musicologist "Musicologist") and others to publish the music. For years he resisted such requests since, as he said, the music played was improvised "on a certain night and should go as quickly as it comes".[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-koln_transcription-12) In 1990, Jarrett finally agreed to publish an authorized transcription but with the recommendation that every pianist intending to play the piece should use the recording itself as the final word. ## Reception | Review scores | | --- | | Source | Rating | | Die")_.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-Dimery-Lydon_2006-21) ## Legacy In 2011 the _Witness_ program on the [BBC World Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_World_Service "BBC World Service") broadcast "Keith Jarrett in Cologne" in which Vera Brandes describes the difficulties surrounding the performance.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-BBC_2011_Witness-7) In 2019 the performance was the subject of an episode of the "Cautionary Tales" podcast, by British journalist and broadcaster [Tim Harford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Harford "Tim Harford"), which looked at the role of obstacles and difficulties in fostering the creative process.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-Harford_2019-22) It became the best-selling piano recording of all time,[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-23)[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-AAJ_2010-24) as well as the best-selling jazz solo album, with sales of around 4 million.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-Sandner_2020-25) ## Usage in popular culture - The 1980 [Nicolas Roeg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolas_Roeg "Nicolas Roeg") movie _[Bad Timing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bad_Timing "Bad Timing")_ has part of the concert in its soundtrack.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] - The 1993 [Nanni Moretti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanni_Moretti "Nanni Moretti") movie _[Caro diario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caro_diario "Caro diario")_ ("Dear Diary") has part of the concert in its soundtrack.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-26) In a 1992 interview with the German magazine __[Der Spiegel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Der_Spiegel "Der Spiegel")__, Jarrett complained that the album had become nothing more than a soundtrack and also said that "We also have to learn to forget music. Otherwise we become addicted to the past."[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-online.wsj.com-8) Several tributes were created for the 50th anniversary of the _Köln Concert._ The German film entitled _[Köln 75](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ln_75 "Köln 75")_, directed by [Ido Fluk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ido_Fluk?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ido Fluk")\[ [de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ido%20Fluk "de:Ido Fluk")\], which tells the story of this concert, premiered at the [Berlinale 2025](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlinale_2025 "Berlinale 2025") with [Vera Brandes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vera_Brandes "Vera Brandes") played by [Mala Emde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mala_Emde "Mala Emde"), Keith Jarrett by [John Magaro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Magaro "John Magaro") and [Manfred Eicher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manfred_Eicher "Manfred Eicher") by [Alexander Scheer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Scheer "Alexander Scheer").[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert#cite_note-27)A French documentary _Köln Tracks_, directed by Vincent Duceau and scheduled for release in 2026, investigates the piano used by Keith Jarrett during this concert.
