[Decca Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decca_Records "Decca Records") (United Kingdom)
Universal Music Group (International) | | Genre | [Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") | | Country of origin | United States | | Location | Los Angeles | | Official website | [bluenote.com](http://bluenote.com/) | **Blue Note Records** is an American [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") record label now owned by [Universal Music Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Music_Group "Universal Music Group") and operated under [Capitol Music Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitol_Music_Group "Capitol Music Group").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-umg-1) Established in 1939 by [German-Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_Germany "History of the Jews in Germany") emigrants [Alfred Lion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Lion "Alfred Lion") and [Max Margulis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Margulis "Max Margulis"), it derived its name from the [blue notes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_note "Blue note") of [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") and the [blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues "Blues"). Originally dedicated to recording traditional jazz and small group swing, the label began to switch its attention to modern jazz around 1947. From there, Blue Note grew to become one of the most prolific, influential and respected jazz labels of the mid-20th century, noted for its role in facilitating the development of [hard bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop "Hard bop"), [post-bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-bop "Post-bop") and [avant-garde jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz"), as well as for its iconic [modernist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernism "Modernism") art direction. ## History \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blue_Note_Records&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: History")\] Historically, Blue Note has principally been associated with the " [hard bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop "Hard bop")" style of jazz (mixing [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop") with other forms of music including [soul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_music "Soul music"), blues, [rhythm and blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues") and [gospel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_music "Gospel music")), but also recorded essential albums in the [avant-garde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde "Avant-garde") and [free](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Jazz "Free Jazz") styles of jazz. [Horace Silver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Silver "Horace Silver"), [Jimmy Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Smith_(musician) "Jimmy Smith (musician)"), [Freddie Hubbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Hubbard "Freddie Hubbard"), [Lee Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Morgan "Lee Morgan"), [Art Blakey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Blakey "Art Blakey"), [Grant Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grant_Green "Grant Green"), [Hank Mobley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hank_Mobley "Hank Mobley"), [Wayne Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter "Wayne Shorter"), [Bobby Hutcherson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Hutcherson "Bobby Hutcherson"), and [Jackie McLean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_McLean "Jackie McLean") were among the label's leading artists. During its heyday, the 1950s and 1960s, the photography and graphic art of [Reid Miles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reid_Miles "Reid Miles") created a series of iconic album covers, often incorporating session photos by [Francis Wolff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Wolff "Francis Wolff"), which added to Blue Note's artistic reputation. ### Early years \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blue_Note_Records&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Early years")\] Lion first heard jazz as a young boy in [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin"). He settled in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") in 1937, and shortly after the first [From Spirituals to Swing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/From_Spirituals_to_Swing "From Spirituals to Swing") concert, recorded pianists [Albert Ammons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ammons "Albert Ammons") and [Meade Lux Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meade_Lux_Lewis "Meade Lux Lewis") in 1939 during a one-day session in a rented studio.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-LarkinGE-2) The Blue Note label initially consisted of Lion and [Max Margulis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Margulis "Max Margulis"), a communist writer who funded the project. The label's first releases were traditional "hot" jazz and [boogie woogie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boogie_woogie "Boogie woogie"), and the label's first hit was a performance of " [Summertime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summertime_(George_Gershwin_song) "Summertime (George Gershwin song)")" by famous soprano saxophonist [Sidney Bechet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidney_Bechet "Sidney Bechet"), which Bechet had been unable to record for the established companies.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-LarkinGE-2) Musicians were supplied with alcoholic refreshments, and recorded in the early hours of the morning after their evening's work in clubs and bars had finished. The label soon became known for treating musicians uncommonly well—setting up recording sessions at congenial times, and allowing the artists to be involved in all aspects of the record's production. Francis Wolff, a professional photographer, emigrated to the US at the end of 1939 and soon joined forces with Lion, a childhood friend.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-LarkinGE-2) In 1941, Lion was drafted into the army for two years. [Milt Gabler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milt_Gabler "Milt Gabler") at the [Commodore Music Store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commodore_Records "Commodore Records") offered storage facilities and helped keep the catalog in print, with Wolff working for him. By late 1943, the label was back in business recording musicians and supplying records to the armed forces. Willing to record artists that most other labels would consider to be uncommercial, in December 1943 the label initiated more sessions with artists such as pianist [Art Hodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Hodes "Art Hodes"), trumpeter [Sidney De Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidney_De_Paris "Sidney De Paris"), clarinetist [Edmond Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmond_Hall "Edmond Hall"), and Harlem stride pianist [James P. Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_P._Johnson "James P. Johnson"),[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-LarkinGE-2) who was returning to a high degree of musical activity after having largely recovered from a stroke suffered in 1940. ### Lion and Wolff embrace bebop \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blue_Note_Records&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Lion and Wolff embrace bebop")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6f/Thelonious_Monk%2C_Minton%27s_Playhouse%2C_New_York%2C_N.Y.%2C_ca._Sept._1947_%28William_P._Gottlieb_06221%29.jpg/250px-Thelonious_Monk%2C_Minton%27s_Playhouse%2C_New_York%2C_N.Y.%2C_ca._Sept._1947_%28William_P._Gottlieb_06221%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Thelonious_Monk,_Minton's_Playhouse,_New_York,_N.Y.,_ca._Sept._1947_(William_P._Gottlieb_06221).jpg) [Thelonious Monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thelonious_Monk "Thelonious Monk") performing in 1947, the same year he would record his first sessions for Blue Note Towards the end of the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War"), saxophonist [Ike Quebec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ike_Quebec "Ike Quebec") was among those who recorded for the label.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-LarkinGE-2) Quebec would act as a talent scout for the label until his death in 1963.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-GMJ-3) Although stylistically belonging to a previous generation, he could appreciate the new bebop style of jazz, the creation of which is usually attributed to [Dizzy Gillespie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie "Dizzy Gillespie") and [Charlie Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Parker "Charlie Parker"). In 1947, pianist [Thelonious Monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thelonious_Monk "Thelonious Monk") recorded his first sessions as a leader for the label, which were also the Blue Note debut of drummer [Art Blakey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Blakey "Art Blakey"), who also recorded his first session as leader for the label at this time.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-LarkinGE-2) Lion recorded several Monk sessions before he began to release the resulting sides. Monk's recordings for Blue Note between 1947 and 1952 did not sell well for some years, but have since come to be regarded as the most important of his career. Other bebop or [modernist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernist "Modernist") musicians who recorded for Blue Note during the late 1940s and early 1950s were pianist [Tadd Dameron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tadd_Dameron "Tadd Dameron"), trumpeters [Fats Navarro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fats_Navarro "Fats Navarro") and [Howard McGhee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_McGhee "Howard McGhee"), saxophonist [James Moody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Moody_(saxophonist) "James Moody (saxophonist)") and pianist [Bud Powell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bud_Powell "Bud Powell").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-LarkinGE-2) The sessions by Powell are commonly ranked among his best. [J. J. Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._J._Johnson "J. J. Johnson") and trumpeter [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis") both recorded several sessions for Blue Note between 1952 and 1954, but by then the musicians who had created bebop were starting to explore other styles. The recording of musicians performing in an earlier jazz idiom, such as [Sidney Bechet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidney_Bechet "Sidney Bechet") and clarinettist [George Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Lewis_(clarinetist) "George Lewis (clarinetist)"), continued into the 1950s. ### Hard bop \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blue_Note_Records&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: Hard bop")\] In 1951, Blue Note issued their first vinyl 10″ releases. The label was soon recording emerging talent such as Horace Silver (who would stay with Blue Note for 25 years) and [Clifford Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_Brown "Clifford Brown"). Meanwhile, [Milt Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milt_Jackson "Milt Jackson") (as the leader of what became the [Modern Jazz Quartet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_Jazz_Quartet "Modern Jazz Quartet")) and the [Jazz Messengers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Messengers "Jazz Messengers") (originally organised as a cooperative, but soon to become Art Blakey's group) recorded for Blue Note. The Milt Jackson Quartet session was a one-off, but Blakey's various groups recorded for the label extensively, if intermittently, for the next decade. [Rudy Van Gelder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudy_Van_Gelder "Rudy Van Gelder") recorded most Blue Note releases from 1953, after Lion and Van Gelder's mutual friend, saxophonist and composer [Gil Melle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gil_Melle "Gil Melle"), introduced them.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-LarkinGE-2) A difference between Blue Note and other independent labels (for example [Prestige Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_Records "Prestige Records"), who also employed Van Gelder) was that musicians were paid for rehearsal time prior to the recording session: this helped ensure a better end result on the record. Producer [Bob Porter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Porter_(record_producer) "Bob Porter (record producer)") of Prestige Records once said that "The difference between Blue Note and Prestige is two days' rehearsal."[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-4) When the recording industry switched to 12″ LP in the mid-1950s, Blue Note was in difficulties. Their catalog on the now outmoded 10″ LP now had to be recreated on the newer format. Lion contemplated selling out to [Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Records "Atlantic Records") at this time, an option which was not acted upon. A musician who was to become one of the label's best sellers was discovered. [Jimmy Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Smith_(musician) "Jimmy Smith (musician)"), the [Hammond organist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hammond_organ "Hammond organ") was signed in 1956,[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-LarkinGE-2) and performed on the label's first 12″ LP album of new recordings. The mid-to-late 1950s saw debut recordings for Blue Note by (among others) [Hank Mobley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hank_Mobley "Hank Mobley"), [Lee Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Morgan "Lee Morgan"), [Herbie Nichols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Nichols "Herbie Nichols"), [Sonny Clark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Clark "Sonny Clark"), [Kenny Dorham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Dorham "Kenny Dorham"), [Kenny Burrell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Burrell "Kenny Burrell"), [Jackie McLean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_McLean "Jackie McLean"), [Donald Byrd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Byrd "Donald Byrd") and [Lou Donaldson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou_Donaldson "Lou Donaldson"). [Sonny Rollins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Rollins "Sonny Rollins") recorded for the label in 1956 and 1957 and Bud Powell briefly returned. [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane")'s _[Blue Train](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Train_(album) "Blue Train (album)")_, and [Cannonball Adderley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannonball_Adderley "Cannonball Adderley")'s _[Somethin' Else](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somethin'_Else_(Cannonball_Adderley_album) "Somethin' Else (Cannonball Adderley album)")_ (featuring [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis") in one of his last supporting roles) were guest appearances on the label. Blue Note was by then recording a mixture of established acts (Rollins, Adderley) and artists who in some cases had recorded before, but often produced performances for the label which by far exceeded earlier recordings in quality ( _Blue Train_ is often considered to be the first significant recording by Coltrane as a leader). Horace Silver and Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers continued to release a series of artistically and commercially successful recordings. The early 1960s saw [Dexter Gordon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dexter_Gordon "Dexter Gordon") join the label.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-LarkinGE-2) Gordon was a saxophonist from the bebop era who had spent several years in prison for narcotic offences, and he made several albums for Blue Note over a five-year period, including several at the beginning of his sojourn in Europe. Gordon also appeared on the debut album by [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock") \- by the mid 1960s, all four of the younger members of the Miles Davis quintet (Hancock, [Wayne Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter "Wayne Shorter"), [Ron Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Carter "Ron Carter") and [Tony Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer) "Tony Williams (drummer)")) were recording for the label, and Hancock and Shorter in particular produced a succession of superb albums in a mix of styles. Carter did not actually record under his own name until the label's revival in the 1980s, but played [double bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_bass "Double bass") on many other musicians' sessions. Many of these also included [Freddie Hubbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Hubbard "Freddie Hubbard"), a trumpeter who also recorded for the label as a leader. One of the features of the label during this period was a "family" of musicians (Hubbard, Hancock, Carter, Grant Green, [Joe Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Henderson "Joe Henderson"), Kenny Dorham, Lee Morgan, [Blue Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mitchell "Blue Mitchell"), Hank Mobley and many others) who would record as sidemen on each other's albums without necessarily being part of the leader's [working group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_group "Working group"). The early 1960s also saw three Blue Note recordings by pianist/composer [Freddie Redd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Redd "Freddie Redd"), one of which, _[The Connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Music_From_The_Connection_(Freddie_Redd_Quartet) "The Music From The Connection (Freddie Redd Quartet)")_, used music written for the play by [Jack Gelber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Gelber "Jack Gelber") and its film version. In 1963, Lee Morgan scored a significant hit with [the title track of](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sidewinder_(song) "The Sidewinder (song)") _[The Sidewinder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sidewinder "The Sidewinder")_ album,[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-LarkinGE-2) and Horace Silver did the same the following year with _[Song for My Father](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Song_for_My_Father_(album) "Song for My Father (album)")_. As a result, Lion was under pressure by independent distributors to come up with similar successes, with the result that many Blue Note albums of this era start with a catchy tune intended for heavy airplay in the United States. At the end of the 1950s, and in the early 1960s, Blue Note headquarters were located in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), at West 61st Street,[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-5)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-7) and at 47 W 63rd Street.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-8) ### The Avant-Garde \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blue_Note_Records&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: The Avant-Garde")\] Although many of the acts on Blue Note were recording jazz for a wide audience, the label also documented some of the emerging avant-garde and [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") players. [Andrew Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Hill_(jazz_musician) "Andrew Hill (jazz musician)"),[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-LarkinGE-2) a highly individual pianist, made many albums for the label, one featuring multi-instrumentalist [Eric Dolphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy "Eric Dolphy"). Dolphy's _[Out to Lunch!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch! "Out to Lunch!")_ (featuring a celebrated cover by [Reid Miles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reid_Miles "Reid Miles")) is perhaps his best-known album. Saxophonist [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman") released two albums recorded with a trio in a Stockholm club, and three studio albums (including _The Empty Foxhole_, with his then ten-year-old son [Denardo Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denardo_Coleman "Denardo Coleman") on drums). Pianist [Cecil Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor "Cecil Taylor") recorded a brace of albums for Blue Note, as did trombonist [Grachan Moncur III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grachan_Moncur_III "Grachan Moncur III"), and saxophonist [Sam Rivers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Rivers_(jazz_musician) "Sam Rivers (jazz musician)"), drummer Tony Williams, vibraphonist [Bobby Hutcherson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Hutcherson "Bobby Hutcherson") and organist [Larry Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Young_(jazz) "Larry Young (jazz)") also recorded albums which diverged from the "hard bop" style usually associated with the label.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-LarkinGE-2) Saxophonist Jackie McLean, a stalwart of the label's hard bop output since the late 1950s, also crossed over into the avant-garde in the early 1960s, whose notable avant-garde albums included _One Step Beyond_, _Destination Out_ and on (as a side man) trombonist Grachan Moncur III's "Evolution". Though these avant-garde records did not sell as well as some other Blue Note releases, Lion thought it was important to document new developments in jazz. [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0b/Art_Hodes_Doctor_Jazz_Blue_Note.jpg/250px-Art_Hodes_Doctor_Jazz_Blue_Note.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Art_Hodes_Doctor_Jazz_Blue_Note.jpg) Iconic Blue Note label design on an [Art Hodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Hodes "Art Hodes") record ### Cover art \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blue_Note_Records&action=edit§ion=6 "Edit section: Cover art")\] Main article: [Album covers of Blue Note Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album_covers_of_Blue_Note_Records "Album covers of Blue Note Records") In 1956, Blue Note employed [Reid Miles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reid_Miles "Reid Miles"), an artist who worked for _[Esquire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esquire_(magazine) "Esquire (magazine)")_ magazine.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-LarkinGE-2) The cover art produced by Miles, often featuring Wolff's photographs of musicians in the studio, was as influential in the world of graphic design as the music within would be in the world of jazz.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-9) Under Miles, Blue Note was known for their striking and unusual album cover designs.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-LarkinGE-2) Miles' graphical design was distinguished by its tinted black and white photographs, creative use of [sans-serif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sans-serif "Sans-serif") typefaces, and restricted color palette (often black and white with a single color), and frequent use of solid rectangular bands of color or white, influenced by the [Bauhaus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bauhaus "Bauhaus") school of design.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-10) Though Miles' work is closely associated with Blue Note and has earned iconic status and frequent homage, Miles was only a casual jazz fan, according to Richard Cook;[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-11) Blue Note gave him several copies of each of the many dozens of albums he designed, but Miles gave most to friends or sold them to second-hand record shops. A few mid-1950s album covers featured drawings by a then-unknown [Andy Warhol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Warhol "Andy Warhol").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-12) Some of his most celebrated designs adorned the sleeves of albums such as _[Midnight Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midnight_Blue_(Kenny_Burrell_album) "Midnight Blue (Kenny Burrell album)")_, _[Out to Lunch!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch! "Out to Lunch!")_, _[Unity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unity_(Larry_Young_album) "Unity (Larry Young album)")_, _[Somethin' Else](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somethin'_Else_(Cannonball_Adderley_album) "Somethin' Else (Cannonball Adderley album)")_, _[Let Freedom Ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Let_Freedom_Ring "Let Freedom Ring")_, _[Hub-Tones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hub-Tones "Hub-Tones")_, _[No Room for Squares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_Room_for_Squares "No Room for Squares")_, _[Cool Struttin'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cool_Struttin' "Cool Struttin'")_, and _[The Sidewinder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sidewinder "The Sidewinder")_. ### Lion retires; Wolff dies \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blue_Note_Records&action=edit§ion=7 "Edit section: Lion retires; Wolff dies")\] Blue Note was acquired by [Liberty Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberty_Records "Liberty Records") in 1965 and Lion, who had difficulties working within a larger organization, retired in 1967.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-LarkinGE-2) Reid Miles' association with the label ended in late 1967. In 1968, Liberty Records was acquired by [Transamerica Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transamerica_Corporation "Transamerica Corporation"), a holding company. The same year, [United Artists Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Artists_Records "United Artists Records") merged with Liberty, along with its subsidiary labels including Blue Note. In 1972, the group was consolidated into one entity as United Artists Records. From late 1967 to 1971, recording sessions were produced by Wolff or pianist [Duke Pearson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Pearson "Duke Pearson"), who had succeeded Ike Quebec in A&R in 1963 (following Quebec's death). Francis Wolff died in 1971 and Pearson left the label in the same year.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-GMJ-3) At the end of the 1960s, the company headquarters were moved to 1776 Broadway.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-13) ### Revival and ownership history \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blue_Note_Records&action=edit§ion=8 "Edit section: Revival and ownership history")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/Blue_Note_Advert_1969.png/250px-Blue_Note_Advert_1969.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Blue_Note_Advert_1969.png) 1969 advertisement after Blue Note was acquired by [Liberty Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberty_Records "Liberty Records") In 1979, EMI purchased [United Artists Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Artists_Records "United Artists Records"), which had absorbed Liberty Records in 1968,[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-14) and phased out the Blue Note label, which lay dormant until 1985, when it was relaunched as part of [EMI Manhattan Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EMI_Manhattan_Records "EMI Manhattan Records") (both for re-issues and new recordings for which [Bruce Lundvall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Lundvall "Bruce Lundvall") was appointed).[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-LarkinGE-2) Some artists previously associated with Blue Note, such as [McCoy Tyner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner "McCoy Tyner"), made new recordings,[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-LarkinGE-2) while younger musicians such as [Bennie Wallace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bennie_Wallace "Bennie Wallace"), [Joe Lovano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Lovano "Joe Lovano"), [John Scofield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Scofield "John Scofield"), [Greg Osby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greg_Osby "Greg Osby"), [Jason Moran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Moran_(musician) "Jason Moran (musician)") and arranger–composer [Bob Belden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Belden "Bob Belden") have established notable reputations through their Blue Note albums. The label has also found great commercial success with the vocalist [Norah Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norah_Jones "Norah Jones"), and released new albums by established artists on the fringes of jazz such as [Van Morrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison "Van Morrison"), [Al Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Green "Al Green"), [Anita Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anita_Baker "Anita Baker") and newcomer [Amos Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amos_Lee "Amos Lee"), sometimes referred to as the "male Norah Jones". Two of the leading trumpeters of the 1980s Jazz Resurgence, [Wynton Marsalis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wynton_Marsalis "Wynton Marsalis") and [Terence Blanchard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terence_Blanchard "Terence Blanchard") signed with the label in 2003. Hip-hop producer [Madlib](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madlib "Madlib") recorded _[Shades of Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shades_of_Blue_(Madlib_album) "Shades of Blue (Madlib album)")_ in 2003, as a tribute to Blue Note, with samples from earlier records on the label. Blue Note has pursued an active reissue program since the mid-1980s revival, and [Michael Cuscuna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Cuscuna "Michael Cuscuna") has worked as freelance advisor and reissue producer.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-LarkinGE-2) Some of the original Blue Note's output has appeared in CD box sets issued by [Mosaic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosaic_Records "Mosaic Records") (also involving Cuscuna).[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-GMJ-3) Blue Note Records became the flagship jazz label for [Capitol Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitol_Records "Capitol Records"), and was the parent label for the Capitol Jazz, [Pacific Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Jazz_Records "Pacific Jazz Records"), [Roulette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roulette_Records "Roulette Records") and other labels within Capitol's holdings which had possessed a jazz line.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-GMJ-3) The "RVG series", Rudy Van Gelder remastering his own recordings from decades earlier began around 1998. In 2006, EMI expanded Blue Note to create [The Blue Note Label Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Blue_Note_Label_Group "The Blue Note Label Group") by moving its Narada group of labels to New York to join with Blue Note, centralizing EMI's approach to music for the adult market segment. The labels newly under the Blue Note umbrella are [Angel Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angel_Records "Angel Records"), [EMI Classics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EMI_Classics "EMI Classics") and Virgin Classics (classical music), [Narada Productions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narada_Productions "Narada Productions") (contemporary jazz and world-influenced music, including exclusively licensed sub-label [Real World Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_World_Records "Real World Records")), [Back Porch Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back_Porch_Records "Back Porch Records") (folk and Americana), [Higher Octave Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher_Octave_Records "Higher Octave Records") (smooth jazz and [New-age music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New-age_music "New-age music")), and Mosaic Records (devoted exclusively to reissuing jazz recordings in limited-edition boxed sets).[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-15)[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-16) As of June 2007, Bruce Lundvall, founder of [Manhattan Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan_Records "Manhattan Records"), as President/CEO of the Blue Note Label Group, was at the time reporting directly to Eric Nicoli, then Chief Executive Officer of EMI Group.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-17) In 2008, [the Blue Note 7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Blue_Note_7 "The Blue Note 7"), a jazz [septet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Septet "Septet"), was formed in honor of the 70th anniversary of Blue Note Records. The group recorded an album in 2008, entitled _[Mosaic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosaic:_A_Celebration_of_Blue_Note_Records "Mosaic: A Celebration of Blue Note Records")_, which was released in 2009 on Blue Note Records/ [EMI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EMI "EMI"), and toured the United States in promotion of the album from January until April 2009.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-18) The group consists of [Peter Bernstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Bernstein_(guitarist) "Peter Bernstein (guitarist)") (guitar), [Bill Charlap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Charlap "Bill Charlap") (piano), [Ravi Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ravi_Coltrane "Ravi Coltrane") (tenor saxophone), [Lewis Nash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_Nash "Lewis Nash") (drums), [Nicholas Payton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_Payton "Nicholas Payton") (trumpet), [Peter Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Washington "Peter Washington") (bass), and [Steve Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Wilson_(jazz_musician) "Steve Wilson (jazz musician)") (alto saxophone, flute). The group plays the music of Blue Note Records from various artists, with arrangements by members of the band and [Renee Rosnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renee_Rosnes "Renee Rosnes"). Following the acquisition of EMI by Universal, [Don Was](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Was "Don Was") became President of Blue Note in January 2012, after an appointment as CEO a few months earlier, in succession to Bruce Lundvall. Lundvall, who stood down in 2010, became Chairman Emeritus[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-19) In May 2013, Blue Note Records partnered with [ArtistShare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ArtistShare "ArtistShare") to form a label called "Blue Note/ArtistShare". The Blue Note/ArtistShare partnership was forged by ArtistShare founder [Brian Camelio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Camelio "Brian Camelio"), [Bruce Lundvall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Lundvall "Bruce Lundvall"), and [Don Was](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Was "Don Was").[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-20) After [Universal Music Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Music_Group "Universal Music Group") took over EMI, Blue Note Records is now operated under [Capitol Music Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitol_Music_Group "Capitol Music Group"),[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-umg-1) while [Decca Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decca_Records "Decca Records") took over UK distribution of Blue Note.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-21)[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-22) ### Modern era \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blue_Note_Records&action=edit§ion=9 "Edit section: Modern era")\] Blue Note has seen a continuity in releases from older artists such as Shorter, [Charles Lloyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Lloyd_(jazz_musician) "Charles Lloyd (jazz musician)"), [Louis Hayes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Hayes "Louis Hayes"), and [Dr. Lonnie Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lonnie_Smith_(organist) "Lonnie Smith (organist)"). In 2019, the imprint announced the launch of a vinyl reissue series of classic titles,[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-23) with releases selected and produced by [Grammy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Awards "Grammy Awards")-nominated producer and jazz expert Joe Harley.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-24) The series, named the "Tone Poet series" in honor of Harley, reissues several titles each year from the Blue Note catalogue.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-25) In 2020, Blue Note released the debut of South African artist [Nduduzo Makhathini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nduduzo_Makhathini "Nduduzo Makhathini"), called _Modes of Communication: Letters from the Underworlds_. It was named one of the "Best Jazz Albums of 2020" by _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")_, and was followed by _In the Spirit of Ntu_ in 2022, and _uNomkhubulwane_ in 2024.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-26) ## Legacy \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blue_Note_Records&action=edit§ion=10 "Edit section: Legacy")\] There has been much sampling of classic Blue Note tracks by both hip hop artists and for mashing projects. In 1993, the group [Us3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Us3 "Us3") designed the entirety of its [debut album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hand_on_the_Torch "Hand on the Torch") upon samples from classic Blue Note records. In 2003, hip-hop producer [Madlib](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madlib "Madlib") released _[Shades of Blue: Madlib Invades Blue Note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shades_of_Blue_(Madlib_album) "Shades of Blue (Madlib album)")_, a collection of his remixes and interpretations of Blue Note music. [Pete Rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Rock "Pete Rock"), [J Dilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J_Dilla "J Dilla"), and [DJ Spinna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DJ_Spinna "DJ Spinna") have likewise been involved in similar projects. In 2004, Burning Vision Entertainment created the video for Helicopter Girl's "Angel City",[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-27) using the art from numerous Blue Note LP sleeves to startling effect. In 2008, hip-hop producer [Questlove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Questlove "Questlove") of [The Roots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Roots "The Roots") compiled _Droppin' Science: Greatest Samples from the Blue Note Lab_, a collection of original Blue Note recordings sampled by modern-day hip-hop artists such as [Dr. Dre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dr._Dre "Dr. Dre") and [A Tribe Called Quest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Tribe_Called_Quest "A Tribe Called Quest"). ## Notable issues of critical assessment \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blue_Note_Records&action=edit§ion=11 "Edit section: Notable issues of critical assessment")\] ### Publishing rights \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blue_Note_Records&action=edit§ion=12 "Edit section: Publishing rights")\] Any artist who records a song written by another artists is required to pay the statutory royalty to the copyright owner. A royalty is a usage-based fee paid by a licensee (the party wanting to use the copyrighted music) to a licensor (the owner of the copyrighted music). From the 1930s through the 1960s it was commonplace for a songwriter to sign over the rights to his/her work to a company — usually the record label for which they were recording — as part of the terms of the recording contract. Unfortunately, few musicians of this period had sufficient knowledge of US copyright laws or the proper advocator legal advice to ensure they would receive the royalties for their compositions. As a result, whenever any of their pieces were recorded, broadcast, telecast, etc., it was the record company that profited — and the writer received nothing. The majority of jazz musicians fell victim to this practice in that period. Andrew Dowd writes: "The example that still haunts me (and probably always will) is the famous tenor saxophonist Hank Mobley. He recorded countless albums for the storied label Blue Note from 1955 to 1970 (many of them classics) yet he died alone and penniless in a tiny Philadelphia apartment in 1986"[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-28) #### Donald Byrd \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blue_Note_Records&action=edit§ion=13 "Edit section: Donald Byrd")\] Trumpeter Donald Byrd recorded for Blue Note Records, 1959-1967. He encouraged fellow musicians to always retain the publishing rights to their own music and to always negotiate their recording contracts as a standard practice.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-29) #### Herbie Hancock \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blue_Note_Records&action=edit§ion=14 "Edit section: Herbie Hancock")\] According to Tom Cotter: "Hancock credits Byrd with giving him one of the most important pieces of advice of his career – not to give away his publishing rights. When Blue Note offered Hancock the chance to record his first solo LP, label executives tried to convince him to relinquish his publishing in exchange for being able to record the album, but he stuck to Byrd's advice and refused, so the meeting came to an impasse. At this point, he stood up to leave and when it became clear that he was about to walk out, the executives relented and allowed him to retain his publishing. Thanks to Santamaria's subsequent hit cover version of "Watermelon Man", Hancock was soon receiving substantial royalties".[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-30) #### Steve Swallow \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blue_Note_Records&action=edit§ion=15 "Edit section: Steve Swallow")\] During an interview by Ethan Iverson, double bassist Steve Swallow revealed the following about the 1965 Pete La Roca "Basra" LP session: "Another song on the date is my piece, 'Eiderdown,' which is actually the first recording of one of my compositions. It's also the only tune of mine that I don't own. Alfred Lion snatched it right out of my hands. After the date had been done, I got a phone call from Alfred and he said, 'Oh, by the way, "Eiderdown," who is publishing that?' I had no idea what he was talking about. I said, 'Gee, I don't know.' Alfred said, 'No problem.' He then proceeded to offer me this 'wonderful' deal. He would publish it for me and take care of everything and I wouldn't have to worry about a thing. I was so grateful. 'Gee, Alfred. Thank you so much.' I haven't been able to get that tune back after all these years. Blue Note sold it, it's gone around, and some big conglomerate owns it now. I keep trying to buy it back because it has been recorded fairly often. That's another kind of Blue Note story. It is a great blessing to jazz that Blue Note existed, but on the business side they were also sort of gangsters."[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-31) ### Lee Morgan and Grant Green: high volumes of unreleased recordings \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blue_Note_Records&action=edit§ion=16 "Edit section: Lee Morgan and Grant Green: high volumes of unreleased recordings")\] Based on the number of recording dates held, Grant Green and Lee Morgan were the most prolific Blue Note recording artists in the 1960s. It has been conjectured for many years that as the label's major heroin addicts, Green and Morgan would come to Al Lion for "an advance". At his discretion, Lion would then respond by arranging an "ad-hoc" recording session — paying the standard base arrangement at the time: one four-hour rehearsal and one subsequent four-hour recording session. The artists were paid for their time and Lion now owned an LP's worth of recorded music — including the publishing rights — to be used solely at Blue Note's later discretion. Both Green and Morgan were used far more than any other guitarist or trumpeter as participants at other Blue Note sessions during this same period (roughly, 1961-67). Once Al Lion left Blue Note (August 1967), there were no more of these ad hoc recording sessions.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-32) ### Notable participating musicians who did not record as leaders, 1965-1968 \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blue_Note_Records&action=edit§ion=17 "Edit section: Notable participating musicians who did not record as leaders, 1965-1968")\] From 1955 to 1964, Al Lion was relatively prolific in signing quality artists to recording contracts with Blue Note — many of whom were new to the recording industry. During 1955-59, Lion signed multi-LP contracts with the following artists — all of whom would develop into the high-profile artists that would define Blue Note records into the early 1960s: Art Blakey, Kenny Burrell, Donald Byrd, Paul Chambers, Lou Donaldson, Kenny Dorham, Curtis Fuller, Freddie Hubbard, Thad Jones, Jackie McLean, Hank Mobley, Lee Morgan, Duke Pearson, Horace Silver, and Jimmy Smith.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-my-source-1-33) During 1960-64, Lion signed multi-LP contracts with the following new artists (many of whom had no prior recording contracts) — all of whom would develop into high-profile artists that would further define Blue Note records throughout the 1960s: Grant Green, Herbie Hancock, Joe Henderson, Andrew Hill, Bobby Hutcherson, John Patton, Sam Rivers, Wayne Shorter, Stanley Turrentine, Tony Williams, and Larry Young. The following established artists were also signed: Dexter Gordon, and Blue Mitchell.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-my-source-1-33) #### 1965-68: Liberty \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blue_Note_Records&action=edit§ion=18 "Edit section: 1965-68: Liberty")\] Following Al Lion's and partner Francis Wolff's sale of Blue Note Records to Liberty Records in 1965, there was an immediate reduction in new talent acquisition. Instead, Liberty, which is presumed to have had more working capital than Blue Note, signed the following eight established artist (all of whom had been with previous labels) to multi-LP contracts: Don Cherry, Ornette Coleman, Booker Ervin, Frank Foster, Elvin Jones, Cecil Taylor, McCoy Tyner, and Jack Wilson.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-my-source-1-33) During the Liberty period, no new talent was signed to multi-LP contracts. Liberty, however, did offer single-LP contracts to Pete La Roca in 1965 and Tyrone Washington in 1967 (in Washington's case an unfinished follow-up 1968 session was documented).[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-my-source-1-33) In addition to signing fewer artists to contracts, Liberty also thinned out the current roster of artists under contract at Blue Note. The following artists, who had multi-LP contracts with Blue Note prior to 1965, stopped recording for Blue Note during the Liberty period: Art Blakey, Kenny Burrell, Kenny Dorham, Dexter Gordon, Grant Green, Joe Henderson, Freddie Hubbard, Sam Rivers, and Tony Williams.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-my-source-1-33) Although Lion remained the sole producer at Blue Note until his July 1967 retirement, following the 1965 ownership change he no longer enjoyed authority regarding talent acquisition, which most likely explains why the following new artists — all of whom exhibited unique and pronounced musical aptitude during the 1965-68 Blue Note recording sessions on which they participated — were not offered contracts. ##### Joe Chambers \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blue_Note_Records&action=edit§ion=19 "Edit section: Joe Chambers")\] Chambers first came to Blue Note by way of Freddie Hubbard's _Breaking Point_ session (May 1964) and from 1965-1969 wrote and arranged several stirring and memorable pieces for 8 of 9 Bobby Hutcherson sessions.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-my-source-1-33) Chambers was a unique artist: in addition to being a highly skilled trap drummer, he was equally adroit at orchestral percussion (e.g., marimba), and piano, as well as composition and arranging. In addition to the numerous Hutcherson dates, Chambers participated in sessions for the following artists: Joe Henderson, Andrew Hill, Sam Rivers, Wayne Shorter, and McCoy Tyner. It goes without saying that Chambers was participating in important, pace-setting post-bop dates and that his skill level and artistic abilities clearly contributed to the overall artistic success of those sessions. Liberty may not have offered Chambers a contract in 1965-66 as the label currently had contracts with two drummers (Tony Williams and Pete La Roca — though neither recorded as leaders after 1965). In 1968, Liberty extended a multi-LP contract to drummer Elvin Jones, who was the only drummer at Blue Note under contract at that time.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-my-source-1-33) (Recording contracts extended to drummers and double bassists are uncommon relative to horn players, pianists, and organists.) ##### Chick Corea \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blue_Note_Records&action=edit§ion=20 "Edit section: Chick Corea")\] Corea first came to Blue Note by way of Blue Mitchell's _The Thing To Do_ session (July 1964) as a member of the Blue Mitchell Quintet and played on two subsequent sessions, July 1965 and November 1966.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-my-source-1-33) Corea brought his own compositions to these sessions. Like Herbie Hancock, Corea exhibited a singular aural approach to playing piano, was a formally schooled musician, was a solid composer and arranger, and would even replace Hancock in the Miles Davis Quintet in late 1968. Unfortunately, given Mitchell's hard-bop stylings during 1964-65, Corea's emerging post-bop talent may not have been realized by Al Lion. Akin to Andrew Hill's playing with Hank Mobley in 1963, which did not demonstrate Hill's musical direction, it can be equally said that Corea's 1964-65 contributions to both Blue Mitchell's LPs from this period were similarly unrepresentative of Corea's musical direction. By the time of the quintet's third LP date, January 1966, Lion actually had Corea replaced (by Harold Mabern — in an attempt to inject a stronger R&B feeling into the date, according to Michael Cuscuna.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-34) Yet, by the following November 1966 session for _Boss Horn_, which would be Corea's last with Mitchell, he had already written two pieces that would quickly become jazz standards: "Tones For Joan's Bones" and "Straight Up And Down". Both pieces had made such an impact at the session that arranger Duke Pearson's glowing accolades, writer Nat Hentoff's exuberant critique, and quotes from Corea himself would dominate nearly half of the liner note content.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-35) In 2005, writer Bob Blumenthal further offered: "Chick Corea, the pianist and composer of the two final tracks, had received his first significant exposure in the jazz world on Mitchell's _The Thing To Do_ and _Down With It!_ The present album \[ _Boss Horn_\] served similar notice regarding his talents as a composer, and heralded Corea's arrival as a major voice in music".[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-36) By this time, however, Corea was under contract with Atlantic and in two weeks would himself lead his first session as a leader — including his own recordings of his compositions here (Duke Pearson himself would also record both in 1967 and 1968). On the surface, the excitement and success surrounding the November 1966 recording session suggests not having previously extended a contract to Corea was a missed opportunity for Lion. Though in his defense, Corea's unique talents were not fully on display to Lion until the November 1966 date. To further underscore Lion's presumed unknowingness regarding Corea's emerging talent, one can only wonder: had Lion not replaced Corea for the January 1966 session, what compositions Corea would have brought to that session — and would they have received similar acclaim? In the end, given Liberty's practice of favouring established artists to new talent, it's unknown if lobbying from Al Lion and others would have persuaded Liberty management to sign Corea at that time. ##### Woody Shaw \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blue_Note_Records&action=edit§ion=21 "Edit section: Woody Shaw")\] Shaw first came to Blue Note by way of Horace Silver's _The Cape Verdean Blues_ session (October 1965), and from 1965-1968, he would participate in the recording sessions of Andrew Hill, Jackie McLean, Hank Mobley, Tyrone Washington, and Larry Young — at times contributing his own memorable compositions.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-my-source-1-33) Woody was a skilled technical expert who at the time was frequently compared to Freddie Hubbard. At his own expense, Woody produced his own demo tape in December 1965, to submit to Blue Note / Liberty in hopes of securing a recording contract. To further underscore his goal his demo session included Blue Note artists Herbie Hancock, Joe Henderson and Larry Young as well as Joe Chambers.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records#cite_note-37) Shaw may have been passed over given overarching stylistic similarities to Freddie Hubbard. That said, Hubbard left Blue Note in 1966 seemingly indicating there was a viable vacancy for another trumpet artist — which stylistically would have been a good fit for Shaw and Blue Note at that time. ## Documentary films \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blue_Note_Records&action=edit§ion=22 "Edit section: Documentary films")\] - Julian Benedikt: _Blue Note – A Story of Modern Jazz_. # Contemporary Records Contemporary Records American record label Record label | Contemporary Records | | --- | | [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/Contemporary_Records_logo_1979.svg/500px-Contemporary_Records_logo_1979.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Contemporary_Records_logo_1979.svg)
Logo used from 1979 to the mid-2000s | | Parent company | [Concord Bicycle Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concord_Bicycle_Music "Concord Bicycle Music") | | Founded | 1951(1951) | | Founder | [Lester Koenig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lester_Koenig "Lester Koenig") | | Defunct | 1984(1984) | | Status | Inactive | | Genre | [Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), [West Coast jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Coast_jazz "West Coast jazz") | | Country of origin | U.S. | | Official website | [concord.com](http://www.concord.com//labels/contemporary) | **Contemporary Records** was a [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") record company and label founded by [Lester Koenig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lester_Koenig "Lester Koenig") in [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles") in 1951. Contemporary produced music from a variety of jazz styles and players.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_Records#cite_note-New_Grove-1) ## West Coast players Contemporary became identified with a style of jazz called [West Coast jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Coast_jazz "West Coast jazz") as exemplified by [Art Pepper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Pepper "Art Pepper"), [Chet Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chet_Baker "Chet Baker"), [Shelly Manne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelly_Manne "Shelly Manne"), and [André Previn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A9_Previn "André Previn").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_Records#cite_note-New_Grove-1) In the mid-1960s the company fell into relative limbo, but limited new recordings were made in the late 1970s, including a series of albums by Art Pepper recorded at the [Village Vanguard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Village_Vanguard "Village Vanguard") club in New York. After Les Koenig's death in 1977, the label was run for seven years by his son,[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_Records#cite_note-New_Grove-1) John, who produced albums by [George Cables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Cables "George Cables"), [Joe Farrell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Farrell "Joe Farrell"), [Joe Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Henderson "Joe Henderson"), [Bobby Hutcherson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Hutcherson "Bobby Hutcherson"), [Peter Erskine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Erskine "Peter Erskine"), and [Chico Freeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chico_Freeman "Chico Freeman"). In 1984 Contemporary was purchased by [Fantasy Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fantasy_Records "Fantasy Records"), which used the name for a short time. Most Contemporary titles were reissued by Fantasy. Also, some titles have found new life among today's audiophiles as high-quality LP [remasters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_mastering "Audio mastering") from [Analogue Productions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analogue_Productions "Analogue Productions") and other [audiophile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audiophile "Audiophile") labels. The Fantasy catalog, including Contemporary and its associated labels, [Good Time Jazz Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_Time_Jazz_Records "Good Time Jazz Records"), Society for Forgotten Music, and Contemporary Composers Series, was sold to [Concord Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concord_Records "Concord Records") in 2004. Over the years, a number of major figures in the music business worked for Contemporary. Among them were [Atlantic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Records "Atlantic Records") executive [Nesuhi Ertegun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nesuhi_Ertegun "Nesuhi Ertegun"), writers [Nat Hentoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nat_Hentoff "Nat Hentoff") and [Leonard Feather](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Feather "Leonard Feather"), producer [Joe Boyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Boyd "Joe Boyd"), recording engineer and studio designer Howard Holzer, and mastering engineer [Bernie Grundman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernie_Grundman "Bernie Grundman"). ## Recording Lester Koenig was very particular about high-fidelity sounds.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_Records#cite_note-2) In 1956 Koenig hired away Roy DuNann from [Capitol Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitol_Records "Capitol Records"), and DuNann provided some creative recording techniques for the label.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_Records#cite_note-3) He said Koenig provided him with German ( [Neumann/Telefunken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georg_Neumann "Georg Neumann") U-47) and Austrian ( [AKG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AKG_Acoustics "AKG Acoustics") C-12) condenser microphones and he immediately noted the very high output of these microphones, especially close-in on jazz musicians' dynamic playing. DuNann achieved his signature sound—crisp, clear and balanced without distortion or unpleasant "peak presence"—by keeping his microphone setups very simple (generally one per musician) and avoided the use of pre-amplifiers for them. He built a simple passive mixing system that directly fed the electronics of his [Ampex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ampex#Audio_technology "Ampex") 350 and 351 tape machines. Also, DuNann told _Stereophile_ that Contemporary sessions were recorded "dry" (without electronic echo added or in a reverberant room). Sometimes, such as in the case of Sonny Rollins' _[Way Out West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Way_Out_West_(Sonny_Rollins_album) "Way Out West (Sonny Rollins album)")_, a plate reverb unit was inserted between the tape machine and the [LP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LP_album "LP album") [disc cutting lathe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disc_cutting_lathe "Disc cutting lathe"). This is why some later LP and [CD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_Disc "Compact Disc") reissues of Contemporary albums sound "dry" and "dead" compared to the original LPs mastered by DuNann. ## **Impulse! Records** (occasionally styled as "¡mpulse! Records" and "¡!") is an American [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") [record label](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Record_label "Record label") established by [Creed Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creed_Taylor "Creed Taylor") in 1960. [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane") was among Impulse!'s earliest signings. Thanks to consistent sales and positive critiques of his recordings, the label came to be known as "the house that Trane built".[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records#cite_note-1)

## History

Impulse!'s parent company, [ABC-Paramount Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC-Paramount_Records "ABC-Paramount Records"), was established in 1955 as the recording division of the American Broadcasting Company ( [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Broadcasting_Company "American Broadcasting Company")). In the 1940s and 1950s, ABC benefitted from the U.S. government's [antitrust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antitrust "Antitrust") actions against broadcasters and film studios who were forced to divest parts of their companies. In the early 1950s, ABC acquired the [Blue Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Network "Blue Network") of radio stations from [NBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC "NBC") and later merged with the newly independent Paramount Theaters chain, formerly owned by [Paramount Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount_Pictures "Paramount Pictures").

The new recording division was located at [1501 Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1501_Broadway "1501 Broadway"), above the [Paramount Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount_Theatre_(New_York_City) "Paramount Theatre (New York City)") in [Times Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Square "Times Square").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records#cite_note-2) Under the leadership of [Leonard Goldenson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Goldenson "Leonard Goldenson"), the former head of Paramount Pictures, the company "sought to establish itself as a cross-media force in television, theaters and sound recordings".[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records#cite_note-3) It enjoyed early success in TV with _[The Mickey Mouse Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mickey_Mouse_Club "The Mickey Mouse Club")_, a joint venture with [Disney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disney "Disney").

To market music from the successful TV show, ABC-Paramount established the Am-Par Record Corporation and the ABC-Paramount label in early 1955, appointing Sam Clark, a Boston record distributor, as president, with Larry Newton as sales manager and Harry Levine the A&R director. The new recording company enjoyed Goldenson's full support. Sid Feller, a producer and arranger, was the first salaried employee on July 15, 1955.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records#cite_note-4) The label achieved early success in [pop music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music "Pop music") with [Paul Anka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Anka "Paul Anka"). A young producer named [Creed Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creed_Taylor "Creed Taylor"), who also worked for a period at [Bethlehem Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethlehem_Records "Bethlehem Records") in 1955, produced some of ABC-Paramount/Am-Par's earliest albums for musicians such as [Urbie Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urbie_Green "Urbie Green"), [Billy Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Taylor "Billy Taylor"), [Oscar Pettiford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oscar_Pettiford "Oscar Pettiford"), [Kenny Dorham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Dorham "Kenny Dorham") and [Zoot Sims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoot_Sims "Zoot Sims").

In 1960, Am-Par established a jazz subsidiary and hired Taylor as producer and A&R manager. He chose the name "Pulse" but then learned there was already a label with that name, so he added a prefix. In the mid-1960s, the headquarters of Impulse! was moved to 1130 [Avenue of the Americas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avenue_of_the_Americas "Avenue of the Americas").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records#cite_note-5)

### Design

Impulse!'s albums are known for their visual appeal. The black, orange, and white [livery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Livery "Livery") was devised by [Fran Attaway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran_Attaway?action=edit&redlink=1 "Fran Attaway") (then known as Fran Scott), whom Taylor also credits with establishing the label's tradition of using cutting-edge photographers for its covers.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records#cite_note-6) The color scheme was chosen for its brightness and because no other label used this combination.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records#cite_note-7)

The label's logo featured the Impulse! name in a heavy, sans-serif, lower-cased font, followed by an exclamation mark that mirrors the lower-case "i" at the beginning. For most of the 1960s, Impulse!'s album covers featured the logo in orange letters in a white circle, with black-and-orange exclamation marks above it, and the catalog number below it. One exception is the album _[A Love Supreme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme "A Love Supreme")_, which used the design in black and white. In 1968 the circular front-cover badge was replaced by a one-color design featuring a simplified Impulse! logo and the ABC Records logo side by side within a divided rectangular border.

Album covers often featured stylish, large-format photographs or paintings, usually in color, which were typically bled out to the edges of the cover and printed on glossy laminated stock. Many of the best-known Impulse! covers were designed by art director [Robert Flynn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Flynn_(graphic_designer)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Robert Flynn (graphic designer)") and photographed by a small group that included [Pete Turner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Turner_(photographer) "Pete Turner (photographer)"), who shot covers for Verve, [A&M](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A&M_Records "A&M Records"), and [CTI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CTI_Records "CTI Records"); [Chuck Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Stewart "Chuck Stewart"); [Arnold Newman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_Newman "Arnold Newman"); [Ted Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Russell_(photographer)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ted Russell (photographer)"); and [Joe Alper](https://web.archive.org/web/20090323120015/http://www.bobdylanphotobook.com/), who was known for his early ’60s photographs of [Bob Dylan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Dylan "Bob Dylan")) The sparse black-and-white back covers bore the slogan "The New Wave of Jazz is on IMPULSE!" Most Impulse! LPs were issued in a gatefold sleeve, with photographs, liner notes, and, in some cases, multi-page booklets.

### Early success

Taylor achieved early success by signing [Ray Charles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Charles "Ray Charles"), who had just ended his contract with [Atlantic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Records "Atlantic Records"). Charles's _[Genius + Soul = Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genius_+_Soul_=_Jazz "Genius + Soul = Jazz")_ gave the label its first hit and became the fourth-highest charting album of his career.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records#cite_note-8) Other early successes included _[Out of the Cool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_of_the_Cool "Out of the Cool")_ by [Gil Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gil_Evans "Gil Evans"). Taylor also signed [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records#cite_note-9)

Another significant early release was _[The Blues and the Abstract Truth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Blues_and_the_Abstract_Truth "The Blues and the Abstract Truth")_ by [Oliver Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Nelson "Oliver Nelson"), who led an all-star group that featured [Freddie Hubbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Hubbard "Freddie Hubbard"), [Eric Dolphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy "Eric Dolphy"), [Bill Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans "Bill Evans"), [Paul Chambers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Chambers "Paul Chambers"), and [Roy Haynes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Haynes "Roy Haynes"). Nelson played an important role in the label's early years before relocating to Los Angeles, where he became an arranger for film and television.

Taylor left Impulse! in the summer of 1961 after being approached by MGM to become the head of [Verve Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verve_Records "Verve Records").

### The Thiele Years: 1961–69

[Bob Thiele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Thiele "Bob Thiele"), Taylor's successor, produced most of the albums in the 1960s. He had worked for [Decca Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decca_Records "Decca Records") and its subsidiaries [Coral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coral_Records "Coral Records") and [Brunswick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brunswick_Records "Brunswick Records"), where his production credits included [Alan Dale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Dale "Alan Dale"), [the McGuire Sisters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_McGuire_Sisters "The McGuire Sisters"), [Pearl Bailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl_Bailey "Pearl Bailey"), and [Theresa Brewer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theresa_Brewer "Theresa Brewer"), whom he married. Despite resistance from Decca executives who were suspicious of rock and roll, Thiele signed [Buddy Holly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddy_Holly "Buddy Holly") in 1957.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records#cite_note-10)

Thiele's first Impulse! production was Coltrane's _[Live! at the Village Vanguard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live!_at_the_Village_Vanguard "Live! at the Village Vanguard")_, released in March 1962. Although unfamiliar with the "new jazz" movement, Thiele backed his artists, afforded them unprecedented freedom in their repertoire, and gave leading acts like Coltrane _[carte blanche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blank_cheque "Blank cheque")_ in the studio. Impulse! during the Thiele years is recognized as a key outlet for [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") and the musical movement spearheaded by Coltrane, [Freddie Hubbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Hubbard "Freddie Hubbard"), [Archie Shepp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Shepp "Archie Shepp"), and [McCoy Tyner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner "McCoy Tyner"). In addition to avant-garde releases, Thiele also produced collaborations between Coltrane and two of their mutual heroes, [Duke Ellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Ellington "Duke Ellington") and [Coleman Hawkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coleman_Hawkins "Coleman Hawkins"). Other notable performers who recorded for Impulse! during this period included [Charles Mingus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus "Charles Mingus").

Aided by good promotion and ABC-Paramount's well-established distribution chain, Coltrane enjoyed the highest profile and the strongest and most consistent sales of any Impulse! artist. In addition to its artistic influence, Coltrane's 1965 LP _[A Love Supreme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme "A Love Supreme")_ became one of the most successful jazz albums ever released, selling over 100,000 copies[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records#cite_note-11) on its first release. By 1970 it had sold more than half a million. [Roger McGuinn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_McGuinn "Roger McGuinn") of [the Byrds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Byrds "The Byrds") has stated that he listened to Coltrane extensively in this period, and that Coltrane's saxophone playing influenced his 12-string guitar playing on the hit " [Eight Miles High](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eight_Miles_High "Eight Miles High")".

Thiele severed his ties with Impulse! in 1969, setting up a short-lived deal to provide independently produced recordings, before leaving the label entirely to establish his own imprint, [Flying Dutchman Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_Dutchman_Records "Flying Dutchman Records"). Thiele's departure was in part precipitated by the breakdown of his relationship with [Larry Newton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Newton "Larry Newton"), the president of ABC Records.

One of Thiele's last productions was the Louis Armstrong song " [What a Wonderful World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What_a_Wonderful_World "What a Wonderful World")", which Thiele co-wrote and produced for ABC's pop division shortly before Armstrong's death. Although the musicians were apparently unaware of the drama, the recording session is reported to have been the scene of a clash between Thiele and Newton. When Newton arrived at the session he became upset when he discovered that Armstrong was recording a ballad rather than a [Dixieland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dixieland_jazz "Dixieland jazz")-style number like his earlier hit " [Hello Dolly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hello,_Dolly!_(song) "Hello, Dolly! (song)")". According to Thiele's own account, this led to a screaming match; Newton then had to be locked out of the studio and he stood outside throughout the session, banging on the door and yelling to be let in. The single was released with little promotion from ABC and it sold relatively poorly in the U.S.. In Europe, it sold more than 1.5 million copies and went to #1 in the UK. Demand from ABC's European distributor [EMI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EMI "EMI") for an album forced ABC to issue one, but they did not promote the album and it did not chart in the U.S. Twenty years later, it became the most successful recording of both Armstrong's and Thiele's careers, thanks to its inclusion on the soundtrack _[Good Morning, Vietnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_Morning,_Vietnam "Good Morning, Vietnam")_.

### The 1970s

Under the guidance of [Ed Michel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Michel "Ed Michel"), Thiele's successor, Impulse! continued to issue significant recordings. The company also acquired LP masters that [Sun Ra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Ra "Sun Ra") had recorded for his private label, making them more widely available for the first time.

In the early 1970s, ABC restructured its recording division, merging the ABC label with its other pop-rock subsidiary, [Dunhill Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunhill_Records "Dunhill Records"), whose roster included [The Mamas & the Papas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mamas_&_the_Papas "The Mamas & the Papas"), [Steppenwolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band) "Steppenwolf (band)"), [Three Dog Night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Dog_Night "Three Dog Night"), and [The Grass Roots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Grass_Roots "The Grass Roots"). Impulse! was moved to share headquarters with ABC-Dunhill in [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"). By this time, pop-rock acts dominated the company's output, with Impulse! releases accounting for only 5 percent of total sales. It was also during this time that Impulse! became the first all-jazz label to release a rock album when it issued _[Trespass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trespass_(album) "Trespass (album)")_, the second album by [Genesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genesis_(band) "Genesis (band)"), in the U.S. in 1970.

In 1974, ABC acquired the [Famous Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Famous_Music "Famous Music") labels and catalog from [Gulf+Western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf+Western "Gulf+Western"), and subsequently, that company's jazz recordings were incorporated into the Impulse! catalog. New recordings from the label ceased in the late 1970s, but ABC reissued titles until the company was sold to [MCA Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MCA_Records "MCA Records") in 1979. The label lay dormant until it was resurrected in 1992 as part of MCA’s [GRP Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GRP_Records "GRP Records"), during which time the label started releasing important titles that had otherwise been unavailable and began signing new artists during the late 1990s. In 1999, Impulse! became part of [Universal Music Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Music_Group "Universal Music Group")'s jazz holdings, under the aegis of [the Verve Label Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verve_Records "Verve Records"), where it has remained until the present.
