John Coltrane in 1963 | | Studio albums | 45 | | Live albums | 11 | | Compilation albums | 23 | | Singles | 19 | | Video albums | 2 | | Appearances | 59 | | Documentaries | 3 | | Television | 2 | This article presents the [discography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discography "Discography") of the American [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") [saxophonist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxophone "Saxophone") and [bandleader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bandleader "Bandleader") [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane") (1926–1967). ## Introduction \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Coltrane_discography&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Introduction")\] Coltrane participated in his first recording sessions while enlisted in the Navy from August 6, 1945, to August 11, 1946.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane_discography#cite_note-1) He performed eight numbers in a pickup band that included trumpeter Dexter Culbertson.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane_discography#cite_note-2) These were private recordings not made for official release. However, one track from the session, " [Hot House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_House_(composition) "Hot House (composition)")", eventually appeared on the 1992 compilation _[The Last Giant: The John Coltrane Anthology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Giant:_Anthology "The Last Giant: Anthology")._[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane_discography#cite_note-3) There are conflicting sources as to whether he made his first professional recording session with [Dinah Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinah_Washington "Dinah Washington"): Jazzdisco.org[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane_discography#cite_note-4) lists the session as September 27, 1949 in New York City, but Lewis Porter's _John Coltrane: His Life and Music_ states that he was on tour with the [Dizzy Gillespie Big Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie "Dizzy Gillespie") during that time.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane_discography#cite_note-5) Most sources confirm that he recorded with Billy Valentine on November 7 in Los Angeles for [Mercury Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_Records "Mercury Records"). In subsequent years, Coltrane sat in on recording sessions with Gillespie, [Johnny Hodges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Hodges "Johnny Hodges"), [Earl Bostic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_Bostic "Earl Bostic"), and Gay Crosse. In September 1955, Coltrane joined the [Miles Davis Quintet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis_Quintet "Miles Davis Quintet")[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane_discography#cite_note-6) and appeared on several [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")-led recordings, including _['Round About Midnight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/'Round_About_Midnight "'Round About Midnight")_ and _[Milestones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milestones_(Miles_Davis_album) "Milestones (Miles Davis album)")_. He briefly joined [Thelonious Monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thelonious_Monk "Thelonious Monk") in May 1957, and their handful of recordings together have been collected on albums such as 1961's _[Thelonious Monk with John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thelonious_Monk_with_John_Coltrane "Thelonious Monk with John Coltrane")_. In 1958, he rejoined Davis' band and stayed until April 1960; during that time he participated in the 1959 _[Kind of Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue "Kind of Blue")_ sessions. In April 1957, he signed a contract with [Prestige Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_Records "Prestige Records"); it is unclear if this was a two-year deal or a one-year contract plus a one-year option.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane_discography#cite_note-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane_discography#cite_note-8) Many of Coltrane's recordings for Prestige could be classified as "sideman" recordings and informal [jam sessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jam_sessions "Jam sessions") (or "blowing sessions", in the then-current terminology). He also made his first albums as a group leader, including his 1957 debut, _[Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coltrane_(1957_album) "Coltrane (1957 album)")_. That same year, Prestige allowed him to fulfill a promise that he would make an album for [Blue Note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records"),[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane_discography#cite_note-9) leading to 1958's _[Blue Train](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Train_(album) "Blue Train (album)")_. After Coltrane gained prominence in the early 1960s, Prestige reissued a number of Coltrane's sideman and jam sessions under his name to capitalize on his success. _[The Prestige Recordings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Complete_Prestige_Recordings_(John_Coltrane_album) "The Complete Prestige Recordings (John Coltrane album)")_ collects all of Coltrane's recordings for Prestige with the exception of his sideman work with Davis. When his Prestige contract expired, Coltrane signed a two-year contract (one year, plus a one-year option) with [Atlantic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Records "Atlantic Records") in April 1959.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane_discography#cite_note-10)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane_discography#cite_note-11) He was the leader of all of these sessions except _[Bags & Trane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bags_&_Trane "Bags & Trane")_ and _[The Avant-Garde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Avant-Garde_(album) "The Avant-Garde (album)")_, where he was featured with [Milt Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milt_Jackson "Milt Jackson") and [Don Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter) "Don Cherry (trumpeter)") respectively. Albums from this period include _[Giant Steps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant_Steps "Giant Steps")_ and _[My Favorite Things](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_Favorite_Things_(John_Coltrane_album) "My Favorite Things (John Coltrane album)")_. The _[Heavyweight Champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavyweight_Champion:_The_Complete_Atlantic_Recordings_(album) "Heavyweight Champion: The Complete Atlantic Recordings (album)")_ box collects his recordings for Atlantic, including all known outtakes. Coltrane became the first artist to sign with the new [Impulse! Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records "Impulse! Records") when it bought out his Atlantic contract in April 1961.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane_discography#cite_note-12) He would record for the label until the end of his life, and his success earned Impulse! a reputation as "The House That Trane Built".[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane_discography#cite_note-13) Albums from this final period include the live album _[Live at Birdland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_at_Birdland_(1964_John_Coltrane_album) "Live at Birdland (1964 John Coltrane album)")_, _[A Love Supreme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme "A Love Supreme")_, and _[Ascension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album) "Ascension (John Coltrane album)")_. All of the companies Coltrane worked with during his lifetime have compiled and reissued his material. In addition, Impulse! has issued several previously unreleased live recordings, including _[Live in Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_in_Japan_(John_Coltrane_album) "Live in Japan (John Coltrane album)")_ and _[The Olatunji Concert: The Last Live Recording](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olatunji_Concert "Olatunji Concert")_. Coltrane's concert, television and radio performances generated dozens of unauthorized and [bootleg recordings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bootleg_recording "Bootleg recording"). [Pablo Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pablo_Records "Pablo Records"), a label that specializes in live recordings,[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane_discography#cite_note-14) purchased rights to several tapes of his performances,[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane_discography#cite_note-15) and is therefore considered a legitimate source despite never See Wikipedia's [guide to writing better articles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Writing_better_articles#Tone "Wikipedia:Writing better articles") for suggestions._(October 2023)__([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance_template_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))_ | _([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance_template_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))_ | The term " **M-Base**" is a term coined in the 1980s by American musician [Steve Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Coleman "Steve Coleman") to describe a new theory about creative expression. "M-Base-concept" is short for " **m** acro **-b** asic **a** rray of **s** tructured **e** xtemporization", and critics have used this term to categorize this scene's music as a style of [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-1) But Coleman stressed "M-Base" doesn't denote a musical style but a way of thinking about creating music.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-2) However, Coleman has expressed discomfort with the term “jazz” to describe his music and also says M-Base was intended to be more expansive than describing music alone. M-Base was associated with a loose collective of young African American musicians and other performers active in and around [Brooklyn, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn,_New_York "Brooklyn, New York"). The M-Base collective included Coleman, [Graham Haynes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graham_Haynes "Graham Haynes"), [Cassandra Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassandra_Wilson "Cassandra Wilson"), [Geri Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geri_Allen "Geri Allen"), [Robin Eubanks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Eubanks "Robin Eubanks"), and [Greg Osby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greg_Osby "Greg Osby"). However, the musicians of the M-Base movement, which also included dancers and poets, strived for common creative musical languages, so their early recordings show many similarities reflecting their common ideas, the experiences of working together, and their similar cultural background. To label this kind of music, jazz critics have established the word "M-Base" as a jazz style for lack of a better term, distorting its original meaning.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-3) ## Music associated with the term "M-Base" \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=M-Base&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Music associated with the term \"M-Base\"")\] In 1991 a significant number of M-Base participants labelled as "M-Base Collective" recorded the CD _Anatomy of a Groove_. Most of them previously contributed to CDs by alto saxophonist Steve Coleman, whose creativity has been a pivotal factor in that movement,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-4) although he refused to be called its leader or founder. Coleman and his friend Greg Osby, who plays alto saxophone in a related style, together led the group Strata Institute, which recorded two CDs (the second with tenor saxophonist Von Freeman as a further leader). Under the name of Osby, a number of CDs with a specific character have been released starting in 1987, which also coined the perception of "M-Base" jazz. Tenor saxophonist and flutist Gary Thomas admittedly didn't take part in the M-Base initiative, but joined them, and there were similarities in his way of playing. He can be heard on recordings of Coleman and Osby, and his own CDs are also labelled as "M-Base-style". All three saxophonists contributed to the CD _[Jumpworld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jumpworld "Jumpworld")_ by singer Cassandra Wilson. Pianist [Andrew Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Hill_(jazz_musician) "Andrew Hill (jazz musician)") said about Greg Osby: "He has an incredible sense of rhythm and harmonic accuracy, and picks the right notes with a precision that isn't common to people with his technical versatility. He's developed into a fully rounded artist who can play various styles extremely well – better than most."[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-5) Greg Osby said about [Gary Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Thomas_(musician) "Gary Thomas (musician)"): "He's extremely intelligent and has a capacity for absorption that exceeds that of most people that I know \[…\] He has his own compositional and improvisational method that is peerless in my opinion. He's my favourite tenor saxophone player on the contemporary scene."[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-6) Clarinettist and composer Don Byron called Steve Coleman "an exceptional personality of American music history."[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-7) Antecedents to M-Base were identified by jazz critic [Bill Milkowski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Milkowski "Bill Milkowski") as the [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")-led band featured on recordings like 1975's _[Agharta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album) "Agharta (album)")_; he noted the combination of [Sonny Fortune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Fortune "Sonny Fortune")'s acerbic saxophone lines atop the syncopated [grooves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groove_(music) "Groove (music)") performed by the rhythm section of drummer [Al Foster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Foster "Al Foster"), bassist [Michael Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Henderson "Michael Henderson"), and rhythm guitarist [Reggie Lucas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggie_Lucas "Reggie Lucas").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-8) ## Further history \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=M-Base&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Further history")\] The ideas of the M-Base concept were largely incompatible with the requirements of music business. Most participants of the M-Base movement turned to more conventional music. Cassandra Wilson's blues- and folk-influenced music has been fairly suitable for an adaption to the taste of a larger audience. Wilson has been signed to [Blue Note Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records") since 1993. Though two of Gary Thomas' recordings were highly rated by _[DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat")_[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-9) he only had a contract with a small European company and his performance opportunities were virtually limited to Europe. Since 1997, he has put his career as a bandleader on hold to teach at Peabody Music Institute.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-10) Greg Osby signed with Blue Note Records in 1990 and developed a specific balancing act between an enhanced reverence to tradition and maintaining his new direction. In 2008, Osby launched his own small label.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-11) Steve Coleman has developed his music further in accordance with the M-Base concept. In the 1990s his CDs were released by the major label [BMG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertelsmann_Music_Group "Bertelsmann Music Group"). Thereafter he became practically an underground artist in the U.S. again, in that his music was only available as imports, distributed by a small French label.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-12) In 2007 [John Zorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Zorn "John Zorn")'s small label [Tzadik Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tzadik_Records "Tzadik Records") released a solo CD of Coleman. In 2010 the small advanced label [Pi Recordings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pi_Recordings "Pi Recordings") began to release Steve Coleman's recordings. Although the musical line initially called "M-Base" became more than ever focused on Steve Coleman, a number of younger musicians (e.g. a range of excellent drummers) have made substantial creative contributions to his music and his influence is to be found in several musical fields – both in terms of music technique and of the music's meaning. Pianist [Vijay Iyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vijay_Iyer "Vijay Iyer") (who was chosen as "Jazz Musician of the Year 2010" by the [Jazz Journalists Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Journalists_Association "Jazz Journalists Association")) said, "It's hard to overstate Steve \[Coleman's\] influence. He's affected more than one generation, as much as anyone since John Coltrane. It's not just that you can connect the dots by playing seven or 11 beats. What sits behind his influence is this global perspective on music and life. He has a point of view of what he does and why he does it."[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-13) ## M-Base concept \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=M-Base&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: M-Base concept")\] Steve Coleman explained the substantial elements of the concept as: - improvisation and structure - contemporary relevance - music as expression of life experience - growth through creativity and philosophical broadening - use of non-western concepts The M-Base concept reminds of the creative energy of the bebop originators, their loose collective, and also of their musical goals.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base#cite_note-14) The concept does not include "neo-classical jazz", [free](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation "Free improvisation") music without structures, [fusion music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fusion_music "Fusion music"), music which isn't mainly improvised, or music shaped with respect to commercial aspects. ## References \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=M-Base&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: References")\] 01. - What is free jazz?







Free jazz emerged in the late 1950s as an approach to jazz improvisation that reached its height in the 60s and has remained a major development since then. The main characteristic of [free jazz](https://www.britannica.com/art/free-jazz/Introduction#ref1) is that there are no rules. Musicians don’t adhere to a fixed harmonic structure as they improvise; instead, they modulate at will.



Free jazz performers often improvise without observing fixed metres or tempos, and solo and accompaniment roles tend to be fluid. Effectively, free jazz began with the small groups led in 1958–59 by alto saxophonist [Ornette Coleman](https://www.britannica.com/art/jazz/Free-jazz-the-explorations-of-Ornette-Coleman#ref215432), from whose album _Free Jazz_ (1960) the idiom received its name.

- How is free jazz different from other types of jazz?







Free jazz distinguishes itself from other jazz forms through its rejection of fixed structures. Unlike traditional jazz, free jazz musicians do not adhere to predetermined [chord progressions](https://www.britannica.com/art/free-jazz/Introduction#ref1) or [time signatures](https://www.britannica.com/art/jazz/Free-jazz-the-explorations-of-Ornette-Coleman#ref215432). Improvisation is central, with musicians modulating keys at will and phrasing in chromatic intervals and harmonies, sometimes achieving atonality.



Roles are fluid, and the balance between composition and improvisation shifts. Free improvisation, the ultimate form of free jazz, abandons fixed instrumental roles and harmonic, rhythmic, and melodic structures, eliminating composition altogether. [Ornette Coleman](https://www.britannica.com/art/jazz/Free-jazz-the-explorations-of-Ornette-Coleman#ref215432)'s work in the late 1950s and early 1960s significantly influenced this movement, with his album _Free Jazz_ (1960) giving the idiom its name.

- Who were some important musicians in free jazz?







Free jazz emphasizes improvisation without fixed rules, allowing musicians to freely modulate keys and tempos.



Key figures include [Ornette Coleman](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ornette-Coleman/Introduction), whose album _Free Jazz_ (1960) gave the movement its name, and who developed the "harmolodic theory" that released jazz from fixed harmonic structures. [John Coltrane](https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-Coltrane/Introduction) and [Eric Dolphy](https://www.britannica.com/art/free-jazz/Introduction#ref1) also created individual versions of free jazz. [Cecil Taylor](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Cecil-Taylor/Introduction) and [Albert Ayler](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Albert-Ayler/Introduction) were also innovators in free jazz.

- What instruments are commonly used in free jazz?







Free jazz emphasizes improvisation without fixed rules, and any instrument can be used. Common instruments include saxophones, especially alto and tenor saxophones, as exemplified by [John Coltrane](https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-Coltrane/Introduction) and [Ornette Coleman](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ornette-Coleman/Introduction), who were pioneers in the genre.



Other instruments frequently used are the trumpet, clarinet, trombone, piano, and drums. Some free jazz groups may exclude rhythm section instruments entirely.

- How do musicians improvise in free jazz?







In free jazz, improvisation throws out the rule book, freeing musicians from fixed harmonic structures and predetermined chord progressions. Instead, they can modulate keys at will, using chromatic intervals and harmonies, sometimes even exploring atonality through microtones, overtones, multiphonics, and tone clusters.



Improvisation in free jazz also often disregards fixed meters or tempos, with solo and accompaniment roles becoming fluid, as does the balance between composition and improvisation. This leads to free improvisation, which abandons fixed instrumental roles, harmonic, rhythmic, or melodic structures, and even composition itself.

- How did free jazz influence later styles of music?







Free jazz, which emerged in the late 1950s, has significantly impacted later music styles by breaking traditional jazz rules. This genre, characterized by the absence of fixed harmonic structures, allows musicians to modulate keys freely and improvise without adhering to set meters or tempos.



One notable influence of free jazz is its contribution to the development of [jazz-rock](https://www.britannica.com/art/jazz-rock/Introduction#ref1), where the improvisation of modern jazz combines with rock music's instrumentation, drumming, and bass lines. Free jazz also stimulated composers to explore new sounds and melodic expressions, enriching ensemble music. However, the recurring patterns of rock tended to dominate, reducing jazz improvisation.

**free jazz**, an approach to jazz [improvisation](https://www.britannica.com/art/improvisation-music) that emerged during the late 1950s, reached its height in the ’60s, and remained a major development in [jazz](https://www.britannica.com/art/jazz) thereafter.

The main characteristic of free jazz is that there are no rules. Musicians do not adhere to a fixed harmonic structure (predetermined [chord](https://www.britannica.com/art/chord-music) progressions) as they improvise; instead, they modulate (i.e., change keys) at will. Free jazz improvisers typically phrase in chromatic intervals and harmonies, and some achieve [atonality](https://www.britannica.com/art/atonality) while playing in microtones, overtones, multiphonics (simultaneous notes played on one horn), and tone clusters. Free jazz performers often improvise without observing fixed metres or tempos. Solo and accompaniment roles tend to be fluid, as does the balance of [composition](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/composition) and improvisation in a performance. The ultimate development of free jazz is free improvisation, which combines all these qualities—using no fixed instrumental roles or harmonic, rhythmic, or melodic structures and abandoning composition altogether.

As early as the 1940s, jazz musicians, most notably pianist [Lennie Tristano](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Lennie-Tristano) and composer Bob Graettinger, created a handful of works using free jazz elements. Effectively, free jazz began with the small groups led in 1958–59 by alto saxophonist [Ornette Coleman](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ornette-Coleman), from whose album _Free Jazz_ (1960) the [idiom](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/idiom) received its name. Shortly afterward, saxophonists [John Coltrane](https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-Coltrane) and [Eric Dolphy](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Eric-Dolphy) and pianist [Cecil Taylor](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Cecil-Taylor) began creating individual versions of free jazz. “Energy music,” later called “noise,” became an identifying label for high-energy, [collective](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/collective) improvisations in which dense sound textures were created from furiously generated note sequences. In the mid-1960s Coltrane and fellow saxophonist Pharaoh Sanders adopted styles using soaring runs and distorted wails and shrieks, and [Albert Ayler](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Albert-Ayler) played saxophone solos using indeterminate pitches, multiphonic honks, and overtone screams. Such drummers as Sunny Murray and Andrew Cyrille accompanied these improvisations with pure accent and without direct reference to tempo or metre. [Sun Ra](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Sun-Ra)’s Arkestra, with instrumentalists, singers, and dancers, enriched free jazz with a colourful sense of spectacle, and the [Art Ensemble of Chicago](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Art-Ensemble-of-Chicago) and other musicians [affiliated](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/affiliated) with that city’s [Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Association-for-the-Advancement-of-Creative-Musicians) explored new sound colours and melodic expressions that returned an emphasis on lyricism to free jazz.

There were other [innovations](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/innovations) as well: saxophonists [Anthony Braxton](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Anthony-Braxton), Steve Lacy, and Evan Parker performed unaccompanied improvisations at their solo concerts, and unprecedented groups began to appear that had no [rhythm](https://www.britannica.com/art/rhythm-music) section instruments whatsoever. Free improvisation also flourished in Europe and Great Britain, where native musical traditions often influenced the players as much as did traditional jazz. The Ganelin Trio from the [Soviet Union](https://www.britannica.com/place/Soviet-Union) improvised on Russian folk songs, and exiles from [South Africa](https://www.britannica.com/place/South-Africa) in the Brotherhood of Breath fused free jazz with [kivela](https://www.britannica.com/art/kwela) (kwela) [music](https://www.britannica.com/art/music). The free-jazz [idiom](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/idiom) proved to be a stimulus to composers for large and small ensembles, resulting in a remarkable variety of composed music by Coleman, Barry Guy, Leo Smith, [Henry Threadgill](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Henry-Threadgill), Alex Schlippenbach, David Murray, Pierre Dørge, [John Zorn](https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-Zorn), and Roscoe Mitchell, among others.

**improvisation**, in [music](https://www.britannica.com/art/music), the [extemporaneous](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/extemporaneous) [composition](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/composition) or free performance of a [musical](https://www.britannica.com/art/musical) passage, usually in a manner conforming to certain stylistic norms but unfettered by the [prescriptive](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/prescriptive) features of a specific musical text. Music originated as improvisation and is still extensively improvised in Eastern traditions and in the modern Western tradition of jazz.

Many of the great composers of Western classical music were masters of improvisation, especially on keyboard instruments, which offered such celebrated composer-performers as [Johann Sebastian Bach](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Johann-Sebastian-Bach), W.A. Mozart, [Felix Mendelssohn](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Felix-Mendelssohn), and [Frédéric Chopin](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Frederic-Chopin) virtually boundless opportunities for the spontaneous unfolding of their rich musical imaginations. Many an idea so generated eventually appeared in a written composition. Some composers have regarded improvisation as an indispensable warm-up for their creative task.

Prior to the instrumental era in the West, improvisation within the systematized musical [context](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/context) was largely limited to ornamental variants of vocal parts in polyphonic [compositions](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/compositions) and to instrumental [adaptations](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/adaptations) of vocal compositions, especially by lute and keyboard virtuosos. The monodic textures that originated about 1600, on the other hand, were ready-made, indeed in large measure intended, for improvisational enhancement, not only of the treble parts but also, almost by definition, of the bass, which was figured to suggest no more than a minimal chordal outline.

In essentially monophonic musical [cultures](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/cultures), whether Western or non-Western, improvisation has been of paramount importance, if only because successful improvisation is always more readily achieved by soloists than by groups. A monophonic oral musical tradition, however, does not necessarily imply the prevalence of improvisational practices. Quite to the contrary, oral traditions have been prone to preserve the [integrity](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/integrity) of particular songs and dances from generation to generation with a degree of precision virtually unknown in literate musical [contexts](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/contexts).

It is generally assumed that early European music from Roman Catholic chant to [medieval](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/medieval) polyphony was rooted in such improvisational practices as the exploration of motivic possibilities in the church modes ( _see_ [church mode](https://www.britannica.com/art/church-mode)) and the addition of a second melody to a preexisting melody or [cantus firmus](https://www.britannica.com/art/cantus-firmus). Modal improvisations have remained central to much non-Western music, including the chant of the Jewish synagogue, Islāmic _maqām_ elaborations, and Indian [raga](https://www.britannica.com/art/raga) performances.

In the West, cantus firmus improvisation inspired a great deal of instrumental music as well, beginning with late Renaissance improvisations over ostinato basses (relatively short repeated bass patterns) and maintained through the centuries especially by organists who embraced such popular ostinato [genres](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/genres) as the passacaglia and chaconne. Organists have remained in the forefront of improvisation as a primary musical activity in no way at odds with written composition, while keyboard improvisation in turn has been responsible for compositions of a freely associative character of the sort found among hundreds of preludes, toccatas, and fantasies written during the past three centuries. Improvisations on Protestant hymn tunes gave birth to the important 17th- and 18th-century [genre](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/genre) the [chorale prelude](https://www.britannica.com/art/chorale-prelude). In the later 18th century, improvisation, often based on variation techniques but not excluding the strictly polyphonic procedures of canon and fugue, challenged the ingenuity of virtuoso-composers repeatedly in public improvisational contests, such as those that pitted Mozart against [Muzio Clementi](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Muzio-Clementi) and [Ludwig van Beethoven](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ludwig-van-Beethoven) against Joseph Wölfl.

In modern times, improvisation survives as one of the chief distinguishing characteristics of [jazz](https://www.britannica.com/art/jazz). Here, too, the process is usually inspired by, and structured (however loosely) in accordance with, [salient](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/salient) characteristics of the model in question, be it a well-known show tune or a [ground bass](https://www.britannica.com/art/ground-bass). During the second half of the 20th century, there arose among certain avant-garde composers and performers a tendency away from any vestige of traditional structure. A “composition” from this experimental school might be entirely devoid of conventional notation, consisting rather of a verbal instruction, a prescription for duration, or an [idiosyncratic](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/idiosyncratic) graphic code. Some works required performers to combine at random “building blocks” of brief musical phrases or entire sections presented by the composer; it has been asserted that such a process embodies a more profound creative collaboration between composer and performer than does the interpretation of a fully notated work or the express but limited freedom accorded performers at crucial moments in certain fixed compositions ( _e.g.,_ the da capo section of an 18th-century aria or the cadenza near the end of a solo concerto movement). _See also_ [aleatory music](https://www.britannica.com/art/aleatory-music).

## Quick Summary

"Third stream" refers to music that blends elements of classical music and jazz. This concept emerged in the 1950s and 1960s, though composers had been incorporating jazz into classical music and vice versa for decades.12

Key characteristics of third stream music include:

\\* **Fusion:** It combines the structures and techniques of classical music with the improvisation and rhythms of jazz.2

\\* **Two-way Influence:** Unlike earlier trends, third stream saw a mutual exchange of ideas between classical and jazz musicians.2

\\* **Broader Scope:** The concept also extended to integrating ethnic and vernacular music traditions.2

While the term "third stream" is used less frequently today, its ideal of true musical fusion continues to influence contemporary music, sometimes referred to as crossover, fusion, or world music.2

[Blues](https://www.britannica.com/art/blues-music) and [jazz](https://www.britannica.com/art/jazz) are both profoundly influential African American [music](https://www.britannica.com/art/music) styles that developed in the [South](https://www.britannica.com/place/the-South-region) about the turn of the 20th century. So closely are they related that jazz great [Billie Holiday](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Billie-Holiday) titled her 1956 autobiography _Lady Sings the Blues_. [Yet](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/Yet) there are key differences between the two music forms.

## Differences in origins and development

First, blues is slightly older than jazz. Blues developed after the [Civil War](https://www.britannica.com/event/American-Civil-War) (1861–65) and was influenced by 19th-century [work songs](https://www.britannica.com/art/work-song-music) and field hollers, [minstrel show](https://www.britannica.com/art/minstrel-show) music, [ragtime](https://www.britannica.com/art/ragtime), and [church music](https://www.britannica.com/topic/liturgical-music) such as [spirituals](https://www.britannica.com/art/spiritual) and [hymns](https://www.britannica.com/topic/hymn), as well as the [folk](https://www.britannica.com/art/folk-music) and [popular music](https://www.britannica.com/art/popular-music) of white Southerners. The earliest references to blues date to the 1890s and early 1900s. Jazz arose in the earliest years of the 20th century, springing from blues and ragtime. In this sense, blues is a grandparent of jazz, which also contains elements of popular dance music, music for [brass](https://www.britannica.com/art/brass-instrument) bands, funeral processions, and parades (think of the tune “When the Saints Go Marching In”), and touches of European [opera](https://www.britannica.com/art/opera-music), theater, and concert music.

Second, blues began as a rural music. Early blues was largely played by Southern Black men, most of whom were agricultural workers. Key regions in its development include [Texas](https://www.britannica.com/place/Texas-state), [Georgia](https://www.britannica.com/place/Georgia-state), the Carolinas, and, of course, the [Mississippi](https://www.britannica.com/place/Mississippi-River) [Delta](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/Delta). Eventually, blues traveled north to [Chicago](https://www.britannica.com/place/Chicago) and other urban centers, but not until the 1920s and ’30s. By contrast, jazz was born in the city, specifically in [New Orleans](https://www.britannica.com/place/New-Orleans-Louisiana)—to be more exact, in Congo Square, a public square in the Tremé neighborhood that was set aside by city officials for enslaved and free African people to dance, worship, and play music, especially [drums](https://www.britannica.com/art/drum-musical-instrument). At first, the gathered musicians played the [rhythms](https://www.britannica.com/art/rhythm-music) brought from Africa and the Caribbean. But over time they began embellishing and improvising, just as later jazz musicians would do.

This highlights another difference between the two styles of music: Blues was initially performed by solo musicians, whereas jazz, from the very beginning, was communal, involving an interplay between multiple musicians. In time, however, blues musicians came together to form [bands](https://www.britannica.com/art/band-music), and soloing became a notable feature of jazz performances.

In terms of form, blues is [characterized](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/characterized) by a repeating [harmonic](https://www.britannica.com/art/harmony-music) structure with [melodic](https://www.britannica.com/art/melody) emphasis on the flatted (or “blue”) third and seventh [notes](https://www.britannica.com/art/note-staff-notation) of the [scale](https://www.britannica.com/art/scale-music). Other notable characteristics are its 12-bar pattern, which uses the [chords](https://www.britannica.com/art/chord-music) of the first, fourth, and fifth notes of the scale, and its “blues stanza,” a three-line lyric stanza in which the words of the second line repeat those of the first. This is also described as an AAB pattern, as in the opening lines of [Robert Johnson](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Robert-Johnson-American-musician)’s “Love in Vain.”

> And I followed her to the station with a suitcase in my hand (A)

Another common feature of blues is call-and-response, which can be thought of as a conversation between two parts of music. Both parts may be vocal or instrumental, or they may be a mix of the two. For example, listen to the way the instruments respond to [Muddy Waters](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Muddy-Waters)’ call—essentially to each vocal line—in his classic song “Mannish Boy.”

Jazz uses most of these elements but with much more deviation from the basic structure. Again, in jazz, [improvisation](https://www.britannica.com/art/improvisation-music) is the name of the game, and the heights of it can be heard in saxophonist [John Coltrane](https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-Coltrane)’s rendition of “ [My Favorite Things](https://open.spotify.com/track/3ZikLQCnH3SIswlGENBcKe),” from the [Richard Rodgers](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Richard-Rodgers) and [Oscar Hammerstein](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Oscar-Hammerstein-II) musical _[The Sound of Music](https://www.britannica.com/topic/The-Sound-of-Music-film-by-Wise)_. Coltrane’s fully instrumental version famously takes a familiar tune and steers it into uncharted musical waters.

Indeed, jazz musicians are [notorious](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/notorious) for employing complex chord changes and more [syncopation](https://www.britannica.com/art/syncopation-music), in which “off” [beats](https://www.britannica.com/art/beat-music) disrupt the standard metrical patterns in a tune and create a fast-tempo, forward-driving momentum. You hear it in [swing](https://www.britannica.com/art/swing-music). These elements, especially improvisation, can be expressed vocally too, as in [scat](https://www.britannica.com/art/scat-music).

Another difference between blues and jazz is the choice of instruments. In blues the human voice is preeminent, although there are many examples of instrumental blues songs. Other important instruments in blues are [guitar](https://www.britannica.com/art/guitar), [harmonica](https://www.britannica.com/art/harmonica), and [piano](https://www.britannica.com/art/piano). Bass ( [double](https://www.britannica.com/art/double-bass) or [electric](https://www.britannica.com/art/bass-guitar)) provides the foundational, driving rhythm of ensemble blues, while drums set the tempo and backbeat.

Common instruments in jazz include piano, [double bass](https://www.britannica.com/art/double-bass), [trombone](https://www.britannica.com/art/trombone), [trumpet](https://www.britannica.com/art/trumpet), [saxophone](https://www.britannica.com/art/saxophone), [clarinet](https://www.britannica.com/art/clarinet), and [drums](https://www.britannica.com/art/drum-musical-instrument), with an [emphasis](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/emphasis) on the mighty [cymbal](https://www.britannica.com/art/cymbal). The prominence of [horns](https://www.britannica.com/art/horn-musical-instrument-group) in jazz influenced blues; these instruments began to be used in bigger blues bands, especially in New Orleans-style blues.

Subgenres of jazz, such as [jazz-rock](https://www.britannica.com/art/jazz-rock) and [Latin jazz](https://www.britannica.com/art/Latin-jazz), introduced more electronic- and guitar-based sounds and a wide range of [percussion instruments](https://www.britannica.com/art/percussion-instrument), from conga and [bongo](https://www.britannica.com/art/bongo-drum) drums to [vibraphone](https://www.britannica.com/art/vibraphone). Notwithstanding the many great jazz vocalists, including [Ella Fitzgerald](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ella-Fitzgerald), [Frank Sinatra](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Frank-Sinatra), [Dinah Washington](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Dinah-Washington), [Sarah Vaughan](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Sarah-Vaughan), and [Nat King Cole](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Nat-King-Cole) (a few of whom, like Billie Holiday, also sang the blues), jazz became a primarily instrumental music early on in its development.

A final difference between blues and jazz is the ingredient of [emotion](https://www.britannica.com/science/emotion). Although jazz can be powerfully expressive of a composer or musician’s personal [idiosyncrasies](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/idiosyncrasies) and attitude (think of [Miles Davis](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Miles-Davis) or [Sun Ra](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Sun-Ra)), blues is the domain of raw emotion. Some musicians tell stories, and some inspire their listeners to dance, but blues singers, perhaps more than any other popular musical artists, express their feelings.

They accomplish this through specific vocal techniques such as inserting [falsetto](https://www.britannica.com/art/falsetto) breaks, howls, and [yodels](https://www.britannica.com/art/yodel) or sustaining a single syllable across several pitches (known as melisma). Many instrumental techniques of blues are also intended to imitate the emotion of human speech, such as “choking” or bending guitar strings on the neck or applying a metal slide or bottleneck to the strings to create a plaintive or whining sound. This is as true of the electrified [Chicago blues](https://www.britannica.com/art/Chicago-blues) of Muddy Waters, [Howlin’ Wolf](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Howlin-Wolf), and [Koko Taylor](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Koko-Taylor) and the blues-based [rock](https://www.britannica.com/art/rock-music) of such bands as [the Rolling Stones](https://www.britannica.com/topic/the-Rolling-Stones) and the Black Keys as it is of early [acoustic](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/acoustic) blues.

# ‘It didn’t adhere to any of the rules’: the fascinating history of free jazz

This article is more than 5 years old

In documentary Fire Music, the hostile reaction that met the unusual genre soon turns into deep appreciation and a lasting influence

When [Miles Davis](https://www.theguardian.com/music/miles-davis) first heard the music of Eric Dolphy, a key figure in the free jazz movement, he described it as “ridiculous”, “sad” and just plain “bad”. Upon encountering the early sounds of free jazz pioneer Ornette Coleman, Thelonious Monk said “there’s nothing beautiful in what he’s playing. He’s just playing loud and slurring the notes. Anybody can do that.” The editors at the jazz world’s bible, Downbeat Magazine, went further, initially criticising the entire genre as a force that’s “poisoning the minds of young players”, jazz critic Gary Giddins recalled.

[![Alan Skidmore performing in the late 1960s.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/d13d9804ec56203cd9329e4a30c29e0fb63319e4/0_105_3696_2218/master/3696.jpg?width=460&quality=85&auto=format&fit=max&s=2d1e29e31391d2ca01331624de754927)\\
\\
‘Rawness, freedom, experimentation’: the Brit jazz boom of the 60s and 70s\\
\\
Read more](https://www.theguardian.com/music/2021/aug/18/rawness-freedom-experimentation-british-jazz-john-surman-tony-higgins)

Given the revolutionary nature of the music, it’s no surprise that many in the field greeted it with such disdain. “Free jazz didn’t adhere to any of the rules of what was considered music at the time,” said Tom Surgal, director of the new documentary Fire Music, which covers the history and breadth of the movement. “There wasn’t a single musical tenet this music did not defy.”

That included everything from its approach to chords to the placement of the beat to the role of the solos to the basic notions of melody and harmony. Atonality and abrasion were embraced, polyrhythmic and polytonal modes were amplified and risk idealized, paving the way for some of the most extreme and, to some ears, difficult, music ever made. As even Surgal admits, “this is not easily digestible music”.

A foundational figure in the genre, Cecil Taylor, had a word of advice about that. “The same way that musicians have to prepare, listeners have to prepare,” he said in a vintage interview used in the film. But when the movement started in the late 50s and early 60s, few were in any way prepared. Bebop ruled jazz at the time, exemplified by well-established stars like Max Roach, Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie, each of whom presented then codified approaches to solos, rhythms and melody. As exciting, erudite and skilled as their work may have been, their approach had become familiar enough to spur artists like pianist Taylor and saxophonist Coleman to seek something new.

Taylor began to capture that on record with his 1956 debut, [Jazz](https://www.theguardian.com/music/jazz) Advance, in which he displayed a highly percussive approach to his instrument, performing with equal degrees of energy and technique. The music created by his quartet expanded the use of improvisation, bringing a wildness to original pieces, as well as standards like Cole Porter’s You’d Be So Nice to Come Home To. On Taylor’s two albums released in 1960, Air and The World of Cecil Taylor, he pushed further, leaving more traces of bebop behind to play in a world of his own making.

Coleman followed a similar trajectory. His first album, Something Else!!!, issued in 1958, had a daring that would grow exponentially. The title track of his 1960 album, Change of the Century, could be taken literally as it heralded fresh ways to balance dissonance, cacophony and virtuosity. But the real line-in-the-sand moment didn’t arrive until the next year, with the release of an album that gave this emerging style both its name and its mission: Free Jazz: A Collective Improvisation. Credited to the Ornette Coleman Double Quartet, the set featured two self-contained groups of players performing at once. Each quartet featured a bass and drum player as well as two wind instruments. On the left channel listeners could hear Coleman on sax and Don Cherry on trumpet; on the right Eric Dolphy on bass clarinet and Freddie Hubbard on trumpet. The near 40 minutes of music they spun represented an almost unbroken improvisation, anchored by a few set sections that, ironically, tended to be the most disruptive. Still, the result had its own sense of order and logic, not to mention a surprising beauty, once you adjust to it. “This wasn’t a musical circle jerk,” said Surgal. “It was a symbiosis. There’s a lot of interplay and empathy at work. It’s very much about musicians listening to each other.”

It’s also about their balance of freedom and discipline. “Improvisation is informed by passion and conditioned by knowledge,” Taylor said in a vintage interview used in the film.

![Free jazz musician Ornette Coleman performing in 1971.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/8f2ce6eb1afbb3de2087abe3db2caf1dee4b4f77/0_0_683_1024/master/683.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)[View image in fullscreen](https://www.theguardian.com/film/2021/sep/07/fire-music-history-free-jazz-documentary#img-2)

Free jazz musician Ornette Coleman performing in 1971. Photograph: Jean-Pierre Roche/Photo credit: JP Roche. Image courtesy of Submarine Deluxe

As controversial as this work may have been at the time, Surgal said its creators didn’t feel they were in any way refuting their predecessors. “The free jazz musicians weren’t casting aspersions on what came before,” he said. “In their minds, they were simply creating the next step.”

More, even the wildest of them had firm roots in established genres, informed by music from the places in which they grew up. In the music of the Fort Worth-born Coleman, for instance, Surgal believes “you can hear the rough-hewn Texan sound of Arnette Cobb or Eddie ‘Lockjaw’ Davis. To me, Ornette was always playing the blues. He just had a unique interpretation of it.”

The freshness of such interpretations mirrored parallel mid-century movements in the worlds of art and literature. Its accent on improvisation and internalization echoed both the Beat authors’ love of spontaneous writing and the attitudes and techniques of the abstract artists of the era. (The cover of the Free Jazz album featured a reproduction of Jackson Pollock’s 1954 painting The White Light.) Likewise, the music’s anger and edge reflected the politics of the day. “This music was coming out of the civil rights movement which metamorphosed into the Black militant movement,” said the director. “It also reflected the anti-war movement. The cry of wailing saxophones and the beating of drums was the perfect complement to the radicalism in the air at the time.”

At the same time, the exploratory quality of the music reflected the musicians’ experimentation with their own psyches. “A lot of the free jazz musicians, especially the ones in New York, were experimenting with hallucinogens and that experience was informing the music,” Surgal said. “In many ways, this is the undocumented psychedelia.”

Small wonder, the rock musicians of the day took note. The expansive and noisy solos of late 60s psychedelic rock used some of the principles of free jazz to blow out the bounds of the blues that first inspired them. The fractured guitars in songs like the Byrds’ Eight Miles High borrowed from the angularity and skittishness of free jazz. Leader Roger McGuinn has often spoken of the cues he took from John Coltrane, who himself moved from bebop to the world of free jazz with his classic, 1966 album Ascension. Paul McCartney listened to the music of the free jazz saxophonist Albert Ayler while writing songs for the Revolver album and various Beatles attended shows by the London-based free improv band AMM. You can hear the clear influence of this music on British art-jazz bands like Soft Machine as well as on the avant garde UK keyboardist Keith Tippett, who channeled the very soul of Cecil Taylor with his unhinged piano work in pieces like King Crimson’s 1970 single Cat Food.

Coleman’s frenetic style didn’t only influence the sounds of musicians but, in one prominent case, the movements. After a young Iggy Pop heard Coleman for the first time, he had a revelation: “I can do that,” he told a reporter, “ _with my body_.”

By the mid-70s, a second wave of New York avant garde players created a scene of their own. Due to their difficulty in getting gigs, they began hosting shows in their own living spaces, spawning the loft jazz movement. Their efforts just preceded, and sometimes mingled, with the city’s no wave “punk jazz” movement, led by acts like the Contortions, Mars and DNA.

Not only did the New York-bred free jazz movement affect artists beyond the genre, it also seeded scenes across the US, in places like Chicago and St Louis, as well as ones in Europe and the UK. In one case, it may even have had a connection to outer space: the free jazz artist Sun Ra claimed that he and his music came straight from Saturn. Importantly, each of these artists and scenes had their own take on the music. “Free jazz is not one thing,” said Surgal. “This music is nothing if not varied.”

At the same time, the artists found unity in their uncompromising nature. Unfortunately, that often made it difficult for them to make a living. Club owners were resistant to it, so gigs were hard to come by, at least in the US. The film chronicles several attempts by the musicians to organize themselves to gain decent pay, but their independent natures made coordinated efforts a challenge. More, the movement was marred by the young deaths of some of its central players during its prime era. In 1964, Eric Dolphy died at the age of 36 from issues related to his undiagnosed diabetes. Three years later, Coltrane succumbed to liver cancer at 40, and Ayler died in a presumed suicide in 1970 at 34.

By the 1980s, key parts of jazz began to take a more conservative turn. A new movement, dubbed rebop, aimed to return the genre to pre-free jazz values. Surgal blames the subsequent refutation of the avant garde on “a conspiracy of revisionists”. He fingers, in particular, “Wynton Marsalis and his brother Branford who have done everything they could to minimize the exposure of this music and to denigrate its contributions. The critic Stanley Crouch led the assault.”

Meanwhile, in the world of alt-rock, devotees abound, from Thurston Moore of Sonic Youth and Nels Cline of Wilco (who each serve as executive producers of Fire Music), to members of Superchunk. Today, some young, math-rock groups, like Black Midi and Squid, have applied free jazz’s dissonance and mania to guitar-oriented sounds. However well-regarded many of these musicians may be in certain circles, however, Surgal sees them as outsiders and so, by necessity, exemplars of the DIY tradition. “DIY is normally used in relation to punk or hardcore but these guys were the OGs of that,” he said. “They had to self-release records and find alternative places to play when they were turned away by the clubs. Their story is a great example of self-determined people who believed in a sound they knew deserved to be heard.”
