[David H. Rosenthal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_H._Rosenthal "David H. Rosenthal") contends in his book _Hard Bop_ that the genre is, to a large degree, the natural creation of a generation of [African-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African-American "African-American") musicians who grew up at a time when bebop and rhythm and blues were the dominant forms of black American music.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-rosenthal-2):24 Prominent hard bop musicians included [Horace Silver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Silver "Horace Silver"), [Clifford Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_Brown "Clifford Brown"), [Charles Mingus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus "Charles Mingus"), [Art Blakey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Blakey "Art Blakey"), [Cannonball Adderley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannonball_Adderley "Cannonball Adderley"), [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis"), [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane"), [Hank Mobley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hank_Mobley "Hank Mobley"), [Sonny Clark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Clark "Sonny Clark"), [Thelonious Monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thelonious_Monk "Thelonious Monk"), [Lee Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Morgan "Lee Morgan"), [Wes Montgomery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wes_Montgomery "Wes Montgomery"), and [Pat Martino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pat_Martino "Pat Martino"). ## Characteristics Hard bop is sometimes referred to as "funky hard bop".[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-gridley-1)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-tanner-3) The "funky" label refers to the rollicking, rhythmic feeling associated with the style.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-tanner-3) The descriptor is also used to describe [soul jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz "Soul jazz"), which is commonly associated with hard bop.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-gridley-1)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-tanner-3) According to Mark C. Gridley, soul jazz more specifically refers to music with "an earthy, bluesy melodic concept and...repetitive, dance-like rhythms. Some listeners make no distinction between 'soul-jazz' and 'funky hard bop,' and many musicians don't consider 'soul-jazz' to be continuous with 'hard bop.'"[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-gridley-1) The term " [soul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_music "Soul music")" suggests the church, and traditional [gospel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_music "Gospel music") elements such as the [plagal cadence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plagal_cadence "Plagal cadence") seemed to suddenly appear in jazz during the era.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-tanner-3) [Amiri Baraka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amiri_Baraka "Amiri Baraka") noted a combination of "wider and harsher tones" with "accompanying piano chords \[that\] became more basic and simplified" in this era. He cited saxophonist [Sonny Rollins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Rollins "Sonny Rollins")' playing as one of the best examples of the style.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-4) Jazz critic Scott Yanow distinguished hard bop from the broader world of bop by saying that "\[t\]empos could be just as blazing but the melodies were generally simpler, the musicians (particularly the saxophonists and pianists) tended to be familiar with (and open to the influence of) rhythm & blues and the bass players (rather than always being stuck in the role of a metronome) were beginning to gain a little more freedom and solo space."[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-:1-5) Hard bop has been seen by some critics as a response to [cool jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cool_jazz "Cool jazz") and [West Coast jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Coast_jazz "West Coast jazz").[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-carr-6) As [Paul Tanner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tanner "Paul Tanner"), Maurice Gerow, and David Megill explain, "the hard bop school...saw the new instrumentation and compositional devices used by cool musicians as gimmicks rather than valid developments of the jazz tradition."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-tanner-3) However, [Shelly Manne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelly_Manne "Shelly Manne") suggested that cool jazz and hard bop simply reflected their respective geographic environments: the relaxed cool jazz style reflected a more relaxed lifestyle in California, while driving bop typified the hectic atmosphere of New York City.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-manne-7) Some writers, such as [James Lincoln Collier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Lincoln_Collier "James Lincoln Collier"), suggest that the style was an attempt to recapture jazz as a form of African-American expression.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-collier-8) Whether or not this was the intent, many musicians quickly adopted the style, regardless of race.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-tanner-3) ## History ### Origins [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b2/Nachtconcert_van_het_Horeca_Silverquintet_in_het_concertgebouw_te_Amsterdam%2C_Bestanddeelnr_910-1687.jpg/500px-Nachtconcert_van_het_Horeca_Silverquintet_in_het_concertgebouw_te_Amsterdam%2C_Bestanddeelnr_910-1687.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nachtconcert_van_het_Horeca_Silverquintet_in_het_concertgebouw_te_Amsterdam,_Bestanddeelnr_910-1687.jpg) Horace Silver Quintet in Amsterdam, 1959 According to [Nat Hentoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nat_Hentoff "Nat Hentoff") in his 1957 liner notes for the [Art Blakey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Blakey "Art Blakey") album _Hard Bop_, the phrase was originated by music critic and pianist [John Mehegan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Mehegan "John Mehegan"), jazz reviewer of the _[New York Herald Tribune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Herald_Tribune "New York Herald Tribune")_ at that time. Hard bop first developed in the mid-1950s, and is generally seen as originating with [the Jazz Messengers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Jazz_Messengers "The Jazz Messengers"), a group led by Blakey.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-tanner-3)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-carr-6) Alternatively, Anthony Macias points to [Detroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit "Detroit") as an early center in the rise of bop and hard bop, noting the influence of Detroit musicians [Barry Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_Harris "Barry Harris") and [Kenny Burrell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Burrell "Kenny Burrell") and the fact that Miles Davis lived in the city from 1953 to 1954. [Billy Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Mitchell_(saxophonist) "Billy Mitchell (saxophonist)"), a tenor saxophone player, organized a band that played at the [Blue Bird Inn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Bird_Inn "Blue Bird Inn") in Detroit during the early 1950s that "anchored the city's Jazz scene" and attracted hard bop musicians to the city.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-9) [Michael Cuscuna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Cuscuna "Michael Cuscuna") maintains that Silver and Blakey's efforts were in response to the New York bebop scene: > Both Art and Horace were very, very aware of what they wanted to do. They wanted to get away from the jazz scene of the early '50s, which was the [Birdland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birdland_(jazz_club) "Birdland (jazz club)") scene—you hire [Phil Woods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Woods "Phil Woods") or [Charlie Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Parker "Charlie Parker") or [J. J. Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._J._Johnson "J. J. Johnson"), they come and sit in with the [house rhythm section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_band "House band"), and they only play blues and [standards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_standard "Jazz standard") that everybody knows. There's no rehearsal, there's no thought given to the audience. Both Horace and Art knew that the only way to get the jazz audience back and make it bigger than ever was to really make music that was memorable and planned, where you consider the audience and keep everything short. They really liked digging into blues and gospel, things with universal appeal. So they put together what was to be called the Jazz Messengers.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-schaffer-10) David Rosenthal sees the development of hard bop as a response to both a decline in bebop and the rise of rhythm and blues: > The early fifties saw an extremely dynamic [Rhythm and Blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_Blues "Rhythm and Blues") scene take shape.... This music, and not cool jazz, was what chronologically separated bebop and hard bop in ghettos. Young jazz musicians, of course, enjoyed and listened to these R & B sounds which, among other things, began the amalgam of blues and gospel that would later be dubbed ' [soul music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_music "Soul music").' And it is in this vigorously creative black pop music, at a time when bebop seemed to have lost both its direction and its audience, that some of hard bop's roots may be found.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-rosenthal-2):24 [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d5/Horace_Silver.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Horace_Silver.jpg) Horace Silver A key recording in the early development of hard bop was Silver's composition " [The Preacher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Preacher_(Horace_Silver_song) "The Preacher (Horace Silver song)")", which was considered "old-timey" or "corny", such that [Blue Note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records") head [Alfred Lion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Lion "Alfred Lion") was hesitant to record the song.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-rosenthal-2):38[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-schaffer-10) However, the song became a hit.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-schaffer-10) Miles Davis, who had performed the title track of his album _[Walkin'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walkin' "Walkin'")_ at the inaugural [Newport Jazz Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport_Jazz_Festival "Newport Jazz Festival") in 1954, would form the [Miles Davis Quintet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis_Quintet "Miles Davis Quintet") with [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane") in 1955, becoming prominent in hard bop before moving on to other styles.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-carr-6) Other early documents were the two volumes of the Blue Note [albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LP_album "LP album") _[A Night at Birdland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Night_at_Birdland_Vol._1 "A Night at Birdland Vol. 1")_, also from 1954, recorded by the Blakey's quintet at Birdland months before the Davis set at Newport. [Clifford Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_Brown "Clifford Brown"), the trumpeter on the Birdland albums, formed the Brown–Roach Quintet with drummer [Max Roach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Roach "Max Roach"). Among the pianists in the band were [Richie Powell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richie_Powell "Richie Powell")[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-11) and [Carl Perkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Perkins_(pianist) "Carl Perkins (pianist)"),[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-tanner-3) both of whom died at a young age. ### Mainstream David Ake notes that by the mid-1950s, "the bop world clearly was not the 'closed' circle it had been in its earliest days." This coincided with a competitive spirit among bop musicians to play with "virtuousity and complexity", along with what Ake calls "jazz masculinity."[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-12) The broadening influence of hard bop coincided with a generation of jazz pianists who rose to prominence in the late 1950s – among them [Tommy Flanagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tommy_Flanagan_(musician) "Tommy Flanagan (musician)"), [Kenny Drew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Drew "Kenny Drew"), and [Wynton Kelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wynton_Kelly "Wynton Kelly") – who took "altered" approaches to bebop. Although these musicians did not work exclusively or specifically within hard bop, their association with hard bop saxophone players put them within the genre's broader circle.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-:0-13) West Coast Jazz's diminishing influence during the late 1950s accelerated hard bop's rise to prominence, while the transition to 33 rpm records facilitated the shifts toward longer solos that were typical of hard bop albums.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-:1-5) During a fifteen-year stretch from 1952 to 1967, Blue Note Records recruited musicians and promoted hard bop described by Yanow as "classy."[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-:1-5) A critical album that cemented hard bop's mainstream presence in jazz was _[A Blowin' Session](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Blowin'_Session "A Blowin' Session")_ (1957), including saxophonists [Johnny Griffin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Griffin "Johnny Griffin"), John Coltrane, and Hank Mobley; trumpeter Lee Morgan; pianist Wynton Kelly; bassist [Paul Chambers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Chambers "Paul Chambers"); and Art Blakey. Described by Al Campbell as "one of the greatest hard bop jam sessions ever recorded" and "filled with infectious passion and camaraderie", it was the only studio session ever recorded including all three saxophonists. It cemented "Coltrane's ability to navigate complex chord changes over a fast tempo" and is associated with Griffin's reputation as "the world's fastest saxophonist".[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-14) In 1956, The Jazz Messengers recorded an album titled _[Hard Bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_Bop_(album) "Hard Bop (album)")_, which was released in 1957, including [Bill Hardman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Hardman "Bill Hardman") on trumpet and saxophonist [Jackie McLean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_McLean "Jackie McLean"), with a mix of hard bop compositions and [jazz standards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_standard "Jazz standard").[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-15) Shortly after, in 1958, The Jazz Messengers, with a new line-up including Lee Morgan on trumpet and Benny Golson on saxophone,[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-16) recorded the quintessential hard bop album _[Moanin'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moanin' "Moanin'")_,[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-:1-5) with the album pioneering in soul jazz. Golson and Morgan formed their own bands and produced further records in the hard bop genre: Golson's Jazztet with [Art Farmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Farmer "Art Farmer") on trumpet recorded the album _[Meet the Jazztet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meet_the_Jazztet "Meet the Jazztet")_ in 1960, which was given a five-star rating by [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic"), and Morgan explored hard bop and sister genres in records like _[The Sidewinder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sidewinder "The Sidewinder")_, known for its "funky, danceable groov\[e\] that drew from soul-jazz, [Latin boogaloo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boogaloo "Boogaloo"), blues, and R&B."[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-:2-17) Morgan's albums attracted rising stars in the jazz world, particularly saxophonists [Joe Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Henderson "Joe Henderson") and [Wayne Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter "Wayne Shorter"); Morgan formed a "long-standing partnership" with the latter.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-:2-17) Meanwhile, in the late 1950s to early 1960s John Coltrane was a prominent saxophonist within the hard bop genre, with albums such as _[Blue Train](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Train_(album) "Blue Train (album)")_ and _[Giant Steps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant_Steps "Giant Steps")_ exemplifying his ability to play within this style. His album _Stardust_ (1958), for instance, included on trumpet a young [Freddie Hubbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Hubbard "Freddie Hubbard"),[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-18) who would go on to become "a hard bop stylist."[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-19) _Blue Train_ was described by Richard Havers as "Coltrane's Hard-Bop Masterpiece", although an edit made to one of the album's tracks caused controversy following disapproval from sound engineer [Rudy Van Gelder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudy_Van_Gelder "Rudy Van Gelder").[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-20) In the early to mid-1960s, prior to his death, Coltrane experimented in free jazz but again drew influences from hard bop in his 1965 album _[A Love Supreme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme "A Love Supreme")_.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-21) Coltrane was a longtime member of Miles Davis' band, which bridged the gap between hard bop and modal jazz with albums such as _[Milestones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milestones_(Miles_Davis_album) "Milestones (Miles Davis album)")_ and _[Kind of Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue "Kind of Blue")_. These albums represented a transition toward more experimental jazz, but Davis maintained core ideas of hard bop, such as the "call-and-response theme" found on one of _Kind of Blue_'s best-known tracks, " [So What](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/So_What_(Miles_Davis_composition) "So What (Miles Davis composition)")".[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-:4-22) The earlier album _Milestones_ was described as "indebted to hard bop" due to its "fast speeds, angular phrases and driving rhythms".[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-:4-22) In the early 1960s, Joe Henderson formed a band with [Kenny Dorham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Dorham "Kenny Dorham"), which recorded for Blue Note Records, and played extensively as a sideman in the bands of Horace Silver and [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"); however, he received less recognition after he moved to [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco") and began recording for [Milestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milestone_Records "Milestone Records").[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-:3-23) Other hard bop musicians went to Europe, such as pianist [Bud Powell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bud_Powell "Bud Powell") (elder brother of Richie Powell) in 1959 and saxophonist [Dexter Gordon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dexter_Gordon "Dexter Gordon") in 1962. Powell, a bebop pianist, continued to record albums in the early 1960s, while Gordon's _[Our Man in Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Our_Man_in_Paris "Our Man in Paris")_ became "one of his most iconic albums" for Blue Note.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-24) Other musicians who contributed to the hard bop style include [Donald Byrd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Byrd "Donald Byrd"), [Tina Brooks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tina_Brooks "Tina Brooks"), [Sonny Clark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Clark "Sonny Clark"), [Lou Donaldson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou_Donaldson "Lou Donaldson"), [Blue Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mitchell "Blue Mitchell"), [Sonny Rollins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Rollins "Sonny Rollins"), and [Sonny Stitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Stitt "Sonny Stitt"). David Rosenthal considers six albums among the high points of the hard bop era: _[Ugetsu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ugetsu_(album) "Ugetsu (album)")_, _Kind of Blue_, _[Saxophone Colossus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxophone_Colossus "Saxophone Colossus")_, _[Let Freedom Ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Let_Freedom_Ring "Let Freedom Ring")_, _[Mingus Ah Um](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mingus_Ah_Um "Mingus Ah Um")_, and _[Brilliant Corners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brilliant_Corners "Brilliant Corners")_, referring to these as being some of the genre's "masterpieces".[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-:0-13) ### Decline and revival [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3b/Wynton-Marsalis_DSC07326.jpg/500px-Wynton-Marsalis_DSC07326.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wynton-Marsalis_DSC07326.jpg) Wynton Marsalis, an important figure in the revival of bop Scott Yanow described hard bop in the late 1960s as "running out of gas." Blue Note Records' sale and decline in the late 1960s and early 1970s, combined with the rapid ascendance of [soul jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz "Soul jazz") and [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion"), largely replaced hard bop's prevalence within jazz, although bop would see a major revival in the 1980s ( [neo-bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-bop "Neo-bop")).[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-:1-5) Yanow also attributes hard bop's temporary decline in the 1970s to "\[t\]he rise of commercial rock and the consolidation of most of the independent record labels."[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-:1-5) With rock groups such as [the Beatles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beatles "The Beatles") capturing hard bop's charisma and [avant-garde jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz") bringing "division and controversy into the jazz community," Miles Davis and other former hard boppers left the genre.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-25) Davis led other jazz musicians toward the fusion genre, particularly other trumpet players. For example, Donald Byrd's shift toward commercial fusion and [smooth jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_jazz "Smooth jazz") recordings of the early 1970s, while celebrated within some circles, was considered a "betrayal" by fans of hard bop. His album _[Black Byrd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Byrd "Black Byrd")_ (1973), Blue Note's most successful album, neared the #1 spot on the R&B charts despite the opposition of jazz purists.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-26) In 1985, the filmed concert _[One Night with Blue Note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Night_with_Blue_Note "One Night with Blue Note")_ brought together thirty predominantly hard bop musicians including Art Blakey, [Ron Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Carter "Ron Carter"), Johnny Griffin, and Freddie Hubbard.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-27) Following fusion's decline, younger musicians started a bop revival known as neo-bop, the best-known proponent of this being trumpeter [Wynton Marsalis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wynton_Marsalis "Wynton Marsalis"). The revival was a "resurgence" by the 1990s,[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-28) and by the 1990s, hard bop's revival had become so prominent that Yanow referred to it as "the foundation of modern acoustic jazz."[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-:1-5) Veteran saxophonist Joe Henderson, for instance, was described by Yanow as a "national celebrity and a constant poll winner" in jazz circles after signing to [Verve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verve_Records "Verve Records") in the 1990s, largely due to changes in marketing.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-:3-23) ## Legacy Rosenthal observed that "\[t\]he years 1955 to 1965 represent the last period in which jazz effortlessly attracted the hippiest young black musicians, the most musically advanced, those with the most solid technical skills and the strongest sense of themselves, not only as entertainers but as artists." In the same text he laments hard bop's "many detractors and few articulate defenders," describing some of the comments made by its critics as "derogatory cliches."[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-:0-13) Alternatively, Yanow suggests a slightly longer period, from 1955 to 1968, during which hard bop was "the most dominant jazz style."[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop#cite_note-:1-5) Although the hard bop style enjoyed its greatest popularity in the 1950s and 1960s, hard bop performers and elements of the music remain present in jazz. ## See also - [![icon](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/Saxo_Boca1.JPG/60px-Saxo_Boca1.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Saxo_Boca1.JPG)[Jazz portal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portal:Jazz "Portal:Jazz") - [List of hard bop musicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_hard_bop_musicians "List of hard bop musicians") ## References 01. # Post-bop Post-bop Genre of small-combo jazz **Post-bop** is a [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") term with several possible definitions and usages.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-bop#cite_note-Yudkin_p._125-1) It has been variously defined as a musical period, a musical genre, a musical style, and a body of music, sometimes in different chronological periods, depending on the writer. Musicologist [Barry Kernfeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_Kernfeld "Barry Kernfeld") wrote in _[The New Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_Grove_Dictionary_of_Music_and_Musicians "The New Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians")_ that post-bop is "a vague term, used either stylistically or chronologically (with divergent results) to describe any continuation or amalgamation of [bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop"), [modal jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz "Modal jazz"), and [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz"); its meaning sometimes extends into [swing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing_music "Swing music") and earlier styles or into [fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") and third stream styles."[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-bop#cite_note-Grove-2) ## Definitions and uses The term post-bop has a variety of usages which vary widely.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-bop#cite_note-Grove-2) Jazz historian [Stuart Nicholson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Nicholson_(jazz_historian) "Stuart Nicholson (jazz historian)") wrote that "The term post-bop is a wonderful catch-all, used not so much to describe what a style of music is, but more what it isn't. Post-bop isn't [free](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") or [fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fusion_jazz "Fusion jazz") or [hard-bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard-bop "Hard-bop") or [modal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz "Modal jazz") or [avant-garde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz")."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-bop#cite_note-3) Some writers have defined post-bop with specificity, but these sources conflict with one another.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-bop#cite_note-Yudkin_p._125-1) One potential definition of post-bop is a musical period in which modern jazz was at its greatest mainstream popularity extending from the mid-1950s through to the mid-1960s.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-bop#cite_note-Yudkin_p._125-1)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-bop#cite_note-4) Others have written that post-bop is not a musical period but a specific body of music that emerged in the late 1950s and 1960s that combined principles of bebop, [hard bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop "Hard bop"), [modal jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz "Modal jazz"), [avant-garde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz") and [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz"), but also departed from earlier traditions in jazz.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-bop#cite_note-Waters_2019-5) Still other writers have defined post-bop as a genre of small-combo jazz that evolved in the early to mid 1960s in the United States that was pioneered by [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis") (the central figure in the development of this genre), in conjunction with [Charles Mingus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus "Charles Mingus"), [Wayne Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter "Wayne Shorter"), [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"), [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane") and [Jackie McLean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_McLean "Jackie McLean"), which crafted syntheses of hard bop with contemporaneous developments in [avant-garde jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz"), modal jazz and free jazz that resulted in music with a complex and experimental flavor though still rooted in bop tradition, featuring less of the [blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues "Blues") and [soul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_music "Soul music") leanings predominant in hard bop. The movement had a significant impact on subsequent generations of both acoustic jazz and [fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") musicians.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-bop#cite_note-Yudkin_p._125-1) According to [musicologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musicology "Musicology") Jeremy Yudkin, post-bop does not follow "the conventions of bop or the apparently formless freedom of the new jazz".[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-bop#cite_note-Bailey-6) He wrote in his definition of the subgenre: > [Forms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Form_(music) "Form (music)"), [tempos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tempo "Tempo"), and [meters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meter_(music) "Meter (music)") are freer, all the compositions are new, and the band members themselves are featured composers.... \[A\]n approach that is abstract and intense in the extreme, with space created for rhythmic and coloristic independence of the drummer—an approach that incorporated [modal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mode_(music) "Mode (music)") and chordal harmonies, flexible form, structured choruses, melodic [variation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variation_(music) "Variation (music)"), and [free improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation "Free improvisation")."[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-bop#cite_note-Bailey-6) According to scholar Keith Waters, some of the traits found in post-bop recordings are: a slower harmonic rhythm characteristic of modal jazz, techniques for playing "inside" and "outside" the underlying harmonic structure, an interactive (or conversational) approach to rhythm section accompaniment, unusual harmonic progressions, use of harmonic or metric superimposition, unusual underlying formal designs for head statements and chorus structure improvisation, or the abandonment entirely of underlying chorus structure beneath improvisation.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-bop#cite_note-Waters_2019-5) [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis") was particularly influential in the development of small-combo jazz post-bop in the 1960s. His second quintet was active during 1964 to 1968 and featured pianist [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"), bassist [Ron Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Carter "Ron Carter"), saxophonist [Wayne Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter "Wayne Shorter"), and drummer [Tony Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer) "Tony Williams (drummer)"). They recorded six studio albums that, according to [All About Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_About_Jazz "All About Jazz")'s C. Michael Bailey, introduced post-bop: _[E.S.P.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E.S.P._(Miles_Davis_album) "E.S.P. (Miles Davis album)")_ (1965), _[Miles Smiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Smiles "Miles Smiles")_ (1967), _[Sorcerer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sorcerer_(Miles_Davis_album) "Sorcerer (Miles Davis album)")_ (1967), _[Nefertiti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nefertiti_(Miles_Davis_album) "Nefertiti (Miles Davis album)")_ (1968), _[Miles in the Sky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_in_the_Sky "Miles in the Sky")_ (1968), and _[Filles de Kilimanjaro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filles_de_Kilimanjaro "Filles de Kilimanjaro")_ (1968).[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-bop#cite_note-Bailey-6) ## See also - [Category:Post-bop jazz musicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Post-bop_jazz_musicians "Category:Post-bop jazz musicians") ## References 1. - [gospel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_music "Gospel music") | | Cultural origins | 1950s | | Fusion genres | | [Jazz-funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk "Jazz-funk") | **Soul jazz** or **funky jazz** is a subgenre of [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") that incorporates strong influences from [hard bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop "Hard bop"), [blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues "Blues"), [soul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_music "Soul music"), [gospel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_music "Gospel music") and [rhythm and blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues"). Soul jazz is often characterized by [organ trios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organ_trio "Organ trio") featuring the [Hammond organs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hammond_organ "Hammond organ") and small combos including [saxophones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxophone "Saxophone"), [brass instruments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brass_instrument "Brass instrument"), [electric guitars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_guitar "Electric guitar"), [double basses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_bass "Double bass"), [bass guitars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_guitar "Bass guitar"), [drums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drums "Drums"), [pianos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano "Piano"), [vocals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vocal "Vocal") and [electric organs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_organ "Electric organ"). Its origins were in the 1950s and early 1960s, with its heyday with popular audiences preceding the rise of [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") in the late 1960s and 1970s. Prominent names in fusion ranged from bop pianists including [Bobby Timmons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Timmons "Bobby Timmons") and [Junior Mance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junior_Mance "Junior Mance") to a wide range of organists, saxophonists, pianists, drummers and electric guitarists including [Jack McDuff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_McDuff "Jack McDuff"), [Eddie "Lockjaw" Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_%22Lockjaw%22_Davis "Eddie \"Lockjaw\" Davis"), and [Grant Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grant_Green "Grant Green").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-1) ## Musical style Soul jazz is often associated with [hard bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop "Hard bop").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-gridley-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-tanner-3)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-carr-4) Mark C. Gridley, writing for the _[All Music Guide to Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Music_Guide_to_Jazz "All Music Guide to Jazz")_, explains that soul jazz more specifically refers to music with "an earthy, bluesy melodic concept" and "repetitive, dance-like rhythms.... Note that some listeners make no distinction between 'soul-jazz' and 'funky hard bop,' and many musicians don't consider 'soul-jazz' to be continuous with 'hard bop.'"[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-gridley-2) According to Nick Morrison, the subgenre "usually begins with the bass player" who "take\[s\] a strong bass line, establish\[es\] a steady groove between the bass and drums", before the band can "embellish that groove with riffs and melody lines".[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-:0-5) Jazz pianist Horace Silver stated that "\[f\]unky means earthy and blues-based. It might not be blues itself, but it does have that 'down-home' feel to it. Soul is basically the same, but there's an added dimension of feeling and spirit."[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-6) ## History ### Origins [Roy Carr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Carr "Roy Carr") has described soul jazz as an outgrowth of hard bop, with the terms "funk" and "soul" appearing in a jazz context as early as the mid-1950s to describe "gospel-informed, down-home, call-and-response blues".[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-carr-4) Carr has also noted the influence of [Ray Charles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Charles "Ray Charles")' small group recordings (which included saxophonists [David "Fathead" Newman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_%22Fathead%22_Newman "David \"Fathead\" Newman") and [Hank Crawford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hank_Crawford "Hank Crawford")) on [Horace Silver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Silver "Horace Silver"), [Art Blakey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Blakey "Art Blakey"), [Cannonball Adderley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannonball_Adderley "Cannonball Adderley").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-carr-4) In his view, [David Sanborn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Sanborn "David Sanborn") and [Maceo Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maceo_Parker "Maceo Parker") are in a line of [alto saxophonists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alto_saxophone "Alto saxophone") that includes [Earl Bostic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_Bostic "Earl Bostic"), [Tab Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tab_Smith "Tab Smith"), Adderley, and [Lou Donaldson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou_Donaldson "Lou Donaldson") as the strongest links in the chain of the genre's evolution.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-carr-4) In the early to mid-1950s, after he left the [Count Basie Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_Basie_Orchestra "Count Basie Orchestra"), saxophonist Eddie "Lockjaw" Davis was among the first to form a jazz group with both organ and saxophone, first with [Bill Doggett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Doggett "Bill Doggett") and later [Shirley Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirley_Scott "Shirley Scott").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-7) For this and his "full bodied yet reedy tone that was equally at home in rhythm & blues settings as more modern contexts," he "provided a link" between big band swing and soul jazz.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-8) Soul jazz continued to develop in the late 1950s, reaching public awareness with the release of _[The Cannonball Adderley Quintet in San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Cannonball_Adderley_Quintet_in_San_Francisco "The Cannonball Adderley Quintet in San Francisco")_.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-NPR-9)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-10) Cannonball Adderley noted: "We were pressured quite heavily by [Riverside Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riverside_Records "Riverside Records") when they discovered there was a word called 'soul'. We became, from an image point of view, soul jazz artists. They kept promoting us that way and I kept deliberately fighting it, to the extent that it became a game."[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-11) Late 1950s, soul jazz artist [Curtis Fuller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curtis_Fuller "Curtis Fuller") recorded "Five Spot after Dark".[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-12) ### Mainstream [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2e/Het_Less_McCann_trio_op_Schiphol%2C_vlnr_Less_McCann_%28piano%29%2C_Hurby_Loui_%28bas%29%2C_Bestanddeelnr_914-5091.jpg/500px-Het_Less_McCann_trio_op_Schiphol%2C_vlnr_Less_McCann_%28piano%29%2C_Hurby_Loui_%28bas%29%2C_Bestanddeelnr_914-5091.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Het_Less_McCann_trio_op_Schiphol,_vlnr_Less_McCann_(piano),_Hurby_Loui_(bas),_Bestanddeelnr_914-5091.jpg) [Les McCann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_McCann "Les McCann") Trio Jimmy Smith's shift into soul jazz demonstrated the organ's potential within the genre with his albums _[Home Cookin'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_Cookin'_(album) "Home Cookin' (album)")_ (1961) and _[Back at the Chicken Shack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back_at_the_Chicken_Shack "Back at the Chicken Shack")_ (1963). Other organists who recorded in the soul jazz genre during this period include [Jack McDuff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_McDuff "Jack McDuff"), [Shirley Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirley_Scott "Shirley Scott"), and [Charles Earland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Earland "Charles Earland").[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-13) With the addition of former bebop and hard-bop musicians to the genre, the number of musicians within various facets of the style increased as soul jazz became a subgenre in its own right; and like its bop predecessor, the new genre of jazz reworked popular songs, such as " [Got My Mojo Workin'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Got_My_Mojo_Working "Got My Mojo Working")," while saxophone and trumpet players recently converted to the genre composed hits including " [The Sidewinder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sidewinder_(composition) "The Sidewinder (composition)")", " [Mercy, Mercy, Mercy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercy,_Mercy,_Mercy "Mercy, Mercy, Mercy")" and "Listen Here" during the mid-1960s.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-:0-5) [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d7/Jimmy_Oscar_Smith_Hammond.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jimmy_Oscar_Smith_Hammond.JPG) [Jimmy Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Smith_(musician) "Jimmy Smith (musician)") on a [Hammond organ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hammond_organ "Hammond organ") An accelerating factor in soul jazz's development was the [Black Power movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Power_movement "Black Power movement"), which led African-American musicians to return to the African roots of their music. Tunes recorded within the genre, including "Mercy, Mercy, Mercy" and "Let My People Go" were direct references to the [civil rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_rights_movement "Civil rights movement") and Black Power movements.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-14) For instance, Adderley's music from the period has been described as containing an "irrepressible exuberance". Interest in the genre broadened when Adderley introduced Austrian-born keyboardist [Joe Zawinul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Zawinul "Joe Zawinul") to soul jazz through his Quintet, with Zawinul contributing to its repertoire with his own compositions.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-15) Likewise [Stanley Turrentine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Turrentine "Stanley Turrentine"), who began recording with Jimmy Smith in 1960 and rapidly expanded his audience, lamented the lack of jazz on radio and TV, saying that more people, and particularly African Americans, would have listened to soul jazz had it received as much exposure as rock music.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-16) The tenor saxophone player recorded a number of soul jazz albums throughout the 1960s, including _[Never Let Me Go](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Never_Let_Me_Go_(Stanley_Turrentine_album) "Never Let Me Go (Stanley Turrentine album)")_ (1963) with his wife Shirley Scott. Jazz critic Thom Jurek noted that on the recording "the organ acts as the testifying pulpit from which to speak, and Turrentine not only speaks, he weeps and whispers and wails."[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-17) Turrentine's following album, _[A Chip Off the Old Block](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Chip_Off_the_Old_Block_(album) "A Chip Off the Old Block (album)")_ (1963), marked the first shift in influence, in this case from the swing/big band era with compositions by [Count Basie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_Basie "Count Basie") and [Neal Hefti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neal_Hefti "Neal Hefti"). Turrentine's wife again contributed in addition to hard bop trumpeter [Blue Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mitchell "Blue Mitchell").[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-18) In the mid- to late-1960s, Turrentine evolved his soul jazz style from the small-group setting traditionally associated with the subgenre to an ensemble format,[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-:1-19) with _[Joyride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyride_(Stanley_Turrentine_album) "Joyride (Stanley Turrentine album)")_ (1965) arranged by fellow jazz saxophonist [Oliver Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Nelson "Oliver Nelson").[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-20) [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/98/KPLU_In-Studio_Performance_Ramsey_Lewis_2.jpg/330px-KPLU_In-Studio_Performance_Ramsey_Lewis_2.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:KPLU_In-Studio_Performance_Ramsey_Lewis_2.jpg) [Ramsey Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramsey_Lewis "Ramsey Lewis") While Turrentine developed the core of the "soul" in soul jazz, Latin and funky influences developed soul jazz upon the foundation of bop. Pianist Herbie Hancock, for instance, was instrumental in pushing the boundaries of music theory and chord progressions during the 1960s.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-21) Hancock's first album _[Takin' Off](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takin'_Off "Takin' Off")_ (1962) featured the funky " [Watermelon Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watermelon_Man_(composition) "Watermelon Man (composition)")", a composition recorded by both Hancock and [Mongo Santamaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongo_Santamar%C3%ADa "Mongo Santamaría"), and was notable for "spare, funky piano riffing and tight, focused solo statements" that enabled Hancock to "begin pushing the boundaries of hard bop."[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-22) The 1960s saw Hancock and trumpeter Lee Morgan's compositions be used in TV, with " [Maiden Voyage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maiden_Voyage_(composition) "Maiden Voyage (composition)")" by Hancock appearing in a [Fabergé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Faberg%C3%A9 "House of Fabergé") commercial and Morgan's "The Sidewinder" in a [Chrysler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chrysler "Chrysler") commercial.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-:2-23) Popularizations of jazz compositions, such as the renditions of "Watermelon Man" by Santamaria and [Gloria Lynne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gloria_Lynne "Gloria Lynne"), went further to make soul jazz appealing to Black audiences, particularly in the early to mid-1960s, though this shifted over the course of the decade so much that by the late 1960s, the jazz musicians themselves were producing hit records, with six Jimmy Smith/ [Blue Note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records") albums reaching the top 200. However, jazz labels such as Blue Note found it difficult to compete with larger record companies for advertising opportunities.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-:2-23) [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/4f/Eddie_Harris.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Eddie_Harris.jpg) Saxophonist [Eddie Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Harris "Eddie Harris") The growing popularity of soul jazz meant that, for many hard bop musicians, the shift from bop to soul jazz was not clearly defined, with Horace Silver releasing hard bop album _[The Jody Grind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Jody_Grind "The Jody Grind")_ in 1966,[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-24) and the more soul-influenced _[Serenade to a Soul Sister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serenade_to_a_Soul_Sister "Serenade to a Soul Sister")_ – starring Turrentine – in 1968. The latter album was described by Steve Huey as "one of the pianist's most infectiously cheerful, good-humored outings." Silver wrote in the album's liner notes that he believed his music should avoid "politics, hatred, or anger."[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-25) Tenor saxophonist Hank Mobley took even longer to make the shift, playing primarily within the hard bop genre until 1968, when he recorded _[Reach Out!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reach_Out!_(Hank_Mobley_album) "Reach Out! (Hank Mobley album)")_ with a light soul jazz feel.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-26) His following album _[The Flip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Flip_(album) "The Flip (album)")_ (1969) blended soul jazz and hard bop on its title track, according to Jurek.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-27) Other jazz artists, such as Lee Morgan, wavered in and out of the soul jazz genre. Drawing influence from the reliably hard bop Jazz Messengers, Morgan's albums of the mid-1960s could be described as both hard bop and soul jazz. Morgan hired bop musicians for the album but recorded soul-influenced material, for instance on the album _[Cornbread](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornbread_(album) "Cornbread (album)")_ (1965).[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-28) Other soul jazz musicians had their roots almost entirely in soul and blues. Organist Jack McDuff, for example, was known for his particularly bluesy style, which enabled him to collaborate with young jazz talents including saxophonist [Johnny Griffin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Griffin "Johnny Griffin") and guitarist [George Benson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Benson "George Benson").[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-29) McDuff's band focused on "groove-centric" music but in the later '60s experimented with popular songs and larger ensembles, particularly on his album _Tobacco Road_ (1967).[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-30) In contrast, former McDuff sideman and guitarist [Pat Martino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pat_Martino "Pat Martino") utilized an organ trio format during the late 1960s, with the live _[Young Guns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young_Guns_(album) "Young Guns (album)")_ (2014) album recorded at Club 118 in 1968 and 1969 featuring [Gene Ludwig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_Ludwig "Gene Ludwig") on organ and [Randy Gelispie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Gelispie "Randy Gelispie") on drums.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-31) Among the best-known soul jazz recordings from the era are [Lee Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Morgan "Lee Morgan")'s _[The Sidewinder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sidewinder "The Sidewinder")_ (1963), [Frank Foster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Foster_(jazz_musician) "Frank Foster (jazz musician)")'s _Samba Blues_ (1963), [Nat Adderley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nat_Adderley "Nat Adderley")'s " [Work Song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Work_Song_(Adderley_song) "Work Song (Adderley song)")", Horace Silver's " [Song for My Father](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Song_for_My_Father_(song) "Song for My Father (song)")" (1964), [Ramsey Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramsey_Lewis "Ramsey Lewis")'s " [The 'In' Crowd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_'In'_Crowd_(song) "The 'In' Crowd (song)")" (a top-five hit in 1965[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-carr-4)), Cannonball Adderley's " [Mercy, Mercy, Mercy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercy,_Mercy,_Mercy "Mercy, Mercy, Mercy")"[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-carr-4) (1966) (also popularized further when covered as a top-40 pop song by [the Buckinghams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Buckinghams "The Buckinghams") the following year), and Young Holt Unlimited "Soulful Strut". [Les McCann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_McCann "Les McCann") and [Eddie Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Harris "Eddie Harris")'s album _[Swiss Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swiss_Movement "Swiss Movement")_ (1969) was a [hit record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hit_record "Hit record"), as was the accompanying [single](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_(music) "Single (music)") " [Compared to What](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compared_to_What "Compared to What")", with both selling millions of units.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-carr-4) ### Fusion Soul jazz began to mold into [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") by the late 1960s, with musicians such as Turrentine moving to the [CTI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CTI_Records "CTI Records") fusion label in the early 1970s[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-:1-19) and free jazz saxophonist [Albert Ayler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler "Albert Ayler") moving into jazz-rock during the late 1960s before his untimely death in 1970.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-32) With the temporary decline of Blue Note and the rapid rise of the CTI label, soul jazz moved toward smooth jazz and popular music of the day, with the label's founder [Creed Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creed_Taylor "Creed Taylor") remarking that his original goal of creating jazz for listening had "backfired" into the development of background music.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-33) Others pushed the boundaries of soul jazz to the extent it became fused with other genres. Tenor saxophonist Eddie Harris switched to the electric saxophone for his album titled _[The Electrifying Eddie Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Electrifying_Eddie_Harris "The Electrifying Eddie Harris")_ (1968).[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-34) His experiments in "funk-influenced fusion, outside improvisations, bizarre electronic effects, new crossbreedings of traditional instruments, blues crooning, and even comedy," according to Steve Huey, "fell outside the bounds of what critics considered legitimate, serious jazz." He [returned to bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-bop_jazz "Neo-bop jazz") late in his career.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-35) ## Legacy Although soul jazz was most popular during the mid-to-late 1960s, its musicians and musical influences remained popular past this time period. In the late 1960s and 1970s, the genre saw increased [crossover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossover_music "Crossover music") with fusion. The Jazz Crusaders, for example, evolved from soul jazz to [soul music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_music "Soul music"), becoming [the Crusaders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Crusaders_(Houston_group) "The Crusaders (Houston group)") in the process.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz#cite_note-carr-4) ## See also - [![icon](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/Saxo_Boca1.JPG/60px-Saxo_Boca1.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Saxo_Boca1.JPG)[Jazz portal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portal:Jazz "Portal:Jazz") - [List of jazz genres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_jazz_genres "List of jazz genres") - [List of soul-jazz musicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_soul-jazz_musicians "List of soul-jazz musicians") - [Category:Soul-jazz musicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Soul-jazz_musicians "Category:Soul-jazz musicians") ## References 01. [Alto saxophonist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alto_saxophone "Alto saxophone") [Charlie Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Parker "Charlie Parker") was a leading performer and composer of the bebop era. He is pictured here with [Tommy Potter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tommy_Potter "Tommy Potter"), [Max Roach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Roach "Max Roach") and [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis") at the Three Deuces club in New York City. | | Stylistic origins | - [Swing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing_music "Swing music")
