(1959) | | _**Kind of Blue**_ is a [studio album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio_album "Studio album") by American [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") musician [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis"), released on August17,1959, by [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records"). For this album, Davis led a [sextet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sextet "Sextet") featuring saxophonists [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane") and [Julian "Cannonball" Adderley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannonball_Adderley "Cannonball Adderley"), pianist [Bill Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans "Bill Evans"), bassist [Paul Chambers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Chambers "Paul Chambers"), and drummer [Jimmy Cobb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Cobb "Jimmy Cobb"), with new band pianist [Wynton Kelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wynton_Kelly "Wynton Kelly") replacing Evans on " [Freddie Freeloader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Freeloader "Freddie Freeloader")". The album was recorded at Columbia's [30th Street Studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS_30th_Street_Studio "CBS 30th Street Studio") in New York City in two sessions on March2 and April22,1959. Influenced in part by Evans, who had been a member of the ensemble in 1958 and was called back for this album, Davis departed further from his early [hard bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop "Hard bop") style in favor of greater experimentation with [musical modes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_mode "Musical mode"), as on the title track of his previous album, _[Milestones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milestones_(Miles_Davis_album) "Milestones (Miles Davis album)")_ (1958). Basing _Kind of Blue_ entirely on [modality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz "Modal jazz"), Davis gave each performer a set of scales that encompassed the parameters of their improvisation and style and consequently more creative freedom with melodies; Coltrane later expanded on this modal approach in his own solo career. _Kind of Blue_ is regarded by many critics as Davis's masterpiece, the greatest jazz album ever recorded, and one of the greatest albums of all time. Its influence on jazz, rock, and classical music has also led writers to describe it as one of the most influential albums ever made. In 2002, it was among the first fifty recordings selected by the [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress") for inclusion in the National Recording Registry as "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant." In 2003, it ranked number 12 on _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ magazine's list of the "500 Greatest Albums of All Time"; it was repositioned at number 31 in the 2020 revision. The [Recording Industry Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America "Recording Industry Association of America") (RIAA) certified the album quintuple platinum in 2019, representing five million album-equivalent units in the United States. It remained the highest-certified jazz album until August 2026, when [Vince Guaraldi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vince_Guaraldi "Vince Guaraldi")'s _[A Charlie Brown Christmas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Charlie_Brown_Christmas_(soundtrack) "A Charlie Brown Christmas (soundtrack)")_ was certified 6x platinum, making _Kind of Blue_ the second-best-selling jazz album in the United States based on RIAA certification.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-6mil-1) ## Background \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kind_of_Blue&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Background")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fa/Miles_Davis_by_Palumbo.jpg/250px-Miles_Davis_by_Palumbo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Miles_Davis_by_Palumbo.jpg) [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis") in 1956 [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Bill_Evans_%281961_publicity_photo_by_Steve_Schapiro%29.jpg/250px-Bill_Evans_%281961_publicity_photo_by_Steve_Schapiro%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bill_Evans_(1961_publicity_photo_by_Steve_Schapiro).jpg) [Bill Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans "Bill Evans") in 1961 By late 1958, trumpeter Miles Davis employed one of the most acclaimed and profitable [hard bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop "Hard bop") bands in the business. Bassist [Paul Chambers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Chambers "Paul Chambers") had been with the group from its beginning in 1955, alto saxophonist [Julian "Cannonball" Adderley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannonball_Adderley "Cannonball Adderley") joined in late 1957, and tenor saxophonist [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane") returned in early 1958.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-kahn86-2) Drummer [Jimmy Cobb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Cobb "Jimmy Cobb") replaced [Philly Joe Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philly_Joe_Jones "Philly Joe Jones") in May 1958,[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-3) and pianist [Wynton Kelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wynton_Kelly "Wynton Kelly") replaced Bill Evans in November 1958.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-kahn86-2) The Davis band played a mixture of [pop standards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_standards "Pop standards"), [blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues "Blues"), and [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop") originals by composers such as [Charlie Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Parker "Charlie Parker"), [Thelonious Monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thelonious_Monk "Thelonious Monk"), [Dizzy Gillespie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie "Dizzy Gillespie"), [Tadd Dameron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tadd_Dameron "Tadd Dameron"), and Davis himself. As with all bebop-based jazz, Davis's groups [improvised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_improvisation "Musical improvisation") on the [chord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chord_(music) "Chord (music)") changes of a given song.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-kahn86-2) Davis was one of many jazz musicians growing dissatisfied with bebop, however, and saw its increasingly complex chord changes as hindering creativity.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-kindofblue67-68-4) In 1953, the composer and theorist [George Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Russell_(composer) "George Russell (composer)") published his _[Lydian Chromatic Concept of Tonal Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization "Lydian Chromatic Concept of Tonal Organization")_,[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-lydian-5) which offered an alternative to improvisation based on chords. Abandoning the traditional major and minor [key](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Key_(music) "Key (music)") relationships, his concept introduced the idea of chord/scale unity and was the first theory to explore the vertical relationship between chords and scales. These insights helped lead the way to [modal jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz "Modal jazz").[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-modal-6) Influenced by Russell's ideas, Davis implemented his first modal composition with the title track of his studio album _[Milestones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milestones_(Miles_Davis_album) "Milestones (Miles Davis album)")_ (1958). Satisfied with the results, Davis prepared an entire album based on modality.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-reissuenotes-7) Evans, who had studied and recorded with Russell but had left the Davis group to pursue his own career, was drafted back into the project.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-kindofblue83-8) ## Recording \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kind_of_Blue&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Recording")\] _Kind of Blue_ was recorded on three-track tape in two sessions at [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records")' [30th Street Studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS_30th_Street_Studio "CBS 30th Street Studio") in New York City. On March 2, 1959, the tracks " [So What](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/So_What_(composition) "So What (composition)")", " [Freddie Freeloader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Freeloader "Freddie Freeloader")", and " [Blue in Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_in_Green "Blue in Green")" were recorded for side one of the original [LP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LP_record "LP record"), and on April 22 the tracks " [All Blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Blues "All Blues")" and "Flamenco Sketches" were recorded, making up side two.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-LPnotes-9) As was Davis's penchant, he called for almost no rehearsal and the musicians had little idea what they were to record. As described in the original liner notes by pianist Bill Evans, Davis had only given the band sketches of scales and melody lines on which to improvise.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-ch34-10) Once the musicians were assembled, Davis gave brief instructions for each piece and then set to taping the sextet in studio. While the results were impressive with so little preparation, the persistent legend that the entire album was recorded in one pass is untrue.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-ch34-10) Only "Flamenco Sketches" yielded a complete take on the first try. That take, which is not the master, was added to the 1997 CD reissue of the album as a bonus track.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-ch34-10) The five master takes issued were the only other complete takes; an insert for the ending to "Freddie Freeloader" was recorded, but was not used for release or on the issues of _Kind of Blue_ prior to the 1997 reissue.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-ch34-10) Pianist [Wynton Kelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wynton_Kelly "Wynton Kelly") may not have been happy to see the man he replaced, Bill Evans, back in his old seat. Perhaps to assuage the pianist's feelings, Davis had Kelly play instead of Evans on the album's most [blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues_music "Blues music")-oriented number, "Freddie Freeloader."[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-ch34-10) The live album _[Miles Davis at Newport 1958](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/At_Newport_1958 "At Newport 1958")_ documents the sextet during Evans's tenure; however, it is in a hard bop style, rather than the modal approach of _Kind of Blue_.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-11) The more ruminative side of Evans's playing while he was a member of the band can best be heard on his lengthy solo on " [My Funny Valentine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_Funny_Valentine "My Funny Valentine")" from _[Jazz at the Plaza Vol. I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_at_the_Plaza_Vol._I "Jazz at the Plaza Vol. I")_.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-12) ### Production credit \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kind_of_Blue&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Production credit")\] _Kind of Blue_ was produced by [Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records") staff producer [Irving Townsend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irving_Townsend "Irving Townsend").[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-Kahn2002-13):195 However, Davis' subsequent producer, [Teo Macero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teo_Macero "Teo Macero"), has incorrectly received partial or full credit. "In the case of _Kind of Blue_ there were two producers: Teo Macero and Irving Townsend", said jazz historian [Eric Nisenson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Nisenson "Eric Nisenson"). "Macero's role, however, was clearly that of an apprentice and observer." The recording session was also cited by Nisenson as Macero's first experience with "the highs and lows of working with Miles." From Macero's own recollection, his involvement in the recording included "box\[ing\] everyone in so that there would be a physical closeness among the musicians, not like today when the musicians are spread all over the place."[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-14) According to _[High Fidelity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Fidelity_(magazine) "High Fidelity (magazine)")_, "though his role in _Kind of Blue_ has been disputed", the recording was "made under the auspices" of Macero.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-15) However, it is Townsend's voice heard on the session tapes, who became Davis's producer after the departures of [George Avakian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Avakian "George Avakian") and [Cal Lampley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cal_Lampley "Cal Lampley"). Macero did not produce Davis until after Townsend took over West Coast production duties for Columbia Records, when Macero took his place.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-Kahn2002-13):90 Macero's first Davis production was his next record, _[Sketches of Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sketches_of_Spain "Sketches of Spain")_.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-Kahn2002-13):166 The original LP did not credit a producer.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-1959LP-16) The first release with a producer credit was the 1987 CD, which credited only Macero.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-17) However, this was in error; Macero only produced that reissue, not the sessions for the original album.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-Kahn2002-13):195 The 1997 [MiniDisc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MiniDisc "MiniDisc") reissue credited both Townsend and Macero,[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-18) but the subsequent 1997,[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-19) 1999,[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-20) 2004,[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-21) 2008,[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-22) and 2015[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-23) reissues all correctly credit only Townsend. ## Composition \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kind_of_Blue&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: Composition")\] _Kind of Blue_ is based entirely on [modality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz "Modal jazz"), diverging from Davis's earlier [hard bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop "Hard bop") style of jazz with its complex [chord progression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chord_progression "Chord progression") and [improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Improvisation_(music) "Improvisation (music)").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-reissuenotes-7) The entire album was a series of _modal sketches_, with each performer given a set of scales that encompassed the parameters of their improvisation and style.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-1997notes-24) This recording style contrasted with the typical preparation of providing musicians with the [complete score](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheet_music "Sheet music") or, for improvisational jazz, providing the musicians with a [chord progression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chord_progression "Chord progression") or series of [harmonies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmony "Harmony").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-kindofblue67-68-4) Modal jazz was not unique to this album. Davis himself had previously used the same method on his 1958 _[Milestones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milestones_(Miles_Davis_album) "Milestones (Miles Davis album)")_ album, the _'58 Sessions_, and _[Porgy and Bess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porgy_and_Bess_(Miles_Davis_album) "Porgy and Bess (Miles Davis album)")_ (1958), on which he used modal influences for collaborator [Gil Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gil_Evans "Gil Evans")'s [third stream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_stream "Third stream") compositions.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-kindofblue67-68-4) Modal composition, with its reliance on scales and modes, represented, as Davis called it,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-kindofblue67-68-4) "a return to melody".[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-1997notes-24) In a 1958 interview with [Nat Hentoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nat_Hentoff "Nat Hentoff") of _[The Jazz Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Jazz_Review "The Jazz Review")_, Davis elaborated on this form of composition in contrast to the chord progression predominant in bebop, stating: > No chords ... gives you a lot more freedom and space to hear things. When you go this way, you can go on forever. You don't have to worry about changes and you can do more with the \[melody\] line. It becomes a challenge to see how melodically innovative you can be. When you're based on chords, you know at the end of 32 bars that the chords have run out and there's nothing to do but repeat what you've just done—with variations. I think a movement in jazz is beginning away from the conventional string of chords ... there will be fewer chords but infinite possibilities as to what to do with them.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-kindofblue67-68-4) Bill Evans wrote in the LP liner notes, "Miles conceived these settings only hours before the recording dates."[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-LPnotes-9) Evans continued with an introduction concerning the modes used in each composition on the album. " [So What](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/So_What_(Miles_Davis_composition) "So What (Miles Davis composition)")" consists of two modes: sixteen measures of the first, followed by eight measures of the second, and then eight again of the first.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-LPnotes-9) " [Freddie Freeloader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Freeloader "Freddie Freeloader")" is a standard [twelve-bar blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twelve-bar_blues "Twelve-bar blues") form. " [Blue in Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_in_Green "Blue in Green")" consists of a ten-measure cycle following a short four-measure introduction.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-LPnotes-9) " [All Blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Blues "All Blues")" is a twelve-bar blues form in [**6**\\ \\ **8** time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/6/8_time "6/8 time"). "Flamenco Sketches" consists of five scales, which are each played "as long as the soloist wishes until he has completed the series".[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-LPnotes-9) The liner notes list Davis as author of all compositions, but many scholars and fans believe that Bill Evans wrote part or the whole of "Blue in Green" and "Flamenco Sketches".[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-25) Bill Evans assumed co-credit with Davis for "Blue in Green" when recording it on his _[Portrait in Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portrait_in_Jazz "Portrait in Jazz")_ album, and the Davis estate acknowledged Evans' authorship in 2002.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-26) ## Reception and legacy \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kind_of_Blue&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: its release on August 17, 1959,[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-36) _Kind of Blue_ has been regarded by critics as Davis's greatest work. It is his most acclaimed album, and became, along with Davis's 1970 album _[Bitches Brew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew "Bitches Brew")_, his best-selling record, cementing him as one of the most successful jazz artists in history.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-37)[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-38)[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-39)[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-40)[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-41) Music writer Chris Morris cited _Kind of Blue_ as "the distillation of Davis's art."[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-Morris-42) Cobb said the album "must have been made in heaven".[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-43) _Kind of Blue_ has been lauded as one of the most influential albums in the history of jazz. One reviewer has called it a "defining moment of twentieth century music".[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-44) Several of the pieces from the album have become [jazz standards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_standards "Jazz standards"). _Kind of Blue_ is consistently ranked among the greatest albums of all time.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-45) In a review of the album, [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") senior editor [Stephen Thomas Erlewine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Thomas_Erlewine "Stephen Thomas Erlewine") stated: > _Kind of Blue_ isn't merely an artistic highlight for Miles Davis, it's an album that towers above its peers, a record generally considered as the definitive jazz album, a universally acknowledged standard of excellence. Why does _Kind of Blue_ possess such a mystique? Perhaps because this music never flaunts its genius. ... It's the pinnacle of modal jazz— tonality and solos build from the overall key, not chord changes, giving the music a subtly shifting quality. ... It may be a stretch to say that if you don't like _Kind of Blue_, you don't like jazz— but it's hard to imagine it as anything other than a cornerstone of any jazz collection.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-Erlewine-27) In 1959, the arrival of [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman") on the jazz scene via his fall residency at the [Five Spot Café](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Spot_Caf%C3%A9 "Five Spot Café"), consolidated by the release of his _[The Shape of Jazz to Come](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shape_of_Jazz_to_Come "The Shape of Jazz to Come")_ LP in 1959, muted the initial impact of _Kind of Blue_, a happenstance that irritated Davis greatly.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-46) Though Davis and Coleman both offered alternatives to the rigid rules of bebop, Davis would never reconcile himself to Coleman's [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") innovations, although he would incorporate musicians amenable to Coleman's ideas with his great quintet of the mid-1960s, and offer his own version of "free" playing with his [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") outfits in the 1970s.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-47) The influence of _Kind of Blue_ did build, and all of the sidemen from the album went on to achieve success on their own. Evans formed his influential jazz trio with bassist [Scott LaFaro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_LaFaro "Scott LaFaro") and drummer [Paul Motian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Motian "Paul Motian"); "Cannonball" Adderley fronted popular bands with his brother [Nat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nat_Adderley "Nat Adderley"); Kelly, Chambers and Cobb continued as a touring unit, recording under Kelly's name as well as in support of Coltrane and [Wes Montgomery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wes_Montgomery "Wes Montgomery"), among others; and Coltrane went on to become one of the most revered and innovative of all jazz musicians. Even more than Davis, Coltrane took the modal approach and ran with it during his career as a leader in the 1960s, leavening his music with Coleman's ideas as the decade progressed.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-48) _Kind of Blue_ has appeared on professional listings of the greatest albums. In 1994, it was ranked number one in [Colin Larkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Larkin "Colin Larkin")'s _[Top 100 Jazz Albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Time_Top_1000_Albums "All Time Top 1000 Albums")_. Larkin described it as "the greatest jazz album in the world".[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-49) In 2002, it was one of 50 recordings chosen for the very first year of induction by the [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress") to be added to the [National Recording Registry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Recording_Registry "National Recording Registry").[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-50) In selecting the album as number 12 on its 2003 list of [the 500 greatest albums of all time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone's_500_Greatest_Albums_of_All_Time "Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Albums of All Time"), maintaining the rating in a 2012 revised list,[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-51) _Rolling Stone_ magazine stated: "This painterly masterpiece is one of the most important, influential and popular albums in jazz".[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-rs500-52) The rating descended to number 31 in _Rolling Stone's_ revised list in 2020.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-53) On December 16, 2009, the [United States House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") passed a resolution honoring the 50th anniversary of _Kind of Blue_ and "reaffirming jazz as a national treasure".[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-Jarenwattananon-54) It is included in the 2005 book _[1001 Albums You Must Hear Before You Die](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1001_Albums_You_Must_Hear_Before_You_Die "1001 Albums You Must Hear Before You Die")_, described by reviewer Seth Jacobson as "a genre-defining moment in twentieth-century music, period"..[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-55) It was voted number 14 in Colin Larkin's [All Time Top 1000 Albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Time_Top_1000_Albums "All Time Top 1000 Albums") 3rd Edition (2000).[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-Larkin-56) _[The Penguin Guide to Jazz Recordings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Penguin_Guide_to_Jazz_Recordings "The Penguin Guide to Jazz Recordings")_ lists the album as part of its suggested "core collection", and also awards it a crown, indicating a recording of particular merit.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-Penguin-31) _Kind of Blue_ remains popular with listeners. Between 1991 (when [Nielsen SoundScan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nielsen_SoundScan "Nielsen SoundScan") started tracking sales) and 2016, the album sold 3.6million copies in the US.[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-57)[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-58) In 2019, the [Recording Industry Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America "Recording Industry Association of America") (RIAA) certified the album [five-times platinum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RIAA_certification "RIAA certification"), indicating five million units recorded there.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-RIAAcert-59) ### Influence \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kind_of_Blue&action=edit§ion=6 "Edit section: Influence")\] The album's influence has reached beyond jazz, as musicians of such genres as rock and classical have been influenced by it, while critics have written about it as one of the most influential albums of all time.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-60)[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-61) Many improvisatory rock musicians of the 1960s referred to _Kind of Blue_ for inspiration, along with other Davis albums, as well as Coltrane's modal records _[My Favorite Things](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_Favorite_Things_(John_Coltrane_album) "My Favorite Things (John Coltrane album)")_ (1961) and _[A Love Supreme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme "A Love Supreme")_ (1965). Guitarist [Duane Allman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duane_Allman "Duane Allman") of [the Allman Brothers Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Allman_Brothers_Band "The Allman Brothers Band") said his soloing on songs such as " [In Memory of Elizabeth Reed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_Memory_of_Elizabeth_Reed "In Memory of Elizabeth Reed")," "comes from Miles and Coltrane, and particularly _Kind of Blue_. I've listened to that album so many times that for the past couple of years, I haven't hardly listened to anything else."[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-62) [Pink Floyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pink_Floyd "Pink Floyd") keyboardist [Richard Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Wright_(musician) "Richard Wright (musician)") said that the chord progressions on the album influenced the structure of the introductory chords to the song " [Breathe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breathe_(Pink_Floyd_song) "Breathe (Pink Floyd song)")" on the album _[The Dark Side of the Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dark_Side_of_the_Moon "The Dark Side of the Moon")_ (1973).[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-pinkfloyd-63) In his book _Kind of Blue: The Making of a Miles Davis Masterpiece_, writer [Ashley Kahn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashley_Kahn "Ashley Kahn") wrote "still acknowledged as the height of hip, four decades after it was recorded, _Kind of Blue_ is the premier album of its era, jazz or otherwise. Its vapory piano introduction is universally recognized".[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-Kahn-p19-64) Producer [Quincy Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quincy_Jones "Quincy Jones"), one of Davis's longtime friends, wrote: "That \[ _Kind of Blue_\] will always be my music, man. I play _Kind of Blue_ every day—it's my orange juice. It still sounds like it was made yesterday".[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-Kahn-p19-64) Pianist [Chick Corea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chick_Corea "Chick Corea"), one of Miles's acolytes, was also struck by its majesty, later stating "It's one thing to just play a tune, or play a program of music, but it's another thing to practically create a new language of music, which is what _Kind of Blue_ did."[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-65) [Gary Burton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Burton "Gary Burton"), of [Berklee College of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berklee_College_of_Music "Berklee College of Music"), noted the consistent innovation present throughout the album, stating: "It wasn't just one tune that was a breakthrough, it was the whole record. When new jazz styles come along, the first few attempts to do it are usually kind of shaky. Early Charlie Parker records were like this. But with _Kind of Blue_ \[the sextet\] all sound like they're fully into it."[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-66) Along with _[Time Out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_Out_(album) "Time Out (album)")_ by the [Dave Brubeck Quartet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Brubeck_Quartet "Dave Brubeck Quartet") (1959) and Coltrane's _[Giant Steps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant_Steps "Giant Steps")_ (1960), _Kind of Blue_ has often been recommended by music writers as an introductory jazz album, for similar reasons: the music on both records is very melodic, and the relaxed quality of the songs makes the [improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_improvisation "Jazz improvisation") easy for listeners to follow, without sacrificing artistry or experimentation.[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-67) Upon the release of the 50th anniversary collector's edition of the album, a columnist for _[All About Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_About_Jazz "All About Jazz")_ stated " _Kind of Blue_ heralded the arrival of a revolutionary new American music, a post-bebop modal jazz structured around simple scales and melodic improvisation. Trumpeter/band leader/composer Miles Davis assembled a sextet of legendary players to create a sublime atmospheric masterpiece. Fifty years after its release, _Kind of Blue_ continues to transport listeners to a realm all its own while inspiring musicians to create to new sounds—from acoustic jazz to post-modern ambient—in every genre imaginable."[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-collectors-68) Renowned hip-hop artist and rapper [Q-Tip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Q-Tip_(musician) "Q-Tip (musician)") reaffirmed the album's reputation and influence when discussing the significance of _Kind of Blue_, stating "It's like the Bible—you just have one in your house."[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-69) The singer [Bilal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bilal_(American_singer) "Bilal (American singer)") names it among his 25 favorite albums and "an important record" for him.[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-70) The 2014 album _Blue_ by [Mostly Other People Do the Killing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mostly_Other_People_Do_the_Killing "Mostly Other People Do the Killing") is a note-for-note reproduction of _Kind of Blue_.[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-71) The _Kind of Blue_ musicians appeared together in further recorded ventures through the 1960s. Davis had made a rare post-1953 sideman appearance in 1958 on Adderley's _[Somethin' Else](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somethin'_Else_(Cannonball_Adderley_album) "Somethin' Else (Cannonball Adderley album)")_ album; Evans and Adderley collaborated on the latter's LP _[Know What I Mean?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Know_What_I_Mean%3F "Know What I Mean?")_ from 1961. Kelly and Chambers backed [Hank Mobley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hank_Mobley "Hank Mobley") on _[Soul Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_Station "Soul Station")_ in 1960, and Evans and Chambers played on the sessions for _[The Blues and the Abstract Truth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Blues_and_the_Abstract_Truth "The Blues and the Abstract Truth")_ by [Oliver Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Nelson "Oliver Nelson") in 1961. The rhythm section of Kelly, Chambers, and Cobb played on _[Cannonball Adderley Quintet in Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannonball_Adderley_Quintet_in_Chicago "Cannonball Adderley Quintet in Chicago")_, supported Benny Golson on _[Turning Point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turning_Point_(Benny_Golson_album) "Turning Point (Benny Golson album)")_ and Coltrane for _[Coltrane Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coltrane_Jazz "Coltrane Jazz")_ and one track on Coltrane's landmark _Giant Steps_, which featured Chambers throughout. That trio stayed with Davis for the recordings _[Someday My Prince Will Come](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Someday_My_Prince_Will_Come_(Miles_Davis_album) "Someday My Prince Will Come (Miles Davis album)")_[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-72) and the live sets [at the Blackhawk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_Person_Friday_and_Saturday_Nights_at_the_Blackhawk,_Complete "In Person Friday and Saturday Nights at the Blackhawk, Complete") and [at Carnegie Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis_at_Carnegie_Hall "Miles Davis at Carnegie Hall").[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-73)[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-74) ### Davis in retrospect \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kind_of_Blue&action=edit§ion=7 "Edit section: Davis in retrospect")\] Late in his life, from the electric period on, Davis repeatedly disregarded his earlier work, such as the music of _[Birth of the Cool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_of_the_Cool "Birth of the Cool")_ or _Kind of Blue_. In Davis's view, remaining static stylistically was the wrong option.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-75) > "So What" or _Kind of Blue_, they were done in that era, the right hour, the right day, and it happened. It's over .... What I used to play with Bill Evans, all those different modes, and substitute chords, we had the energy then and we liked it. But I have no feel for it anymore—it's more like warmed-over turkey. —Interview with [Ben Sidran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Sidran "Ben Sidran"), 1986.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-76) When [Shirley Horn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirley_Horn "Shirley Horn") insisted, in 1990, that Davis reconsider playing the gentle ballads and modal tunes of his _Kind of Blue_ period, he demurred: "Nah, it hurts my lip."[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-77) ## Release history \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kind_of_Blue&action=edit§ion=8 "Edit section: Release history")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/1/19/KindofBlue_JM.jpg/250px-KindofBlue_JM.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:KindofBlue_JM.jpg) 1986 _[Columbia Jazz Masterpieces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Jazz_Masterpieces "Columbia Jazz Masterpieces")_ compact disc reissue cover _Kind of Blue_ was released as a 12-inch [vinyl record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gramophone_record "Gramophone record"), in both [stereo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereophonic "Stereophonic") and mono, and was reissued multiple times. On some editions, the label switched the order for the two tracks on side two, "All Blues" and "Flamenco Sketches". The album was [remastered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remastered "Remastered") many times during the compact disc era, including in 1982 by CBS/Sony Japan catalog number 35DP 62 and the 1986 [Columbia Jazz Masterpieces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Jazz_Masterpieces "Columbia Jazz Masterpieces") reissue.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-discogs-78) The significant 1992 remaster corrected the original recording speed of side one, which had caused all prior releases to be slightly off- [pitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitch_(music) "Pitch (music)").[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-79) The 1997 reissue added the alternative take of "Flamenco Sketches".[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-discogs-78) In 2005, a [DualDisc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DualDisc "DualDisc") release included the original album, a [digital remastering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_remastering "Digital remastering") in [5.1 Surround Sound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surround_sound "Surround sound") and [LPCM Stereo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LPCM "LPCM"), and a 25-minute documentary _Made in Heaven_ about the making and influence of _Kind of Blue_.[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-80) _Kind of Blue_ was re-issued on a rare 24-carat gold CD collectors version.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-discogs-78) A two-disc CD [box set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_set "Box set") "50th Anniversary Collector's Edition" was released on September 30, 2008, by Columbia and Legacy.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-50th-81) The album was released in other [audio formats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_format "Audio format"), which are only available second hand. - [Two-track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-track "Two-track") open-reel tape (US only), Columbia GCB 60, from which "Freddie Freeloader" and "Flamenco Sketches" were omitted to reduce cost. This release was on the market less than a year and was discontinued some time after July 1961, after _Sketches of Spain_ had been released as four-track only. Sonically, it was reportedly better than the four-track counterpart that replaced it. The rumor that the two-track version was the only one to be issued at correct speed for the tracks from the first album side is false.[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-ReferenceA-82) It was not issued at the correct speed.[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-speedissues-83) - Four-track open-reel tape (US only), Columbia CQ 379, as the complete five-track album. This release replaced the two-track release and remained in the Columbia catalog for a few years. Some tracks are available on other reel tapes issued current at the time of or following the original release of the album, as by Various Artists. None issued were at the correct speed.[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-speedissues-83) "All Blues" is included on the _Greatest Hits_ album.[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-ReferenceA-82) - [Armed Forces Radio and Television Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armed_Forces_Radio_and_Television_Service "Armed Forces Radio and Television Service") 16-inch transcription discs. These are monaural and the track on side P-6925 marked "Flamenco Sketches" actually holds "All Blues". None issued were at the correct speed.[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-speedissues-83) - Philips [Compact Cassette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_Cassette "Compact Cassette") versions of the original album prior to the Jazz Masterpiece remaster, and of the 1987 Jazz Masterpiece remaster. Neither are at the correct speed.[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue#cite_note-speedissues-83) - [MiniDisc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MiniDisc "MiniDisc"), Columbia CM 40579 (US) from a master prior to 1997, but not the Jazz Masterpiece remaster. It was unavailable by the end of the 1990s when production of Jazz Masterpiece series had ceased. **Soul Jazz Records** is a British record label based in London.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_Jazz_Records#cite_note-about-1) Outside of releasing records, the label also publishes books, occasionally films and performs as a DJ set.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_Jazz_Records#cite_note-about-1) The music releases labels from a variety of genres, including [reggae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggae "Reggae"), [house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_music "House music"), [hip hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip_hop_music "Hip hop music"), [punk rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punk_rock "Punk rock"), [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk"), [bossa nova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bossa_nova "Bossa nova") and [soul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_music "Soul music").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_Jazz_Records#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMagni2012-2)

## History

\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Soul_Jazz_Records&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")\]

Soul Jazz Records was founded by Stuart Baker in 1991.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_Jazz_Records#cite_note-FOOTNOTELees2005-3)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_Jazz_Records#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilder2001-4)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_Jazz_Records#cite_note-souljazz1299-5) Baker purchased his first record at the age of 10 and prior to starting the label, had his roots selling records at a secondhand record vinyl stall in the [Camden Market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camden_Market "Camden Market") in the late 1980s.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_Jazz_Records#cite_note-FOOTNOTELees2005-3)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_Jazz_Records#cite_note-sohoradio-6)

The label initially worked doing straight reissues of old albums before releasing _[Nu Yorica!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nu_Yorica! "Nu Yorica!")_, a double album of classic [salsa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salsa_music "Salsa music") and [Latin funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_funk "Latin funk") from the 1970s.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_Jazz_Records#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilder2001-4) Peter Reilly spoke on the labels behalf that _Nu Yorica_ was their first "really successful record" form Soul Jazz noting that "it was more of a kind of cult thing up until then. It opened it up to a lot of people." and that the album sold specifically well in New York.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_Jazz_Records#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilder2001-4)

The reggae releases were praised by important people of the genre, such as [Chris Blackwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Blackwell "Chris Blackwell") of [Island records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Island_records "Island records") who called the _It's Dynamite!_ compilations as the "university of reggae."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_Jazz_Records#cite_note-FOOTNOTELees2005-3) [Radio 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Radio_1 "BBC Radio 1")'s [Gilles Peterson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilles_Peterson "Gilles Peterson") commented that "Soul Jazz put out the best compilations. They've consistently done it, from the Studio One stuff to the free jazz stuff to the acid house compilations. As a reissue label, they're the best."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_Jazz_Records#cite_note-FOOTNOTELees2005-3) [Grant Marshall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grant_Marshall "Grant Marshall") of [Massive Attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massive_Attack "Massive Attack") stated that one thing he wanted to do when entering the music business was to release [Studio One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio_One_(record_label) "Studio One (record label)") records in England and tried to deal with the [Coxsone Dodd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coxsone_Dodd "Coxsone Dodd") of [Studio One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio_One_(record_label) "Studio One (record label)").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_Jazz_Records#cite_note-FOOTNOTELees2005-3) Baker managed to talk to Dodd to let him have access to their archives after Dodd had put out rare jazz compilations.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_Jazz_Records#cite_note-FOOTNOTELees2005-3) Dodd died in 2004 leading to the labels relationship to continue via his daughter Carol and his wife Norma Dodd, who died in 2010.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_Jazz_Records#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMagni2012-2) These deaths briefly led to breaks in releasing Studio One related material.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_Jazz_Records#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMagni2012-2)

The booklets of Soul Jazz Records album are often written by Baker himself, with Baker explaining that he likes to describe the relationships between music and society, the connections between genres, and the history of the music industry.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_Jazz_Records#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavet2011-7)

Soul Jazz has released album through sublabels. These include Universal Sound, which was described by the Soul Jazz website as both a sister label and a subsidiary label.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_Jazz_Records#cite_note-souljazz1299-5)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_Jazz_Records#cite_note-discoSJMar2000-8) Soul Jazz described Universal Sound as containing "releases that are slightly more specialist. Mainly artist releases rather than compilations they often follow on from an earlier Soul Jazz Release. Many of these releases come with extensive sleeve notes and original photos."[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_Jazz_Records#cite_note-discoSJMar2000-8) Another was Satellite Records, which was a label home to bands such as [Add N to X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Add_N_to_X "Add N to X"), [Sand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sand_(band) "Sand (band)"), Bell, and Yossarian.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_Jazz_Records#cite_note-satellite0201-9)

[Randy Cain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Cain "Randy Cain") | **The Delfonics** were an American [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues")/ [soul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_music "Soul music") vocal group from [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia"). The Delfonics were most popular in the late 1960s and early 1970s. Their most notable hits include " [La-La (Means I Love You)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La-La_(Means_I_Love_You) "La-La (Means I Love You)")", " [Didn't I (Blow Your Mind This Time)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Didn't_I_(Blow_Your_Mind_This_Time) "Didn't I (Blow Your Mind This Time)")", "Break Your Promise", " [I'm Sorry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I'm_Sorry_(Delfonics_song) "I'm Sorry (Delfonics song)")", and " [Ready or Not Here I Come (Can't Hide from Love)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ready_or_Not_Here_I_Come_(Can't_Hide_from_Love) "Ready or Not Here I Come (Can't Hide from Love)")".[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-1) Their hit songs were primarily written by lead vocalist and founding member William "Poogie" Hart, and [arranger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrangement "Arrangement") and [producer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Record_producer "Record producer") [Thom Bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thom_Bell "Thom Bell"). [Wilbert Hart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilbert_Hart "Wilbert Hart") is the last surviving founding member. Their songs have been used in film soundtracks, including [Quentin Tarantino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quentin_Tarantino "Quentin Tarantino")'s 1997 movie _[Jackie Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Brown_(soundtrack) "Jackie Brown (soundtrack)")_, in which "La-La (Means I Love You)" and "Didn't I (Blow Your Mind This Time)" underscore the pivotal relationship between the characters played by [Pam Grier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pam_Grier "Pam Grier") and [Robert Forster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Forster "Robert Forster"). Their songs "Ready or Not Here I Come (Can't Hide from Love)" and "Funny Feeling" were used in the video game _[Grand Theft Auto V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Theft_Auto_V "Grand Theft Auto V")_ on the fictional radio station The Lowdown 91.1. ## Career \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Delfonics&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Career")\] ### Early days \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Delfonics&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Early days")\] Prior to forming the Delfonics, William "Poogie" Hart sang in a variety of groups including Little Hart and The Everglows, [the Veltones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Vel-Tones "The Vel-Tones"), the Four Guys, and the Four Gents. Members of some of these early groups included brothers William and [Wilbert Hart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilbert_Hart "Wilbert Hart"), Ritchie Daniels, [Randy Cain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Cain "Randy Cain"), and Jimmy Wroten, [Stan Lathan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Lathan "Stan Lathan"), and Donald Cannon, friends who met at [Overbrook High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overbrook_High_School_(Philadelphia) "Overbrook High School (Philadelphia)") in the 1960s.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-2) Circa 1964, William "Poogie" Hart and his brother, Wilbert Hart, formed a group called The Orphonics, consisting of themselves plus Randy Cain and Richie Daniels. After Daniels joined the armed services, they used Ricky Johnson. Randy Cain later rejoined, and the original trio of [William Hart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Hart_(singer) "William Hart (singer)"), [Wilbert Hart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilbert_Hart "Wilbert Hart"), and [Randy Cain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Cain "Randy Cain") became The Orphonics. The name came from a stereophonic machine the Harts had in their basement. In 1965, William Hart was working in a barbershop in Philadelphia. A man named Stan Watson came into the barbershop one day, where Hart, who had written quite a few songs by this point, would sing while playing his guitar. Watson told Hart that he knew a young arranger/producer for [Cameo-Parkway Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cameo-Parkway_Records "Cameo-Parkway Records") named [Thom Bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thom_Bell "Thom Bell"), who was at the time working with [Chubby Checker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chubby_Checker "Chubby Checker"). Watson thereafter introduced the group to Bell. Hart recalls that the first song he presented to Bell was an original composition of his entitled "He Don't Really Love You".[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-3) Bell immediately produced the music arrangement to that song and it was released on Moon Shot, which later became Cameo-Parkway Records. ### Hit years \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Delfonics&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Hit years")\] The Orphonics were soon renamed "The Delfonics," and their first recording, "He Don't Really Love You" b/w "Without You", which had been arranged and produced by Thom Bell, was released on the small Moon Shot Records label in around August 1966. (The artist on first pressings of the 45 RPM record was actually listed as "The Del Fonics" and Thom Bell was credited as "Tommy Bell." Following the increased popularity of the group, the Moon Shot record was reissued in April 1968, and on this later release it was distributed by Calla Records.) The second Delfonics' recording, "You've Been Untrue" b/w "I Was There," once again arranged/produced by Bell (now credited as "Thom Bell") was released in April 1967 on Cameo Records. [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/3/3c/Delfonics_1970%27s_early_70%27s.JPG/250px-Delfonics_1970%27s_early_70%27s.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Delfonics_1970's_early_70's.JPG) The Delfonics promo photo, 1971 By the end of 1967, Cameo-Parkway Records announced that it would soon no longer exist as a record company. In December of that year, Thom Bell took the Delfonics into Cameo-Parkway's recording studio to record a William Hart composition, entitled " [La-La (Means I Love You)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La-La_(Means_I_Love_You) "La-La (Means I Love You)")", which featured Hart on falsetto lead.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-LarkinSM-4) With Cameo-Parkway about to be defunct, Stan Watson started up his own label entitled [Philly Groove Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philly_Groove_Records "Philly Groove Records") and, in December 1967, "La-La (Means I Love You)" was first released to the local Philadelphia music market.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-LarkinSM-4) After gaining national distribution/promotion with New York's Amy-Mala-Bell, the single became a hit in 1968, selling over one million copies. It reached No. 4 on the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100"),[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-chart-history-5) and was awarded a [gold disc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_recording_sales_certification "Music recording sales certification"). The group's debut album _[La La Means I Love You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_La_Means_I_Love_You_(album) "La La Means I Love You (album)")_, released on Philly Groove Records in 1968,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-LarkinSM-4) featured the hit original compositions "La-La (Means I Love You)", "Break Your Promise", "I'm Sorry", and "Can You Remember"; along with covers of the [Hal David](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hal_David "Hal David")/ [Burt Bacharach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burt_Bacharach "Burt Bacharach") compositions " [Alfie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfie_(Burt_Bacharach_song) "Alfie (Burt Bacharach song)")" and " [The Look of Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Look_of_Love_(1967_song) "The Look of Love (1967 song)")". Four more Bell-produced albums appeared in the next few years: _[The Sound of Sexy Soul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sound_of_Sexy_Soul "The Sound of Sexy Soul")_, _The Delfonics Super Hits_, _[The Delfonics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics_(album) "The Delfonics (album)")_ and _[Tell Me This Is a Dream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tell_Me_This_Is_a_Dream "Tell Me This Is a Dream")_.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-LarkinSM-4) Among the Delfonics' popular hits were the [Grammy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award "Grammy Award")–winning "Didn't I (Blow Your Mind This Time)", "(For The Love) I Gave To You", "Ready or Not Here I Come (Can't Hide from Love)", and "Hey! Love", written by Wilbert Hart.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-6)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-LarkinSM-4) The Delfonics and Bell had to work with a basic budget on the first creation as Thom explained "When I took them into the studio we didn't have any money to pay for string players and an orchestra so I played most of the instruments myself!"—a far cry from the full classical productions from 1968 to the beginning of the 1970s.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-7) "Didn't I (Blow Your Mind This Time)" also sold a million copies and by March 1970 received a gold disc from the [R.I.A.A.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R.I.A.A. "R.I.A.A.") By 1972, the Delfonics racked up twelve top-20 hits on _Billboard_'s R&B/Soul Single Chart.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-8) Randy Cain left the group in 1971 after completing their fourth album,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-LarkinSM-4) and in 1973 had a hand in forming [Blue Magic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Magic_(band) "Blue Magic (band)"). Cain was replaced by [Major Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_Harris_(singer) "Major Harris (singer)"); by then, however, Thom Bell had moved on to produce [The Stylistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Stylistics "The Stylistics") and later, [The Spinners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spinners_(American_group) "The Spinners (American group)").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-LarkinSM-4) The Delfonics swiftly produced another album, _[Alive & Kicking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alive_&_Kicking_(Delfonics_album) "Alive & Kicking (Delfonics album)")_ (1974), produced by Stan Watson.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-LarkinSM-4) However, in the absence of Bell, the Delfonics' career declined sharply, and with the exception of the aforementioned "Hey Love" and the minor hits "When You Get Right Down to It", "I Don't Want to Make You Wait" and "I Told You So", success eluded them after 1975.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-LarkinSM-4) ("(For the Love) I Gave to You", although popular, was never released as a [single](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_(music) "Single (music)").) Most of their songs at this point were written by lead singer William Hart. ### 1974–1980s \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Delfonics&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: 1974–1980s")\] Late 1974, Major Harris started his solo career by signing with [Atlantic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Records "Atlantic Records"),[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-LarkinSM-4) and releasing his 1975 No. 1 R&B hit single, " [Love Won't Let Me Wait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love_Won't_Let_Me_Wait "Love Won't Let Me Wait")",[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-9) which peaked at No. 5 on the US [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100") [chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Record_chart "Record chart")[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-10) and was awarded a [gold disc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_recording_sales_certification "Music recording sales certification") by the [R.I.A.A.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R.I.A.A. "R.I.A.A.") on June 25, 1975. The group split around 1975; one group featured Major Harris and Wilbert Hart, with new member Frank Washington, formerly of the Futures. The other group featured William Hart with new members. Line-ups would become confusing as members shifted between groups and multiple groups toured.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-11) Harris moved to William's group around 1980, with their third member being the returning Randy Cain. Washington also switched from Wilbert Hart's group, joining in 1985. While the main recording line-up of the group was William Hart, Harris, and Washington, they would tour as two separate trios with additional members added. One group featured William Hart, Randy Cain, and Garfield Fleming, and the other consisted of Washington, Harris, and Freddy Ingleton. William Hart also toured with another line-up consisting of himself, Johnny ("JJ") Johnson and Pat Palmer,[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-12) and toured in Japan at least one time with Ingleton and Dr. Salaam Love.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-13) In 1989, Wilbert Hart, Harris, and Washington appeared on _[The Arsenio Hall Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arsenio_Hall_Show "The Arsenio Hall Show")_.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] ### 1990–2000 \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Delfonics&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: 1990–2000")\] Through the 1990s, the Delfonics groups continued to perform. The William Hart's with Major Harris and Frank Washington made several recordings, including backing vocals on the track "After the Smoke is Clear", on the 1996 hip hop album, _[Ironman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ironman_(Ghostface_Killah_album) "Ironman (Ghostface Killah album)")_ by [Ghostface Killah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghostface_Killah "Ghostface Killah").[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-14) The groups reorganized again in the 1990s. William Hart began touring with Johnnie Johnson and Garfield Fleming; this group recorded as the Delfonics. Major Harris toured with Frank Washington and Pat Palmer. Wilbert Hart's group included Salaam Love (formerly in William's group) and Eban Brown who formerly performed with [Ray, Goodman & Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray,_Goodman_&_Brown "Ray, Goodman & Brown") and a short stay with [the Manhattans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Manhattans "The Manhattans") as lead tenor. Brown was lead tenor with Wilbert Hart's group for five years, from 1993 until his departure to take a two-year break from the industry in 1998. Brown and Love were replaced by first tenor Van Fields and New York native Greg Hill around 1999. After a short stay with Wilbert Hart's group, Fields left and joined [the Stylistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Stylistics "The Stylistics") in 2000 and Hill left in 2005 and was replaced by Dr. Salaam Love. William Hart's group with Johnson and Fleming were featured in concert on the DVDs _The Big Show_ and _'70s Soul Jam_, whereas Hart's group is featured on the DVD _Old School Soul Party Live!_, which was part of the PBS My Music series. Harris is also featured on the re-released DVD _Blue Magic/Margie Joseph/Major Harris Live!_, which was recorded in 1975. Hart released a CD in 2005 entitled _Fonic Zone_,[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-15) which he wrote and produced. [Rick Ross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Ross "Rick Ross") was featured on the single entitled "Here For U". ### 2005–present \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Delfonics&action=edit§ion=6 "Edit section: 2005–present")\] William "Poogie" Hart continued touring with his group, Johnson and Fleming while Wilbert Hart continued touring with his group, Branch and Salaam. Randy Cain reunited with the brothers at the Rhythm and Blues Foundation Awards in Philadelphia to perform for the first time together in years, and were honored with the Pioneer Award.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-16) Soon after, Cain joined William Hart on his tour and stayed with that unit until his death in 2009. William Hart, along with [Russell Thompkins Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Thompkins_Jr. "Russell Thompkins Jr."), the original lead singer of [the Stylistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Stylistics "The Stylistics") and Ted Mills the original lead singer of [Blue Magic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Magic_(band) "Blue Magic (band)") came together to record a CD entitled, _The Three Tenors of Soul_,[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-17) which was produced by songwriter and producer, [Bobby Eli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Eli "Bobby Eli") and released in 2007. Randy Cain died on April 9, 2009, at age 63.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-18) Major Harris died on November 9, 2012, at age 65.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-19) In 2015, Wilbert Hart's group performed on the Soul Train Cruise.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-20) In 2020, William Hart and Wilbert Hart celebrated their 55th anniversary in the music industry. Lead singer William "Poogie" Hart died on July 14, 2022, at age 77.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-soultracks-21) Upon the death of William "Poogie" Hart, Johnnie Johnson and Garfield Fleming returned to the group (now named "William Hart's Delfonics") joined by Michael Muse, who replaced Eban Brown as lead singer for the Stylistics for a short period of time. On April 24, 2023, The Delfonics were inducted into The National R&B Music Society Atlantic City Walk of Fame.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-22)[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-23) Wilbert Hart is the only surviving original member of the Delfonics still performing as of 2025. His group performed for a second time on the Soul Train Cruise in January 2025.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-24) ## Legacy \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Delfonics&action=edit§ion=7 "Edit section: Legacy")\] The Delfonics songs are covered and sampled by multiple artists and they are used in TV shows and in films. In 1997, the song was sampled by [Missy Elliott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missy_Elliott "Missy Elliott") for her song " [Sock It 2 Me](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sock_It_2_Me "Sock It 2 Me")" featuring [Da Brat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Da_Brat "Da Brat"). - In 2000, the song was sampled on "Who Run It" by [Three 6 Mafia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_6_Mafia "Three 6 Mafia") on their album _[When the Smoke Clears: Sixty 6, Sixty 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/When_the_Smoke_Clears:_Sixty_6,_Sixty_1 "When the Smoke Clears: Sixty 6, Sixty 1")_. - In 2008, the song was sampled by [Bliss n Eso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bliss_n_Eso "Bliss n Eso") in their song " [The Sea is Rising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sea_is_Rising "The Sea is Rising")". - In 2012, [Bridgit Mendler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridgit_Mendler "Bridgit Mendler") interpolated the chorus of the song on her single " [Ready Or Not](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ready_or_Not_(Bridgit_Mendler_song) "Ready or Not (Bridgit Mendler song)")". - In 2014, the song was sampled by [Lil' Kim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lil'_Kim "Lil' Kim") in the chorus of her song "Whenever You See Me" from her mixtape, _Hardcore 2K14_. - In 2016, the song was covered by [Laura Mvula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laura_Mvula "Laura Mvula"). " **Hey Love**" - The Notorious B.I.G. incorporated a reconstructed version of "Hey Love" for his song, "Playa Hater" from his 1997 album _[Life After Death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_After_Death_(album) "Life After Death (album)")_. [Grammy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award "Grammy Award") – William Hart, Wilbert Hart and Randy Cain won a Grammy Award for best R&B performance for their song, " [Didn't I (Blow Your Mind This Time)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Didn't_I_(Blow_Your_Mind_This_Time) "Didn't I (Blow Your Mind This Time)")",[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-29) at the [13th Annual Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/13th_Annual_Grammy_Awards "13th Annual Grammy Awards"). - [RIAA Gold Record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RIAA_certification "RIAA certification") – On March 18, 1970, the Delfonics were awarded a Gold Record for sales of one million units.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-30) - Philadelphia Music Alliance Walk of Fame – In 1995, William Hart, Wilbert Hart, Randy Cain, and Major Harris were inducted as the Delfonics into the Philadelphia Music Alliance Walk of Fame.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-31) - [The Rhythm and Blues Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rhythm_and_Blues_Foundation "The Rhythm and Blues Foundation") – In 2006, William Hart, Wilbert Hart, and Randy Cain received the Rhythm and Blues Pioneer Award.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-32) - The National Rhythm and Blues Music Society – In 2013, William & Wil Hart were honored with, Lifetime Achievement Awards and Major Harris and Randy Cain received Posthumous Awards at [Resorts Casino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resorts_Casino_Hotel "Resorts Casino Hotel") in Atlantic City, New Jersey.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-33)[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delfonics#cite_note-34) - - [John Mayall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Mayall "John Mayall") | Musical artist **Richard Allen**" **Blue**" **Mitchell** (March 13, 1930 – May 21, 1979)[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mitchell#cite_note-LarkinJazz-1) was an American [trumpeter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trumpet "Trumpet") and [composer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composer "Composer") who worked in [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), [rhythm and blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues"), [soul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_music "Soul music"), [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music"), and [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk"). He recorded albums as leader and sideman for [Riverside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riverside_Records "Riverside Records"), [Mainstream Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainstream_Records "Mainstream Records"), and [Blue Note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mitchell#cite_note-ALLMUSIC-2) He is also credited as the most recorded trumpeter with jazz [organ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hammond_organ "Hammond organ"), accumulating 27 sideman recordings in the genre.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mitchell#cite_note-3) ## Early life Mitchell was born and raised in [Miami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami "Miami"), Florida, United States.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mitchell#cite_note-ALLMUSIC-2) He began playing the trumpet in high school, aged 17,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mitchell#cite_note-:1-4) with the nickname "Blue".[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mitchell#cite_note-ALLMUSIC-2) His early influences included [Dizzy Gillespie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie "Dizzy Gillespie"), [Fatts Navarro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fats_Navarro "Fats Navarro"), [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis"), [Kenny Dorham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Dorham "Kenny Dorham"), and [Clifford Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_Brown "Clifford Brown").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mitchell#cite_note-:2-5) ## Career After high school, Blue Mitchell began playing with local musicians in Miami.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mitchell#cite_note-:2-5) By [Sam Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Jones_(musician) "Sam Jones (musician)")'s telegram request, Mitchell joined the touring [Paul Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Williams_(saxophonist) "Paul Williams (saxophonist)") Orchestra in [Detroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit "Detroit").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mitchell#cite_note-:2-5) He later called this his first tour with a professional band.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mitchell#cite_note-:2-5) While on tour in 1952, Mitchell passed through New York, where he made his first recordings.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mitchell#cite_note-:2-5) These were later released on the compilation album _[Quartet/Quintet/Sextet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quartet/Quintet/Sextet "Quartet/Quintet/Sextet")_ by [Lou Donaldson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou_Donaldson "Lou Donaldson").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mitchell#cite_note-:2-5) Mitchell remained in New York following the conclusion of the tour and was hired to join [Earl Bostic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_Bostic "Earl Bostic")'s touring band from 1952 to 1955.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mitchell#cite_note-:2-5)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mitchell#cite_note-ALLMUSIC-2)[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mitchell#cite_note-LarkinJazz-1) Following his stint with Earl Bostic, in 1955, Blue Mitchell returned to Miami and was heard by saxophonist [Cannonball Adderley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannonball_Adderley "Cannonball Adderley"), a fellow Floridian.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mitchell#cite_note-ALLMUSIC-2)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mitchell#cite_note-:2-5) Adderley recommended Mitchell to [Riverside Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riverside_Records "Riverside Records")' producer, [Orrin Keepnews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orrin_Keepnews "Orrin Keepnews"), who flew to Miami to hear Mitchell perform.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mitchell#cite_note-:1-4)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mitchell#cite_note-6) Keepnews, impressed, signed Mitchell to record a string of his own albums for Riverside.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mitchell#cite_note-:0-7) Mitchell joined the [Horace Silver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Silver "Horace Silver") Quintet in 1958,[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mitchell#cite_note-ALLMUSIC-2) playing with tenor saxophonist [Junior Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junior_Cook "Junior Cook"), bassist [Gene Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_Taylor_(bassist) "Gene Taylor (bassist)"), and drummer [Louis Hayes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Hayes "Louis Hayes"), who was later replaced by [Roy Brooks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Brooks "Roy Brooks"). Mitchell stayed with Silver's group until the band's break-up in 1964, after which Mitchell formed a group with members from the Silver quintet, substituting the young pianist [Chick Corea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chick_Corea "Chick Corea") for Silver and replacing Brooks with drummer [Al Foster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Foster "Al Foster").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mitchell#cite_note-ALLMUSIC-2) This group produced a number of records for [Blue Note Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records") with some variation in personnel, disbanding in 1969.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mitchell#cite_note-ALLMUSIC-2)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mitchell#cite_note-:0-7) Mitchell then toured with [Ray Charles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Charles "Ray Charles") until 1971.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mitchell#cite_note-ALLMUSIC-2) From 1971 to 1973, Mitchell performed with [John Mayall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Mayall "John Mayall"), appearing on _[Jazz Blues Fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Blues_Fusion "Jazz Blues Fusion")_ and subsequent albums.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mitchell#cite_note-ALLMUSIC-2) In 1974, he moved to Los Angeles, California.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mitchell#cite_note-:0-7) During this period, he recorded and worked as a studio musician in the genres [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues"), [soul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_music "Soul music"), [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music"), and [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk"), and performed with the [big band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_band "Big band") leaders [Louie Bellson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louie_Bellson "Louie Bellson"), [Bill Holman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Holman_(musician) "Bill Holman (musician)"), and [Bill Berry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Berry_(trumpeter) "Bill Berry (trumpeter)"), and was the principal soloist for [Tony Bennett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett "Tony Bennett") and [Lena Horne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lena_Horne "Lena Horne").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mitchell#cite_note-ALLMUSIC-2) ## Death Mitchell co-led a quintet with saxophonist [Harold Land](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Land "Harold Land"), while in California, until his death from cancer on May 21, 1979, aged 49.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mitchell#cite_note-8)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mitchell#cite_note-:0-7) ## Discography ### As leader/co-leader | Recording date | Title |
