in Los Angeles, he studied [music theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_theory "Music theory") and harmony and developed an idiosyncratic take on [country blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_blues "Country blues") and [folk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music "Folk music") forms.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shape_of_Jazz_to_Come#cite_note-pbs-grove-11) Coleman's big break came in Los Angeles when he caught the attention of bassist [Percy Heath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percy_Heath "Percy Heath") and pianist [John Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lewis_(pianist) "John Lewis (pianist)") of the [Modern Jazz Quartet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_Jazz_Quartet "Modern Jazz Quartet"). Lewis encouraged Coleman and his trumpeter, Don Cherry, to attend the [Lenox School of Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenox_School_of_Jazz "Lenox School of Jazz") summer program in Massachusetts in 1959, at which Lewis was the director. Lewis also secured Coleman a deal with Atlantic Records, which paid his tuition at the Lenox School.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shape_of_Jazz_to_Come#cite_note-Kaplan,_Fred_M._2009-4)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shape_of_Jazz_to_Come#cite_note-pbs-grove-11)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shape_of_Jazz_to_Come#cite_note-Johnson,_Martin_2009-13) Though both Coleman and Cherry were already rather accomplished by this point in their careers, Lewis wanted to use their attendance at Lenox to generate buzz amongst jazz circles. Their presence at the school was not without friction amongst students and faculty alike, but in the end, their attending the school accomplished what Lewis hoped to achieve. Coleman was subsequently booked by Lewis to play at the 1959 Monterey Jazz Festival in California.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shape_of_Jazz_to_Come#cite_note-14) In June 1959, Coleman suggested to Atlantic jazz producer [Nesuhi Ertegun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nesuhi_Ertegun "Nesuhi Ertegun") that he was considering abandoning music in order to study religion. Ertegun, confident of Coleman's potential, urged him to reconsider.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shape_of_Jazz_to_Come#cite_note-Kaplan,_Fred_M._2009-4) ## Content Coleman's quartet, like [Gerry Mulligan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerry_Mulligan "Gerry Mulligan")'s, was unusual in that it did not employ a chordal instrument such as a piano or guitar. Each composition contains a brief thematic statement, then several minutes of free improvisation, followed by a repetition of the main theme. While this resembles the conventional head-solo-head structure of [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop"), it abandons the use of chord structures. _The Shape of Jazz to Come_ found Coleman and his quartet elaborating on the sound and themes he had been developing throughout his career. One prominent feature of Coleman's signature sound was that he played a plastic [Grafton saxophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grafton_saxophone "Grafton saxophone"), which contributed to the harshness of his timbre. He coined the term " [harmolodic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmolodics "Harmolodics")", a combination of harmony, movement, and melody, to describe his philosophy of improvisation which heavily emphasized melody rather than harmony. It was early in his career, in an attempt to further emphasize focus on melody over harmony, that he stopped including a piano as a part of his ensembles. Coleman continues with this tradition on _The Shape of Jazz to Come_, dispensing with harmonic accompaniment and focusing solely on improvised melodies and variations on themes and motifs. His use of microtonal intervals was central to his sound, and he even went as far as to suggest that the same pitch should sound different when played in different contexts, stating that "jazz is the only music in which the same note can be played night after night, but differently each time".[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shape_of_Jazz_to_Come#cite_note-15) The album was a breakthrough and helped to establish the [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") movement. Later [avant-garde jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz") was often very different from Coleman's work, but the work helped to lay the foundation upon which much subsequent avant-garde and free jazz would be built. ### "Lonely Woman" The album contains one of the few Coleman compositions to achieve [jazz standard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_standard "Jazz standard") status, " [Lonely Woman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lonely_Woman_(composition) "Lonely Woman (composition)")". Coleman was moved to compose the song when, while on a lunch break from his job in a department store stock room in Los Angeles in the early 1950s, he came across a photograph of a woman in a gallery. Coleman describes the photograph as follows: > In the background there was everything you could imagine that was wealthy – all in her background – but she was so sad. And I said, 'Oh my goodness. I understand this feeling. I have not experienced this wealth, but I understand the feeling.' I went home and wrote 'Lonely Woman'... I related the condition to myself, wrote this song, and ever since it has grown and grown and grown.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shape_of_Jazz_to_Come#cite_note-16) Fred Kaplan wrote: > 'Lonely Woman' begins with Haden playing a slow bass dirge. Higgins follows with a fast drum riff (a pairing of slow bass and fast drums was unusual enough). Then Coleman and Cherry, in unison, blow a sorrowful melody, both of them bending notes, wailing, so naked with emotion that it still raises shivers a half century later. After reciting the theme a couple times, Coleman takes his solo, which wanders off in a different direction; if you were expecting to hear an improvisation on harmony, it might seem like a different song. But he's improvising on other aspects of the song, especially its emotion. The other players do the same. Somehow it all hangs together, and toward the end, they come back to the theme, come back down to Earth, with aplomb.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shape_of_Jazz_to_Come#cite_note-Kaplan,_Fred_M._2009-4) ## Reception and legacy | Review scores | | --- | | Source | Rating | | The [recording session](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_session "Recording session") took place on December 21, 1960, at A&R Studios in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"). The sole outtake from the album session, "First Take," was later released on the 1971 compilation _[Twins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twins_(Ornette_Coleman_album) "Twins (Ornette Coleman album)")_ and subsequent CD reissues of _Free Jazz_. ## Music \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Free_Jazz:_A_Collective_Improvisation&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Music")\] The album presents a continuous free improvisation with only a few brief pre-determined sections, recorded in one take with no overdubbing or editing.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Jazz:_A_Collective_Improvisation#cite_note-6) It features what Coleman called a "double quartet," i.e., two self-contained jazz quartets: each with a reed instrument, trumpet, bass, and drums.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Jazz:_A_Collective_Improvisation#cite_note-7) The two quartets are heard in separate channels, with Coleman's working quartet at the time (as featured on _[Ornette!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette! "Ornette!")_) in the left channel, and the second quartet, including the former Coleman rhythm section of [Charlie Haden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Haden "Charlie Haden") and [Ed Blackwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Blackwell "Ed Blackwell"), on the right.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Jazz:_A_Collective_Improvisation#cite_note-rhino-8) The two quartets play simultaneously, with the two rhythm sections providing a dense rhythmic foundation over which the wind players either solo or provide freeform commentaries, interspersed with pre-composed passages. The composed thematic material can be considered a series of brief, [dissonant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consonance_and_dissonance "Consonance and dissonance") [fanfares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fanfare "Fanfare") for the horns which serve as interludes between solos. _Free Jazz_ was the first album-length improvisation at thirty-seven minutes, unheard of at the time. The original LP package incorporated [Jackson Pollock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_Pollock "Jackson Pollock")'s 1954 painting _The White Light_.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Jazz:_A_Collective_Improvisation#cite_note-9) The cover was a gatefold with a cutout window in the lower right corner allowing a glimpse of the painting; opening the cover revealed the full artwork, along with liner notes by critic [Martin Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Williams_(writer) "Martin Williams (writer)"). Coleman was a fan of Pollock's work and a painter himself; the cover of his 1966 album _[The Empty Foxhole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Empty_Foxhole "The Empty Foxhole")_ would feature his own artwork.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Jazz:_A_Collective_Improvisation#cite_note-10)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Jazz:_A_Collective_Improvisation#cite_note-11) ## Reception \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Free_Jazz:_A_Collective_Improvisation&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Reception")\] In the January 18, 1962 issue of _[Down Beat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Down_Beat "Down Beat")_ magazine, in a special review titled "Double View of a Double Quartet," [Pete Welding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Welding "Pete Welding") awarded the album five stars while John A. Tynan rated it "no stars".[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Jazz:_A_Collective_Improvisation#cite_note-rhino-8)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Jazz:_A_Collective_Improvisation#cite_note-12) [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") critic Steve Huey described it in his five-star retrospective review as "a staggering achievement" which "practically defies superlatives in its historical importance."[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Jazz:_A_Collective_Improvisation#cite_note-13) It served as the blueprint for later large-ensemble free jazz recordings such as _[Ascension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album) "Ascension (John Coltrane album)")_ by [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane") and _[Machine Gun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine_Gun_(Peter_Br%C3%B6tzmann_album) "Machine Gun (Peter Brötzmann album)")_ by [Peter Brötzmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Br%C3%B6tzmann "Peter Brötzmann"). On March 3, 1998, _Free Jazz_ was reissued on [compact disc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_disc "Compact disc") by [Rhino Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhino_Records "Rhino Records") as part of its "Atlantic 50" series marking Atlantic Records' fiftieth anniversary. The title track, split into two sections for each side of the LP, appeared here in continuous uninterrupted form, along with the previously issued "First Take". ## Track listing \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Free_Jazz:_A_Collective_Improvisation&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Track listing")\] ### Original LP \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Free_Jazz:_A_Collective_Improvisation&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: Original LP")\] All tracks are written by Ornette Coleman. | No. | Title | Length | | --- | --- | --- | | 1. | "Free Jazz (Part One)" | 19:55 | | Total length: | 19:55 | Side one | No. | Title | Length | | --- | --- | --- | | 1. | "Free Jazz (Part Two)" | 16:28 | | Total length: | 16:28 36:23 | Side two ### 1998 CD reissue \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Free_Jazz:_A_Collective_Improvisation&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: 1998 CD reissue")\] All tracks are written by Ornette Coleman. | No. | Title | Length | | --- | --- | --- | | 1. | "Free Jazz" | 37:03 | | 2. | "First Take" | 17:06 | | Total length: | 54:09 | ### Timing of the various sections \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Free_Jazz:_A_Collective_Improvisation&action=edit§ion=6 "Edit section: Timing of the various sections")\] | | | | --- | --- | | ![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/b/b4/Ambox_important.svg/40px-Ambox_important.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail) | This section **may contain [original research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:No_original_research "Wikipedia:No original research")**. | Professional ratings _**Unit Structures**_ is a studio album by the American jazz pianist [Cecil Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor "Cecil Taylor"), released in October 1966 by [Blue Note Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records"). ## Background _Unit Structures_ was Taylor's first album on Blue Note; he would record _[Conquistador!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquistador! "Conquistador!")_ for the label later the same year with a similar lineup, although it was not released until 1968.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_Structures#cite_note-6) The album was accompanied by an essay written by Taylor entitled "Sound Structure of Subculture Becoming Major Breath/Naked Fire Gesture".[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_Structures#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBartlett1995276-7) ## Music Jesse Jarnow of _[Pitchfork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitchfork_(website) "Pitchfork (website)")_ described _Unit Structures_ as "among the most intense of the early [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") albums".[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_Structures#cite_note-Pitchfork-8) He continued: "The album is by no means [easy listening](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Easy_listening "Easy listening"); the [atonality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atonality "Atonality") is unrepentant. But Taylor’s septet finds numerous gorgeous spaces as they interpret “free jazz” not just as the freedom to [improvise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_improvisation "Jazz improvisation") but the freedom to invent musical worlds and hidden [syntaxes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syntax "Syntax"). The only way to tap into the 'rhythm-sound energy found in the [amplitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amplitude "Amplitude") of each time unit,' as Taylor wrote in the liner notes, is to listen reverently."[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_Structures#cite_note-:0-9) ## Critical reception and legacy _[AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic")_ gave the album five stars, with reviewer [Scott Yanow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Yanow "Scott Yanow") opining that "Taylor's high-energy atonalism fit in well with the free jazz of the period but he was actually leading the way rather than being part of a movement...it could be safely argued that no jazz music of the era approached the ferocity and intensity of Cecil Taylor's".[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_Structures#cite_note-allmusic-2) _[The Penguin Guide to Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Penguin_Guide_to_Jazz "The Penguin Guide to Jazz")_ awarded it three and a half stars of a possible four, writing: " _Unit Structures_ is both as mathematically complex as its title suggests and as rich in colour and sound as the ensemble proposes, with the orchestrally varied sounds of the two bassists — [Grimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Grimes "Henry Grimes") a strong, elemental driving force, [Silva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Silva "Alan Silva") tonally fugitive and mysterious — while [Stevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Gale "Eddie Gale") and [McIntyre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Makanda_Ken_McIntyre "Makanda Ken McIntyre") add other hues and [Lyons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Lyons_(saxophonist) "Jimmy Lyons (saxophonist)") improvises with and against them."[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_Structures#cite_note-Penguin-4) In 2008, webzine _[Cokemachineglow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cokemachineglow "Cokemachineglow")_ included _Unit Structures_ on their "30 'Other' Albums of the 1960s" list.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_Structures#cite_note-10) In 2013, _[Spin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin_(magazine) "Spin (magazine)")_ included it on their "Top 100 Alternative Albums of the 1960s" list.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_Structures#cite_note-11) In 2017, _[Pitchfork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitchfork_(website) "Pitchfork (website)")_ placed it at number 197 on their list of the "200 Best Albums of the 1960s".[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_Structures#cite_note-Pitchfork-8) In 2017, Jesse Jarnow of _[Pitchfork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitchfork_(website) "Pitchfork (website)")_ wrote: " _Unit Structures_ still challenges notions of musical freedom. Recorded during the same season that the psychedelic ballroom scene was starting to bubble in San Francisco, _Unit Structures_ did more to disassemble music than nearly all of the light-show-drenched psychedelia that followed."[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_Structures#cite_note-:0-9) ## Track listing All tracks are written by [Cecil Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor "Cecil Taylor"). | No. | Title | Length | | --- | --- | --- | | 1. | "Steps" | 10:20 | | 2. | "Enter, Evening" | 11:06 | | 3. | "Enter, Evening (Alternate Take)" (CD edition bonus track) | 10:11 | | 4. | "Unit Structure/As of a Now/Section" | 17:47 | | 5. | "Tales (8 Whisps)" | 7:14 | ## Personnel Credits adapted from liner notes.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_Structures#cite_note-12) ‹The [template](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Template "Help:Template") below ( _[Col-begin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Template:Col-begin "Template:Col-begin")_) is being considered for deletion. (1965) | | _**Spiritual Unity**_ is a 1965 [studio album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio_album "Studio album") by the American [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") saxophonist [Albert Ayler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler "Albert Ayler"). It was recorded on July 10, 1964, with bassist [Gary Peacock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Peacock "Gary Peacock") and drummer [Sunny Murray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunny_Murray "Sunny Murray"). It was the first album recorded for [Bernard Stollman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Stollman "Bernard Stollman")'s [ESP-Disk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESP-Disk "ESP-Disk") label, and it brought the "shockingly different" Ayler to international attention.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-wilmer139-2) It also established ESP-Disk as "a major source for [avant-garde jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz")".[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-DeVeaux-3) ## Background In late December 1963, Bernard Stollman, who had been toying with the idea of starting a record label, went, at the insistence of a friend, to hear Ayler at the Baby Grand Café on 125th Street in Harlem.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-4) Ayler had moved to New York City earlier in the year, and had recently been playing with a variety of musicians, including [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman"), with whom Ayler made an informal recording earlier that month,[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-5) and [Cecil Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor "Cecil Taylor"), with whom he would perform on New Years Eve on a concert at Philharmonic Hall, [Lincoln Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln_Center "Lincoln Center") that would also feature the [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane") quintet and [Art Blakey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Blakey "Art Blakey") and [the Jazz Messengers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Jazz_Messengers "The Jazz Messengers").[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-6) According to Stollman, upon arriving at the Baby Grand Cafe, > Elmo Hope was at the piano, with his trio, on an elevated stage. I sat and listened to them. Several minutes later, a small man in a gray leather suit, holding a large saxophone, brushed by me and jumped up on the stage. He had a black beard, with a little patch of white in it. He was not introduced and, ignoring the trio, he began to blow his horn. The other musicians stopped and looked at him. No words were exchanged. Elmo Hope quietly closed his piano, the bass player parked his bass, the drummer put his sticks down, and they all sat back to listen. He was playing solo, and he kept right on playing for twenty to thirty minutes, just a burst of music. It seemed like a second; it was no time at all! Then he stopped and jumped down from the platform, covered with sweat.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-weiss21-7) Stollman then approached Ayler, told him he was starting a record label, and asked him to be his first artist, offering a $500 advance.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-8) Ayler agreed, and stated that he would contact Stollman after fulfulling a commitment to record material at Atlantic Studios.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-weiss21-7) In early 1964, Ayler briefly joined a quartet led by [Paul Bley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Bley "Paul Bley").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-schwartz-9) This occasion introduced Ayler to bassist Gary Peacock, who had been playing with Bley for several years, and who had also recently recorded with [Bill Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans "Bill Evans"). Bley's group also included drummer Sunny Murray, with whom Ayler had played in Cecil Taylor's group.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-schwartz-9) The Bley quartet did not record, and made only one public appearance at the Take 3 coffeehouse in [Greenwich Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenwich_Village "Greenwich Village").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-schwartz-9) By late spring, Ayler, Peacock, and Murray had formed a trio after Peacock left [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")' group, where he was substituting for [Ron Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Carter "Ron Carter").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-10) On June 14, the trio played at the Cellar Café in New York and recorded the material that would be released on the album _[Prophecy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophecy_(Albert_Ayler_album) "Prophecy (Albert Ayler album)")_, which features some of the pieces that would be recorded for _Spiritual Unity_ less than a month later. ## Recording and release That same month, Ayler called Stollman and told him he would like to make a recording. According to [Val Wilmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Val_Wilmer "Val Wilmer"), Ayler's decision to join Stollman's label, which would be called [ESP-Disk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESP-Disk "ESP-Disk"), was made "against the advice of Cecil Taylor and other musicians who thought that artists should hold out for a price commensurate with their talent."[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-11) Ayler justified his decision, stating: "I felt my art was so important that I had to get it out. At that time I was musically out of this world. I knew I had to play this music for the people."[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-wilmer139-2) Stollman booked a session for July 10, 1964, at Variety Arts Studio, a small and inexpensive studio near [Times Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Square "Times Square") which had been used frequently by [Moses Asch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moses_Asch "Moses Asch"), the owner of [Folkways Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folkways_Records "Folkways Records"),[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-weiss21-7) for whom Stollman had done legal work.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-weiss20-12) Stollman recalled: > Just before 1 PM, Sunny Murray arrived, a large, genial walrus, moving and speaking with an easy agility that belied his appearance. Gary Peacock was next, tall, thin, ascetic looking, and soft spoken, with an introspective and kindly demeanor. Albert Ayler was last, small, wary and laconic.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-espdisk-13) The recording engineer left the studio door open, and Stollman and Peacock's then-wife [Annette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annette_Peacock "Annette Peacock") sat in the reception area.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-weiss21-7) According to Stollman, > As the music played, I was enthralled, exhilarated, jubilant. I exchanged glances with Annette and said, "What an auspicious beginning for a record label!" She nodded her head in agreement.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-weiss21-7) At one point, "the engineer fled the control room for a few minutes, but returned in time to change the tape for the next selection".[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-espdisk-13) Stollman was "horrified" to learn that the session had been recorded in [mono](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monaural_sound "Monaural sound"), though he later reflected that "In forty-plus years, no one has ever cared".[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-weiss21-7) The musicians were paid and signed recording agreements after the session, in a nearby cafe.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-espdisk-13) Stollman hired Jordan Matthews, formerly a producer for ABC, as his art director, and Matthews brought in Howard Bernstein to do the cover art.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-14) Stollman stated that he decided to [silkscreen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silkscreen "Silkscreen") the cover, lending it "a primal quality".[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-15) Though it was the first dedicated ESP-Disk recording, _Spiritual Unity_ was released in 1965 as the second item in the label's catalog, following a record titled _Ni Kantu En Esperanto_, which Stollman described as "just an exercise" resulting from his interest in [Esperanto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esperanto "Esperanto").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-weiss20-12) Early releases of _Spiritual Unity_ contained a booklet titled "Ayler - Peacock - Murray - You and the Night and the Music" with text by [Paul Haines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Haines_(poet) "Paul Haines (poet)").[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-16) The album [liner notes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liner_notes "Liner notes") state that the symbol "Y" that appears on the back cover "pre-dates recorded history and has always represented the rising spirit of man. We thought the sign particularly apt for this album."[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-17) The booklet has never been included in any CD reissue, but it was included in the "Holy Ghost" box set. Ayler reflected on the session that "Most people would have thought this impossible but it actually happened. The most important thing is to stay in tune with each other but it takes spiritual people to do this... We weren't _playing_, we were listening to each other."[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-wilmer139-2) Following its release, Ayler sent a copy of the album to [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane"); soon afterwards, Coltrane urged [Impulse! Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records "Impulse! Records") to sign Ayler. In June 1965, Coltrane recorded the album _[Ascension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album) "Ascension (John Coltrane album)")_; following the recording session, Coltrane "called Ayler and told him, 'I recorded an album and found that I was playing just like you.' Albert's reply: 'No man, don't you see, you were playing like yourself. You were just feeling what I feel and were just crying out for spiritual unity."[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-18) Stollman was energized by the experience, and recalled: "I was thrilled with that record, so I was very much charged up with the idea of going forward. I wanted to explore this new music."[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-19) A week following the _Spiritual Unity_ session, Ayler, Peacock, and Murray, along with [Don Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter) "Don Cherry (trumpeter)"), [John Tchicai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Tchicai "John Tchicai"), and [Roswell Rudd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roswell_Rudd "Roswell Rudd"), recorded _[New York Eye and Ear Control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Eye_and_Ear_Control "New York Eye and Ear Control")_, which would also be released by ESP-Disk. The label would issue several additional Ayler albums, including _[Bells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bells_(album) "Bells (album)")_ and _[Spirits Rejoice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spirits_Rejoice "Spirits Rejoice")_. According to Stollman, following Ayler's death in 1970, he represented the musician's estate.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-20) ## Critical reception | Review scores | Professional ratings Initial critical reaction to _Spiritual Unity_ was polarized. Scott Deveaux and [Gary Giddins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Giddins "Gary Giddins") observed that the album "was both cheered and ridiculed" and Ayler's playing "evoked lusty hysteria".[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-DeVeaux-3) In July 1965, _[DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat")_ magazine published an article which featured a zero-star review of the album by trumpeter [Kenny Dorham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Dorham "Kenny Dorham"), who called it "not worth the paper it takes to review it," alongside a positive review by Bill Mathieu, who wrote: "Ayler's music, as well as most avant-garde music, is, at best, difficult to listen to. It is nevertheless a very direct statement, the physical manifestation of a spiritual or mystical ritual. Its logic is the logic of human flesh in the sphere of the spirit."[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-25) Retrospectively, the album has come to be regarded as a pioneering classic of free jazz. The authors of _[The Penguin Guide to Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Penguin_Guide_to_Jazz "The Penguin Guide to Jazz")_ selected the album as part of their suggested "Core Collection," awarding it a "crown" in addition to a four-star rating, and commenting: "the 1964 Ayler trio was quintessentially a listening band, locked in a personal struggle which it is possible only to observe, awestruck, from the sidelines."[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-Penguin-26) In 2013, _[Spin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin_(magazine) "Spin (magazine)")_ included it on the "Top 100 Alternative Albums of the 1960s" list.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-27) In 2017, _[Pitchfork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitchfork_(website) "Pitchfork (website)")_ placed it at number 30 on the "200 Best Albums of the 1960s" list.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-28) [John Fordham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Fordham_(jazz_critic) "John Fordham (jazz critic)"), writing in _[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Guardian "The Guardian")_, commented: "Half a century since the trio unleashed this music in a tiny Times Square studio, it still blazes, uplifts and unnerves. Ayler emerges from a Sonny Rollins-like jauntiness into slurred-pitch flurries and klaxon hoots over Peacock's prodding lines and Murray's shadings on the opening 'Ghosts'; barges ferociously through seamless runs on 'The Wizard'; and calls imploringly in a tone somewhere between an impassioned singer and a microtonal viola player on the meditative 'Spirits'. It still sounds like music on the edge".[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-29) [Shabaka Hutchings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shabaka_Hutchings "Shabaka Hutchings") wrote that the first time he listened to _Spiritual Unity_, he "didn't understand anything!... My brain couldn't compute it." He commented: "It sounded like he was crying through the saxophone. You can hear vocalisation in [Sidney Bechet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidney_Bechet "Sidney Bechet") and the older guys, but this was the first time I'd heard someone follow through on that and not try to mesh it with something more conventional". Eventually, he stated, "The more I listened, the more I realised that it's in what [Anthony Braxton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Braxton "Anthony Braxton") calls 'an emotional zone' – whatever Ayler does, it's about the emotional intent behind it. I wanted to see whether I could get into that space where you're free to do that. It's all about the big picture – more like painting."[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-30) ## Track listing All tracks are written by [Albert Ayler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler "Albert Ayler"). | No. | Title | Length | | --- | --- | --- | | 1. | "Ghosts: First Variation" | 5:12 | | 2. | "The Wizard" | 7:20 | | 3. | "Spirits" | 6:46 | | 4. | "Ghosts: Second Variation" | 10:01 | | Total length: | 29:13 | | No. | Title | Length | | --- | --- | --- | | 5. | "Vibrations" | 7:49 | | Total length: | 37:17 | 2014 reissue edition bonus track ## Personnel Credits adapted from liner notes. - [Albert Ayler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler "Albert Ayler") – tenor saxophone - [Gary Peacock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Peacock "Gary Peacock") – double bass - [Sunny Murray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunny_Murray "Sunny Murray") – percussion ## References 01. (1970) | | _**Emergency!**_ is the debut [double album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_album "Double album") by the American [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") group [the Tony Williams Lifetime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tony_Williams_Lifetime "The Tony Williams Lifetime") featuring Williams with guitarist [John McLaughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McLaughlin_(musician) "John McLaughlin (musician)") and organist [Larry Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Young_(musician) "Larry Young (musician)"). It was recorded and released in 1969 and was one of the first significant [fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") recordings.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency!_(album)#cite_note-2) The album is commonly regarded as an influential album in the [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music"), and [fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fusion_(music) "Fusion (music)") genres.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency!_(album)#cite_note-3) ## Composition \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Emergency!_(album)&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Composition")\] According to jazz scholar Christopher Meeder, the Lifetime eschewed the funk influence of [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")' early fusion music with a mixture of heavy rock drumming and the "light, rapid [swing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing_(jazz_performance_style) "Swing (jazz performance style)")" that was Williams' signature. " _Emergency!_ synthesized the best elements of [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz"), [modal jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz "Modal jazz"), and [British rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_rock "British rock")", Meeder wrote, "and added a rhythmic complexity in tracks like 'Via the Spectrum Road,' a blues of sorts in the [unusual time signature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_signature#Complex_time_signatures "Time signature") of 11/8."[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency!_(album)#cite_note-Meeder-4) In [Paul Hegarty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Hegarty_(musician) "Paul Hegarty (musician)")'s opinion, the music was more oriented with [progressive music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_music "Progressive music")'s rock side rather than its jazz, fusing psychedelic elements while featuring "reprises, crescendos, an oscillation between the simpler time signatures of rock and the more progressive metres of jazz". He cited "Via the Spectrum Road" as an example of how Williams' singing approached the "non-rock, non-jazz softness" of progressive rock pioneer [Robert Wyatt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Wyatt "Robert Wyatt").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency!_(album)#cite_note-5) "Via the Spectrum Road" was viewed by [Stuart Nicholson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Nicholson_(jazz_historian) "Stuart Nicholson (jazz historian)") as one of the album's most blatant explorations of rock rhythms. "Spectrum", on the other hand, utilized rhythms from [post-bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-bop "Post-bop"). Composed by McLaughlin, it was first recorded for his 1969 _[Extrapolation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extrapolation_(album) "Extrapolation (album)")_ debut and was regarded by Nicholson as an extension of that album's "free-flowing approach ... but reinforced by the volume and energy associated with rock".[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency!_(album)#cite_note-6) A mistake during _Emergency_'s production led Meeder to believe it helped lend a "raw power" to the music: "A cynical engineer used to recording mainstream jazz recorded the band carelessly, allowing the tape to distort, unintentionally adding satisfyingly raw edges to the album."[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency!_(album)#cite_note-Meeder-4) ## Release and reception \[ originally released in 1969 by [Polydor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polydor_Records "Polydor Records")/ [PolyGram Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PolyGram_Records "PolyGram Records"),[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency!_(album)#cite_note-Fellezs-15) receiving widespread acclaim from major American publications.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency!_(album)#cite_note-Coda-16) In a contemporary review for _[The Village Voice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Village_Voice "The Village Voice")_, [Robert Christgau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Christgau "Robert Christgau") hailed Williams as "probably the best drummer in the world" and was astonished by the album,[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency!_(album)#cite_note-VV-14) calling it "a frank extrapolation on the most raucous qualities of new thing jazz and wah-wah mannerist rock".[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency!_(album)#cite_note-17) _[Coda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coda_(magazine) "Coda (magazine)")_ was less enthusiastic, finding it "intriguing" with some "substantial" pieces of music but not as much as other [hard rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock "Hard rock") bands attempting the same kind of music, nor as imaginative and coherent as the music Williams, McLaughlin, and Young had made outside the group.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency!_(album)#cite_note-Coda-16) The album was later issued on [CD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_Disc "Compact Disc") by [Polydor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polydor_Records "Polydor Records")/ [PolyGram Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PolyGram_Records "PolyGram Records") in 1991 but with a "restoration" remix by [Phil Schaap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Schaap "Phil Schaap") to overcome "Marked sonic problems". The original album mix was reissued on CD for the first time by [Verve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verve_Records "Verve Records")/ [PolyGram Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PolyGram_Records "PolyGram Records") in 1997.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency!_(album)#cite_note-Fellezs-15) According to [J. D. Considine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._D._Considine "J. D. Considine") in _[The Rolling Stone Album Guide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rolling_Stone_Album_Guide "The Rolling Stone Album Guide")_ (1992), [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") started on _Emergency!_ where McLaughlin was first given the chance to combine jazz and rock.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency!_(album)#cite_note-RSguide-12) In a retrospective review for [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic"), Leo Stanley said that it "shattered the boundaries between jazz and rock" with its "dense, adventurous, unpredictable soundscapes".[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency!_(album)#cite_note-AM-7) Dennis Polkow of the _[Chicago Tribune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Tribune "Chicago Tribune")_ wrote that in spite of the album's questionable sound quality, the music has an "energy and spirit" that has never been surpassed in fusion.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency!_(album)#cite_note-CT-8) According to Nicholson, recordings like _Emergency!_ and the 1975 [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis") LP _[Agharta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album) "Agharta (album)")_ showed jazz rock paralleling [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") by being "on the verge of creating a whole new musical language in the 1960s", suggesting the genre's "potential of evolving into something that might eventually define itself as a wholly independent genre quite apart from the sound and conventions of anything that had gone before." This development was stifled by commercialism, he said, as the genre "mutated into a peculiar species of jazz-inflected pop music that eventually took up residence on FM radio" at [the end of the 1970s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980s_in_jazz "1980s in jazz").[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency!_(album)#cite_note-18) _[Mojo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mojo_(magazine) "Mojo (magazine)")_ regarded it as "jazz-rock's equivalent of _[Are You Experienced?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Are_You_Experienced%3F "Are You Experienced?")_".[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency!_(album)#cite_note-19) ## Track listing \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Emergency!_(album)&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Track listing")\] Side one 1.
