1976 North American edition | | | | | _**Agharta**_ is a 1975 live [double album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_album "Double album") by American [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") trumpeter, composer, and bandleader [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis"). By the time he recorded the album, Davis was 48 years old and had alienated many in the jazz community while attracting younger [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music") audiences with his radical electric [fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") music. After experimenting with different line-ups, he established a stable live band in 1973 and toured constantly for the next two years, despite physical pain from worsening health and emotional instability brought on by substance abuse. During a three-week tour of Japan in 1975, the trumpeter performed two concerts at the [Festival Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Festival_Hall,_Osaka "Festival Hall, Osaka") in [Osaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osaka "Osaka") on February 1; the afternoon show produced _Agharta_, and the evening show was released as _[Pangaea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pangaea_(album) "Pangaea (album)")_ the following year. Davis led a [septet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Septet "Septet") at the concert; he, saxophonist [Sonny Fortune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Fortune "Sonny Fortune"), and guitarist [Pete Cosey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Cosey "Pete Cosey") were given space to improvise against a dense backdrop of [riffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riff_(music) "Riff (music)"), electronic effects, [cross-beats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-beat "Cross-beat"), and [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk") [grooves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groove_(music) "Groove (music)") from the [rhythm section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_section "Rhythm section") – drummer [Al Foster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Foster "Al Foster"), bassist [Michael Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Henderson "Michael Henderson"), guitarist [Reggie Lucas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggie_Lucas "Reggie Lucas"), and percussionist [James Mtume](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Mtume "James Mtume"). Davis controlled their rhythmic and musical direction with hand and head gestures, [phrases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phrase_(music) "Phrase (music)") played on his [wah-wah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wah-wah_pedal "Wah-wah pedal") processed trumpet, and [drones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drone_(music) "Drone (music)") from an accompanying [electronic organ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_organ "Electronic organ"). The evolving nature of the performance led to the widespread misunderstanding that it had no compositional basis, while its dark, angry, and somber musical qualities were seen as a reflection of the bandleader's emotional and spiritual state at the time. _Agharta_ was first released in Japan by [CBS/Sony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_Music_Entertainment_Japan "Sony Music Entertainment Japan") in August 1975 just before Davis temporarily retired due to increasingly poor health and exhaustion. At the record label's suggestion, it was titled after [the legendary subterranean city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta "Agharta"). Davis enlisted Japanese artist [Tadanori Yokoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tadanori_Yokoo "Tadanori Yokoo") to design its artwork, which depicted the cityscape of an advanced civilization with elements inspired by [Eastern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_world "Eastern world") subterranean myths, [Afrofuturism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afrofuturism "Afrofuturism"), and [ufology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ufology "Ufology"). An alternate cover was produced for its 1976 release in North America by [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records"). A highly divisive record, _Agharta_ further challenged Davis' jazz audience and was widely panned by contemporary critics; reviewers found the music discordant and complained of Cosey's loud guitar sounds and Davis' sparse trumpet playing. It was reevaluated positively in subsequent years, however, as a generation of younger musicians was influenced by the band's abrasive music and cathartic playing, particularly Cosey's [effects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effects_unit "Effects unit")-laden [free improvisations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation "Free improvisation"). _Agharta_ has since been viewed as an important jazz-rock record, a dramatically dynamic group performance, and the culmination of Davis' [electric period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_Miles "Electric Miles") spanning the late 1960s and mid-1970s. ## Background [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/72/Miles_Davis-140916-0016-103WP_%28cropped%29.jpg/500px-Miles_Davis-140916-0016-103WP_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Miles_Davis-140916-0016-103WP_(cropped).jpg) [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis") in 1971 In the early 1970s, Miles Davis continued exploring directions radically different from the jazz music that made him renowned in the 1950s and 1960s.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson200360-1) The music from this [electric period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#1968%E2%80%931975:_The_electric_period "Miles Davis") in his career found him experimenting with [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music"), [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk"), [African rhythms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_in_Sub-Saharan_Africa "Rhythm in Sub-Saharan Africa"), emerging [electronic music technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_technology_(electronic_and_digital) "Music technology (electronic and digital)"), and an ever-changing lineup of musicians who played electric instruments.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreeman200510%E2%80%9311,_155%E2%80%93156-2) The trumpeter attracted younger audiences as his [fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") music became more radical and abstract while alienating older listeners, musicians, and critics in the jazz scene who accused him of [selling out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selling_out "Selling out").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-3) After recording his 1972 _[On the Corner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner "On the Corner")_ album, Davis began to focus more on performing live, working in the studio only sporadically and haphazardly; the 1974 releases _[Big Fun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Fun_(Miles_Davis_album) "Big Fun (Miles Davis album)")_ and _[Get Up with It](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Get_Up_with_It "Get Up with It")_ compiled recordings he made between 1969 and 1974.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreeman200510,_110-4) By 1973, Davis had established most of his band's line-up, a [septet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Septet "Septet") featuring bassist [Michael Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Henderson "Michael Henderson"), guitarists [Pete Cosey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Cosey "Pete Cosey") and [Reggie Lucas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggie_Lucas "Reggie Lucas"), drummer [Al Foster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Foster "Al Foster"), percussionist [James Mtume](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Mtume "James Mtume"), and saxophonist [Dave Liebman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Liebman "Dave Liebman"); Liebman left the group the following year and was replaced by [Sonny Fortune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Fortune "Sonny Fortune").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-5) Lucas, Henderson, Foster, and Mtume functioned as the band's [rhythm section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_section "Rhythm section"), while Cosey, and Fortune were given space to improvise as soloists.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreeman2005134-6) Their concerts – played frequently at rock venues and festivals – became opportunities for Davis and his sidemen to test new musical ideas and ways to exploit electronic equipment.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreeman20057,_152-7) Davis toured relentlessly for two years while tolerating intense physical pain and difficulty walking, caused by joint pain from [sickle-cell anaemia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sickle-cell_anaemia "Sickle-cell anaemia"), badly damaged ankles after a 1972 car wreck, and [osteoporosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osteoporosis "Osteoporosis") in his left hip, which had been operated on a decade earlier.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-8) He had also developed [nodules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vocal_fold_nodule "Vocal fold nodule") on his [larynx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larynx "Larynx") that often left him short of breath, especially when playing the trumpet.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChambers1998277-9) To numb the pain, he became increasingly dependent on [self-medicating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-medication "Self-medication") with painkillers, cocaine, and morphine, which combined with his alcohol and [recreational drug use](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recreational_drug_use "Recreational drug use") led to mood swings; he would by turns feel vulnerable and hostile.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-10) By the end of 1974, a disappointing showing in _[DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat")_ magazine's readers poll reinforced to Davis that his reputation had diminished.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChambers1998274-11) Unfazed by detractors and personal troubles, he kept his touring schedule intense.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChambers1998158-12) As Henderson recounted: > He was like the general looking at the fort and they had a moat and we were going to get in that fort. That was the attitude of the band. We didn't give a shit what the critics said. People are gonna like what they like, but if you don't like it, respect it. Respect that I have the right to do what I do. Because with or without you, we're going to do it anyway.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTECole200727-13) ### Tour of Japan In 1975, the 48-year old Davis embarked on a three-week tour of Japan. Between January 22 and February 8, he played 14 concerts in large-hall venues to capacity crowds and enthusiastic reviews.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-14) Japanese critic Keizo Takada said at the time that Davis is leading his "magnificent and energetic" band just as [Duke Ellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Ellington "Duke Ellington") had his orchestra: "Miles must be _the_ genius of managing men and bringing out their hidden talent."[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChambers1998274-11) [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/be/Festival_hall_Osaka02bs2400.jpg/500px-Festival_hall_Osaka02bs2400.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Festival_hall_Osaka02bs2400.jpg) [Festival Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osaka_Festival_Hall "Osaka Festival Hall") (left center) in [Osaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osaka "Osaka"), where _Agharta_ was recorded Throughout the tour, Davis was sick with [pneumonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pneumonia "Pneumonia") and a bleeding ulcer that grew worse, while his hip occasionally and unpredictably slipped out of its socket. Unable to work his trumpet's volume and [effects pedals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effects_pedals "Effects pedals") because of the pain in his legs, he would go down on his knees to press them with his hand during performances. To relieve his pain and perform, he used codeine and morphine, smoked, and drank large quantities of [Heineken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heineken "Heineken") beer. On several occasions, Davis was able to play two concerts in one day, as he did on February 1 at the [Festival Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Festival_Hall,_Osaka "Festival Hall, Osaka") in [Osaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osaka "Osaka").[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTESzwed2004342-15) The Festival Hall performances were recorded by Japan's [CBS/Sony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_Music_Entertainment_Japan "Sony Music Entertainment Japan") record label under the supervision of [Teo Macero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teo_Macero "Teo Macero"), Davis' producer of 15 years.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTESzwed2004209,_342-16) "The Japanese people were very beautiful", Henderson recalled from the concerts. "They came in with their suit and ties on and we proceeded to blow the roof off the suckers with a million amplifiers."[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTECole200727-13) ## Composition and performance > Our concerts began like a balloon that was incredibly compressed. After that it was a matter of gradually letting the air out. The energy it took us to play at that level was enormous. There were times that we had to lie down after we had finished playing. Before the concert we'd build this energy up. We looked at each other, and said, "Let's go through the wall." That was our slogan. It meant taking it as far as we could physically. To stay at that level of concentration and energy for two to three hours was going through the wall. — [James Mtume](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Mtume "James Mtume") (2001)[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTETingen2001164-17) For the first of the afternoon concert's two [sets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_list "Set list"), the band performed the compositions "Tatu", "Agharta Prelude", and "Maiysha" (from _Get Up with It_), making up _Agharta_'s first disc of music. The second-set performances of "Right Off" (from Davis' 1971 _[Jack Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Johnson_(album) "Jack Johnson (album)")_ album), "Ife" (from _Big Fun_), and "Wili (= For Dave)" spanned the second disc; between the "Right Off" and "Ife" segments, the band improvised a passage based on " [So What](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/So_What_(Miles_Davis_composition) "So What (Miles Davis composition)")" (from the 1959 album _[Kind of Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue "Kind of Blue")_) for 41 seconds after Henderson started to play its [ostinato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostinato "Ostinato").[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-18) The pieces were performed in [medleys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_musical_medleys "List of musical medleys"), which were given generic track titles on _Agharta_, such as "Prelude" and "Interlude".[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTETingen2001151-19) As with his other live releases in the 1970s, Davis refused to have individual compositions specified in the track listing because he felt critics and other listeners often overlooked the music's intrinsic meaning by indulging in abstract [musical analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_analysis "Musical analysis"). "I'm not doing anything, it doesn't need an explanation", he later told [Leonard Feather](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Feather "Leonard Feather").[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTETingen2001115-20) Music scholars were able to identify the pieces through an examination of what Davis researcher Enrico Merlin called "coded [phrases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phrase_(music) "Phrase (music)")", which Davis played on trumpet or organ to signify the end of one segment and direct the band toward the next section. He first used such cues and [modulations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulation_(music) "Modulation (music)") when recording " [Flamenco Sketches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flamenco_Sketches "Flamenco Sketches")" in 1959, Merlin said.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTETingen200172-21) The pieces featured on _Agharta_ were part of a typical set list for the group, but their performances of each sometimes changed almost beyond recognition from concert to concert. This, along with the track names, led to the widespread misunderstanding that the music was mostly or entirely improvised and unstructured.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTETingen2001115,_152-22) Lucas explained that the band started each performance with a "very defined compositional basis" before developing it further in a highly structured yet "very free way"; the "Right Off" segment, for instance, was improvised from the original recording's [E-flat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E-flat_major "E-flat major") riff.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTETingen2001152,_317-23) Davis had the band play around a single [chord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chord_(music) "Chord (music)") in a piece for several minutes with [variations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variation_(music) "Variation (music)") as each member performed in a different [time signature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_signature "Time signature"); Foster might have been playing in [common time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_time "Common time") and Mtume in [compound duple metre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compound_duple_metre "Compound duple metre") or [septuple time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Septuple_meter "Septuple meter"), while the guitarists would [comp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comping_(jazz) "Comping (jazz)") in another tempo altogether. "That's a lot of intricate shit we were working off this one chord", Davis remarked.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJeske19914-24) From Lucas' perspective, this kind of "structured improvisation" resulted in significant interplay between the rhythm section and allowed the band to improvise "a lot more than just the notes that were being played in the solos; we were improvising the entire song as we went along."[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTETingen2001152-25) [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/Michael_Henderson-140915-0040WP_%28cropped%29.jpg/500px-Michael_Henderson-140915-0040WP_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Michael_Henderson-140915-0040WP_(cropped).jpg) [Michael Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Henderson "Michael Henderson") (1971), the bassist in Davis' rhythm section Like _[Pangaea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pangaea_(album) "Pangaea (album)")_ and _[Dark Magus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_Magus "Dark Magus")_ – the two other live albums showcasing the septet – _Agharta_ revealed what [Amiri Baraka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amiri_Baraka "Amiri Baraka") described as Davis' affinity for [minimalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_music "Minimal music").[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-26) He abandoned melodic and harmonic conventions in favor of riffs, [cross-rhythms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-rhythm "Cross-rhythm"), and funk [grooves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groove_(music) "Groove (music)") as a backdrop for soloists to improvise throughout.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJurek2002315-27) Davis had preferred understated compositions throughout his career but by the mid 1970s he showed a deeper embrace of rhythm, inspired by [Afrocentric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afrocentricism "Afrocentricism") politics.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBayles200119-28) When Mtume and Cosey joined the band, his live music lost most of its "European sensibilities" and "settled down into a deep African thing, a deep African-American groove" emphasizing rhythm and drums rather than individual solos, Davis said, although he did not completely reject melody. "We ain't in Africa, and we don't play just chants. There's some theory under what we do."[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-29) Categorizing _Agharta_ as a jazz-rock record, [Simon Reynolds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Reynolds "Simon Reynolds") wrote in _[The Wire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wire_(magazine) "The Wire (magazine)")_ that the music "offered a drastic intensification of rock's three most radical aspects: space, [timbre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbre "Timbre"), and groove".[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReynolds2011182,_269-30) In [Martha Bayles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Bayles "Martha Bayles")' opinion, it drew from jazz only in its element of [free improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation "Free improvisation") and from rock only in its use of electronics and "ear-bleeding volume".[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBayles200119-28) The album also showcased Davis' [avant-garde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_music "Avant-garde music") impulses and exploration of [ambient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambient_music "Ambient music") sounds. According to [Greg Tate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greg_Tate "Greg Tate"), the septet created "a pan-ethnic web of avant-garde music", while Sputnikmusic's Hernan M. Campbell said they explored "progressive ambiences" particularly within the record's second half; Phil Alexander from _[Mojo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mojo_(magazine) "Mojo (magazine)")_ characterized _Agharta_ as "both ambient yet thrashing, melodic yet coruscating", and suggestive of [Karlheinz Stockhausen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karlheinz_Stockhausen "Karlheinz Stockhausen")'s electronic experiments.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-31) ### Dynamics and effects During the concert, Davis directed approximately 50 stops or [breaks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Break_(music) "Break (music)") to the band, particularly the rhythm section, by gesturing with his head or hand.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-32) These stops served as dramatic turning points in the [tension-release](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tension_(music) "Tension (music)") structure of the performances, changing their tempo and allowing the band to alternate between quiet passages and intense climaxes.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTETingen2001163-33) He also interjected the performances with [drone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drone_(music) "Drone (music)") washes from his [Yamaha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yamaha_Corporation "Yamaha Corporation") organ, achieving a "strange, nearly perverse presence" that [Mikal Gilmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikal_Gilmore "Mikal Gilmore") believed "defined the temper" of the music.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlkyerEnrightKoransky2007271,_330-34) Lucas said Davis applied a feel for [dynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamics_(music) "Dynamics (music)") he had developed earlier in his career playing jazz, but with a greater array of [contrasts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contrast_(music) "Contrast (music)"), including [atonal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atonality "Atonality"), dissonant chords, and his own [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop") trumpet playing set against the group's funk rhythms. "Extreme [textures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texture_(music) "Texture (music)") and extreme volume", Lucas explained, "were as much part of the palette as the contrasting chord and rhythmic structures. Being equipped like a full rock band, we sometimes literally blew the walls out."[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTETingen2001163-33) ![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg/120px-Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail) ["Prelude"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Miles_Davis_-_Prelude.ogg "File:Miles Davis - Prelude.ogg") A 30-second sample featuring the "Prelude" theme, played on _Agharta_ with more pronounced riffs and [tonality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonality "Tonality") * * * _Problems playing this file? See [media help](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Media "Help:Media")._ During the "Tatu" and "Agharta Prelude" segments, Davis abruptly stopped and started the septet several times to shift tempos by playing a dissonant, cacophonous organ figure, giving Cosey space to generate eccentric, [psychedelic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelic_music "Psychedelic music") figures and effects.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-35) The main theme for "Tatu" had been played at a slower tempo when Cosey first joined the band, but they played it faster as their rapport grew, especially by the time of the Japanese tour. Cosey credited Davis with having the ability to "transmit thoughts and ideas" to the soloists with his playing.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEColen.d.-36) According to [John Szwed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Szwed "John Szwed"), the "Prelude" theme was played here with more pronounced riffs and [tonality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonality "Tonality") than in past performances of the piece.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTESzwed2004342-15) [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/41/SynthiAKSStack_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SynthiAKSStack_(cropped).jpg) An [EMS Synthi A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EMS_Synthi_A "EMS Synthi A"), which [Pete Cosey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Cosey "Pete Cosey") used as an [effects unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effects_unit "Effects unit") The rhythmic direction of the music was occasionally interrupted by densely layered percussive and electronic effects, including repeated whirring and grinding sounds. Cosey generated these sounds by running his guitar through a [ring modulator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_modulator "Ring modulator") and an [EMS Synthi A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EMS_Synthi_A "EMS Synthi A").[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrzaskowski197674-37) The latter device was an early synthesizer with knobs and buttons but no keyboard, making it useful for producing abstract noises rather than exact pitches and melodies. While serving as an effects unit for his improvisations, it was also used by Cosey to suggest a certain [soundscape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soundscape "Soundscape") during each performance. "Whether we were in space, or underwater or a group of Africans playing – just different soundscapes", he later explained.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-38) Onstage, Cosey also had a table set up holding a [mbira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mbira "Mbira"), [claves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claves "Claves"), [agogo bells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agogo_bells "Agogo bells"), and several other [hand percussion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hand_percussion "Hand percussion") instruments, which he played or struck with a mallet to indicate a different break or stop. "I would hit them just like they do at \[boxing\] fights!", Cosey recalled.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-39) His synthesizer sometimes interacted with the experimental sounds Mtume was able to generate from his drum machine, as during the "Ife" segment. Davis gave the instrument to Mtume after receiving it from Yamaha, the Japanese tour's sponsor, and told him "see what you can do with it." Rather than use it to create rhythms, Mtume processed the drum machine through several different pedals and [phase shifters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phaser_(effect) "Phaser (effect)") such as the [Mu-Tron Bi-Phase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mu-Tron#Mu-tron_Bi-Phase "Mu-Tron"), creating a sound he said was "total tapestry". "I'm also using a volume pedal, so I'm bringing the sounds in and out", Mtume recalled. "Unless you were told, you'd have no idea that you heard a rhythm machine."[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTETingen2001165-40) ### Soloists [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/Sonny_Fortune_photo.jpg/500px-Sonny_Fortune_photo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sonny_Fortune_photo.jpg) [Sonny Fortune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Fortune "Sonny Fortune") (2007), a featured soloist on _Agharta_ Unlike Davis' previous recordings, the [cadenzas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadenza "Cadenza") throughout _Agharta_ were mostly played by Fortune and Cosey.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTESzwed2004342-15) Fortune alternated between soprano and alto saxophones and the flute, performing with a "substance and structure" Gilmore believed was very much indebted to [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane") during his _[A Love Supreme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme "A Love Supreme")_ (1965) period.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlkyerEnrightKoransky2007271-41) In his estimation of Fortune's solos on the album, Gilmore said the saxophonist "floats over formidable rhythmic density, taking long and graceful breaks that wing off into a private reverie".[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlkyerEnrightKoransky2007271-41) Fortune performed his longest alto saxophone solo on "Right Off", which opened the record's second disc in a "propulsive" segment Gilmore said "flies by like a train ride in a dream, where scenes flash past the window in a fascinating and illusive dream".[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-42) Cosey played a [Guild S-100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guild_S-100 "Guild S-100") electric guitar and heavily employed [chromaticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromaticism "Chromaticism"), [dissonance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consonance_and_dissonance "Consonance and dissonance"), and [feedback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_feedback "Audio feedback") in his improvisations on _Agharta_.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-43) He alternated between several effects pedals set up underneath his table of percussion instruments, including a [fuzzbox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distortion_(music) "Distortion (music)") for distorting guitar sounds and two different [wah-wah pedals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wah-wah_pedal "Wah-wah pedal") he used during solos or when playing more mellow [tones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tone_(musical_instrument) "Tone (musical instrument)").[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGluckin2015-44) Cosey often arranged his guitar strings in different places on the [fretboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fretboard "Fretboard") and never played in [standard tuning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_tuning "Standard tuning"), using at least 36 different [tuning systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuning_system "Tuning system"), each of which altered the style and sound of his playing.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-45) According to [Tzvi Gluckin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tzvi_Gluckin "Tzvi Gluckin") from _Premier Guitar_, his experimental guitar playing was rooted in the [blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues "Blues") and displayed a sense of [phrasing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_phrasing "Musical phrasing") that was aggressive and "blistering" yet "somehow also restrained", particularly in his control of feedback.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGluckin2015-44) Davis had enlisted Cosey to provide his music with sounds from the [electric blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_blues "Electric blues") and [Jimi Hendrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimi_Hendrix "Jimi Hendrix"), whose use of distortion and the [E-flat tuning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E-flat_tuning "E-flat tuning") was shared by Cosey.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-46) According to [Charles Shaar Murray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Shaar_Murray "Charles Shaar Murray"), he evoked the guitarist's echoic, [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz")-inspired solos while Lucas performed in the manner of Hendrix's more lyrical [rhythm and blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues") songs; Cosey's guitar was separated to the left [channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_channel "Audio channel") and Lucas' to the right on _Agharta_.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-47) Jazz scholar [Stuart Nicholson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Nicholson_(jazz_historian) "Stuart Nicholson (jazz historian)") wrote that Davis utilized his guitarists in a way which realized the "waves of [harmonic distortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_distortion "Harmonic distortion")" Hendrix had explored in his own music.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTENicholson1998128,_130-48) In Murray's view, the album invoked his influence on the trumpeter more explicitly than any other of his records; Nicholson considered it to be the "closest approximation" to the music they could have recorded together.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-49) ### Davis on trumpet Davis veered from succinct and expressive solos to unsentimental wails during the concert, which suggested he was still mourning [Hendrix's 1970 death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_of_Jimi_Hendrix "Death of Jimi Hendrix"), Murray surmised.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMurray1991202-50) That year, Davis had started playing with a wah-wah pedal affixed to his trumpet in order to emulate the [register](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Register_(music) "Register (music)") Hendrix achieved on his guitar.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMilkowski2000508-51) The pedal created what _[The Penguin Guide to Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Penguin_Guide_to_Jazz "The Penguin Guide to Jazz")_ (2006) described as "surges and ebbs in a harmonically static line, allowing Miles to build huge melismatic variations on a single note".[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTECookMorton2006330-52) Davis eventually developed what Philip Freeman called "a new tone, the wiggly, shimmering ribbons of sound that are heard on _Agharta_", where his wah-wah processed solos often sounded frantic and melancholic, like "twisted streams of raw pain".[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreeman2005152-53) ![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg/120px-Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail) ["Interlude/Theme from Jack Johnson"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Miles_Davis_-_Interlude_Theme_from_Jack_Johnson.ogg "File:Miles Davis - Interlude Theme from Jack Johnson.ogg") A 30-second sample of Davis' final trumpet passage in the "Wili" segment, representative of the sense of melancholy throughout the album. * * * _Problems playing this file? See [media help](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Media "Help:Media")._ Davis played his trumpet sparsely throughout the concert, often sounding obscured by the rhythm section. His presence on _Agharta_ reflected what Szwed called "the feel and shape of a musician's late work, an egoless music that precedes its creator's death". Drawing on [Theodor W. Adorno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodor_W._Adorno "Theodor W. Adorno")'s commentary of [Ludwig van Beethoven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_van_Beethoven "Ludwig van Beethoven")'s late works, Szwed said "the disappearance of the musician into the work is a bow to mortality. It was as if Miles were testifying to all that he had been witness to for the past thirty years, both terrifying and joyful."[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTESzwed2004342%E2%80%9343-54) According to [Richard Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Cook_(journalist) "Richard Cook (journalist)"), Davis' final trumpet passage from the "Wili (= For Dave)" segment typified a "sense of gloom, even exhaustion", that colored many interpretations of _Agharta_'s "dark" music.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook2007259%E2%80%9360-55) After Lucas' first and only solo of the show climaxed the "Ife" segment, Davis introduced "Wili (= For Dave)" with a few organ chords, culminating in Cosey's final solo and a trumpet passage by Davis, which [Paul Tingen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tingen "Paul Tingen") characterized as plaintive and introspective. According to him, live music shows typically developed toward reaching a final climax, but Davis' concerts "often dissolved into entropy". On _Agharta_, Tingen observed a "deep sadness" hanging over the music as the energy of the "Wili (= For Dave)" piece "slowly drained away" to the record's [fade out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fade_(audio_engineering) "Fade (audio engineering)").[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTETingen2001164-17) ## Title and packaging _Agharta_'s title was proposed by CBS/Sony as a reference to [the subterranean utopian city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta "Agharta").[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-56) The city's legend was one of several [Eastern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_world "Eastern world") versions of the [Hollow Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollow_Earth "Hollow Earth") theory, which proposed that an ancient [high culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_culture "High culture") originally lived on the Earth's surface but was forced to flee below because of some political or geological crisis.[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBuchwald20129-57) The myth depicted the city as a divine source of power, claiming that its inhabitants were highly spiritual, advanced beings who would save the Earth from materialism and destructive technology after a cataclysmic event.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-58) It was first conceived by 19th-century French thinker [Louis Jacolliot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Jacolliot "Louis Jacolliot") as a land ruled by an [Ethiopian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aethiopia "Aethiopia") ruler; [Alexandre Saint-Yves d'Alveydre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandre_Saint-Yves_d'Alveydre "Alexandre Saint-Yves d'Alveydre") later described it as "drowning in celestial radiances all visible distinctions of race in a single chromatic of light and sound, singularly removed from the usual notions of perspective and acoustics."[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTESzwed2004342-15) The album's artwork was designed by Japanese artist [Tadanori Yokoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tadanori_Yokoo "Tadanori Yokoo"), who had been creating silkscreen prints on themes of Agharta and the mythical kingdom of [Shambhala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shambhala "Shambhala") the year before the Festival Hall concert; his design for [Santana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band) "Santana (band)")'s _[Lotus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lotus_(Santana_album) "Lotus (Santana album)")_ (1974) featured such themes.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-59) In the early 1970s, Yokoo had found his growing popularity in Japan distracting and moved to the United States, where he was able to get more of his work published. After returning to Japan, he received a phone call from Davis, who had seen his art and wanted him to create a cover for _Agharta_.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThorgersonPowell199921-60) Before designing the cover, Yokoo listened to a preliminary tape of the concert, meditated, and reflected on his reading of [Raymond W. Bernard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raymond_W._Bernard "Raymond W. Bernard")'s 1969 book _The Hollow Earth_.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThorgersonPowell199920-61) Bernard had written that the city existed in a large cavern in the center of the Earth where displaced inhabitants of [Atlantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantis "Atlantis") had taken refuge following its destruction, using mythological aircraft known as [vimanas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vimana "Vimana") as transport, although Yokoo said he believed "Agharta could be down there under the sea like Atlantis or even hidden in the jungle like the lost city of [El Dorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Dorado "El Dorado")."[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-62) Yokoo also drew on elements from other Eastern subterranean myths and [Afrofuturism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afrofuturism "Afrofuturism") in his design.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBuchwald2012109-63) Critics who eventually saw the album's packaging thought he had been inspired instead by the [psychedelic drugs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelic_drug "Psychedelic drug") popular at the time.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThorgersonPowell199920-61) [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/7/77/Agharta_back_gatefold.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Agharta_back_gatefold.jpg) The back cover design by [Tadanori Yokoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tadanori_Yokoo "Tadanori Yokoo"), who was inspired by the legendary city of [Agartha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agartha "Agartha") The front cover depicted an advanced civilization with a vast landscape of skyscrapers and red, sunburst-like flames rising out of the cityscape as representations of Agharta's power.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-64) Yokoo used a combination of collage, airbrushing, and painting techniques as he had with his previous work, along with postcards collected from his trips to [Tahiti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tahiti "Tahiti") and New York City; the cityscape on the front cover was taken from one of his postcards.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThorgersonPowell199921-60) The back cover showed the city submerged in water, embedded in coral reefs, and hovered over by a diver, fish, and a squid ascending from the city.[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBuchwald2012110-65) According to graphic designers [Storm Thorgerson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storm_Thorgerson "Storm Thorgerson") and [Aubrey Powell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aubrey_Powell_(designer) "Aubrey Powell (designer)"), Yokoo depicted groups of jellyfish, coral reefs, and brightly colored fish to suggest an association between Agharta and Atlantis.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThorgersonPowell199920-61) The foreground of the back cover's illustration featured a [reptilian creature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reptilian_humanoid "Reptilian humanoid"). Cultural studies researcher Dagmar Buchwald interpreted this image as an allusion to similar ideas about [Lemuria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lemuria_(continent) "Lemuria (continent)"); this mythological continent supposedly existed during the Earth's prehistory and was inhabited by an [advanced civilization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silurian_hypothesis "Silurian hypothesis"), later forced under the Earth's surface after its homeland was destroyed by a [great flood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flood_myth "Flood myth").[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBuchwald2012110-65) A [UFO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unidentified_flying_object "Unidentified flying object") was depicted on the back cover, flying in a spotlight over Agharta, while the album's inside packaging featured images of winged superhuman beings known as the Agharta supermen, who guarded the city's entrances and secret tunnels.[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-66) An inscription in the LP's [gatefold sleeve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gatefold "Gatefold") explained the connection between the UFO and the Agharta supermen: > During various periods in history the supermen of Agharta came to the surface of Earth to teach the human race how to live together in peace and save us from wars, catastrophe, and destruction. The apparent sighting of several flying saucers soon after the [bombing of Hiroshima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombing_of_Hiroshima "Bombing of Hiroshima") may represent one visitation.[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBuchwald2012110-65)[\[nb 1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-68) _Agharta_'s North American release had different artwork designed by John Berg, the art director from Davis' U.S. label, [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records").[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAnon.1976-69) In its liner notes, an inscription said the record should be listened to at the highest possible volume, and the [arrangements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrangement "Arrangement") were credited to Davis.[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-70) After it was released, Macero received a complaint from Columbia's accounting department about the trumpeter being compensated $2,500 per arrangement, arguing that none of the music sounded as if it had been arranged.[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTESzwed2004343-71) ## Release [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ad/Teo_Macero_%28cropped%29.jpg/500px-Teo_Macero_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Teo_Macero_(cropped).jpg) Davis' producer [Teo Macero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teo_Macero "Teo Macero") (1996) prepared _Agharta_'s original release. Davis was reportedly so dissatisfied with his performance on the Festival Hall recordings that he conceded the preparation of their release to Macero.[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChristgau1981103-72) The producer abstained from editing and splicing them with pre-recorded parts, a departure from his usual approach to Davis' electric-era albums. As he later explained to _[Musician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musician_(magazine) "Musician (magazine)")_ magazine, "the Japanese specifically wanted me to leave in the spacy things."[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReese198786-73) They were released as two [double albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_album "Double album") – _Agharta_, featuring the afternoon concert, was first released in Japan in August 1975 and later in North America in 1976; the evening show was issued exclusively in Japan as _Pangaea_ in 1976.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-74)[\[nb 2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-76) _Agharta_ was reissued several times. In January 1991, Columbia re-released it in the U.S. on CD, featuring a [remaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remaster "Remaster") Tingen deemed inferior to the original LP in sound and [mix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_mixing_(recorded_music) "Audio mixing (recorded music)") quality. "Had the CD been my first introduction, I might never have liked the album much", he said.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-77) Sony later remastered _Agharta_ again as part of their Davis reissue campaign and Master Sound series in Japan, with improved sound using [Super Bit Mapping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bit_Mapping "Super Bit Mapping").[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTETingen2001142,_286-78) This 1996 Japanese CD edition restored nine additional minutes of atmospheric feedback, percussion, and synthesizer sounds to the end of the final track.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTETingen2001164-17) Another remaster of the album was engineered by Mark Wilder and Maria Triana at New York's Battery Studios. It was made available in the U.S. in 2009, when _Agharta_ was one of 52 albums re-issued in [mini-LP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mini-LP "Mini-LP") replica sleeves as a part of _[Miles Davis: The Complete Columbia Album Collection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis:_The_Complete_Columbia_Album_Collection "Miles Davis: The Complete Columbia Album Collection")_, a box set commissioned by [Sony Legacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legacy_Recordings "Legacy Recordings").[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-79) According to Tingen, this edition sounded "like a woolen blanket has been lifted from the previous \[1991\] CD", clarifying especially Cosey, who had sounded muted in the mix. He still found it somewhat low on bass, which he attributed to the original master tapes: "The LP version also didn't have a lot of bass, but I always assumed this was due to the LP cut: with long album lengths the grooves can hold less bass information."[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTETingen2009-80) ## Reception The Festival Hall concert itself had been received enthusiastically by the Osaka audience. "I had no idea what \[they\] were going to do", Henderson recalled. "They gave us a standing ovation that was almost as long as the concert."[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTECole200727-13) The music translated poorly to the commercial marketplace, however, as _Agharta_ was ill-suited for "FM airplay, dancing, or passive listening", in Nicholson's words. The LP's only appearance on a popular music chart was in April 1976 on the American [_Billboard_ chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200"), where it spent five weeks and reached a peak position of 168.[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-81) ### Critical reviews _Agharta_ was also largely unsuccessful with professional critics.[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTESvorinich2015152-82) According to [Robert Christgau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Christgau "Robert Christgau"), it proved the most widely panned of Davis' double albums in the 1970s.[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChristgau1981103-72) _[The Stranger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Stranger_(newspaper) "The Stranger (newspaper)")_'s Dave Segal claims it was one of the most divisive records ever, challenging both critics and the artist's core audience much in the same way [Lou Reed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou_Reed "Lou Reed")'s _[Metal Machine Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metal_Machine_Music "Metal Machine Music")_ album had in 1975.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTESegal2015-83) [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0b/Gary_Giddins.JPG/500px-Gary_Giddins.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gary_Giddins.JPG) [Gary Giddins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Giddins "Gary Giddins") (2009), one of several jazz critics who originally disliked the album, though he later warmed to it Reviewing for _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")_ in April 1976, [Robert Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Palmer_(American_writer) "Robert Palmer (American writer)") said _Agharta_ is marred by long stretches of "sloppy, one-chord jams", disjointed sounds, and a banal quality clearly rendered by the impeccable Japanese engineering. He complained that Davis' use of the wah-wah pedal inhibits his ability to phrase notes and that the septet sounds poor "by rock standards", particularly Cosey, whose overamplified guitar "whines and rumbles like a noisy machine shop" and relegates Lucas to background riffs.[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPalmer1976REC2-84) _[Jazz Forum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Forum_(magazine) "Jazz Forum (magazine)")_ reviewer [Andrzej Trzaskowski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrzej_Trzaskowski "Andrzej Trzaskowski") wrote that Fortune seems to be the only jazz musician on the record, finding his solos often flawless, while disparaging the performances of Davis, Lucas, and Cosey, whose guitar and synthesizer effects he found pointlessly brutal. In Trzaskowski's opinion, the individual segments do not cohere as a whole and are further hampered by the clichéd "rock phraseology" of the guitarists, who he said lack wit, harmony, and taste.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrzaskowski197674-37) Jazz critic [Ian Carr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Carr "Ian Carr") thought the album "suffers from a monotony of sound" that he attributed mostly to Lucas and Cosey's relentlessly eruptive guitar playing. Alongside the band's intense rhythms, Davis' trumpet sounds fatigued, dejected, and out of place to Carr. In general, he deemed the music "too non- [Western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_culture "Western culture") in the sense of too much rhythm and not enough structure".[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-85) [Gary Giddins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Giddins "Gary Giddins") penned an angrily dismissive review of _Agharta_ in _[The Village Voice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Village_Voice "The Village Voice")_, in which he charged Davis with failing to assert his musical presence on what he said is not "just a bad record" but also "a sad one". In Giddins' mind, the trumpeter "doesn't exploit the backbeat, he succumbs to it, and the worst consequence is not the ensuing monotony, which theoretically a soloist could turn to his advantage."[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-86) A few days after his review was published, he was sent a package full of large cotton swabs, industrial-strength [scouring pads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scouring_pad "Scouring pad"), and a card that read, "The next time you review Miles Davis clean out your head."[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGiddins2006186-87) _Agharta_ received some positive contemporary commentary. Nathan Cobb from _[The Boston Globe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Boston_Globe "The Boston Globe")_ appraised the record favorably in 1976, calling it "a kind of firestorm for the '70s" with a "positively cosmic" rhythmic foundation. In conclusion, he regarded Davis as "the one who leads the others through the unknown waters of electronic jazz rock".[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTECobb1976A8-88) In _DownBeat_, Gilmore said the band sounds best on the breakneck segments opening each of the two discs, where Cosey's ferocious improvisations "achieve a staggering emotional dimension" lacking on the slower passages, which he felt are still redeemed by Davis' elegiac trumpet playing. He rated the album four stars, out of a possible five.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlkyerEnrightKoransky2007271-41) [Lester Bangs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lester_Bangs "Lester Bangs") found _Agharta_ too difficult to definitively assess but nonetheless more fascinating than most other music being released at the time. He wrote in _[Phonograph Record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phonograph_Record_(magazine) "Phonograph Record (magazine)")_ that Davis' new music is the product of his heart's once luminous "emotional capacities" having been shattered by "great, perhaps unbearable suffering".[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBangs2008170%E2%80%9371-89) He went on to write: > In [Patti Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patti_Smith "Patti Smith")'s words, his music now to me is "a branch of cold flame," and I think that, crushed as that heart is, the soul beyond it has not been and cannot ever be destroyed. Like [Graham Greene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graham_Greene "Graham Greene")'s " [burnt-out case](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Burnt-Out_Case "A Burnt-Out Case")" (and he was not referring to drugs), perhaps that is all that is left. But in a curious way that almost glows uniquely brighter in its own dark coldness; and that, that which is all that is left, is merely the universe.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBangs2008171-90) ## Aftermath and legacy [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c2/Jazz_group_at_AghaRTA.jpg/500px-Jazz_group_at_AghaRTA.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jazz_group_at_AghaRTA.jpg) A [Czech jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_in_Czechoslovakia "Jazz in Czechoslovakia") group at [Prague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague "Prague")'s AghaRTA Jazz Centrum in 2008 By the time of the second Osaka concert (captured on _Pangaea_), the band's level of energy had diminished significantly, and Davis sounded particularly absent. As Mtume recounted, "he became ill in the evening, and you can hear the difference in the energy."[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTETingen2001165-40) Upon returning from Japan, the trumpeter fell ill again and was hospitalized for three months.[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTENicholson1998128-91) He held a few more shows and studio sessions with the band, but his health worsened; their last show on September 5, 1975, in [Central Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Park "Central Park") ended abruptly when Davis left the stage and began to cry in pain.[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-92) Davis retired soon after – citing physical, spiritual, and creative exhaustion – and lived as a recluse for the next several years, often struggling with bouts of depression and further medical treatment.[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-93) After resuming his recording career in 1980, he abandoned the direction he had pursued in the 1970s, instead playing a style of fusion far more melodic and accessible to audiences, until his death in 1991.[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-94) The day after he died, Prague's [Wenceslas Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wenceslas_Square "Wenceslas Square") saw the opening of the AghaRTA Jazz Centrum, a small jazz club named after the album, hosting nightly performances and an annual festival played by local and international Hull (critic)")_ | A–[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHulln.d.-102) | Retrospective professional reviews _Agharta_ underwent positive critical reassessment, beginning in 1980 when Davis returned to the jazz scene.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlkyerEnrightKoransky2007118-103) Of the albums documenting his 1973–75 band, it was considered by many critics to be the best, in retrospect.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGluckin2015-44) For Giddins, it had become one of his favorite albums from the trumpeter's electric period, as he reevaluated its elements of drama, relentless tension, and what he considered the best performances of Fortune and Cosey's careers. "There really is not a moment when the music fails to reflect the ministrations of the sorcerer himself", he later said.[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGiddins2006186%E2%80%937-104) In _[Christgau's Record Guide: Rock Albums of the Seventies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christgau's_Record_Guide:_Rock_Albums_of_the_Seventies "Christgau's Record Guide: Rock Albums of the Seventies")_ (1981), Christgau saw _Agharta_ as Davis' finest music since _Jack Johnson_. He called it an "angry, dissociated, funky" record built on the septet's virtuosic performance, particularly Foster's "guileless show of chops" and Fortune's performance, which he deemed the best [woodwind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodwind_instrument "Woodwind instrument") playing on a Davis album from this decade.[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChristgau1981103-72)[\[nb 3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-106) Reflecting on the trumpeter's 1970s concert recordings in _[The Rolling Stone Album Guide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rolling_Stone_Album_Guide "The Rolling Stone Album Guide")_ (1992), [J. D. Considine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._D._Considine "J. D. Considine") contended that _Agharta_'s "alternately audacious, poetic, hypnotic, and abrasive" music had endured the passage of time best.[\[104\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEConsidine1992182-107) Davis biographer [Jack Chambers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Chambers_(linguist) "Jack Chambers (linguist)") believed it proved far better than most of his other electric albums, and that the "Maiysha" and "Jack Johnson" segments in particular "magically brought into focus the musical forces over which many thought Davis had lost control".[\[105\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChambers1998234,_275-108) Although Davis' use of wah-wah was frequently dismissed in the past as a failed experiment, Richard Cook and [Brian Morton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Morton_(Scottish_writer) "Brian Morton (Scottish writer)") believed the effects pedal had in fact helped Davis achieve remarkably adventurous playing on _Agharta_.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTECookMorton2006330-52) Cook named it among Davis' best works and the culmination of the music he had begun to explore on _[Bitches Brew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew "Bitches Brew")_ (1970). While possessing an "epic" sound and scope, _Agharta_ is also "a great band record", in his opinion: "Even though Davis contributed only telling details, he still cued exceptional performances from his men."[\[106\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-109) In Tingen's mind, it represents the "high plateau" of Davis' electric explorations. He said that, because Davis gave the band leeway for constant interplay, the music exhibits an "organic and fluid quality" as well as a greater variety of textures, rhythms, timbres, and moods than _Dark Magus_.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTETingen2001163-33) [Henry Kaiser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Kaiser_(musician) "Henry Kaiser (musician)") called it the best ensemble performance of jazz's electric era, and Steve Holtje, writing in _[MusicHound Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MusicHound "MusicHound")_ (1998), credited Davis with [conducting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conducting "Conducting") the album's "heroes" to sculpt "moments of shattering beauty and soul-rending vehemence".[\[107\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-110) In the _[All Music Guide to Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Music_Guide_to_Jazz "All Music Guide to Jazz")_ (2002), Thom Jurek considered the album inarguably the "greatest electric funk-rock jazz record ever" and declared, "there is simply nothing like _Agharta_ in the canon of recorded music."[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJurek2002315-27) ### Influence > Back in the mid-1970s, fans who had formed emotional attachments to the moody soundscapes of _[Filles de Kilimanjaro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filles_de_Kilimanjaro "Filles de Kilimanjaro")_ and _[In a Silent Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way "In a Silent Way")_ had trouble adjusting to the electronic firestorms of _Agharta_. While Mr. Davis was being treated for two broken legs and a bone disease, a newer generation of listeners and musicians was inspired by the abrasive music his last band of the 70's had recorded. — [Robert Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Palmer_(American_writer) "Robert Palmer (American writer)") (1985)[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPalmer1985-111) Despite being one of Davis' lesser-known records, _Agharta_ belonged to a period in his career that influenced artists in [British jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_jazz "British jazz"), [new wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_wave_music "New wave music"), and [punk rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punk_rock "Punk rock"), including guitarists [Robert Quine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Quine "Robert Quine") and [Tom Verlaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Verlaine "Tom Verlaine").[\[109\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-112) It inspired a generation of musicians to focus on cathartic playing rather than precise instrumentation and composition.[\[110\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlkyerEnrightKoransky2007307-113) Quine was particularly fascinated by Cosey's electric guitar sounds; Bangs, who attended Quine's performance with [the Voidoids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Hell_and_the_Voidoids "Richard Hell and the Voidoids") in 1977, claimed "he steals from _Agharta_! And makes it _work_!"[\[111\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-114) Writers have since lauded the quality and originality of Cosey's playing on the album, viewing it as a standard for guitar mastery and contrast.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGluckin2015-44) Jazz critic [Bill Milkowski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Milkowski "Bill Milkowski") credited his excursive style for "spawning an entire school of 'sick' guitar playing" and said the combination of Fortune's acerbic sax lines atop Foster, Henderson, and Lucas' syncopated grooves were 10 years ahead of [Steve Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Coleman "Steve Coleman") and [Greg Osby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greg_Osby "Greg Osby")'s [M-Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M-Base "M-Base") experiments.[\[110\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlkyerEnrightKoransky2007307-113) Tingen found Cosey's solos amazingly revealing and advanced when heard decades later: "Sometimes growling, scurrying around all corners like a caged tiger, sometimes soaring like a bird, sometimes deliriously abstract, sometimes elegantly melodic and tender, his electric guitar concept is one of the most original to have been devised on the instrument."[\[112\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMilkowski2007-115) In Christgau's opinion, the noises he produced on the first track's second half "comprise some of the greatest free improvisations ever heard in a 'jazz'-'rock' context."[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChristgau1981103-72) [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d0/Guild_s-100.jpg/330px-Guild_s-100.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Guild_s-100.jpg) A [Guild S-100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guild_S-100 "Guild S-100"), played by [Pete Cosey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Cosey "Pete Cosey") on _Agharta_ According to Nicholson, _Agharta_ and other jazz-rock recordings such as _[Emergency!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency!_(album) "Emergency! (album)")_ (1970) by [the Tony Williams Lifetime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tony_Williams_Lifetime "The Tony Williams Lifetime") suggested the genre was progressing toward "a whole new musical language... a wholly independent genre quite apart from the sound and conventions of anything that had gone before". This development dwindled with the commercialism of [jazz in the 1980s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980s_in_jazz "1980s in jazz"), although _Agharta_ remained a pivotal and influential record through the 1990s, especially on artists in the [experimental rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experimental_rock "Experimental rock") genre.[\[113\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-116) It became one of the favorite albums for English musician [Richard H. Kirk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_H._Kirk "Richard H. Kirk"), who recalled playing it often while working at [Chris Watson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Watson_(musician) "Chris Watson (musician)")'s loft during their early years in the band [Cabaret Voltaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabaret_Voltaire_(band) "Cabaret Voltaire (band)"). "I can see how this album might have annoyed people but for me it was really nice grooves with improvisation and would open out and become more minimal", Kirk later told _[The Quietus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Quietus "The Quietus")_.[\[114\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAcharya2016-117) Along with _On the Corner_, it was also a major influence on the [Beastie Boys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beastie_Boys "Beastie Boys")' 1994 album _[Ill Communication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ill_Communication "Ill Communication")_.[\[115\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReynolds2011182-118) In 1998, composer and bandleader [David Sanford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Sanford_(composer) "David Sanford (composer)") completed his [dissertation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissertation "Dissertation") on _Agharta_ as a doctoral student in composition at [Princeton University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princeton_University "Princeton University"). In it, he argued that the album demonstrated how jazz has utilized a variety of external influences "to evolve or modernize itself". In an interview several years later, Sanford said it was an important work that had gone to the "fringes of jazz" and a place most other music has not explored since.[\[116\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-119) Visual artist [Arthur Jafa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Jafa "Arthur Jafa"), among the generation of fans originally attracted to _Agharta_, later drew on the album as a predominant influence behind his digitally animated film _AGHDRA_ (2021), an abstract meditation on trauma in the [African-American experience](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African-American_experience "African-American experience") expressed through visuals of an eruptive sea and a soundtrack recalling Davis' experimental sounds and arrangements.[\[117\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYablonsky2021-120)[\[nb 4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta_(album)#cite_note-121) ## Track listing
