(1973) | | _**On the Corner**_ is a studio album by the American jazz trumpeter, bandleader, and composer [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis"). It was recorded in June and July 1972 and released on October 11 of that year by [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records"). The album continued Davis' exploration of [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion"), and explicitly drew on the [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk") of [Sly Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sly_Stone "Sly Stone") and [James Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Brown "James Brown"), the [experimental music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experimental_music "Experimental music") of [Karlheinz Stockhausen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karlheinz_Stockhausen "Karlheinz Stockhausen"), the [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") of [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman"), and the work of collaborator [Paul Buckmaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Buckmaster "Paul Buckmaster").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-1) Recording sessions for the album featured a changing lineup of musicians including bassist [Michael Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Henderson "Michael Henderson"), guitarist [John McLaughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McLaughlin_(musician) "John McLaughlin (musician)"), and keyboardists [Chick Corea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chick_Corea "Chick Corea") and [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"), with Davis playing his trumpet through a [wah-wah pedal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wah-wah_pedal "Wah-wah pedal").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-Christgau-2) Davis and producer [Teo Macero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teo_Macero "Teo Macero") then [spliced and edited](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reel-to-reel_audio_tape_recording#As_a_musical_instrument "Reel-to-reel audio tape recording") various takes into compositions. The album's packaging did not credit any musicians, in an attempt to make the instruments less discernible to critics. Its artwork features [Corky McCoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corky_McCoy "Corky McCoy")'s cartoon designs of urban [African-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Americans "African Americans") characters. _On the Corner_ was in part an effort by Davis to reach a younger African-American audience who had largely left jazz for funk and rock music; instead, due to Columbia's lack of [target marketing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Target_market "Target market"), it was one of Davis' worst-selling albums, and was scorned by jazz critics and many of Davis' contemporaries at the time of its release.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-3)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-Chinen-4) It would be Davis's last studio album of the 1970s conceived as a complete work; subsequently, he recorded haphazardly and focused on live performance before temporarily retiring in 1975.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-5) Critical and popular reception of _On the Corner_ has improved dramatically with the passage of time.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-Reynolds-6) Many outside the jazz community have since called it an innovative musical statement anticipating subsequent developments in styles including funk, jazz, [post-punk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-punk "Post-punk"), [electronica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronica "Electronica"), and [hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip-hop "Hip-hop"). In 2007, _On the Corner_ was reissued as part of the six-disc box set _[The Complete On the Corner Sessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Complete_On_the_Corner_Sessions "The Complete On the Corner Sessions")_. ## Background [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/72/Miles_Davis-140916-0016-103WP_%28cropped%29.jpg/500px-Miles_Davis-140916-0016-103WP_%28cropped%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Miles_Davis-140916-0016-103WP_(cropped).jpg) Davis performing in Germany, 1971 Following his turn to [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") in the late 1960s and the release of rock- and funk-influenced albums such as _[Bitches Brew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew "Bitches Brew")_ (1970) and _[Jack Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Johnson_(album) "Jack Johnson (album)")_ (1971), Miles Davis received backlash from the jazz community.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-nashville-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-milestones-8) Critics accused him of abandoning his talents and pandering to commercial trends, though his recent albums had been commercially unsuccessful by his standards. Other jazz contemporaries, such as [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"), [Cecil Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor "Cecil Taylor"), and [Gil Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gil_Evans "Gil Evans"), defended Davis; the latter stated that "jazz has always used the rhythm of the time, whatever people danced to". In early 1972, Davis began conceiving _On the Corner_ as an attempt to reconnect with a young [African-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African-American "African-American") audience which had largely forsaken jazz for the [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk") of artists such as [Sly and the Family Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sly_and_the_Family_Stone "Sly and the Family Stone") and [James Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Brown "James Brown").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-milestones-8) In an interview with _[Melody Maker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melody_Maker "Melody Maker")_, Davis stated: > "I don't care who buys the record so long as they get to the black people so I will be remembered when I die. I'm not playing for any white people, man. I wanna hear a black guy say 'Yeah, I dig Miles Davis.'"[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-milestones-8) [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/ba/Karlheinz_Stockhausen_par_Claude_Truong-Ngoc_1980_%28cropped%29.jpg/500px-Karlheinz_Stockhausen_par_Claude_Truong-Ngoc_1980_%28cropped%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Karlheinz_Stockhausen_par_Claude_Truong-Ngoc_1980_(cropped).jpg) _On the Corner_ was partly inspired by the musical concepts of [Karlheinz Stockhausen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karlheinz_Stockhausen "Karlheinz Stockhausen") (pictured in 1980). Davis also cited German experimental composer [Karlheinz Stockhausen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karlheinz_Stockhausen "Karlheinz Stockhausen") as an influence, in particular his forays into [electronic music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_music "Electronic music") and tape manipulation.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-stockhausen-9)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-popmatters-10) Davis was first introduced to Stockhausen's work in 1972 by collaborator [Paul Buckmaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Buckmaster "Paul Buckmaster"), and the trumpeter reportedly kept a cassette recording of Stockhausen's electroacoustic composition _[Hymnen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hymnen "Hymnen")_ (1966–67) in his [Lamborghini Miura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamborghini_Miura "Lamborghini Miura").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-popmatters-10)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-11) The electronic sound processing found in _Hymnen_ and _[Telemusik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telemusik "Telemusik")_ (1966) and the development of musical structures by expanding and minimizing [processes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Process_music "Process music") based on preconceived principles, as featured in _[Plus-Minus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plus-Minus_(Stockhausen) "Plus-Minus (Stockhausen)")_ and other Stockhausen works from the 1960s and early 1970s, appealed to Davis.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-Gluck107-12) Davis began to apply these ideas to his music by adding and taking away instrumentalists and other aural elements throughout a recording to create a progressively changing soundscape.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-Gluck107-12) He later wrote in his autobiography: > I had always written in a circular way and through Stockhausen I could see that I didn't want to ever play again from eight bars to eight bars, because I never end songs: they just keep going on. Through Stockhausen I understood music as a process of elimination and addition.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-13) The work of Buckmaster, who played [electric cello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_cello "Electric cello") on the album and contributed some arrangements, and the [harmolodic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmolodics "Harmolodics") theory of avant-garde jazz saxophonist [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman"), whom Davis had previously disparaged,[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-14) would also influence the album; Davis later described _On the Corner_ as "Stockhausen plus funk plus Ornette Coleman."[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-wire-15) Using this conceptual framework, Davis reconciled ideas from [contemporary classical music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_classical_music "Contemporary classical music"), jazz, and rhythm-based [dance music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dance_music "Dance music").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-Gluck107-12) ## Recording and production [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/Michael_Henderson-140915-0040WP_%28cropped%29.jpg/500px-Michael_Henderson-140915-0040WP_%28cropped%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Michael_Henderson-140915-0040WP_(cropped).jpg) Bassist [Michael Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Henderson "Michael Henderson") was a fixture throughout the recording sessions. Recording sessions for _On the Corner_ began in June 1972. Both sides of the record consisted of repetitive drum and bass grooves based around a one-chord [modal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz "Modal jazz") approach,[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-nashville-7)[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-Tingen-16) with the final cut edited down from hours of jams featuring changing lineups underpinned by bassist [Michael Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Henderson "Michael Henderson").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-milestones-8) Other musicians involved in the recording included guitarist [John McLaughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McLaughlin_(musician) "John McLaughlin (musician)"), drummers [Jack DeJohnette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_DeJohnette "Jack DeJohnette") and [Billy Hart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Hart "Billy Hart"), and keyboardists Herbie Hancock and [Chick Corea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chick_Corea "Chick Corea").[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-strangerafs-17) _On the Corner_ utilized three keyboardists, as on _Bitches Brew_, while pairing Hart—who had also played in Hancock's _[Mwandishi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mwandishi "Mwandishi")_-era band—with DeJohnette and two percussionists. [Bennie Maupin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bennie_Maupin "Bennie Maupin"), Hancock's woodwind player at the time, played [bass clarinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_clarinet "Bass clarinet"), and [Dave Liebman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Liebman "Dave Liebman") was recruited as saxophonist.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-Gluck107-12) Jazz historian [Robert Gluck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Gluck "Robert Gluck") later discussed the performances: > "The recording functions on two layers: a relatively static, dense thicket of rhythmic pulse provided by McLaughlin's percussive guitar attack, the multiple percussionists, and Henderson's funky bass lines, plus keyboard swirls on which the horn players solo. Segments of [tabla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabla "Tabla") and [sitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sitar "Sitar") provide a change of mood and pace. Aside from 'Black Satin,' most of the material consists of intense [vamps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vamp_(music) "Vamp (music)") and rhythmic layering."[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-Gluck107-12) Compared to Davis' previous recordings, _On the Corner_ found him playing the trumpet scarcely.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-Gleason_2011-18)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-milestones-8) The album also saw his producer, [Teo Macero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teo_Macero "Teo Macero"), employ tape editing procedures which he had first used on Davis' 1969 album _[In a Silent Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way "In a Silent Way")_ to combine various takes into a single cohesive work.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-Tingen-16)[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-stereogum.com-19) Macero's tape editing technique was informed by his experiences with New York-based avant-garde and electronic composers such as [Edgard Varèse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgard_Var%C3%A8se "Edgard Varèse") and [Vladimir Ussachevsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Ussachevsky "Vladimir Ussachevsky") in the 1950s and 1960s.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-20)[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-21) The tape editing process also allowed Macero and Davis to overdub and add effects after the sessions.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-Tingen-16) Some of the musicians expressed misgivings about the unconventional musical direction of the sessions; Liebman opined that "the music appeared to be pretty chaotic and disorganized,"[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-nashville-7) while Buckmaster called it his "least favorite Miles album."[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-Tingen-16) ## Packaging The album cover featured an illustration by cartoonist [Corky McCoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corky_McCoy "Corky McCoy") depicting [ghetto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghetto "Ghetto") caricatures.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-milestones-8) The packaging only featured one stylized photograph of Davis, and was originally released with no musician credits, leading to ongoing confusion about which musicians appeared on the album. Davis later admitted to doing this intentionally:[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-Feather-22) "I didn't put those names on _On the Corner_ specially for that reason, so now the critics have to say, 'What's this instrument, and what's this?' ... I'm not even gonna put my picture on albums anymore. Pictures are dead, man. Gleason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_J._Gleason "Ralph J. Gleason") found the music very "lyrical and rhythmic" while praising the dynamic stereo recording and calling Davis "a magician". He concluded by saying that "the impact of the whole is greater than the sum of any part."[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-Gleason_2011-18) The album's commercial performance was as limited as that of Davis's albums since _[Bitches Brew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew "Bitches Brew")_, topping the _[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_(magazine) "Billboard (magazine)")_ jazz chart but only peaking at No. 156 in the more heterogeneous [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200"). Tingen wrote that "predictably, this impenetrable and almost tuneless concoction of avant-garde classical, [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz"), [African](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_of_Africa "Music of Africa"), [Indian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindustani_classical_music "Hindustani classical music") and acid funk bombed spectacularly, leading to decades in the wilderness. | Professional ratings _**Outward Bound**_ is the debut [album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album "Album") by [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") multi-instrumentalist [Eric Dolphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy "Eric Dolphy"), released in 1960. It is oriented towards straight [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop"), and slightly less adventurous than the majority of his later recordings.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outward_Bound_(Eric_Dolphy_album)#cite_note-Simosko44-4) The album was recorded at [Van Gelder Studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Gelder_Studio "Van Gelder Studio") in New Jersey and features Dolphy in a quintet with trumpeter [Freddie Hubbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Hubbard "Freddie Hubbard"), pianist [Jaki Byard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaki_Byard "Jaki Byard"), bassist [George Tucker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Tucker_(musician) "George Tucker (musician)") and drummer [Roy Haynes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Haynes "Roy Haynes"). Hubbard had shared living space with Dolphy when they both first arrived in New York City.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outward_Bound_(Eric_Dolphy_album)#cite_note-5) The cover artwork was by Dolphy's friend [Richard "Prophet" Jennings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Slater_Jennings "Richard Slater Jennings").[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outward_Bound_(Eric_Dolphy_album)#cite_note-6) Of the three Dolphy originals on the album, "G.W." is dedicated to the [Californian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California") bandleader [Gerald Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Wilson "Gerald Wilson"),[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outward_Bound_(Eric_Dolphy_album)#cite_note-Simosko44-4) "Les" is named after the [trombonist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trombone "Trombone") Lester Robertson,[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outward_Bound_(Eric_Dolphy_album)#cite_note-payne-7) and "245" was the number of Dolphy's house on Carlton Avenue, in Brooklyn's [Fort Greene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Greene,_Brooklyn "Fort Greene, Brooklyn") neighborhood.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outward_Bound_(Eric_Dolphy_album)#cite_note-8) ## Reception \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Outward_Bound_(Eric_Dolphy_album)&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Reception")\] Jazz critic [Martin Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Williams_(writer) "Martin Williams (writer)") wrote: "From the first selection on Dolphy's first album under his own name... it was obvious that fresh and important talent had arrived."[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outward_Bound_(Eric_Dolphy_album)#cite_note-9) _[All About Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_About_Jazz "All About Jazz")_ reviewer Douglas Payne described the album as "an ardently passionate gathering with pristine contributions from some of jazz's most flexible avatars... The music ranks, perhaps, as some of Dolphy's most accessible and most easily enjoyed."[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outward_Bound_(Eric_Dolphy_album)#cite_note-payne-7) Regarding "G.W.", J. Hunter wrote: "While the rest of the band lays down beats and fills that would not be out of place on any bop date, Dolphy steps out of the head to blister us with a mind-boggling, lightning-fingered alto solo that threatens to go over a cliff at any moment. Dolphy and his partners maintain this unorthodox balancing act throughout the 1960 session."[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outward_Bound_(Eric_Dolphy_album)#cite_note-10) Writing for _[PopMatters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PopMatters "PopMatters")_, Sean Murphy stated that _Outward Bound_ "brings together a handful of the finest musicians who ever played their respective instruments, and it's more than a little coincidental that, when put in the same environment with a common purpose, there was an affinity and extra edge they conjured up, seemingly out of nowhere... If you've never experienced the joy that is Eric Dolphy, there is no better place to begin since this is where it all officially began. If, in the final analysis, it is not the unqualified masterpiece that _Out To Lunch_ would be, and does not possess the truly strange and unfathomable wonder of _Out There_, it can contentedly settle for merely being a great album. _Outward Bound_, in sum, is a top tier effort from a tremendous quintet, and it signals the start of an abbreviated but incendiary burst of creative genius."[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outward_Bound_(Eric_Dolphy_album)#cite_note-11) ## Track listing \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Outward_Bound_(Eric_Dolphy_album)&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Track listing")\] All compositions by Eric Dolphy except where noted. 1. (1968) | | _**Point of Departure**_ is a studio album by American [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") pianist and composer [Andrew Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Hill_(jazz_musician) "Andrew Hill (jazz musician)"), recorded in 1964 and released in 1965 on the [Blue Note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records") label. It features Hill in a sextet with alto saxophonist [Eric Dolphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy "Eric Dolphy"), tenor saxophonist [Joe Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Henderson "Joe Henderson"), trumpeter [Kenny Dorham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Dorham "Kenny Dorham"), bassist [Richard Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Davis_(bassist) "Richard Davis (bassist)") and drummer [Tony Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer) "Tony Williams (drummer)"). _Point of Departure_ was reissued on CD by [Blue Note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records") in 1988 and again in 1999 when recording engineer [Rudy Van Gelder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudy_Van_Gelder "Rudy Van Gelder") [remastered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remaster "Remaster") the album, adding alternate takes of "New Monastery", "Flight 19", and "Dedication". ## Reception | Review scores | | --- | | ( [Dubois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eug%C3%A8ne_Dubois "Eugène Dubois"), 1893) | _**Homo erectus**_ ([/ˌhoʊmoʊəˈrɛktəs/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")lit.'[upright](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/erectus "wikt:erectus") man') is an [extinct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extinction "Extinction") [species](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Species "Species") of [archaic human](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo "Homo") from the [Pleistocene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pleistocene "Pleistocene"), spanning nearly 2 million years. It is the first human species to evolve a humanlike [body plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Body_plan "Body plan") and [gait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_gait "Human gait"), to [leave Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_expansions_of_hominins_out_of_Africa "Early expansions of hominins out of Africa") and colonize Asia and Europe, and to [wield fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Control_of_fire_by_early_humans "Control of fire by early humans"). Some populations of _H. erectus_ were ancestors of later human species, including _[H. heidelbergensis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_heidelbergensis "Homo heidelbergensis")_—the [last common ancestor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_common_ancestor "Last common ancestor") of [modern humans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human "Human"), [Neanderthals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neanderthal "Neanderthal"), and [Denisovans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denisovan "Denisovan"). As such a widely distributed species both geographically and temporally, _H. erectus_ anatomy varies considerably. Subspecies are sometimes recognized: _[H. e. erectus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Java_Man "Java Man")_, _[H. e. pekinensis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peking_Man "Peking Man")_, _[H. e. soloensis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solo_Man "Solo Man")_, _[H. e. ergaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_ergaster "Homo ergaster")_, _[H. e. georgicus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dmanisi_hominins "Dmanisi hominins")_, and _[H. e. tautavelensis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tautavel_Man "Tautavel Man")_. The species was first [described](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Species_description "Species description") by [Eugène Dubois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eug%C3%A8ne_Dubois "Eugène Dubois") in 1893 as " _[Pithecanthropus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthropopithecus "Anthropopithecus") erectus_" using a skullcap, [molar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molar_(tooth) "Molar (tooth)"), and [femur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Femur "Femur") from [Java](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Java "Java"), Indonesia. Further discoveries around East Asia were used to contend that humanity evolved out of Asia. Based on [historical race concepts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_race_concepts "Historical race concepts"), it was argued that local _H. erectus_ populations evolved directly into local modern human populations ( [polycentrism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiregional_origin_of_modern_humans "Multiregional origin of modern humans")) rather than all humanity sharing a single [anatomically modern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_modern_human "Early modern human") ancestor ( [monogenism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monogenism "Monogenism")). As the fossil record improved over the mid-to-late 20th century, the ["Out of Africa"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_expansions_of_hominins_out_of_Africa "Early expansions of hominins out of Africa") theory and monogenism became the consensus. The typical skull has a pronounced brow ridge, a protruding jaw, and large teeth. The bones are much thicker than in modern humans. East Asian populations normally have an even more robust skeleton and larger brain volume—averaging 1,000cc (61cuin). Western _H. erectus_ brain volume could be as low as 546cc (33.3cuin) in _H. e. georgicus_. _H. erectus_ probably had a faster apelike [growth trajectory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_height "Human height"), lacking the [extended childhood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altriciality "Altriciality") required for [language acquisition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Language_acquisition "Language acquisition"). Reconstructed adult body dimensions range from 141–167cm (4ft 8in– 5ft 6in) in height and about 50kg (110lb) in weight. _H. erectus_ invented the [Acheulean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acheulean "Acheulean") [tool industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industry_(archaeology) "Industry (archaeology)"), a major innovation of large, heavy-duty [stone tools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone_tools "Stone tools"). These may have been used in butchery, vegetable processing, and woodworking of [spears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spear "Spear") and [digging sticks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digging_stick "Digging stick"). _H. erectus_ was a major predator of large herbivores on the expanding savannas during the [Quaternary glaciation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaternary_glaciation "Quaternary glaciation"). The species is usually characterized as the first [hunter-gatherer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunter-gatherer "Hunter-gatherer") and the first to practice [sexual division of labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_division_of_labor "Sexual division of labor"). Fire usage and cave habitation were probably not important aspects of daily life. Similarly, _H. erectus_ may not have often ventured into colder regions or cooked meat. The last known occurrence of _H. erectus_ is 108,000 to 117,000 years ago ( _H. e. soloensis_) in Southeast Asia, until the last savannas in the region gave way to jungle. ## Taxonomy See also: [Human taxonomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_taxonomy "Human taxonomy") ### Research history [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5e/Hypothetical_sketch_of_the_monophylitic_origin_and_of_the_diffusion_of_the_12_varieties_of_men_from_Lemuria_over_the_earth_LCCN2014649358.jpg/500px-Hypothetical_sketch_of_the_monophylitic_origin_and_of_the_diffusion_of_the_12_varieties_of_men_from_Lemuria_over_the_earth_LCCN2014649358.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hypothetical_sketch_of_the_monophylitic_origin_and_of_the_diffusion_of_the_12_varieties_of_men_from_Lemuria_over_the_earth_LCCN2014649358.jpg) In 1868, [Ernst Haeckel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Haeckel "Ernst Haeckel") suggested that early humans dispersed from the now-disproven hypothetical continent " [Lemuria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lemuria_(continent) "Lemuria (continent)")".[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-HsiaoPei2014-5)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-6) While [Charles Darwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Darwin "Charles Darwin") had hypothesized in his 1871 _[Descent of Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Descent_of_Man "Descent of Man")_ that humans most likely evolved in Africa,[\[note 2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-8) many late-19th century evolutionary naturalists postulated that Asia was the birthplace of humankind. Asia is midway between all continents via land routes or short sea crossings, providing optimal dispersal routes throughout the world. Among the major proponents of "Out of Asia" theory was [Ernst Haeckel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Haeckel "Ernst Haeckel"), who argued that the first human species (which he speculatively named _Homo primigenius_) evolved on a now-disproven hypothetical continent " [Lemuria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lemuria_(continent) "Lemuria (continent)")" from a species he termed _[Pithecanthropus alalus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthropopithecus "Anthropopithecus")_ (speechless ape-man). "Lemuria" had supposedly sunk below the [Indian Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Ocean "Indian Ocean"), accounting for the lack of fossil evidence.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-HsiaoPei2014-5) Dutch scientist [Eugène Dubois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eug%C3%A8ne_Dubois "Eugène Dubois") joined the [Royal Netherlands East Indies Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Netherlands_East_Indies_Army "Royal Netherlands East Indies Army") to search for the " [missing link](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missing_link_(human_evolution) "Missing link (human evolution)")" of human evolution in [Java](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Java "Java").[\[note 3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-10) At the [Trinil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinil "Trinil") site, his team found a skullcap and [molar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molar_(tooth) "Molar (tooth)") in 1891, and a [femur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Femur "Femur") in 1892 ( [Java Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Java_Man "Java Man")), which he named " _Pithecanthropus erectus_" in 1893.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-FOOTNOTETheunissen198954%E2%80%9359-11) He attempted to convince the European scientific community that he had found an upright-walking ape-man dating to the [late Pliocene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Pliocene "Late Pliocene") or [Early Pleistocene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Pleistocene "Early Pleistocene"); they dismissed his findings as some kind of non-human ape.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-HsiaoPei2014-5) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0c/Homo_erectus_Sangiran_17_IMG_5644_BMNH.jpg/500px-Homo_erectus_Sangiran_17_IMG_5644_BMNH.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Homo_erectus_Sangiran_17_IMG_5644_BMNH.jpg) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3c/Sinanthropus_Skull_XII.png/500px-Sinanthropus_Skull_XII.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sinanthropus_Skull_XII.png) Using fossils like [Sangiran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sangiran "Sangiran") (left) and [Peking Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peking_Man "Peking Man") (right), [Franz Weidenreich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franz_Weidenreich "Franz Weidenreich") and [Ralph von Koenigswald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustav_Heinrich_Ralph_von_Koenigswald "Gustav Heinrich Ralph von Koenigswald") argued that [Java Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Java_Man "Java Man") was an ancient human. Dubois argued that " _P. erectus_" was a [gibbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibbon "Gibbon")-like ape which was the precursor to a more familiar human body plan, but in the 1930s, Jewish-German anatomist [Franz Weidenreich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franz_Weidenreich "Franz Weidenreich") noticed a striking similarity with ancient human remains recently being unearthed in China ( [Peking Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peking_Man "Peking Man"), " _Sinanthropus pekinensis_").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-FOOTNOTETheunissen1989p._156-12)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBoazCiochon2004pp._59%E2%80%9360-13) This characterization became better supported as German-Dutch palaeontologist [Gustav Heinrich Ralph von Koenigswald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustav_Heinrich_Ralph_von_Koenigswald "Gustav Heinrich Ralph von Koenigswald") discovered more Indonesian ancient human remains over the decade at [Mojokerto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mojokerto_child "Mojokerto child"), [Sangiran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sangiran "Sangiran"), and [Ngandong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solo_Man "Solo Man").[\[note 4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-15)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBoazCiochon2004pp._60%E2%80%9362-16)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-17) Weidenreich believed that they were the direct ancestors of the local modern human [_Homo sapiens_ subspecies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_taxonomy#Homo_sapiens_subspecies "Human taxonomy"), in accord with [historical race concepts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_race_concepts "Historical race concepts") ( [polycentricism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiregional_origin_of_modern_humans "Multiregional origin of modern humans"))—that is, Peking Man was the direct ancestor of specifically [Chinese people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_people "Chinese people"), and Java Man of [Aboriginal Australians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aboriginal_Australian "Aboriginal Australian").[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Weidenreich1940-18)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Mayr1950-19) As the significance of racial distinction diminished with the development of [modern evolutionary synthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_evolutionary_synthesis "Modern evolutionary synthesis"), many fossil human species and genera around Asia, Africa, and Europe (including " _Pithecanthropus_" and " _Sinanthropus_") were reclassified as subspecies of _Homo erectus_.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Schwartz2010-20)[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBoazCiochon2004pp._70%E2%80%9373-21) During the late 20th century, some of the oldest _H. erectus_ fossils were discovered across Africa, the first being Kenyan archeologist [Louis Leakey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Leakey "Louis Leakey")'s [Olduvai Hominin 9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chellean_Man "Chellean Man") in 1960.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBoazCiochon2004pp._68%E2%80%9372-22) As the human fossil record expanded, the "Out of Africa" theory and [monogenism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monogenism "Monogenism") became the consensus: that all modern humans share a fully [anatomically modern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_modern_human "Early modern human") common ancestor. _H. erectus_ is now generally considered to be an African species which later dispersed across Eurasia, with later African populations giving rise to the modern human lineage.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBoazCiochon2004pp._151%E2%80%93153-23) ### Subspecies [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/Altruistic_behaviour_of_Homo_erectus.jpg/500px-Altruistic_behaviour_of_Homo_erectus.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Altruistic_behaviour_of_Homo_erectus.jpg) Artistic depiction of a group of _[Homo erectus georgicus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus_georgicus "Homo erectus georgicus")_, based on early hominin discoveries from [Dmanisi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dmanisi_historic_site "Dmanisi historic site"). By the middle of the 20th century, [human taxonomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_taxonomy "Human taxonomy") was in turmoil, with many poorly defined species and genera described across Europe, Asia, and Africa, which exaggerated the differences among them.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBoazCiochon2004p._65-24) In 1940, Weidenreich was the first to suggest reclassifying " _Sinanthropus pekinensis_" and " _Pithecanthropus erectus_" as subspecies of _H. erectus_.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Weidenreich1940-18) In 1950, German-American evolutionary biologist [Ernst Mayr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Mayr "Ernst Mayr") entered this field. Surveying a "bewildering diversity of names" and many proposals for consolidation, he decided to reclassify human fossils into three species of _[Homo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo "Homo")_: " _H. transvaalensis_" (the [australopithecines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australopithecine "Australopithecine")), _H. erectus_ (including " _Sinanthropus_", " _Pithecanthropus_", and various other Asian, African, and European taxa), and _H. sapiens_ (including anything younger than _H. erectus_, such as modern humans and Neanderthals). Mayr defined these species as a sequential lineage, each evolving into the next ( [chronospecies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chronospecies "Chronospecies")).[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Mayr1950-19) Though later Mayr changed his opinion on the australopithecines (recognizing _[Australopithecus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australopithecus "Australopithecus")_), his more [conservative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lumpers_and_splitters "Lumpers and splitters") view of [archaic human](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaic_human "Archaic human") diversity became widely adopted in the subsequent decades.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Schwartz2010-20) > ...never more than one species of man existed on the earth at any one time... If fossils of [Congo pygmies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_pygmies "African pygmies") and of [Watusi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tutsi "Tutsi") were to be found in the same deposit by a paleontologist, a million years hence, he might well think that they belonged to two different species. — [Ernst Mayr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Mayr "Ernst Mayr"), 1950[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Mayr1950-19) In the 1970s, as [population genetics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_genetics "Population genetics") was being formulated, the anatomical variation of _H. erectus_ across its wide geographic and temporal range (the basis for the subspecies distinctions) became better understood as [clines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cline_(biology) "Cline (biology)")—different populations which attained some anatomical regionality but were not reproductively isolated.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBoazCiochon2004pp._151%E2%80%93153-23) In general, subspecies names for _H. erectus_ are now used for convenience to indicate time and region rather than specific anatomical trends.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Anton2002-25) > ...to paleontologists in general, subspecies are epiphenomena which do not merit the attention paid to species... The pursuit of subspecies in the fossil record is at best fraught with difficulty, and is more probably futile. — [Ian Tattersall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Tattersall "Ian Tattersall"), 1986[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-26) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6f/Ergaster_Skull.png/330px-Ergaster_Skull.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ergaster_Skull.png) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e8/Erectus_Skull.png/330px-Erectus_Skull.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Erectus_Skull.png) Reconstructions of _[H. e. ergaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_ergaster "Homo ergaster")_ ( [KNM ER 3733](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KNM_ER_3733 "KNM ER 3733")) left and _[H. e. pekinensis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peking_Man "Peking Man")_ right The more commonly used subspecies (if any are used) are:[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAnt%C3%B3n2003p._153-27) - _[H. e. erectus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Java_Man "Java Man")_ for earlier Indonesian fossils - _[H. e. pekinensis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peking_Man "Peking Man")_ for Chinese fossils - _[H. e. soloensis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solo_Man "Solo Man")_ for the latest-surviving Indonesian fossils - _[H. e. ergaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_ergaster "Homo ergaster")_ for African fossils - _[H. e. georgicus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dmanisi_hominins "Dmanisi hominins")_ for an early group of fossils from [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prehistoric_Georgia "Prehistoric Georgia")[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Rightmire2006-28) - _[H. e. tautavelensis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tautavel_Man "Tautavel Man")_ for Western European fossils[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Lumley2015-29) The ancient Georgia fossils have variably been classified as _H. e. ergaster_ (or quadrinomial _H. e. ergaster georgicus_),[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-30) as their own subspecies as _H. e. georgicus_, or as their own species _H. georgicus_.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Rightmire2006-28) Some authors may also elevate _H. ergaster_,[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-31) _H. soloensis_,[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-32) and _H. pekinensis_ to species level.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-33) Fossils relegated to _H. e. tautavelensis_ are traditionally assigned to _[H. heidelbergensis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_heidelbergensis "Homo heidelbergensis")_.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Lumley2015-29) ### Evolution and dispersal See also: [Human evolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_evolution "Human evolution") and [Early expansions of hominins out of Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_expansions_of_hominins_out_of_Africa "Early expansions of hominins out of Africa") [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1f/Dmanisi_fossils_D_2282_%2B_D_211_%28Replika%29.JPG/500px-Dmanisi_fossils_D_2282_%2B_D_211_%28Replika%29.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dmanisi_fossils_D_2282_+_D_211_(Replika).JPG) _[H. e. georgicus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dmanisi_hominins "Dmanisi hominins")_ (above) represents one of the earliest dispersals out of Africa about 1.8 million years ago.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Ferring2011-34) _H. erectus_ evolved in Africa from a population of _[H. habilis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_habilis "Homo habilis")_[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBoazCiochon2004pp._143%E2%80%93144-35)[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Zaim2011-36) and they coexisted for about half a million years.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-37) During this time interval, _H. erectus_ populations could display a mix of more "classically _erectus_" or "classically _habilis_" cranial anatomy and a wide range of brain volumes.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Baab2025-38) The oldest identified _H. erectus_ specimen is a 2.04 million year old skull, DNH 134, from [Drimolen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drimolen "Drimolen"), South Africa, coexisting with the australopithecine _[Paranthropus robustus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paranthropus_robustus "Paranthropus robustus")_.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Herries2020-1) _H. erectus_ dispersed out of Africa soon after evolution, the earliest recorded instances being _H. e. georgicus_ 1.78 to 1.85 million years ago in Georgia,[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Ferring2011-34) the Indonesian Mojokerto and Sangiran sites 1.6 to 1.8 million years ago,[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAnt%C3%B3n2003p._142-39)[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBoazCiochon2004p._162-40) and the Chinese [Yunxian Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yunxian_Man "Yunxian Man") 1.77 million years ago.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-41) Populations may have pushed into northwestern Europe at around the same time.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-42) While _H. erectus_ is usually considered the first [hominin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hominin "Hominin") to leave Africa, stone tools that may date to as far back as 2.48 and 2.1 million years ago (from [Zarqa Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zarqa_River "Zarqa River"), Jordan, and [Shangchen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shangchen "Shangchen"), China, respectively) could indicate that an earlier hominin species left Africa.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-43) Since _H. erectus_ was first defined in East Asia, those populations are sometimes distinguished as _H. erectus sensu stricto_ ("in the strict sense"), and African and West Eurasian populations as _H. erectus sensu lato_ ("in the broad sense"), but this may not reflect how these populations are actually related to each other.[\[note 5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-44)[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Anton2002-25)[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Zaim2011-36) Once established around the [Old World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_World "Old World"), _H. erectus_ evolved into other later species in the genus _Homo_, including: _H. heidelbergensis_, _[H. antecessor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_antecessor "Homo antecessor")_,[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Stringer2012-45) _[H. floresiensis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_floresiensis "Homo floresiensis")_,[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-46) and _[H. luzonensis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_luzonensis "Homo luzonensis")_.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-47) _H. heidelbergensis_, in turn, is usually placed as the [last common ancestor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_common_ancestor "Last common ancestor") of [Neanderthals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neanderthal "Neanderthal") ( _H. neanderthalensis_), [Denisovans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denisovan "Denisovan"), and modern humans.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Stringer2012-45) _H. erectus_ is thus a non-natural, [paraphyletic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraphyletic "Paraphyletic") grouping of fossils and does not include all the descendants of a last common ancestor.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Ni2021-48) Despite being designated as a different species, _H. erectus_ may have [interbred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interbreeding_between_archaic_and_modern_humans "Interbreeding between archaic and modern humans") with some of its descendant species, namely the common ancestor of Neanderthals and Denisovans ("Neandersovans").[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-49)[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-50) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/Spreading_homo_sapiens_la.svg/1280px-Spreading_homo_sapiens_la.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Spreading_homo_sapiens_la.svg) Successive dispersals of _Homo erectus_ (yellow), _[Homo neanderthalensis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neanderthal "Neanderthal")_ (ochre) and _[Homo sapiens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human "Human")_ (red, _[Out of Africa II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_of_Africa_II "Out of Africa II")_) The dispersal of _H. erectus_ is generally ascribed to the evolution of obligate [bipedalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biped "Biped"), better technology, and adoption of a carnivorous diet.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Carotenuto2016-51) However, the sudden adoption of carnivory could be [sampling bias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sampling_bias "Sampling bias"), with earlier species consuming the same amount of meat.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-52) Populations spread out via open grassland and woodland [savannas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savanna "Savanna"), which were expanding due to a global [aridification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aridification "Aridification") trend at the onset of the [Quaternary glaciation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaternary_glaciation "Quaternary glaciation").[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Carotenuto2016-51) _H. erectus_ is usually thought to have occupied the [Sahara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sahara "Sahara") and West Asia during [humid periods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_humid_period "African humid period"), but populations may have persisted into desert periods.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-53) Most _H. erectus sensu lato_ specimens date to 1 to 1.8 million years ago in the Early Pleistocene before giving way to descendant species.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Rizal2020-2) The classification of [Middle Pleistocene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Pleistocene "Middle Pleistocene") _Homo_ has been a controversial topic, termed "the muddle in the middle".[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Lumley2015-29)[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-54) _H. erectus sensu stricto_ persisted much longer than _sensu lato_, with the youngest population ( _H. e. soloensis_) dating to 108,000 to 117,000 years ago in [Late Pleistocene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Pleistocene "Late Pleistocene") Java.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Rizal2020-2) This population appears to have died out when the savannah corridors closed and tropical jungle took over.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-55) A 2021 phylogeny of some _H. erectus_ fossils using [tip dating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tip_dating "Tip
