## Biology As such a widely distributed species both across regions and through time, the anatomy of _H. erectus_ can vary considerably (regionality). Among living [primates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primate "Primate"), the degree of regionality achieved by _H. erectus_ ( [phenotypic plasticity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phenotypic_plasticity "Phenotypic plasticity")) is only observed in modern humans.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Anton2016-57) ### Head [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Solo_Man_reconstruction.png/500px-Solo_Man_reconstruction.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Solo_Man_reconstruction.png) [Franz Weidenreich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franz_Weidenreich "Franz Weidenreich")'s reconstruction of the _[H. e. soloensis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solo_Man "Solo Man")_ skull Dubois originally described the species using a skullcap, noting the traits of a low and thickened [cranial vault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cranial_vault "Cranial vault") and a continuous bar of bone forming the brow ridge (supraorbital torus).[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAnt%C3%B3n2003p._132-58) _H. erectus_ fossils typically share these traits, but the Kenyan [Koobi Fora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koobi_Fora "Koobi Fora") skulls notably have thinner skulls and weaker supraorbital tori.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAnt%C3%B3n2003p._147-59) He also used several other traits now considered more typical of _H. erectus sensu stricto_, such as a [sagittal keel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sagittal_keel "Sagittal keel") running across the midline of the skullcap, a bar of bone across the back of the skull ( [occipital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occipital_bone "Occipital bone") torus), and a strong crest on the [mastoid part of the temporal bone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mastoid_part_of_the_temporal_bone "Mastoid part of the temporal bone").[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAnt%C3%B3n2003p._132-58) These traits can be still be found, nonetheless, in a few _H. erectus sensu lato_ specimens, namely the 1.47 million year old Olduvai Hominin 9.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAnt%C3%B3n2003p._136-60) Compared to _H. erectus sensu lato_, the skullcap of _sensu stricto_ narrows considerably at the front, the face is bigger and presumably more [prognathic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prognathism "Prognathism") (it juts out more, but the face is poorly documented), and the molars are larger particularly in Indonesian fossils.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAnt%C3%B3n2003pp._146%E2%80%93147-61) _H. erectus_ was the first human species with a fleshy [nose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_nose "Human nose"), which is generally thought to have evolved in response to breathing dry air in order to retain moisture.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-62) Compared to earlier _Homo_, _H. erectus_ has smaller teeth, thinner [enamel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tooth_enamel "Tooth enamel"), and weaker [mandibles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandible "Mandible") (jawbone), likely due to a greater reliance on tool use and food processing.[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Ungar2006-63) The brain size of _H. erectus_ varies considerably, but is generally smaller in _H. erectus sensu lato_, as low as 546cc (33.3cuin) in [Dmanisi skull 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dmanisi_skull_5 "Dmanisi skull 5").[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-64) East Asian _H.erectus_ overall are rather big-brained, averaging roughly 1,000 cc,[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Anton2016-57) staying within the range of variation for modern humans.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-65) The late-surviving _H. e. soloensis_ has the biggest brain volume with one specimen measuring 1,251cc (76.3cuin).[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAnt%C3%B3n2003p._136-60) ### Body [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d6/Neanderthal_Museum_15.jpg/500px-Neanderthal_Museum_15.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Neanderthal_Museum_15.jpg) [Turkana Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkana_Boy "Turkana Boy") at the [Neanderthal Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neanderthal_Museum "Neanderthal Museum") The rest of the body is primarily understood by three partial skeletons from the Kenyan [Lake Turkana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Turkana#Anthropology "Lake Turkana") site, notably [Turkana Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkana_Boy "Turkana Boy"). Other postcranial fossils (all bones aside from the skull) attributed to _H. erectus_ are not associated with a skull, making attribution unverifiable. Though the body plan of earlier _Homo_ is poorly understood, _H. erectus_ is usually characterized as the first _Homo_ species with a human body plan, distinct from non-human apes.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAnt%C3%B3n2003pp._147%E2%80%93152-66)[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Anton2016-57)[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-67) The chest may have been short and [barrel-shaped](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barrel_chest "Barrel chest"), like other archaic humans.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Bastir2020-68) [Fossil tracks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fossil_track "Fossil track") near [Ileret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ileret "Ileret"), Kenya, suggest a [human gait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_gait "Human gait"). This adaptation is implicated in the dispersal of _H. erectus_ across the Old World.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Hatala-69) It is unclear when human ancestors [lost most of their body hair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prehistory_of_nakedness_and_clothing "Prehistory of nakedness and clothing"). Genetic analysis suggests that high activity in the [melanocortin 1 receptor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melanocortin_1_receptor "Melanocortin 1 receptor"), which produces dark skin, dates back to 1.2 million years ago. This could indicate the evolution of hairlessness around this time, as a lack of body hair would have left the skin exposed to harmful [UV radiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UV_radiation "UV radiation").[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-70) It is possible that populations in higher latitudes developed lighter skin to prevent [vitamin D deficiency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitamin_D_deficiency "Vitamin D deficiency"),[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-71) though a 300,000 to 500,000 year old Turkish _H. erectus_ specimen presents the earliest case of [tuberculous meningitis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuberculous_meningitis "Tuberculous meningitis"), which is typically exacerbated by vitamin D deficiency in dark-skinned people living in higher latitudes.[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-72) Hairlessness is generally thought to have facilitated sweating,[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-73) but it may also have helped to reduce parasite load, and was possibly reinforced by [sexual selection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_selection "Sexual selection").[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-74)[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-75) ### Size Height reconstructions range approximately 141–167cm (4ft 8in– 5ft 6in), with tropical populations typically reconstructed as scoring on the higher end like modern human populations. Adult weight is harder to approximate, but about 50kg (110lb) may have been normal. _H. erectus_ is usually thought to be the first human species with little size-specific [sexual dimorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_dimorphism "Sexual dimorphism"), but the variability of postcranial material makes this unclear.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Anton2016-57) A 2010 study estimates that the [Turkana Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkana_Boy "Turkana Boy") would have reached a height of 163cm (5ft 4in) if he had reached adulthood.[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-76) ### Growth and development The dimensions of a 1.8million years old adult female _H. e. ergaster_ pelvis from [Gona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gona,_Ethiopia "Gona, Ethiopia"), Ethiopia, suggests that she would have been capable of birthing children with a maximum prenatal brain size of 315cc (19.2cuin), about 30–50% of adult brain size, falling between [chimpanzees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chimpanzee "Chimpanzee") (~40%) and modern humans (28%).[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Simpson2008-77) Similarly, a 1.5 million year old infant skull from Mojokerto had a brain volume of about 72–84% the size of an adult, which suggests a brain growth trajectory more similar to that of non-human apes.[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Coqueugniot2004-78) This suggests that the childhood growth and development of _H. erectus_ was intermediate between that of chimpanzees and modern humans,[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Simpson2008-77) and the faster development rate suggests that [altriciality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altriciality "Altriciality") (an extended childhood) evolved at a later stage in human evolution.[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Coqueugniot2004-78) The faster development rate might also indicate a shorter expected lifespan compared to later _Homo_.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-79) ### Bone thickness [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/17/Homo_erectus_skull_cross-section.png/500px-Homo_erectus_skull_cross-section.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Homo_erectus_skull_cross-section.png) Cross sections of [Peking Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peking_Man "Peking Man") Skulls III (A) and XII (B), and [Java Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Java_Man "Java Man") Skull II (C) The bones are extraordinarily thickened, particularly in _Homo erectus sensu stricto_, so much so that skull fragments have sometimes been confused for fossil turtle [carapaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carapace "Carapace").[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBoazCiochon2004p._74-80) The [medullary canal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medullary_canal "Medullary canal") in the [long bones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_bone "Long bone") (where the [bone marrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bone_marrow "Bone marrow") is stored, in the limbs) is extremely narrowed (medullary [stenosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stenosis "Stenosis")). This degree of thickening is usually exhibited in semi-aquatic animals which use their heavy ( [pachyosteosclerotic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pachyosteosclerosis "Pachyosteosclerosis")) bones as ballasts to help them sink, induced by [hypothyroidism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypothyroidism "Hypothyroidism").[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Kennedy1985-81) It is unclear what function intense bone thickening could have served. Before more complete skeletons were discovered, Weidenreich suggested _H. erectus_ was a gigantic species.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-82) Other explanations include a far more violent and impact-prone lifestyle than other _Homo_, or pathological nutrient deficiencies.[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBoazCiochon2004pp._80%E2%80%9386-83) The supraorbital torus thickens with age, and may be a response to [bending](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bending "Bending") stresses from habitual loading of the front teeth.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-84) ## Culture ### Subsistence See also: [Hunting hypothesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunting_hypothesis "Hunting hypothesis") [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f1/Megalochelys_AMNH.jpg/500px-Megalochelys_AMNH.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Megalochelys_AMNH.jpg) _H. erectus_ overhunting may have led to the extinction of _[Megalochelys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megalochelys "Megalochelys")_ (above).[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Rhodin2015-85) _H. erectus_ was early-on portrayed as the earliest [hunter-gatherer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunter-gatherer "Hunter-gatherer") and a skilled predator of big game, relying on running. The few identified specimens of the _H. e. ergaster_ torso and pelvis may indicate a body plan more conducive for power running, unlike modern humans better [adapted for endurance running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endurance_running_hypothesis "Endurance running hypothesis").[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Bastir2020-68) The gradual shift to " [top predator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apex_predator "Apex predator")" may have led to its dispersal throughout Afro-Eurasia.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Carotenuto2016-51) Though scavenging may have instead played a bigger role at least in some populations, _H. erectus_ fossils are often associated with the butchered remains of large herbivores,[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBoazCiochon2004p._105-86) especially [elephants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elephant "Elephant"), [rhinos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhino "Rhino"), [hippos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippo "Hippo"), [bovines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bovine "Bovine"), and [boars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boar "Boar"). Tracking complex prey behaviors as well as the nutritional value of meat have been connected to brain volume growth.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-BenDor2011-87) _H. erectus_ is usually assumed to have practiced [sexual division of labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_division_of_labor "Sexual division of labor") much like recent hunter-gatherer societies, with men hunting and women gathering. This model is supported by a fossil trackway from Ileret, Kenya, made by a probably all-male band of over 20 _H. erectus_ individuals, possibly a hunting party or (similar to chimpanzees) a border patrol group.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Hatala-69) Since common modern human tapeworms began to diverge from those of other predators roughly 1.7 million years ago (specifically the [pork tapeworm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taenia_solium "Taenia solium"), [beef tapeworm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taenia_saginata "Taenia saginata"), and [Asian tapeworm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taenia_asiatica "Taenia asiatica")), not only was _H. erectus_ consuming meat regularly enough for speciation to occur in these parasites, but meat was probably consumed raw more often than not.[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBoazCiochon2004p._105%E2%80%93107-88) Some populations were collecting aquatic resources like fish, shellfish, and turtles at waterside sites, such as Lake Turkana[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-89) and Trinil.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-90) Underground [storage organs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storage_organ "Storage organ") (roots, tubers, etc.) were likely also major dietary components, and traces of the edible plant _[Celtis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celtis "Celtis")_ have been documented at several _H. erectus_ sites.[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Hardy2018-91) Possibly due to overhunting of the biggest game available, the dispersal of _H. erectus_ and descendant species may be implicated in the extinctions of large herbivores and the gradual reduction of average herbivore size over the Pleistocene.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-92) _H. erectus_ overhunting has been blamed by some authors for the decline of [proboscidean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proboscidea "Proboscidea") species as well as competing carnivores,[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-BenDor2011-87)[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-93)[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Faith2020-94) but their decline may be better attributed to the spread of grasslands.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Faith2020-94)[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-95) The giant tortoise _[Megalochelys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megalochelys "Megalochelys")_ may have been driven to extinction by _H. erectus_ in [Sundaland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sundaland "Sundaland") (what is now [Island Southeast Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Island_Southeast_Asia "Island Southeast Asia")), since species went extinct shortly after the arrival of _H. erectus_.[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Rhodin2015-85) ### Technology #### Stone tools [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Pi%C3%A8ce_bifaciale_Saint-Acheul_La_Garenne_Arch%C3%A9ologie_Nationale_01042018.jpg/500px-Pi%C3%A8ce_bifaciale_Saint-Acheul_La_Garenne_Arch%C3%A9ologie_Nationale_01042018.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pi%C3%A8ce_bifaciale_Saint-Acheul_La_Garenne_Arch%C3%A9ologie_Nationale_01042018.jpg) A [handaxe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handaxe "Handaxe") from the [Saint-Acheul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amiens "Amiens") site at the [Musée d'Archéologie nationale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_France "National Archaeological Museum, France"), France _H. erectus_ manufactured [Lower Paleolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Paleolithic "Lower Paleolithic") technologies, and is credited with the invention of the [Acheulean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acheulean "Acheulean") stone tool [industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industry_(archaeology) "Industry (archaeology)") at latest 1.95 million years ago.[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-96) This was a major technological breakthrough featuring large, heavy-duty tools; most iconically, the [handaxe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handaxe "Handaxe"). Over hundreds of thousands of years, the Acheulean eventually replaced its predecessor—the [Oldowan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oldowan "Oldowan") (a [chopper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chopper_(archaeology) "Chopper (archaeology)") and [flake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithic_flake "Lithic flake") industry)—in Africa, and spread out across Western Eurasia.[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Torre2016-97) This sudden innovation was typically explained as a response to environmental instability in order to process more types of food and broaden the diet combined with increasing brain size, which also allowed _H. erectus_ to colonize Eurasia. Despite this characterization of the Acheulean, the small-brained _H. e. georgicus_ was able to leave Africa despite only manufacturing Oldowan-style tools,[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Carotenuto2016-51)[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Torre2016-97) the 1.6 million year old DAN5/P1 specimen from [Gona, Ethiopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gona,_Ethiopia "Gona, Ethiopia") is associated with Acheulean style tools despite its low brain volume of 598cc (36.5cuin),[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Baab2025-38) and the handaxe does not seem to have been manufactured commonly in East Asia.[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-98) The lack of East Asian handaxes was first noted by American archaeologist [Hallam L. Movius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hallam_L._Movius "Hallam L. Movius") in 1948, who drew the " [Movius Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movius_Line "Movius Line")", dividing the East into a "chopping-tool culture" and the West into a "hand axe culture".[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Movius1948-99) Movius took this as evidence of inferiority of Far Eastern populations: > ...as early as [Lower Palaeolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Paleolithic "Lower Paleolithic") times Southern and Eastern Asia as a whole was a region of cultural retardation...very primitive forms of Early Man apparently persisted there long after types at a comparable stage of physical evolution had become extinct elsewhere. — [Hallam L. Movius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hallam_L._Movius "Hallam L. Movius"), 1948[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Movius1948-99) _H. erectus_ seems to have been using stone tools in butchery, vegetable processing, and woodworking (maybe manufacturing [spears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spear "Spear") and [digging sticks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digging_stick "Digging stick")).[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Hardy2018-91)[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Dominguez2001-100) In Africa, Oldowan sites are typically found alongside major fossil assemblages, but Acheulean sites normally feature more stone tools than fossils, so _H. erectus_ could have been using choppers and handaxes for different activities.[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Dominguez2001-100) These stone tools probably were not [hafted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hafting "Hafting") onto spears; this innovation is associated with the transition to the [Middle Paleolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Paleolithic "Middle Paleolithic") and the emergence of Neanderthals and modern humans.[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-101) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/31/Homo-erectus_Turkana-Boy_%28Ausschnitt%29_Fundort_Nariokotome%2C_Kenia%2C_Rekonstruktion_im_Neanderthal_Museum.jpg/960px-Homo-erectus_Turkana-Boy_%28Ausschnitt%29_Fundort_Nariokotome%2C_Kenia%2C_Rekonstruktion_im_Neanderthal_Museum.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Homo-erectus_Turkana-Boy_(Ausschnitt)_Fundort_Nariokotome,_Kenia,_Rekonstruktion_im_Neanderthal_Museum.jpg) Reconstruction of [Turkana Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkana_Boy "Turkana Boy") at the [Neanderthal Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neanderthal_Museum "Neanderthal Museum") wearing a cloak and hoisting a wooden [carrying pole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrying_pole "Carrying pole") Materials for stone tools were normally sourced locally, and it seems [blanks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithic_reduction "Lithic reduction") were usually chosen based on size rather than material quality.[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Torre2016-97) _H. erectus_ also produced tools from shells at Sangiran[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-102) and Trinil.[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Joordens2015-103) #### Fire Main article: [Control of fire by early humans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Control_of_fire_by_early_humans "Control of fire by early humans") _H. erectus_ is credited as the first human species to wield fire. The earliest claimed fire site is [Wonderwerk Cave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wonderwerk_Cave "Wonderwerk Cave"), South Africa, at 1.7 million years old.[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Beaumont2011-104) While the species' dispersal far out of Africa has often been attributed to fire and cave dwelling, fire does not become common in the archaeological record until 300,000 to 400,000 years ago,[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Roebroeks2011-105) and cave-dwelling about 600,000 years ago.[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-106) Therefore, _H. erectus_ may have only been scavenging fire opportunistically. Similarly, _H. erectus_ sites usually stay within warmer tropical or subtropical latitudes.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Carotenuto2016-51) The dating of northerly populations (namely Peking Man) could suggest that they were retreating to warmer refugia during [glacial periods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glacial_period "Glacial period"), but the precise age of the Peking Man fossils is poorly resolved.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAnt%C3%B3n2003p._132-58)[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-auto-107) There have been claims of manmade hearths and "clear-cut evidence for intentional fire use",[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-108) ostensibly as far back as 770,000 years ago in the supposed cave home of Peking Man.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-auto-107) At the French Caune de L'Arago, Tautavel Man does not seem to have been using fire at all, even though occupation sequences span two cold periods.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Lumley2015-29) #### Healthcare See also: [Prehistoric medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prehistoric_medicine "Prehistoric medicine") [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/93/Dmanisi_fossils_D_3444_%2B_D_3900_%28Replika%29.jpg/500px-Dmanisi_fossils_D_3444_%2B_D_3900_%28Replika%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dmanisi_fossils_D_3444_+_D_3900_(Replika).jpg) The single-toothed _[H. e. georgicus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dmanisi_hominins "Dmanisi hominins")_ specimen (above) is the earliest probable example of human group care.[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Spikins2019-109) Like other primates, _H. erectus_ probably used [medicinal plants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicinal_plant "Medicinal plant")[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Hardy2018-91) and infirmed sick group members. The earliest probable example of human group care is a 1.77 million year old _H. e. georgicus_ specimen who had lost all but one tooth due to age or [gum disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gum_disease "Gum disease") (the earliest example of severe chewing impairment) yet still survived for several years afterwards.[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Spikins2019-109) #### Seafaring _H. erectus_ made long sea crossings to arrive on the islands of [Flores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flores "Flores"), [Luzon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luzon "Luzon"),[\[104\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-D%C3%A9troit2019-110) and some [Mediterranean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean_Sea "Mediterranean Sea") islands. Some authors have asserted that _H. erectus_ intentionally made these crossings by inventing watercrafts and seafaring so early in time, speaking to advanced cognition and language skills. These populations could have also been founded by [natural rafting events](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanic_dispersal "Oceanic dispersal") instead.[\[105\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-:6-111) ### Art and rituals See also: [Prehistoric art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prehistoric_art "Prehistoric art") In East Asia, _H. erectus_ is usually represented only by skullcaps, which used to be interpreted as widespread [cannibalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_cannibalism "Human cannibalism") and ritual [headhunting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Headhunting "Headhunting"). This had been reinforced by the historic practice of headhunting and cannibalism in some recent Indonesian, Australian, and Polynesian cultures, which were formerly believed to have directly descended from these _H. erectus_ populations. The lack of the rest of the skeleton is now normally explained by natural phenomena.[\[106\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-112) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/Homo_Erectus_shell_with_geometric_incisions_circa_500%2C000_BP%2C_Naturalis_Biodiversity_Center%2C_Netherlands_%28with_detail%29.jpg/960px-Homo_Erectus_shell_with_geometric_incisions_circa_500%2C000_BP%2C_Naturalis_Biodiversity_Center%2C_Netherlands_%28with_detail%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Homo_Erectus_shell_with_geometric_incisions_circa_500,000_BP,_Naturalis_Biodiversity_Center,_Netherlands_(with_detail).jpg) Engraved _[Pseudodon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudodon "Pseudodon")_ shell [DUB1006-fL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudodon_shell_DUB1006-fL "Pseudodon shell DUB1006-fL") from [Trinil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinil "Trinil"), [Java](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Java "Java") Art-making could be evidence of symbolic thinking. An engraved _[Pseudodon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudodon "Pseudodon")_ shell [DUB1006-fL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudodon_shell_DUB1006-fL "Pseudodon shell DUB1006-fL") from Trinil, Java, with geometric markings could possibly be the earliest example of art-making, dating to 436,000 to 546,000 years ago.[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Joordens2015-103)[\[107\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-113)[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Dickson1992-114) _H. erectus_ was also the earliest human to collect red-colored pigments, namely [ochre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ochre "Ochre"). Ochre lumps at Olduvai Gorge, Tanzania, associated with the 1.4 million year old Olduvai Hominid 9 may have been purposefully shaped and trimmed by a [hammerstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hammerstone "Hammerstone"). Red ochre is normally recognized as bearing symbolic value when associated with modern humans.[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Dickson1992-114) ### Language See also: [Origin of language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Origin_of_language "Origin of language") and [Origin of speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Origin_of_speech "Origin of speech") The [spinal column](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spinal_column "Spinal column") of the 1.6 million year old Turkana boy would not have supported properly developed respiratory muscles required to produce speech;[\[109\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-115)[\[110\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-116) and a 1.5 million year old infant _H. erectus_ skull from Mojokerto, Java, shows that this population did not have an extended childhood, which is a prerequisite for [language acquisition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Language_acquisition "Language acquisition").[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Coqueugniot2004-78) On the other hand, despite the [cochlear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochlea "Cochlea") (ear) anatomy of Sangiran 2 and 4 retaining several traits reminiscent of australopithecines, the hearing range may have included the higher frequencies used to discern speech.[\[111\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-117) Given expanding brain size and technological innovation, _H. erectus_ may have been using some basic proto-language in combination with gesturing, and built the basic framework around which fully-fledged languages would eventually be formed.[\[112\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-118) ## See also - [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_ref-4)The Java Man [femur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Femur "Femur") presents a noticeable [osteocyte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osteocyte "Osteocyte"), likely [Paget's disease of bone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paget's_disease_of_bone "Paget's disease of bone") and [osteopetrosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osteopetrosis "Osteopetrosis") (thickening of the bone), probably stemming from [skeletal fluorosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skeletal_fluorosis "Skeletal fluorosis") caused by ingestion of food contaminated by [fluoride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluoride_toxicity "Fluoride toxicity")-filled [volcanic ash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanic_ash#ingesting_ash "Volcanic ash") (as the specimen was found in ash-filled [strata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stratum_(geology) "Stratum (geology)")). Livestock that graze on volcanic ash-ridden fields typically die of [acute toxicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acute_toxicity "Acute toxicity") within a few days or weeks.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-3) 2. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_ref-8)Darwin's work mainly aimed to demonstrate that his [theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_theory "Scientific theory") of [common descent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_descent "Common descent") with modification by [natural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_selection "Natural selection") and [sexual selection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_selection_in_humans "Sexual selection in humans") applied to humans, "The sole object of this work is to consider, firstly, whether man, like every other species, is descended from some pre-existing form; secondly, the manner of his development; and thirdly, the value of the [differences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Darwinism "Social Darwinism") between the so-called [races of man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_race_concepts "Historical race concepts")."[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-7) 3. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_ref-10)Dubois was studying the anatomy and evolution of the [larynx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larynx "Larynx") in [vertebrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertebrate "Vertebrate") in [Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam "Amsterdam") with German anatomist [Max Fürbringer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_F%C3%BCrbringer "Max Fürbringer"), but fed up with both the research and Fürbringer, he decided to drop everything and board the [SS Prinses Amalia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SS_Prinses_Amalia "SS Prinses Amalia") to the Dutch East Indies on 29 October 1887. Dubois said his interest in human evolution began in secondary school (the State [Hogere Burgerschool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hogere_Burgerschool "Hogere Burgerschool")), where he heard of lectures given by [Carl Vogt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Vogt "Carl Vogt") in 1868.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-FOOTNOTETheunissen1989pp._27%E2%80%9330-9) 4. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_ref-15)Dubois never accepted that the Java Man was a type of human, and continued to fight Weidenreich and von Koenigswald until his death in 1940. Sir [Arthur Keith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Keith "Arthur Keith") described Dubois in an obituary notice as, "an idealist, his ideas being so firmly held that his mind tended to bend facts rather than alter his ideas to fit them."[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-FOOTNOTETheunissen1989pp._159%E2%80%93165-14) 5. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_ref-44)There may have been two different _H. erectus_ dispersals into East Asia: an early one that led to the Sangiran [Java Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Java_Man "Java Man") (specifically the older material), and a later one which led to the northern Chinese [Peking Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peking_Man "Peking Man"). That is, the older Sangiran material may be more closely related to _H. erectus sensu lato_ than to Peking Man. The younger Sangiran material, though, possibly descended from or interbred with Chinese _H. erectus_.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Zaim2011-36) 6. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_ref-56)_H. heidelbergensis_ is also a [paraphyletic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraphyly "Paraphyly") assemblage of fossils.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus#cite_note-Ni2021-48) ## References 001. [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/39/Bailey1.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bailey1.jpg) [Derek Bailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Bailey_(guitarist) "Derek Bailey (guitarist)")

**European free jazz** is a part of the global [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") scene with its own development and characteristics. It is hard to establish who are the founders of European free jazz because of the different developments in different European countries. One can, however, make an argument that European free jazz took its development from American [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz"), where musicians such as [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman") revolutionised the way of playing. As the British drummer [Eddie Prévost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Pr%C3%A9vost "Eddie Prévost"), of long-standing improvising ensemble AMM, has put it, 'the music of Ornette Coleman and Albert Ayler gave us _permission to disobey_.'[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-1) Yet at much the same time, there were significant European innovations: for example, the same year as Coleman's [_Free Jazz_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Jazz:_A_Collective_Improvisation "Free Jazz: A Collective Improvisation") album was released (1961), in the UK the Jamaican alto saxophonist [Joe Harriott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Harriott "Joe Harriott") released the first of his experimental albums, _[Free Form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Form_(Joe_Harriott_album) "Free Form (Joe Harriott album)")._ It was recorded in late 1960, the month before Coleman's.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-2)

## American origin

Free jazz got its name from the album _Free Jazz_ (Atlantic, 1961) by Ornette Coleman to describe American avant-garde jazz of the 1960s.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-New_Grove1-3) Besides "avant-garde", it was called "the New Wave", "the New Thing", "action jazz", and in Europe "improvised music".[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-New_Grove1-3) Germans played a form of free jazz that had something in common with the [aleatoric music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleatoric_music "Aleatoric music") of [Bernd Alois Zimmermann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernd_Alois_Zimmermann "Bernd Alois Zimmermann") and was performed by [Derek Bailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Bailey_(guitarist) "Derek Bailey (guitarist)"), [Joachim Kuhn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joachim_Kuhn "Joachim Kuhn"), [Albert Mangelsdorff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Mangelsdorff "Albert Mangelsdorff"), [Manfred Schoof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manfred_Schoof "Manfred Schoof"), [John Surman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Surman "John Surman"), and [Alexander von Schlippenbach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_von_Schlippenbach "Alexander von Schlippenbach").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-New_Grove1-3)

Free jazz was unpopular and didn't sell well.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-New_Grove1-3) It was viewed as a musical, political, and social backlash to the structure of jazz and of American society at the time. "For some performers the style was loosely linked to the [Black Power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Power "Black Power") movement in the USA, partly because of the radical political outlook of some of its practitioners and advocates (e.g., [Archie Shepp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Shepp "Archie Shepp") and [LeRoi Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LeRoi_Jones "LeRoi Jones") – later known as Amiri Baraka) and partly owing to the explosive, expressionistic nature of the music itself".[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-4) Due to the lack of commercial success of the free jazz music as well as the racial issues, like the [Civil Rights Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Rights_Movement "Civil Rights Movement"), many American free jazz musicians began touring the European continent, playing and spreading their new avant-garde style throughout Europe.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-autogenerated1-5) Jazz musicians like Ornette Coleman, [Albert Ayler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler "Albert Ayler"), [Don Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter) "Don Cherry (trumpeter)"), [Bud Powell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bud_Powell "Bud Powell"), [Don Byas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Byas "Don Byas") traveled and performed throughout Europe.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-6) In contrast to the lack of commercial success in America, many American free jazz musicians experienced both commercial success and acceptance in Europe, leading to tours of Europe and extended residencies.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-7) "A number of jazz musicians migrated to other parts of the world, where they received an opposite response, being considered the ultimate expression of high culture. Thus, many of them remained in exile, and they enjoyed unparalleled success in France, Germany, Japan, Scandinavia, and the Netherlands after the world wars".[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-8)

Although much of American public believed this music to be structure-less, provocative, and ridiculous, some European listeners enjoyed the "dissonant and seemingly chaotic music".[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-9) "Many Europeans viewed free jazz as the descriptor most used by the media on both sides of the Atlantic for a musical movement that ignited like a flare in the African-American... and Western European...jazz communities. The social context in both cases included a reaction by musicians against a mainstream jazz culture they felt to be colluding with an oppressive Western hegemony that was intrinsically racist, historically imperialistic and exploitive, venally decadent and vicious as its power was challenged".[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-10) Due in part to the provocative nature of the music as well as the freedom it granted both the musician and the listener, many Europeans associated the backlash toward American society conveyed in free jazz with the [counter-culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterculture_of_the_1960s "Counterculture of the 1960s") and anti-imperialist movements in Europe during the late 1960s.

## European acceptance

Contrary to the societal reaction free jazz music received in the United States, many Europeans (musicians, critics and young people alike) identified with this style of music. While many African-Americans associated this avant-garde style with the Civil Rights Movement in America, many Europeans in the 1960s, especially college-aged students, associated this style of music with anti-colonialist movements occurring throughout Europe at the same time.

> The music under the "free-jazz" rubric – that of Ornette Coleman, Cecil Taylor, Albert Ayler, John Coltrane, Sun Ra and their bands, to name the major pioneers with the most impact in Europe – ignited the jazz scenes there in the mid-to-late 1960s. The subsequent free-jazz movement in their countries was linked to the events and spirit of the 1968 student protests and riots in Paris and Berlin (the " '68ers") as it was to new assertions of black identity in America. The racial conflict specific to the United States translated in Europe to an international radical leftism – one with a youthful white more than an angry black face – hostile to Western imperialistic capitalism and faux-culture.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-11)

As American free jazz musicians continued to play throughout Europe, the free jazz genre and the cultural movements in Europe associated with it began to spread as well, influencing many European jazz musicians to imitate the avant-garde style of playing as well as adopting its techniques to create their own individual sound. "Reflecting their diverse backgrounds, these musicians often blend personal narrative reminiscent of an Afrological perspective with some sonic imagery characteristic of European forms spanning several centuries".[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-12)

## European development of free jazz

[![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/58/Deuker_J%C3%B6rgensmann_Rolin_30_10_09_Photo_by_Herb_Weisrock_%2885%29.JPG/500px-Deuker_J%C3%B6rgensmann_Rolin_30_10_09_Photo_by_Herb_Weisrock_%2885%29.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Deuker_J%C3%B6rgensmann_Rolin_30_10_09_Photo_by_Herb_Weisrock_(85).JPG) Theo Jörgensmann, 2009

The introduction of this new, avant-garde style influenced many European jazz musicians like the German saxophonist [Peter Brötzmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Br%C3%B6tzmann "Peter Brötzmann"), who is known as one of the first European free jazz musicians. The founders of European free jazz usually came from a classic jazz background and then went over bebop and [hard bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop "Hard bop") into [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz"). Brötzmann began playing free jazz in 1964, and he formed a quintet with "Peter Kowald and Sven-Åke Johansson. The following year he toured Europe in a quintet led by Mike Mantler and Carla Bley, and they began an association with the Globe Unity Orchestra that lasted until 1981".[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-autogenerated2-13)

Brötzmann is renowned for his high-strung, fast playing, although the harmonies in his playing are often overlooked. His collaborator [Peter Kowald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Kowald "Peter Kowald") interpreted free jazz on double bass. Kowald helped in creating such organizations as "FMP (1969), which sponsors performances and issues recordings of free jazz, the Wuppertal Free Jazz Workshop, and 360° Spielraum für Ideen, an art gallery and performance space in Wuppertal".[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-autogenerated2-13)

Trombonist [Albert Mangelsdorff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Mangelsdorff "Albert Mangelsdorff"), although coming from a more classic background, also had great influence. He toured Asia, the United States, and South America and was one "finest trombonists in modern jazz".[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-14)

[Alexander von Schlippenbach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_von_Schlippenbach "Alexander von Schlippenbach")'s [Globe Unity Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Globe_Unity_Orchestra "Globe Unity Orchestra") created a scandal at its debut in Berlin.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-15) In Germany some of the second generation free jazz players came from a more European music background, like Georg Gräwe, [Theo Jörgensmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theo_J%C3%B6rgensmann "Theo Jörgensmann"), or [Hannes Bauer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannes_Bauer "Hannes Bauer").[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-16) In East Germany, trombonist [Conny Bauer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conny_Bauer "Conny Bauer") and drummer [Günter Sommer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%BCnter_Sommer "Günter Sommer") spread free jazz in the [Socialist bloc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Bloc "Eastern Bloc").[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-17) Bauer "formed Doppelmoppel, a quartet of two trombones and two guitars"[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-18) in 1982 and participated in the European Jazz Ensemble which celebrated its 20th-anniversary tour in 1996.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-19) In the UK saxophonist [Evan Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evan_Parker "Evan Parker"), who was highly influenced by [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane"), took on the role of Brötzmann for Britain. Guitarist Derek Bailey and trombonist [Paul Rutherford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Rutherford_(trombone_player) "Paul Rutherford (trombone player)") also developed the British scene. Both Paul Rutherford and Evan Parker experimented with solo improvisation for extended periods of their careers.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-20) Slava/Viacheslav/Ganelin, from Soviet Lithuania, came out with a bang in the late 70's, playing with Vladimir Chekasin and percussionist Vladimir Tarasov. Leo Feigin of [Leo Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Records "Leo Records") produced dozens of their albums, as well of other musicians from the Eastern Bloc.

In addition to the rise of free jazz musicians in Europe, during the 1960s there was a "sudden surge in critical interest...the emergence of a new cohort of critics – young intellectuals such as Yves Buin, Michel Le Bris, Guy Kopelowicz and Jean-Louis Comolli – who took up the cause of experimental jazz".[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-21) During this time, free jazz was based less on its American origin and became more European.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-22) Through the use of "spontaneous improvisation theoretically free of the diatonic/chromatic and metric systems governing harmony, melody, and rhythm of both pre-free jazz and other Western music",[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-23) European free jazz musicians created interpretations based on their experience in western Europe.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-24) In Europe, this style of music achieved the relative level of success that "'bop,' 'early jazz,' and 'swing' enjoy\[ed\] in America," [\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-25) during their respective musical periods. According to Oxford Music Online, "In Europe (especially England) free jazz is also known simply as 'improvised music,' particularly in performances which emphasize stylistic connections to avant-garde art music rather than to sounds of African-American origin".[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-autogenerated1-5)

## Free jazz as an art form in Europe

As free jazz, or 'improvised music' grew and developed as a popular genre of music in Europe, so did its supporters – both casual and scholarly. While there had always been a close association between free jazz and political and social strife in Europe, many supporters of the genre began pushing to depoliticize the music, urging listeners to consider free jazz as an art form rather than simply a provocative statement on society bereft of any actual musicality. Many listeners of the time believed that, "free jazz was as much a political as a musical phenomenon".[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-26) During this time, there were fears that if free jazz was only considered as a mechanism for political commentary, that it would lose its validity as an art form, or at worst, be subject to censorship by European governments.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-27) Due to this possibility, there was a surge amongst the free jazz community to dissociate the word "free" with the political environment it is so commonly associated with.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-28) In addition to the depoliticizing of this genre of music, other critics asserted that,"Were jazz to be valued henceforth according to its capacity to reveal something of the social conditions under which it was produced or the political beliefs that its producers espoused, then its relevance for those outside the particular community from which it issues would be limited.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-29) In other words, by only associating jazz or free jazz with a particular ideology or thought process, in effect only those of a similar thought process can understand or appreciate it fully. Rather, if the free jazz genre was dissociated from the view that it is simply a vehicle for political commentary, and instead it was viewed objectively as a form of art, it would not only would be accessible to a larger audience, but it would allow itself to be judged as an art rather than the political statement it may or may not be attempting to make.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-30)

## Aftermath of free jazz

After the popularity of the late 1960s and 1970s in Europe, improvised music began to influence and became influenced by other genres of music.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-autogenerated3-31) In the United States, Europe, and the rest of the world, musicians continued to play improvisational music, but they also looked to other genres for inspiration. This term 'improvised music' may, of course, be used in the common dictionary sense, and it is particularly useful in references to the pan-genre eclecticism which has characterized much music-making from the 1980s onwards, as musicians draw freely from, or meld together, not only jazz and contemporary art music but also aspects of various mainstream popular musics (blues, rock, soul, pop), [heavy metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_metal_music "Heavy metal music") and world music (ethnic traditions).[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-autogenerated3-31)

[Los Angeles, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles,_California "Los Angeles, California"), U.S. | | Genre | [Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") | | Occupations | Musician, composer | | Instruments | Piano, trombone | | Years active | 1950s–1990s | | Label | [Arabesque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabesque_Records "Arabesque Records") | Musical artist **Horace Elva Tapscott** (April 6, 1934– February 27, 1999) was an American [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") pianist and composer.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-amg-1) He formed the Pan Afrikan Peoples Arkestra (also known as P.A.P.A., or The Ark) in 1961 and led the ensemble through the 1990s.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-ucla-bio-2) ## Early life \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Horace_Tapscott&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Early life")\] Tapscott was born in [Houston, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston,_Texas "Houston, Texas"), and moved to [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), at the age of nine.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-LarkinJazz-3) By this time he had begun to study piano and trombone.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-LarkinJazz-3) He played with [Frank Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Morgan_(musician) "Frank Morgan (musician)"), [Don Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter) "Don Cherry (trumpeter)"), Bobby Bradford, and [Billy Higgins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Higgins "Billy Higgins") as a teenager. ## Later life and career \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Horace_Tapscott&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Later life and career")\] After service in the [Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Air_Force "United States Air Force") in [Wyoming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyoming "Wyoming"), he returned to Los Angeles and played trombone with various bands, notably [Lionel Hampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionel_Hampton "Lionel Hampton") (1959–61). Soon after, though, he quit playing trombone and focused on piano.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-Grove-4) In 1961, Tapscott formed the Pan Afrikan Peoples Arkestra,[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-5) with the aim of preserving, developing and performing African-American music. As his vision grew, this became just one part of a larger organization in 1963, the Underground Musicians Association (UGMA),[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-LarkinJazz-3) which later changed name to the [Union of God's Musicians and Artists Ascension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_of_God's_Musicians_and_Artists_Ascension "Union of God's Musicians and Artists Ascension") (UGMAA).[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-Grove-4) [Arthur Blythe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Blythe "Arthur Blythe"), [Stanley Crouch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Crouch "Stanley Crouch"), [Butch Morris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butch_Morris "Butch Morris"), [Wilber Morris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilber_Morris "Wilber Morris"), [David Murray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Murray_(saxophonist) "David Murray (saxophonist)"), [Jimmy Woods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Woods "Jimmy Woods"), [Nate Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nate_Morgan "Nate Morgan") and [Guido Sinclair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guido_Sinclair "Guido Sinclair") all performed in Tapscott's Arkestra at one time or another.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-ucla-bio-2) Tapscott and his work are the subjects of the [UCLA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Los_Angeles "University of California, Los Angeles") Horace Tapscott Jazz Collection.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-oac-6) Enthusiasts of his music formed two labels in the 1970s and 1980s, Interplay and Nimbus, for which he recorded.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-Grove-4) From [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic"): "His pianistic technique was hard and percussive, likened by some to that of [Thelonious Monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thelonious_Monk "Thelonious Monk") and [Herbie Nichols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Nichols "Herbie Nichols") and every bit as distinctive. In contexts ranging from freely improvised duos to highly arranged big bands, Tapscott exhibited a solo and compositional voice that was his own." ## Death and legacy \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Horace_Tapscott&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Death and legacy")\] Having been suffering from brain cancer, Tapscott died aged 64 on February 27, 1999, the day before a planned tribute concert in his honor took place at Los Angeles' [Leimert Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leimert_Park,_Los_Angeles "Leimert Park, Los Angeles").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-7) An engraving in the sidewalk along Degnan Boulevard in the Leimert Park neighborhood reads: "Horace Tapscott, the local pianist and organizer whose ensemble, the Pan Afrikan Peoples Arkestra, gave many musicians their first gigs and helped heal a community impacted by racism."[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-8) His personal archive of manuscripts, arrangements and recordings was donated to [UCLA Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UCLA_Library "UCLA Library") in 2003 by his wife, Cecilia Tapscott.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-9) ## Discography \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Horace_Tapscott&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: Discography")\] ### As leader \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Horace_Tapscott&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: As leader")\] - BAG is known for the convergence of free jazz and experimental theater.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group#cite_note-washu-thesource-bag-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group#cite_note-looker-bag-book-2) ## Members Members included saxophonists [Julius Hemphill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Hemphill "Julius Hemphill"),[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group#cite_note-LarkinJazz-3) [Oliver Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Lake "Oliver Lake"),[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group#cite_note-LarkinJazz-3) [Lester Bowie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lester_Bowie "Lester Bowie"), [J. Parran"), [Hamiet Bluiett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamiet_Bluiett "Hamiet Bluiett"), and [Luther Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luther_Thomas "Luther Thomas"); trumpeters [Baikida Carroll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baikida_Carroll "Baikida Carroll")[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group#cite_note-LarkinJazz-3) and [Floyd LeFlore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floyd_LeFlore "Floyd LeFlore"); trombonist [Joseph Bowie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Bowie "Joseph Bowie");[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group#cite_note-LarkinJazz-3) drummers [Bensid Thigpen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bensid_Thigpen?action=edit&redlink=1 "Bensid Thigpen") and [Charles "Bobo" Shaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_%22Bobo%22_Shaw "Charles \"Bobo\" Shaw");[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group#cite_note-LarkinJazz-3) bassist Bobby Reed, [Arzinia Richardson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arzinia_Richardson?action=edit&redlink=1 "Arzinia Richardson"); stage directors [Malinke Robert Elliott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malinke_Robert_Elliott?action=edit&redlink=1 "Malinke Robert Elliott"), [Vincent Terrell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_Terrell?action=edit&redlink=1 "Vincent Terrell"), and [Muthal Naidoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muthal_Naidoo?action=edit&redlink=1 "Muthal Naidoo"); actors [LeRoi S. Shelton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LeRoi_S._Shelton?action=edit&redlink=1 "LeRoi S. Shelton"); poets [Ajule (Bruce) Rutlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajule_(Bruce)_Rutlin?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ajule (Bruce) Rutlin")[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group#cite_note-LarkinJazz-3) and [Shirley LeFlore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirley_LeFlore "Shirley LeFlore"); dancers [Georgia Collins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Collins?action=edit&redlink=1 "Georgia Collins") and [Luisah Teish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luisah_Teish "Luisah Teish"); and painters [Emilio Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emilio_Cruz_(artist) "Emilio Cruz (artist)") and [Oliver Lee Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Lee_Jackson "Oliver Lee Jackson"). While Jackson was not officially a member, he was deeply involved with BAG and is usually listed as a member.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group#cite_note-4) In addition, [Ronnie Burrage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronnie_Burrage "Ronnie Burrage") was considered one of the youngest members (11 and 12 years old) of BAG as he began to perform with various members in 1971 and 1972.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group#cite_note-stlpublicradio-bag-5) ## History Members Oliver Lake, Lester Bowie, and Floyd LeFlore studied music in the jazz program at [Sumner High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sumner_High_School_(St._Louis) "Sumner High School (St. Louis)"). They continued music education at [Lincoln University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln_University_(Missouri) "Lincoln University (Missouri)") alongside Julius Hemphill. Several members were drafted into military service, and all played music in St. Louis through the 1960s. Frustration with discrimination and limited opportunities brought the musical artists together with black actors marginalized from the theater scene, and they began collaborating on artistic productions around [LaClede Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LaClede_Town "LaClede Town"), the [Circle Coffee Shop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle_Coffee_Shop?action=edit&redlink=1 "Circle Coffee Shop"), and [Berea Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berea_Church?action=edit&redlink=1 "Berea Church").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group#cite_note-looker-bag-book-2) While strongly influenced by [Chicago's Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Ensemble_of_Chicago "Art Ensemble of Chicago"), the Black Artists Group was unique in including artists from dance, theater, visual arts, and creative writing. They incorporated as a not-for-profit organization under the name "The Black Artists' Group, Inc" in 1968.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group#cite_note-looker-bag-book-2) BAG received major grant funding from the [Danforth Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danforth_Foundation "Danforth Foundation") and the [Rockefeller Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockefeller_Foundation "Rockefeller Foundation"). In July 1969, the group paid $1 annual rent for a building at 2665 Washington Blvd.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group#cite_note-washu-thesource-bag-1) Many of the BAG members relocated to Paris and then New York in the 1970s.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group#cite_note-washu-thesource-bag-1) A recording of a 1973 performance in Paris was released on an LP titled _[In Paris, Aries 1973](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_Paris,_Aries_1973 "In Paris, Aries 1973")_;[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group#cite_note-6) it was the only album ever issued under the BAG name until the 2024 release of _For Peace And Liberty, In Paris Dec 1972_.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group#cite_note-wire-7) ## Legacy BAG inspired other groups and artistic collectives to form around the United States and influenced [Chicago's Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Ensemble_of_Chicago "Art Ensemble of Chicago").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group#cite_note-allaboutjazz-bag-8) [Oliver Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Lake "Oliver Lake"), [Julius Hemphill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Hemphill "Julius Hemphill") and [Hamiet Bluiett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamiet_Bluiett "Hamiet Bluiett") formed the [African Continuum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Continuum?action=edit&redlink=1 "African Continuum") and organized the 1971 multimedia concert "Images: Sons/Ancestors" at [Powell Symphony Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Powell_Hall "Powell Hall"), which was delayed by a bomb threat.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group#cite_note-looker-bag-book-2) They went on to form the [World Saxophone Quartet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Saxophone_Quartet "World Saxophone Quartet") and were notable in the "loft-jazz" scene of New York's underground in the 1980s.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group#cite_note-washu-thesource-bag-1) ## Discography **Albums** - _[In Paris, Aries 1973](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_Paris,_Aries_1973 "In Paris, Aries 1973")_ (1973, self-release; reissued in 2011 and 2018) - _For Peace And Liberty, In Paris Dec 1972_ (2024, Wewantsounds) ## (1961) | | _**Change of the Century**_ is a studio album by [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") saxophonist [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman"). It was released through [Atlantic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Records "Atlantic Records") in May 1960.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Change_of_the_Century#cite_note-BbApr60-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Change_of_the_Century#cite_note-CbApr60-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Change_of_the_Century#cite_note-CbMay60-3) It sold very well from soon after its release.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Change_of_the_Century#cite_note-BbMay60-4) Recording sessions for the album took place on October 8 and 9, 1959, in New York City.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Change_of_the_Century#cite_note-6) In the liner notes, Coleman stressed that the album was "a group effort," and wrote: "When our group plays, before we start out to play, we do not have any idea what the end result will be. Each player is free to contribute what he feels in the music at any given moment... our final results depend entirely on the musicianship, emotional make-up and taste of the individual (1959) | | _**Tomorrow Is the Question!**_, subtitled _The New Music of Ornette Coleman!_, is the second album by American [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") musician [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman"), originally released in 1959 by [Contemporary Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_Records "Contemporary Records"). It was Coleman's last album for the label before he began a highly successful multi-album series for [Atlantic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Records "Atlantic Records") in 1959. As well as regular sideman [Don Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(jazz) "Don Cherry (jazz)") on trumpet, the album features bassists [Percy Heath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percy_Heath "Percy Heath") and [Red Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Mitchell "Red Mitchell"), and drummer [Shelly Manne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelly_Manne "Shelly Manne"). ## Reception | Review scores | | --- | | Source | Rating | | [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") | ![Star](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Star_full.svg/40px-Star_full.svg.png)![Star](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Star_full.svg/40px-Star_full.svg.png)![Star](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Star_full.svg/40px-Star_full.svg.png)![Star](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Star_full.svg/40px-Star_full.svg.png)![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Star_empty.svg/40px-Star_empty.svg.png)[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomorrow_Is_the_Question!#cite_note-1) | | [Yahoo! [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic")'s Thom Jurek notes the interplay of Coleman and Cherry on tunes he described as "knottier and tighter in their arrangement style" than those of the previous album.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomorrow_Is_the_Question!#cite_note-5) Ekkehard Jost, in his book _Free Jazz_, noted that "as early as the 1958/59 recordings for Contemporary, the most pronounced features of Coleman's saxophone playing were set. His bent for improvisations that were largely unrestrained harmonically is evident, even in pieces whose outward make-up is anything but revolutionary."[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomorrow_Is_the_Question!#cite_note-jost-6) Others have hailed the removal of the piano as a positive move: for Mike Andrews, "a marked conceptual improvement can be immediately recognized" as the lack of harmonic instrument allowed greater freedom for the soloists.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomorrow_Is_the_Question!#cite_note-andrews-7) ## Release history Released as an [LP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gramophone_record "Gramophone record") by [Contemporary Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_Records "Contemporary Records") in 1959. (1958) | | _**Jazz Advance**_ is the debut album by [pianist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pianist "Pianist") [Cecil Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor "Cecil Taylor"), recorded for the [Transition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transition_Records "Transition Records") label in September 1956. The album features performances by Taylor with [Buell Neidlinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buell_Neidlinger "Buell Neidlinger"), [Denis Charles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denis_Charles "Denis Charles") and [Steve Lacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Lacy_(saxophonist) "Steve Lacy (saxophonist)"). ## Music \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jazz_Advance&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Music")\] The album contains three Taylor originals, three [standards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_standard "Jazz standard"), and one standard-to-be, [Thelonious Monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thelonious_Monk "Thelonious Monk")'s " [Bemsha Swing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bemsha_Swing "Bemsha Swing")," first recorded only four years before Taylor's version. This track is played "cryptically and succinctly, the lines breaking up into jagged fragments and jutting chords." "Charge 'Em Blues" is in **4** **4** time. The chords and light treble playing towards the beginning of "Azure" are similar to the sound of [Abdullah Ibrahim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdullah_Ibrahim "Abdullah Ibrahim"), but then "the cross-rhythmic improvised piano patterns clattering chords typical of later Taylor emerge."[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Advance#cite_note-1) ## Reception \[ **Black Saint** and **Soul Note** are two affiliated [Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy") [independent record labels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_record_label "Independent record label"). Since their conception in the 1970s, they have released albums from a variety of influential jazz musicians, particularly in the genre of [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz").

## History

Black Saint was established in 1975 by Giacomo Pellicciotti and devoted to recording avant-garde musicians who might not have an opportunity elsewhere.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Saint/Soul_Note#cite_note-LarkinGE-1) In 1979, a sister label, Soul Note, was established as a home for artists who, while being no less creative, might be considered slightly closer to the mainstream.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Saint/Soul_Note#cite_note-LarkinGE-1)

The labels specialize in avant-garde jazz stemming from the free jazz tradition.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Saint/Soul_Note#cite_note-LarkinGE-1) Some of its roster of artists were members of the Chicago-based music association [Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians "Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians") and the St. Louis-based multidisciplinary arts collectives [Black Artists Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group "Black Artists Group") and the [Human Arts Ensemble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Arts_Ensemble "Human Arts Ensemble").

The company was based in [Tribiano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tribiano "Tribiano"), Italy. Many of the recordings were made in Milan, as the performers passed through the area on tour,[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Saint/Soul_Note#cite_note-2) although many leading Italian musicians, such as [Giorgio Gaslini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giorgio_Gaslini "Giorgio Gaslini"), have also recorded for the label.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Saint/Soul_Note#cite_note-LarkinGE-1) Giovanni Bonandrini's son Flavio ran the company until its sale in 2008, the elder Bonandrini having retired, and has supervised many recording sessions in New York City.

Starting in 1984, Black Saint/Soul Note won the _[Down Beat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Down_Beat "Down Beat")_ Critics Poll for best record label for six subsequent years until they were replaced by [Blue Note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records") in 1990.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Saint/Soul_Note#cite_note-3)

Cam Jazz acquired the company in 2008.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Saint/Soul_Note#cite_note-4)
