Koester and the label moved to Chicago, Illinois, in 1958, and the label's name became **Delmark**. Koester sold the label assets in 2018, and the label since operates as **Delmark Records LLC.** ## History \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Delmark_Records&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: History")\] Born in 1932 in [Wichita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wichita,_Kansas "Wichita, Kansas"), Kansas, [Bob Koester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Koester "Bob Koester") was the son of a petroleum engineer. While in the hospital with polio when he was a child, he listened to the radio and was cheered up when he heard [Eddie Condon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Condon "Eddie Condon") and [Benny Goodman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benny_Goodman "Benny Goodman"). In his teens, he was a dedicated jazz fan who began buying old records from a Salvation Army store. At concerts in Kansas City, he heard [Red Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Allen "Red Allen"), [Count Basie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_Basie "Count Basie"), [Jimmy Rushing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Rushing "Jimmy Rushing"), [Tommy Douglas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tommy_Douglas_(clarinetist) "Tommy Douglas (clarinetist)"), [Lionel Hampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionel_Hampton "Lionel Hampton"), and [Jay McShann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jay_McShann "Jay McShann").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delmark_Records#cite_note-Kennedy-2) Moving from Wichita to St. Louis to attend college, Koester began his career as a record trader in his dormitory room. Joining a local jazz club gave Koester his first taste of live jazz, seeing [Clark Terry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clark_Terry "Clark Terry") perform. Koester made acquaintance with a fellow jazz club member, Ron Fister, with whom he opened his first record shop, K & F Sales. Shortly after opening in an old restaurant storefront, they changed the name to the Blue Note Record Shop. About a year after this joint venture, Fister and Koester decided to part ways, with Koester moving to the corner of Delmar and Olive streets in St. Louis. Taking the name from the street his shop was on, Koester recorded a local jazz group the Windy City Six in 1953. Shortly thereafter, Koester found local talent such as [James Crutchfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Crutchfield "James Crutchfield"), [Speckled Red](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speckled_Red "Speckled Red"), [J.D. Short](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J.D._Short "J.D. Short"), and [Big Joe Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Joe_Williams "Big Joe Williams"). Koester moved to Chicago in August 1958. He bought Seymour's Jazz Mart, and in renaming the storefront the Jazz Record Mart, Delmark Records found its new home in the basement of the record shop. By 1963, Koester had moved the shop to a location at 7 West Grand. During this period in Chicago, Delmark released albums by, [Barney Bigard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barney_Bigard "Barney Bigard"), [Donald Byrd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Byrd "Donald Byrd"), [Jimmy Forrest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Forrest_(musician) "Jimmy Forrest (musician)"), [George Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Lewis_(clarinetist) "George Lewis (clarinetist)"), [Bud Powell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bud_Powell "Bud Powell"), and [Ira Sullivan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ira_Sullivan "Ira Sullivan"). Throughout the 1960s and 1970s, Delmark recorded the [Art Ensemble of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Ensemble_of_Chicago "Art Ensemble of Chicago"), [Sonny Stitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Stitt "Sonny Stitt"), [Junior Wells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junior_Wells "Junior Wells"),[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delmark_Records#cite_note-3) [Luther Allison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luther_Allison "Luther Allison"), [Arthur Crudup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Crudup "Arthur Crudup"), [Jimmy Dawkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Dawkins "Jimmy Dawkins"), [Sleepy John Estes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_John_Estes "Sleepy John Estes"), [Buddy Guy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddy_Guy "Buddy Guy"), [J. B. Hutto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._B._Hutto "J. B. Hutto"),[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delmark_Records#cite_note-4)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delmark_Records#cite_note-5) [Jimmy Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Johnson_(blues_guitarist) "Jimmy Johnson (blues guitarist)"), [Magic Sam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magic_Sam "Magic Sam"), [Robert Nighthawk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Nighthawk "Robert Nighthawk"), [Yank Rachell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yank_Rachell "Yank Rachell"), [Otis Rush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otis_Rush "Otis Rush"), [Roosevelt Sykes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roosevelt_Sykes "Roosevelt Sykes"), and [Malachi Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malachi_Thompson "Malachi Thompson"). In 1966, [Chuck Nessa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nessa_Records "Nessa Records"), manager of the Jazz Record Mart, convinced Koester to release albums by musicians associated with the [Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians "Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians"). The first record was [Roscoe Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roscoe_Mitchell "Roscoe Mitchell")'s _[Sound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_(Roscoe_Mitchell_album) "Sound (Roscoe Mitchell album)")_ (1966) which received a five star review in _[Downbeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downbeat_(magazine) "Downbeat (magazine)")_. This was followed by [Muhal Richard Abrams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhal_Richard_Abrams "Muhal Richard Abrams")' _[Levels and Degrees of Light](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levels_and_Degrees_of_Light "Levels and Degrees of Light")_ (1968), [Kalaparusha Maurice McIntyre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalaparusha_Maurice_McIntyre "Kalaparusha Maurice McIntyre")'s _Humility in the Light of the Creator_ (1969) and [Anthony Braxton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Braxton "Anthony Braxton")'s _[For Alto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/For_Alto "For Alto")_ (1969). Delmark released two of the earliest [Sun Ra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Ra "Sun Ra") albums, _[Sun Song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_by_Sun_Ra "Jazz by Sun Ra")_ and _[Sound of Joy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_of_Joy "Sound of Joy")_, in 1967 and 1968 respectively. Delmark has also released albums by [Fred Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Anderson_(musician) "Fred Anderson (musician)"), [Frank Catalano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Catalano "Frank Catalano"), [Rob Mazurek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rob_Mazurek "Rob Mazurek"), [Nicole Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicole_Mitchell_(musician) "Nicole Mitchell (musician)"), [Ken Vandermark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Vandermark "Ken Vandermark"), [Roy Campbell, Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Campbell,_Jr. "Roy Campbell, Jr."), and [Ethnic Heritage Ensemble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnic_Heritage_Ensemble "Ethnic Heritage Ensemble"); and blues musicians including [Zora Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zora_Young "Zora Young"), [Ken Saydak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Saydak "Ken Saydak"), [Byther Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byther_Smith "Byther Smith"), [Michael Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Coleman_(blues_musician) "Michael Coleman (blues musician)"), [Little Arthur Duncan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Arthur_Duncan "Little Arthur Duncan"), [Eddie C. Campbell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_C._Campbell "Eddie C. Campbell"), [Jimmy Burns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Burns "Jimmy Burns"), and [ragtime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ragtime "Ragtime") musicians including [Terry Waldo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terry_Waldo "Terry Waldo"). In March 2010, Delmark announced the release of the album _Revisit_ by the Polish duo [Mikrokolektyw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikrokolektyw "Mikrokolektyw"). This album was Delmark's first by a European [avant-garde jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz") group in its 57-year history.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delmark_Records#cite_note-6) In 2012, Delmark released two [Chicago blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_blues "Chicago blues") albums by [Linsey Alexander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linsey_Alexander "Linsey Alexander") and [Mike Wheeler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Wheeler_(musician) "Mike Wheeler (musician)").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delmark_Records#cite_note-Album_Discography-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delmark_Records#cite_note-AllMusic-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delmark_Records#cite_note-9) In May 2018, Koester retired and sold Delmark Records to Delmark Records LLC, of which Julia A. Miller is the Managing Member. Julia A. Miller became the label President & CEO and Elbio Barilari became the Vice President & Artistic Director. They are two musicians from Chicago and Uruguay, respectively. The sale included Delmark's subsidiary labels, CD and LP inventory, the catalog of masters, and Riverside Studio.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delmark_Records#cite_note-Reich-10) ## | Professional ratings _**Om**_ is a posthumously released album by [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane"), recorded on October 1, 1965, one day after the recording of _[Live in Seattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_in_Seattle_(John_Coltrane_album) "Live in Seattle (John Coltrane album)")_, and one day prior to the recording of the music heard on _[A Love Supreme: Live in Seattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme:_Live_in_Seattle "A Love Supreme: Live in Seattle")_. The album, which features Coltrane's quartet plus three additional players, consists of a single 29-minute work that was split into two parts when released on LP. _Om_ was issued by [Impulse!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records "Impulse! Records") in 1968, and was also included on _[The Major Works of John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Major_Works_of_John_Coltrane "The Major Works of John Coltrane")_, a compilation CD released in 1992. ## Background \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Om_(John_Coltrane_album)&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Background")\] During September 14–26, 1965, the John Coltrane Quartet played an engagement at the [Jazz Workshop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Workshop "Jazz Workshop") in [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco").[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-jcref-6) The saxophonist [Pharoah Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharoah_Sanders "Pharoah Sanders"), whose music Coltrane admired, and who had previously recorded with Coltrane on _[Ascension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album) "Ascension (John Coltrane album)")_, went to hear the group and was invited to sit in. According to Sanders, "\[H\]e told me then that he was thinking of changing the group and changing the music, to get different sounds. He asked me to play with him."[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-7) At the same time, the multi-instrumentalist [Donald Garrett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Garrett "Donald Garrett"), who had played with Coltrane's group in 1961 as a second bassist,[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-8) was also asked to sit in. At the end of the two-week gig, both Sanders and Garrett were asked to join the band, and accompanied it to the next engagement, September 27 - October 2, at [The Penthouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Penthouse_(Seattle) "The Penthouse (Seattle)") in [Seattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle "Seattle").[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-jcref-6) During the stay in Seattle, Coltrane decided to document the newly expanded group at his own expense, hiring the recording engineer Jan Kurtis for the September 30 gig.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-porter_265-9)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-10) Music from this date was released in 1971 on _Live in Seattle_, with additional tracks issued in 2011 on _The Unissued Seattle Broadcast_. The next day, the whole band, with the addition of [Joe Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Brazil "Joe Brazil"), traveled to Kurtis' studio, Camelot Sound Studios, in a rented house in [Lynnwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynnwood,_Washington "Lynnwood, Washington"), to record _Om_.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-11)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-12) On the following day, the band wrapped up their Seattle engagement at The Penthouse with a performance of "A Love Supreme", a recording of which was issued in 2021 on _A Love Supreme: Live in Seattle_, then headed to [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles") for an eleven-day stay at the It Club,[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-13) during which they recorded the tracks "Kulu Sé Mama (Juno Sé Mama)" and "Selflessness", both of which appear on the CD version of the album _[Kulu Sé Mama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kulu_S%C3%A9_Mama "Kulu Sé Mama")_.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-14) It is believed that Coltrane was using [LSD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LSD "LSD") during the recording, though this is disputed.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-15) [Lewis Porter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_Porter "Lewis Porter") wrote that "Coltrane may have been tripping on LSD when he recorded _Om_. It is certain that he did begin using LSD around this time,"[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-porter_265-9) "according to four reliable sources, speaking off the record."[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-16) However, Porter was careful to point out that Coltrane's playing "is perfectly coherent on all his late recordings - in fact, incredibly so", adding: "he probably felt or hoped that LSD could help him in the direction he already wanted to go".[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-17) ## Music \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Om_(John_Coltrane_album)&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Music")\] The album's title refers to the [sacred sound and spiritual symbol in Indian religions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om "Om"). Coltrane described _Om_ as "the first vibration - that sound, that spirit, which set everything else into being. It is The Word from which all men and everything else comes, including all possible sounds that man can make vocally. It is the first syllable, the primal word, the word of power."[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-liner-18) The recording begins with quiet percussion, after which the musicians chant in unison a verse from chapter nine of the _[Bhagavad Gita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhagavad_Gita "Bhagavad Gita")_: > Rites that the Vedas ordain, and the rituals taught by the scriptures, all these am I, and the offering made to the ghosts of the fathers, herbs of healing and food. The mantram. The clarified butter. I, the oblation and I, the flame into which it is offered. I am the sire of the world, and this world's mother and grandsire. I am he who awards to each the fruit of his action. I make all things clean. I am Om![\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-Ratliff-19)[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-20) Regarding the next section, writer Peter Bebergal commented: > Coltrane and his compatriots start chanting "om" as if they are caught on fire by it. It's not meditative, but rather honors the actual meaning of the Sanskrit, "to shout." But the word "om" is also a vibration, a reflection of the unity of all things before creation. It is the manifestation of the truth essential to Hindu philosophy that Brahman (God) and the Atman (Soul) are one; their separateness is an illusion. The acknowledgement of this truth, or rather the attempt to get inside of it, is what Coltrane seems to be doing with Om.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-quietus-21) ( [Guerino Mazzola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guerino_Mazzola "Guerino Mazzola") and Paul Cherlin suggested that the _Live in Seattle_ track "Evolution", recorded the previous day, and featuring "trance-like moaning", can be heard as a direct forebear to the chanting in _Om_.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-22)) The chanting is succeeded by a dense, loud ensemble passage, after which Coltrane, Sanders, and Tyner solo.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-flow_26-23) The solos are followed by what has been described as "jungle sound" in which "the culture of jazz, or of any kind of civilization, is left behind".[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-flow_26-23) This section features, among other things, quavering flutes, animal noises, a yodeling voice, and both basses playing bowed harmonics and glissandi. This leads to a Coltrane / Sanders duet and a climactic ensemble passage, after which the word "om" is once again heard, followed by a closing recitation of the verse from the Bhagavad Gita.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-flow_26-23) In the liner notes, [Nat Hentoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nat_Hentoff "Nat Hentoff") wrote: "It may be that to break the circumscribed limits of conventional hearing, the ear must be propelled to hear sounds and pitches it has rejected in the past, just as compassion is not come by in conventional comfort. And once heard and absorbed, these sounds lead to further extensions of listening and feeling capacities... In so far as one can ever advise anyone else in how to listen, I would suggest that they start by not worrying about how it is all structured, where it's leading. Let the music come in without any pre-set definitions of what jazz has to be, of what music has to be."[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-liner-18) ## Legacy and reception \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Om_(John_Coltrane_album)&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Legacy and reception")\] According to [Eric Nisenson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Nisenson "Eric Nisenson"), Coltrane, "clearly embarrassed by _Om_, instructed [Bob Thiele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Thiele "Bob Thiele") that he never wanted it released."[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-Nisenson-24) However, Thiele, the director and producer of [Impulse!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records "Impulse! Records"), did release it in 1968 to capitalize on Coltrane's death and on the growing psychedelic rock scene at the time. Upon its release, "a copy was almost immediately placed in the window of the [Haight-Ashbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haight-Ashbury "Haight-Ashbury") Psychedelic Shop."[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-Nisenson-24) Coltrane scholar [Ashley Kahn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashley_Kahn "Ashley Kahn") wrote: "In title and cover, it could not have been more timely, tying into the look and feel of the year that brought forth the Summer of Love."[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-house184-25) Opinions regarding _Om_ have been mixed. According to Lewis Porter, "Some fans were taken aback by the group chanting... Coltrane was allowing an informality and spiritualism into his recordings and performances that some found amateurish; others found it freeing and revolutionary."[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-porter_265-9) David Nelson McCarthy called it "Coltrane's only major release of questionable quality... featuring screechy playing and moaning vocals, this is for true believers and historical interest only."[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-26) [Ben Ratliff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Ratliff "Ben Ratliff") described it as "a fairly disjointed, agitated, muddy, twenty-nine-minute catharsis."[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-Ratliff-19) In an [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") review, Stacia Proefrock commented: "Condemned by many critics as John Coltrane's worst album, _Om_ suffers only in comparison to the great works that preceded it... _Om_... seems... like a pure release of energy... Regardless of its seeming chaos, this is a deeply spiritual work... _Om_ resonates with passion and yearning, but has a frantic edge that suggests that opening up to all of that powerful spiritual energy might have been a frightening experience... _Om_ doesn't deserve the dismissal it has been given by critics. It is an important work in the history of free jazz that opens up considerably by the end of its 29 minutes, revealing the expansive contents of a jazz master's mind."[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-allmusic-2) Guerino Mazzola and Paul Cherlin wrote that "Compared to the other LPs of that year (1965), _Om_ lives on another planet... This journey is not for beginners... It would be fair to listen to this performance without any reference to jazz or to any other disciplined utterance of music."[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-flow_26-23) In an article for [All About Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_About_Jazz "All About Jazz"), Simon Weil wrote: " _Om_ qualifies as fearsome. There are moments, particularly during the closing unison passages, when it feels like one is getting beaten over the head with a blunt instrument. It becomes unbearable. But I believe that such an effect was in line with Coltrane's intentions... Coltrane is trying to evoke the voice of God at the Dawn of Creation in this track. But hearing the voice of God at the Dawn of Creation is much like confronting the face of God. This is going to be an awesome and overwhelming experience—which one can only take for so long. But I think there ought therefore to be some unbearability in the music as well —because one should neither really be able to look God full in the face, nor hear his voice without quailing somewhat. So then _Om_ must be 'difficult'."[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-27) Ashley Kahn described _Om_ as "a single spiraling, epic composition that... musically fused the spontaneous energy of _Ascension_ with the spiritual resonance of _A Love Supreme_".[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-house184-25) A reviewer for Norman Records called _Om_ "one of the most singular psychedelic experiences in music, an all-engulfing kaleidoscope that offers us a rare glimpse at a completely unencumbered Coltrane", and concluded: "If you’re looking for catharsis in Coltrane’s discography, _Om_ is where you’ll find it."[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-28) In an essay for [The Quietus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Quietus "The Quietus"), Peter Bebergal stated: "The fierceness of Coltrane's playing indicates that he knows the divine cannot be contained in a thin tube of molded brass. But this is all he has. This is all anyone of us really has. Music binds us to the body. It is where we hear it and where we make it. With _Om_, Coltrane often plays as if he is trying to escape the bonds of the instrument, but his feet won't leave the Earth... Coltrane is trying to give us a glimpse of his heaven, but the noise of his saxophone contains its own holiness by virtue of it being the vessel through which the divine reveals itself". He concluded: "while _Om_ might not easily alter the consciousness of the listener, it still comes awfully close to revealing the intense spiritual desire of Coltrane that shapes the almost desperate mood. It is, however, also a glimpse into the vast spectrum of non-ordinary states of consciousness... Coltrane's ache to break through is humbled by the living organism of the band and the session itself... There is a strange and frightening purity here, one that you don't want to get too close to, but demands respect... Coltrane is the ever-building ascension, over and over again, wanting nothing more than for God to open the gates, all the while begging him to please keep them closed."[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-quietus-21) ## Track listing \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Om_(John_Coltrane_album)&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: Track listing")\] | No. | Title | Length | | --- | --- | --- | | 1. | "Om, Part 1" | 15:06 | Side A | No. | Title | Length | | --- | --- | --- | | 2. | "Om, Part 2" | 14:01 | Side B _Note: while some CD configurations had "Om" as a single track, others kept the original LP record's two-track configuration._ ## Personnel \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Om_(John_Coltrane_album)&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: Personnel")\] - Defined as "something of an irregular institution, a band that has come together intermittently through the years",[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musica_Elettronica_Viva#cite_note-Perkis-1994-1) Musica Elettronica Viva's founding members were Allan Bryant, [Alvin Curran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alvin_Curran "Alvin Curran"), Jon Phetteplace and [Frederic Rzewski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederic_Rzewski "Frederic Rzewski"),[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musica_Elettronica_Viva#cite_note-2) [Richard Teitelbaum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Teitelbaum "Richard Teitelbaum"),[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musica_Elettronica_Viva#cite_note-Perkis-1994-1) and [Carol Plantamura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Plantamura "Carol Plantamura").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musica_Elettronica_Viva#cite_note-3) Other members include [Ivan Vandor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Vandor "Ivan Vandor") and [Steve Lacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Lacy_(saxophonist) "Steve Lacy (saxophonist)").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musica_Elettronica_Viva#cite_note-4) [Garrett List](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garrett_List "Garrett List") and [George E. Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_E._Lewis "George E. Lewis") subsequently joined the group.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musica_Elettronica_Viva#cite_note-Perkis-1994-1) Musica Elettronica Viva were early experimenters in the use of synthesizers. A 1967 performance in [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin") featured a rendition of [John Cage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cage "John Cage")'s _Solo for Voice 2_ with Plantamura's voice transformed through a [Moog synthesizer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moog_synthesizer "Moog synthesizer"). At the end of the 1960s, they took part in the group [Lo Zoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lo_Zoo?action=edit&redlink=1 "Lo Zoo"), founded by artist [Michelangelo Pistoletto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelangelo_Pistoletto "Michelangelo Pistoletto"). They also used such "non-musical" objects as amplified panes of glass and motor oil cans. Their performances achieved mainstream notoriety in Italy for generating vocal audience participation, occasionally resulting in riots, for example at the Musee d'Art Moderne in Paris, at Queen Anne's Hall in London where the police and the fire department kicked the group out, and at the Teatro Regio in Parma where the authorities shut the house lights down and emptied the hall, inspiring a street demonstration led by Jean-Jacques Lebel. Musica Elettronica Viva disbanded in 2017 after a final tour, though at least two CDs were released subsequently. Among the many who performed with the group, Jon Phetteplace died decades ago, Steve Lacy in 2004, Maryanne Amacher in 2009, Garrett List in 2019, Ivan Vandor and Richard Teitelbaum in 2020, and Frederic Rzewski in 2021.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musica_Elettronica_Viva#cite_note-5) ## Discography - _Spacecraft_, recorded in Cologne in 1967 by Bryant, Curran, Rzewski, Teitelbaum and Vandor - _Unified Patchwork Theory_, recorded in Zurich in 1990 by Curran, Rzewski, Teitelbaum, Steve Lacy, and [Garrett List](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garrett_List "Garrett List") Both of the above first issued in 2001 on CD as "Spacecraft/Unified Patchwork Theory" (Alga Marghen, Plana-M 15NMN.038). - _Friday_, recorded in London in 1969 by Curran, Rzewski, Teitelbaum, Franco Cataldi and Gunther Carius, reissued 2008 (ALGA 073CD) - _The Sound Pool_, recorded 1969, reissued 1998 (Spalax CD14969) - _United Patchwork_, recorded November 1977 in Rome by Curran, Rzewski, Teitelbaum, Lacy, List, and [Karl Berger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Berger "Karl Berger") (Horo 2xLP HDP 15-16) - _MEV 40_, recorded 1967–2007, a 4-CD set of previously unpublished performances issued by [New World Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_World_Records "New World Records") in 2008 (CD80675) - _Apogee_, a double CD (Matchless Recordings, MRCD61, 2005) shared with another of the electronic improvisational ensembles that emerged during the 1960s: [AMM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AMM_(group) "AMM (group)"). The first CD is a studio recording in a joint session in [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England") on April 30, 2004 featuring MEV's Curran, Teitelbaum and Rzewski with the three members of [AMM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AMM_(group) "AMM (group)"). This is the first occasion that the two ensembles have performed together, but not the first time they have shared a split release - each outfit filled a side of the LP Live Electronic Music Improvised, released on a US label (Mainstream) in 1968. The second CD consists of the performances that each group gave at a festival held in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London") on May 1, 2004. - Symphony No 106, Les Disques Victo, 2016 VICTO CD 129, 2016, and digital album - Symphony No. 105, a Café Oto download available as 320k MP3 or 24bit FLAC, 2016 - Symphony No 108, Live at Brno Philharmonic, Hermes' Ear - HE CD 015 / aSB 03, 2017 - Spacecraft Alga Marghen CD 2001, Our Swimmer LP, welle 104LP, 2021 - Symphony No. 107 - The Bard, Black Truffle 104, June 2023 ## References 1. # Globe Unity Orchestra Globe Unity Orchestra Free jazz ensemble The **Globe Unity Orchestra** is a [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") ensemble. Globe Unity was formed in autumn 1966 with a commission received by [Alexander von Schlippenbach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_von_Schlippenbach "Alexander von Schlippenbach") from the [Berlin Jazz Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JazzFest_Berlin "JazzFest Berlin").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Globe_Unity_Orchestra#cite_note-as-1) It had its debut at the [Berliner Philharmonie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berliner_Philharmonie "Berliner Philharmonie") on 3 November combining [Gunter Hampel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunter_Hampel "Gunter Hampel")'s quartet with [Manfred Schoof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manfred_Schoof "Manfred Schoof")' s quintet and [Peter Brötzmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Br%C3%B6tzmann "Peter Brötzmann")'s trio:[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Globe_Unity_Orchestra#cite_note-2) Hampel (bcl, fl); [Willem Breuker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willem_Breuker "Willem Breuker") (bs, ss); Schoof (tp) with [Gerd Dudek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerd_Dudek "Gerd Dudek") (ts); [Alexander von Schlippenbach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_von_Schlippenbach "Alexander von Schlippenbach") (p); [Buschi Niebergall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buschi_Niebergall "Buschi Niebergall") (b) and [Jaki Liebezeit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaki_Liebezeit "Jaki Liebezeit") (d) on one side, Brötzmann (saxophones), [Peter Kowald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Kowald "Peter Kowald") (b, tuba), [Sven-Åke Johansson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sven-%C3%85ke_Johansson "Sven-Åke Johansson") (d) on the other. During the next years this core group was completed by other European and American musicians: [Johannes Bauer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannes_Bauer "Hannes Bauer") (tb), [Anthony Braxton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Braxton "Anthony Braxton") (as, cl), [Willem Breuker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willem_Breuker "Willem Breuker") (ts), [Rüdiger Carl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C3%BCdiger_Carl?action=edit&redlink=1 "Rüdiger Carl") (as, ts), [Günter Christmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%BCnter_Christmann?action=edit&redlink=1 "Günter Christmann") (tb), [Gunter Hampel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunter_Hampel "Gunter Hampel") (bcl), [Toshinori Kondo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toshinori_Kondo "Toshinori Kondo") (tp), [Steve Lacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Lacy_(saxophonist) "Steve Lacy (saxophonist)") (ss), [Paul Lovens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Lovens "Paul Lovens") (drums), [Paul Lytton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Lytton "Paul Lytton") (drums), [Albert Mangelsdorff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Mangelsdorff "Albert Mangelsdorff") (tb), [Evan Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evan_Parker "Evan Parker") (ss, ts), [Michel Pilz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michel_Pilz "Michel Pilz") (bcl, cl, bars), [Ernst-Ludwig Petrowsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst-Ludwig_Petrowsky "Ernst-Ludwig Petrowsky") (as, cl, fl), [Enrico Rava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enrico_Rava "Enrico Rava") (tp), [Paul Rutherford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Rutherford_(trombonist) "Paul Rutherford (trombonist)") (tb), [Heinz Sauer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinz_Sauer "Heinz Sauer") (ss, ts), [Bob Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Stewart_(musician) "Bob Stewart (musician)") (tuba), [Tomasz Stańko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomasz_Sta%C5%84ko "Tomasz Stańko") (tp), and [Kenny Wheeler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Wheeler "Kenny Wheeler") (tp). The Orchestra has been described as providing "the most remarkable assemblies of outside jazz talent since the AACM big bands".[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Globe_Unity_Orchestra#cite_note-3) They performed in New Delhi, India for the Jazz Yatra in late 1970s. They performed at the Ashoka Hotel, New Delhi in 1978. The final concert in the group's main lifetime was at the [Chicago Jazz Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Jazz_Festival "Chicago Jazz Festival") in 1987.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Globe_Unity_Orchestra#cite_note-as-1) The 40th anniversary line-up for the 2006 concerts and recordings were the saxophone players Evan Parker, Ernst-Ludwig Petrowsky, Gerd Dudek, [Rudi Mahall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudi_Mahall "Rudi Mahall") (bcl), the trumpets Kenny Wheeler, Manfred Schoof, Axel Dörner, Jean-Luc Cappozzo and trombonists Paul Rutherford, [George E. Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_E._Lewis "George E. Lewis"), [Jeb Bishop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeb_Bishop "Jeb Bishop"), J. - [Weather Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report "Weather Report") | | | | Website | [wayneshorter.com (archived)](https://web.archive.org/web/20160330174015/http://www.wayneshorter.com/) | Musical artist **Wayne Shorter** (August 25, 1933 – March 2, 2023) was an American [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") saxophonist, composer, and bandleader, widely regarded as one of the most important and influential figures in the history of jazz. Over a career spanning more than six decades, he received 12 [Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Awards "Grammy Awards") and the [Polar Music Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polar_Music_Prize "Polar Music Prize"), and was acclaimed worldwide for his originality, compositional depth, and transformative approach to [musical improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_improvisation "Musical improvisation").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-grammy-ws-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-chow-2) Shorter first rose to mainstream prominence in 1959 after joining [Art Blakey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Blakey "Art Blakey")'s [Jazz Messengers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Messengers "Jazz Messengers"), where he quickly became the ensemble's primary composer and one of its defining creative voices. In 1964, he joined [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")'s [Second Great Quintet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis_Quintet#Second_Great_Quintet "Miles Davis Quintet"), contributing compositions and performances that helped shape one of the most innovative and influential periods in jazz history. In 1970, he co-founded the [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") band [Weather Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report "Weather Report"), which achieved international success and redefined the possibilities of electric jazz. As a bandleader, Shorter recorded more than 20 albums, and many of his compositions—including works written for Davis, Weather Report, and his own groups—became enduring [jazz standards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_standard "Jazz standard"). His music is noted for its harmonic sophistication, narrative structure, and philosophical depth, earning sustained critical praise and influence across generations of musicians. Shorter was especially acclaimed for his mastery of the [soprano saxophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soprano_saxophone "Soprano saxophone"), having shifted his primary focus from the [tenor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenor_saxophone "Tenor saxophone") in the late 1960s. Beginning in 1970, he dominated _[DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat")_ magazine's annual critics' and readers' polls on soprano saxophone, winning the critics' poll for 10 consecutive years and the readers' poll for 18.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-3) In 2008, _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")_ music critic [Ben Ratliff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Ratliff "Ben Ratliff") described Shorter as "probably jazz's greatest living small-group composer and a contender for greatest living improviser," a characterization that reflected his towering status within the genre.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-Ratliff-4) ## Early life and education \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wayne_Shorter&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")\] Wayne Shorter was born in [Newark, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newark,_New_Jersey "Newark, New Jersey"),[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-Larkin-5) the son of Louise and Joseph Shorter.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-6) He graduated from [Newark Arts High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newark_Arts_High_School "Newark Arts High School")[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-8) in 1952. Encouraged by his parents, Shorter began taking [clarinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarinet "Clarinet") lessons at age 16 and later switched to [tenor saxophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenor_saxophone "Tenor saxophone"). While in high school, Wayne performed with the Nat Phipps Band in Newark. His older brother [Alan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Shorter "Alan Shorter") played [alto saxophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alto_saxophone "Alto saxophone") before switching to the [trumpet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trumpet "Trumpet") in college. Shorter enrolled at [New York University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_University "New York University") in 1952 and graduated with a degree in [music education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_education "Music education") in 1956. After graduating, Shorter spent two years in the [U.S. Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army "United States Army"), during which time he played briefly with [Horace Silver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Silver "Horace Silver"). After his discharge, he played with [Maynard Ferguson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maynard_Ferguson "Maynard Ferguson"). While growing up, Shorter loved comic books and science fiction as well as music. In his youth, Shorter acquired the nickname "Mr. Gone", which later became an album title for Weather Report.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-9) ## Career \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wayne_Shorter&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Career")\] | | | | --- | --- | | [![icon](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/99/Question_book-new.svg/60px-Question_book-new.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Question_book-new.svg) | This section **needs [more citations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")**. In 1959, Shorter joined [Art Blakey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Blakey "Art Blakey")'s Jazz Messengers where he stayed for four years, eventually becoming [musical director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_director "Music director") and composing pieces for the band.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-10) Together they toured the US, Japan, and Europe, recording several albums. During this time, Shorter "established himself as one of the most gifted of the young saxophonists", and received international acknowledgment.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-Rough_Guide_to_Jazz-11) ### With Miles Davis (1964–70) \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wayne_Shorter&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: With Miles Davis (1964–70)")\] [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock") said of Shorter's tenure in [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")'s [Second Great Quintet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis_Quintet#Second_Great_Quintet "Miles Davis Quintet"): "The master writer to me, in that group, was Wayne Shorter. He still is a master. Wayne was one of the few people who brought music to Miles that didn't get changed."[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-Lyons-12) Davis said, "Wayne is a real composer. He writes scores, writes the parts for everybody, just as he wants them to sound. ... Wayne also brought in a kind of curiosity about working with musical rules. If they didn't work, then he broke them, but with musical sense; he understood that freedom in music was the ability to know the rules, in order to bend them to your own satisfaction and taste."[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-13) [Ian Carr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Carr "Ian Carr"), musician and [Rough Guide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rough_Guides "Rough Guides") author, said that with Davis, Shorter found his own voice as a player and composer. "Blakey's hard-driving, straight-ahead rhythms had brought out the muscularity in Shorter's tenor playing, but the greater freedom of the Davis rhythm-section allowed him to explore new emotional and technical dimensions."[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-Rough_Guide_to_Jazz-11) Shorter remained in Davis's band after the breakup of the quintet in 1968, playing on early [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") recordings including _[In a Silent Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way "In a Silent Way")_ and _[Bitches Brew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew "Bitches Brew")_ (both 1969). His last live dates and studio recordings with Davis were in 1970. Until 1968, he played [tenor saxophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenor_saxophone "Tenor saxophone") exclusively. The final album on which he played tenor in the regular sequence of Davis albums was _[Filles de Kilimanjaro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filles_de_Kilimanjaro "Filles de Kilimanjaro")_. In 1969, he played the [soprano saxophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soprano_saxophone "Soprano saxophone") on the Davis album _[In a Silent Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way "In a Silent Way")_ and on his own _[Super Nova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Nova_(Wayne_Shorter_album) "Super Nova (Wayne Shorter album)")_ (recorded with then-current Davis sidemen [Chick Corea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chick_Corea "Chick Corea") and [John McLaughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McLaughlin_(musician) "John McLaughlin (musician)")). When performing live with Davis, and on recordings from summer 1969 to early spring 1970, he played both soprano and tenor saxophones: by the early 1970s, however, he chiefly played soprano. #### Solo Blue Note recordings \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wayne_Shorter&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: Solo Blue Note recordings")\] Simultaneous with his time in the Davis quintet, Shorter recorded several albums for [Blue Note Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records"), featuring, almost exclusively, his own compositions, with a variety of line-ups, quartets and larger groups, including Blue Note favorites such as trumpeter [Freddie Hubbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Hubbard "Freddie Hubbard"). His first Blue Note album (of 11 in total recorded from 1964 to 1970) was _[Night Dreamer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Night_Dreamer "Night Dreamer")_, recorded at [Rudy Van Gelder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudy_Van_Gelder "Rudy Van Gelder")'s studio in 1964 with [Lee Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Morgan "Lee Morgan") (trumpet), [McCoy Tyner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner "McCoy Tyner") (piano), [Reggie Workman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggie_Workman "Reggie Workman") (bass) and [Elvin Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elvin_Jones "Elvin Jones") (drums). Two more albums were recorded in 1964, _[JuJu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JuJu_(album) "JuJu (album)")_ and _[Speak No Evil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_No_Evil_(Wayne_Shorter_album) "Speak No Evil (Wayne Shorter album)")_. Of the three Blue Note albums Shorter recorded in 1965, _[The All Seeing Eye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_All_Seeing_Eye "The All Seeing Eye")_ (rec. 1965, rel. 1966) was a workout with a larger group, while _[Adam's Apple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam's_Apple_(album) "Adam's Apple (album)")_ (rec. 1966, rel. 1967) was back to carefully constructed melodies by Shorter leading a quartet. Then a sextet again in the following year for _[Schizophrenia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schizophrenia_(Wayne_Shorter_album) "Schizophrenia (Wayne Shorter album)")_ (rec. 1967, rel. 1969) with Herbie Hancock, bassist [Ron Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Carter "Ron Carter"), trombonist [Curtis Fuller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curtis_Fuller "Curtis Fuller"), alto saxophonist/flautist [James Spaulding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Spaulding "James Spaulding") and strong rhythms by drummer [Joe Chambers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Chambers "Joe Chambers"). Shorter also recorded occasionally as a [sideman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sideman "Sideman") (again mainly for Blue Note) with trumpeter [Donald Byrd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Byrd "Donald Byrd"), McCoy Tyner, trombonist [Grachan Moncur III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grachan_Moncur_III "Grachan Moncur III"), Freddie Hubbard, Lee Morgan, as well as bandmates Herbie Hancock and drummer [Tony Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer) "Tony Williams (drummer)"). ### Weather Report (1971–1986) \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wayne_Shorter&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: Weather Report (1971–1986)")\] Following the release of _[Odyssey of Iska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odyssey_of_Iska "Odyssey of Iska")_ in 1970, Shorter formed the fusion group [Weather Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report "Weather Report") with Davis veteran keyboardist [Joe Zawinul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Zawinul "Joe Zawinul") and bassist [Miroslav Vitouš](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miroslav_Vitou%C5%A1 "Miroslav Vitouš"). The other original members were percussionist [Airto Moreira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airto_Moreira "Airto Moreira"), and drummer [Alphonse Mouzon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphonse_Mouzon "Alphonse Mouzon"). After Vitouš's departure in 1973, Shorter and Zawinul co-led the group until the band's break-up in late 1985. A variety of musicians would make up Weather Report over the years (most notably the revolutionary bassist [Jaco Pastorius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaco_Pastorius "Jaco Pastorius") and drummers [Peter Erskine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Erskine "Peter Erskine") and [Omar Hakim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omar_Hakim "Omar Hakim")) helping the band produce many high quality recordings in diverse styles, with funk, [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop"), [Latin jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz "Latin jazz"), ethnic music, and [futurism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Futurism "Futurism") being the most prevalent denominators. #### Solo and side projects \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wayne_Shorter&action=edit§ion=6 "Edit section: Solo and side projects")\] Shorter also recorded critically acclaimed albums as a bandleader, notably 1974's _[Native Dancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_Dancer_(album) "Native Dancer (album)")_, which featured Hancock and Brazilian composer and vocalist [Milton Nascimento](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton_Nascimento "Milton Nascimento"). [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/Wayne_Shorter_Berkeley_1980.jpg/250px-Wayne_Shorter_Berkeley_1980.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wayne_Shorter_Berkeley_1980.jpg) Shorter at the [UC Berkeley Jazz Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berkeley_Jazz_Festival "Berkeley Jazz Festival"), May 25, 1980 In the late 1970s and the early 1980s, he toured in the [V.S.O.P. quintet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V.S.O.P._(group) "V.S.O.P. (group)"). This group was a revival of the 1960s Davis quintet, except that Freddie Hubbard filled the trumpet chair. Shorter appeared with the same former Davis bandmates on the [Carlos Santana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Santana "Carlos Santana") double LP _[The Swing of Delight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Swing_of_Delight "The Swing of Delight")_ (1980), for which he also composed a number of pieces. From 1977 through 2002, he appeared on 10 [Joni Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joni_Mitchell "Joni Mitchell") studio albums, gaining him a wider audience. He played an extended solo on [the title track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aja_(song) "Aja (song)") of [Steely Dan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steely_Dan "Steely Dan")'s 1977 album _[Aja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aja_(album) "Aja (album)")_.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-14) ### Later career \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wayne_Shorter&action=edit§ion=7 "Edit section: Later career")\] After leaving Weather Report in 1986, Shorter continued to record and lead groups in [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") styles, including touring in 1988 with guitarist [Carlos Santana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Santana "Carlos Santana"), who appeared on _[This is This!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/This_is_This! "This is This!")_ (1986), the last Weather Report disc. There is a concert video recorded at the [Lugano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lugano "Lugano") Jazz Festival in 1987, with [Jim Beard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Beard "Jim Beard") (keyboards), Carl James (bass), [Terri Lyne Carrington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terri_Lyne_Carrington "Terri Lyne Carrington") (drums), and [Marilyn Mazur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marilyn_Mazur "Marilyn Mazur") (percussion). In 1989, he contributed to a hit on the rock charts, playing the soprano saxophone solo on [Don Henley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Henley "Don Henley")'s song " [The End of the Innocence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_End_of_the_Innocence_(song) "The End of the Innocence (song)")" and also produced the album _Pilar_ by the Portuguese singer-songwriter [Pilar Homem de Melo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilar_Homem_de_Melo "Pilar Homem de Melo"). He also maintained an occasional working relationship with Herbie Hancock, including [a tribute album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Tribute_to_Miles "A Tribute to Miles") recorded shortly after Miles Davis's death with Herbie Hancock, Ron Carter, Tony Williams and [Wallace Roney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallace_Roney "Wallace Roney"). He continued to appear on Mitchell's records in the 1990s, and can be heard on the soundtrack of the [Harrison Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrison_Ford "Harrison Ford") film _[The Fugitive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fugitive_(1993_film) "The Fugitive (1993 film)")_ (1993). In 1995, Shorter released the album _[High Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Life_(Wayne_Shorter_album) "High Life (Wayne Shorter album)")_, his first solo recording for seven years. It was also his debut as a leader for [Verve Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verve_Records "Verve Records"). Shorter composed all the compositions on the album and co-produced it with the bassist [Marcus Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Miller "Marcus Miller") with pianist, [synthesist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analog_synthesizer "Analog synthesizer"), and sound designer [Rachel Z](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Z "Rachel Z"). _High Life_ received the [Grammy Award for Best Contemporary Jazz Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Contemporary_Jazz_Album "Grammy Award for Best Contemporary Jazz Album") in 1996. Shorter worked with Herbie Hancock once again in 1997, on the much acclaimed and heralded album _[1+1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1+1_(Herbie_Hancock_and_Wayne_Shorter_album) "1+1 (Herbie Hancock and Wayne Shorter album)")_. The song "Aung San Suu Kyi" (named for the [Burmese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myanmar "Myanmar") pro-democracy [activist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aung_San_Suu_Kyi "Aung San Suu Kyi")) won both Hancock and Shorter a Grammy Award. In 2009, he was announced as one of the headline acts at the [Gnaoua World Music Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gnaoua_World_Music_Festival "Gnaoua World Music Festival") in Essaouira, Morocco. His 2013 live album _[Without a Net](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Without_a_Net_(Wayne_Shorter_album) "Without a Net (Wayne Shorter album)")_ (rec. 2010) is his first with Blue Note Records since _[Odyssey of Iska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odyssey_of_Iska "Odyssey of Iska")_ (rec. 1970, rel. 1971). #### Quartet \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wayne_Shorter&action=edit§ion=8 "Edit section: Quartet")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ad/Wayne_Shorter_quartet.jpg/330px-Wayne_Shorter_quartet.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wayne_Shorter_quartet.jpg) The Wayne Shorter Quartet at the Teatro degli Arcimboldi, [Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milan "Milan"), 2010 In 2000, Shorter formed the first permanent acoustic group under his name, a quartet with pianist [Danilo Perez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danilo_Perez "Danilo Perez"), bassist [John Patitucci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Patitucci "John Patitucci"), and drummer [Brian Blade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Blade "Brian Blade"), playing his own compositions, many of them reworkings of tunes going back to the 1960s. Four albums of live recordings have been released: _[Footprints Live!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footprints_Live! "Footprints Live!")_ (rec. live 2001, rel. 2002); _[Beyond the Sound Barrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beyond_the_Sound_Barrier "Beyond the Sound Barrier")_ (rec. live 2002–2004, rel. 2005); _[Without a Net](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Without_a_Net_(Wayne_Shorter_album) "Without a Net (Wayne Shorter album)")_ (rec. live 2010, rel. 2013); and _[Emanon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emanon_(Wayne_Shorter_album) "Emanon (Wayne Shorter album)")_ (2018), with the latter, in addition to live material, including Shorter's quartet in a studio session with the 34-piece [Orpheus Chamber Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orpheus_Chamber_Orchestra "Orpheus Chamber Orchestra"). The quartet has received great acclaim from fans and critics, especially for the strength of Shorter's tenor saxophone playing. The biography _Footprints: The Life and Work of Wayne Shorter_ by journalist Michelle Mercer examines the working life of the musicians as well as Shorter's thoughts and Buddhist beliefs.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-15) _Beyond the Sound Barrier_ received the 2006 [Grammy Award for Best Jazz Instrumental Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Jazz_Instrumental_Album "Grammy Award for Best Jazz Instrumental Album"). Shorter's 2003 album _[Alegría](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alegr%C3%ADa_(Wayne_Shorter_album) "Alegría (Wayne Shorter album)")_ (his first studio album for 10 years, since _High Life_) received the 2004 Grammy Award for Best Jazz Instrumental Album; it features the quartet with a host of other musicians, including pianist [Brad Mehldau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brad_Mehldau "Brad Mehldau"), drummer [Terri Lyne Carrington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terri_Lyne_Carrington "Terri Lyne Carrington") and former Weather Report percussionist [Alex Acuña](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Acu%C3%B1a "Alex Acuña"). Shorter's compositions, some new, some reworked from his Miles Davis period, feature the complex Latin rhythms that he specialized in during his Weather Report days. #### _Wayne Shorter: Zero Gravity_ \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wayne_Shorter&action=edit§ion=9 "Edit section: Wayne Shorter: Zero Gravity")\] In 2015, producer/director Dorsay Alavi began filming a documentary about the life of Wayne Shorter called _Wayne Shorter: Zero Gravity_.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-16) A number of high-profile musicians, including [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"), [Esperanza Spalding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esperanza_Spalding "Esperanza Spalding"), and [Terri Lyne Carrington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terri_Lyne_Carrington "Terri Lyne Carrington"), performed at a donor event to raise funds for the documentary; two of the largest donations came from the [Herb Alpert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Alpert "Herb Alpert") Foundation and [Carlos Santana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Santana "Carlos Santana").[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-17) In 2018, a four-hour preliminary cut was completed. Subsequently, [Brad Pitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brad_Pitt "Brad Pitt") joined the project with his production company. After some delay, partly due to the Covid crisis, from August 2023, the documentary is available as a three-hour miniseries on [Amazon Prime Video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Prime_Video "Amazon Prime Video").[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-18)[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-19) #### Mega Nova \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wayne_Shorter&action=edit§ion=10 "Edit section: Mega Nova")\] In 2016, it was announced that Shorter, Carlos Santana, and Herbie Hancock would begin touring under the name Mega Nova. Also included within the [supergroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supergroup_(music) "Supergroup (music)") was bassist [Marcus Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Miller "Marcus Miller") and drummer [Cindy Blackman Santana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cindy_Blackman_Santana "Cindy Blackman Santana").[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-20) Their first show together was on August 24, 2016, at the [Hollywood Bowl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood_Bowl "Hollywood Bowl").[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-21)[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-22) #### _Iphigenia_ \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wayne_Shorter&action=edit§ion=11 "Edit section: Iphigenia")\] In 2018, Shorter retired from his near 70-year performing career due to health issues. He continued working as a composer, creating a "new operatic work" titled _[Iphigenia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iphigenia_(opera) "Iphigenia (opera)")_, a loose adaptation of the [ancient Greek myth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iphigenia#Adaptations_of_the_story "Iphigenia"); with [Esperanza Spalding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esperanza_Spalding "Esperanza Spalding") writing the libretto and architect [Frank Gehry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry "Frank Gehry") designing the sets, which premiered on November 12, 2021, at the [Cutler Majestic Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cutler_Majestic_Theatre "Cutler Majestic Theatre").[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-23)[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-24)[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-25) ## Personal life \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wayne_Shorter&action=edit§ion=12 "Edit section: Personal life")\] In 1961, Shorter met Teruko Nakagami, a [Japanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_people "Japanese people") woman. They married and had a daughter, Miyako. Some of his compositions are copyrighted as "Miyako Music" and Shorter dedicated the pieces "Miyako" and "Infant Eyes" to his daughter. The couple separated in 1964.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-people-26) Shorter met Ana Maria Patricio in 1966 and they married in 1970.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-people-26) In 1986, their daughter Iska died of a [grand mal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_mal "Grand mal") seizure at age 14.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-27) Ana Maria and the couple's niece, Dalila, were killed in the explosion of [TWA Flight 800](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TWA_Flight_800 "TWA Flight 800"), off the coast of [Long Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Island "Long Island") on July 17, 1996 while traveling to visit Shorter in Italy.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-28) Dalila was the daughter of Ana Maria Shorter's sister and her husband, jazz vocalist [Jon Lucien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Lucien "Jon Lucien").[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-people-26) In 1999, Shorter married Carolina Dos Santos, a close friend of Ana Maria. Composer and producer [Rick Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Shorter "Rick Shorter") (1934–2017) was Shorter's cousin.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-29) Shorter practiced [Nichiren Buddhism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nichiren_Buddhism "Nichiren Buddhism") for more than 50 years as a longtime member of the Buddhist association [Soka Gakkai International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soka_Gakkai_International "Soka Gakkai International").[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-30) Singer and actress [Tina Turner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tina_Turner "Tina Turner") credits Shorter with saving her life. In Turner's 2020 spiritual memoir _[Happiness Becomes You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Happiness_Becomes_You_(book) "Happiness Becomes You (book)")_, she states that Shorter and Ana Maria gave her critical refuge at their home for six months in 1976 after Turner left her abusive husband, [Ike Turner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ike_Turner "Ike Turner").[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-31) Shorter died in Los Angeles, California, on March 2, 2023, aged 89.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-32) ## Honors and recognition \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wayne_Shorter&action=edit§ion=13 "Edit section: Honors and recognition")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0b/Wayne_Shorter.jpg/250px-Wayne_Shorter.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wayne_Shorter.jpg) Shorter performing in 2006 In 1999, Shorter received an Honorary Doctorate of Music from the [Berklee College of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berklee_College_of_Music "Berklee College of Music").[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-33) On September 17, 2013, Shorter received a Lifetime Achievement Award from the [Herbie Hancock Institute of Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock_Institute_of_Jazz "Herbie Hancock Institute of Jazz") (formerly [Thelonious Monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thelonious_Monk "Thelonious Monk") Institute of Jazz).[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-34) On December 18, 2014, the Recording Academy announced that Shorter had been awarded the [Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Lifetime_Achievement_Award "Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award") in honor of his "prolific contributions to our culture and history".[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-35) In 2016, Shorter was awarded a [Guggenheim Fellowship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guggenheim_Fellowship "Guggenheim Fellowship") in music composition, the only jazz artist to receive the honor that year.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-36) In 2017, Shorter was announced as the joint winner of the [Polar Music Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polar_Music_Prize "Polar Music Prize"). The award committee stated: "Without the musical explorations of Wayne Shorter, modern music would not have drilled so deep."[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-chow-2) In 2018, Shorter received the [Kennedy Center Honors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Center_Honors "Kennedy Center Honors") Award from the [John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy_Center_for_the_Performing_Arts "John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts") for his lifetime of contributions to the arts.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-37) On April 29, 2022, Shorter's hometown of Newark renamed a street in his honor. Park Place was renamed "Wayne Shorter Way".[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-38) On April 22, 2023, the [BBC Radio Three](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Radio_Three
