- [MCA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MCA_Records "MCA Records") | | Spinoff of | [The Sparrows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sparrows_(band) "The Sparrows (band)") | | | | Past members | - [List](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Steppenwolf_members "List of Steppenwolf members") | | | | Website | [steppenwolf.com](http://steppenwolf.com/) | **Steppenwolf** (later known as **John Kay & Steppenwolf**) was a Canadian-American rock band formed in Los Angeles in 1967.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-AllMusic-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-Biography-OS-2) The group was founded by singer/rhythm guitarist [John Kay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kay_(musician) "John Kay (musician)"), keyboardist [Goldy McJohn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_McJohn "Goldy McJohn") and drummer [Jerry Edmonton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Edmonton "Jerry Edmonton"), all formerly of the Canadian band [the Sparrows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sparrows_(band) "The Sparrows (band)").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-The_Great_Rock_Discography-5) Guitarist [Michael Monarch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Monarch "Michael Monarch") and bassist [Rushton Moreve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushton_Moreve "Rushton Moreve") were recruited via notices placed in Los Angeles–area record and musical instrument stores. Steppenwolf sold over 25 million records worldwide,[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-6) released seven gold albums and one platinum album, and had 13 [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100") singles, of which seven were [Top 40](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Top_40 "Top 40") [hits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hit_record "Hit record"),[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-7) including three top 10 successes: " [Born to Be Wild](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Born_to_Be_Wild "Born to Be Wild")", " [Magic Carpet Ride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magic_Carpet_Ride_(Steppenwolf_song) "Magic Carpet Ride (Steppenwolf song)")", and " [Rock Me](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_Me_(Steppenwolf_song) "Rock Me (Steppenwolf song)")". Steppenwolf enjoyed worldwide success from 1968 to 1972, but clashing personalities led to the end of the core lineup. From 1980 to 2018, John Kay was the only original member involved, having been the lead singer since 1967. The band was called John Kay & Steppenwolf from 1980 to 2018. In [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RPM_(magazine) "RPM (magazine)"), they had four top 10 songs, 12 top 40 and 14 in the top 100.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-8) In 2016, the [Rock and Roll Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_Roll_Hall_of_Fame "Rock and Roll Hall of Fame") nominated the band for induction in 2017.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-9) Although the band fell short of enough votes to qualify for induction that year, in 2018 the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame selected one of its biggest singles—1968's "Born to Be Wild"—as an inaugural selection in its singles category.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-10) ## History ### The Sparrows In 1965, John Kay joined [the Sparrows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sparrows_(band) "The Sparrows (band)") and was followed by Goldy McJohn. The group eventually broke up.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-stone-11) ### Breakthrough, success, and decline (1967–1972) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1d/Steppenwolf_original_lineup.jpg/500px-Steppenwolf_original_lineup.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Steppenwolf_original_lineup.jpg) The original lineup of Steppenwolf. Clockwise from top left: McJohn, Edmonton, Moreve, Monarch, Kay In late 1967, [Gabriel Mekler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel_Mekler "Gabriel Mekler") urged Kay to re-form the Sparrows and suggested the name change to Steppenwolf, inspired by [Hermann Hesse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Hesse "Hermann Hesse")'s [1927 novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(novel) "Steppenwolf (novel)").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-12)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-The_Great_Rock_Discography-5)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-stone-11) Steppenwolf's first two singles were "A Girl I Knew" and "Sookie Sookie". The band finally rocketed to worldwide fame after their third single, "Born to Be Wild", was released in 1968, as well as their version of [Hoyt Axton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoyt_Axton "Hoyt Axton")'s " [The Pusher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pusher "The Pusher")". Both of these tunes were used prominently in the 1969 [counterculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterculture_of_the_1960s "Counterculture of the 1960s") [cult film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cult_film "Cult film") _[Easy Rider](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Easy_Rider "Easy Rider")_[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-Grdn-13) (both titles originally had been released on the band's [debut album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(Steppenwolf_album) "Steppenwolf (Steppenwolf album)")).[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-The_Great_Rock_Discography-5) In the movie _Easy Rider_, the song "The Pusher" accompanies a drug deal, and [Peter Fonda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Fonda "Peter Fonda") stuffing dollar bills into his Stars and Stripes-clad fuel tank, after which "Born to Be Wild" is heard in the opening credits, with Fonda and [Dennis Hopper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennis_Hopper "Dennis Hopper") riding their Harley choppers through the America of the late 1960s. The song, which has been closely associated with motorcycles ever since, introduced to rock lyrics the signature term " [heavy metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_metal_music "Heavy metal music")"[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-The_Great_Rock_Discography-5) (though not about a kind of music, but about a motorcycle: "I like smoke and lightning, heavy metal thunder, racin' with the wind...").[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-Grdn-13) Written by Sparrow guitarist Dennis Edmonton, who had begun using the pen name [Mars Bonfire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars_Bonfire "Mars Bonfire") and inspired by a billboard roadside advertisement Bonfire liked which depicted a motorcycle tearing through the billboard artwork, the song had already reached number two on the _Billboard_ Hot 100 in August 1968.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-The_Great_Rock_Discography-5) It sold over one million copies, and was awarded a [gold disc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_recording_sales_certification "Music recording sales certification").[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-The_Book_of_Golden_Discs-14) In 1968, Steppenwolf played one of their biggest shows up to that time at the [Fillmore East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fillmore_East "Fillmore East") to rave reviews, sharing the bill with [Buddy Rich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddy_Rich "Buddy Rich") and Children of God.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-15) The group's following albums had several more hit singles, including " [Magic Carpet Ride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magic_Carpet_Ride_(Steppenwolf_song) "Magic Carpet Ride (Steppenwolf song)")" from _[The Second](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Second "The Second")_ which reached number three and also sold over one million copies,[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-The_Book_of_Golden_Discs-14) and "Rock Me" from _[At Your Birthday Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/At_Your_Birthday_Party "At Your Birthday Party")_ which reached number 10.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-The_Great_Rock_Discography-5) _[Monster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monster_(Steppenwolf_album) "Monster (Steppenwolf album)")_, which questioned US [Vietnam War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War") policy, was the band's most political album. Following the _Monster_ album from 1969, the following year, the band released _[Steppenwolf 7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_7 "Steppenwolf 7")_, which included the song "Snowblind Friend", another Hoyt Axton-penned song about the era and attitudes of drugs and associated problems.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-Larkin-16) Several changes in the group's personnel were made after the first few years.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-The_Great_Rock_Discography-5) Bassist Rushton Moreve was fired from the group in 1968 for missing gigs after he became afraid to return to Los Angeles, convinced by his girlfriend that it was going to be leveled by an earthquake and fall into the sea. Rob Black briefly filled in for Moreve until former Sparrow bandmate [Nick St. Nicholas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_St._Nicholas "Nick St. Nicholas") came aboard in the latter months of 1968. Michael Monarch quit the group in August 1969 as his relationship with Kay deteriorated. [Larry Byrom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Byrom "Larry Byrom"), who had been in TIME with Nick St. Nicholas, ably replaced Monarch on guitar.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-Larkin-16) But Nick St. Nicholas was let go in mid-1970. He had supposedly appeared in nothing but rabbit ears and a jock strap at the Fillmore East in April 1970[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-17) – and his habit of wearing muumuus and kaftans on stage began to wear on Kay, whose penchant for leather vests and pants was more in line with the image he wanted for the band. [George Biondo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Biondo "George Biondo") was then recruited, and the band lineup for their live performances in the middle of 1970 was John Kay, Jerry Edmonton, Goldy McJohn, Larry Byrom, and George Biondo. However this lineup was also unable to remain together, as Byrom became upset with McJohn over personal issues and quit the band in the early part of 1971. Guitarist [Kent Henry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_Henry "Kent Henry") then replaced Byrom.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-The_Great_Rock_Discography-5) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/68/Steppenwolf_%281970%29.png/500px-Steppenwolf_%281970%29.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Steppenwolf_(1970).png) In 1970 In November 1971, the band released _For Ladies Only_, with the lineup consisting of Kay, Henry, Biondo, McJohn and Edmonton. The album was notable for several reasons, most notably the controversial LP inside cover art, the romantic, political, social lyrical content and the fact that it featured several of the group members on lead vocals. ### Breakup (1972–1973) The band broke up after a farewell concert in Los Angeles on Valentine's Day, 1972.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-Larkin-16) Kay went on to a brief solo career, scoring a minor solo hit in 1972 with "I'm Movin' On" from his album _Forgotten Songs and Unsung Heroes_. Although it was generally praised by most critics, album sales were disappointing in the US.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-The_Great_Rock_Discography-5) Kay released a second solo album in 1973 on the [Dunhill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunhill_Records "Dunhill Records") label titled _My Sportin' Life_. This album sold less than his first solo album and was less gritty and more LA studio-polish in sound. Following the first official breakup of Steppenwolf, and after the release of Kay's first solo album, a late summer and autumn 1972 tour in the US and Europe occurred, which featured Kay heading both the John Kay Band and Steppenwolf, at the top of the bill. Dunhill had released an album of a collection of Steppenwolf songs titled _Rest in Peace_. Thus, the tour was known as the RIP tour.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-18) ### Reunion (1974–1976) Steppenwolf reformed in 1974 with its core lineup of Kay, Edmonton and McJohn, along with longtime bassist Biondo and newcomer [Bobby Cochran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Cochran "Bobby Cochran"), [Eddie Cochran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Cochran "Eddie Cochran")'s nephew, on lead guitar.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-The_Great_Rock_Discography-5) The band signed with [Mums Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mums_Records "Mums Records") in retaliation for what Kay perceived as a lack of support by Dunhill Records for his solo albums. Their first reunion album was _Slow Flux_, which included their last top 40 hit, "Straight Shootin' Woman".[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-The_Great_Rock_Discography-5) In February 1975, McJohn was dismissed for what Kay described as a decline in the quality of his performances, as well as erratic behavior. McJohn was replaced by [Andy Chapin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Chapin "Andy Chapin") on _Hour of the Wolf_ in 1975, though McJohn appeared in artwork for the single to _Caroline_. After the album peaked at number 155, Kay attempted to dissolve the band again, but the label, now having been absorbed by [Epic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epic_Records "Epic Records"), insisted Steppenwolf record one more album to satisfy their contractual obligations. The ensuing album, _Skullduggery_ (1976), featuring [Wayne Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Cook_(musician) "Wayne Cook (musician)") on keyboards, was released without a tour to support it, and by the early fall of 1976, Steppenwolf disbanded a second time. Kay appeared in a segment of the popular music television show _The Midnight Special_ to announce the end of Steppenwolf and also played a solo version of the song "Hey I'm Alright". This song appeared on Kay's third solo album _All In Good Time_, released on Mercury Records in 1978.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-The_Great_Rock_Discography-5) ### "New Steppenwolf" revival act (1976–1980) After Kay disbanded Steppenwolf, former members [Goldy McJohn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_McJohn "Goldy McJohn") and [Nick St. Nicholas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_St._Nicholas "Nick St. Nicholas") formed a "revival act" called "New Steppenwolf". McJohn did not last long, but St. Nicholas continued with the venture for several years. Various incarnations included, according to author [Dave Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Thompson_(author) "Dave Thompson (author)"), a "revolving door of musicians" consisting of "jobbing players".[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-19) Among those players were vocalist Tom Holland (who would go on to form the B'zz and later Holland) and drummer [Steve Riley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Riley_(drummer) "Steve Riley (drummer)") of future [W.A.S.P.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W.A.S.P._(band) "W.A.S.P. (band)") and [L.A. Guns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L.A._Guns "L.A. Guns") fame. Yet another musician involved, guitarist Glen Bui, went on to work with Goldy McJohn until he died in 2017. _The Rolling Stone Encyclopedia of Rock & Roll_ described these bands as "unprofessional, bogus versions" of Steppenwolf.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-stone-11) Although Kay and Edmonton had originally licensed the use of the "New Steppenwolf" name, they later sued for breach of contract. St. Nicholas agreed in 1980 to cease use of the name, but legal disputes about promotional use of the Steppenwolf name continued until 2000.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-20) ### John Kay and Steppenwolf (1980–2018) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/38/John_Kay.JPG/500px-John_Kay.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:John_Kay.JPG) Kay and Steppenwolf performing in [Lillehammer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lillehammer "Lillehammer"), Norway, May 2007 Kay had a few meetings with David Pesnell about management, concert promotions and producing a new album for the band. Pesnell wanted to produce an album featuring new songs on side A, by the reformed band [Three Dog Night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Dog_Night "Three Dog Night") and with side B of the album featuring songs by Steppenwolf. The album's working name was "Back to Back", a play on each band having a side of the album and the fact the bands were back together again. Pesnell's concept was simple: each band should record four new songs, with a fifth song on each side featuring a medley of the band's past songs. This would give the Pesnell-produced album a double release of singles to support a concert tour featuring the two bands. Though both bands liked the concept of the album and tour, the arguments included who would be side A and side B and which of the two would headline the upcoming concert tour. The reformed John Kay and Steppenwolf line-up featured John Kay, Michael Palmer (guitars, backing vocals), Steve Palmer (drums, backing vocals), Danny Ironstone (keyboards, backing vocals), and Kurtis Teel on bass. The Palmer brothers had played in a group called Tall Water and had also been involved with Kay in his solo career playing live gigs in the late 1970s. Teel was replaced by Chad Peery and Ironstone by Brett Tuggle by 1981, and the new grouping released _Live in London_ overseas. Tuggle was then displaced by [Michael Wilk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Wilk "Michael Wilk") and a new studio album, _[Wolftracks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolftracks "Wolftracks")_, was released in 1982. _Wolftracks_ was one of the earliest digitally recorded albums in the industry. It was recorded live on a two-track Sony digital recording system. Bassist [Welton Gite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welton_Gite "Welton Gite"), who appeared on this album, left shortly after its completion and was replaced by Gary Link, formerly with [Dokken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back_in_the_Streets "Back in the Streets"). Another album, _Paradox_, followed in 1984. In December 1984, the band as it was disbanded and Kay and Wilk decided to continue in early 1985 with a pared-down quartet composed of Kay, Wilk, Wilk's friend Ron Hurst (drums, backing vocals), and Rocket Ritchotte (guitars, backing vocals). Wilk also handled bass duties from his sequencing computer keyboards from then on. This line-up released _Rock N' Roll Rebels_ (1987) and _Rise & Shine_ (1990); these were on the Qwil and [I.R.S. Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I.R.S._Records "I.R.S. Records") imprints, respectively. Ritchotte had departed temporarily in 1989 to be replaced by [Les Dudek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_Dudek "Les Dudek") and then Steve Fister, but then returned in 1990 for three more years. Fister (ex– [Iron Butterfly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Butterfly "Iron Butterfly")) then came back in late 1993, but turned guitar duties over to Danny Johnson (formerly of Derringer, [Rod Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rod_Stewart "Rod Stewart") and others) in 1996. As the band was named after the novel _[Der Steppenwolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(novel) "Steppenwolf (novel)")_ by German author [Hermann Hesse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Hesse "Hermann Hesse"), who was born in the [Black Forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Forest "Black Forest") town of [Calw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calw "Calw"), the city invited them to come over and play in the International Hermann-Hesse-Festival 2002,[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-21) along with other bands inspired by Hesse, such as [Anyone's Daughter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anyone's_Daughter "Anyone's Daughter"). The band performed what they then labeled their "Farewell Concert" on October 6, 2007, at [Ripken Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripken_Stadium "Ripken Stadium") in [Aberdeen, Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberdeen,_Maryland "Aberdeen, Maryland"), featuring Kay, keyboardist and programmer Michael Wilk, drummer Ron Hurst and guitarist Danny Johnson. However, the band, rejoined by bassist Gary Link, began touring again in June 2009.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-22) Steppenwolf was nominated for the [Rock and Roll Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_Roll_Hall_of_Fame "Rock and Roll Hall of Fame") in 2017, but was not inducted.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-23)[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-24) On November 22, 2019, John Kay announced that the band's show on October 14, 2018, was its last.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band)#cite_note-25) ## Band members Main article: [List of Steppenwolf members](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Steppenwolf_members "List of Steppenwolf members") **Original lineup** - [John Kay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kay_(musician) "John Kay (musician)") – lead vocals, rhythm guitar, harmonica (1967–1972, 1974–1976, 1980–2018) - [Michael Monarch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Monarch "Michael Monarch") – lead guitar, backing vocals (1967–1969) - [Rushton Moreve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushton_Moreve "Rushton Moreve") – bass guitar, lead & backing vocals (1968–1969; died 1981) - [Jerry Edmonton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Edmonton "Jerry Edmonton") – drums, backing vocals (1967–1972, 1974–1976; died 1993) - [Goldy McJohn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_McJohn "Goldy McJohn") – keyboards, backing vocals (1967–1972, 1974; died 2017) **Final lineup** - [John Kay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kay_(musician) "John Kay (musician)") – lead vocals, rhythm guitar, harmonica (1967–1972, 1974–1976, 1980–2018) - - [Rykodisc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rykodisc "Rykodisc") | | Formerly of | - [The Mothers of Invention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mothers_of_Invention "The Mothers of Invention") | | Musical artist | | Website | [zappa.com](http://zappa.com/) | **Frank Vincent Zappa**[\[nb 1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-2) (December 21, 1940– December 4, 1993) was an American composer, songwriter, guitarist, conductor, actor, satirist, filmmaker, and activist. In a career spanning more than 30years, Zappa composed [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music"), [pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music "Pop music"), [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion"), [orchestral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orchestra "Orchestra") and _[musique concrète](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musique_concr%C3%A8te "Musique concrète")_ works; he additionally produced nearly all the 60-plus albums he released with his band [the Mothers of Invention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mothers_of_Invention "The Mothers of Invention") and as a solo artist.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-WRAM-3) His [discography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa_discography "Frank Zappa discography") is characterized by [nonconformity](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/nonconformity "wikt:nonconformity"), [improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_improvisation "Musical improvisation"),[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-dweezilimprov-4) sonic experimentation, [musical virtuosity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtuoso "Virtuoso") and [satire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satire "Satire") of American culture.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-semley2012-5) Zappa also directed feature-length films and [music videos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_video "Music video"), and designed album covers. He is considered one of the most innovative and stylistically diverse musicians of the 20th century.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-6)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-museobit-7) As a mostly self-taught composer and performer, Zappa had diverse musical influences that led him to create music that was sometimes difficult to categorize. While in his teens, he acquired a taste for 20th-century classical [modernism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernism_(music) "Modernism (music)"), African-American [rhythm and blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues"), and [doo-wop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doo-wop "Doo-wop") music.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-teentastes-8) He began writing classical music in high school, while simultaneously playing drums in rhythm-and-blues bands, later switching to electric guitar. His debut studio album with the Mothers of Invention, _[Freak Out!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freak_Out! "Freak Out!")_ (1966), combined satirical but seemingly conventional [rock-and-roll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock-and-roll "Rock-and-roll") songs with extended sound collages. He continued this eclectic and experimental approach throughout his career. Zappa's output is unified by a conceptual continuity he termed "Project/Object", with numerous musical phrases, ideas and characters reappearing throughout his albums.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-semley2012-5) His lyrics reflected his iconoclastic views of established social and political processes, structures and movements, often humorously so, and he has been described as the "godfather" of [comedy rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_rock "Comedy rock").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Comedy_rock-9) He was a strident critic of mainstream education and organized religion, and a forthright and passionate advocate for [freedom of speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_speech "Freedom of speech"), [self-education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-education "Self-education"), political participation and the abolition of censorship. Unlike many other rock musicians of his generation, he disapproved of recreational drug use, but supported decriminalization and regulation. Zappa was a highly productive and prolific musician with a controversial critical standing; supporters of his music admired its compositional complexity, while detractors found it lacking emotional depth.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-wp-10) He had greater commercial success outside the U.S., particularly in Europe. Though he worked as an [independent artist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_music "Independent music"), Zappa mostly relied on distribution agreements he had negotiated with the major [record labels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Record_label "Record label"). He remains a major influence on musicians. His many honors include his posthumous 1995 induction into the [Rock and Roll Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_Roll_Hall_of_Fame "Rock and Roll Hall of Fame") and the 1997 [Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Lifetime_Achievement_Award "Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award"). ## 1940–1965: Early life and career ### Childhood Zappa was born on December 21, 1940, in [Baltimore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore "Baltimore"), Maryland, to Rose Marie ([née](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_name#Maiden_and_married_names "Birth name") Colimore) and Francis Vincent Zappa. His father was born in [Partinico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partinico "Partinico"), Sicily. Zappa was predominantly of Sicilian descent but also had Greek, Arbërëshe and French ancestors.[\[nb 2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-11) The eldest of four children, he was raised in an Italian-American household where Italian was often spoken by his grandparents.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):6[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Rolling_Stone_Book-12) The family moved often because his father, a [chemist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemist "Chemist") and mathematician, worked in the defense industry. After a time in [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida") in the 1940s, the family returned to [Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryland "Maryland"), where Zappa's father worked at the [Edgewood Arsenal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgewood_Arsenal "Edgewood Arsenal") chemical warfare facility—since incorporated into the adjacent [Aberdeen Proving Ground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberdeen_Proving_Ground "Aberdeen Proving Ground")—run by the [U.S. Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Army "U.S. Army"). Due to their home's proximity to the arsenal, which stored [mustard gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mustard_gas "Mustard gas"), gas masks were kept in the home in case of an accident.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):20–23 This living arrangement had a profound effect on Zappa, and references to germs, germ warfare, ailments and the defense industry occur frequently throughout his work.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):8–9 Zappa's father often brought [mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(element) "Mercury (element)")-filled lab equipment home from his workplace and gave it to Zappa to play with.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):19 Zappa said that as a child he "used to play with it all the time", often by putting liquid mercury on the floor and using a hammer to spray out mercury droplets in a circular pattern, eventually covering the entire floor of his bedroom with them.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-14) Zappa was often sick as a child, suffering from [asthma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asthma "Asthma"), [earaches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earache "Earache") and [sinus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paranasal_sinuses "Paranasal sinuses") problems. A doctor treated his sinusitis by inserting a pellet of [radium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radium "Radium") into each of Zappa's nostrils. At the time, little was known about the potential dangers of even small amounts of therapeutic radiation and mercury exposure.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):10 Nasal imagery and references appear in his music and lyrics, as well as in the collage album covers created by his long-time collaborator [Cal Schenkel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cal_Schenkel "Cal Schenkel"). Zappa believed his childhood diseases might have been due to exposure to mustard gas released by the nearby chemical warfare facility, and his health worsened when he lived in Baltimore.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):20–23[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):10 In 1952, his family relocated for health reasons to [Monterey, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monterey,_California "Monterey, California"), where his father taught [metallurgy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallurgy "Metallurgy") at the [Naval Postgraduate School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_Postgraduate_School "Naval Postgraduate School").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):22 They soon moved to the [San Diego](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Diego "San Diego") neighborhood of [Clairemont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clairemont,_San_Diego "Clairemont, San Diego"),[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-slaven03-15):46 and then to the nearby city of [El Cajon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Cajon "El Cajon"), before finally returning to San Diego.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-16) ### First musical interests > Since I didn't have any kind of formal training, it didn't make any difference to me if I was listening to [Lightnin' Slim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lightnin'_Slim "Lightnin' Slim"), or a vocal group called the Jewels..., or [Webern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Webern "Webern"), or [Varèse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Var%C3%A8se "Varèse"), or [Stravinsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stravinsky "Stravinsky"). To me it was all good music. —Frank Zappa, 1989[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):34 At the age of 12, Zappa started learning [drum rudiments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drum_rudiment "Drum rudiment") at a summer school group course in Monterey, California with a teacher named Keith McKillop. Frank said "Instead of drums, he had us practicing on wooden planks."[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):13 Zappa joined his first band at [Mission Bay High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mission_Bay_High_School "Mission Bay High School") in San Diego as a drummer.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):29 At about the same time, his parents bought a [phonograph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phonograph "Phonograph"), which allowed him to develop his interest in music, and to begin building his record collection.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):22 According to _[The Rough Guide to Rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rough_Guide "Rough Guide")_ (2003), "as a teenager Zappa was simultaneously enthralled by black R&B ( [Johnny 'Guitar' Watson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_%22Guitar%22_Watson "Johnny \"Guitar\" Watson"), [Guitar Slim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar_Slim "Guitar Slim")), doo-wop ( [The Channels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Channels "The Channels"), [The Velvets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Velvets "The Velvets")), and modern composers, such as [Igor Stravinsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Igor_Stravinsky "Igor Stravinsky"), [Anton Webern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anton_Webern "Anton Webern") and [Edgard Varèse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgard_Var%C3%A8se "Edgard Varèse")."[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-teentastes-8) R&B singles were early purchases for Zappa, starting a large collection he kept for the rest of his life.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):36 He was interested in sounds for their own sake, particularly the sounds of drums and other percussion instruments. By age twelve, he had obtained a snare drum and began learning the basics of orchestral percussion.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):29 Zappa's deep interest in modern classical music began[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-idol-17) when he read a _[LOOK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Look_(American_magazine) "Look (American magazine)")_ magazine article about the [Sam Goody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Goody "Sam Goody") record store chain that lauded its ability to sell an LP as obscure as _The Complete Works of Edgard Varèse, Volume One_.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):30–33 The article described Varèse's percussion composition _[Ionisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionisation_(Var%C3%A8se) "Ionisation (Varèse)")_, produced by [EMS Recordings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EMS_Recordings "EMS Recordings"), as "a weird jumble of drums and other unpleasant sounds". Zappa decided to seek out Varèse's music. After searching for over a year, Zappa found a copy (he noticed the LP because of the "mad scientist" looking photo of Varèse on the cover). Not having enough money with him, he persuaded the salesman to sell him the record at a discount.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):30–33 Thus began his lifelong passion for Varèse's music and that of other modern classical composers. He also liked the Italian classical music listened to by his grandparents, especially [Puccini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puccini "Puccini")'s opera arias.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/3e/Frank_Zappa_HS_Yearbook.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Frank_Zappa_HS_Yearbook.jpg) Zappa's senior yearbook photo, 1958 By 1956, the Zappa family had moved to [Lancaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancaster,_California "Lancaster, California"), a small [aerospace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerospace "Aerospace") and farming town in the [Antelope Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antelope_Valley "Antelope Valley") of the [Mojave Desert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mojave_Desert "Mojave Desert") close to [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base"); he would later refer to Sun Village (a town close to Lancaster) in the 1973 track "Village of the Sun".[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-18) Zappa's mother encouraged him in his musical interests. Although she disliked Varèse's music, she was indulgent enough to give her son a long-distance call to the New York composer as a fifteenth birthday present.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):30–33 Unfortunately, Varèse was in Europe at the time, so Zappa spoke to the [composer's wife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Var%C3%A8se "Louise Varèse") and she suggested he call back later. In a letter, Varèse thanked him for his interest, and told him about a composition he was working on called " [Déserts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%A9serts "Déserts")". Living in the desert town of Lancaster, Zappa found this very exciting. Varèse invited him to visit if he ever came to New York. The meeting never took place (Varèse died in 1965), but Zappa framed the letter and kept it on display for the rest of his life.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-idol-17)[\[nb 3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-20) At [Antelope Valley High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antelope_Valley_High_School "Antelope Valley High School"), Zappa met Don Glen Vliet (who later changed his name to Don Van Vliet and adopted the stage name [Captain Beefheart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_Beefheart "Captain Beefheart")). Zappa and Vliet became close friends, sharing an interest in R&B records and influencing each other musically throughout their careers.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-slaven03-15):29–30 Around the same time, Zappa started playing drums in a local band, the Blackouts.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-watson96-21):13 The band was racially diverse and included [Euclid James "Motorhead" Sherwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid_James_%22Motorhead%22_Sherwood "Euclid James \"Motorhead\" Sherwood") who later became a member of the Mothers of Invention. Zappa's interest in the guitar grew, and in 1957 he was given his first instrument. Among his early influences were [Johnny "Guitar" Watson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_%22Guitar%22_Watson "Johnny \"Guitar\" Watson"), [Howlin' Wolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howlin'_Wolf "Howlin' Wolf") and [Clarence "Gatemouth" Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarence_%22Gatemouth%22_Brown "Clarence \"Gatemouth\" Brown"). In the 1970s and '80s, Zappa invited Watson to perform on several albums. Zappa considered guitar solos the equivalent of forming "air sculptures",[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-22) and developed an eclectic, innovative and highly personal style.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-23) He was also influenced by Egyptian composer [Halim El-Dabh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halim_El-Dabh "Halim El-Dabh"), an early proponent of [tape music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tape_music "Tape music").[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Holmes-24) Zappa's interest in composing and arranging flourished in his last high school years. By his final year, he was writing, [arranging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arranging "Arranging") and conducting avant-garde performance pieces for the school orchestra.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):40 He graduated from Antelope Valley High School in 1958, and later acknowledged two of his music teachers on the sleeve of the 1966 album _[Freak Out!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freak_Out! "Freak Out!")_[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-walley80-25):23 Due to his family's frequent moves, Zappa attended at least six different high schools, and as a student he was often bored and given to distracting the rest of the class with juvenile antics.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):48 In 1959, he attended [Chaffey College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaffey_College "Chaffey College") but left after one semester, and maintained thereafter a disdain for formal education, taking his children out of school at age 15 and refusing to pay for their college.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):345 While in college, Zappa met [Terry Kirkman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terry_Kirkman "Terry Kirkman") and played gigs at local [coffee houses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffee_house "Coffee house") with him.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-26) Zappa left home in 1959, and moved into a small apartment in [Echo Park, Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Echo_Park,_Los_Angeles "Echo Park, Los Angeles"). After he met Kathryn J. "Kay" Sherman during his short period of private composition study with Prof. [Karl Kohn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Kohn "Karl Kohn") of [Pomona College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pomona_College "Pomona College"), they moved in together in [Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario,_California "Ontario, California"),[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-27)[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-28) and were married December 28, 1960.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):58 Zappa worked for a short period in advertising as a copywriter. His sojourn in the commercial world was brief, but gave him valuable insights into its workings.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):40[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-29) Throughout his career, he took a keen interest in the visual presentation of his work, designing some of his album covers and directing his own films and videos. ### Studio Z Zappa attempted to earn a living as a musician and composer, and played different nightclub gigs, some with a new version of the Blackouts.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):59 Zappa's earliest professional recordings, two soundtracks for the low-budget films _[The World's Greatest Sinner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_World's_Greatest_Sinner "The World's Greatest Sinner")_ (1962) and _[Run Home, Slow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Run_Home,_Slow "Run Home, Slow")_ (1965) were more financially rewarding. The former score was commissioned by actor-producer [Timothy Carey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_Carey "Timothy Carey") and recorded in 1961. It contains many themes that appeared on later Zappa records.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):63 The latter soundtrack was recorded in 1963 after the film was completed, but it was commissioned by one of Zappa's former high school teachers in 1959 and Zappa may have worked on it before the film was shot.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):55 Excerpts from the soundtrack can be heard on the posthumous album _[The Lost Episodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Lost_Episodes "The Lost Episodes")_ (1996). During the early 1960s, Zappa wrote and produced songs for other local artists, often working with singer-songwriter [Ray Collins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Collins_(musician) "Ray Collins (musician)") and producer Paul Buff. Their " [Memories of El Monte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memories_of_El_Monte "Memories of El Monte")" was recorded by [the Penguins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Penguins "The Penguins"), although only Cleve Duncan of the original group was featured.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-30) Buff owned the small [Pal Recording Studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pal_Recording_Studio "Pal Recording Studio") in [Cucamonga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rancho_Cucamonga,_California "Rancho Cucamonga, California"), which included a unique five-track tape recorder he had built. At that time, only a handful of the most sophisticated commercial studios had [multi-track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multitrack_recording "Multitrack recording") facilities; the industry standard for smaller studios was still mono or two-track.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):42 Although none of the recordings from the period achieved major commercial success, Zappa earned enough money to allow him in 1963 to stage a concert of his orchestral music and to broadcast and record it.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):74 In March of that same year Zappa appeared on [Steve Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Allen "Steve Allen")'s syndicated late night show playing a bicycle as a musical instrument[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-31)[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-slaven96-32):35–36—using drum sticks and a bow borrowed from the band's bass player he proceeded to pluck, bang, and bow the spokes of the bike, producing strange, comical sounds from his newfound instrument. With Captain Beefheart, Zappa recorded some songs under the name of the Soots. They were rejected by [Dot Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dot_Records "Dot Records"). Later, in 1965, the Mothers were also rejected by [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records") for having "no commercial potential", a verdict Zappa subsequently quoted on the sleeve of _[Freak Out!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freak_Out! "Freak Out!")_[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-watson96-21):27 The Columbia Records demo tape was rediscovered by a collector in 1993 and quickly returned to the Zappa estate.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-33) In 1964, after his marriage started to break up, he moved into the Pal studio and began routinely working 12hours or more per day recording and experimenting with [overdubbing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overdubbing "Overdubbing") and [audio tape manipulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reel-to-reel_audio_tape_recording#As_a_musical_instrument "Reel-to-reel audio tape recording"). This established a work pattern that endured for most of his life.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):43 Aided by his income from film composing, Zappa took over the studio from Paul Buff, who was now working with [Art Laboe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Laboe "Art Laboe") at [Original Sound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Original_Sound "Original Sound"). It was renamed Studio Z.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):80–81 Studio Z was rarely booked for recordings by other musicians. Instead, friends moved in, notably James "Motorhead" Sherwood.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):82–83 Zappa started performing in local bars as a guitarist with a [power trio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_trio "Power trio"), the Muthers, to support himself.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-watson96-21):26 An article in the local press describing Zappa as "the Movie King of Cucamonga" prompted the local police to suspect that he was making [pornographic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pornographic "Pornographic") films.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):85 In March 1965, Zappa was approached by a [vice squad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_squad "Vice squad") undercover officer, and accepted an offer of $100 (equivalent to $1,020in 2025) to produce a suggestive audio tape for an alleged [bachelor party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_party "Bachelor party"). Zappa and a female friend recorded a faked erotic episode. When Zappa was about to hand over the tape, he was arrested, and the police stripped the studio of all recorded material.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):85 The press was tipped off beforehand, and next day's _[The Daily Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Daily_Report "The Daily Report")_ wrote that "Vice Squad investigators stilled the tape recorders of a free-swinging, a-go-go film and recording studio here Friday and arrested a self-styled movie producer".[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-34) Zappa was charged with "conspiracy to commit pornography".[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):57 This [felony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felony "Felony") charge was reduced and he was sentenced to six months in jail on a [misdemeanor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Misdemeanor "Misdemeanor"), with all but ten days suspended.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):86–87 His brief imprisonment left a permanent mark, and was central to the formation of his anti-authoritarian stance.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):xv Zappa lost several recordings made at Studio Z in the process, as the police returned only 30 of 80 hours of tape seized.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):87 Eventually, he could no longer afford to pay the rent on the studio and was evicted.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-slaven96-32):40 Zappa managed to recover some of his possessions before the studio was torn down in 1966.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):90–91 ## 1965–1970: The Mothers of Invention ### Formation By April 1965, [Ray Collins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Collins_(musician) "Ray Collins (musician)"), one of Zappa's friends during the early Studio Z days, was the singer of an R&B band called the Soul Giants, based in [Pomona, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pomona,_California "Pomona, California"). That month, he asked Zappa to take over as guitarist in the Soul Giants, following a fight between Collins and the group's original guitarist.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Rolling_Stone_Book-12) Zappa accepted, and soon assumed leadership and the role as co-lead singer (even though he never considered himself a singer, then or later[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-HighTimes1980-35)). He convinced the other members that they should play his music to increase the chances of getting a record contract.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):65–66 The band – comprising Zappa, Collins, [Roy Estrada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Estrada "Roy Estrada"), and [Jimmy Carl Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carl_Black "Jimmy Carl Black") – debuted at the Broadside Club and was renamed the Mothers since this gig took place on May 10, 1965– [Mother's Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mother's_Day_(United_States) "Mother's Day (United States)").[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-slaven03-15):42 They increased their bookings after beginning an association with manager [Herb Cohen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Cohen "Herb Cohen"), and gradually gained attention on the burgeoning Los Angeles [underground music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underground_music "Underground music") scene.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-walley80-25):58 Under Zappa's leadership, the Mothers' lineup would be ever-changing during their time together, with members including Collins, Estrada, Black, [Elliot Ingber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliot_Ingber "Elliot Ingber"), brothers [Bunk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunk_Gardner "Bunk Gardner") and [Buzz Gardner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buzz_Gardner "Buzz Gardner"), [Don Preston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Preston "Don Preston"), [Billy Mundi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Mundi "Billy Mundi"), [Jim Fielder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Fielder "Jim Fielder"), [Jim "Motorhead" Sherwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Sherwood "Jim Sherwood"), [Ian Underwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Underwood "Ian Underwood"), [Art Tripp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Tripp "Art Tripp"), and [Lowell George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lowell_George "Lowell George"). ### Signing to Verve Records See also: [Freak Out!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freak_Out! "Freak Out!"), [Absolutely Free](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolutely_Free "Absolutely Free"), and [Lumpy Gravy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lumpy_Gravy "Lumpy Gravy") In early 1966, the Mothers were spotted by leading record producer [Tom Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Wilson_(record_producer) "Tom Wilson (record producer)") when playing "Trouble Every Day", a song about the [Watts riots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watts_riots "Watts riots").[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):103 Wilson had earned acclaim as the producer for [Bob Dylan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Dylan "Bob Dylan") and [Simon & Garfunkel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Garfunkel "Simon & Garfunkel"), and was one of the few African-Americans working as a major label pop music producer at this time. Wilson signed the Mothers to the [Verve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verve_Records "Verve Records") division of [MGM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MGM_Records "MGM Records"), which had built up a strong reputation for its releases of modern jazz recordings in the 1940s and 1950s, but was attempting to diversify into pop and rock audiences. Verve insisted that the band change their name, as _Mother_ was short for _[motherfucker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motherfucker "Motherfucker")_—a term that, apart from its profane meanings, can denote a skilled musician.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-36) As a compromise, Zappa expanded the band's name to "The Mothers of Invention".[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-37) With Wilson credited as producer, the Mothers of Invention, augmented by a studio orchestra, recorded the groundbreaking _[Freak Out!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freak_Out! "Freak Out!")_ (1966), which, after Bob Dylan's _[Blonde on Blonde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blonde_on_Blonde "Blonde on Blonde")_, was the second rock [double album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_album "Double album") ever released. It mixed R&B, [doo-wop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doo-wop "Doo-wop"), [musique concrète](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musique_concr%C3%A8te "Musique concrète"),[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-lowe-38):25 and experimental [sound collages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_collage "Sound collage") that captured the [Los Angeles freak scene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_freak_scene "Los Angeles freak scene").[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-walley80-25):60–61 Although he was dissatisfied with the final product, _Freak Out_ immediately established Zappa as a radical new voice in rock music, providing an antidote to the "relentless consumer culture of America".[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):115 The sound was raw, but the arrangements were sophisticated. While recording in the studio, some of the additional [session musicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Session_musician "Session musician") were shocked that they were expected to read the notes on sheet music from [charts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chord_chart "Chord chart") with Zappa conducting them, since it was not standard when recording rock music.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):112 The lyrics praised non-conformity, disparaged authorities, and had [dadaist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dada "Dada") elements. Yet, there was a place for seemingly conventional love songs.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-watson05-39):10–11 Most compositions are Zappa's, which set a precedent for the rest of his recording career. He had full control over the arrangements and musical decisions and did most [overdubs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overdubs "Overdubs"). Wilson provided the industry clout and connections and was able to provide the group with the financial resources needed.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):123 Although Wilson was able to provide Zappa and the Mothers with an extraordinary degree of artistic freedom for the time, the recording did not go entirely as planned. In a 1967 radio interview, Zappa explained that the album's outlandish 11-minute closing track, "Return of the Son of Monster Magnet" was not finished. The track as it appears on the album was only a backing track for a much more complex piece, but MGM refused to allow the additional recording time needed for completion. Much to Zappa's chagrin, it was issued in its unfinished state.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-40) ![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/Gnome-mime-audio-openclipart.svg/120px-Gnome-mime-audio-openclipart.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail) ["Hungry Freaks Daddy" (1966)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Zappa_HungryFreaks.ogg "File:Zappa HungryFreaks.ogg") The opening track on _[Freak Out!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freak_Out! "Freak Out!")_. The album has "consistently been voted as one of top 100 greatest albums ever made".[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):115 * * * _Problems playing this file? See [media help](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Media "Help:Media")._ During the recording of _Freak Out!_, Zappa moved into a house in [Laurel Canyon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Canyon "Laurel Canyon") with friend Pamela Zarubica, who appeared on the album.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):112 The house became a meeting (and living) place for many LA musicians and [groupies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groupie "Groupie") of the time, despite Zappa's disapproval of their illicit drug use.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):122 After a short promotional tour following the release of _Freak Out!_, Zappa met [Adelaide Gail Sloatman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adelaide_Gail_Sloatman "Adelaide Gail Sloatman"). He fell in love within "a couple of minutes", and she moved into the house over the summer.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):65–66 They married in 1967, had four children and remained together until Zappa's death. Wilson nominally produced the Mothers' second album _[Absolutely Free](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolutely_Free "Absolutely Free")_ (1967), which was recorded in November 1966, and later [mixed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_mixing_(recorded_music) "Audio mixing (recorded music)") in New York, although by this time Zappa was in _de facto_ control of most facets of the production. It featured extended playing by the Mothers of Invention and focused on songs that defined Zappa's compositional style of introducing abrupt rhythm changes into songs that were built from diverse elements.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-lowe-38):5 Examples are "Plastic People" and "Brown Shoes Don't Make It", which contained lyrics that lampooned the hypocrisy and conformity of American society, but also of the [counterculture of the 1960s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterculture_of_the_1960s "Counterculture of the 1960s").[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-lowe-38):38–43 As Zappa put it, "\[W\]e're satirists, and we are out to satirize everything."[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):135–138 At this time, Zappa had also recorded material for an album of orchestral works to be released under his own name, _[Lumpy Gravy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lumpy_Gravy_(1967_album) "Lumpy Gravy (1967 album)"),_ to be released by [Capitol Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitol_Records "Capitol Records") in 1967. Due to contractual problems, the album was held back. Zappa took the opportunity to radically restructure the material, adding newly recorded improvised dialogue. After the contractual problems were resolved, [a new album of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lumpy_Gravy "Lumpy Gravy") was issued by Verve in 1968.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):140–141 It is an "incredible ambitious musical project",[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-lowe-38):56 a "monument to [John Cage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cage "John Cage")",[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-walley80-25):86 which intertwines orchestral themes, spoken words and electronic noises through radical [audio editing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_engineer "Audio engineer") techniques.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-lowe-38):56[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-41)[\[nb 4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-42) ### Move to New York and beginning of Straight and Bizarre Records See also: [We're Only in It for the Money](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/We're_Only_in_It_for_the_Money "We're Only in It for the Money"), [Cruising with Ruben & the Jets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cruising_with_Ruben_&_the_Jets "Cruising with Ruben & the Jets"), [Uncle Meat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncle_Meat "Uncle Meat"), and [Ahead of Their Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahead_of_Their_Time "Ahead of Their Time") [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6a/Zappa_c_1967.png/500px-Zappa_c_1967.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Zappa_c_1967.png) Zappa in 1967 The Mothers of Invention played in New York in late 1966 and were offered a contract at the [Garrick Theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garrick_Cinema "Garrick Cinema") (at 152 [Bleecker Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bleecker_Street "Bleecker Street"), above the [Cafe au Go Go](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cafe_au_Go_Go "Cafe au Go Go")) during Easter 1967. This proved successful and Herb Cohen extended the booking, which eventually lasted half a year.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-james-43):62–69 As a result, Zappa and his wife Gail, along with the Mothers of Invention, moved to New York.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):140–141 Their shows became a combination of improvised acts showcasing individual talents of the band as well as tight performances of Zappa's music. Everything was directed by Zappa using hand signals.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):147 Guest performers and audience participation became a regular part of the Garrick Theater shows. One evening, Zappa managed to entice some U.S. Marines from the audience onto the stage, where they proceeded to dismember a big baby doll, having been told by Zappa to pretend that it was a " [gook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gook "Gook") baby".[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):94 In 1967, filmmaker [Ed Seeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Seeman "Ed Seeman") paid Zappa $2,000 to produce music for a [Luden's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luden's "Luden's") cough drops television commercial.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-44) Zappa's music was matched with Seeman's animation and the advertisement won a [Clio Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clio_Award "Clio Award") for "Best Use of Sound".[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-45)[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-46) An alternate version of the soundtrack, called "The Big Squeeze", later appeared on Zappa's posthumous 1996 album _[The Lost Episodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Lost_Episodes "The Lost Episodes")_. This version lacks Seeman's narration. While living in New York City, and interrupted by the band's first European tour, the Mothers of Invention recorded the album widely regarded as the peak of the group's late 1960s work, _[We're Only in It for the Money](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/We're_Only_in_It_for_the_Money "We're Only in It for the Money")_ (released 1968).[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-47) It was produced by Zappa, with Wilson credited as executive producer. From then on, Zappa produced all albums released by the Mothers of Invention and as a solo artist. _We're Only in It for the Money_ featured some of the most creative audio editing and production yet heard in pop music, and the songs ruthlessly satirized the [hippie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippie "Hippie") and [flower power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flower_power "Flower power") phenomena.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-walley80-25):90[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-watson05-39):15 He sampled surf music from his Studio Z days in the audio collage _Nasal Retentive Caliope Music_. The cover photo parodied that of [the Beatles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beatles "The Beatles")' _[Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sgt._Pepper's_Lonely_Hearts_Club_Band "Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band")_.[\[nb 5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-48) The cover art was provided by [Cal Schenkel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cal_Schenkel "Cal Schenkel") whom Zappa met in New York. This initiated a lifelong collaboration in which Schenkel designed covers for numerous Zappa and Mothers albums.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-watson96-21):88 [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/be/The_Mothers_of_Invention_%281968%29.jpg/500px-The_Mothers_of_Invention_%281968%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Mothers_of_Invention_(1968).jpg) Zappa (back) with the Mothers, 1968 Reflecting Zappa's eclectic approach to music, the next album, _[Cruising with Ruben & the Jets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cruising_with_Ruben_&_the_Jets "Cruising with Ruben & the Jets")_ (1968), was very different. It represented a collection of [doo-wop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doo-wop "Doo-wop") songs; listeners and critics were not sure whether the album was a satire or a tribute.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-lowe-38):58 Zappa later remarked that the album was conceived like Stravinsky's compositions in his neo-classical period: "If he could take the forms and clichés of the classical era and pervert them, why not do the same... to doo-wop in the fifties?"[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):88 The opening theme from Stravinsky's _[The Rite of Spring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rite_of_Spring "The Rite of Spring")_ is sung in "Fountain of Love". In 1967 and 1968, Zappa made two appearances with [the Monkees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Monkees "The Monkees"). The first appearance was on an episode of [their TV series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Monkees_(TV_series) "The Monkees (TV series)"), "The Monkees Blow Their Minds", where Zappa, dressed up as [Mike Nesmith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Nesmith "Mike Nesmith"), interviews Nesmith who is dressed up as Zappa. After the interview, Zappa destroys a car with a sledgehammer as the song "Mother People" plays. He later provided a cameo in the Monkees' movie [_Head_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_(film) "Head (film)") where, leading a cow, he tells [Davy Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davy_Jones_(musician) "Davy Jones (musician)") "the youth of America depends on you to show them the way." Zappa respected the Monkees and attempted to recruit [Micky Dolenz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micky_Dolenz "Micky Dolenz") to the Mothers but RCA/Columbia/Colgems would not release Dolenz from his contract.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):158–159 During the late 1960s, Zappa continued to develop the business side of his career. He and Herb Cohen formed the [Bizarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bizarre_Records "Bizarre Records") and [Straight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straight_Records "Straight Records") labels to increase creative control and produce recordings by other artists. These labels were distributed in the US by [Warner Bros. Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros._Records "Warner Bros. Records"). Zappa/Mothers recordings appeared on Bizarre along with [Wild Man Fischer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_Man_Fischer "Wild Man Fischer") and [Lenny Bruce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenny_Bruce "Lenny Bruce").[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):173–175 Straight released the double album _[Trout Mask Replica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trout_Mask_Replica "Trout Mask Replica")_ for [Captain Beefheart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_Beefheart "Captain Beefheart"), and releases by [Alice Cooper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_Cooper "Alice Cooper"), [The Persuasions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Persuasions "The Persuasions"), and [the GTOs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_GTOs "The GTOs"). The Mothers' first album on Bizarre was 1969's _[Uncle Meat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncle_Meat "Uncle Meat")_, which Zappa described as "most of the music from the Mothers' movie of the same name which we haven't got enough money to finish yet". A version of the _[Uncle Meat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncle_Meat_(film) "Uncle Meat (film)")_ film was released direct-to-video in 1987. Principal photography having never been completed, the VHS videocassette is a "making of" documentary showing rehearsals and background footage from 1968 and interviews with people involved with the
