See [media help](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Media "Help:Media")._ Zappa and the Mothers of Invention returned to Los Angeles in mid-1968; the Zappas moved into a house on Laurel Canyon Boulevard, only to move again to Woodrow Wilson Drive.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):178 This was Zappa's home for the rest of his life. Despite being successful in Europe, the Mothers of Invention were not doing well financially.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-walley80-25):116 Their first records were vocally oriented, but as Zappa wrote more instrumental jazz and classical style music for the band's concerts, audiences were confused. Zappa felt that audiences failed to appreciate his "electrical chamber music".[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):185–187[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-slaven03-15):119–120 In 1969, there were nine band members and Zappa was supporting the group from his publishing [royalties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royalties "Royalties") whether they played or not.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-walley80-25):116 In late 1969, Zappa broke up the band. He often cited the financial strain as the main reason,[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):107 but also commented on the band members' lack of diligence.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-slaven03-15):120 Many band members were bitter about Zappa's decision, and some took it as a sign of Zappa's perfectionism at the expense of human feeling.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):185–187 Others were irritated by 'his [autocratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autocratic "Autocratic") ways',[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):123 exemplified by Zappa's never staying at the same hotel as the band members.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):116 Several members would play with Zappa again in subsequent years, while Lowell George and Roy Estrada went on to form the band [Little Feat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Feat "Little Feat"). Zappa assembled remaining unreleased recordings of the band on the albums _[Burnt Weeny Sandwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burnt_Weeny_Sandwich "Burnt Weeny Sandwich")_ and _[Weasels Ripped My Flesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weasels_Ripped_My_Flesh "Weasels Ripped My Flesh")_, both released in 1970. After he disbanded the Mothers of Invention, Zappa released the acclaimed solo album _[Hot Rats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_Rats "Hot Rats")_ (1969).[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):194[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-52) It features, for the first time on record, Zappa playing extended guitar solos and contains one of his most enduring compositions, " [Peaches en Regalia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peaches_en_Regalia "Peaches en Regalia")", which reappeared several times on future recordings.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-lowe-38):74 He was backed by jazz, blues and R&B session players including violinist [Don "Sugarcane" Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_%22Sugarcane%22_Harris "Don \"Sugarcane\" Harris"), drummers [John Guerin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Guerin "John Guerin") and [Paul Humphrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Humphrey_(American_musician) "Paul Humphrey (American musician)"), multi-instrumentalist and former Mothers of Invention member Ian Underwood, and multi-instrumentalist [Shuggie Otis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuggie_Otis "Shuggie Otis") on bass, along with a guest appearance by [Captain Beefheart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_Beefheart "Captain Beefheart") on the only vocal track, "Willie the Pimp". It became a popular album in England,[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):109 and had a major influence on the development of [jazz-rock fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-rock_fusion "Jazz-rock fusion").[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):194[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-lowe-38):74 ## 1970–1980: Highs and lows ### Rebirth of the Mothers and filmmaking See also: [Chunga's Revenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chunga's_Revenge "Chunga's Revenge"), [Fillmore East – June 1971](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fillmore_East_%E2%80%93_June_1971 "Fillmore East – June 1971"), [200 Motels (soundtrack)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/200_Motels_(soundtrack) "200 Motels (soundtrack)"), [Just Another Band from L.A.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Just_Another_Band_from_L.A. "Just Another Band from L.A."), and [Playground Psychotics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playground_Psychotics "Playground Psychotics") [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/64/Frank_Zappa%2C_1970_-_19.jpg/500px-Frank_Zappa%2C_1970_-_19.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Frank_Zappa,_1970_-_19.jpg) Zappa in 1970 [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fa/Frank_Zappa%2C_Theatre_de_Clichy%2C_Paris%2C_1971.jpg/250px-Frank_Zappa%2C_Theatre_de_Clichy%2C_Paris%2C_1971.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Frank_Zappa,_Theatre_de_Clichy,_Paris,_1971.jpg) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3c/FRANK_ZAPPA3.jpg/500px-FRANK_ZAPPA3.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:FRANK_ZAPPA3.jpg) Zappa on stage at the [Theatre de Clichy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boulevard_de_Clichy "Boulevard de Clichy"), Paris, 1971 In 1970, Zappa met conductor [Zubin Mehta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zubin_Mehta "Zubin Mehta"). They arranged a May 1970 concert where Mehta conducted the [Los Angeles Philharmonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Philharmonic "Los Angeles Philharmonic") augmented by a rock band. According to Zappa, the music was mostly written in motel rooms while on tour with the Mothers of Invention. Some of it was later featured in the movie _[200 Motels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/200_Motels "200 Motels")_.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):109 Although the concert was a success, Zappa's experience working with a symphony orchestra was not a happy one.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):88 His dissatisfaction became a recurring theme throughout his career; he often felt that the quality of performance of his material delivered by orchestras was not commensurate with the money he spent on orchestral concerts and recordings.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):142–156 Later in 1970, Zappa formed a new version of the Mothers (from then on, he mostly dropped the "of Invention"). Along with Ian Underwood, the new band also included British drummer [Aynsley Dunbar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aynsley_Dunbar "Aynsley Dunbar"), jazz keyboardist [George Duke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Duke "George Duke"), bassist [Jeff Simmons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Simmons_(musician) "Jeff Simmons (musician)"), and the two lead singers of [the Turtles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Turtles "The Turtles"), [Mark Volman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Volman "Mark Volman") and [Howard Kaylan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Kaylan "Howard Kaylan"), who, due to persistent legal and contractual problems, adopted the stage name "The Phlorescent Leech and Eddie" or " [Flo & Eddie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flo_&_Eddie "Flo & Eddie")" for short.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):201 Another member of the Turtles, [Jim Pons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Pons "Jim Pons"), would join on bass in February 1971, following Simmons' departure the previous month and his brief replacement by Martin Lickert. This version of the Mothers debuted on Zappa's next solo album _[Chunga's Revenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chunga's_Revenge "Chunga's Revenge")_ (1970),[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):205 which was followed by [the double-album soundtrack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/200_Motels_(album) "200 Motels (album)") to the movie _[200 Motels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/200_Motels "200 Motels")_ (1971), featuring the Mothers, the [Royal Philharmonic Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Philharmonic_Orchestra "Royal Philharmonic Orchestra"), [Ringo Starr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ringo_Starr "Ringo Starr"), [Theodore Bikel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Bikel "Theodore Bikel"), and [Keith Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Moon "Keith Moon"). Co-directed by Zappa and [Tony Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Palmer_(director) "Tony Palmer (director)"), it was filmed in a week at [Pinewood Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinewood_Studios "Pinewood Studios") outside London.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-watson96-21):183 Tensions between Zappa and several cast and crew members arose before and during shooting.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-watson96-21):183 The film deals loosely with life on the road as a rock musician.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):207 It was the first feature film photographed on [videotape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Videotape "Videotape") and transferred to [35mm film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/35_mm_movie_film "35 mm movie film"), a process that allowed for novel visual effects.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-53) It was released to mixed reviews.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-lowe-38):94 The score relied extensively on orchestral music, and Zappa's dissatisfaction with the classical music world intensified when a concert, scheduled at the [Royal Albert Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Albert_Hall "Royal Albert Hall") after filming, was canceled because a representative of the venue found some of the lyrics obscene. In 1975, he lost a lawsuit against the Royal Albert Hall for breach of contract.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):119–137 After _200 Motels_, the band went on tour, which resulted in two live albums, _[Fillmore East – June 1971](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fillmore_East_%E2%80%93_June_1971 "Fillmore East – June 1971")_ and _[Just Another Band from L.A.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Just_Another_Band_from_L.A. "Just Another Band from L.A.")_; the latter included the 20-minute track " [Billy the Mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_the_Mountain "Billy the Mountain")", Zappa's satire on rock opera set in Southern California. This track was representative of the band's theatrical performances—which used songs to build sketches based on _200 Motels_ scenes, as well as new situations that often portrayed the band members' sexual encounters on the road.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):203–204[\[nb 6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-54) ### Accident, attack, and aftermath [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2f/Frank_Zappa_Mothers_of_Invention_1971.JPG/500px-Frank_Zappa_Mothers_of_Invention_1971.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Frank_Zappa_Mothers_of_Invention_1971.JPG) Zappa with the Mothers, 1971 On December 4, 1971, Zappa suffered his first of two serious setbacks. While performing at [Casino de Montreux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casino_de_Montreux "Casino de Montreux") in Switzerland, the Mothers' equipment was destroyed when a flare set off by an audience member started a fire that burned down the casino.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):112–115[Deep Purple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_Purple "Deep Purple") were booked to record in the casino after Zappa's performance, and wrote about the incident in their 1972 song " [Smoke on the Water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smoke_on_the_Water "Smoke on the Water")". A recording of the incident and immediate aftermath can be heard on the bootleg album _Swiss Cheese/Fire_, released legally as part of Zappa's _[Beat the Boots II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_the_Boots_II "Beat the Boots II")_ box set. After losing $50,000 (equivalent to $397,000in 2025) worth of equipment and a week's break, the Mothers played at the [Rainbow Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow_Theatre "Rainbow Theatre"), London, with rented gear. During the encore, an audience member, jealous because of his girlfriend's infatuation with Zappa, pushed him off the stage and into the concrete-floored orchestra pit.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Reed-55) The band thought Zappa had been killed—he had suffered serious fractures, head trauma and injuries to his back, leg, and neck, as well as a crushed [larynx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larynx "Larynx"), which ultimately caused his voice to drop a [third](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_third "Major third") after healing.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):112–115 A recording of the whole concert, including the attack, was released on the posthumous album _[The Mothers 1971](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mothers_1971 "The Mothers 1971")_ in 2022. [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/be/Frank-Zappa_in_glory.jpg/500px-Frank-Zappa_in_glory.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Frank-Zappa_in_glory.jpg) Zappa on Stage in Hamburg, December 1971 After the attack, Zappa needed to use a wheelchair for an extended period; this made touring impossible for over half a year. Upon return to the stage in September 1972, Zappa was still wearing a leg brace, had a noticeable limp and could not stand for very long while on stage. Zappa noted that one leg healed "shorter than the other" (a reference later found in the lyrics of songs "Zomby Woof" and " [Dancin' Fool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dancin'_Fool "Dancin' Fool")"), resulting in chronic back pain.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):112–115 Meanwhile, the Mothers were left in limbo and eventually formed the core of Flo and Eddie's band as they set out on their own. ### _Waka/Jawaka_ and _The Grand Wazoo_ See also: [Waka/Jawaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waka/Jawaka "Waka/Jawaka") and [The Grand Wazoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Grand_Wazoo "The Grand Wazoo") ![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/Gnome-mime-audio-openclipart.svg/120px-Gnome-mime-audio-openclipart.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail) ["Waka/Jawaka" (1972)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Zappa_WakaJawaka.ogg "File:Zappa WakaJawaka.ogg") The closing track on _[Waka/Jawaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waka/Jawaka "Waka/Jawaka")_, one of Zappa's jazz-oriented albums. * * * _Problems playing this file? See [media help](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Media "Help:Media")._ In 1972, Zappa released two strongly jazz-oriented solo LPs, _[Waka/Jawaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waka/Jawaka "Waka/Jawaka")_ and _[The Grand Wazoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Grand_Wazoo "The Grand Wazoo")_, which were recorded during the forced layoff from concert touring, using floating lineups of session players and Mothers alumni.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-lowe-38):101 Musically, the albums were akin to _Hot Rats,_ in that they featured extended instrumental tracks with extended soloing.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):225–226 Zappa began touring again in late 1972.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):225–226 His first effort was a series of concerts in September 1972 with a 20-piece [big band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_band "Big band") referred to as the Grand Wazoo. 1973–1975 band".[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-lowe-38):114–122 life.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):372 ### Business breakups and continued touring See also: [Zoot Allures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoot_Allures "Zoot Allures"), [Zappa in New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zappa_in_New_York "Zappa in New York"), [Studio Tan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio_Tan "Studio Tan"), [Sleep Dirt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleep_Dirt "Sleep Dirt"), and [Orchestral Favorites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orchestral_Favorites "Orchestral Favorites") In 1976, Zappa produced the album _[Good Singin', Good Playin'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_Singin',_Good_Playin' "Good Singin', Good Playin'")_ for [Grand Funk Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Funk_Railroad "Grand Funk Railroad"). His relationship with long-time manager Herb Cohen ended in May 1976.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-chron76-62) After Cohen cashed one of Zappa's royalty checks from Warner and kept the money for himself, Zappa sued him.[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-lafp77-63) Zappa was also upset with Cohen for signing acts he did not approve.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):250[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-valleynews-64) Cohen filed a lawsuit against Zappa in return, which froze the money the pair were expecting to receive from an out-of-court settlement with [MGM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MGM_Records "MGM Records")/ [Verve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verve_Records "Verve Records") over the rights to Zappa's early [Mothers of Invention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mothers_of_Invention "Mothers of Invention") recordings. The MGM settlement was finalized in mid-1977 after two years of negotiations.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-dmreg77-65) Litigation with Cohen also prevented Zappa having access to any of his previously recorded material during the trials. Zappa therefore took his personal master copies of the album _[Zoot Allures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoot_Allures "Zoot Allures")_ (1976) directly to Warner, while bypassing DiscReet.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):253,258–259 Cohen countersued, claiming that the Warner release violated the terms of his DiscReet contract with Zappa.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-guardian-66) So the final four albums of Zappa's recording contract were then assigned back to DiscReet, against Zappa's objection. Following the split with Cohen, Zappa hired Bennett Glotzer as new manager.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-melmak77-67) [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c4/Zappa_16011977_01_300.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Zappa_16011977_01_300.jpg) Zappa performing in Oslo, January 1977 By late 1976, Zappa was upset with Warner over inadequate promotion of his DiscReet recordings and he was eager to move on as soon as possible.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-mumedia-68) In March 1977, Zappa delivered four albums (five full-length LPs) to Warner to complete his contract: _[Zappa in New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zappa_in_New_York "Zappa in New York")_ (a 2-LP set), _[Studio Tan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio_Tan "Studio Tan")_, _[Sleep Dirt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleep_Dirt "Sleep Dirt")_ and _[Orchestral Favorites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orchestral_Favorites "Orchestral Favorites")_.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-valleynews-64) These albums contained recordings mostly made between 1972 and 1976. Warner failed to pay Zappa on delivery of the four albums and to meet other contractual obligations.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-valleynews-64) In response Zappa filed a multi-million dollar breach of contract lawsuit.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Collage77-69) During a lengthy legal debate, Warner eventually released the four disputed albums during 1978 and 1979, _Zappa in New York_ having been censored to remove references to guitarist [Punky Meadows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punky_Meadows "Punky Meadows"). Following his completion of the Warner contract, Zappa reconfigured the four disputed albums, along with some other material, into a quadruple album called _[Läther](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A4ther "Läther")_ (pronounced "leather") and negotiated distribution with [Phonogram Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phonogram_Inc. "Phonogram Inc.") for release on the new [Zappa Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zappa_Records "Zappa Records") label. _Läther_ was scheduled for release on [Halloween](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halloween "Halloween") 1977, but legal action from Warner forced Zappa to shelve this project.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):261 In December 1977, Zappa appeared on the [Pasadena, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasadena,_California "Pasadena, California") radio station [KROQ-FM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KROQ-FM "KROQ-FM") and played the entire _Läther_ album, while encouraging listeners to make tape recordings of the broadcast.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-slaven03-15):248 The album integrates many aspects of Zappa's 1970s work: heavy rock, orchestral works, and complex jazz instrumentals, along with Zappa's distinctive guitar solos. _Läther_ was officially released posthumously in 1996. It has been debated as to whether Zappa had conceived the material as a four-LP set from the beginning, or only later when working with Phonogram.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):267[\[nb 7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-70) Gail Zappa claimed in 1996 that _Läther_ was Zappa's original intention.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-71)[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-72) However, Zappa himself stated in an October 1978 radio interview that " _Läther_ was made out of four albums. Warners has released two of them already and they have two more that they're probably gonna release."[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-CFNY-73) Although Zappa eventually gained the rights to all his material created under the MGM and Warner contracts,[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-watson05-39):49 the various lawsuits meant that for a period Zappa's only income came from touring, which he therefore did extensively in 1975–1977 with relatively small, mainly rock-oriented, bands.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):261 Drummer [Terry Bozzio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terry_Bozzio "Terry Bozzio") became a regular band member, Napoleon Murphy Brock stayed on for a while, and original Mothers of Invention bassist [Roy Estrada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Estrada "Roy Estrada") joined. Among other musicians were bassist [Patrick O'Hearn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_O'Hearn "Patrick O'Hearn"), singer-guitarist [Ray White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_White "Ray White") and former [Roxy Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roxy_Music "Roxy Music") keyboardist/violinist [Eddie Jobson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Jobson "Eddie Jobson"). In December 1976, Zappa appeared as a featured musical guest on the [NBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC "NBC") television show _[Saturday Night Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturday_Night_Live "Saturday Night Live")_.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):262 Zappa's song " [I'm the Slime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I'm_the_Slime "I'm the Slime")" was performed with a voice-over by _SNL_ booth announcer [Don Pardo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Pardo "Don Pardo"), who also introduced "Peaches En Regalia" on the same airing. In 1978, Zappa served both as host and musical act on the show. The performances included an impromptu musical collaboration with cast member [John Belushi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Belushi "John Belushi") during the instrumental piece "The Purple Lagoon". Belushi appeared as his [Samurai Futaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samurai_Futaba "Samurai Futaba") character playing the tenor sax with Zappa conducting.[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-74) However, he earned a ban from the show after the latter episode because he had done what producers called "a disastrous job of hosting" (Zappa reportedly did not get along with cast and crew in the lead-up to recording, then told the audience he was simply reading from cue cards).[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-banned-75) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f8/Frank_Zappa_in_Toronto%2C_Sept._24_1977.jpg/500px-Frank_Zappa_in_Toronto%2C_Sept._24_1977.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Frank_Zappa_in_Toronto,_Sept._24_1977.jpg) Zappa in Toronto, 1977 Zappa's band had a series of Christmas shows in New York City in 1976, recordings of which appear on _[Zappa in New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zappa_in_New_York "Zappa in New York")_ and _Läther_. The band included Ruth Underwood and a horn section featuring the [Brecker Brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brecker_Brothers "Brecker Brothers"). It mixes complex instrumentals such as " [The Black Page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Black_Page "The Black Page")" and humorous songs like "Titties and Beer".[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-lowe-38):132 The former composition, written originally for drum kit but later developed for larger bands, is notorious for its complexity in rhythmic structure and short, densely arranged passages.[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-76)[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-77) ![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/Gnome-mime-audio-openclipart.svg/120px-Gnome-mime-audio-openclipart.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail) ["The Black Page Drum Solo/Black Page #1" (recorded 1976, released 1978)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Zappa_BlackPage1.ogg "File:Zappa BlackPage1.ogg") One of Zappa's complex, percussion-based compositions featured on _[Zappa in New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zappa_in_New_York "Zappa in New York")_. * * * _Problems playing this file? See [media help](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Media "Help:Media")._ _Zappa in New York_ also featured a song about sex criminal [Michael H. Kenyon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_H._Kenyon "Michael H. Kenyon"), "The Illinois Enema Bandit", in which Don Pardo provides the opening narrative. Like many songs on the album, it contained numerous sexual references,[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-lowe-38):132 leading to many critics objecting and being offended by the content.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-lowe-38):134[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-lowe-38):261–262 Zappa dismissed the criticism by noting that he was acting as a "journalist" reporting on life as he saw it.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):234 Predating his later fight against censorship, he remarked: "What do you make of a society that is so primitive that it clings to the belief that certain words in its language are so powerful that they could corrupt you the moment you hear them?"[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-HighTimes1980-35) The remaining albums released by Warner without Zappa's approval were _[Studio Tan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio_Tan "Studio Tan")_ in 1978 and _[Sleep Dirt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleep_Dirt "Sleep Dirt")_ and _[Orchestral Favorites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orchestral_Favorites "Orchestral Favorites")_ in 1979. These releases were not promoted and were largely overlooked in the midst of the press about Zappa's legal problems.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-lowe-38):138 The 1991 CD releases of these albums marked the first time they were issued with Zappa's full approval.[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-78) ### Zappa Records See also: [Sheik Yerbouti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheik_Yerbouti "Sheik Yerbouti"), [Joe's Garage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe's_Garage "Joe's Garage"), and [Baby Snakes (soundtrack)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baby_Snakes_(soundtrack) "Baby Snakes (soundtrack)") ![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/Gnome-mime-audio-openclipart.svg/120px-Gnome-mime-audio-openclipart.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail) ["Bobby Brown" (1979)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Zappa_BobbyBrown.ogg "File:Zappa BobbyBrown.ogg") The single became a hit in non-English speaking countries and helped _[Sheik Yerbouti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheik_Yerbouti "Sheik Yerbouti")_ become a best-seller.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-watson96-21):351 * * * _Problems playing this file? See [media help](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Media "Help:Media")._ Zappa released two of his most important projects in 1979. The double LP _[Sheik Yerbouti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheik_Yerbouti "Sheik Yerbouti")_ appeared in March and was the first release on Zappa Records. It became the best-selling album of his career.[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-79) The album contained the [Grammy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy "Grammy")-nominated single "Dancin' Fool", which reached No.45 on the _Billboard_ charts.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-BBsingles-59) It also contained " [Jewish Princess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish_Princess_(song) "Jewish Princess (song)")", which received attention when the [Anti-Defamation League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Defamation_League "Anti-Defamation League") (ADL) attempted to prevent the song from receiving radio airplay due to its alleged [antisemitic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antisemitic "Antisemitic") lyrics.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):234 Zappa vehemently denied any antisemitic sentiments, and dismissed the ADL as a "noisemaking organization that tries to apply pressure on people in order to manufacture a stereotype image of Jews that suits their idea of a good time."[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-80) The album's commercial success was attributable in part to " [Bobby Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Brown_(song) "Bobby Brown (song)")". Due to its explicit lyrics, the song did not get airplay in the U.S., but it topped the charts in several European countries where English is not the primary language.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-watson96-21):351 _[Joe's Garage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe's_Garage "Joe's Garage")_ has been described as a "bona fide masterpiece".[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-lowe-38):140 The project initially had to be released in two parts due to economic conditions.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-islandear-81) The first was a single LP _Joe's Garage Act I_ in September 1979, followed by a double LP _Joe's Garage Acts II and III_ in November 1979. The story features singer [Ike Willis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ike_Willis "Ike Willis") as the lead character in a [rock opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_opera "Rock opera") about the danger of [political systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_system "Political system"),[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-lowe-38):140 the suppression of [freedom of speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_speech "Freedom of speech") and music—inspired in part by the 1979 [Islamic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam "Islam") [Iranian revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iranian_revolution "Iranian revolution") that had made music illegal[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):277—and about the "strange relationship Americans have with sex and sexual frankness".[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-lowe-38):140 The _Act I_ album reached number 27 on the [Billboard 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") chart. It contains the song "Catholic Girls" (a [riposte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riposte "Riposte") to the controversies of "Jewish Princess")[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-watson05-39):59 and the title track, which was also released as a single. The second and third acts have extended guitar improvisations, which were recorded live, then combined with studio backing tracks. Zappa described this process as [xenochrony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xenochrony "Xenochrony"). The band included drummer [Vinnie Colaiuta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinnie_Colaiuta "Vinnie Colaiuta") (with whom Zappa had a particularly strong musical rapport)[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):180 Included is one of Zappa's guitar "signature pieces", " [Watermelon in Easter Hay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watermelon_in_Easter_Hay "Watermelon in Easter Hay")".[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-watson05-39):61[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-DZlinernotes-82) In 1987, all three acts were reissued together as a 3-LP and 2-CD set. Zappa had been known for his long hair since the mid-1960s, but he had Gail cut it short around August 1979.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-islandear-81) That autumn he cancelled tour plans to stay home with newborn daughter Diva, and celebrate the birthdays of children Moon and Dweezil in September.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-gcfreep-83) At this time Zappa also completed the [Utility Muffin Research Kitchen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utility_Muffin_Research_Kitchen "Utility Muffin Research Kitchen") (UMRK) studios, which were located at his house,[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Mix2003-84) thereby giving him complete freedom in his work.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):269 On Zappa's 39th birthday, December 21, 1979, his film _[Baby Snakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baby_Snakes "Baby Snakes")_ premiered in New York City. He described it as "A movie about people who do stuff that is not normal".[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-85) The 2hour and 40minute movie shows concerts in New York during Halloween 1977, with a band featuring keyboardist [Tommy Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tommy_Mars "Tommy Mars"), percussionist [Ed Mann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Mann "Ed Mann") and guitarist [Adrian Belew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrian_Belew "Adrian Belew"). It also contained [clay animation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clay_animation "Clay animation") by [Bruce Bickford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Bickford_(animator) "Bruce Bickford (animator)") who had earlier worked with Zappa on a 1974 TV special (later seen in the 1982 video _[The Dub Room Special](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dub_Room_Special "The Dub Room Special")_).[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):282 The movie had a highly successful initial release in Manhattan, but did not do well in theatrical distribution,[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-86) It later won the Premier Grand Prix at the First International Music Festival in Paris in 1981.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):282 ## 1980–1993: Later years ### Beginning of Barking Pumpkin Records See also: [Tinsel Town Rebellion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tinsel_Town_Rebellion "Tinsel Town Rebellion"), [Shut Up 'n Play Yer Guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shut_Up_'n_Play_Yer_Guitar "Shut Up 'n Play Yer Guitar"), and [You Are What You Is](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You_Are_What_You_Is "You Are What You Is") [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/58/Zappa-buffalo-ny.jpg/500px-Zappa-buffalo-ny.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Zappa-buffalo-ny.jpg) Zappa performing at the [Memorial Auditorium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo_Memorial_Auditorium "Buffalo Memorial Auditorium"), [Buffalo, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo,_New_York "Buffalo, New York"), October 1980. The concert was released in 2007 as _[Buffalo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo_(Frank_Zappa_album) "Buffalo (Frank Zappa album)")_. Zappa cut ties with Phonogram after the distributor refused to release his song " [I Don't Wanna Get Drafted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Don't_Wanna_Get_Drafted "I Don't Wanna Get Drafted")", which was recorded in February 1980.[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-87) The single was released independently by Zappa in the United States and was picked up by CBS Records internationally.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-88) After spending much of 1980 on the road, Zappa released _[Tinsel Town Rebellion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tinsel_Town_Rebellion "Tinsel Town Rebellion")_ in 1981. It was the first release on his own [Barking Pumpkin Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barking_Pumpkin_Records "Barking Pumpkin Records"),[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-lowe-38):161 and featured live recordings from 1979 and 1980, as well as a new studio track, "Fine Girl". The album is a mixture of complicated instrumentals and Zappa's use of _[sprechstimme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sprechstimme "Sprechstimme")_ (speaking song or voice)—a compositional technique utilized by such composers as [Arnold Schoenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_Schoenberg "Arnold Schoenberg") and [Alban Berg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alban_Berg "Alban Berg")—showcasing some of the most accomplished bands Zappa ever had (mostly featuring drummer [Vinnie Colaiuta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinnie_Colaiuta "Vinnie Colaiuta")).[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-lowe-38):161 While some lyrics still raised controversy among critics, some of whom found them sexist,[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):284 the political and sociological satire in songs like the title track and "The Blue Light" have been described as a "hilarious critique of the willingness of the American people to believe anything".[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-lowe-38):165 The album is also notable for the presence of guitarist [Steve Vai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Vai "Steve Vai"), who joined Zappa's touring band in late 1980.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):283 In 1981, Zappa also released three instrumental albums, _[Shut Up 'n Play Yer Guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shut_Up_'n_Play_Yer_Guitar "Shut Up 'n Play Yer Guitar")_, _Shut Up 'N Play Yer Guitar Some More_, and _The Return of the Son of Shut Up 'N Play Yer Guitar_, which were initially sold via [mail order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mail_order "Mail order"), but later released as one 3-LP set through CBS Records (now [Sony Music Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_Music_Entertainment "Sony Music Entertainment")) due to popular demand.[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-89) The albums consist entirely of tracks in which Zappa is featured as a guitar soloist, and they are predominantly live recordings from 1979 to 1980; they highlight Zappa's improvisational skills with "beautiful performances from the backing group as well".[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-90) Another guitar-only album, _[Guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar_(Frank_Zappa_album) "Guitar (Frank Zappa album)")_, was released in 1988, and a third, The album mainly consisted of rock songs with Zappa's sardonic social commentary—satirical lyrics directed at teenagers, the media, and religious and political hypocrisy.[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-92) "Dumb All Over" is a tirade against religion, as is "Heavenly Bank Account", wherein Zappa rails against [TV evangelists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Televangelism "Televangelism") such as [Jerry Falwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Falwell "Jerry Falwell") and [Pat Robertson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pat_Robertson "Pat Robertson") for their purported influence on the U.S. administration as well as their use of religion as a means of raising money.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-lowe-38):169–175 Songs like "Society Pages" and "I'm a Beautiful Guy" show Zappa's dismay with the [Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reagan "Reagan") era and its "obscene pursuit of wealth and happiness".[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-lowe-38):169–175 Zappa made his only music video for a song from this album – "You Are What You Is" – directed by Jerry Watson, produced by Paul Flattery. The video was banned from [MTV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTV "MTV"), though was later featured by [Mike Judge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Judge "Mike Judge") in the _[Beavis & Butthead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beavis_&_Butthead "Beavis & Butthead")_ episode "Canoe".[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-93) Also included is the guitar instrumental, "Theme from the 3rd Movement of Sinister Footwear" which he adapted from a ballet performed with the Berkeley Symphony Orchestra in 1984. charts).[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-BBsingles-59) In her improvised lyrics to the song, Zappa's daughter [Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon_Zappa "Moon Zappa") satirized the [patois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patois "Patois") of teenage girls from the [San Fernando Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Fernando_Valley "San Fernando Valley"), which out".[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-97) The first of Zappa's lawsuits against Warner was scheduled to go to court starting in January 1982.[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-98)[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-99) All of Zappa's Bizarre and DiscReet recordings also went out of print when the Warner distribution agreement ended in 1982. The Los Angeles Times quoted a Warner representative saying that Zappa's releases of the 1970s "consistently sold hundreds of thousands of units, which wasn't huge, but it was substantial."[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-100) Zappa said in 1983 that a lawsuit had recently been resolved, and that he was once again able to access his vault of tape and film, which had been locked up by "another person". This allowed him to restart work on unfinished projects, such as the Uncle Meat film.[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-101) The unnamed person was, presumably, his former manager Herb Cohen. A 1983 album _[The Man from Utopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Man_from_Utopia "The Man from Utopia"),_ featured an anti-drug single " [Cocaine Decisions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cocaine_Decisions "Cocaine Decisions")". "The Dangerous Kitchen" and "The Jazz Discharge Party Hats" are continuations of the sprechstimme vocal excursions on _Tinseltown Rebellion_, and the album also has jazzy rock instrumentals "Mōggio" and "We Are Not Alone". A second 1983 album, _[London Symphony Orchestra, Vol. I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Symphony_Orchestra,_Vol._I "London Symphony Orchestra, Vol. I")_, includes orchestral Zappa compositions conducted by [Kent Nagano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_Nagano "Kent Nagano") and performed by the [London Symphony Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Symphony_Orchestra "London Symphony Orchestra") (LSO). A second record of these sessions, _[London Symphony Orchestra, Vol. II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Symphony_Orchestra,_Vol._II "London Symphony Orchestra, Vol. II")_ was released in 1987. The material was recorded under a tight schedule with Zappa providing all funding, helped by the commercial success of "Valley Girl".[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):146–156 Zappa was not satisfied with the LSO recordings. He drew particular attention to the performance of "Strictly Genteel", which was recorded after the trumpet section had been out for drinks on a break: the track needed 40 edits to hide out-of-tune notes.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):146–156 Conductor Nagano, who was pleased with the experience, noted that "in fairness to the orchestra, the music is humanly very, very difficult".[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):315 Some reviews noted that the recordings were the best representation of Zappa's orchestral work so far.[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-102) In 1984 Zappa teamed again with Nagano and the Berkeley Symphony Orchestra[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-103) for a live performance of _A Zappa Affair_ with augmented orchestra, life-size puppets, and moving stage sets. Although critically acclaimed, the work was a financial failure, and only performed twice. Zappa was invited by conference organizer [Thomas Wells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Wells_(composer) "Thomas Wells (composer)") to be the keynote speaker at the American Society of University Composers at the [Ohio State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_State_University "Ohio State University"). It was there Zappa delivered an address entitled "Bingo! There Goes Your Tenure",[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-104) and had two of his orchestra pieces, "Dupree's Paradise" and "Naval Aviation in Art?" performed by the [Columbus Symphony Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Symphony_Orchestra "Columbus Symphony Orchestra") and ProMusica Chamber Orchestra of Columbus.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):323[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-105) Zappa's management relationship with Bennett Glotzer ended in 1984.[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-106) Starting in 1985 Gail began managing much of the Zappa business empire, which included a record label, a mail-order company, a video company and a music publishing firm.[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-capitalistrocker-107) ### Beginning of Synclavier works See also: [The Perfect Stranger (Frank Zappa album)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Perfect_Stranger_(Frank_Zappa_album) "The Perfect Stranger (Frank Zappa album)"), [Them or Us](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Them_or_Us "Them or Us"), [Thing-Fish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thing-Fish "Thing-Fish"), [Francesco Zappa (album)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Zappa_(album) "Francesco Zappa (album)"), and [Does Humor Belong in Music? See [media help](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Media "Help:Media")._ In 1983, Zappa began using the [Synclavier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synclavier "Synclavier"), an early digital synthesizer that over time became his primary compositional and performance tool.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):172–173 According to Zappa, "With the Synclavier, any group of imaginary instruments can be invited to play the most difficult passages... with _one-millisecond_ accuracy—every time".[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):172–173 Even though it essentially did away with the need for musicians,[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):319 Zappa viewed the Synclavier and real-life musicians as separate.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):172–173 In late 1984, he released four albums. _[The Perfect Stranger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Perfect_Stranger_(Frank_Zappa_album) "The Perfect Stranger (Frank Zappa album)")_ contains orchestral works commissioned and conducted by celebrated conductor, composer, and pianist [Pierre Boulez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Boulez "Pierre Boulez") (who was listed as an influence on _Freak Out!_), and performed by his [Ensemble intercontemporain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ensemble_intercontemporain "Ensemble intercontemporain"). These were juxtaposed with premiere Synclavier pieces. Again, Zappa was not satisfied with the performances of his orchestral works, regarding them as under-rehearsed, but in the album liner notes he respectfully thanks Boulez's demands for precision.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-watson05-39):73 The Synclavier pieces stood in contrast to the orchestral works, as the sounds were electronically generated and not, as became possible shortly thereafter, [sampled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sampling_(music) "Sampling (music)"). _[Them or Us](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Them_or_Us "Them or Us")_ is a two LP set of studio and live rock recordings. It includes a version of the [Allman Brothers Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allman_Brothers_Band "Allman Brothers Band") song " [Whipping Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whipping_Post_(song) "Whipping Post (song)")" and "Be in My Video", Zappa's satirical take on perceived visual clichés of the [MTV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTV "MTV") channel. _[Francesco Zappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Zappa_(album) "Francesco Zappa (album)")_, a Synclavier rendition of works by 18th-century composer [Francesco Zappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Zappa "Francesco Zappa"), was also released in 1984.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-108) The album _[Thing-Fish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thing-Fish "Thing-Fish")_ was an ambitious three-record set in the style of a Broadway play dealing with a [dystopian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dystopia "Dystopia") "what-if" scenario involving feminism, homosexuality, manufacturing and distribution of the AIDS virus, and a [eugenics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugenics "Eugenics") program conducted by the United States government.[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-109) New vocals were combined with previously released tracks and new Synclavier music; "the work is an extraordinary example of _[bricolage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bricolage "Bricolage")_".[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-110) ### Merchandising Zappa's mail-order merchandise business, Barfko-Swill, established during the 1980s by Zappa's wife Gail, offers t-shirts, videos, posters, sheet music, and collector's recordings, most of them unavailable through other media.[\[104\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-111) Gail has explained why Barfko-Swill was founded: "Just piles and piles of fan mail sitting around unanswered or with no response. The first thing that we did was put a list together from the fan mail and made a Barking Pumpkin t-shirt available which we still have – same old shirt, same old logo, same old price – just to see what would happen. Everybody would write to us and ask us if there was something they could get besides records. ... That was really the primary reason for getting into the business – for setting up Barfko-Swill – in those days was to be independent. To not have to rely on a major record company's interest and ability to promote your product. And that was what the challenge was for me. I prefer the autonomy."[\[105\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-112) From 1983 to 1993, Barfko-Swill was run by [Gerry Fialka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerry_Fialka "Gerry Fialka");[\[106\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-113) Fialka also worked for Zappa as archivist, production assistant, tour assistant, and [factotum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handyman "Handyman"),[\[107\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-114)[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-115)[\[109\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-:12-116)[\[110\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-:10-117) and answered the phone for Zappa's [Barking Pumpkin Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barking_Pumpkin_Records "Barking Pumpkin Records") hotline.[\[111\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-118)[\[112\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-119) The 1987 [VHS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VHS "VHS") release of Zappa's film _[Baby Snakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baby_Snakes "Baby Snakes")_ includes, as an extra feature, Fialka giving a tour of Barfko-Swill. He is credited on-screen as "Gerald Fialka Cool Guy Who Wraps Stuff So It Doesn't Break".[\[113\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-120) A short clip of this tour is also included in the 2020 documentary film _Zappa_. ### Digital medium and last tour See also: [Frank Zappa Meets the Mothers of Prevention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa_Meets_the_Mothers_of_Prevention 1970s, and early 1980s albums for the new digital compact disc (CD) medium.[\[nb 8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-121) Certain aspects of these re-issues have been criticized by some fans as being unfaithful to the original recordings, with changes made to _We're Only in It for the Money_, _Cruising with Ruben & the Jets_, _Uncle Meat_, and _Sleep Dirt_ being the most strongly criticized.[\[114\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-122) Nearly twenty years before the advent of online music stores, Zappa had proposed to replace "phonographic record merchandising" of music by "direct digital-to-digital transfer" through phone or cable TV (with royalty payments and consumer billing automatically built into the accompanying software).[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):337–339 In 1989, Zappa considered his idea a "miserable flop".[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):337–339 The album _[Jazz from Hell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_from_Hell "Jazz from Hell"),_ released in 1986, Performance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Best_Rock_Instrumental_Performance "Best Rock Instrumental Performance"). Except for one live guitar solo ("St. Etienne"), the album exclusively featured compositions brought to life by the Synclavier. Zappa's last tour began on February 2, 1988, in Albany, New York and ended on June 6 in Genoa, Italy.[\[115\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-123) By the end the band had a repertoire of over 100 mostly Zappa compositions. With 12 members, it was one of his largest touring ensembles, including a five piece horn section. The group split up early under acrimonious circumstances before Zappa's intended completion date.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):346–350 The tour was documented on the albums _[Broadway the Hard Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_the_Hard_Way "Broadway the Hard Way")_ (new material featuring songs with strong political emphasis); _[The Best Band You Never Heard in Your Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Best_Band_You_Never_Heard_in_Your_Life "The Best Band You Never Heard in Your Life")_ (Zappa "standards" and an eclectic collection of cover tunes, ranging from [Maurice Ravel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Ravel "Maurice Ravel")'s _[Boléro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bol%C3%A9ro "Boléro")_ to [Led Zeppelin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Led_Zeppelin "Led Zeppelin")'s " [Stairway to Heaven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stairway_to_Heaven "Stairway to Heaven")"); and _[Make a Jazz Noise Here](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Make_a_Jazz_Noise_Here "Make a Jazz Noise Here")_ (a selection of Zappa's more instrumentally complex and jazz orientated material). An album of guitar solos from this tour also appeared as the posthumous 2006 album _[Trance-Fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trance-Fusion "Trance-Fusion")_, a follow-up to the _Shut Up 'n Play Yer Guitar_ and _Guitar_ albums. More recordings from the 1988 tour would appear as part of _[You Can't Do That on Stage Anymore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You_Can't_Do_That_on_Stage_Anymore_(disambiguation) "You Can't Do That on Stage Anymore (disambiguation)")_, a series of six double CDs compiled by Zappa from unreleased live recordings, dating back to the earliest Mothers recordings from 1965. The six volumes were released between 1988 and 1992. _[The Real Frank Zappa Book](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Real_Frank_Zappa_Book "The Real Frank Zappa Book")_, co-written with Peter Occhiogrosso, was published by [Poseidon Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poseidon_Press "Poseidon Press") in 1989. Zappa appeared on the TV interview show _[Larry King Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_King_Live "Larry King Live")_ to promote it. He explained the title by saying he wrote it in response to previous unauthorized books, which he considered to be stupid and exploitative.[\[116\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-124) ### Health deterioration See also: [The Yellow Shark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Yellow_Shark "The Yellow Shark") ![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/Gnome-mime-audio-openclipart.svg/120px-Gnome-mime-audio-openclipart.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail) ["N-Lite" (recorded circa 1991-1992, released 1994)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Zappa_Nlite.ogg "File:Zappa Nlite.ogg") One of Zappa's works for Synclavier on _[Civilization Phaze III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civilization_Phaze_III "Civilization Phaze III")_, cited as his "last great work".[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-watson05-39):100 * * * _Problems playing this file? See [media help](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Media "Help:Media")._ In 1990, Zappa was diagnosed with terminal [prostate cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prostate_cancer "Prostate cancer"). The disease had been developing unnoticed for years and was considered inoperable.[\[117\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-A.C._Grimes-125)[\[118\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Pulse1993-126) After the diagnosis, Zappa devoted most of his energy to modern orchestral and [Synclavier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synclavier "Synclavier") works. Shortly before his death in 1993 he completed _[Civilization Phaze III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civilization_Phaze_III "Civilization Phaze III")_, a major Synclavier work that he had begun in the 1980s.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):374–375[\[nb 9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-127) In 1991, Zappa was chosen to be one of four featured composers at the Frankfurt Festival in 1992 (the others were [John Cage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cage "John Cage"), [Karlheinz Stockhausen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karlheinz_Stockhausen "Karlheinz Stockhausen"), and [Alexander Knaifel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Knaifel "Alexander Knaifel")).[\[119\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-128) Zappa was approached by the German chamber ensemble [Ensemble Modern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ensemble_Modern "Ensemble Modern"), which was interested in playing his music for the event. Although ill, he invited them to Los Angeles for rehearsals of new compositions and new arrangements of older material.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):369 Zappa also got along with the musicians, and the concerts in Germany and Austria were set up for later in the year.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):369 Zappa also performed in 1991 in [Prague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague "Prague"), claiming that "was the first time that he had a reason to play his guitar in 3 years", and that that moment was just "the beginning of a new country", and asked the public to "try to keep your country unique, do not change it into something else".[\[120\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-129)[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-130) [John Kricfalusi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kricfalusi "John Kricfalusi"), creator of [Nickelodeon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nickelodeon "Nickelodeon")'s _[The Ren & Stimpy Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ren_&_Stimpy_Show "The Ren & Stimpy Show")_, idolized Zappa and got him to voice the [Pope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope "Pope") in the episode " [Powdered Toast Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Powdered_Toast_Man_(episode) "Powdered Toast Man (episode)")"; as Zappa was too ill to head to [Spümcø](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sp%C3%BCmc%C3%B8 "Spümcø") at [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"), he recorded his lines at his residence. The episode aired in August 1992 to significant controversy unrelated to Zappa's appearance.[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKomorowski2017145-131) In September 1992, the concerts went ahead as scheduled but Zappa could only appear at two in Frankfurt due to illness. At the first concert, he conducted the opening "Overture" and the final " [G-Spot Tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G-Spot_Tornado "G-Spot Tornado")", as well as the theatrical "Food Gathering in Post-Industrial America, 1992" and "Welcome to the United States" (the remainder of the program was conducted by the ensemble's regular conductor [Peter Rundel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Rundel "Peter Rundel")). Zappa received a 20-minute ovation.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):371 "G-Spot Tornado" was performed with Canadian dancer [Louise Lecavalier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Lecavalier "Louise Lecavalier"). It was Zappa's last professional public appearance, as the cancer was spreading to such an extent that he was in too much pain to enjoy an event that he otherwise found "exhilarating".[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):371 Recordings from the concerts appeared on _[The Yellow Shark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Yellow_Shark "The Yellow Shark")_ (1993), Zappa's last release during his lifetime, and some material from studio rehearsals appeared on the posthumous _[Everything Is Healing Nicely](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everything_Is_Healing_Nicely "Everything Is Healing Nicely")_ (1999). ## Death On December 4, 1993, Zappa died from [prostate cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prostate_cancer "Prostate cancer") at his home with his wife and children by his side. On December 6, his family publicly announced that "Composer Frank Zappa left for his final tour just before 6:00 P.M. on Saturday".[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-slaven03-15):320 He was buried at a private ceremony in a grave at the [Westwood Village Memorial Park Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westwood_Village_Memorial_Park_Cemetery "Westwood Village Memorial Park Cemetery"), in Los Angeles. The grave remains unmarked and located just to the right of actor [Lew Ayres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lew_Ayres "Lew Ayres")' grave. Zappa was 52 years old.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):379–380[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-watson05-39):552 ## Artistry ###
