rock").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-semley2012-5) ### Influences Zappa grew up influenced by [avant-garde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde "Avant-garde") composers such as [Edgard Varèse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgard_Var%C3%A8se "Edgard Varèse"), [Igor Stravinsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Igor_Stravinsky "Igor Stravinsky"), and [Anton Webern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anton_Webern "Anton Webern"); 1950s [blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues "Blues") artists [Clarence "Gatemouth" Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarence_%22Gatemouth%22_Brown "Clarence \"Gatemouth\" Brown"), [Guitar Slim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar_Slim "Guitar Slim"), [Howlin' Wolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howlin'_Wolf "Howlin' Wolf"), [Johnny "Guitar" Watson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_%22Guitar%22_Watson "Johnny \"Guitar\" Watson"), and [B.B. King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B.B._King "B.B. King");[\[129\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-138) Egyptian composer [Halim El-Dabh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halim_El-Dabh "Halim El-Dabh");[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Holmes-24) R&B and [doo-wop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doo-wop "Doo-wop") groups (particularly local [pachuco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pachuco "Pachuco") groups); and [modern jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_jazz "Modern jazz"). His own heterogeneous ethnic background, and the diverse social and cultural mix in and around greater Los Angeles, were crucial in the formation of Zappa as a practitioner of [underground music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underground_music "Underground music") and of his later distrustful and openly critical attitude towards "mainstream" social, political and musical movements. He frequently lampooned musical fads like [psychedelia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelia "Psychedelia"), [rock opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_opera "Rock opera") and [disco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disco "Disco").[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-watson96-21):13[\[nb 10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-140) Television also exerted a strong influence, as demonstrated by quotations from show themes and advertising jingles found in his later works.[\[131\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-quotes-141) In his book _The Real Frank Zappa Book_, Zappa credited composer [Spike Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spike_Jones "Spike Jones") for his frequent use of funny sound effects, mouth noises, and humorous percussion interjections. After explaining his ideas on this, he said "I owe this part of my musical existence to Spike Jones."[\[132\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-142) ### Project/Object Zappa's albums make extensive use of [segued](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Segue "Segue") tracks, breaklessly joining the elements of his albums.[\[133\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-segue-143) His total output is unified by a conceptual continuity he termed "Project/Object", with numerous musical phrases, ideas, and characters reappearing across his albums.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-semley2012-5) He also called it a "conceptual continuity", meaning that any project or album was part of a larger project. Everything was connected, and musical themes and lyrics reappeared in different form on later albums. Conceptual continuity clues are found throughout Zappa's entire œuvre.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):160[\[131\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-quotes-141) ### Techniques #### Guitar playing Zappa is widely recognized as one of the most significant electric guitar soloists. In a 1983 issue of _[Guitar World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar_World "Guitar World")_, John Swenson declared: "the fact of the matter is that \[Zappa\] is one of the greatest guitarists we have and is sorely unappreciated as such."[\[134\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-144) His idiosyncratic style developed gradually and was mature by the early 1980s, by which time his live performances featured lengthy improvised solos during many songs. A November 2016 feature by the editors of _Guitar Player_ magazine wrote: "Brimming with sophisticated motifs and convoluted rhythms, Zappa's extended excursions are more akin to symphonies than they are to guitar solos." The symphonic comparison stems from his habit of introducing melodic themes that, like a symphony's main melodies, were repeated with variations throughout his solos. He was further described as using a wide variety of scales and modes, enlivened by "unusual rhythmic combinations". His left hand was capable of smooth [legato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legato "Legato") technique, while Zappa's right was "one of the fastest pick hands in the business."[\[135\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-145) In 2016, [Dweezil Zappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dweezil_Zappa "Dweezil Zappa") explained a distinctive element of his father's guitar improvisation technique was relying heavily on upstrokes much more than many other guitarists, who are more likely to use downstrokes with their picking.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-dweezilimprov-4) His song "Outside Now" from _[Joe's Garage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe's_Garage "Joe's Garage")_ poked fun at the negative reception of Zappa's guitar technique by those more commercially minded, as the song's narrator lives in a world where music is outlawed and he imagines "imaginary guitar notes that would irritate/An executive kind of guy", lyrics that are followed by one of Zappa's characteristically quirky solos in 11/8 time.[\[136\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-146) Zappa transcriptionist Kasper Sloots wrote, "Zappa's guitar solos aren't meant to show off technically (Zappa hasn't claimed to be a big virtuoso on the instrument), but for the pleasure it gives trying to build a composition right in front of an audience without knowing what the outcome will be."[\[137\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-147) Zappa's guitar style was not without its critics. English guitarist and bandleader [John McLaughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McLaughlin_(musician) "John McLaughlin (musician)"), whose band [Mahavishnu Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra "Mahavishnu Orchestra") toured with the Mothers of Invention in 1973, opined that Zappa was "very interesting as a human being and a very interesting composer" and that he "was a very good musician but he was a dictator in his band," and that he "was taking very long guitar solos \[when performing live\]—10–15 minute guitar solos and really he should have taken two or three minute guitar solos, because they were a little bit boring."[\[138\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-148) In 2000, he was ranked No. 36 on [VH1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VH1 "VH1")'s _100 Greatest Artists of Hard Rock_.[\[139\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-youtube.com-149) In 2004, _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ magazine ranked him at No. 71 on its [list of the "100 Greatest Artists of All Time"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone's_100_Greatest_Artists_of_All_Time "Rolling Stone's 100 Greatest Artists of All Time"),[\[140\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-150) and in 2011 at No. 22 on its list of the "100 Greatest Guitarists of All Time".[\[141\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-151) #### Tape manipulation During recording sessions in New York in 1967, Zappa increasingly used [tape editing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_engineer "Audio engineer") as a compositional tool.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):160 A prime example is found on the double album _[Uncle Meat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncle_Meat "Uncle Meat")_ (1969),[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-james-43):104 where the track "King Kong" is edited from various studio and live performances. Zappa had begun regularly recording concerts,[\[nb 11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-152) and because of his insistence on precise [tuning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_tuning#Tuning_practice "Musical tuning") and timing, he was able to augment his studio productions with excerpts from live shows, and vice versa.[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Mix2003-84) Later, he combined recordings of different compositions into new pieces, irrespective of the [tempo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tempo "Tempo") or [meter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meter_(music) "Meter (music)") of the sources. He dubbed this process " [xenochrony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xenochrony "Xenochrony")" (strange synchronizations[\[142\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-153))—ref from the Greek "xeno" (alien or strange) and "chronos" (time).[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Mix2003-84) ## Personal life ### Family Main articles: [Gail Zappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gail_Zappa "Gail Zappa"), [Moon Zappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon_Zappa "Moon Zappa"), [Dweezil Zappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dweezil_Zappa "Dweezil Zappa"), [Ahmet Zappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmet_Zappa "Ahmet Zappa"), and [Diva Zappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diva_Zappa "Diva Zappa") [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/fc/Simon_Prentis_%26_Frank_Zappa_%26_Gerry_Fialka_%26_Gail_Zappa.webp?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Simon_Prentis_&_Frank_Zappa_&_Gerry_Fialka_&_Gail_Zappa.webp) Left to right: Simon Prentis (Zappa's "Semantic Scrutinizer"), Zappa, Zappa's production assistant [Gerry Fialka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerry_Fialka "Gerry Fialka"), and Zappa's second wife Gail outside Zappa's home recording studio [Utility Muffin Research Kitchen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utility_Muffin_Research_Kitchen "Utility Muffin Research Kitchen") in 1986. Prentis holds a preview cassette of the album _[Jazz From Hell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_From_Hell "Jazz From Hell")_ that Fialka had just delivered for Zappa's approval.[\[143\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-154) Zappa's parents were Francis Vincent Zappa and Rose Marie Zappa (née Colimore). Frank was the second of five children, preceded by his half-sister Ann and followed by his brothers Bobby and Carl and sister Patrice (also known as Candy). Zappa was married to Kathryn J. "Kay" Sherman from 1960 to 1963. In 1967, he married [Adelaide Gail Sloatman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adelaide_Gail_Sloatman "Adelaide Gail Sloatman").[\[144\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-155)[\[145\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-156) He and his second wife had four children: [Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon_Zappa "Moon Zappa") (born 1967), [Dweezil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dweezil "Dweezil") (born 1969), [Ahmet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmet_Zappa "Ahmet Zappa") (born 1974), and [Diva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diva_Zappa "Diva Zappa") (born 1979).[\[146\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-157) Moon and Ahmet sang on Frank's 1981 album _[You Are What You Is](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You_Are_What_You_Is "You Are What You Is")_, while Moon also provided the " [Valley girl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valley_girl "Valley girl")" voice on [the song of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valley_Girl_(song) "Valley Girl (song)") on 1982's _[Ship Arriving Too Late to Save a Drowning Witch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ship_Arriving_Too_Late_to_Save_a_Drowning_Witch "Ship Arriving Too Late to Save a Drowning Witch")_. The song became Frank's only US Top 40 hit single and is credited with popularizing [valspeak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valspeak "Valspeak") and valley girl culture, despite being intended by Frank and Moon as a parody and criticism of it.[\[147\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-158)[\[148\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-159)[\[149\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-160) An accomplished guitarist in his own right, Dweezil made several guest appearances on stage with Frank during the 1982, 1984, and 1988 tours, and Frank produced Dweezil's first album _[Havin' a Bad Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Havin'_a_Bad_Day "Havin' a Bad Day")_ in 1986. Following Zappa's death, his widow Gail created the Zappa Family Trust, which owns the rights to Zappa's music and some other creative output: 62 albums released during Zappa's lifetime and 73 released posthumously as of September 2026. Upon Gail's death in October 2015, the Zappa children received shares of the trust; Ahmet and Diva received 30% each, Moon and Dweezil received 20% each.[\[150\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-:1-161) The original trust, signed by Frank and Gail in 1990, assured the four children would receive equal shares, but this was altered by Gail sometime after Frank's death.[\[151\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-162) In the mid-1980s, Zappa learned of an obscure 18th century Italian composer and cellist named [Francesco Zappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Zappa "Francesco Zappa"). Initially assuming him to be an ancestor, Frank recorded and released an album of Francesco's music, _[Francesco Zappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Zappa_(album) "Francesco Zappa (album)")_, in 1984. It was subsequently found that Frank and Francesco were not actually related, which Frank confirmed in _[The Real Frank Zappa Book](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Real_Frank_Zappa_Book "The Real Frank Zappa Book")_ in 1989. ### Captain Beefheart Main article: [Captain Beefheart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_Beefheart "Captain Beefheart") Zappa and [Don Van Vliet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Van_Vliet "Don Van Vliet") met when they were both teenagers and shared an interest in [rhythm and blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues") and [Chicago blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_blues "Chicago blues").[\[152\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Taylor-163) They collaborated from this early stage with Zappa's scripts for "teenage operettas", such as "Captain Beefheart & the Grunt People", with Vliet eventually adopting the Captain Beefheart name. The earliest known recording of either Zappa or Beefheart is a collaboration between them, "Lost in a Whirlpool", recorded around 1958/1959 and included on the posthumous Zappa album _[The Lost Episodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Lost_Episodes "The Lost Episodes")_ in 1996. In 1963, the pair recorded a demo at the [Pal Recording Studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pal_Recording_Studio "Pal Recording Studio") in Cucamonga as the Soots, seeking support from a major label. Their efforts were unsuccessful, as Vliet's [Howlin' Wolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howlin'_Wolf "Howlin' Wolf")-influenced vocal style and Zappa's distorted guitar were "not on the agenda" at the time.[\[152\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Taylor-163) In 1965, while Zappa formed the Mothers of Invention, Beefheart assembled Captain Beefheart and His Magic Band. Their third album, 1969's critically acclaimed _[Trout Mask Replica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trout_Mask_Replica "Trout Mask Replica")_, was produced by Zappa. That same year, Beefheart provided the vocal on "Willie the Pimp" on the _[Hot Rats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_Rats "Hot Rats")_ album. Beefheart also played the harmonica on "San Ber'dino" (credited as "Bloodshot Rollin' Red") on _[One Size Fits All](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Size_Fits_All_(Frank_Zappa_album) "One Size Fits All (Frank Zappa album)")_ (1975) and " [Find Her Finer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Find_Her_Finer "Find Her Finer")" on _[Zoot Allures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoot_Allures "Zoot Allures")_ (1976).[\[153\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-164) Over the years, Zappa and Beefheart's friendship was sometimes complicated by rivalry, as musicians drifted back and forth between their groups. Beefheart joined Zappa's band on the early 1975 tour, documented on the _[Bongo Fury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bongo_Fury "Bongo Fury")_ album,[\[154\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-165) mainly because conflicting contractual obligations made Beefheart unable to tour or record independently at the time. Their relationship grew acrimonious on the tour to the point that they refused to talk to one another. Zappa became irritated by Beefheart, who drew constantly, including while on stage, filling one of his large sketch books with rapidly executed portraits and warped caricatures of Zappa. Musically, Beefheart's primitive style contrasted sharply with Zappa's compositional discipline and abundant technique. Mothers of Invention drummer [Jimmy Carl Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carl_Black "Jimmy Carl Black") described the situation as "two geniuses" on "ego trips".[\[155\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-166) Estranged for years afterwards, they reconciled by the end of Zappa's life. ## Beliefs and politics ### Drugs Zappa stated, "Drugs do not become a problem until the person who uses the drugs does something to you, or does something that would affect your life that you don't want to have happen to you, like an airline pilot who crashes because he was full of drugs."[\[156\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-167) Zappa was a heavy [tobacco smoker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tobacco_smoker "Tobacco smoker") for most of his life, and critical of anti-tobacco campaigns.[\[nb 12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-169) While he disapproved of drug use, he criticized the [war on drugs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_on_drugs "War on drugs"), comparing it to [alcohol prohibition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcohol_prohibition "Alcohol prohibition"); he stated that the [United States Treasury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Treasury "United States Treasury") would benefit from the decriminalization and regulation of drugs.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):329 Describing his philosophical views, Zappa stated, "I believe that people have a right to decide their own destinies; people own themselves. I also believe that, in a democracy, government exists because (and only so long as) individual citizens give it a 'temporary license to exist'—in exchange for a promise that it will behave itself. In a democracy, you own the government—it doesn't own you."[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):315–316,323–324,329–330 ### Government and religion [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/Praga_7_zappa_havel.jpg/500px-Praga_7_zappa_havel.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Praga_7_zappa_havel.jpg) Zappa with [Václav Havel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V%C3%A1clav_Havel "Václav Havel"), 1990 In a 1991 interview, Zappa reported that he was a registered [Democrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") but added "that might not last long—I'm going to shred that."[\[158\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-170) Describing his political views, Zappa categorized himself as a " [practical conservative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservatism_in_the_United_States "Conservatism in the United States")."[\[nb 13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-171) He favored [limited government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limited_government "Limited government") and low [taxes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxes "Taxes"); he also stated that he approved of national defense, [social security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Security_(United_States) "Social Security (United States)"), and other federal programs, but only if citizens are willing and able to pay for them.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):315–316,323–324,329–330 He opposed military drafts, saying that military service should be voluntary.[\[159\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-172) He favored capitalism, [entrepreneurship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entrepreneurship "Entrepreneurship"), and independent business, stating that musicians could make more from owning their own businesses than from collecting royalties.[\[160\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-:0-173) He [opposed communism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-communism "Anti-communism"), stating, "A system that doesn't allow ownership... has—to put it mildly—a fatal design flaw."[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):315–316,323–324,329–330 He had placed messages on his album covers to encourage his fans to [register to vote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Register_to_vote "Register to vote"); further, throughout 1988, Zappa had registration booths at his concerts.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):348 He even considered running for president of the United States as an independent.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):365[\[161\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-174) Zappa was an [atheist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atheist "Atheist").[\[162\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-175)[\[163\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-176) He recalled his parents being "pretty religious" and trying to make him go to Catholic school despite his resentment. He felt disgust towards [organized religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organized_religion "Organized religion") (Christianity in particular) because he believed that it promoted ignorance and [anti-intellectualism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-intellectualism "Anti-intellectualism"). He held the view that the Garden of Eden story shows that the essence of Christianity is to oppose gaining knowledge.[\[164\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-177) Some of his songs, concert performances, interviews and public debates in the 1980s criticized and derided Republicans and their policies—President [Ronald Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan"), the [Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_Defense_Initiative "Strategic Defense Initiative"), [televangelism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Televangelism "Televangelism"), and the [Christian Right](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Right "Christian Right")—and warned that the United States government was in danger of becoming a " [fascist theocracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_fascism "Christian fascism")."[\[165\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-178)[\[166\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-CNN_TV_Debate-179) In early 1990, Zappa visited [Czechoslovakia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czechoslovakia "Czechoslovakia") at the request of [President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Czech_Republic "President of the Czech Republic") [Václav Havel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V%C3%A1clav_Havel "Václav Havel"). The meeting had been arranged by keyboardist [Michael Kocáb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Koc%C3%A1b "Michael Kocáb"). A longtime admirer of Zappa's commitment to individualism, Havel designated him as Czechoslovakia's "Special Ambassador to the West on Trade, Culture and Tourism."[\[167\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Pompilio-180) Havel was a lifelong fan of Zappa, who had great influence in the avant-garde and underground scene in Central Europe in the 1970s and 1980s. [The Plastic People of the Universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Plastic_People_of_the_Universe "The Plastic People of the Universe"), a Czechoslovak jazz rock group associated with [Prague underground culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague_underground_(culture) "Prague underground (culture)"), took its name from Zappa's 1967 song " [Plastic People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plastic_People "Plastic People")".[\[168\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-181) Under pressure from Secretary of State, [James Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Baker "James Baker"), Zappa's posting (as Czech 'Special Ambassador') was withdrawn.[\[169\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-182) Havel made Zappa an unofficial [cultural attaché](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_attach%C3%A9 "Cultural attaché") instead.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):357–361 Zappa planned to develop an international consulting enterprise to facilitate trade between the former Eastern Bloc and Western businesses.[\[118\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Pulse1993-126) ### Anti-censorship activism Zappa expressed opinions on [censorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Censorship "Censorship") when he appeared on [CNN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNN "CNN")'s _[Crossfire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossfire_(U.S._TV_program) "Crossfire (U.S. TV program)")_ TV series and debated issues with _Washington Times_ commentator [John Lofton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lofton "John Lofton") in 1986.[\[166\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-CNN_TV_Debate-179) On September 19, 1985, Zappa testified before the [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") Commerce, Technology, and Transportation committee, attacking the [Parents Music Resource Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parents_Music_Resource_Center "Parents Music Resource Center") (PMRC), an organization co-founded by [Tipper Gore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tipper_Gore "Tipper Gore"), wife of then-senator [Al Gore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore "Al Gore").[\[170\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-183) The PMRC consisted of many wives of politicians, including the wives of five members of the committee, and was founded to address the issue of song lyrics with sexual or satanic content.[\[171\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-184) During Zappa's testimony, he stated that there was a clear conflict of interest between the PMRC due to the relations of its founders to the politicians who were then trying to pass what he referred to as the "Blank Tape Tax." Kandy Stroud, a spokeswoman for the PMRC, announced that Senator Gore (who co-founded the committee) was a co-sponsor of that legislation. Zappa suggested that record labels were trying to get the bill passed quickly through committees, one of which was chaired by Senator [Strom Thurmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strom_Thurmond "Strom Thurmond"), who was also affiliated with the PMRC. Zappa further said that this committee was being used as a distraction from that bill being passed, which would lead only to the benefit of a select few in the music industry.[\[172\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-pmrc-statement-185)[\[173\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-cspan-186) Zappa saw their activities as on a path towards censorship[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):267 and called their proposal for voluntary [labelling of records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parental_Advisory "Parental Advisory") with explicit content "extortion" of the music industry.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Occhiogrosso-1):262 In his prepared statement, he said: > The PMRC proposal is an ill-conceived piece of nonsense which fails to deliver any real benefits to children, infringes the civil liberties of people who are not children, and promises to keep the courts busy for years dealing with the interpretational and enforcemental problems inherent in the proposal's design. It is my understanding that, in law, [First Amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Amendment "First Amendment") issues are decided with a preference for the least restrictive alternative. In this context, the PMRC's demands are the equivalent of treating [dandruff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dandruff "Dandruff") by [decapitation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decapitation "Decapitation").... The establishment of a rating system, voluntary or otherwise, opens the door to an endless parade of moral quality control programs based on things certain Christians do not like. What if the next bunch of Washington wives demands a [large yellow "J"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_badge "Yellow badge") on all material written or performed by Jews, in order to save helpless children from exposure to concealed Zionist doctrine?[\[172\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-pmrc-statement-185)[\[173\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-cspan-186)[\[174\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-187) Zappa set excerpts from the PMRC hearings to Synclavier music in his composition "Porn Wars" on the 1985 album _[Frank Zappa Meets the Mothers of Prevention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa_Meets_the_Mothers_of_Prevention "Frank Zappa Meets the Mothers of Prevention")_, and the full recording was released in 2010 as _[Congress Shall Make No Law...](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_Shall_Make_No_Law... "Congress Shall Make No Law...")_ Zappa is heard interacting with Senators [Fritz Hollings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fritz_Hollings "Fritz Hollings"), [Slade Gorton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slade_Gorton "Slade Gorton") and [Al Gore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore "Al Gore").[\[175\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-lowe194-188) ## Legacy Main article: [Frank Zappa in popular culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa_in_popular_culture "Frank Zappa in popular culture") Zappa was a controversial figure. As [Geoffrey Himes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffrey_Himes "Geoffrey Himes") noted in 1993 after the artist's death, Zappa was hailed as a genius by conductor [Kent Nagano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_Nagano "Kent Nagano") and nominated by Czechoslovak President [Václav Havel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V%C3%A1clav_Havel "Václav Havel") to the country's cultural ambassadorship; however, in his lifetime, Zappa was rejected twice for admission into the [Rock and Roll Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_Roll_Hall_of_Fame "Rock and Roll Hall of Fame"). In _[Christgau's Record Guide: Rock Albums of the Seventies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christgau's_Record_Guide:_Rock_Albums_of_the_Seventies "Christgau's Record Guide: Rock Albums of the Seventies")_ (1981), [Robert Christgau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Christgau "Robert Christgau") dismissed Zappa's music as "sexist adolescent drivel ... with meters and voicings and key changes that are as hard to play as they are easy to forget."[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-wp-10) According to Himes: > Admirers and detractors agree that Zappa's music—with its odd time signatures, unorthodox harmonies and fiendishly difficult lines—boasts a rare cerebral complexity. But that's where the agreement ends. Some fans find his sophomoric jokes ("Don't Eat the Yellow Snow") and pop music parodies ("Sheik Yerbouti") a crucial counterbalance to the rarefied density of the music; other devotees find the jokes an irrelevant sideshow to music best appreciated in a chamber or orchestral setting. The critics find the humor's smug iconoclasm a symptom of the essential emptiness of Zappa's intellectual exercises.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-wp-10) ### Acclaim and honors > Frank Zappa was one of the first to try tearing down the barriers between rock, jazz, and classical music. In the late Sixties his Mothers of Invention would slip from [Stravinsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stravinsky "Stravinsky")'s " [Petroushka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petrushka_(ballet) "Petrushka (ballet)")" into [The Dovells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dovells "The Dovells")' " [Bristol Stomp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Stomp "Bristol Stomp")" before breaking down into saxophone squeals inspired by [Albert Ayler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler "Albert Ayler"). — _The Rolling Stone Illustrated History of Rock & Roll_, p. 497 _[The Rolling Stone Album Guide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rolling_Stone_Album_Guide "The Rolling Stone Album Guide")_ (2004) writes: "Frank Zappa dabbled in virtually all kinds of music—and, whether guised as a satirical rocker, jazz-rock fusionist, guitar virtuoso, electronics wizard, or orchestral innovator, his eccentric genius was undeniable."[\[176\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-189) Even though his work drew inspiration from many different genres, Zappa was seen as establishing a coherent and personal expression. In 1980, biographer David Walley noted that "The whole structure of his music is unified, not neatly divided by dates or time sequences and it is all building into a composite".[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-walley80-25):3 On commenting on Zappa's music, politics and philosophy, [Barry Miles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_Miles "Barry Miles") noted in 2004 that they cannot be separated: "It was all one; all part of his 'conceptual continuity'."[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-miles-13):383 [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e6/Zappa.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Zappa.jpg) Zappa in 1977 _[Guitar Player](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar_Player "Guitar Player")_ devoted a special issue to Zappa in 1992, and asked on the cover "Is FZ America's Best Kept Musical Secret?" Editor Don Menn remarked that the issue was about "The most important composer to come out of modern popular music".[\[177\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-190) Among those contributing to the issue was composer and [musicologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musicologist "Musicologist") [Nicolas Slonimsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolas_Slonimsky "Nicolas Slonimsky"), who conducted premiere performances of works of [Ives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Ives "Charles Ives") and Varèse in the 1930s.[\[178\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-191) He became friends with Zappa in the 1980s,[\[179\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-192) and said, "I admire everything Frank does, because he practically created the new musical millennium. He does beautiful, beautiful work... It has been my luck to have lived to see the emergence of this totally new type of music."[\[180\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-193) Conductor [Kent Nagano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_Nagano "Kent Nagano") remarked in the same issue that "Frank is a genius. That's a word I don't use often... In Frank's case it is not too strong... He is extremely literate musically. I'm not sure if the general public knows that."[\[181\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-194) [Pierre Boulez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Boulez "Pierre Boulez") told _[Musician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musician_(magazine) "Musician (magazine)")_ magazine's posthumous Zappa tribute article that Zappa "was an exceptional figure because he was part of the worlds of rock and classical music and that both types of his work would survive."[\[182\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-195) In 1994, jazz magazine _[DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat")_'s critics poll placed Zappa in its Hall of Fame.[\[183\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-196) Zappa was posthumously inducted into the [Rock and Roll Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_Roll_Hall_of_Fame "Rock and Roll Hall of Fame") in 1995. There, it was written that "Frank Zappa was rock and roll's sharpest musical mind and most astute social critic. He was the most prolific composer of his age, and he bridged genres—rock, jazz, classical, avant-garde and even novelty music—with masterful ease".[\[184\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-197) He was ranked No. 36 on [VH1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VH1 "VH1")'s _100 Greatest Artists of Hard Rock_[\[139\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-youtube.com-149) in 2000. ### References in arts and sciences [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0e/Doberan_Zappa-Denkmal3.jpg/500px-Doberan_Zappa-Denkmal3.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Doberan_Zappa-Denkmal3.jpg) Frank Zappa bust by Vaclav Cesak in [Bad Doberan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bad_Doberan "Bad Doberan"), Germany Scientists from various fields have honored Zappa by naming new discoveries after him. In 1967, paleontologist Leo P. Plas Jr., identified an extinct [mollusc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mollusc "Mollusc") in Nevada and named it _Amaurotoma zappa_ with the motivation that, "The [specific name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Specific_name_(zoology) "Specific name (zoology)"), _zappa_, honors Frank Zappa".[\[253\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-268) In the 1980s, biologist Ed Murdy named a [genus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genus "Genus") of [gobiid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gobiid "Gobiid") fishes of New Guinea _Zappa_, with a [species](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Species "Species") named _Zappa confluentus_.[\[254\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-269) Biologist Ferdinando Boero named a Californian [jellyfish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jellyfish "Jellyfish") _Phialella zappai_ (1987), noting that he had "pleasure in naming this species after the modern music composer".[\[255\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-270) Belgian biologists Bosmans and Bosselaers discovered in the early 1980s a Cameroonese spider, which they in 1994 named _[Pachygnatha zappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pachygnatha_zappa "Pachygnatha zappa")_ because "the ventral side of the abdomen of the female of this species strikingly resembles the artist's legendary moustache".[\[256\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-271) A gene of the bacterium _[Proteus mirabilis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proteus_mirabilis "Proteus mirabilis")_ that causes urinary tract infections was in 1995 named _zapA_ by three biologists from Maryland. In their scientific article, they "especially thank the late Frank Zappa for inspiration and assistance with genetic nomenclature".[\[257\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-272) Repeating regions of the genome of the human tumor virus [KSHV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaposi's_sarcoma-associated_herpesvirus "Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus") were named _frnk_, _vnct_ and _zppa_ in 1996 by [Yuan Chang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuan_Chang "Yuan Chang") and [Patrick S. Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_S._Moore "Patrick S. Moore") who discovered the virus. Also, a 143 base pair repeat sequence occurring at two positions was named _waka/jwka_.[\[258\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-273) In the late 1990s, American paleontologists Marc Salak and Halard L. Lescinsky discovered a [metazoan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metazoan "Metazoan") fossil, and named it _Spygori zappania_ to honor "the late Frank Zappa... whose mission paralleled that of the earliest paleontologists: to challenge conventional and traditional beliefs when such beliefs lacked roots in logic and reason".[\[259\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-274) In 1994, lobbying efforts initiated by psychiatrist John Scialli led the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union")'s [Minor Planet Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minor_Planet_Center "Minor Planet Center") to name an [asteroid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asteroid "Asteroid") in Zappa's honor: [3834 Zappafrank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3834_Zappafrank "3834 Zappafrank").[\[260\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-275) The asteroid was discovered in 1980 by Czechoslovak astronomer [Ladislav Brožek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ladislav_Bro%C5%BEek "Ladislav Brožek"), and the citation for its naming says that "Zappa was an eclectic, self-trained artist and composer... Before 1989 he was regarded as a symbol of democracy and freedom by many people in Czechoslovakia".[\[261\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-276) In 1995, a bust of Zappa by sculptor Konstantinas Bogdanas was installed in [Vilnius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vilnius "Vilnius"), [Lithuania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithuania "Lithuania"). The choice of Zappa was explained as "a symbol that would mark the end of communism, but at the same time express that it wasn't always doom and gloom."[\[167\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-Pompilio-180) A replica was offered to the city of Baltimore in 2008, and on September 19, 2010—the twenty-fifth anniversary of Zappa's testimony to the U.S. Senate—a ceremony dedicating the replica was held, and the bust was unveiled at a library in the city.[\[262\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-277)[\[263\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa#cite_note-278) For the radio format, see [Smooth jazz radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_jazz_radio "Smooth jazz radio"). | Smooth jazz | | --- | | [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/46/George_benson_1986_montreux_16_3.jpg/500px-George_benson_1986_montreux_16_3.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:George_benson_1986_montreux_16_3.jpg)

- [Soul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_music "Soul music") | | Cultural origins | 1970s, United States | | Fusion genres | | [Crossover jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossover_jazz "Crossover jazz") | | Other topics | | [List of musicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_smooth_jazz_musicians "List of smooth jazz musicians") | **Smooth jazz** is a commercially oriented sub-genre style of jazz music by R&B, funk, rock and pop music styles (separately, or in any combination). Beginning in the early-1970s, [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") (aka "fusion") was a movement by some jazz musicians to merge the instrumental virtuosity and improvisation of traditional jazz, with a modern, electronic sensibility. The instrument that has become the most widely-associated with the genre is the saxophone inspired by players like [Grover Washington Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Washington_Jr. "Grover Washington Jr."), [Ronnie Laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronnie_Laws "Ronnie Laws"), [Wayne Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter "Wayne Shorter") and [Nathan Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_Davis_(saxophonist) "Nathan Davis (saxophonist)"); plus a gentle, [legato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legato "Legato") [electric guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_guitar "Electric guitar") (influenced by players like [Wes Montgomery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wes_Montgomery "Wes Montgomery") and [Grant Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grant_Green "Grant Green")). Jazz fusion ensembles such as [Weather Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report "Weather Report"), [Spyro Gyra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spyro_Gyra "Spyro Gyra"), [Hiroshima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroshima_(band) "Hiroshima (band)") and [Bob James' Fourplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_James_(musician) "Bob James (musician)") were vital to the development of the genre. Modern derivatives of the genre includes the more recent New Adult Contemporary format broadcast radio. "Smooth jazz" has been successful as a radio format; however in 2007, the popularity of the format began to decline. Consequently, it was abandoned by several high-profile radio stations across the U.S.A., perhaps notably in [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") and [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco"). Many industry insiders have speculated that the smooth jazz format may die out, particularly with the industry giant [Clear Channel Communications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clear_Channel_Communications "Clear Channel Communications") dropping the genre. Critics of the company, however, blame Clear Channel for the format's decline, citing too much repetition of a sharply-reduced number of tracks on Clear Channel–owned stations that alienated many listeners. Despite the format's demise on commercial radio, a growing number of non-commercial stations have taken up the music. In addition, smooth jazz concerts, recording sales – as well as increased smooth jazz offerings on the Internet – continue to show strong fan support for the genre. ## Description In general, a smooth jazz track is downtempo (the most widely played tracks are in the 90–105 BPM range), layering a lead, melody-playing instrument (saxophones – especially soprano and tenor – are the most popular with guitars a close second) over a backdrop that typically consists of programmed rhythms and various pads and/or samples. Smooth jazz groups or recording artists tend to play their instruments in a melodic fashion such that they are recognizable within just a few measures; this category includes names such as saxophonists [Kenny G](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_G "Kenny G"), [Najee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Najee "Najee"), [David Sanborn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Sanborn "David Sanborn"), [George Howard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Howard_(jazz) "George Howard (jazz)") and [Art Porter Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Porter_Jr. "Art Porter Jr."); guitarists [George Benson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Benson "George Benson"), [Earl Klugh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_Klugh "Earl Klugh"), [Marc Antoine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Antoine_(musician) "Marc Antoine (musician)"), [Peter White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_White_(musician) "Peter White (musician)"), [Jonathan Butler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Butler "Jonathan Butler"), [Norman Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Brown_(guitarist) "Norman Brown (guitarist)"), [Ronny Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronny_Jordan "Ronny Jordan"), and [Yves Vincent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yves_Vincent "Yves Vincent"); keyboardist/pianists [Joe Sample](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Sample "Joe Sample"), [David Benoit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Benoit "David Benoit"), and [Bradley Joseph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bradley_Joseph "Bradley Joseph"). Some performers, such as [Dave Koz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Koz "Dave Koz"), Bob James, and [Nathan East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_East "Nathan East") are notable for their numerous collaborations with many of the genre's big names. Groups include [Fourplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourplay "Fourplay"), [Pieces of a Dream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pieces_of_a_Dream_(band) "Pieces of a Dream (band)"), [Acoustic Alchemy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acoustic_Alchemy "Acoustic Alchemy"), [Airbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airbourne_(band) "Airbourne (band)") and [the Rippingtons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rippingtons "The Rippingtons"). Female performers includes [Keiko Matsui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keiko_Matsui "Keiko Matsui"), [Joyce Cooling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyce_Cooling "Joyce Cooling"), [Mindi Abair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mindi_Abair "Mindi Abair"), [Candy Dulfer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candy_Dulfer "Candy Dulfer"), [Sade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sade_(band) "Sade (band)"), [Brenda Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brenda_Russell "Brenda Russell"), [Pamela Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pamela_Williams "Pamela Williams"), [Regina Belle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regina_Belle "Regina Belle") and [Anita Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anita_Baker "Anita Baker"). ## History Smooth jazz may be thought of as commercially-oriented, crossover jazz which came to prominence in the 1980s, displacing the more venturesome [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") from which it emerged. It avoids the [improvisational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_improvisation "Jazz improvisation") "risk-taking" of jazz fusion, emphasizing melodic form, and much of the music was initially "a combination of jazz with easy-listening [pop music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music "Pop music") and lightweight [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues")."[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_jazz#cite_note-fushion-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_jazz#cite_note-explore_amg-2) During the mid-1970s in the United States, it was known as "smooth radio"; the genre was not termed "smooth jazz" until the 1980s.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_jazz#cite_note-Gioia2011-3) The term itself seems to have been birthed directly out of radio marketing efforts. In an industry focus group in the late 1980s, one participant coined the phrase "smooth jazz" – and it stuck.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_jazz#cite_note-4)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_jazz#cite_note-5) The popularity of smooth jazz as a radio format grew in the '80s and '90s, but gradually declined in the early 2000s. By 2009, many stations including in NYC, Washington, DC, and Boston had switched away from the format.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_jazz#cite_note-6) ## Pioneers and notable songs See also: [List of smooth jazz musicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_smooth_jazz_musicians "List of smooth jazz musicians") Smooth jazz was arguably pioneered in the early 1970s, with notable songs and artists including: " [Grazing in the Grass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grazing_in_the_Grass "Grazing in the Grass")" (1968), by trumpeter [Hugh Masekela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Masekela "Hugh Masekela"), " [Nautilus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nautilus_(song) "Nautilus (song)")" (1974) by keyboardist [Bob James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_James_(musician) "Bob James (musician)"), and " [Mister Magic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mister_Magic "Mister Magic")" (1975) by saxophonist [Grover Washington, Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Washington,_Jr. "Grover Washington, Jr.") Other early popular releases include guitarist [George Benson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Benson "George Benson")'s 1976 cover/version of " [Breezin'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breezin'_(song) "Breezin' (song)")" and [flugelhorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flugelhorn "Flugelhorn") player [Chuck Mangione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Mangione "Chuck Mangione")'s " [Feels So Good](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feels_So_Good_(composition) "Feels So Good (composition)")" in 1977. Others are " [What You Won't Do for Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What_You_Won't_Do_for_Love_(song) "What You Won't Do for Love (song)")" by [Bobby Caldwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Caldwell "Bobby Caldwell") in 1978, jazz fusion group [Spyro Gyra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spyro_Gyra "Spyro Gyra")'s 1979 instrumental song " [Morning Dance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morning_Dance "Morning Dance")"[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_jazz#cite_note-Gioia2011-3) and the 1981 collaboration between [Grover Washington Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Washington_Jr. "Grover Washington Jr.") and [Bill Withers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Withers "Bill Withers") on " [Just the Two of Us](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Just_the_Two_of_Us_(Grover_Washington,_Jr._song) "Just the Two of Us (Grover Washington, Jr. song)")". Smooth jazz grew in popularity in the 1980s and 1990s as [Anita Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anita_Baker "Anita Baker"), [Sade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sade_(singer) "Sade (singer)"), [Al Jarreau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jarreau "Al Jarreau"), [Grover Washington Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Washington_Jr. "Grover Washington Jr.") and [Kenny G](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_G "Kenny G") released multiple hit songs.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_jazz#cite_note-7) ## Critical and public reception The smooth jazz genre experienced a backlash exemplified by critical complaints about the "bland" sound of top-selling saxophonist Kenny G, whose popularity peaked with his 1992 album _[Breathless](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breathless_(Kenny_G_album) "Breathless (Kenny G album)")_.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_jazz#cite_note-Gioia2011-3) Music reviewer George Graham argues that the "so-called 'smooth jazz' sound of people like Kenny G has none of the fire and creativity[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_jazz#cite_note-8) that marked the best of the fusion scene during its heyday in the 1970s".[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_jazz#cite_note-9) [Digby Fairweather](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digby_Fairweather "Digby Fairweather"), before the start of UK jazz station [theJazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TheJazz "TheJazz"), denounced the change to a smooth jazz format on defunct radio station [102.2 Jazz FM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/102.2_Jazz_FM "102.2 Jazz FM"); he stated that the owners [GMG Radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GMG_Radio "GMG Radio") were responsible for the "attempted rape and (fortunately abortive) re-definition of the music — is one that no true jazz lover within the boundaries of the [M25](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M25_motorway "M25 motorway") will ever find it possible to forget or forgive."[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_jazz#cite_note-10) ## See also - [Rhythm and blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues") - [Lofi hip hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lofi_hip_hop "Lofi hip hop") - [Neo-soul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-soul "Neo-soul") - [Mallsoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mallsoft "Mallsoft") - [Quiet storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quiet_storm "Quiet storm") - [Sophisti-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophisti-pop "Sophisti-pop") - [Yacht rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yacht_rock "Yacht rock") - [Smooth jazz radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_jazz_radio "Smooth jazz radio") ## References 01. # Jazz-funk Jazz-funk Subgenre of jazz music This article is about the music genre. For the dance style, see [Hip-hop dance §Jazz-funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip-hop_dance#Jazz-funk "Hip-hop dance"). "Jazz Funk" redirects here. For the Incognito album, see [Jazz Funk (album)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Funk_(album) "Jazz Funk (album)"). | Jazz-funk | | --- | | [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/40/Herbie_Hancock-Chameleon_Live.jpg/500px-Herbie_Hancock-Chameleon_Live.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Herbie_Hancock-Chameleon_Live.jpg)
[Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"), one of the pioneers of jazz-funk | | Stylistic origins | - [Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz")
- [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk")
- [soul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_music "Soul music")
- [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues") | | Cultural origins | Late 1960s – 1970s, United States | | Subgenres | | [Free funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_funk "Free funk") | | Other topics | | [Jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion"), [rare groove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rare_groove "Rare groove") | **Jazz-funk** is a subgenre of [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") music characterized by a strong [back beat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music) "Beat (music)"), electrified sounds,[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-1) and [analog synthesizers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analog_synthesizers "Analog synthesizers"). The integration of [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk"), [soul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_music "Soul music"), and [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues") music and styles into jazz resulted in the creation of a genre that ranges from pure [jazz improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_improvisation#Jazz_improvisation "Musical improvisation") to soul, funk or [disco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disco "Disco") with jazz arrangements, jazz [riffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riff "Riff"), jazz solos, and sometimes soul vocals.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-allmusic-2) Similar genres to jazz funk include [acid jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acid_jazz "Acid jazz").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-3) ## History Jazz-funk generally exhibits a simple structure based around one or two riffs, and a harmonic structure that allows musicians to improvise.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-4) Modern jazz funk music was influenced by [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-5) The [Mizell Brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mizell_Brothers "Mizell Brothers") were producers for many jazz and soul artists. Examples of early jazz funk albums include [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")' _[On the Corner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner "On the Corner")_ (1972)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-6) and [Jimmy Smith's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Smith_(musician) "Jimmy Smith (musician)") _[Root Down](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Root_Down_(album) "Root Down (album)")_ (1972).[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-7) [The Last Poets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Poets "The Last Poets"), [Gil Scott-Heron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gil_Scott-Heron "Gil Scott-Heron"), [Lightnin' Rod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lightnin'_Rod "Lightnin' Rod"),[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-8) [T.S. Monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T.S._Monk "T.S. Monk"), [Pleasure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pleasure_(Oregon_band) "Pleasure (Oregon band)"), [Boogaloo Joe Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boogaloo_Joe_Jones "Boogaloo Joe Jones"), [Lenny White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenny_White "Lenny White"), [Don Blackman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Blackman "Don Blackman"), [Monk Higgins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monk_Higgins "Monk Higgins"), [Wilbur Bascomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilbur_Bascomb "Wilbur Bascomb"),[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-9) the Blackbyrds, [Donald Byrd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Byrd "Donald Byrd") and [Les DeMerle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_DeMerle "Les DeMerle")[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-10) and [Michael Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Henderson "Michael Henderson")[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-11) released jazz funk albums. Jazz funk musicians used electric instruments, such as the [Rhodes Piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodes_Piano "Rhodes Piano") or electric guitar, [bass guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_guitar "Bass guitar"), organ, particularly in [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-12) Herbie Hancock played ARP Odyssey synthesizer and [clavinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clavinet "Clavinet") on album _[Head Hunters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_Hunters "Head Hunters")_ (1973).[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-13) The controversy\[ _[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_\] may have helped jazz find a larger audience.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-14) By contrast, pop audiences found it "too jazzy" and, therefore, too complex.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-15) Some mainstream artists in [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") used specialist producers to commercial success. Larry and Fonce Mizell[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-16) produced jazz-funk artists such as [Johnny "Hammond" Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_%22Hammond%22_Smith "Johnny \"Hammond\" Smith"), [Gary Bartz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Bartz "Gary Bartz"), Roger Glenn, the Blackbyrds, and [Donald Byrd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Byrd "Donald Byrd").[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-17) ## UK jazz funk See also: [Brit funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brit_funk "Brit funk") In the UK's nightclubs of the mid-late 1970s, DJs including [Colin Curtis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Curtis_(DJ) "Colin Curtis (DJ)") in [Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester "Manchester"), [Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham "Birmingham")'s Graham Warr and [Shaun Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaun_Williams_(DJ) "Shaun Williams (DJ)"), and [Leeds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leeds "Leeds")-based Ian Dewhirst and Paul Schofield championed the genre, along with [Chris Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Hill_(DJ) "Chris Hill (DJ)") and Bob Jones in the South.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-18) London-based jazz funk pioneers drew a new audience to jazz: notably [pirate radio stations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pirate_radio "Pirate radio") Invicta 92.4 and JFM. In the late 1980s, [rare groove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rare_groove "Rare groove") crate diggers–DJs in England who were interested in looking back into the past and re-discovering old tunes– [Norman Jay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Jay "Norman Jay") and [Gilles Peterson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilles_Peterson "Gilles Peterson") achieved prominence.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-19) While the majority of jazz-funk bands are American, [British jazz-funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brit_funk "Brit funk") artists and bands emerged in the late 1970s and early 1980s.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-20) They were encouraged by club DJs such as [Chris Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Hill_(DJ) "Chris Hill (DJ)") and [Robbie Vincent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robbie_Vincent "Robbie Vincent"), who was then on [BBC Radio London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_London_94.9 "BBC London 94.9"), and [Greg Edwards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greg_Edwards_(DJ) "Greg Edwards (DJ)"), who had a show on London's first commercial radio station, [Capital Radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Radio "Capital Radio"). They launched a jazz festival in 1980, where the jazz-funk band [Light of the World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_of_the_World_(band) "Light of the World (band)") performed.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-21) Jazz-funk was also played on Europe's first soul station, [Radio Invicta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_Invicta_(London_pirate_station) "Radio Invicta (London pirate station)"), and [pirate radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_pirate_radio "UK pirate radio") stations such as [Solar Radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_Radio "Solar Radio"), Horizon, and [Kiss FM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiss_100 "Kiss 100").[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-22) The first of these bands to establish a UK identity was Light of the World, formed by Kenny Wellington,[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-23) [Jean-Paul 'Bluey' Maunick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Paul_'Bluey'_Maunick "Jean-Paul 'Bluey' Maunick") and other musicians. [Acid jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acid_jazz "Acid jazz") is a related jazz genre, but places more emphasis on groove, similar to funk, hip hop, and club dance music.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-24) [Incognito](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incognito_(band) "Incognito (band)"), [The Brand New Heavies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Brand_New_Heavies "The Brand New Heavies"), [Jamiroquai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamiroquai "Jamiroquai"), and the [James Taylor Quartet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Taylor_Quartet "James Taylor Quartet") helped the acid jazz movement surge in popularity. UK group [US3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US3 "US3") signed to [Acid Jazz Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acid_Jazz_Records "Acid Jazz Records"), founded by Peterson and [Eddie Piller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Piller "Eddie Piller"). US3 covered " [Cantaloupe Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantaloupe_Island "Cantaloupe Island")", originally recorded by [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock").[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-25) ## See also - [![icon](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/Saxo_Boca1.JPG/60px-Saxo_Boca1.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Saxo_Boca1.JPG)[Jazz portal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portal:Jazz "Portal:Jazz") - [Chase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chase_(band) "Chase (band)") ## References 01.
