- [space rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_rock "Space rock") | **Progressive rock** (shortened to **prog rock** or simply **prog**) is a broad [genre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_genre "Music genre") of [rock music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music")[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin199871%E2%80%9375-9) that primarily developed in the United States and United Kingdom through the mid- to late 1960s. Initially termed " [progressive pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_pop "Progressive pop")", the style emerged from [psychedelic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelic_music "Psychedelic music") bands who abandoned standard [pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music "Pop music") or [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music") traditions in favour of [instrumental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instrumentation_(music) "Instrumentation (music)") and [compositional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composition_(music) "Composition (music)") techniques more commonly associated with [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), [folk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music "Folk music"), or [classical music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_music "Classical music"), while retaining the instrumentation typical of rock music. Additional elements contributed to its " [progressive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_music "Progressive music")" label: lyrics were more poetic, technology was harnessed for new sounds, music approached the condition of " [art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_music "Art music")", and the studio, rather than the stage, [became the focus of musical activity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_studio_as_an_instrument "Recording studio as an instrument"), which often involved creating music for listening rather than dancing. Progressive rock includes a fusion of styles, approaches and genres, and tends to be diverse and [eclectic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eclecticism_in_music "Eclecticism in music"). Progressive rock is often associated with long solos, extended pieces, fantastic lyrics, grandiose stage sets and costumes, and an obsessive dedication to technical skill and [virtuosity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtuoso "Virtuoso"). While the genre is often cited for its merging of [high culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_culture "High culture") and [low culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_culture "Low culture"), few artists incorporated Western classical themes in their work to a significant degree, with only a minority of groups ( [Emerson, Lake & Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerson,_Lake_&_Palmer "Emerson, Lake & Palmer"), [Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance_(band) "Renaissance (band)"), [Ekseption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ekseption "Ekseption"), etc.) directly emulating or referencing classical music. In the early to mid-1970s, progressive rock groups such as [Pink Floyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pink_Floyd "Pink Floyd") and [Yes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band) "Yes (band)") experienced great worldwide success; in the late 1970s, it declined in popularity, and has never fully recovered.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell20111-10) [Conventional wisdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conventional_wisdom "Conventional wisdom") holds that the rise of [punk rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punk_rock "Punk rock") caused this, but several more factors contributed to the decline.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell20111-10) Music critics, who often labelled the style of progressive rock as "pretentious" and the sounds as "pompous" and "overblown", tended to be hostile towards the genre or to completely ignore it.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTELucky20007-11) After the late 1970s, progressive rock fragmented into numerous forms. Some bands achieved commercial success well into the 1980s (albeit with changed lineups and more compact song structures) or crossed into [symphonic pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphonic_pop "Symphonic pop"), [arena rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arena_rock "Arena rock"), or [new wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_wave_music "New wave music"). Early groups who exhibited progressive features are retroactively described as " [proto-prog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-prog "Proto-prog")". The [Canterbury scene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_scene "Canterbury scene"), originating in the late 1960s, denotes a subset of progressive rock bands who emphasised the use of [wind instruments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind_instrument "Wind instrument"), complex chord changes and long improvisations. [Rock in Opposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_in_Opposition "Rock in Opposition"), from the late 1970s, was more [avant-garde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde "Avant-garde"), and when combined with the Canterbury style, created [avant-prog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-prog "Avant-prog"). In the 1980s, a new subgenre, [neo-prog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-prog "Neo-prog"), enjoyed some commercial success, although it was also accused of being derivative and lacking in innovation. [Post-progressive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-progressive "Post-progressive") draws upon newer developments in popular music and the avant-garde since the mid-1970s. ## Definition and characteristics \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Progressive_rock&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Definition and characteristics")\] Further information: [Progressive music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_music "Progressive music") ### Scope and related terms \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Progressive_rock&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Scope and related terms")\] ![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg/60px-Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail) [The Fourth Colour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Fourth_Colour.mp3 "File:The Fourth Colour.mp3") [Play audio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Fourth_Colour.mp3 "Play audio") Duration: 6 minutes and 13 seconds.6:13 _[The Fourth Colour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fourth_Colour "The Fourth Colour")_, a progressive rock song by [King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Gizzard_and_the_Lizard_Wizard "King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard"). * * * _Problems playing this file? See [media help](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Media "Help:Media")._ See also: [Progressive pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_pop "Progressive pop") and [Art rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_rock "Art rock") The term "progressive rock" is related to and sometimes considered [synonymous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synonym "Synonym") with " [art rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_rock "Art rock")", "classical rock" (not to be confused with [classic rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classic_rock "Classic rock")), and "symphonic rock".[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECovach19975-12) Historically, "art rock" has been used to describe at least two related, but distinct, types of rock music.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBannister200737-13) The first is progressive rock as it is generally understood, while the second usage refers to [experimental rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experimental_rock "Experimental rock") groups who rejected [psychedelia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelia "Psychedelia") and the [hippie counterculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterculture_of_the_1960s "Counterculture of the 1960s") in favour of a [modernist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernist "Modernist"), [avant-garde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde "Avant-garde") approach.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBannister200737-13)[\[nb 1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-15)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-16) Similarities between the two terms are that they both describe a mostly British attempt to elevate rock music to new levels of artistic credibility. However, art rock is more likely to have experimental or avant-garde influences.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-AMProg-17) "Prog" was devised in the 1990s[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTERobinson2017223-18) as a shorthand term, but later became a transferable adjective, also suggesting a wider palette than that drawn on by the most popular 1970s bands.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell20119-19) Progressive rock is varied and is based on fusions of styles, approaches, and genres, tapping into broader cultural resonances that connect to avant-garde art, [classical music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_music "Classical music") and [folk music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music "Folk music"), performance and the moving image.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell201113-20) Although a unidirectional English "progressive" style emerged in the late 1960s, by 1967, progressive rock had come to constitute a diversity of loosely associated style codes.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECotner200090-21) When the "progressive" label arrived, the music was dubbed " [progressive pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_pop "Progressive pop")" before it was called "progressive rock",[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoore200422-22)[\[nb 2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-24) with the term "progressive" referring to the wide range of attempts to break with standard pop music formula.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHaworthSmith1975126-25) A number of additional factors contributed to the acquired "progressive" label: lyrics were more poetic; technology was harnessed for new sounds; music approached the condition of "art"; some harmonic language was imported from jazz and [19th-century classical music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romantic_music "Romantic music"); [the album format overtook singles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album_Era "Album Era"); and the studio, rather than the stage, became the focus of musical activity, which often involved creating music for listening, not dancing.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoore2016201%E2%80%93202-26) > One of the best ways to define progressive rock is that it is a heterogeneous and troublesome genre – a formulation that becomes clear the moment we leave behind characterizations based only on the most visible bands of the early to mid-1970s — [Paul Hegarty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Hegarty_(musician) "Paul Hegarty (musician)") and Martin Halliwell[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell201113-20) Critics of the genre often limit its scope to a stereotype of long solos, overlong albums, fantasy lyrics, grandiose stage sets and costumes, and an obsessive dedication to technical skill.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell20112-27) While progressive rock is often cited for its merging of high culture and low culture, few artists incorporated literal classical themes in their work to any great degree,[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHolm-Hudson201316,_85%E2%80%9387-28) and only a handful of groups purposely emulated or referenced classical music.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell201113-20) Writer Emily Robinson says that the narrowed definition of "progressive rock" was a measure against the term's loose application in the late 1960s, when it was "applied to everyone from [Bob Dylan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Dylan "Bob Dylan") to [the Rolling Stones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rolling_Stones "The Rolling Stones")". Debate over the genre's criterion continued to the 2010s, particularly on [Internet forums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_forum "Internet forum") dedicated to prog.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTERobinson2017223-18) According to musicologists [Paul Hegarty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Hegarty_(musician) "Paul Hegarty (musician)") and Martin Halliwell, [Bill Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Martin_(philosophy) "Bill Martin (philosophy)") and Edward Macan authored major books about progressive rock while "effectively accept\[ing\] the characterization of progressive rock offered by its critics. ... they each do so largely unconsciously."[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell20112-27) Academic John S. Cotner contests Macan's view that progressive rock cannot exist without the continuous and overt assimilation of classical music into rock.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECotner200090-21) Author Kevin Holm-Hudson agrees that "progressive rock is a style far more diverse than what is heard from its mainstream groups and what is implied by unsympathetic critics."[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHolm-Hudson201316-29) ### Relation to art and social theories \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Progressive_rock&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Relation to art and social theories")\] See also: [Formalism (music)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formalism_(music) "Formalism (music)") and [Eclecticism in music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eclecticism_in_music "Eclecticism in music") In early references to the music, "progressive" was partly related to [progressive politics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_politics "Progressive politics"), but those connotations were lost during the 1970s.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTERobinson2017223-18) On "progressive music", Holm-Hudson writes that it "moves continuously between explicit and implicit references to genres and strategies derived not only from European art music, but other cultural domains (such as East Indian, Celtic, folk, and African) and hence involves a continuous aesthetic movement between [formalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formalism_(art) "Formalism (art)") and [eclecticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eclecticism_in_music "Eclecticism in music")".[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHolm-Hudson201385%E2%80%9387-30)[\[nb 3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-32) Cotner also says that progressive rock incorporates both formal and eclectic elements, "It consists of a combination of factors – some of them intramusical ('within'), others extramusical or social ('without')."[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECotner200091-33) One way of conceptualising [rock and roll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_roll "Rock and roll") in relation to "progressive music" is that progressive music pushed the genre into greater complexity while retracing the roots of romantic and classical music.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWillis2014204,_219-34) Sociologist [Paul Willis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Willis "Paul Willis") believes: "We must never be in doubt that 'progressive' music followed rock 'n' roll, and that it could not have been any other way. We can see rock 'n' roll as a deconstruction and 'progressive' music as a reconstruction."[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWillis2014219-35) Author Will Romano states that "rock itself can be interpreted as a progressive idea... Ironically, and quite paradoxically, 'progressive rock', the classic era of the late 1960s through the mid- and late 1970s, introduces not only the explosive and exploratory sounds of technology... but traditional music forms (classical and European folk) and (often) a pastiche compositional style and artificial constructs ( [concept albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concept_album "Concept album")) which suggests [postmodernism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postmodernism "Postmodernism")."[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTERomano201024-36) ### Use of synthesizers \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Progressive_rock&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: Use of synthesizers")\] [Synthesizers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthesizer "Synthesizer") have a long history in the creation of progressive rock, beginning with the perhaps most well known early electronic instrument, the [Theremin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theremin "Theremin"). Synthesizers rose in stature in the 1960s and 1970s as groups like [Emerson, Lake & Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerson,_Lake_&_Palmer "Emerson, Lake & Palmer"), [Genesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genesis_(band) "Genesis (band)") and [Yes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band) "Yes (band)") incorporated synthesizers as part of their music.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-CR-37) ## History \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Progressive_rock&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/Beatles_and_George_Martin_in_studio_1966.JPG/250px-Beatles_and_George_Martin_in_studio_1966.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Beatles_and_George_Martin_in_studio_1966.JPG) [The Beatles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beatles "The Beatles") rehearsing in the studio with producer [George Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Martin "George Martin"), 1966 In 1966, the level of social and artistic correspondence among British and American rock musicians dramatically accelerated for bands like [the Beatles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beatles "The Beatles"), [the Beach Boys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beach_Boys "The Beach Boys") and [the Byrds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Byrds "The Byrds") who fused elements of [cultivated music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultivated_music "Cultivated music") with the [vernacular traditions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernacular_music "Vernacular music") of rock.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHolm-Hudson201385-38) Progressive rock, originating in the later 1960s, was inspired by [progressive pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_pop "Progressive pop") groups from the 1960s: those who combined rock and roll with various other music styles such as Indian [ragas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raga "Raga"), [oriental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_of_Asia "Music of Asia") melodies and [Gregorian chants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregorian_chant "Gregorian chant"), like the Beatles and [the Yardbirds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Yardbirds "The Yardbirds").[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrownNewquist199778-39) The Beatles' [Paul McCartney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_McCartney "Paul McCartney") said in 1967 that the band "got a bit bored with 12 bars all the time, so we tried to get into something else. Then came Dylan, [the Who](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Who "The Who"), and the Beach Boys. ... We're all trying to do vaguely the same kind of thing".[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPhilo2014119-40) The term _progressive_ here refers to an intentional break from the more standard, predictable, and popular conventions of rock music of the time.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] Rock musicians started to take their music more seriously, paralleling earlier movements in jazz (such as how [swing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing_music "Swing music") gave way to [bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop"), a shift appealing to smaller but devoted audiences). In this period, the [popular song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_song "Popular song") began signalling a new possible means of expression that went beyond the three-minute [love song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love_song "Love song"), leading to an intersection between the "underground" and the "establishment" for listening publics.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoore2016201-41)[\[nb 4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-43) Hegarty and Halliwell identify the Beatles, the Beach Boys, [the Doors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doors "The Doors"), [the Pretty Things](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretty_Things "The Pretty Things"), [the Zombies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Zombies "The Zombies"), [the Byrds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Byrds "The Byrds"), [the Grateful Dead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Grateful_Dead "The Grateful Dead") and [Pink Floyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pink_Floyd "Pink Floyd") "not merely as precursors of progressive rock but as essential developments of progressiveness in its early days".[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell201111-44) According to musicologist [Walter Everett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Everett_(musicologist) "Walter Everett (musicologist)"), the Beatles' "experimental timbres, rhythms, tonal structures, and poetic texts" on their albums _[Rubber Soul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubber_Soul "Rubber Soul")_ (1965) and _[Revolver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolver_(Beatles_album) "Revolver (Beatles album)")_ (1966) "encouraged a legion of young bands that were to create progressive rock in the early 1970s".[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEverett199995-45) Dylan's poetry, [the Mothers of Invention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mothers_of_Invention "The Mothers of Invention")'s album _[Freak Out!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freak_Out! "Freak Out!")_ (1966) and the Beatles' _[Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sgt._Pepper's_Lonely_Hearts_Club_Band "Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band")_ (1967) were all important in progressive rock's development.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-AMProg-17) The productions of [Phil Spector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Spector "Phil Spector") were key influences,[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin199847-46) as they introduced the possibility of using the recording studio to create music that otherwise could never be achieved.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTETamm199529-47) Other influences include the Beach Boys' _[Pet Sounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pet_Sounds "Pet Sounds")_ (1966), which [Brian Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Wilson "Brian Wilson") intended as an answer to _Rubber Soul_[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-48) and which in turn influenced the Beatles when they made _Sgt. Pepper_.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin199853-49)[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECotner200130-50) Dylan introduced a literary element to rock through his fascination with the [Surrealists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrealism "Surrealism") and the [French Symbolists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symbolism_(movement) "Symbolism (movement)"), and his immersion in the New York City art scene of the early 1960s.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurtis1987156-7-51) The trend of bands with names drawn from literature, such as [the Doors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doors "The Doors"), [Steppenwolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band) "Steppenwolf (band)") and [the Ides of March](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ides_of_March_(band) "The Ides of March (band)"), were a further sign of rock music aligning itself with high culture.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurtis1987179-52) Dylan also led the way in blending rock with folk music styles. This was followed by folk rock groups such as the Byrds, who based their initial sound on that of the Beatles.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-53) In turn, the Byrds' vocal harmonies inspired those of [Yes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band) "Yes (band)"),[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin19964-54) and [British folk rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_folk_rock "British folk rock") bands like [Fairport Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairport_Convention "Fairport Convention"), who emphasised instrumental virtuosity.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell201154%E2%80%9355-55) Some of these artists, such as [the Incredible String Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Incredible_String_Band "The Incredible String Band") and [Shirley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirley_Collins "Shirley Collins") and [Dolly Collins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolly_Collins "Dolly Collins"), would prove influential through their use of instruments borrowed from world music and [early music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_music "Early music").[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTESweers200472,204-56) #### _Pet Sounds_ and _Sgt. Pepper_ \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Progressive_rock&action=edit§ion=8 "Edit section: Pet Sounds and Sgt. Pepper")\] Main articles: [Pet Sounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pet_Sounds "Pet Sounds") and [Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sgt._Pepper's_Lonely_Hearts_Club_Band "Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band") > Many groups and musicians played important roles in this development process, but none more than [the Beach Boys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beach_Boys "The Beach Boys") and [the Beatles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beatles "The Beatles")... \[They\] brought expansions in [harmony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmony "Harmony"), [instrumentation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrangement "Arrangement") (and therefore [timbre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbre "Timbre")), [duration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duration_(music) "Duration (music)"), [rhythm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm "Rhythm"), and the use of [recording technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_multitrack_recording "History of multitrack recording"). Of these elements, the first and last were the most important in clearing a pathway toward the development of progressive rock. —Bill Martin[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin199839-57) _Pet Sounds_ and _Sgt. Pepper_, with their lyrical unity, extended structure, complexity, eclecticism, experimentalism, and influences derived from classical music forms, are largely viewed as beginnings in the progressive rock genre[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan199715,20-58)[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin199839%E2%80%9340-59) and as turning points wherein rock, which previously had been considered dance music, became music that was made for listening to.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECovach19973-60)[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin199839-57) Between _Pet Sounds_ and _Sgt. Pepper_, the Beach Boys released the single " [Good Vibrations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_Vibrations "Good Vibrations")" (1966), dubbed a " [pocket symphony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pocket_symphony "Pocket symphony")" by [Derek Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Taylor "Derek Taylor"), the band's publicist. The song contained an eclectic array of exotic instruments and several disjunctive key and modal shifts.[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBooneCovach199741%E2%80%9346-61) Scott Interrante of _[Popmatters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popmatters "Popmatters")_ wrote that its influence on progressive rock and the psychedelic movement "can't be overstated".[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-62) Martin likened the song to the Beatles' " [A Day in the Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Day_in_the_Life "A Day in the Life")" from _Sgt. Pepper_, in that they showcase "the same reasons why much progressive rock is difficult to dance to".[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin199840-63) Although _Sgt. Pepper_ was preceded by several albums that had begun to bridge the line between "disposable" pop and "serious" rock, it successfully gave an established "commercial" voice to an alternative youth culture[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHolm-Hudson200810-64) and marked the point at which the [LP record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LP_record "LP record") emerged as a creative format whose importance was equal to or greater than that of the single.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-pirenne1-65)[\[nb 5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-67) [Bill Bruford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Bruford "Bill Bruford"), a veteran of several progressive rock bands, said that _Sgt. Pepper_ transformed both musicians' ideas of what was possible and audiences' ideas of what was acceptable in music.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeigel2012b-68) He believed that: "Without the Beatles, or someone else who had done what the Beatles did, it is fair to assume that there would have been no progressive rock."[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBruford2012159-69) In the aftermath of _Sgt. Pepper_, magazines such as [Melody Maker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melody_Maker "Melody Maker") drew a sharp line between "pop" and "rock". Americans increasingly used the adjective "progressive" for groups like [Jethro Tull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jethro_Tull_(band) "Jethro Tull (band)"), [Family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_(British_band) "Family (British band)"), [East of Eden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_of_Eden_(British_band) "East of Eden (British band)"), [Van der Graaf Generator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_der_Graaf_Generator "Van der Graaf Generator") and [King Crimson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Crimson "King Crimson").[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZoppo2014[[Category:Wikipedia_articles_needing_page_number_citations_from_December_2016]]%3Csup_class=%22noprint_Inline-Template_%22_style=%22white-space:nowrap;%22%3E[%3Ci%3E[[Wikipedia:Citing_sources|%3Cspan_title=%22This_citation_requires_a_reference_to_the_specific_page_or_range_of_pages_in_which_the_material_appears. Pink Floyd and [Soft Machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine "Soft Machine") functioned as [house bands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_band "House band") at all-night events at locations such as [Middle Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Earth_(club) "Middle Earth (club)") and the [UFO Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UFO_Club "UFO Club"), where they experimented with sound textures and long-form songs.[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTESweers2004114%E2%80%9315-71)[\[nb 6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-74) Many psychedelic, folk rock and early progressive bands were aided by exposure from [BBC Radio 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Radio_1 "BBC Radio 1") DJ [John Peel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Peel "John Peel").[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTESweers2004119-75) [Jimi Hendrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimi_Hendrix "Jimi Hendrix"), who rose to prominence in the London scene and recorded with a band of English musicians, initiated the trend towards guitar virtuosity and eccentricity in rock music.[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin1998164%E2%80%9365-76) The Scottish band 1-2-3, later renamed [Clouds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clouds_(60s_rock_band) "Clouds (60s rock band)"), were formed in 1966 and began performing at London clubs a year later. According to _Mojo_'s George Knemeyer: "some claim \[that they\] had a vital influence on prog-rockers such as Yes, The Nice and Family."[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHogg1994-77) Symphonic rock artists in the late 1960s had some chart success, including the singles " [Nights in White Satin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nights_in_White_Satin "Nights in White Satin")" (the Moody Blues, 1967) and " [A Whiter Shade of Pale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Whiter_Shade_of_Pale "A Whiter Shade of Pale")" (Procol Harum, 1967).[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FowlesWade2012-78) The Moody Blues established the popularity of symphonic rock when they recorded _Days of Future Passed_ together with the [London Festival Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Festival_Orchestra "London Festival Orchestra").[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan199721%E2%80%9322-79) Classical influences sometimes took the form of pieces adapted from or inspired by classical works, such as [Jeff Beck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Beck "Jeff Beck")'s _[Beck's Bolero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beck's_Bolero "Beck's Bolero")_, [Love Sculpture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love_Sculpture "Love Sculpture")'s[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-80) [_Farandole (Arlésienne Suite No 2. Movement 4)_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L'Arl%C3%A9sienne_(Bizet) "L'Arlésienne (Bizet)") and parts of the Nice's _[Ars Longa Vita Brevis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ars_Longa_Vita_Brevis_(album) "Ars Longa Vita Brevis (album)")_. The latter, along with such tracks as " [Rondo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Rondo_%C3%A0_la_Turk "Blue Rondo à la Turk")" and " [America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/America_(West_Side_Story_song) "America (West Side Story song)")", reflect a greater interest in music that is entirely instrumental. _Sgt. Pepper's_ and _Days_ both represent a growing tendency towards [song cycles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Song_cycle "Song cycle") and suites made up of multiple [movements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movement_(music) "Movement (music)").[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan199721%E2%80%9322-79) [Focus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Focus_(band) "Focus (band)") incorporated and articulated jazz-style chords, and irregular off-beat drumming into their later rock-based riffs, and several bands that included jazz-style [horn sections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horn_section "Horn section") appeared, including [Blood, Sweat & Tears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood,_Sweat_&_Tears "Blood, Sweat & Tears") and [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_(band) "Chicago (band)"). Of these, Martin highlights Chicago in particular for their experimentation with suites and extended compositions, such as the " [Ballet for a Girl in Buchannon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballet_for_a_Girl_in_Buchannon "Ballet for a Girl in Buchannon")" on _[Chicago II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_(album) "Chicago (album)")_.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin1998163%E2%80%93164-81) Jazz influences appeared in the music of British bands such as [Traffic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traffic_(band) "Traffic (band)"), [Colosseum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colosseum_(band) "Colosseum (band)") and [If](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_(band) "If (band)"), together with [Canterbury scene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_scene "Canterbury scene") bands such as [Soft Machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine "Soft Machine") and [Caravan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caravan_(band) "Caravan (band)"). Canterbury scene bands emphasised the use of wind instruments, complex chord changes and long improvisations.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan199720-82) Martin writes that in 1968, "full-blown progressive rock" was not yet in existence; however, albums were released by three bands who would later come to the forefront of the music: Jethro Tull, Caravan and Soft Machine.[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin1998168-83) ![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg/60px-Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail) ["The Court of the Crimson King" (1969)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:King_Crimson_-_The_Court_of_the_Crimson_King.ogg "File:King Crimson - The Court of the Crimson King.ogg") [Play audio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:King_Crimson_-_The_Court_of_the_Crimson_King.ogg "Play audio") Duration: 38 seconds.0:38 Macan writes that King Crimson's album "displays every element of the mature progressive rock genre... \[and\] exerted a powerful extramusical influence on later progressive rock bands".[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan199723-84) * * * _Problems playing this file? See [media help](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Media "Help:Media")._ The term "progressive rock", which appeared in the liner notes of Caravan's 1968 [self-titled debut LP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caravan_(Caravan_album) "Caravan (Caravan album)"), came to be applied to bands that used classical music techniques to expand the styles and concepts available to rock music.[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan199726-85)[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBowman2001184-86) The Nice, the Moody Blues, Procol Harum and Pink Floyd all contained elements of what is now called progressive rock, but none represented as complete an example of the genre as several bands that formed soon after.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan199722%E2%80%9323-87) Almost all of the genre's major bands, including Jethro Tull, King Crimson, Yes, [Genesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genesis_(band) "Genesis (band)"), [Van der Graaf Generator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_der_Graaf_Generator "Van der Graaf Generator"), [ELP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerson,_Lake_&_Palmer "Emerson, Lake & Palmer"), [Gentle Giant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentle_Giant "Gentle Giant"), [Barclay James Harvest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barclay_James_Harvest "Barclay James Harvest") and [Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance_(band) "Renaissance (band)"), released their debut albums during the years 1968–1970. Most of these were folk-rock albums that gave little indication of what the bands' mature sound would become, but King Crimson's _[In the Court of the Crimson King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_the_Court_of_the_Crimson_King "In the Court of the Crimson King")_ (1969) and Yes' [self-titled debut album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(Yes_album) "Yes (Yes album)") (1969) were early, fully formed examples of the genre.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan199723-84)[\[nb 7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-88) ### 1970s–1980s \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Progressive_rock&action=edit§ion=10 "Edit section: 1970s–1980s")\] #### Peak years (1971–1976) \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Progressive_rock&action=edit§ion=11 "Edit section: Peak years (1971–1976)")\] See also: [Krautrock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krautrock "Krautrock") [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8f/DarkSideOfTheMoon1973.jpg/250px-DarkSideOfTheMoon1973.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:DarkSideOfTheMoon1973.jpg) [Pink Floyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pink_Floyd "Pink Floyd") performing _[The Dark Side of the Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dark_Side_of_the_Moon "The Dark Side of the Moon")_ (1973), the best-selling album of the entire progressive rock period[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPriore200579-89) Most of the genre's major bands released their most critically acclaimed albums during the years 1971–1976.[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan199727-90) The genre experienced a high degree of commercial success during the early 1970s. Between them, the bands Jethro Tull, [ELP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerson,_Lake_&_Palmer "Emerson, Lake & Palmer"), [the Moody Blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Moody_Blues "The Moody Blues"), Yes, and Pink Floyd had five albums that reached number one in the US charts, and sixteen that reached the top ten.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan199728-91)[\[nb 8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-96) [Mike Oldfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Oldfield "Mike Oldfield")'s _[Tubular Bells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tubular_Bells "Tubular Bells")_ (1973), an excerpt of which was used as the theme for the film _[The Exorcist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Exorcist "The Exorcist")_, sold 16 million copies.[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-97) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b5/Emerson%2C_Lake_%26_Palmer_01.jpg/250px-Emerson%2C_Lake_%26_Palmer_01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Emerson,_Lake_&_Palmer_01.jpg) [Emerson, Lake & Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerson,_Lake_&_Palmer "Emerson, Lake & Palmer") were one of the most commercially successful progressive rock bands of the 1970s. Many of these groups were very influential even among bands that had little enthusiasm for the symphonic variety of progressive rock.[\[113\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin200282-124) ##### Avant-prog \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Progressive_rock&action=edit§ion=12 "Edit section: Avant-prog")\] See also: [Zeuhl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeuhl "Zeuhl") **Avant-prog** (originally known as **avant-garde progressive rock** or **experimental prog**) is a subgenre of progressive rock that emerged in the 1970s. The style drew influences from [avant-garde music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_music "Avant-garde music"), [modern classical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_classical "Modern classical"), [avant-garde jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz"), [experimental rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experimental_rock "Experimental rock"), [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") and [psychedelic rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelic_rock "Psychedelic rock"). Times")_ calls Wonder's mid-1970s albums "prog soul of the highest order, pushing the form yet always heartfelt, ambitious and listenable".[\[118\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-129) #### Decline and fragmentation \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Progressive_rock&action=edit§ion=14 "Edit section: Decline and fragmentation")\] See also: [Punk rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punk_rock "Punk rock") and [Symphonic pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphonic_pop "Symphonic pop") Political and social trends of the late 1970s shifted away from the early 1970s [hippie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippie "Hippie") attitudes that had led to the genre's development and popularity. The rise in [punk cynicism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punk_ideologies "Punk ideologies") made the utopian ideals expressed in progressive rock lyrics unfashionable.[\[119\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin200278-130) Virtuosity was rejected, as the expense of purchasing quality instruments and the time investment of learning to play them were seen as barriers to rock's energy and immediacy.[\[120\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin2002115-131) There were also changes in the music industry, as record companies disappeared and merged into large [media conglomerates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Media_conglomerates "Media conglomerates"). Promoting and developing experimental music was not part of the [marketing strategy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marketing_strategy "Marketing strategy") for these large corporations, who focused their attention on identifying and targeting profitable [market niches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niche_market "Niche market").[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin2002108%E2%80%93110-132) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/Robert_Fripp_2.jpg/250px-Robert_Fripp_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Robert_Fripp_2.jpg) King Crimson's [Robert Fripp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Fripp "Robert Fripp") believed that the prog movement had gone "tragically off course".[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011177-133) Four of progressive rock's most successful bands – King Crimson, Yes, ELP and Genesis – went on hiatus or experienced major personnel changes during the mid-1970s.[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011177-133) Macan notes the September 1974 breakup of King Crimson as particularly significant, noting that Fripp (much later) referred to 1974 as the point when "all English bands in the genre should have ceased to exist".[\[123\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997179-134) More of the major bands, including Van der Graaf Generator, Gentle Giant and [U.K.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.K._(band) "U.K. (band)"), dissolved between 1978 and 1980.[\[124\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997187%E2%80%93188-135) Many bands had by the mid-1970s reached the limit of how far they could experiment in a rock context, and fans had wearied of the extended, epic compositions. The sounds of the [Hammond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hammond_organ "Hammond organ"), [Minimoog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimoog "Minimoog") and [Mellotron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mellotron "Mellotron") had been thoroughly explored, and their use became clichéd. Those bands who continued to record often simplified their sound, and the genre fragmented from the late 1970s onwards.[\[125\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997181%E2%80%93183-136) In [Robert Fripp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Fripp "Robert Fripp")'s opinion, once "progressive rock" ceased to cover new ground – becoming a set of conventions to be repeated and imitated – the genre's premise had ceased to be "progressive".[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997206-137) The era of record labels investing in their artists, giving them freedom to experiment and limited control over their content and marketing ended with the late 1970s.[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoore2016202-138) Corporate [artists and repertoire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artists_and_repertoire "Artists and repertoire") staff exerted an increasing amount of control over the creative process that had previously belonged to the artists,[\[128\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin1996188-139) and established acts were pressured to create music with simpler harmony and song structures and fewer changes in meter. A number of symphonic pop bands, such as [Supertramp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supertramp "Supertramp"), [10cc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10cc "10cc"), [the Alan Parsons Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Alan_Parsons_Project "The Alan Parsons Project") and the [Electric Light Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_Light_Orchestra "Electric Light Orchestra"), brought the orchestral-style arrangements into a context that emphasised pop singles while allowing for occasional instances of exploration. Jethro Tull, Gentle Giant and Pink Floyd opted for a harder sound in the style of [arena rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arena_rock "Arena rock").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997187-5) Few new progressive rock bands formed during this era, and those who did found that record labels were not interested in signing them.[\[129\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-derogatis98-140) The short-lived supergroup U.K. was a notable exception since its members had established reputations; they produced two albums that were stylistically similar to previous artists and did little to advance the genre.[\[130\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997183-141) Part of the genre's legacy in this period was its influence on other styles, as several European guitarists brought a progressive rock approach to [heavy metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_metal_music "Heavy metal music") and laid the groundwork for [progressive metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_metal "Progressive metal"). [Michael Schenker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Schenker "Michael Schenker"), of [UFO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UFO_(band) "UFO (band)"); and [Uli Jon Roth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uli_Jon_Roth "Uli Jon Roth"), who replaced Schenker in [Scorpions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scorpions_(band) "Scorpions (band)"), expanded the modal vocabulary available to guitarists.[\[131\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlackett2001-142)\[ _[further explanation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_\] Roth studied classical music with the intent of using the guitar in the way that classical composers used the violin.[\[132\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGress2007-143) Finally, the Dutch-born and classically trained [Alex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Van_Halen "Alex Van Halen") and [Eddie Van Halen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Van_Halen "Eddie Van Halen") formed [Van Halen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Halen "Van Halen"), featuring ground-breaking whammy-bar, tapping and cross-picking guitar performances[\[133\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGress1993-144) that influenced " [shred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shred_guitar "Shred guitar")" music in the 1980s.[\[134\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-145) ##### Commercialisation \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Progressive_rock&action=edit§ion=15 "Edit section: Commercialisation")\] > By the early 1980s, progressive rock was thought to be all but dead as a style, an idea reinforced by the fact that some of the principal progressive groups had developed a more commercial sound. ... What went out of the music of these now ex-progressive groups ... was any significant evocation of art music. —John Covach[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECovach19975-12) Some established artists moved towards music that was simpler and more commercially viable.[\[135\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011182-146)\[ _[verification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_\][\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECovach19975-12) Arena rock bands like [Journey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journey_(band) "Journey (band)"), [Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_(band) "Kansas (band)"), [Styx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Styx_(band) "Styx (band)"), [GTR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GTR_(band) "GTR (band)"), [ELO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_Light_Orchestra "Electric Light Orchestra") and [Foreigner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreigner_(band) "Foreigner (band)") either had begun as progressive rock bands or included members with strong ties to the genre. These groups retained some of the song complexity and orchestral-style arrangements, but they moved away from lyrical mysticism in favour of more conventional themes such as relationships.[\[136\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011181%E2%80%93182-147) These radio-friendly groups have been called "prog lite".[\[137\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECateforis2011154%E2%80%93159-148) Genesis transformed into a successful pop act, the prog supergroup [Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia_(band) "Asia (band)") (consisting of members of Yes, King Crimson, and ELP) scored a number-one album in 1982,[\[138\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-149) and a re-formed Yes released the relatively mainstream _[90125](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/90125_(album) "90125 (album)")_ (1983), which yielded their only US number-one single, " [Owner of a Lonely Heart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owner_of_a_Lonely_Heart "Owner of a Lonely Heart")". One band who remained successful into the 1980s while maintaining a progressive approach was Pink Floyd, who released _[The Wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wall "The Wall")_ late in 1979. The album, which brought punk anger into progressive rock,[\[139\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011174-150) was a huge success and was later filmed as _[Pink Floyd – The Wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pink_Floyd_%E2%80%93_The_Wall "Pink Floyd – The Wall")_.[\[nb 12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-158) #### Post-punk and post-progressive \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Progressive_rock&action=edit§ion=16 "Edit section: Post-punk and post-progressive")\] Main articles: [Post-punk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-punk "Post-punk") and [Post-progressive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-progressive "Post-progressive") See also: [New wave music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_wave_music "New wave music") Punk and progressive rock were not necessarily as opposed as is commonly believed. Both genres reject commercialism, and punk bands did see a need for musical advancement.[\[147\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin1996189%E2%80%93190-159)[\[nb 13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-164) Author Doyle Green noted that [post-punk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-punk "Post-punk") emerged as "a kind of 'progressive punk'".[\[152\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGreene2014173-165) Post-punk artists rejected the high cultural references of 1960s rock artists like the Beatles and Bob Dylan as well as paradigms that defined rock as "progressive", "art", or "studio perfectionism".[\[153\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBannister200736%E2%80%9337-166) In contrast to punk rock, it balances punk's energy and skepticism with art school consciousness, [Dadaist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dadaist "Dadaist") experimentalism, and atmospheric, ambient soundscapes. [World music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_music "World music"), especially African and Asian traditions, was also a major influence.[\[154\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTERojek201128-167) Progressive rock's impact was felt in the work of some post-punk artists, although they tended not to emulate classical rock or Canterbury groups but rather [Roxy Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roxy_Music "Roxy Music"), King Crimson, and German [krautrock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krautrock "Krautrock") bands, particularly [Can](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Can_(band) "Can (band)"), [Neu!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neu! "Neu!"), and [Faust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faust_(band) "Faust (band)") as key inspirations.[\[155\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-168)[\[156\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-ClassicRock-169)[\[nb 14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-171) [Punishment of Luxury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punishment_of_Luxury "Punishment of Luxury")'s music borrowed from both progressive and punk rock,[\[158\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-172) whilst [Alternative TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_TV "Alternative TV"), who were fronted by the founder of the influential punk fanzine _[Sniffin' Glue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sniffin'_Glue "Sniffin' Glue")_ [Mark Perry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Perry_(musician) "Mark Perry (musician)"), toured and released a split live album with [Gong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gong_(band) "Gong (band)") offshoot [Here & Now](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Here_&_Now_(band) "Here & Now (band)").[\[159\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-173) The term " [post-progressive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-progressive "Post-progressive")" identifies progressive rock that returns to its original principles while dissociating from 1970s progressive rock styles,[\[160\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011225-174) and may be located after 1978.[\[161\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin199820-175) Martin credits [Roxy Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roxy_Music "Roxy Music")'s [Brian Eno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Eno "Brian Eno") as the sub-genre's most important catalyst, explaining that his 1973–77 output merged aspects of progressive rock with a prescient notion of new wave and punk.[\[162\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin1998251-176) New wave, which surfaced around 1978–79 with some of the same attitudes and aesthetic as punk, was characterised by Martin as "progressive" multiplied by "punk".[\[163\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin200299-177) Bands in the genre tended to be less hostile towards progressive rock than the punks, and there were crossovers, such as Fripp and Eno's involvement with [Talking Heads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talking_Heads "Talking Heads"), and Yes' replacement of Rick Wakeman and Jon Anderson with the pop duo [the Buggles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Buggles "The Buggles").[\[163\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin200299-177) When King Crimson reformed in 1981, they released an album, _[Discipline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discipline_(King_Crimson_album) "Discipline (King Crimson album)")_, which Macan says "inaugurated" the new post-progressive style.[\[164\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997205-178) The new King Crimson line-up featured guitarist and vocalist [Adrian Belew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrian_Belew "Adrian Belew"), who also collaborated with Talking Heads, playing live with the band and featuring on their 1980 album _[Remain in Light](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remain_in_Light "Remain in Light")_.[\[165\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-179)[\[166\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-180) According to Martin, Talking Heads also created rock").[\[176\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTERomano2010[httpsbooksgooglecombooksid2lVMAgAAQBAJpgPT390_%22Marillion%22]-190) The genre's most successful band, See [media help](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Media "Help:Media")._ Progressive rock and [heavy metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_metal_music "Heavy metal music") have similar timelines. Both emerged from late-1960s psychedelia to achieve great early-1970s success despite a lack of radio airplay and support from critics, then faded in the mid-to-late 1970s and experienced revivals in the early 1980s. Each genre experienced a fragmentation of styles at this time, and many metal bands from the [new wave of British heavy metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_wave_of_British_heavy_metal "New wave of British heavy metal") – most notably [Iron Maiden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Maiden "Iron Maiden") – onwards displayed progressive rock influences.[\[187\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011259%E2%80%93260-201) [Progressive metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_metal "Progressive metal") reached a point of maturity with [Queensrÿche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queensr%C3%BFche "Queensrÿche")'s 1988 concept album _[Operation: Mindcrime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation:_Mindcrime "Operation: Mindcrime"),_ [Voivod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voivod_(band) "Voivod (band)")'s 1989 _[Nothingface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nothingface_(Voivod_album) "Nothingface (Voivod album)")_, which featured abstract lyrics and a King Crimson-like texture, and [Dream Theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dream_Theater "Dream Theater")'s 1992 _[Images and Words](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Images_and_Words "Images and Words")_.[\[188\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011260%E2%80%93262-202) Progressive rock elements appear in other metal subgenres. [Death metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_metal "Death metal")'s [guttural vocals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_growl "Death growl") are sometimes used by bands who can be classified as progressive, such as [Mastodon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mastodon_(band) "Mastodon (band)"), [Mudvayne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mudvayne "Mudvayne") and [Opeth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opeth "Opeth").[\[189\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011264,_266-203) [Symphonic metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphonic_metal "Symphonic metal") is an extension of the tendency towards orchestral passages in early progressive rock.[\[190\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011266%E2%80%93267-204) Progressive rock has also served as a key inspiration for genres such as [post-rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-rock "Post-rock"),[\[191\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-allen-205) [post-metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-metal "Post-metal") and [avant-garde metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_metal "Avant-garde metal"),[\[192\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-caramanica-206) [math rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Math_rock "Math rock"),[\[193\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-tudor-207) [power metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_metal "Power metal") and [neo-classical metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-classical_metal "Neo-classical metal").[\[194\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-miers-208) #### New prog \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Progressive_rock&action=edit§ion=21 "Edit section: New prog")\] Not to be confused with [Neo-prog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-prog "Neo-prog"). **New prog** describes the wave of progressive rock bands in the 2000s who revived the genre. According to _[Entertainment Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment_Weekly "Entertainment Weekly")_'s Evan Serpick, "success stories like [System of a Down](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/System_of_a_Down "System of a Down") and up-and-comers like the [Dillinger Escape Plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dillinger_Escape_Plan "Dillinger Escape Plan"), [Lightning Bolt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lightning_Bolt_(band) "Lightning Bolt (band)"), [Coheed and Cambria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coheed_and_Cambria "Coheed and Cambria"), and [the Mars Volta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mars_Volta "The Mars Volta") create incredibly complex and inventive music that sounds like a heavier, more aggressive version of '70s behemoths such as Led Zeppelin and King Crimson."[\[195\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-209) #### Wider influence \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Progressive_rock&action=edit§ion=22 "Edit section: Wider influence")\] The turn of the millennium also saw the rise of a number of bands to mainstream success who, whilst not explicitly identifying as progressive rock, have incorporated influences from it and embraced an experimentalism and complexity in their music which has been regarded as being in keeping with the genre's traditions. [Radiohead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiohead "Radiohead") have been embraced by some progressive rock fans and musicians, with Rush's [Geddy Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geddy_Lee "Geddy Lee") declaring _[OK Computer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OK_Computer "OK Computer")_ as one of his favourite albums and arguing that they carried on the torch from bands like Yes and Genesis. Radiohead's drummer [Philip Selway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Selway "Philip Selway") has cited King Crimson and Pink Floyd as influences, and the band's eclectic and experimental style has drawn on a range of sources, including jazz, electronic music, art rock, krautrock, post-rock and the work of [Captain Beefheart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_Beefheart "Captain Beefheart").[\[196\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-210) [Tool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tool_(band) "Tool (band)") and King Crimson have acknowledged each other as
