During this time, Portnoy released 40 albums, 24 of them with Morse, while Morse released an additional 5 albums of his own.[\[205\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-219) During the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic") in 2020, the Prog Report launched a virtual concert, _Prog From Home_, bringing together many of the biggest artists active in the genre.[\[206\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-220) On April 3, 2022, "The Alien" won a [Grammy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Awards "Grammy Awards") for [Best Metal Performance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Metal_Performance "Grammy Award for Best Metal Performance"), giving [Dream Theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dream_Theater "Dream Theater") their first Grammy.[\[207\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-221) ## Festivals \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Progressive_rock&action=edit§ion=24 "Edit section: Festivals")\] Many prominent progressive rock bands got their initial exposure at large [rock festivals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_festival "Rock festival") that were held in Britain during the late 1960s and early 1970s. King Crimson made their first major appearance at the [1969 Hyde Park free concert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stones_in_the_Park "Stones in the Park"), before a crowd estimated to be as large as 650,000, in support of [the Rolling Stones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rolling_Stones "The Rolling Stones").[\[208\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFripp1975-222) Emerson, Lake & Palmer debuted at the [1970 Isle of Wight Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isle_of_Wight_Festival_1970 "Isle of Wight Festival 1970"), at which [Supertramp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supertramp "Supertramp"), [Family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_(British_band) "Family (British band)") and Jethro Tull also appeared.[\[209\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell201150%E2%80%9351-223) Jethro Tull were also present at the 1969 [Newport Jazz Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport_Jazz_Festival "Newport Jazz Festival"), the first year in which that festival invited rock bands to perform. [Hawkwind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawkwind "Hawkwind") appeared at many British festivals throughout the 1970s, although they sometimes showed up uninvited, set up a stage on the periphery of the event, and played for free.[\[210\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell201150-224) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/Supertramp0062.jpg/250px-Supertramp0062.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Supertramp0062.jpg) Supertramp performing in 1979[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/da/King_Crimson_-_Dour_Festival_2003_%2801%29.jpg/250px-King_Crimson_-_Dour_Festival_2003_%2801%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:King_Crimson_-_Dour_Festival_2003_(01).jpg) [King Crimson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Crimson "King Crimson") performing at the Dour Festival, 2003 Renewed interest in the genre in the 1990s led to the development of progressive rock festivals.[\[182\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGill1995-196) ProgFest, organised by Greg Walker and David Overstreet in 1993, was first held in [UCLA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UCLA "UCLA")'s Royce Hall,[\[211\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECovach2000-225) and featured Sweden's Änglagård, the UK's IQ, Quill and Citadel. CalProg was held annually in Whittier, California during the early 2000s.[\[212\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-226) The North East Art Rock Festival, or [NEARfest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NEARfest "NEARfest"),[\[184\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKarnick2003-198) held its first event in 1999 in [Bethlehem, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethlehem,_Pennsylvania "Bethlehem, Pennsylvania") and held annual sold-out concerts until 2012's NEARfest Apocalypse, which featured headliners [U.K.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.K._(band) "U.K. (band)") and Renaissance.[\[213\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeigel2012e-227) Other festivals include the annual ProgDay (the longest-running and only outdoor progressive music festival) in [Chapel Hill, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_Hill,_North_Carolina "Chapel Hill, North Carolina"); the annual Rites of Spring Festival (RoSfest) in [Sarasota, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarasota,_Florida "Sarasota, Florida"); [The Rogue Independent Music Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rogue_Independent_Music_Festival "The Rogue Independent Music Festival") in Atlanta, Georgia; [Baja Prog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baja_Prog "Baja Prog") in [Mexicali, Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexicali "Mexicali"); [ProgPower USA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ProgPower_USA "ProgPower USA") in Atlanta, Georgia; [ProgPower Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ProgPower_Europe "ProgPower Europe") in [Baarlo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baarlo "Baarlo"), Netherlands; and ProgStock in Rahway, NJ, which held its first event in 2017.[\[214\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-228) Another popular prog festival is Cruise to the Edge; 2026's line-up included [Marillion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marillion "Marillion"), [Steven Hackett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Hackett "Steve Hackett"), and [Big Big Train](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Big_Train "Big Big Train").[\[215\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-229) ## Reception \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Progressive_rock&action=edit§ion=25 "Edit section: Reception")\] The genre has received both critical acclaim and criticism throughout the years. Progressive rock has been described as parallel to the classical music of [Igor Stravinsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Igor_Stravinsky "Igor Stravinsky") and [Béla Bartók](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9la_Bart%C3%B3k "Béla Bartók").[\[211\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECovach2000-225) This desire to expand the boundaries of rock, combined with some musicians' dismissiveness toward mainstream rock and pop, dismayed critics and led to accusations of elitism. Its intellectual, fantastic and apolitical lyrics, and shunning of rock's blues roots, were abandonments of the very things that many critics valued in rock music.[\[216\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997168%E2%80%9373-230) Progressive rock also represented the maturation of rock as a genre, but there was an opinion among critics that rock was and should remain fundamentally tied to adolescence, so rock and maturity were mutually exclusive.[\[217\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin2002107-231) Criticisms over the complexity of their music provoked some bands to create music that was even more complex.[\[nb 15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-235) BBC radio DJ [John Peel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Peel "John Peel"), who was one of the first people to play progressive rock on British radio, later said "the one distinguishing feature about early-70s progressive rock was that it didn't progress".[\[221\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-236) Most of the musicians involved were male, as was the case for most rock of the time,[\[222\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011204-237) although [Annie Haslam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annie_Haslam "Annie Haslam") of [Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance_(band) "Renaissance (band)") was a notable exception. Female singers were better represented in [progressive folk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_folk "Progressive folk") bands,[\[223\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997135-238) who displayed a broader range of vocal styles than the progressive rock bands[\[224\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTESweers2004204-239) with whom they frequently toured and shared band members.[\[225\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTESweers2004131-240) British and European audiences typically followed concert hall behaviour protocols associated with classical music performances and were more reserved in their behaviour than audiences for other forms of rock. This confused musicians during US tours, as they found American audiences less attentive and more prone to outbursts during quiet passages.[\[226\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997263-241) These aspirations towards [high culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_culture "High culture") reflect progressive rock's origins as a music created largely by [upper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_class "Upper class")\- and [middle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_class "Middle class")-class, [white-collar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White-collar_workers "White-collar workers"), college-educated males from [Southern England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_England "Southern England"). The music never reflected the concerns of or was embraced by working-class listeners,[\[227\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997144%E2%80%9348-242) except in the US, where listeners appreciated the musicians' virtuosity.[\[228\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997156-243) Progressive rock's exotic, literary topics were considered particularly irrelevant to British youth during the late 1970s, when the nation suffered from a poor economy and frequent strikes and shortages.[\[229\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHegartyHalliwell2011163%E2%80%93164-244) Even King Crimson leader Robert Fripp dismissed progressive rock lyrics as "the philosophical meanderings of some English half-wit who is circumnavigating some inessential point of experience in his life".[\[230\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTETamm1990-245) Bands whose darker lyrics avoided utopianism, such as King Crimson, Pink Floyd and Van der Graaf Generator, experienced less critical disfavour.[\[231\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan199778-246) In 2002, Pink Floyd guitarist [David Gilmour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Gilmour "David Gilmour") said, "I wasn't a big fan of most of what you'd call progressive rock. I'm like [Groucho Marx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groucho_Marx "Groucho Marx"): I don't want to belong to any club that would have me for a member."[\[232\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-247) In 2014, [Peter Gabriel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel "Peter Gabriel") remarked, "Despite prog probably being the most derided musical genre of all time there were—as today—a lot of extraordinary musicians trying to break down the barriers to reject the rules of music. It was genuinely pioneering at the time. We didn't always get it right, but when it did work we could move people and get some magic happening. I see it all as a very healthy part of growing up."[\[233\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-248) [Ian Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Anderson "Ian Anderson"), the frontman of Jethro Tull, commented: > I still like the original term that comes from 1969: progressive rock – but that was with a small "p" and a small "r". Prog Rock, on the other hand, has different connotations – of grandeur and pomposity \[...\] I think looking back on it that most of it was a pretty good experience for musicians and listeners alike. Some of it was a little bit overblown, but in the case of much of the music, it was absolutely spot on.[\[234\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-249) While music fans for years have declared progressive rock to be dead,[\[235\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-250) the scene is still active with many sub-genres.[\[236\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-251) ## List of progressive rock artists \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Progressive_rock&action=edit§ion=26 "Edit section: List of progressive rock artists")\] Main article: [List of progressive rock artists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_progressive_rock_artists "List of progressive rock artists") ## See also \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Progressive_rock&action=edit§ion=27 "Edit section: See also")\] [![Wiktionary logo](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/99/Wiktionary-logo-en-v2.svg/40px-Wiktionary-logo-en-v2.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wiktionary-logo-en-v2.svg) Look up _**[progressive rock](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/progressive%20rock "wiktionary:progressive rock")**_ in Wiktionary, the free dictionary. - [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_ref-15 "Jump up")In the rock music of the 1970s, the "art" descriptor was generally understood to mean "aggressively avant-garde" or "pretentiously progressive".[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-ArtPunkMurray-14) 02. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_ref-24 "Jump up")From about 1967, "pop music" was increasingly used in opposition to the term "rock music", a division that gave generic significance to both terms.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-23) 03. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_ref-32 "Jump up")Formalism refers to a preoccupation with established external compositional systems, structural unity, and the autonomy of individual art works. Eclecticism, like formalism, connotes a predilection towards style synthesis, or integration. However, contrary to formalist tendencies, eclecticism foregrounds discontinuities between historical and contemporary styles and electronic media, sometimes referring simultaneously to vastly different musical genres, idioms and cultural codes. Examples include [the Beatles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beatles "The Beatles")' " [Within You Without You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Within_You_Without_You "Within You Without You")" (1967) and [Jimi Hendrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimi_Hendrix "Jimi Hendrix")'s 1969 version of " [The Star-Spangled Banner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Star-Spangled_Banner "The Star-Spangled Banner")".[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECotner200093-31) 04. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_ref-43 "Jump up")Allan Moore writes: "It should be clear by now that, although this history appears to offer a roughly chronological succession of styles, there is no single, linear history to that thing we call _popular song_.... Sometimes it appears that there are only peripheries. Sometimes, audiences gravitate towards a centre. The most prominent period when this happened was in the early to mid 1960s when it seems that almost everyone, irrespective of age, class or cultural background, listened to the Beatles. But by 1970 this monolothic position had again broken down. Both [the Edgar Broughton Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Edgar_Broughton_Band "The Edgar Broughton Band")'s ' [Apache Dropout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apache_Dropout?action=edit&redlink=1 "Apache Dropout (page does not exist)")' and [Edison Lighthouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edison_Lighthouse "Edison Lighthouse")'s ' [Love grows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love_Grows_(Where_My_Rosemary_Goes) "Love Grows (Where My Rosemary Goes)")' were released in 1970 with strong Midlands/London connections, and both were audible on the same radio stations, but were operating according to very different aesthetics."[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoore2016199%E2%80%93200-42) 05. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_ref-67 "Jump up")LP sales first overtook those of singles in 1969.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTESweers2004120-66) 06. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_ref-74 "Jump up")Beatles member [John Lennon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lennon "John Lennon") is known to have attended at least one such event, a [happening](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Happening "Happening") called [the 14 Hour Technicolor Dream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_14_Hour_Technicolor_Dream "The 14 Hour Technicolor Dream").[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEO'Brien1999-72) [Paul McCartney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_McCartney "Paul McCartney") was deeply connected to the underground through his involvement with the [Indica Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indica_Gallery "Indica Gallery").[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles1999-73) 07. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_ref-96 "Jump up")Tull alone scored 11 [gold albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_album "Gold album") and 5 [platinum albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platinum_album "Platinum album").[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECleveland2005-92) Pink Floyd's 1970 album _[Atom Heart Mother](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atom_Heart_Mother "Atom Heart Mother")_ reached the top spot on the UK charts. Their 1973 album _[The Dark Side of the Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dark_Side_of_the_Moon "The Dark Side of the Moon")_, which united their extended compositions with the more structured kind of composing employed when [Syd Barrett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syd_Barrett "Syd Barrett") was their songwriter,[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhiteley199234%E2%80%9335-93) spent more than two years at the top of the charts[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhiteley19924,_38-94) and remained on the [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") album chart for fifteen years.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFriedlander1998245-95) 09. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_ref-101 "Jump up")Radio airplay was less important in the UK, where popular music recordings had limited air-time on official radio stations (as opposed to on [pirate radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pirate_radio_in_the_United_Kingdom "Pirate radio in the United Kingdom")) until the 1967 launch of [BBC Radio 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Radio_1 "BBC Radio 1").[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-pirenne1-65) UK audiences were accustomed to hearing bands in clubs, and British bands could support themselves through touring. US audiences were first exposed to new music on the radio, and bands in the US required radio airplay for success.[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurtis1987296-7-99) Radio stations were averse to progressive rock's longer-form compositions, which hampered [advertising sales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_advertisement "Radio advertisement").[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-100) 10. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_ref-113 "Jump up")Van der Graaf Generator were much more popular there than in their own country. Genesis were hugely successful in Continental Europe at a time when they were still limited to a [cult following](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cult_following "Cult following") in Britain and the US.[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-spicer-112)\[ _[importance of example(s)?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Template:Refexample#Self-sourcing "Template:Refexample")_\] 11. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_ref-120 "Jump up")This can be heard in [Triumvirat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triumvirat "Triumvirat"), an organ trio in the style of ELP; [Ange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ange_(band) "Ange (band)") and [Celeste](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celeste%20(gruppo%20musicale) "it:Celeste (gruppo musicale)") who have had a strong King Crimson influence.[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997267-118) Others brought national elements to their style: Spain's [Triana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triana_(band) "Triana (band)") introduced [flamenco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flamenco "Flamenco") elements, groups such as the Swedish [Samla Mammas Manna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samla_Mammas_Manna "Samla Mammas Manna") drew from the folk music styles of their respective nations, and Italian bands such as [Il Balletto di Bronzo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Il_Balletto_di_Bronzo "Il Balletto di Bronzo"), Rustichelli & Bordini, leaned towards an approach that was more overtly emotional than that of their British counterparts.[\[109\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997184-119) 12. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_ref-158 "Jump up")Pink Floyd were unable to repeat that combination of commercial and critical success, as their sole follow-up, _[The Final Cut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Final_Cut_(album) "The Final Cut (album)")_, was several years in coming[\[140\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997188-151) and was essentially a [Roger Waters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Waters "Roger Waters") solo project[\[141\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-merc-152) that consisted largely of material that had been rejected for _The Wall_.[\[142\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-tsmith-153) The band later reunited without Waters and restored many of the progressive elements that had been downplayed in the band's late-1970s work.[\[143\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacan1997195-154) This version of the band was very popular,[\[144\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-harrington87-155) but critical opinion of their later albums is less favourable.[\[145\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-graves-156)[\[146\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-wyman-157) 13. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_ref-164 "Jump up")[Sex Pistols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_Pistols "Sex Pistols") frontman [Johnny Rotten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lydon "John Lydon") famously wore a T-shirt that read "I hate Pink Floyd",[\[129\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-derogatis98-140) but he expressed admiration for Van der Graaf Generator,[\[148\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-boros-160) Can,[\[149\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-lydon-161) and many years later, Pink Floyd themselves.[\[150\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-162) [Brian Eno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Eno "Brian Eno") expressed a preference for the approach of the punk and new wave bands in New York, as he found them to be more experimental and less personality-based than the English bands.[\[151\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTETamm199530-163) 14. [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_ref-171 "Jump up")[Julian Cope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_Cope "Julian Cope") of [the Teardrop Explodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Teardrop_Explodes "The Teardrop Explodes") wrote a history of the krautrock genre, _[Krautrocksampler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krautrocksampler "Krautrocksampler")_.[\[157\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-170)\[ _[importance of example(s)?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Template:Refexample#Self-sourcing "Template:Refexample")_\] 15. - [soft rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_rock "Soft rock") | **Hard rock** or **heavy rock**[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-1) is a heavier subgenre of [rock music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music") typified by vocals and electric guitars that are aggressive and distorted relative to traditional rock music. Hard rock began in the mid-1960s with the [garage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garage_rock "Garage rock"), [psychedelic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelic_rock "Psychedelic rock"), and [blues rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues_rock "Blues rock") movements. Some of the earliest hard rock music was produced by [the Kinks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Kinks "The Kinks"), [the Who](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Who "The Who"), [the Yardbirds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Yardbirds "The Yardbirds"), [the Rolling Stones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rolling_Stones "The Rolling Stones"), [Cream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cream_(band) "Cream (band)"), [Vanilla Fudge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanilla_Fudge "Vanilla Fudge"), and [the Jimi Hendrix Experience](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Jimi_Hendrix_Experience "The Jimi Hendrix Experience"). In the late 1960s, bands such as [Blue Cheer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Cheer "Blue Cheer"), [the Jeff Beck Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Jeff_Beck_Group "The Jeff Beck Group"), [Iron Butterfly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Butterfly "Iron Butterfly"), [Led Zeppelin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Led_Zeppelin "Led Zeppelin"), [Creedence Clearwater Revival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creedence_Clearwater_Revival "Creedence Clearwater Revival"), [Golden Earring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Earring "Golden Earring"), [Steppenwolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band) "Steppenwolf (band)"), [Grand Funk Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Funk_Railroad "Grand Funk Railroad"), [Free](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_(band) "Free (band)"), and [Deep Purple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_Purple "Deep Purple") also produced hard rock. The genre developed into a major form of [popular music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_music "Popular music") in the 1970s, with the Who, Led Zeppelin and Deep Purple being joined by [Black Sabbath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Sabbath "Black Sabbath"), [Alice Cooper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_Cooper "Alice Cooper"), [Aerosmith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerosmith "Aerosmith"), [Kiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiss_(band) "Kiss (band)"), [Queen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_(band) "Queen (band)"), [AC/DC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AC/DC "AC/DC"), [Thin Lizzy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thin_Lizzy "Thin Lizzy") and [Van Halen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Halen "Van Halen"). During the 1980s, some hard rock bands moved away from their hard rock roots and more towards [pop rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_rock "Pop rock").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-AMQueen-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-Bogdanov2002Queen-3) Established bands made a comeback in the mid-1980s and hard rock reached a commercial peak in the 1980s with [glam metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glam_metal "Glam metal") bands such as [Mötley Crüe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%B6tley_Cr%C3%BCe "Mötley Crüe"), [Bon Jovi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bon_Jovi "Bon Jovi"), [Def Leppard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Leppard "Def Leppard") and [Poison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poison_(band) "Poison (band)"), as well as the rawer sounds of [Guns N' Roses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guns_N'_Roses "Guns N' Roses") which followed with great success in the later part of that decade. Hard rock began losing popularity with the commercial success of [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues"), [hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip-hop "Hip-hop"), [urban pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_contemporary_music "Urban contemporary music"), [grunge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grunge "Grunge"), and later [Britpop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Britpop "Britpop") in the 1990s. Despite this, many [post-grunge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-grunge "Post-grunge") bands adopted a hard rock sound, and the 2000s saw renewed interest in established bands, revival attempts, and new hard rock bands. In the 2000s, only a few hard rock bands from the 1970s and 1980s managed to sustain highly successful recording careers. ## Definitions \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hard_rock&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Definitions")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d8/Backbeat_chop.png/330px-Backbeat_chop.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Backbeat_chop.png) Drum notation for a [backbeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backbeat "Backbeat")[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-4) Hard rock is a form of loud, aggressive rock music. The electric guitar is often emphasised, used with [distortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distortion_(music) "Distortion (music)") and other effects, both as a rhythm instrument using repetitive [riffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riff "Riff") with a varying degree of complexity, and as a solo [lead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead_guitar "Lead guitar") instrument.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-AllMusicHard-5) Drumming characteristically focuses on driving rhythms, strong bass drum and a [backbeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#Backbeat "Beat (music)") on snare, sometimes using cymbals for emphasis.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-Shuker2005-6) The bass guitar works in conjunction with the drums, occasionally playing riffs, but usually providing a backing for the rhythm and lead guitars.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-Allmusicheavymetal-7) Vocals are often growling, raspy, or involve screaming or wailing, sometimes in a high range, or even [falsetto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falsetto "Falsetto") voice.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-8) In the late-1960s, the term [heavy metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_metal_music "Heavy metal music") was used interchangeably with hard rock, but gradually began to be used to describe music played with even more volume and intensity.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-9) While hard rock maintained a bluesy [rock and roll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_roll "Rock and roll") identity, including some [swing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing_(music) "Swing (music)") in the back beat and riffs that tended to outline [chord progressions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chord_progression "Chord progression") in their hooks, heavy metal's riffs often functioned as stand-alone melodies and had no swing in them.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-AllMusicHard-5) In the 1980s, heavy metal developed a number of subgenres, often termed [extreme metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extreme_metal "Extreme metal"), some of which were influenced by [hardcore punk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardcore_punk "Hardcore punk"), and which further differentiated the two styles.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-Allmusicheavymetal-7) Despite this differentiation, hard rock and heavy metal have coexisted with one another, with bands frequently flirting with the boundaries of, or hybridizing the genres.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-10) ## History \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hard_rock&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: History")\] The roots of hard rock can be traced back to the mid-to-late 1950s, particularly [electric blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_blues "Electric blues"),[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-11) which laid the foundations for key elements such as a rough declamatory vocal style, heavy guitar riffs, [string-bending](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_bending "String bending") blues-scale [guitar solos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar_solo "Guitar solo"), strong [beat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music) "Beat (music)"), thick riff-laden [texture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texture_(music) "Texture (music)"), and posturing performances.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-campbell201-12) Electric blues [guitarists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitarist "Guitarist") began experimenting with hard rock elements such as driving rhythms, distorted guitar solos and [power chords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_chord "Power chord") in the 1950s, evident in the work of [Memphis blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis_blues "Memphis blues") guitarists such as [Joe Hill Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Hill_Louis "Joe Hill Louis"), [Willie Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Johnson_(guitarist) "Willie Johnson (guitarist)"), and particularly [Pat Hare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pat_Hare "Pat Hare"),[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-rolling_memphis-13)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-palmer-14) who captured a "grittier, nastier, more ferocious electric guitar sound" on records such as [James Cotton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Cotton "James Cotton")'s " [Cotton Crop Blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotton_Crop_Blues?action=edit&redlink=1 "Cotton Crop Blues (page does not exist)")" (1954).[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-palmer-14) Other antecedents include [Link Wray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Link_Wray "Link Wray")'s instrumental " [Rumble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rumble_(instrumental) "Rumble (instrumental)")" in 1958,[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-15) and the [surf rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surf_rock "Surf rock") instrumentals of [Dick Dale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Dale "Dick Dale"), such as " [Let's Go Trippin'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Let's_Go_Trippin' "Let's Go Trippin'")" (1961) and " [Misirlou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Misirlou "Misirlou")" (1962). ### Origins (1960s) \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hard_rock&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Origins [Grunge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grunge "Grunge") and [Britpop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Britpop "Britpop") Hard rock entered the 1990s as one of the dominant forms of commercial music. The multi-platinum releases of AC/DC's _[The Razors Edge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Razors_Edge_(AC/DC_album) "The Razors Edge (AC/DC album)")_ (1990), Guns N' Roses' _[Use Your Illusion I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Use_Your_Illusion_I "Use Your Illusion I")_ and _[Use Your Illusion II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Use_Your_Illusion_II "Use Your Illusion II")_ (both in 1991),[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-Bogdanov2002Guns&Roses-100) Ozzy Osbourne's _[No More Tears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_More_Tears "No More Tears")_ (1991),[\[113\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-113) and Van Halen's _[For Unlawful Carnal Knowledge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/For_Unlawful_Carnal_Knowledge "For Unlawful Carnal Knowledge")_ (1991) showcased this popularity.[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-AllmusicVanHalen-71) Additionally, [the Black Crowes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Black_Crowes "The Black Crowes") released their debut album, _[Shake Your Money Maker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shake_Your_Money_Maker_(album) "Shake Your Money Maker (album)")_ (1990), which contained a bluesy classic rock sound and sold five million copies.[\[114\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-114)[\[115\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-RIAA-115) In 1992, Def Leppard followed up 1987's _Hysteria_ with _[Adrenalize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrenalize "Adrenalize")_, which went multi-platinum, spawned four Top 40 singles and held the number one spot on the US album chart for five weeks.[\[116\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-116) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Nirvana_around_1992.jpg/250px-Nirvana_around_1992.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nirvana_around_1992.jpg) [Nirvana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nirvana_(band) "Nirvana (band)") were at the forefront of the 1990s [grunge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grunge "Grunge") era. While these few hard rock bands managed to maintain success and popularity in the early part of the decade, [alternative forms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_rock "Alternative rock") of hard rock achieved mainstream success in the form of [grunge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grunge "Grunge") in the US and [Britpop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Britpop "Britpop") in the UK. This was particularly evident after the success of [Nirvana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nirvana_(band) "Nirvana (band)")'s _[Nevermind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevermind "Nevermind")_ (1991), which combined elements of [hardcore punk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardcore_punk "Hardcore punk") and heavy metal into a "dirty" sound that made use of heavy guitar distortion, fuzz and feedback, along with darker lyrical themes than their "hair band" predecessors.[\[117\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-AllmusicGrunge-117)[\[118\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-AllmusicHairMetal-118)[\[119\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-Bogdanov2002Alternative-119) Although most grunge bands had a sound that sharply contrasted mainstream hard rock, several, including [Pearl Jam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl_Jam "Pearl Jam"),[\[120\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-120) [Alice in Chains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_in_Chains "Alice in Chains"), [Mother Love Bone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mother_Love_Bone "Mother Love Bone") and [Soundgarden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soundgarden "Soundgarden"), were more strongly influenced by 1970s and 1980s rock and metal, while [Stone Temple Pilots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone_Temple_Pilots "Stone Temple Pilots") managed to turn alternative rock into a form of stadium rock.[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-121)[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-122) However, all grunge bands shunned the macho, anthemic and fashion-focused aesthetics particularly associated with glam metal.[\[117\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-AllmusicGrunge-117) In the UK, [Oasis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oasis_(band) "Oasis (band)") were unusual among the Britpop bands of the mid-1990s in incorporating a hard rock sound.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-AllMusicHard-5) Welsh band [Manic Street Preachers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manic_Street_Preachers "Manic Street Preachers") emerged in 1991 with a sound [Stephen Thomas Erlewine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Thomas_Erlewine "Stephen Thomas Erlewine") proclaimed to be "crunching hard-rock".[\[123\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-ammanics-123) By 1996, the band enjoyed remarkable vogue throughout much of the world, but were commercially unsuccessful in the U.S.[\[123\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-ammanics-123) In the new commercial climate glam metal bands like Europe, Ratt,[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-AllmusicRatt-80) White Lion[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-AllmusicWhiteLion-81) and Cinderella[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-AllmusicCinderella-94) broke up, Whitesnake went on hiatus in 1990, and while many of these bands would re-unite again in the late 1990s or early 2000s, they never reached the commercial success they saw in the 1980s or early 1990s.[\[118\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-AllmusicHairMetal-118) Other bands such as Mötley Crüe[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-Bogdanov2002MotleyCrue-99) and Poison[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-AllmusicPoison-93) saw personnel changes which impacted those bands' commercial viability during the decade. In 1995, Van Halen released _[Balance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balance_(Van_Halen_album) "Balance (Van Halen album)")_, a multi-platinum seller that would be the band's last with Sammy Hagar on vocals. In 1996, [David Lee Roth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Lee_Roth "David Lee Roth") returned briefly and his replacement, former [Extreme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extreme_(band) "Extreme (band)") singer [Gary Cherone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Cherone "Gary Cherone"), was fired soon after the release of the commercially unsuccessful 1998 album _[Van Halen III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Halen_III "Van Halen III")_ and Van Halen would not tour or record again until 2004.[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-AllmusicVanHalen-71) Guns N' Roses' original lineup was whittled away throughout the decade. Drummer [Steven Adler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Adler "Steven Adler") was fired in 1990, guitarist [Izzy Stradlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izzy_Stradlin "Izzy Stradlin") left in late 1991 after recording _Use Your Illusion I and II_ with the band. Tensions between the other band members and lead singer [Axl Rose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axl_Rose "Axl Rose") continued after the release of the 1993 covers album _[The Spaghetti Incident?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spaghetti_Incident%3F "The Spaghetti Incident?")_ Guitarist [Slash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slash_(musician) "Slash (musician)") left in 1996, followed by bassist [Duff McKagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duff_McKagan "Duff McKagan") in 1997. Axl Rose, the only original member, worked with a constantly changing lineup in recording an album that would take over 15 years to complete.[\[124\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-AllmusicGn-124) Slash and McKagan eventually rejoined the band in 2016 and went on the [Not in this Lifetime... Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Not_in_this_Lifetime..._Tour "Not in this Lifetime... Tour") with them. [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/Foo_Fighters_Live_29.jpg/250px-Foo_Fighters_Live_29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Foo_Fighters_Live_29.jpg) [Foo Fighters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foo_Fighters "Foo Fighters") performing an acoustic show in 2007 Some established acts continued to enjoy commercial success, such as Aerosmith, with their number one multi-platinum albums: _[Get a Grip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Get_a_Grip "Get a Grip")_ (1993), which produced four hit singles and became the band's best-selling album worldwide (going on to sell over 10million copies), and _[Nine Lives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nine_Lives_(Aerosmith_album) "Nine Lives (Aerosmith album)")_ (1997). In 1998, Aerosmith released the hit " [I Don't Want to Miss a Thing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Don't_Want_to_Miss_a_Thing "I Don't Want to Miss a Thing")".[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-AllmusicAerosmith-97) AC/DC produced the double platinum _[Ballbreaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballbreaker "Ballbreaker")_ (1995).[\[125\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-AllmusicAC/DCOnline-125) Bon Jovi appealed to their hard rock audience with songs such as " [Keep the Faith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keep_the_Faith_(Bon_Jovi_song) "Keep the Faith (Bon Jovi song)")" (1992), but also achieved success in [adult contemporary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adult_contemporary "Adult contemporary") radio, with the hit ballads " [Bed of Roses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bed_of_Roses_(Bon_Jovi_song) "Bed of Roses (Bon Jovi song)")" (1993) and " [Always](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Always_(Bon_Jovi_song) "Always (Bon Jovi song)")" (1994).[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-AllmusicBonJovi-103) Bon Jovi's 1995 album _[These Days](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/These_Days_(Bon_Jovi_album) "These Days (Bon Jovi album)")_ was a bigger hit in Europe than it was in the United States,[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-126) spawning four hit singles in the UK.[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-127) Metallica's _[Load](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Load_(album) "Load (album)")_ (1996) and _[ReLoad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reload_(Metallica_album) "Reload (Metallica album)")_ (1997) each sold in excess of 4million copies in the US and saw the band develop a more melodic and blues rock sound.[\[128\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-AllmusicMetallica-128) As the initial impetus of grunge bands faltered in the middle years of the decade, [post-grunge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-grunge "Post-grunge") bands emerged. They emulated the attitudes and music of grunge, particularly thick, distorted guitars, but with a more radio-friendly commercially oriented sound that drew more directly on traditional hard rock.[\[129\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-AllmusicPostGrunge-129) Among the most successful acts were the [Foo Fighters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foo_Fighters "Foo Fighters"), [Candlebox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candlebox "Candlebox"), [Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_(band) "Live (band)"), [Collective Soul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collective_Soul "Collective Soul"), Australia's [Silverchair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silverchair "Silverchair") and England's [Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bush_(British_band) "Bush (British band)"), who all cemented post-grunge as one of the most commercially viable subgenres by the late 1990s.[\[119\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-Bogdanov2002Alternative-119)[\[129\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-AllmusicPostGrunge-129) Similarly, some [post-Britpop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-Britpop "Post-Britpop") bands that followed in the wake of Oasis, including [Feeder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feeder_(band) "Feeder (band)") and [Stereophonics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereophonics "Stereophonics"), adopted a hard rock or "pop-metal" sound.[\[130\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-130)[\[131\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-131) ### Survivals and revivals (2000s) \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hard_rock&action=edit§ion=7 "Edit section: Survivals and revivals (2000s)")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7e/Aerosmith2007.jpg/250px-Aerosmith2007.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Aerosmith2007.jpg) Aerosmith performing at [Quilmes Rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quilmes_Rock "Quilmes Rock") in Buenos Aires, Argentina, on April 15, 2007 A few hard rock bands from the 1970s and 1980s managed to sustain highly successful recording careers. Bon Jovi were still able to achieve a commercial hit with " [It's My Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_My_Life_(Bon_Jovi_song) "It's My Life (Bon Jovi song)")" from their double platinum-certified album _[Crush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crush_(Bon_Jovi_album) "Crush (Bon Jovi album)")_ (2000).[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-AllmusicBonJovi-103) and AC/DC released the platinum-certified _[Stiff Upper Lip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stiff_Upper_Lip_(album) "Stiff Upper Lip (album)")_ (2000)[\[125\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-AllmusicAC/DCOnline-125) Aerosmith released a platinum album, _[Just Push Play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Just_Push_Play "Just Push Play")_ (2001), which saw the band foray further into pop with the hit " [Jaded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaded_(Aerosmith_song) "Jaded (Aerosmith song)")", and a blues cover album, _[Honkin' on Bobo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honkin'_on_Bobo "Honkin' on Bobo")_.[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-AllmusicAerosmith-97) [Heart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_(band) "Heart (band)") achieved their first hit album since the early 90s with _[Red Velvet Car](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Velvet_Car "Red Velvet Car")_ in 2010,[\[132\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-132) becoming the first female-led hard rock band to earn Top 10 albums spanning five decades. There were reunions and subsequent tours from Van Halen (with Hagar in 2004 and then Roth in 2007),[\[133\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-AllmusicVanHalenOnline-133) the Who (delayed in 2002 by the death of bassist [John Entwistle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Entwistle "John Entwistle") until 2006)[\[134\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-134) and Black Sabbath (with Osbourne 1997–2006 and Dio 2006–2010)[\[135\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-135) and even a one-off performance by Led Zeppelin (2007),[\[136\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-136) renewing the interest in previous eras. Additionally, hard rock supergroups, such as [Audioslave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audioslave "Audioslave") (with former members of [Rage Against the Machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rage_Against_the_Machine "Rage Against the Machine") and Soundgarden) and [Velvet Revolver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velvet_Revolver "Velvet Revolver") (with former members of Guns N' Roses, punk band [Wasted Youth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wasted_Youth_(American_band) "Wasted Youth (American band)") and Stone Temple Pilots singer [Scott Weiland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Weiland "Scott Weiland")), emerged and experienced some success. However, these bands were short-lived, ending in 2007 and 2008, respectively.[\[137\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-137)[\[138\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-138) The long-awaited Guns N' Roses album _[Chinese Democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Democracy "Chinese Democracy")_ was finally released in 2008, but only went platinum and failed to come close to the success of the band's late 1980s and early 1990s material.[\[139\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-Certification-139) More successfully, AC/DC released the double platinum-certified _[Black Ice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Ice_(album) "Black Ice (album)")_ (2008).[\[125\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-AllmusicAC/DCOnline-125) Bon Jovi continued to enjoy success, branching into [country music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music") with " [Who Says You Can't Go Home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Who_Says_You_Can't_Go_Home "Who Says You Can't Go Home")", and the rock/country album _[Lost Highway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lost_Highway_(Bon_Jovi_album) "Lost Highway (Bon Jovi album)")_ (2007). In 2009, Bon Jovi released _[The Circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Circle_(Bon_Jovi_album) "The Circle (Bon Jovi album)")_, which marked a return to their hard rock sound.[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-AllmusicBonJovi-103) [Wolfmother](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfmother "Wolfmother"), 2007 The term "retro-metal" has been applied to such bands as Texas based [the Sword](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sword "The Sword"), California's [High on Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_on_Fire "High on Fire"), Sweden's [Witchcraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Witchcraft_(band) "Witchcraft (band)") and Australia's [Wolfmother](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfmother "Wolfmother").[\[140\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-AgeofWinters-140) Wolfmother's [self-titled 2005 debut album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfmother_(album) "Wolfmother (album)") combined elements of the sounds of Deep Purple and Led Zeppelin.[\[141\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-141) Fellow Australians [Airbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airbourne_(band) "Airbourne (band)")'s début album _[Runnin' Wild](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runnin'_Wild_(Airbourne_album) "Runnin' Wild (Airbourne album)")_ (2007) followed in the hard riffing tradition of AC/DC.[\[142\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-142) England's [the Darkness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Darkness_(band) "The Darkness (band)")' _[Permission to Land](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permission_to_Land "Permission to Land")_ (2003), described as an "eerily realistic simulation of '80s metal and '70s glam",[\[143\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-AllmusicTheDarkness-143) went quintuple platinum in the UK. The follow-up, _[One Way Ticket to Hell... and Back](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Way_Ticket_to_Hell..._and_Back "One Way Ticket to Hell... and Back")_ (2005) was also a hit, but the band broke up in 2006,[\[144\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-144) becoming active again in 2011. Los Angeles band [Steel Panther](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steel_Panther "Steel Panther") managed to gain a following by sending up 80s glam metal.[\[145\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-AllmusicSteelPanther-145) A more serious attempt to revive glam metal was made by bands of the sleaze metal movement in Sweden, including [Vains of Jenna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vains_of_Jenna "Vains of Jenna"),[\[146\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-AllmusicVainsofJenna-146) [Hardcore Superstar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardcore_Superstar "Hardcore Superstar")[\[147\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-AllmusicHardcoreSuperstar-147) and [Crashdïet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crashd%C3%AFet "Crashdïet").[\[148\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-148) The Swedish rock band [Ghost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_(Swedish_band) "Ghost (Swedish band)") is among the most successful recent hard-rock bands, being nominated 4 times for the [Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Awards "Grammy Awards"), winning 1 award in the [Best Metal Performance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Metal_Performance "Grammy Award for Best Metal Performance") category for the song [Cirice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cirice "Cirice").[\[149\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-149) Although Foo Fighters continued to be one of the most successful rock acts, with albums like _[In Your Honor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_Your_Honor "In Your Honor")_ (2005), many of the first wave of post-grunge bands began to fade in popularity. Acts like [Creed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creed_(band) "Creed (band)"), [Staind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staind "Staind"), [Puddle of Mudd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puddle_of_Mudd "Puddle of Mudd") and [Nickelback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nickelback "Nickelback") took the genre into the 2000s with considerable commercial success, abandoning most of the angst and anger of the original movement for more conventional anthems, narratives and romantic songs. They were followed in this vein by new acts including [Shinedown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shinedown "Shinedown") and [Seether](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seether "Seether").[\[150\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-Grierson-150) Acts with more conventional hard rock sounds included [Andrew W.K.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_W.K.
