- [Chet Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chet_Baker "Chet Baker") | Musical artist **William John Evans** (August 16, 1929 – September 15, 1980) was an American [jazz pianist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_piano "Jazz piano") and composer who worked primarily as the leader of his trio.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-2) His extensive use of [impressionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impressionism_in_music "Impressionism in music") harmony, [block chords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Block_chord "Block chord"), innovative chord voicings, and trademark rhythmically independent "singing" melodic lines continue to influence [jazz pianists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_jazz_pianists "List of jazz pianists") today. Born in [Plainfield, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plainfield,_New_Jersey "Plainfield, New Jersey"), Evans studied classical music at [Southeastern Louisiana College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Louisiana_College "Southeastern Louisiana College") and the [Mannes School of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mannes_School_of_Music "Mannes School of Music"), in New York City, where he majored in composition and received an [artist diploma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artist_diploma "Artist diploma"). In 1955, he moved to [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), where he worked with bandleader and theorist [George Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Russell_(composer) "George Russell (composer)"). In 1958, Evans joined [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")'s sextet, which in 1959, then immersed in [modal jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz "Modal jazz"), recorded _[Kind of Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue "Kind of Blue")_, the best-selling jazz album of all time.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-:0-3) In late 1959, Evans left Davis's band and began his career as a leader, forming a [trio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_trio "Jazz trio") with bassist [Scott LaFaro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_LaFaro "Scott LaFaro") and drummer [Paul Motian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Motian "Paul Motian"), a group now regarded as a seminal modern jazz trio. They recorded two studio albums, _[Portrait in Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portrait_in_Jazz "Portrait in Jazz")_ and _[Explorations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Explorations_(Bill_Evans_album) "Explorations (Bill Evans album)")_, and two albums recorded during a 1961 engagement at New York's [Village Vanguard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Village_Vanguard "Village Vanguard") jazz club: _[Sunday at the Village Vanguard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunday_at_the_Village_Vanguard "Sunday at the Village Vanguard")_ and _[Waltz for Debby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waltz_for_Debby_(1962_album) "Waltz for Debby (1962 album)")_. A complete set (on three CDs) of their Vanguard recordings was issued decades later. Ten days after this booking ended, LaFaro died in a car crash. After months without public performances, Evans reemerged with a new trio featuring [Chuck Israels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Israels "Chuck Israels") on bass. In 1963, Evans recorded the [Grammy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award "Grammy Award")–winning _[Conversations with Myself](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conversations_with_Myself_(album) "Conversations with Myself (album)")_, a solo album produced with [overdubbing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overdubbing "Overdubbing") technology. In 1966, he met bassist [Eddie Gómez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_G%C3%B3mez_(musician) "Eddie Gómez (musician)"), with whom he worked for the next 11 years. In the mid-1970s, Evans collaborated with the singer [Tony Bennett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett "Tony Bennett") on two critically acclaimed albums: _[The Tony Bennett/Bill Evans Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tony_Bennett/Bill_Evans_Album "The Tony Bennett/Bill Evans Album")_ (1975) and _[Together Again](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Together_Again_(Tony_Bennett_and_Bill_Evans_album) "Together Again (Tony Bennett and Bill Evans album)")_ (1977). Many of Evans's compositions, such as " [Waltz for Debby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waltz_for_Debby_(song) "Waltz for Debby (song)")" and " [Time Remembered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_Remembered "Time Remembered")", have become [standards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_standard "Jazz standard"), played and recorded by many artists. Evans received 31 Grammy nominations and seven awards, and was inducted into the [_DownBeat_ Jazz Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-4) ## Biography \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bill_Evans&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Biography")\] ### Early life \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bill_Evans&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Early life")\] Evans grew up in [North Plainfield, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Plainfield,_New_Jersey "North Plainfield, New Jersey"), the son of Harry and Mary Evans ([née](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_name#Maiden_and_married_names "Birth name") Soroka). His father was of [Welsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welsh_people "Welsh people") descent and ran a golf course; his mother was of [Rusyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rusyns "Rusyns") ancestry and descended from a family of coal miners.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-petrik-5)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-Pat-6) The marriage was stormy because of his father's heavy drinking, gambling, and abuse.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-NYTObit-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-2broth-8) Bill had a brother, Harry (Harold), two years his senior, to whom he was very close.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-2broth-8) Due to Harry Evans Sr.'s destructive behavior, Mary Evans frequently left home with her sons to stay with her sister Justine and the Epps family in nearby [Somerville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somerville,_New_Jersey "Somerville, New Jersey"). During this time, Harry began taking piano lessons with a local teacher named Helen Leland between the ages of five and seven. Although Bill was considered too young for lessons at first, he picked up playing by mimicking what he heard during Harry's lessons.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger20029%E2%80%9310-9) Eventually, at the age of six, Bill began formal piano lessons alongside Harry.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger200210-10) Evans remembered Leland with affection for not insisting on a heavy technical approach, with scales and arpeggios. He quickly developed a fluent sight-reading ability, but Leland considered Harry a better pianist.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger200210-10) Encouraged by his parents to learn multiple instruments, Bill started [violin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violin "Violin") lessons at the age of seven, and soon added [flute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_concert_flute "Western concert flute") and [piccolo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piccolo "Piccolo") to his studies. He soon dropped those instruments, but it is believed they influenced his keyboard style. He later named [Mozart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mozart "Mozart"), [Beethoven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beethoven "Beethoven"), and [Schubert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schubert "Schubert") as composers whose work he often played.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-interv_harry-11) During high school, Evans came in contact with 20th-century music like [Stravinsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Igor_Stravinsky "Igor Stravinsky")'s [_Petrushka_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petrushka_(ballet) "Petrushka (ballet)"), which he called a "tremendous experience", and [Milhaud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darius_Milhaud "Darius Milhaud")'s _[Suite provençale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suite_proven%C3%A7ale "Suite provençale")_, whose bitonal language he said "opened him to new things". Around the same time came his first exposure to jazz; at age 12, he heard [Tommy Dorsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tommy_Dorsey "Tommy Dorsey")'s and [Harry James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_James "Harry James")'s bands on the radio. At 13, Bill stood in for a sick pianist in Buddy Valentino's rehearsal band,[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger200211%E2%80%9312-12) where Harry was already playing the trumpet.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger200211%E2%80%9312-12)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-Allmus-13) Soon he began to perform for dances and weddings throughout New Jersey, playing music like [boogie-woogie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boogie-woogie "Boogie-woogie") and [polkas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polka "Polka") for $1 per hour.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-mcpar-14) Around this time, he met multi-instrumentalist [Don Elliott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Elliott "Don Elliott"), with whom he later recorded. Another important influence was bassist George Platt, who introduced Evans to the theory of harmony.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger200212%E2%80%9313-15) Evans also listened to [Earl Hines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_Hines "Earl Hines"), [Art Tatum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Tatum "Art Tatum"), [Coleman Hawkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coleman_Hawkins "Coleman Hawkins"), [Bud Powell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bud_Powell "Bud Powell"), [George Shearing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Shearing "George Shearing"), [Stan Getz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Getz "Stan Getz"), and [Nat King Cole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nat_King_Cole "Nat King Cole"). He particularly admired Cole.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-16) Evans attended [North Plainfield High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Plainfield_High_School "North Plainfield High School"), graduating in 1946.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-17) > One night I got really adventurous on " [Tuxedo Junction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuxedo_Junction_(song) "Tuxedo Junction (song)")" and I put in a little "ping!" you know, that wasn't written, and this was such an experience! To make music that wasn't indicated. That really got me into starting to want to think about how to make the music. —Interview with Harry Evans. c. 1965.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-interv_harry-11) ### College, army, sabbatical year \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bill_Evans&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: College, army, sabbatical year")\] > I have always admired your teaching as that rare and amazing combination – exceptional knowledge combined with the ability to bring that same knowledge, that lies deep within the student, to life. You were certainly my biggest inspiration in college, and the seeds of the insights that you have sown, have in practice borne fruit many times over. —Bill Evans speaking to Gretchen Magee[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-petrik-5) After high school, in September 1946, Evans attended [Southeastern Louisiana College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Louisiana_College "Southeastern Louisiana College") on a flute scholarship.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-Cramer2009-18)[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-DuBose-Smith2005-19) He studied classical piano interpretation with Louis P. Kohnop, John Venettozzi, and Ronald Stetzel.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger200216-20) A key figure in Evans's development was Gretchen Magee, whose methods of teaching left a big imprint on his compositional style. Around his third year in college, Evans composed his first known tune, "Very Early".[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-mcpar-14) Also around that time he composed a piece called "Peace Piece".[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-Pat-6) Years later, when asked to play it, he said it was a spontaneous improvisation and didn't know it. He was a founding member of SLU's Delta Omega chapter of [Phi Mu Alpha Sinfonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phi_Mu_Alpha_Sinfonia "Phi Mu Alpha Sinfonia"), played [quarterback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quarterback "Quarterback") for the fraternity's football team, and played in the college band. In 1950, he performed a movement of Beethoven's [Piano Concerto No. 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._3_(Beethoven) "Piano Concerto No. 3 (Beethoven)") on his senior recital, graduating with a [Bachelor of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Music "Bachelor of Music") in piano and a bachelor's in music education. Evans regarded his last three years in college as the happiest of his life.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger200216%E2%80%9319-21) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/Bill_Evans_Graduation_Concert.jpg/250px-Bill_Evans_Graduation_Concert.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bill_Evans_Graduation_Concert.jpg) Program of Evans's graduation concert. April 24, 1950. During college, Evans met guitarist [Mundell Lowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mundell_Lowe "Mundell Lowe"), and after graduating, they formed a trio with bassist [Red Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Mitchell "Red Mitchell"). The three moved to New York City but could not attract bookings, prompting them to leave for [Calumet City, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calumet_City,_Illinois "Calumet City, Illinois").[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger200220-22) In July 1950, Evans joined [Herbie Fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Fields "Herbie Fields")'s band, based in Chicago. During the summer, the band did a three-month tour backing [Billie Holiday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billie_Holiday "Billie Holiday"), including East Coast appearances at Harlem's [Apollo Theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_Theater "Apollo Theater") and shows in Philadelphia, Baltimore, and Washington, D.C. The band included trumpeter [Jimmy Nottingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Nottingham "Jimmy Nottingham"), trombonist [Frank Rosolino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Rosolino "Frank Rosolino") and bassist [Jim Aton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Aton "Jim Aton"). Upon its return to Chicago, Evans and Aton worked as a duo in clubs, often backing singer [Lurlean Hunter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lurlean_Hunter "Lurlean Hunter"). Shortly thereafter, Evans received his [draft notice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conscription "Conscription") and entered the [U.S. Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Army "U.S. Army"). During his three-year (1951–54) period in the Army,[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-Allmus-13) Evans played flute, piccolo, and piano in the [Fifth U.S. Army Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army_Band "United States Army Band") at [Fort Sheridan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheridan_Reserve_Center "Sheridan Reserve Center"). He hosted a jazz program on the camp radio station and occasionally performed in Chicago clubs, where he met singer [Lucy Reed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucy_Reed "Lucy Reed"), with whom he became friends and later recorded. He met singer and bassist Bill Scott and Chicago jazz pianist Sam Distefano (his bunkmate in their platoon), both of whom became Evans's close friends. But Evans's stay in the Army was traumatic, and it caused him to have nightmares for years. As people criticized his musical conceptions and playing, he lost confidence for the first time.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger200219%E2%80%9320-23) Around 1953, Evans composed his best-known tune, " [Waltz for Debby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waltz_for_Debby_(song) "Waltz for Debby (song)")", for his young niece.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger200237-24) During this period, he began using recreational drugs, occasionally smoking [marijuana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marijuana "Marijuana").[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger200261-25) Evans was discharged from the Army in January 1954, and entered a period of seclusion triggered by the harsh criticism he had received. He took a sabbatical year and lived with his parents, setting up a studio, acquiring a grand piano, and working on his technique, believing he lacked other musicians' natural fluency. He visited his brother, now in [Baton Rouge, Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baton_Rouge,_Louisiana "Baton Rouge, Louisiana"), recently married and working as a conservatory teacher.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-pettinger-26) ### Return to New York City \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bill_Evans&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: Return to New York City")\] In July 1955, Evans returned to New York City and enrolled in the [Mannes College of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mannes_College_of_Music "Mannes College of Music") for a three-semester postgraduate course in music composition. He also wrote [classical settings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_setting "Musical setting") of poems by [William Blake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Blake "William Blake"). Along with his studies, Evans played in low-profile "Tuxedo gigs" at the Friendship Club and the [Roseland Ballroom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roseland_Ballroom "Roseland Ballroom"), as well as Jewish weddings, intermission spots, and over 40 dances. Better opportunities also arose, such as playing solo opposite the [Modern Jazz Quartet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_Jazz_Quartet "Modern Jazz Quartet") at the [Village Vanguard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Village_Vanguard "Village Vanguard"), where one day he saw [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis") listening to him. During this period, Evans also met [Thelonious Monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thelonious_Monk "Thelonious Monk").[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-pettinger-26) Evans soon began to perform in [Greenwich Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenwich_Village "Greenwich Village") clubs with [Don Elliott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Elliott "Don Elliott"), [Tony Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Scott_(musician) "Tony Scott (musician)"), [Mundell Lowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mundell_Lowe "Mundell Lowe"), and bandleader [Jerry Wald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Wald_(musician)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Jerry Wald (musician) (page does not exist)"). He may have played on some of Wald's discs, but his first proven Wald recording is _Listen to the Music of Jerry Wald_, which also featured his future drummer [Paul Motian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Motian "Paul Motian").[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-pettinger-26) In early 1955, singer [Lucy Reed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucy_Reed "Lucy Reed") moved to New York City to play at the Vanguard and [The Blue Angel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Blue_Angel_(New_York_nightclub) "The Blue Angel (New York nightclub)"), and in August she recorded _The Singing Reed_ with a four-piece group that included Evans. During this period, he met two of Reed's friends: manager [Helen Keane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helen_Keane_(jazz) "Helen Keane (jazz)"), who became his agent seven years later, and [George Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Russell_(composer) "George Russell (composer)"), with whom he soon worked. That year, he recorded with guitarist [Dick Garcia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Garcia "Dick Garcia") on _A Message from Garcia_ on the [Dawn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dawn_Records_(American_label) "Dawn Records (American label)") label. In parallel, Evans kept up his work with Scott, playing in Preview's Modern Jazz Club in Chicago in December 1956 – January 1957, and recording _The Complete Tony Scott_. After the _Complete_ sessions, Scott took a long overseas tour.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-pettinger-26) ### Debut album _New Jazz Conceptions_ \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bill_Evans&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: Debut album New Jazz Conceptions")\] In September 1956, producer [Orrin Keepnews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orrin_Keepnews "Orrin Keepnews") was convinced to record the reluctant Evans by a demo tape [Mundell Lowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mundell_Lowe "Mundell Lowe") played to him over the phone. The result was his debut album, _[New Jazz Conceptions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jazz_Conceptions "New Jazz Conceptions")_, featuring the original versions of " [Waltz for Debby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waltz_for_Debby_(song) "Waltz for Debby (song)")" and "Five".[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-pettinger-26) Eleven songs were recorded in the first session, including Evans's original composition " [Waltz for Debby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waltz_for_Debby_(song) "Waltz for Debby (song)")", which proved to be his most recognized and recorded composition.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-AMB-27) The album began Evans's relationship with [Riverside Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riverside_Records "Riverside Records"), and also marked the formation of the first Bill Evans trio, with Teddy Kotick (bass) and [Paul Motian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Motian "Paul Motian") (drums). [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") critic [Scott Yanow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Yanow "Scott Yanow") said about the album: "Bill Evans' debut as a leader found the 27-year-old pianist already sounding much different than the usual Bud Powell-influenced keyboardists of the time... A strong start to a rather significant career."[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-AM-28) David Rickert of [All About Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_About_Jazz "All About Jazz") noted Bud Powell's influence and wrote, "Even at this stage he had the chops to make this a good piano jazz album, but in the end it's not a very good Bill Evans album... There are glimpses of the later trademarks of Evans' style".[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-AAJ-29) Though a critical success that got good reviews in _[DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat")_ and _[Metronome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metronome_(magazine) "Metronome (magazine)")_ magazines, _New Jazz Conceptions_ was initially a financial failure, selling only 800 copies the first year. "Five" was for some time Evans's trio farewell tune during performances.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-pettinger-26) After the album's release, Evans spent much time studying [J. S. Bach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Sebastian_Bach "Johann Sebastian Bach")'s music to improve his technique.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger200239-30) ### Work with George Russell \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bill_Evans&action=edit§ion=6 "Edit section: Work with George Russell")\] > It was one of those magic moments in your life when you expect a horror story, and the doors of heaven open up. I knew there and then he wasn't going to get away. —George Russell upon hearing Bill Evans for the first time.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-pettinger-26) Evans met composer [George Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Russell_(composer) "George Russell (composer)") during his tenure with Lucy Reed. Russell's first impression of Evans was unfavorable ("this is going to be like pulling teeth all day"), but when he secretly heard Evans play, he changed his mind.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-pettinger-26) Russell was then developing his magnum opus, the treatise _[Lydian Chromatic Concept of Tonal Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_Chromatic_Concept_of_Tonal_Organization "Lydian Chromatic Concept of Tonal Organization")_, in which he argued that the [Lydian mode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_mode "Lydian mode") was more compatible with [tonality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonality "Tonality") than the [major scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_scale "Major scale") ( [Ionian mode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionian_mode "Ionian mode")) used in most music. This was groundbreaking in jazz, and soon influenced musicians like [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis"). Evans, who was already acquainted with these ideas, began to work with Russell in 1956.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-pettinger-26) By this time, [RCA Victor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Victor "RCA Victor") had begun a series of recordings called _Jazz Workshop_, and soon Russell, through the intervention of [Hal McKusick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hal_McKusick "Hal McKusick") and Jack Lewis, gained his own record date, titled [The Jazz Workshop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Jazz_Workshop "The Jazz Workshop") and released in 1957. At that time, Russell assembled trumpeter [Art Farmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Farmer "Art Farmer"), guitarist [Barry Galbraith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_Galbraith "Barry Galbraith"), bassist [Milt Hinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milt_Hinton "Milt Hinton"), and Evans for three recording dates, along with several rehearsal sessions. Initially, for these sessions, only the bassist was given a written part, while the rest were left, and, according to Farmer, "took the parts at home and tried to come to terms with them". The album took a year to make, and was successful enough to enable Russell to escape his penurious lifestyle.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-pettinger-26) Evans performed a significant solo in "Concerto for Billy the Kid".[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-Allmus-13) In 1957, Russell was one of six composers (three jazz, three classical) [Brandeis University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandeis_University "Brandeis University") commissioned to write a piece for its Festival of the Creative Arts in the context of the first experiments in [third stream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_stream "Third stream") jazz. Russell wrote a suite for orchestra, "All About Rosie", that featured Evans, among other soloists.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger200239-30) "All About Rosie" has been cited as one of the few convincing examples of composed [polyphony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyphony "Polyphony") in jazz.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-31) A week before the festival, the piece was previewed on TV, and Evans's performance was deemed "legendary" in jazz circles. During the festival performance on June 6, Evans became acquainted with [Chuck Israels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Israels "Chuck Israels"), who became his bassist years later.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger200240-32) Also during the festival, guitarist [Joe Puma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Puma "Joe Puma") invited Evans to play on the album _Joe Puma/Jazz_.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger200241-33) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/73/Chet_Baker_%281955_portrait%29.jpg/250px-Chet_Baker_%281955_portrait%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Chet_Baker_(1955_portrait).jpg) [Chet Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chet_Baker "Chet Baker") worked with Evans on his album _[Chet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chet_(Chet_Baker_album) "Chet (Chet Baker album)")_ in 1958–1959. That year, Evans also met bassist [Scott LaFaro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_LaFaro "Scott LaFaro") while auditioning him for a place in an ensemble led by trumpeter [Chet Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chet_Baker "Chet Baker"), and was impressed. LaFaro joined his trio three years later.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-interv_lafaro-34) Evans also performed on albums by [Charles Mingus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus "Charles Mingus"), [Oliver Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Nelson "Oliver Nelson"), [Tony Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Scott_(musician) "Tony Scott (musician)"), [Eddie Costa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Costa "Eddie Costa"), and [Art Farmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Farmer "Art Farmer"). ### Work with Miles Davis, _Everybody Digs Bill Evans_, and _Kind of Blue_ \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bill_Evans&action=edit§ion=7 "Edit section: Work with Miles Davis, Everybody Digs Bill Evans, and Kind of Blue")\] Main article: [Kind of Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue "Kind of Blue") [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fa/Miles_Davis_by_Palumbo.jpg/250px-Miles_Davis_by_Palumbo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Miles_Davis_by_Palumbo.jpg) [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis") in 1955, three years before meeting Evans. In February 1958, at [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")'s urging, Russell drove Evans to the Colony Club in [Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn "Brooklyn") to play with [Davis's sextet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis_Quintet "Miles Davis Quintet"). At this time, [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane"), [Cannonball Adderley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannonball_Adderley "Cannonball Adderley"), [Paul Chambers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Chambers "Paul Chambers"), and [Philly Joe Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philly_Joe_Jones "Philly Joe Jones") were the other members of Davis's group. [Red Garland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Garland "Red Garland") had recently been fired, and Evans knew he was not merely filling in for one night but auditioning to become the group's regular pianist. By the end of the night, Davis told Evans that he would play their next engagement in [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia").[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-milesbill-35)[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger200251%E2%80%9352-36) The band had been known for playing a mixture of [jazz standards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_standard "Jazz standard") and [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop") originals, but by the time Evans arrived, Davis had begun his venture into [modal jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz "Modal jazz"), having just released his album _[Milestones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milestones_(Miles_Davis_album) "Milestones (Miles Davis album)")_. Evans formally joined Davis's group in April 1958. The band appeared in radio broadcasts on Saturday nights and, on May 3, the new formation made its first broadcast from [Café Bohemia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caf%C3%A9_Bohemia "Café Bohemia") (its usual locale). The live radio appearance broadcast on May 17, 1958, and also released on the album titled _Makin' Wax_, is the earliest documented evidence of collaboration between Evans and Davis.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger200253-37) By mid-May, [Jimmy Cobb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Cobb "Jimmy Cobb") replaced Philly Joe Jones, with whom Evans had developed a close friendship. On May 26, Evans made his first studio recordings with Davis, which were first issued as part of _Jazz Track_,[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger200254-38) and later reissued on _[1958 Miles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1958_Miles "1958 Miles")_. A performance of the [Ballets Africains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballets_Africains "Ballets Africains") from [Guinea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guinea "Guinea") in 1958 sparked Davis's interest in modal music. This music stayed for long periods of time on a single chord, weaving in and out of consonance and dissonance.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-39) Another influence was [George Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Russell_(composer) "George Russell (composer)")'s treatise. Both influences coalesced in Davis's conception of modal jazz offering an alternative to chord changes and major/minor [key](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Key_(music) "Key (music)") relationships, relying instead on a series of modal scales. He realized that Evans, who had worked with Russell, could follow him into modal music. At the same time, Evans introduced Davis to 20th-century classical composers such as [Sergei Rachmaninoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Rachmaninoff "Sergei Rachmaninoff"), [Maurice Ravel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Ravel "Maurice Ravel"), and [Aram Khachaturian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aram_Khachaturian "Aram Khachaturian").[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-Allmus-13) The band's mostly black followers did not react favorably to the replacement of Garland with a white musician.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-milesbill-35)[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-pettinger-26) Davis used to tease him, and Evans's sensitivity perhaps let it get to him. But the band began to find a new, smoother groove, as Adderley recalled: "When he started to use Bill, Miles changed his style from very hard to a softer approach."[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-milesbill-35) > Bill had this quiet fire that I loved on piano. The way he approached it, the sound he got was like crystal notes or sparkling water cascading down from some clear waterfall. I had to change the way the band sounded again for Bill's style by playing different tunes, softer ones at first. —Miles Davis[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-40) In July 1958, Evans appeared as a sideman on Adderley's album _[Portrait of Cannonball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portrait_of_Cannonball "Portrait of Cannonball")_, featuring the first performance of " [Nardis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nardis_(composition) "Nardis (composition)")", specially written by Davis for the session. While Davis was not very satisfied with the performance, he said that from then on, Evans was the only one to play it in the way he wanted. The piece came to be associated with Evans's future trios, which played it frequently.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-pettinger-26) By the end of the summer, Davis knew Evans was quickly approaching his full professional development and that he would soon leave Davis's group.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-milesbill-35) That year, Evans won the _[DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat")_ International Critics' Poll for his work with Davis and his album _New Jazz Conceptions_.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger200265-41) In September 1958, Evans recorded as a sideman in Art Farmer's album _[Modern Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_Art_(Art_Farmer_album) "Modern Art (Art Farmer album)")_, also featuring [Benny Golson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benny_Golson "Benny Golson"). All three had won the _DownBeat_ poll.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger200265-41) Later, Evans deemed this record one of his favorites. During this period, despite all the successes, Evans was visiting a psychiatrist, as he was unsure whether he wanted to continue as a pianist.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger200266-42) Evans left Davis's sextet in November 1958 and stayed with his parents in Florida and his brother in [Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana "Louisiana"). While he was burned out, one of the main reasons for leaving was his father's illness.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger200266-42) During this sojourn, the always self-critical Evans suddenly felt his playing had improved. "While I was staying with my brother in Baton Rouge, I remember finding that somehow I had reached a new level of expression in my playing. It had come almost automatically, and I was very anxious about it, afraid I might lose it."[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger200266-42) Shortly after, he moved back to New York, and in December Evans recorded the trio album _[Everybody Digs Bill Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everybody_Digs_Bill_Evans "Everybody Digs Bill Evans")_ for Riverside Records with bassist [Sam Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Jones_(musician) "Sam Jones (musician)") and drummer Philly Joe Jones. This was Evans's second album as a leader, the first since _New Jazz Conceptions_, recorded two years earlier. While Keepnews had often tried to persuade Evans to make a second trio recording, the pianist felt he had nothing new to say until then. He had also been too busy traveling with Davis to make a record.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger200267-43) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9f/Bill_Evans_Peace_Piece.png/250px-Bill_Evans_Peace_Piece.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bill_Evans_Peace_Piece.png) Evans built " [Peace Piece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_Piece "Peace Piece")" on a simple one-bar ostinato left-hand figure in C major. Over this static harmonic frame, he freely improvised melodies. One of the pieces to appear on the album was [Leonard Bernstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein "Leonard Bernstein")'s "Some Other Time". Evans started to play an introduction using an [ostinato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostinato "Ostinato") figure. But, according to Keepnews, who was present, Evans spontaneously started to improvise over that harmonic frame, creating the recording that would be named "Peace Piece". According to Evans: "What happened was that I started to play the introduction, and it started to get so much of its own feeling and identity that I just figured, well, I'll keep going." But Gretchen Magee has said the piece was penned as an exercise during Evans's college years, and Peri Cousins says that Evans often played the piece at home.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger200268%E2%80%9369-44) Evans returned to the Davis sextet in early 1959, at the trumpeter's request, to record _[Kind of Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue "Kind of Blue")_, often considered the best-selling jazz album of all time.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-:0-3)[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-:1-45) As usual, during the sessions of _Kind of Blue_, Davis called for almost no rehearsal and the musicians had little idea what they were to record. Davis had given the band only sketches of scales and melody lines on which to improvise. Once the musicians were assembled, Davis gave brief instructions for each piece and then set about taping the sextet in studio.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-KOB_notes-46) During the creative process of _Kind of Blue_, Davis handed Evans a piece of paper with two chords—G minor and A augmented—and asked "What would you do with that?" Evans spent the next night writing what became " [Blue in Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_in_Green "Blue in Green")". But when the album came out, the song was attributed exclusively to Davis. When Evans suggested he deserved a share of the royalties, Davis offered him a check for $25.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-pettinger-26)[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-47) Evans also wrote the liner notes for _Kind of Blue_, comparing jazz improvisation to [Japanese visual art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_art "Japanese art").[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-KOB_notes-46) By the fall of 1959, Evans had started his own trio with [Jimmy Garrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Garrison "Jimmy Garrison") and [Kenny Dennis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Dennis "Kenny Dennis"), but it was short-lived.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-interv_lafaro-34) Sometime during the late 1950s, most probably before joining Davis, Evans began using heroin. Philly Joe Jones has been cited as an especially bad influence in this regard.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-pettinger-26)[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-big_love-48) Davis seems to have tried to help Evans kick his addiction, but failed. Evans's first long-term romance was with a black woman named Peri Cousins (for whom "Peri's Scope" was named), during the second half of the 1950s. The couple had problems booking hotels during Evans's gigs, since most did not allow interracial couples. By the turn of the decade, Evans had met a waitress named Ellaine Schultz, who became his partner for 12 years.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-big_love-48) ### Piano trios
