we could spend a year or two just growing, without ambitions, just allowing the music to grow. And allowing our talents to merge in a very natural way. —Evans in interview with George Clabin, 1966[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-interv_lafaro-34) In mid-1959, Evans was performing at [Basin Street East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basin_Street_East "Basin Street East") and was visited by bassist [Scott LaFaro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_LaFaro "Scott LaFaro"), who was playing with singer and pianist [Bobby Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Scott_(musician) "Bobby Scott (musician)") at a club around the corner.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-49) LaFaro expressed interest in forming a trio, and suggested [Paul Motian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Motian "Paul Motian"), who had appeared on Evans's album [New Jazz Conceptions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jazz_Conceptions "New Jazz Conceptions"), as the drummer.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-interv_lafaro-34) The trio with LaFaro and Motian became one of the most celebrated piano trios in jazz.\[ _[example needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:AUDIENCE "Wikipedia:AUDIENCE")_\] With this group, Evans's focus settled on traditional jazz standards and original compositions, with an added emphasis on interplay among band members. Evans and LaFaro achieved a high level of musical empathy.\[ _[further explanation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_\] In December 1959 the band recorded its first album, _[Portrait in Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portrait_in_Jazz "Portrait in Jazz")_, for [Riverside Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riverside_Records "Riverside Records"). In early 1960, the trio began a tour that brought it to Boston, San Francisco (at [Jazz Workshop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Workshop "Jazz Workshop")), and Chicago (at the [Sutherland Lounge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sutherland_Hotel "Sutherland Hotel")). After returning to New York in February, the band performed at [Town Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Town_Hall_(New_York_City) "The Town Hall (New York City)") on a multi-artist bill, and then began a residency at [Birdland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birdland_(New_York_jazz_club) "Birdland (New York jazz club)"). While the trio produced no studio records in 1960, two bootleg recordings from radio broadcasts from April and May were illegally released in the early 1970s, infuriating Evans.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger200298%E2%80%9399-50) They were posthumously issued as _The 1960 Birdland Sessions_.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-pettinger-26) In parallel with his trio work, Evans kept working as a backing musician for other leaders. In 1960, he performed on singer [Frank Minion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Minion "Frank Minion")'s album _The Soft Land of Make Believe_, featuring versions of the _Kind of Blue_ compositions "Flamenco Sketches" and "So What" with added lyrics. That year, he also recorded _The Soul of Jazz Percussion_ with Philly Joe Jones and Chambers.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-pettinger-26) In May 1960, the trio performed at one of the Jazz Profiles concerts, a series organized by Charles Schwartz. Around this time, Evans hired [Monte Kay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Kay "Monte Kay") as his manager. During one of his concerts at the Jazz Gallery, Evans contracted [hepatitis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hepatitis "Hepatitis") and went to his parents' house in Florida to recuperate. During this period, he also participated in the recordings _[The Great Kai & J. J.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Great_Kai_&_J._J. "The Great Kai & J. J.")_ and _[The Incredible Kai Winding Trombones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Incredible_Kai_Winding_Trombones "The Incredible Kai Winding Trombones")_ for [Impulse! Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records "Impulse! Records"). In May and August 1960, Evans appeared on George Russell's album _[Jazz in the Space Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_in_the_Space_Age "Jazz in the Space Age")._ In late 1960, he performed on _Jazz Abstractions_, an album recorded under the leadership of [Gunther Schuller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunther_Schuller "Gunther Schuller") and [John Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lewis_(pianist) "John Lewis (pianist)").[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-pettinger-26) In February 1961, Evans's trio with Motian and LaFaro recorded _[Explorations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Explorations_(Bill_Evans_album) "Explorations (Bill Evans album)")_, the group's second and final studio album. According to Keepnews, the recording sessions' atmosphere was tense, Evans and LaFaro having argued over extra-musical matters. Evans was also having headaches, and LaFaro was playing with a loaned bass.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-pettinger-26) The disc features Evans's first trio version of "Nardis", the Miles Davis piece Evans had recorded with Cannonball Adderley for [Portrait of Cannonball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portrait_of_Cannonball "Portrait of Cannonball") in 1958. Apart from "Nardis" and "Elsa", the album consisted of jazz standards. After the recording sessions, Evans was initially unwilling to release the album, believing the trio had played badly. But upon hearing the recording, he changed his mind, and later thought of it very favorably.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-interv_lafaro-34) Just after the _Explorations_ sessions, he appeared as a sideman in [Oliver Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Nelson "Oliver Nelson")'s _[The Blues and the Abstract Truth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Blues_and_the_Abstract_Truth "The Blues and the Abstract Truth")_. In late June 1961, Riverside recorded Evans's trio live at the Village Vanguard, resulting in the albums _[Sunday at the Village Vanguard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunday_at_the_Village_Vanguard "Sunday at the Village Vanguard")_ and _[Waltz for Debby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waltz_for_Debby_(1961_album) "Waltz for Debby (1961 album)")._ (Further recordings from this performance were issued in 1984 as _More From The Vanguard._)[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-51)[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-52) Evans later showed special satisfaction with these recordings, seeing them as the culmination of his trio's musical interplay.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-interv_lafaro-34) ### After LaFaro's death \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bill_Evans&action=edit§ion=10 "Edit section: After LaFaro's death")\] The death of 25-year-old LaFaro in a car crash ten days after the Vanguard performances devastated Evans. He did not record or perform in public again for several months. In October 1961, persuaded by Keepnews, Evans returned to the musical scene on the [Mark Murphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Murphy_(singer) "Mark Murphy (singer)") album _[Rah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rah_(Mark_Murphy_album) "Rah (Mark Murphy album)")_. With new bassist Chuck Israels, in December they recorded a session for _[Nirvana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nirvana_(Herbie_Mann_and_the_Bill_Evans_Trio_album) "Nirvana (Herbie Mann and the Bill Evans Trio album)")_ with flutist [Herbie Mann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Mann "Herbie Mann").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-petrik-5) In April and May 1962, Evans completed the duo album _[Undercurrent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undercurrent_(Bill_Evans_and_Jim_Hall_album) "Undercurrent (Bill Evans and Jim Hall album)")_ with guitarist [Jim Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Hall_(musician) "Jim Hall (musician)"). After Evans re-formed his trio in 1962, two albums, _[Moon Beams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon_Beams "Moon Beams")_ and _[How My Heart Sings!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/How_My_Heart_Sings! "How My Heart Sings!")_, resulted. In 1963, at the beginning of his association with [Verve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verve_Records "Verve Records"), he recorded _[Conversations with Myself](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conversations_with_Myself_(album) "Conversations with Myself (album)")_, an album that featured overdubbing, layering up to three tracks of piano for each song. The album won him his first [Grammy award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_award "Grammy award").[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-grammys-53) Evans's heroin addiction worsened after LaFaro's death. His girlfriend Ellaine Schultz was also an addict. Evans habitually borrowed money from friends, and eventually his electricity and telephone services were shut down. He said: "You don't understand. It's like death and transfiguration. Every day you wake in pain like death and then you go out and score, and that is transfiguration. Each day becomes all of life in microcosm."[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-Allmus-13)[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-54) Evans never allowed heroin to interfere with his musical discipline, according to a 2010 BBC article that contrasts his addiction with [Chet Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chet_Baker "Chet Baker")'s.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-55) On one occasion while injecting heroin, Evans hit a nerve and temporarily disabled it, performing a full week's engagement at the Village Vanguard virtually one-handed.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-pettinger-26) During this time, Helen Keane began to have an important influence, as she significantly helped maintain Evans's career despite his self-destructive lifestyle, and the two developed a strong friendship.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-big_love-48) In summer 1963, Evans and Schultz left their flat in New York and settled in his parents' home in Florida, where, it seems, they quit the habit for some time.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-pettinger-26) Even though never legally married, Bill and Ellaine were in all other respects husband and wife. At that time, Schultz meant everything to Evans, and was the only person with whom he felt genuine comfort.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-pettinger-26) Although he recorded many albums for Verve, their artistic quality has typically been viewed as uneven. Despite Israels's fast development and the creativity of new drummer [Larry Bunker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Bunker "Larry Bunker"), the album _[Bill Evans Trio with Symphony Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans_Trio_with_Symphony_Orchestra "Bill Evans Trio with Symphony Orchestra")_, featuring [Gabriel Fauré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel_Faur%C3%A9 "Gabriel Fauré")'s _[Pavane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pavane_(Faur%C3%A9) "Pavane (Fauré)")_ and works of other classical composers arranged by [Claus Ogerman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claus_Ogerman "Claus Ogerman") divided critical opinion. Some recordings in unusual contexts were made, such as a concert recording with a big-band recorded at [Town Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Town_Hall_(New_York_City) "The Town Hall (New York City)") that was never issued owing to Evans's dissatisfaction with it (although the more successful jazz trio portion of the concert was [released](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans_at_Town_Hall "Bill Evans at Town Hall")). Live recordings and bootleg radio broadcasts from this period represent some of the trio's better work. In 1965, the trio with Israels and Bunker went on a well-received European tour. ### Bill Evans meets Eddie Gómez \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bill_Evans&action=edit§ion=11 "Edit section: Bill Evans meets Eddie Gómez")\] In 1966, Evans met Puerto-Rico born, [Juilliard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juilliard "Juilliard")-graduated bassist [Eddie Gómez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_G%C3%B3mez_(musician) "Eddie Gómez (musician)"). In what turned out to be an 11-year stay, Gómez sparked new developments in Evans's trio conception. One of the most significant releases during this period is _[Bill Evans at the Montreux Jazz Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans_at_the_Montreux_Jazz_Festival "Bill Evans at the Montreux Jazz Festival")_ (1968), which won him his second Grammy award.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-grammys-53) It has remained a critical favorite, and is one of two albums Evans made with drummer [Jack DeJohnette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_DeJohnette "Jack DeJohnette"). Other highlights from this period include "Solo – In Memory of His Father" from _[Bill Evans at Town Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans_at_Town_Hall "Bill Evans at Town Hall")_ (1966), which also introduced "Turn Out the Stars"; a second pairing with guitarist Jim Hall, _[Intermodulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intermodulation_(album) "Intermodulation (album)")_ (1966); and the solo album _[Alone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alone_(Bill_Evans_album) "Alone (Bill Evans album)")_ (1968, featuring a 14-minute version of "Never Let Me Go"), that won his third Grammy award.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-grammys-53) In 1968, drummer [Marty Morell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty_Morell "Marty Morell") joined the trio, remaining until 1975, when he retired to family life. This was Evans's stablest, longest-lasting group. Evans had overcome his heroin habit and was entering a period of personal stability. Between 1969 and 1970, Evans recorded _[From Left to Right](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/From_Left_to_Right "From Left to Right")_, featuring his first use of electric piano. Between May and June 1971, Evans recorded _[The Bill Evans Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bill_Evans_Album "The Bill Evans Album")_, which won two Grammy awards.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-grammys-53) This all-originals album (four new) also featured alternation between acoustic and electric piano. One track was "Comrade Conrad", a tune that had originated as a [Crest toothpaste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crest_toothpaste "Crest toothpaste") jingle and later been reelaborated and dedicated to Conrad Mendenhall, a friend who had died in a car crash.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger2002205-56) Other albums included _[The Tokyo Concert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tokyo_Concert "The Tokyo Concert")_ (1973); _[Since We Met](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Since_We_Met "Since We Met")_ (1974); and _[But Beautiful](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/But_Beautiful_(Stan_Getz_&_Bill_Evans_album) "But Beautiful (Stan Getz & Bill Evans album)")_ (1974; released in 1996), featuring the trio plus saxophonist [Stan Getz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Getz "Stan Getz") in live performances in the Netherlands and Belgium. Morell was an energetic, straight-ahead drummer, unlike many of the trio's former percussionists, and many critics feel that this was a period of little growth for Evans. After Morell left, Evans and Gómez recorded two duo albums, _[Intuition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intuition_(Bill_Evans_album) "Intuition (Bill Evans album)")_ and _[Montreux III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreux_III "Montreux III")_. In the early 1970s, Evans was caught at New York's [John F. Kennedy International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy_International_Airport "John F. Kennedy International Airport") with a suitcase containing heroin. Although the police put him in jail for the night, he was not charged, but both he and Schultz had to begin [methadone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methadone "Methadone") treatment.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-big_love-48)[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-57) In 1973, while working in [Redondo Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redondo_Beach,_California "Redondo Beach, California"), California, Evans met and fell in love with Nenette Zazzara, despite his long-term relationship with Schultz.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-pettinger-26) When Evans broke the news to Schultz she pretended to understand, but then died by suicide, throwing herself under a subway train. Evans's relatives believe that Schultz's infertility coupled with Bill's desire to have a son may have influenced those events.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-2broth-8) As a result, Evans went back on heroin for a while before resuming methadone treatment. In August 1973, Evans married Nenette, and in 1975 they had a child, [Evan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evan_Evans_(film_composer) "Evan Evans (film composer)"). The new family, which also included Evans's stepdaughter Maxine, lived in a large house in [Closter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closter,_New_Jersey "Closter, New Jersey"), New Jersey.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-pettinger-26) They remained very close and Nenette and Bill remained married until Evans's death.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-pettinger-26) In 1974, Evans recorded a multimovement jazz concerto written for him by [Claus Ogerman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claus_Ogerman "Claus Ogerman"), _Symbiosis_. ### Collaboration with Tony Bennett \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bill_Evans&action=edit§ion=12 "Edit section: Collaboration with Tony Bennett")\] > There is an intriguing juxtaposition of opposites running through the music—Bennett the expansive, heart on sleeve, vibrato man, Evans the inward looking aesthete—which makes for charged listening, if charged is an adjective which can be applied to something so relaxed. And the projects were genuinely collaborative, with the artists on an equal footing: Evans solos wonderfully throughout and Together Again actually starts with a solo piano piece, "The Bad And The Beautiful", put there at Bennett's suggestion to emphasize that this wasn't just a vocalist-with-accompanist affair.... By the time Bennett and Evans made the second album they'd been performing live together for a year and their partnership, comfortable enough though it was on the first album, is noticeably better oiled. —Chris May on _[The Complete Tony Bennett/Bill Evans Recordings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Complete_Tony_Bennett/Bill_Evans_Recordings "The Complete Tony Bennett/Bill Evans Recordings")_[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-Bennett/Evans-58) During the mid-1970s Evans collaborated with the singer [Tony Bennett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett "Tony Bennett") on two critically acclaimed albums: _[The Tony Bennett/Bill Evans Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tony_Bennett/Bill_Evans_Album "The Tony Bennett/Bill Evans Album")_ (1975) and _[Together Again](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Together_Again_(Bennett_and_Evans_album) "Together Again (Bennett and Evans album)")_ (1977). Bennett initiated the collaboration. The two respected each other's talent, and performed together for about two years. Although Evans was using cocaine regularly during this period, he was reportedly sober when recording the albums with Bennett.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-Bennett/Evans-58) Both Bennett and Evans said it was not just a singer-and-accompanist affair but rather a joint creative effort to enhance some well-known hits with a new twist on familiar melodies and harmonies. Bennett encouraged Evans's harmonically sophisticated arrangements and extended solos to emphasize equally valuable input from both musicians. Bennett and Evans recorded the first album in four studio sessions in June 1975, and the second in four studio sessions in September 1976. Between the two recordings, they performed live as a duo, featuring songs from their recordings, including " [But Beautiful](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/But_Beautiful_(song) "But Beautiful (song)")", " [Days of Wine and Roses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Days_of_Wine_and_Roses_(song) "Days of Wine and Roses (song)")", and " [Dream Dancing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dream_Dancing_(Cole_Porter_song) "Dream Dancing (Cole Porter song)")". ### Last years \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bill_Evans&action=edit§ion=13 "Edit section: Last years")\] In 1975, Morell was replaced by drummer [Eliot Zigmund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliot_Zigmund "Eliot Zigmund"). Several collaborations followed, and the trio did not record an album until 1977. Both _[I Will Say Goodbye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Will_Say_Goodbye "I Will Say Goodbye")_ (Evans's last album for [Fantasy Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fantasy_Records "Fantasy Records")) and _[You Must Believe in Spring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You_Must_Believe_in_Spring_(Bill_Evans_album) "You Must Believe in Spring (Bill Evans album)")_ (for Warner Bros.) highlighted changes that became significant in the last stage of Evans's life. Greater emphasis was placed on group improvisation and interaction, and new harmonic experiments were attempted. [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c8/Bill_Evans.jpg/250px-Bill_Evans.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bill_Evans.jpg) Evans performing at the [Montreux Jazz Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreux_Jazz_Festival "Montreux Jazz Festival") with his trio consisting of [Marc Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Johnson_(jazz_musician) "Marc Johnson (jazz musician)"), bass, and [Philly Joe Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philly_Joe_Jones "Philly Joe Jones"), drums, July 13, 1978. Gómez and Zigmund left Evans in 1978. Evans then asked Philly Joe Jones, the drummer he considered his "all-time favorite", to fill in. Several bassists were tried, with [Michael Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Moore_(bassist) "Michael Moore (bassist)") staying the longest. Evans finally settled on [Marc Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Johnson_(jazz_musician) "Marc Johnson (jazz musician)") on bass and [Joe LaBarbera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_LaBarbera "Joe LaBarbera") on drums. This trio was Evans's last. In April 1979, Evans met Laurie Verchomin, a Canadian waitress (later, a writer) with whom he had a relationship until his death. Verchomin was 28 years younger.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-big_love-48) At the beginning of a several-week tour of the trio through the Pacific Northwest in the spring of 1979, Evans learned that his brother, Harry, who had been diagnosed with [schizophrenia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schizophrenia "Schizophrenia"), had died by suicide at age 52.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-2broth-8)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-Allmus-13)[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-big_love-48) This news shocked him deeply, and some of the concerts were canceled. His friends and relatives believe Harry's death precipitated his own death the next year.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-2broth-8)[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-big_love-48) Marc Johnson recalled: "This fateful trip marks ... the beginning of the end. Bill's willingness to play and work decreased noticeably after the death of Harry, actually it was just the music itself that held him upright. He fulfilled his obligations because he needed money, but these were the few moments in his life when he felt comfortable—the times in between must have been depressing, and he barely showed a willingness to live."[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-petrik-5) In August 1979, Evans recorded his last studio album, _[We Will Meet Again](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/We_Will_Meet_Again "We Will Meet Again")_, featuring a composition of the same name written for his brother. The album won a Grammy award posthumously in 1981, along with _I Will Say Goodbye_.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-grammys-53) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8d/Bill_Evans%27s_tombstone.jpg/250px-Bill_Evans%27s_tombstone.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bill_Evans's_tombstone.jpg) Evans is buried at Roselawn Memorial Park and Mausoleum, [Baton Rouge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baton_Rouge "Baton Rouge"), East Baton Rouge Parish, [Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana "Louisiana"), Section 161, Plot K. During the late 1970s, Evans kicked his heroin habit, with the help of methadone, only to become addicted to cocaine. He started with one gram per weekend, but later started taking several grams daily.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-big_love-48) Harry's death may also have influenced his emotional state after 1979. His sister-in-law Pat Evans has said she knew Bill would not last long after Harry died and wondered whether that is what prompted her to buy three plots in the Baton Rouge Cemetery where Harry was interred.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-2broth-8) Evans voluntarily quit his treatment for chronic hepatitis.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-2broth-8) Laurie Verchomin has said that Evans was sure that he would die in a short time.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-big_love-48) ## Death \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bill_Evans&action=edit§ion=14 "Edit section: Death")\] On September 15, 1980, Evans, who had been in bed for several days with stomach pains at his home in Fort Lee, was accompanied by Joe LaBarbera and Verchomin to the [Mount Sinai Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Sinai_Hospital_(Manhattan) "Mount Sinai Hospital (Manhattan)") in New York City, where he died that afternoon.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-big_love-48) The cause of death was a combination of [peptic ulcer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peptic_ulcer "Peptic ulcer"), [cirrhosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cirrhosis "Cirrhosis"), bronchial [pneumonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pneumonia "Pneumonia"), and untreated hepatitis.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-pettinger-26) Evans's friend [Gene Lees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_Lees "Gene Lees") called Evans's struggle with drugs "the longest suicide in history".[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger20023-59) Evans was interred in [Baton Rouge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baton_Rouge "Baton Rouge") next to his brother. Services were held in Manhattan on September 19.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-60) A tribute, planned by producer [Orrin Keepnews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orrin_Keepnews "Orrin Keepnews") and Tom Bradshaw, was held on September 22 at the [Great American Music Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_American_Music_Hall "Great American Music Hall") in San Francisco.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-61) Fellow musicians paid homage to Evans in the first days of the 1980 [Monterey Jazz Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monterey_Jazz_Festival "Monterey Jazz Festival"), which opened that week: [Dave Brubeck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Brubeck "Dave Brubeck") played his own " [In Your Own Sweet Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_Your_Own_Sweet_Way "In Your Own Sweet Way")" on the 19th, [The Manhattan Transfer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Manhattan_Transfer "The Manhattan Transfer") followed on the 20th, and [John Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lewis_(pianist) "John Lewis (pianist)") dedicated " [I'll Remember April](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I'll_Remember_April_(song) "I'll Remember April (song)")".[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-62) In 1981, Pat Metheny and Lyle Mays released the piece "September Fifteenth (dedicated to Bill Evans)" on their album _[As Falls Wichita, So Falls Wichita Falls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/As_Falls_Wichita,_So_Falls_Wichita_Falls "As Falls Wichita, So Falls Wichita Falls")_. ## Music and style \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bill_Evans&action=edit§ion=15 "Edit section: Music and style")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/d/d4/So_What_Chords_in_Kind_of_Blue.png/250px-So_What_Chords_in_Kind_of_Blue.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:So_What_Chords_in_Kind_of_Blue.png) Evans is credited as creating some new harmonies, like the quartal voicing [Mark Levine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Levine_(musician) "Mark Levine (musician)") calls ["So What" chord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/So_What_chord "So What chord"); first appearing in the opening track of _Kind of Blue_.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-63)[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-Valerio-64)[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ee/Bill_Evans%27s_%22What_Is_This_Thing_Called_Love%22_Viennese_trichord.png/250px-Bill_Evans%27s_%22What_Is_This_Thing_Called_Love%22_Viennese_trichord.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bill_Evans's_%22What_Is_This_Thing_Called_Love%22_Viennese_trichord.png) A [Viennese trichord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viennese_trichord "Viennese trichord") as a part of [6-Z17](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/6-Z17 "6-Z17"), an altered dominant tritone substitution (Db7alt) in the key of C, from Evans's opening to " [What Is This Thing Called Love?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What_Is_This_Thing_Called_Love%3F "What Is This Thing Called Love?")"[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEForte2000-65)[Play](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/d/dc/Bill_Evans%27s_%22What_Is_This_Thing_Called_Love%22_Viennese_trichord.mid/Bill_Evans%27s_%22What_Is_This_Thing_Called_Love%22_Viennese_trichord.mid.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bill_Evans%27s_%22What_Is_This_Thing_Called_Love%22_Viennese_trichord.mid "File:Bill Evans's \"What Is This Thing Called Love\" Viennese trichord.mid"). Evans is credited with influencing the harmonic language of jazz piano.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-Allmus-13)[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEValerio200540-66) His harmonic language was influenced by impressionist composers such as [Claude Debussy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Debussy "Claude Debussy")[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-67) and [Maurice Ravel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Ravel "Maurice Ravel").[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-harmony-68) His versions of jazz standards, as well as his own compositions, often feature thorough reharmonizations. Other features include [added tone chords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Added_tone_chord "Added tone chord"), modal inflections, unconventional [substitutions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chord_substitution "Chord substitution"), and modulations.[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-harmony-68) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ea/Bill_Evans_-_Waltz_For_Debby_-_Bridge_%281961%29.png/250px-Bill_Evans_-_Waltz_For_Debby_-_Bridge_%281961%29.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bill_Evans_-_Waltz_For_Debby_-_Bridge_(1961).png) An example of Evans's harmonies. The chords feature extensions like 9ths and 13ths, are laid around middle C, have smooth voice leading, and leave the root to the bassist. Bridge of the first chorus of "Waltz for Debby" (mm.33–36). From the 1961 album of the same name. One of Evans's distinctive harmonic traits is excluding the root in his chords, leaving it to the bassist, played on another beat of the measure, or just left implied. "If I am going to be sitting here playing roots, fifths and full voicings, the bass is relegated to a time machine." This idea had already been explored by [Ahmad Jamal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Jamal "Ahmad Jamal"), [Erroll Garner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erroll_Garner "Erroll Garner"), and [Red Garland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Garland "Red Garland"). In Evans's system, the chord is expressed as a quality and a color.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-pettinger-26)[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEValerio20054-69) Most of his harmonies feature added-note chords or [quartal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quartal_and_quintal_harmony "Quartal and quintal harmony") voicings.[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEValerio200540-66) Thus, Evans created a self-sufficient language for the left hand, a distinctive voicing, that allowed the transition from one chord to the next while hardly having to move the hand. With this technique, he created an effect of continuity in the piano's central register. Lying around middle C, in this region the harmonic clusters sounded the clearest and at the same time left room for contrapuntal independence with the bass.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-pettinger-26) Evans's improvisations relied heavily on motivic development, either melodically or rhythmically.[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEValerio200540-66) Motives may be broken and recombined to form melodies.[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEValerio200541-70) Another characteristic of Evans's style is rhythmic displacement.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-pettinger-26)[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEValerio200542-71) His melodic contours often describe arches.[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEValerio200543-72) Other characteristics include melodic sequencing and motivic transformation.[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEValerio200543-72) He could play with one hand in 4/4 and the other momentarily in 3/4.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEValerio200546-73) At the beginning of his career, Evans used block chords heavily. He later reduced his use of them.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEValerio200549-74) During a 1978 interview, [Marian McPartland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marian_McPartland "Marian McPartland") asked: "How do you think your playing has changed since you first started? Is it deliberate or is it just happening to change? Evans replied: "Well, it's deliberate, but I stay along the same lines ... I try to get a little deeper into what I'm doing. As far as that kind of playing goes \[jazz playing rather than an earlier example where he played "Waltz for Debbie" without any improvisation or sense of swing\], I think my left hand is a little more competent and of course I worked a lot on inner things happening like inner voices I've worked on."[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-75)[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-76) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/d/d7/Bill_Evans_Time_Remembered2.png/500px-Bill_Evans_Time_Remembered2.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bill_Evans_Time_Remembered2.png) The first line of " [Time Remembered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_Remembered "Time Remembered")", as penned by Evans in the early 1970s. At least during his late years, Evans's favorite keys to play in were A and E.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-mcpar-14) Evans greatly valued [Bach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bach "Bach")'s music, which influenced his playing style and helped him gain good touch and finger independence. "Bach changed my hand approach to playing the piano. I used to use a lot of finger technique when I was younger, and I changed over to a weight technique. Actually, if you play Bach and the voices sing at all, and sustain the way they should, you really can't play it with the wrong approach."[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger200239-30) Evans valued Bach's " [The Well-Tempered Clavier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Well-Tempered_Clavier "The Well-Tempered Clavier")" and " [Two- and Three-Part Inventions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inventions_and_Sinfonias_(Bach) "Inventions and Sinfonias (Bach)")" as excellent practice material.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] In an interview with Len Lyons, Evans said, "for me, technique is the ability to translate your ideas into sound through your instrument."[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-77) ### Influences \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bill_Evans&action=edit§ion=16 "Edit section: Influences")\] In a 1964 interview, Evans called [Bud Powell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bud_Powell "Bud Powell") his single greatest influence.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-78) Biographer Peter Pettinger notes that Evans "assimilated 'a thousand influences'", including pianists [Dave Brubeck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Brubeck "Dave Brubeck"), [George Shearing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Shearing "George Shearing"), [Oscar Peterson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oscar_Peterson "Oscar Peterson"), [Al Haig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Haig "Al Haig"), and [Lou Levy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou_Levy_(pianist) "Lou Levy (pianist)"), and horn players [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis"), [Dizzy Gillespie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dizzy_Gillespie "Dizzy Gillespie"), [Charlie Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Parker "Charlie Parker"), and [Stan Getz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Getz "Stan Getz"). "The biggest influence on Evans \[in his early days\], though, was the pianism of Nat 'King' Cole", whom Evans called "one of the tastiest and just swingin'est and beautifully melodic improvisers and jazz pianists that jazz has ever known, and he was one of the very first that really grabbed me hard."[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger200214%E2%80%9315-79) Pettinger also notes that the "work of the pianist [Lennie Tristano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lennie_Tristano "Lennie Tristano"), with his cool approach to a line" was an important influence on Evans,[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger200234-80) and Lyons observes that Tristano preceded Evans in his use of overdubbing piano tracks.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-81) Evans was also heavily influenced by his deep studies of European classical music: "The constructional knowledge of music that Evans later brought to jazz was firmly rooted in this European tradition, as was his thoroughly trained and exquisitely refined touch at the keyboard."[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger200216-20) As a composer, Evans also assimilated and amalgamated jazz, popular, and classical influences in an "utterly logical" manner.[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger2002129-82) His compositional style shows similarities to and the influence of some of the composers whose works he often played, such as [Earl Zindars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_Zindars "Earl Zindars")[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger2002129-82) and [Michel Legrand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michel_Legrand "Michel Legrand").[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger2002243-83) J. William Murray wrote, "Evans was very adept at drawing Western European compositional techniques into jazz and there are elements of Bach, Chopin, Debussy, and Ravel in his writing."[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-84) ### Views on contemporaneous music tendencies \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bill_Evans&action=edit§ion=17 "Edit section: Views on contemporaneous music tendencies")\] Evans's career began just before the rock explosion in the 1960s. During this decade, jazz was swept into a corner, and most new talents had few opportunities to gain recognition, especially in America.[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger2002197-85) Evans believed he had been lucky to gain exposure before this profound change in the music world, and never had problems gaining bookings and recording opportunities.[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger2002197-85) Evans never embraced new music movements; he kept his style intact. For example, he lamented watching Davis shift his style towards [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") and blamed the change on commercial considerations. Evans said, "I would like to hear more of the consummate melodic master \[Davis\], but I feel that big business and his record company have had a corrupting influence on his material. The rock and pop thing certainly draws a wider audience. It happens more and more these days, that unqualified people with executive positions try to tell musicians what is good and what is bad music."[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-milesbill-35) Still, Evans and Davis kept in touch throughout their lives.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-big_love-48) Evans considered himself an acoustic pianist, but from the 1970 album _[From Left to Right](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/From_Left_to_Right "From Left to Right")_ onward, he also released some material with [Fender-Rhodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fender-Rhodes "Fender-Rhodes") piano intermissions. But unlike other jazz pianists (such as [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock")), he never fully embraced the new instrument, and invariably returned to the acoustic sound. "I don't think too much about the electronic thing, except that it's kind of fun to have it as an alternate voice. ... \[It's\] merely an alternate keyboard instrument that offers a certain kind of sound that's appropriate sometimes. I find that it's a refreshing auxiliary to the piano but I don't need it ... I don't enjoy spending a lot of time with the electric piano. I play it for a period of time, then I quickly tire of it, and I want to get back to the acoustic piano."[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-milesbill-35) He said electronic music "just doesn't attract me. I'm of a certain period, a certain evolution. I hear music differently. For me, comparing electric bass to acoustic bass is sacrilege."[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-milesbill-35) ## Repertoire and compositions \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bill_Evans&action=edit§ion=18 "Edit section: Repertoire and compositions")\] Main article: [List of compositions by Bill Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_compositions_by_Bill_Evans "List of compositions by Bill Evans") Evans's repertoire consisted of established [jazz standards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_standards "Jazz standards"), songs by contemporaries (some of which he helped make standards), and original compositions (some of which have also become standards). Among the major American songwriters, he was particularly drawn to the work of [Jimmy Van Heusen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Van_Heusen "Jimmy Van Heusen"), recording what was reputedly his favorite song, " [But Beautiful](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/But_Beautiful_(song) "But Beautiful (song)")",[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger2002261-86) many times in various settings, as well as many other Van Heusen tunes. Contemporaries whose works he often played include [Michel Legrand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michel_Legrand "Michel Legrand"), [Johnny Mandel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Mandel "Johnny Mandel"), and [Earl Zindars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_Zindars "Earl Zindars") and, to a lesser extent, [Burt Bacharach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burt_Bacharach "Burt Bacharach"), [John Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lewis_(pianist) "John Lewis (pianist)"), [Henry Mancini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Mancini "Henry Mancini"), [Gary McFarland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_McFarland "Gary McFarland"), [Thelonious Monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thelonious_Monk "Thelonious Monk"), [Claus Ogerman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claus_Ogerman "Claus Ogerman"), [Steve Swallow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Swallow "Steve Swallow"), and [Denny Zeitlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denny_Zeitlin "Denny Zeitlin"). Other songs by his contemporaries and colleagues he recorded include " [In Your Own Sweet Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_Your_Own_Sweet_Way "In Your Own Sweet Way")" by [Dave Brubeck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Brubeck "Dave Brubeck"), " [You're Gonna Hear from Me](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You're_Gonna_Hear_from_Me_(song) "You're Gonna Hear from Me (song)")" by [André Previn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A9_Previn "André Previn"), " [The Peacocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Peacocks_(album) "The Peacocks (album)")" by Jimmy Rowles, " [Dolphin Dance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolphin_Dance "Dolphin Dance")" by [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"), and, atypically, " [I Do It for Your Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Do_It_for_Your_Love "I Do It for Your Love")" by [Paul Simon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Simon "Paul Simon"), which nonetheless "continued to inspire the pianist's most complex thoughts" in his final years.[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger2002282-87) " [Nardis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nardis_(composition) "Nardis (composition)")" by [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis") was a special signature tune, often performed in highly extended versions by his final trio.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger2002267-88) During a radio interview, [Marian McPartland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marian_McPartland "Marian McPartland") listened to Evans play "Reflections in D" by [Duke Ellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Ellington "Duke Ellington") and later noted, "Sitting next to him, listening to the rise and fall of the melody, I realized that ... he chooses some of the most romantic, evocative tunes there are. The tune ended softly with a chord so perfect it took my breath away."[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-89) Evans composed more than 50 originals. Many were dedicated to people close to him, including "Waltz for Debby" for his niece; "For Nenette" for his wife; "Letter to Evan" for his son; "NYC's No Lark", an anagram of [Sonny Clark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Clark "Sonny Clark") in memory of the pianist; "Re: Person I Knew", an anagram of [Orrin Keepnews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orrin_Keepnews "Orrin Keepnews"); "We Will Meet Again" for his brother; "Peri's Scope" for Peri Cousins; "One for Helen" and "Song for Helen" for Helen Keane; "B minor Waltz (For Ellaine)" for Ellaine Schultz; "Laurie" for Laurie Verchomin; "Yet Ne'er Broken", an anagram of cocaine dealer Robert Kenney; "Maxine" for his stepdaughter; "Tiffany" for Joe LaBarbera's daughter; and "Knit For Mary F." for fan Mary Franksen from [Omaha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omaha "Omaha").[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger2002276-90) ## Personal life \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bill_Evans&action=edit§ion=19 "Edit section: Personal life")\] Evans was an avid reader, particularly of philosophy and humor. His shelves held works by [Plato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plato "Plato"), [Voltaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voltaire "Voltaire"), [Whitehead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_North_Whitehead "Alfred North Whitehead"), [Santayana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Santayana "George Santayana"), [Freud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freud "Freud"), [Margaret Mead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Mead "Margaret Mead"), [Sartre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sartre "Sartre"), and [Thomas Merton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Merton "Thomas Merton") and he had a special fondness for [Thomas Hardy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Hardy "Thomas Hardy")'s work. He was fascinated with Eastern religions and philosophies including [Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam "Islam"), [Zen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zen "Zen"), and [Buddhism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhism "Buddhism"). Evans introduced [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane") to the philosophy of [Krishnamurti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jiddu_Krishnamurti "Jiddu Krishnamurti").[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-pettinger-26) Evans liked to paint and draw.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger200266-42) He was also a keen golfer, a hobby that began on his father's golf course.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-pettinger-26) Evans had a fondness for horse racing and frequently gambled hundreds of dollars, often winning.[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettinger200266%E2%80%9367-91) During his last years, he owned a racehorse named "Annie Hall" with producer [Jack Rollins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Rollins_(producer) "Jack Rollins (producer)").[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-big_love-48) In 1973, Evans broke up with his girlfriend of 12 years, Ellaine Schultz, to pursue Nenette Zazzara. Schultz then died by suicide, throwing herself in front of a subway train. Evans married Zazzara in August 1973. They met while his trio was performing at [Howard Rumsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Rumsey "Howard Rumsey")'s club Concerts By The Sea in [Redondo Beach, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redondo_Beach,_California "Redondo Beach, California"), where Zazzara was a part-time waitress.[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-92) ## Reception \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bill_Evans&action=edit§ion=20 "Edit section: Reception")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/76/Bill-Evans-1964.jpg/250px-Bill-Evans-1964.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bill-Evans-1964.jpg) Evans in [Helsinki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helsinki "Helsinki") in 1964. Music critic Richard S. Ginell wrote: "With the passage of time, Bill Evans has become an entire school unto himself for pianists and a singular mood unto himself for listeners. There is no more influential jazz-oriented pianist—only [McCoy Tyner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner "McCoy Tyner") exerts nearly as much pull among younger players and journeymen."[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-93) During his short tenure with Davis in 1958, when the band left New York to go on the road, Evans sometimes received cold receptions from the mostly black audiences. Evans later acknowledged that some felt his presence threatened the black pride aspect of Davis's band's success. Pettinger believed in a recording, for his solo on a tune named "Walkin'", Evans received noticeably less applause than the other soloists, and for that on "All Of You", none at all. Davis and the other band members responded, "he's supposed to be there, Miles wants him there", on the bandstand whenever audience members made comments.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-pettinger-26) Davis wrote in his autobiography that Evans was sensitive to the criticism. It might have been a contributing factor to his leaving the band after just seven months. When [Ken Burns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Burns "Ken Burns")'s television miniseries [_Jazz_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_(TV_series) "Jazz (TV series)") was released in 2001, it was criticized for neglecting Evans's work after his departure from Davis's sextet.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-pettinger-26) ## Legacy and influence \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bill_Evans&action=edit§ion=21 "Edit section: Legacy and influence")\] Author and jazz pianist Len Lyons wrote: "Evans was the most influential pianist of the 1960's. The tone, touch, texture, and harmonic richness of his playing affected the majority of pianists who followed him."[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-94) Evans has left his mark on such players as [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"), [Chick Corea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chick_Corea "Chick Corea"), [Paul Kuhn"), [Warren Bernhardt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Bernhardt "Warren Bernhardt"), [Michel Petrucciani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michel_Petrucciani "Michel Petrucciani"), [John Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Taylor_(jazz) "John Taylor (jazz)"), [Vince Guaraldi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vince_Guaraldi "Vince Guaraldi"), [Stefano Krall"), [Ralph Towner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Towner "Ralph Towner"), [John McLaughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McLaughlin_(musician) "John McLaughlin (musician)"), [Lenny [Kronos Quartet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kronos_Quartet "Kronos Quartet"), [Jean-Yves Thibaudet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Yves_Thibaudet "Jean-Yves Thibaudet"), [Roy Evans's style has also influenced some contemporary classical composers. The English composer [Gavin Bryars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gavin_Bryars "Gavin Bryars") wrote "My First Homage" in 1978 "to Bill Evans," the composer explained, "and, more particularly, to the trio that he had from 1959-1961," which "affected me deeply when I first began playing jazz seriously." Bryars also notes that the title of the piece "uses the same initials as ... 'My Foolish Heart'." The 15-minute work is scored principally for two pianos but also for two vibraphones, tuba, and sizzle cymbal and was recorded by Bryars and others in February 1981, shortly after Evans's death.[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-96) The noted Hungarian composer [György Ligeti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gy%C3%B6rgy_Ligeti "György Ligeti") admired Evans and acknowledged his influence in an interview, adding, "As far as touch is concerned, Bill Evans is a sort of Michelangeli of jazz" (in reference to the great classical pianist [Arturo Benedetti Michelangeli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arturo_Benedetti_Michelangeli "Arturo Benedetti Michelangeli")).[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-97) Ligeti's [Fifth Piano Étude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89tudes_(Ligeti)#Book_1 "Études (Ligeti)") (1985), subtitled "Arc-en-ciel" ("Rainbow"), demonstrates this influence clearly, and Ligeti even hand-wrote in the margin of the score, "Play it like Bill Evans."[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-98) Likewise, American minimalist composer and keyboardist [Terry Riley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terry_Riley "Terry Riley") included Evans in "the Pantheon of my teachers and heroes" in the liner notes to his solo piano _Lisbon Concert._[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-99) In 2025, composer [John Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Williams "John Williams") premiered a Piano Concerto, the second movement of which is modeled on Evans's style.[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-100) Many of Evans's own compositions, such as " [Waltz for Debby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waltz_for_Debby_(song) "Waltz for Debby (song)")", " [Peace Piece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_Piece "Peace Piece")", " [Blue in Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_in_Green "Blue in Green")", "Very Early", " [Time Remembered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_Remembered "Time Remembered")", "Turn Out the Stars", "We Will Meet Again", and " [Funkallero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funkallero "Funkallero")", have become oft-recorded jazz standards, and his early death inspired the composition of two widely covered tribute songs, [Phil Woods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Woods "Phil Woods")'s "Goodbye, Mr. Evans" and [Don Sebesky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Sebesky "Don Sebesky")'s "I Remember Bill". During his lifetime, Evans received 31 Grammy nominations and seven Awards.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-grammys-53) In 1994, he posthumously received the [Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Lifetime_Achievement_Award "Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award").[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-101) The Bill Evans Jazz Festival at Southeastern Louisiana University began in 2002.[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-102) A Bill Evans painting hangs in the Recital Hall lobby of the Department of Music and Performing Arts. The Center for Southeastern Louisiana Studies at the Simms Library holds the Bill Evans archives.[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-103) He was named Outstanding Alumnus of the year in 1969.[\[104\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-104) Evans influenced the character Seb's wardrobe in the 2016 film _[La La Land](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_La_Land_(film) "La La Land (film)")_.[\[105\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-105) The 2026 [biographical film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biographical_film "Biographical film") _[Everybody Digs Bill Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everybody_Digs_Bill_Evans_(film) "Everybody Digs Bill Evans (film)")_, directed by [Grant Gee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grant_Gee "Grant Gee"), dramatises a traumatic period of Evans's life following the tragic death of bassist Scott LaFaro in 1961. The film was written by [Mark O’Halloran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_O'Halloran_(writer) "Mark O'Halloran (writer)"), based on the 2013 novel _Intermission_ by Owen Martell.[\[106\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-106)[\[107\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-107) ## Discography \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bill_Evans&action=edit§ion=22 "Edit section: Discography")\] Main article: [Bill Evans discography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans_discography "Bill Evans discography") ## Tribute albums \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bill_Evans&action=edit§ion=23 "Edit section: Tribute albums")\] Main article: [Bill Evans tribute albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans_tribute_albums "Bill Evans tribute albums") - [![icon](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/Saxo_Boca1.JPG/40px-Saxo_Boca1.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Saxo_Boca1.JPG)[Jazz portal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portal:Jazz "Portal:Jazz") ## Notes \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bill_Evans&action=edit§ion=24 "Edit section: Notes")\] 001. # “The Köln Concert”--Keith Jarrett (1975)

## Added to the National Registry: 2025

## Essay by Peter Elsdon (guest post)*

“The Köln Concert” was recorded in the German city of Cologne in January 1975 by jazz musician Keith Jarrett, documenting a single improvised performance. The record’s subsequent fame and popularity are in no small measure due to the sense that it captures a single moment in time, in which a performer, instrument, audience, all interact.

In January 1975, Jarrett was a 29-year-old American jazz musician embarking on a short solo tour of Europe with Manfred Eicher, the owner of one of the record labels he was recording for, ECM (Editions of Contemporary Music). Eicher founded ECM in 1969 and began making recordings of both American and European musicians, especially those associated with progressive or avant-garde approaches to jazz. Jarrett had recorded several albums for ECM before 1975, most notably 1972’s “Facing You” in a studio in Oslo, a record now widely regarded as a milestone in the jazz piano canon. In 1973, ECM had released “Solo Concerts,” a double album documenting two Jarrett solo performances recorded in Germany and Switzerland. These were completely improvised performances where Jarrett would go on stage without any pre-prepared material. ECM and Eicher were instrumental in establishing this approach as a vehicle for Jarrett, including helping to organise his European tours. At the same time, Jarrett was recording for the American label Impulse!, but his contract allowed him the freedom to undertake projects for ECM. Later in his career, from 1978 onwards, he would record exclusively for ECM, marking one of the most extensive and important relationships between an artist and a record label in the history of jazz.

The performance in Cologne took place in challenging circumstances, and countless versions of the same story have been told by the different participants. Jarrett had travelled overnight with Eicher from Switzerland by car. Usually, his tour schedule allowed for a performance every other day, but on this occasion the Cologne performance came the day after a concert in Lausanne, Switzerland. On arriving in Cologne, they discovered the wrong piano was on the stage of the Opera House, and there was no way to move the right piano into place. A local piano tuner did what he could, but the instrument was still problematic with a tonal balance not to Jarrett’s satisfaction. Despite being extremely tired, Jarrett was persuaded to go ahead with the concert by Vera Brandes, the 18-year-old promoter, with recording engineer Martin Wieland on hand to document proceedings. Perhaps a clue as to what happened during the performance is given by the fact that Brandes recalls running to Wieland after the concert, asking simply, “Did you get that?” Eicher and Jarrett apparently listened to the tape in the car on the way to the next concert, and became convinced that despite the problematic conditions, something about the performance demanded that it be released.

On its original LP release, the record contained four tracks: “Part I”, “Part IIa”, “Part IIb”, and “Part IIc.” “Part IIa” and “Part IIb” were a single improvisation split for the purposes of sequencing across the sides of the double LP. “Part IIc” was an encore at the end of the concert, a version of a Jarrett composition which would later appear in printed form entitled “Memories of Tomorrow.”

“The Köln Concert” presents a highly individual approach to the piano Jarrett had been developing over a number of years. His playing nods to a broad range of styles, including blues, gospel, folk, funk, as well the jazz piano language. Partly for this reason, he was considered by parts of the music press as a musician who transcended conventional categories and could not straightforwardly be categorized as a jazz musician, a status from which he benefitted considerably.

The opening of “Part I” is based on a musical language that strips away the extensions and alterations that jazz musicians were apt to add to chords. The harmonies feel open and luminous, with a sound evocative of what might now be called “Americana.” Jarrett gradually extends this approach into a passage where his right hand improvises long lines across the full range of the piano whilst his left hand outlines the bare sonority of the harmony. As the minutes progress it is possible to hear more and more of a jazz influence through the use of the chromatic notes and alterations typical of the jazz piano language. In other places, such as the closing of both “Part I” and “Part IIb,” the music reiterates a single chord, drawing that out into an ecstatic elongation of a single sound. Meanwhile, the opening of “Part IIb” presents a kind of playing most typical of Jarrett: a highly-charged groove- based texture where Jarrett uses left-hand octaves to generate a rhythmic propulsion that powers the music along. Throughout the record, long spans of music lead the listener through these waypoints, following a path which has its own inexorable sense of direction.

In the years after its release, the record went on to become a huge seller for ECM, reportedly bankrolling the label for a number of years. This was not because of a substantial promotional campaign; indeed, at the time of its release, ECM was still a relatively new label for the American record-buying public. But something about the record’s presentation of an improvised acoustic performance in a German opera house gained a deep resonance. Perhaps that was because it tapped into broader cultural ideals, including the stripping away of technology, and a spontaneous kind of self-expression. Whatever the reasons, “The Köln Concert” resonated with a range of record buyers.

Jarrett has often expressed his dislike of the record’s popularity, perhaps because some of his more challenging and thoroughly developed solo piano recordings seemed to be lost in its shadow. The record also came to be linked to the emerging idea of New Age music in America during the 1970s, suggesting its use for purposes such as relaxation or meditation, far from the view of music that Jarrett espoused. Yet it remains a highly significant recording for several reasons. It helped to establish ECM as a major force in jazz, as well demonstrating Manfred Eicher’s complete faith in Jarrett’s abilities. And it established that in a decade when so much jazz was associated with the trappings of amplified and electric instruments, it was possible for acoustic improvised music to connect deeply with an audience, an audience who would not necessarily have considered themselves jazz fans.

*Peter Elsdon is Senior Lecturer in Music at the University of Hull in the UK, and the author* *of “Keith Jarrett’s The Köln Concert,” published by Oxford University Press.*

## 1964 was a great year for cutting-edge jazz records like Albert Ayler’s _Spiritual Unity_, John Coltrane’s _A Love Supreme_ and Andrew Hill’s _Point of Departure_.

But none sounds as far ahead of its time as Eric Dolphy’s masterpiece [_Out to Lunch_](http://amzn.to/2htnlrL), recorded for Blue Note on Feb. 25, 1964. Half a century later it still sounds crazy in a good way. The organized mayhem starts with Dolphy’s tunes, often featuring wide, wide leaps in the melody and ratchet-gear rhythms. His composition “Straight Up and Down” was inspired by the careful walk of a drunk striving to stay upright. He improvised with that same kind of angular energy, and an excitable tone like a goosed goose.

## [Out to Lunch](http://amzn.to/2htnlrL) stands as Eric Dolphy’s magnum opus, an absolute pinnacle of avant-garde jazz in any form or era.

Its rhythmic complexity was perhaps unrivaled since Dave Brubeck’s Time Out, and its five Dolphy originals — the jarring Monk tribute “Hat and Beard,” the aptly titled “Something Sweet, Something Tender,” the weirdly jaunty flute showcase “Gazzelloni,” the militaristic title track, the drunken lurch of “Straight Up and Down” — were a perfect balance of structured frameworks, carefully calibrated timbres, and generous individual freedom. Much has been written about Dolphy’s odd time signatures, wide-interval leaps, and flirtations with atonality. And those preoccupations reach their peak on [Out to Lunch](http://amzn.to/2htnlrL), which is less rooted in bop tradition than anything Dolphy had ever done. But that sort of analytical description simply doesn’t do justice to the utterly alien effect of the album’s jagged soundscapes.

Dolphy uses those pet devices for their evocative power and unnerving hints of dementia, not some abstract intellectual exercise. His solos and themes aren’t just angular and dissonant — they’re hugely so, with a definite playfulness that becomes more apparent with every listen. The whole ensemble — trumpeter Freddie Hubbard, vibist Bobby Hutcherson, bassist Richard Davis, and drummer Tony Williams — takes full advantage of the freedom Dolphy offers, but special mention has to be made of Hutcherson, who has fully perfected his pianoless accompaniment technique. His creepy, floating chords and quick stabs of dissonance anchor the album’s texture, and he punctuates the soloists’ lines at the least expected times, suggesting completely different pulses. Meanwhile, Dolphy’s stuttering vocal-like effects and oddly placed pauses often make his bass clarinet lines sound like they’re tripping over themselves. Just as the title [Out to Lunch](http://amzn.to/2htnlrL) suggests, this is music that sounds like nothing so much as a mad gleam in its creator’s eyes.

The heart of _Out to Lunch_ is its singular vibes-bass-and-drums rhythm trio, starting with Miles Davis’ 18-year-old drum wonder Tony Williams. The following year, Williams would propose to Davis’ band that they play “anti-music” — the opposite of what anyone would expect. Williams is already testing that idea on _Out to Lunch_, rethinking the drum set’s components; his hi-hat alone makes this one of his classics. On “Hat and Beard,” the title a nod to Thelonious Monk, Williams finds myriad ways to provoke Dolphy’s yawping bass clarinet, an instrument Dolphy had pretty much to himself as a soloist.

Williams isn’t the only one avoiding the obvious. Bobby Hutcherson made [_Out to Lunch_](http://amzn.to/2htnlrL) about the weirdest vibraphone showcase ever. More than anyone he gives the album its futuristic quality. All vibists lean on the sustain pedal, to let notes ring like doorbells. But here Hutcherson also takes his foot off the pedal and strikes the metal bars hard, for a rude clanky sound akin to Monk’s piano. Like Monk he leaves in a lot of open space, refers back to the melody often, and uses oblique strategies to prod horn soloists: Dolphy on alto, bass clarinet and flute, and trumpeter Freddie Hubbard.

The equally resourceful bassist is sure-footed Richard Davis. His playing here is a compendium of modern bass strategies: He’ll walk fast, sing with a bow, play counterpoint, toy with the melody, or stubbornly stand his ground. Their interaction anticipates some of what Williams would soon get up to in Miles Davis’ rhythm section.

Dolphy’s creativity was exploding early in 1964, and he was finding more players who could keep up. He was looking forward to spending a year in Europe. But even before the album came out, he was dead of diabetic complications at age 36.

[_Out to Lunch_](http://amzn.to/2htnlrL) was too odd to be an immediate trendsetter, but in time you could hear its influence in Anthony Braxton’s or Roscoe Mitchell’s zigzag solos and odd timbres, in David Murray’s yawping bass clarinet and Jason Adasiewicz’s clanking vibes. You can also hear it in ambitious music by all sorts of modern composers who grapple with the same kind of contradictions Dolphy did. [_Out to Lunch_](http://amzn.to/2htnlrL) is free and focused, dissonant and catchy, wide open and swinging all at once. Fifty years on, there’s plenty there to there to be inspired by.

# OutToLunchWithEricDolphy  - Out To Lunch With Eric Dolphy

April 29, 2013

Free-flying Eric Dolphy veered into the contrarian zone in his musical approach on his one and only Blue Note album, _Out to Lunch_. Breaking away from the clichés of postbop jazz and speaking boldly on his array of instruments (flute and alto sax as well as bass clarinet, seldom heard at the time but sounding profoundly visceral in his hands), Dolphy displayed the avant-garde modus operandi to expect the unexpected. The sometimes abstract and off-kilter yet often whimsical album turned heads and opened ears immediately, and it has gone down in jazz history as one of the genre’s masterpieces. A must-hear. A best bet. A revelation.

The recording took place on February 25, 1964 at engineer Rudy Van Gelder’s Englewood Cliffs, N.J., studio—the home base where most of the Blue Note catalog was being documented. While Dolphy returned to Van Gelder Studio less than a month later as a sideman on Andrew Hill’s _Point of Departure_ on Blue Note, _Out to Lunch_, comprising five Dolphy compositions, proved to be his finale as a leader.

At the age of 36, the Los Angeles native and New York emigrant tragically died on June 29, 1964 in Berlin after setting off on tour to Europe with longtime friend/collective collaborator Charles Mingus as a member of the bassist’s sextet. Much to Mingus’s chagrin, Dolphy told him while on tour that he was staying put on the continent. He had already made that plan while recording _Out to Lunch_, sharing with the album’s original liner note writer A.B. Spellman that he was going to live in Europe for a spell “because I can get more work there playing my own music, and because if you try to do anything different in this country, people put you down for it.”

The angular nature of _Out to Lunch_ may have short-fused some listeners at the time of its release (Miles Davis famously said that he’d like to stomp on the saxophonist’s head). But today, nearly a half-century later, what the mercurial Dolphy concocted with his youthful quintet—two relatively new-on-the-scene cats, trumpeter Freddie Hubbard and vibraphonist Bobby Hutcherson; wunderkind drummer Tony Williams, who was 18 at the time; and bassist Richard Davis, who the leader had enlisted for his 1961 Booker Little date, _At the Five Spot_, in 1961 and later for _Iron Man_ in 1963—sounds so cutting-edge and vital, serving as an important link to what would take place in jazz during the rest of the decade (including in Davis’s own classic ‘60s quintet, with the free improvisation spurred on in part by rhythm maestro Williams).

_Out to Lunch_ captivates from the get-go with the out-leaning “Hat and Beard,” inspired by Thelonious Monk, who in the original liners, Dolphy described as “so musical no matter what he’s doing, even if he’s just walking around.” The playfully creeping 5/4 bass line served up by the leader’s loopy bass clarinet and Davis’s steady acoustic bass creates the perfect 9/4 vehicle for the solos. Of particular note is Hutcherson’s plunks, splashes and shimmers that have a prankster vibe. He contributes unpredictable floating accents and wink-in-the-eye drop-ins throughout the session.

Hubbard and Dolphy connect brilliantly on the slow-paced “Something Sweet, Something Tender,” while the leader flits and twitters on the flute through his “Gazzelloni” tribute to classical flautist Severino Gazzelloni. The capricious title tune, originally the opening track on the second side of the LP, is an irregular epic piece that has extended explorations by each band member, including Dolphy’s twisted alto lines, Hubbard’s soaring trumpet support and the exhilarant rhythm driven by Williams and Davis. The end song, “Straight Up and Down,” is in Dolphy’s words, a tune about a drunkard walking, with the appropriate wobble and weave. After a break of inebriated free playing, the group returns to the theme, walking the straight line without a misstep.

_Out to Lunch is_ a thoroughly engaging 42 minutes of the most profound and far-reaching jazz recorded in 1964. While there’s a flair for the esoteric, it all makes sense upon close listen. After finishing “Straight Up and Down,” don’t be surprised if you stream right back to the “Hat and Beard” beginning. It’s worth the second ride.
