[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-marriage-1) | | Children | 1 | | | | | | Website | [herbiehancock.com](http://herbiehancock.com/) | Musical artist **Herbert Jeffrey Hancock** (born April 12, 1940) is an American [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") musician, bandleader, and composer.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-Britannica-2) He started his career with trumpeter [Donald Byrd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Byrd "Donald Byrd")'s group. Hancock soon joined the [Miles Davis Quintet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis_Quintet "Miles Davis Quintet"), where he helped to redefine the role of a jazz [rhythm section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_section "Rhythm section") and was one of the primary architects of the [post-bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-bop "Post-bop") sound. In the 1970s, he experimented with [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion"), [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk"), and [electro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electro-funk "Electro-funk") styles using a wide array of [synthesizers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthesizers "Synthesizers") and electronics. It was during this time that he released one of his best-known and most influential albums, _[Head Hunters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_Hunters "Head Hunters")_.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-3) Hancock's best-known compositions include " [Cantaloupe Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantaloupe_Island "Cantaloupe Island")", " [Watermelon Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watermelon_Man_(composition) "Watermelon Man (composition)")", " [Maiden Voyage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maiden_Voyage_(composition) "Maiden Voyage (composition)")", and " [Chameleon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chameleon_(composition) "Chameleon (composition)")", all of which are [jazz standards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_standard "Jazz standard"). During the 1980s, he had a hit single with the electronic instrumental " [Rockit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockit_(song) "Rockit (song)")", a collaboration with bassist/producer [Bill Laswell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Laswell "Bill Laswell"). Hancock has won an [Academy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards") and 14 [Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Awards "Grammy Awards"), including [Album of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Album_of_the_Year "Grammy Award for Album of the Year") for his 2007 album _[River: The Joni Letters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River:_The_Joni_Letters "River: The Joni Letters")_, a tribute to his friend [Joni Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joni_Mitchell "Joni Mitchell"). In 2024, [Neil McCormick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_McCormick "Neil McCormick") of _[The Daily Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Daily_Telegraph "The Daily Telegraph")_ ranked Hancock as the greatest keyboard player of all time.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-4) In 2025, he received the [Polar Music Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polar_Music_Prize "Polar Music Prize"). Since 2012, Hancock has served as a professor at the [University of California, Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Los_Angeles "University of California, Los Angeles"), where he teaches at the [UCLA Herb Alpert School of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UCLA_Herb_Alpert_School_of_Music "UCLA Herb Alpert School of Music").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-schoolofmusic.ucla.edu-5) He is also the chairman of the [Herbie Hancock Institute of Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock_Institute_of_Jazz "Herbie Hancock Institute of Jazz")[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-schoolofmusic.ucla.edu-5) (known as the [Thelonious Monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thelonious_Monk "Thelonious Monk") Institute of Jazz until 2019). ## Early life \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Herbie_Hancock&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Early life")\] Hancock was born in [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago"), [Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois "Illinois"), the son of Winnie Belle (née Griffin), a secretary, and Wayman Edward Hancock, a meat inspector for the government. His parents named him after the singer and actor [Herb Jeffries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Jeffries "Herb Jeffries").[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-6) Hancock attended [Hyde Park High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyde_Park_Academy_High_School "Hyde Park Academy High School") in Chicago.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-7) He began playing the piano at the age of seven, and his talent was recognized early on. Like many [jazz pianists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_pianist "Jazz pianist"), Herbie took [classical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_music "Classical music") piano lessons.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-8) Considered to be a [child prodigy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_prodigy "Child prodigy"),[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-Prodigy-9) he played the first movement of [Mozart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfgang_Amadeus_Mozart "Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart")'s [Piano Concerto No. 26 in D Major, K. 537 _(Coronation)_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._26_(Mozart) "Piano Concerto No. 26 (Mozart)") at a young people's concert on February 5, 1952, with the [Chicago Symphony Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Symphony_Orchestra "Chicago Symphony Orchestra") (led by CSO assistant conductor [George Schick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Schick "George Schick")) at the age of 11.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-grove-10) During his teenage years, Herbie Hancock did not have a jazz teacher. He developed his ear and sense of harmony by listening to _[Hard Bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_Bop_(album) "Hard Bop (album)")_ by [Art Blakey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Blakey "Art Blakey")'s [the Jazz Messengers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Jazz_Messengers "The Jazz Messengers"), _[Birth of the Cool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_of_the_Cool "Birth of the Cool")_ by [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis"), and the recordings of jazz pianists, including [George Shearing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Shearing "George Shearing"), [Erroll Garner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erroll_Garner "Erroll Garner"), [Bill Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans "Bill Evans") and [Oscar Peterson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oscar_Peterson "Oscar Peterson"). Hancock was also influenced by records of the vocal group [the Hi-Lo's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hi-Lo's "The Hi-Lo's"). In his words: > By the time I actually heard the Hi-Lo's, I started picking that stuff out; my ear was happening. I could hear stuff and that's when I really learned some much farther-out voicings – like the harmonies I used on _Speak Like a Child_ – just being able to do that. I really got that from [Clare Fischer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clare_Fischer "Clare Fischer")'s arrangements for the Hi-Lo's. Clare Fischer was a major influence on my harmonic concept... he and [Bill Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans "Bill Evans"), and [Ravel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Ravel "Maurice Ravel") and [Gil Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gil_Evans "Gil Evans"), finally. You know, that's where it came from.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-11) In 1960, Hancock heard [Chris Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Anderson_(pianist) "Chris Anderson (pianist)") play just once and begged him to accept him as a student.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-Mapleshade_testimonial-12) Hancock often mentions Anderson as his harmonic guru.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-13) Hancock graduated from [Grinnell College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grinnell_College "Grinnell College") in [Grinnell, Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grinnell,_Iowa "Grinnell, Iowa"), in 1960,[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-Grinnell-14) with degrees in electrical engineering and music. Hancock then moved back to Chicago,[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-Grinnell-14) and began working with [Donald Byrd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Byrd "Donald Byrd") and [Coleman Hawkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coleman_Hawkins "Coleman Hawkins"). During this time, he also took courses at [Roosevelt University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roosevelt_University "Roosevelt University").[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-15) Grinnell also awarded him an honorary Doctor of Fine Arts degree in 1972.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-grove-10)[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-16) Byrd was attending the [Manhattan School of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan_School_of_Music "Manhattan School of Music") in New York at the time and suggested that Hancock study composition with [Vittorio Giannini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vittorio_Giannini "Vittorio Giannini") (which he did for a short time in 1960). The pianist quickly earned a reputation, and played subsequent sessions with [Oliver Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Nelson "Oliver Nelson") and [Phil Woods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Woods "Phil Woods"). Hancock recorded his first solo album, _[Takin' Off](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takin'_Off "Takin' Off")_, for [Blue Note Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records") in 1962. " [Watermelon Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watermelon_Man_(composition) "Watermelon Man (composition)")" (from _Takin' Off_) was to provide [Mongo Santamaría](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongo_Santamar%C3%ADa "Mongo Santamaría") with a hit single, but more importantly for Hancock, _Takin' Off_ caught the attention of [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis"), who was at that time assembling a new band. Hancock was introduced to Davis by the young drummer [Tony Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer) "Tony Williams (drummer)"), a member of the new band. ## Career \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Herbie_Hancock&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Career")\] ### Miles Davis Quintet (1963–1968) and Blue Note Records (1962–1969) \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Herbie_Hancock&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Miles Davis Quintet (1963–1968) and Blue Note Records (1962–1969)")\] Hancock received considerable attention when, in May 1963,[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-grove-10) he joined Davis's [Second Great Quintet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis_Quintet#Second_Great_Quintet_(1964%E2%80%9368) "Miles Davis Quintet"). Davis personally sought out Hancock, whom he saw as one of the most promising talents in jazz. The [rhythm section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_section "Rhythm section") that Davis organized was young but effective, comprising bassist [Ron Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Carter "Ron Carter"), 17-year-old drummer Tony Williams, and Hancock on piano. After [George Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Coleman "George Coleman") and [Sam Rivers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Rivers_(jazz_musician) "Sam Rivers (jazz musician)") each took a turn at the saxophone spot, the quintet gelled with [Wayne Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter "Wayne Shorter") on tenor saxophone. This quintet is often regarded as one of the finest jazz ensembles yet.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-17) While in Davis's band, Hancock also found time to record dozens of sessions for the Blue Note label, both under his own name and as a [sideman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sideman "Sideman") with other musicians such as [Wayne Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter "Wayne Shorter"), Williams, [Grant Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grant_Green "Grant Green"), [Bobby Hutcherson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Hutcherson "Bobby Hutcherson"), Rivers, Byrd, [Kenny Dorham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Dorham "Kenny Dorham"), [Hank Mobley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hank_Mobley "Hank Mobley"), [Lee Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Morgan "Lee Morgan"), [Freddie Hubbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Hubbard "Freddie Hubbard"), and [Eric Dolphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy "Eric Dolphy"). Hancock also recorded several lesser known but still critically acclaimed albums with larger ensembles – _[My Point of View](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_Point_of_View "My Point of View")_ (1963), _[Speak Like a Child](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Like_a_Child_(album) "Speak Like a Child (album)")_ (1968) and _[The Prisoner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Prisoner_(album) "The Prisoner (album)")_ (1969), albums that featured [flugelhorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flugelhorn "Flugelhorn"), [alto flute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alto_flute "Alto flute") and [bass trombone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_trombone "Bass trombone") in addition to the traditional jazz instrumentation. 1963's _[Inventions and Dimensions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inventions_and_Dimensions "Inventions and Dimensions")_ was an album of almost entirely improvised music, teaming Hancock with bassist [Paul Chambers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Chambers "Paul Chambers") and two Latin percussionists, [Willie Bobo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Bobo "Willie Bobo") and Osvaldo "Chihuahua" Martinez. During that period, Hancock also composed the [score](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_scores "Film scores") to [Michelangelo Antonioni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelangelo_Antonioni "Michelangelo Antonioni")'s film _[Blowup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blowup "Blowup")_ (1966), the first of many film [soundtracks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soundtrack "Soundtrack") he recorded in his career. As well as feature film soundtracks, Hancock recorded a number of musical themes used on American television commercials for such well-known products as [Pillsbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pillsbury_Company "Pillsbury Company")'s [Space Food Sticks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Food_Sticks "Space Food Sticks"), [Standard Oil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_Oil "Standard Oil"), [Tab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tab_(soft_drink) "Tab (soft drink)") diet cola, and [Virginia Slims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Slims "Virginia Slims") cigarettes. Hancock also wrote, arranged and conducted a spy type theme for a series of [F. William Free](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F._William_Free "F. William Free") commercials for Silva Thins cigarettes. Hancock liked it so much he wished to record it as a song but the ad agency would not let him. He rewrote the harmony, tempo and tone and recorded the piece as the track "He Who Lives in Fear" from his _The Prisoner_ album of 1969.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-18) Davis had begun incorporating elements of rock and popular music into his recordings by the end of Hancock's tenure with the band. Despite some initial reluctance, Hancock began doubling on electric [keyboards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keyboard_instruments "Keyboard instruments"), including the [Fender Rhodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fender_Rhodes "Fender Rhodes") [electric piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_piano "Electric piano") at Davis's insistence. Hancock adapted quickly to the new instruments, which proved to be important in his future artistic endeavors. In the summer of 1968, after being dismissed from Davis' band under the pretext that he had returned late from a honeymoon in [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil"), Hancock formed his own sextet.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-19) Despite his departure from the band—which was disbanded soon after—Hancock continued to appear on Davis’ records for the next few years. His appearances included _[In a Silent Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way "In a Silent Way")_, _[A Tribute to Jack Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Tribute_to_Jack_Johnson "A Tribute to Jack Johnson"),_ and _[On the Corner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner "On the Corner")_. ### _Fat Albert_ (1969) and Mwandishi era (1971–1973) \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Herbie_Hancock&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: Fat Albert (1969) and Mwandishi era (1971–1973)")\] [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e9/Herbie_hancock_1970.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Herbie_hancock_1970.png) Hancock c. 1970 Hancock left Blue Note in 1969, signing with [Warner Bros. Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros._Records "Warner Bros. Records"). In 1969, Hancock composed the soundtrack for [Bill Cosby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Cosby "Bill Cosby")'s animated prime-time television special _[Hey, Hey, Hey, It's Fat Albert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey,_Hey,_Hey,_It's_Fat_Albert "Hey, Hey, Hey, It's Fat Albert")_.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-20) Music from the soundtrack was later included on _[Fat Albert Rotunda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fat_Albert_Rotunda "Fat Albert Rotunda")_ (1969), an [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues")-inspired album with strong jazz overtones. One of the jazzier songs on the record, the moody ballad "Tell Me a Bedtime Story", was later re-worked as a more electronic sounding song for the [Quincy Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quincy_Jones "Quincy Jones") album _[Sounds...and Stuff Like That!!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sounds...and_Stuff_Like_That!! "Sounds...and Stuff Like That!!")_ (1978). Hancock became fascinated with electronic musical instruments. Together with the profound influence of Davis's _[Bitches Brew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew "Bitches Brew")_ (1970), this fascination culminated in a series of albums in which electronic instruments were coupled with acoustic instruments. Hancock's first ventures into [electronic music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_music "Electronic music") started with a sextet comprising Hancock, bassist [Buster Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buster_Williams "Buster Williams") and drummer [Billy Hart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Hart "Billy Hart"), and a trio of horn players: [Eddie Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Henderson_(musician) "Eddie Henderson (musician)") (trumpet), [Julian Priester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_Priester "Julian Priester") ( [trombone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trombone "Trombone")), and [multireedist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multireedist "Multireedist") [Bennie Maupin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bennie_Maupin "Bennie Maupin"). [Patrick Gleeson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Gleeson "Patrick Gleeson") was eventually added to the mix to play and program the synthesizers. The sextet, later a septet with the addition of Gleeson, made three albums under Hancock's name: _[Mwandishi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mwandishi "Mwandishi")_ (1971), _[Crossings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossings_(Herbie_Hancock_album) "Crossings (Herbie Hancock album)")_ (1972) (both on Warner Bros. Records), and _[Sextant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sextant_(album) "Sextant (album)")_ (1973) (released on [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records")); two more, _[Realization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Realization_(Eddie_Henderson_album) "Realization (Eddie Henderson album)")_ and _[Inside Out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inside_Out_(Eddie_Henderson_album) "Inside Out (Eddie Henderson album)")_, were recorded under Henderson's name with essentially the same personnel. The music exhibited strong improvisational aspect beyond the confines of jazz mainstream and showed influence from the electronic music of [contemporary classical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_classical_music "Contemporary classical music") composers. Hancock's three records released in 1971–73 later became known as the "Mwandishi" albums, so-called after a [Swahili](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swahili_language "Swahili language") name Hancock sometimes used during this era (" _Mwandishi_" is [Swahili](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swahili "Swahili") for "writer"). The first two, including _[Fat Albert Rotunda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fat_Albert_Rotunda "Fat Albert Rotunda")_, were made available on the two-CD set _Mwandishi: the Complete Warner Bros. Recordings_, released in 1994. "Hornets" was later revised on the 2001 album _[Future2Future](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Future2Future "Future2Future")_ as "Virtual Hornets". Among the instruments Hancock and Gleeson used were [Fender Rhodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fender_Rhodes "Fender Rhodes") piano, [ARP Odyssey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARP_Odyssey "ARP Odyssey"), [ARP 2600](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARP_2600 "ARP 2600"), [ARP Pro Soloist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARP_Pro_Soloist "ARP Pro Soloist") Synthesizer, a [Mellotron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mellotron "Mellotron") and the [Moog synthesizer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moog_synthesizer "Moog synthesizer") III. ### From _Head Hunters_ (1973) to _Secrets_ (1976) \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Herbie_Hancock&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: From Head Hunters (1973) to Secrets (1976)")\] See also: [Head Hunters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_Hunters "Head Hunters") [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/79/Herbie_Hancock_and_The_Headhunters_1975.JPG/250px-Herbie_Hancock_and_The_Headhunters_1975.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Herbie_Hancock_and_The_Headhunters_1975.JPG) Hancock (left) with the Headhunters, 1975 Hancock formed [the Headhunters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Headhunters "The Headhunters"), keeping only Maupin from the sextet and adding bassist [Paul Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Jackson_(bassist) "Paul Jackson (bassist)"), percussionist [Bill Summers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Summers_(musician) "Bill Summers (musician)"), and drummer [Harvey Mason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_Mason "Harvey Mason"). The album _[Head Hunters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_Hunters_(album) "Head Hunters (album)")_ (1973) was a hit, crossing over to pop audiences but criticized within his jazz audience.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-21) [Stephen Erlewine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Erlewine "Stephen Erlewine"), in a retrospective summary for [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic"), said, " _Head Hunters_ still sounds fresh and vital three decades after its initial release, and its genre-bending proved vastly influential on not only jazz, but funk, soul, and hip-hop."[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-Headhunters_''Allmusic''_review-22) Brian Case and Stan Britt dismissed the album as uninteresting in _The Illustrated Encyclopedia of Jazz_ in 1978.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-23) Drummer Mason was replaced by [Mike Clark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Clark_(jazz_musician) "Mike Clark (jazz musician)"), and the band released a second album, _[Thrust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrust_(album) "Thrust (album)")_, in 1974. (A live album from a Japan performance, consisting of compositions from those first two _Head Hunters_ releases was released in 1975 as _[Flood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flood_(Herbie_Hancock_album) "Flood (Herbie Hancock album)")_). This was almost as well received as its predecessor, if not attaining the same level of commercial success. The Headhunters made another successful album called _[Survival of the Fittest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Survival_of_the_Fittest_(The_Headhunters_album) "Survival of the Fittest (The Headhunters album)")_ in 1975 without Hancock, while Hancock himself started to make even more commercial albums, often featuring members of the band, but no longer billed as the Headhunters. The Headhunters reunited with Hancock in 1998 for _Return of the Headhunters_, and a version of the band (featuring Clark) continues to play and record. In 1973, Hancock was commissioned to compose the soundtrack for the controversial film _[The Spook Who Sat by the Door](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spook_Who_Sat_by_the_Door_(film) "The Spook Who Sat by the Door (film)")_, based on the [novel of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spook_Who_Sat_by_the_Door_(novel) "The Spook Who Sat by the Door (novel)") by [Sam Greenlee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Greenlee "Sam Greenlee"), who had grown up in the same neighborhood of Chicago as Hancock.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-24)[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-25)[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-26) In the following year, Hancock composed the soundtrack to the first _[Death Wish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_Wish_(1974_film) "Death Wish (1974 film)")_ film. One of his songs, "Joanna's Theme", was re-recorded in 1997 on his duet album with Shorter, _[1+1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1+1_(Herbie_Hancock_and_Wayne_Shorter_album) "1+1 (Herbie Hancock and Wayne Shorter album)")_. Hancock's next jazz-funk albums of the 1970s were _[Man-Child](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man-Child "Man-Child")_ (1975) and _[Secrets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secrets_(Herbie_Hancock_album) "Secrets (Herbie Hancock album)")_ (1976), which point toward the more commercial direction Hancock would take over the next decade. These albums feature the members of the Headhunters band, but also a variety of other musicians in important roles. ### From _V.S.O.P._ (1976) to _Future Shock_ (1983) \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Herbie_Hancock&action=edit§ion=6 "Edit section: From V.S.O.P. (1976) to Future Shock (1983)")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d7/Herbie_Hancock_1976.JPG/250px-Herbie_Hancock_1976.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Herbie_Hancock_1976.JPG) Hancock in 1976 In 1978, Hancock recorded a duet with [Chick Corea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chick_Corea "Chick Corea"), who replaced him in the Davis band a decade earlier. Hancock also released a solo acoustic piano album, _[The Piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Piano_(Herbie_Hancock_album) "The Piano (Herbie Hancock album)")_ (1979), which was released only in Japan. (It was released in the US in 2004). Other Japan-only albums include _[Dedication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedication_(Herbie_Hancock_album) "Dedication (Herbie Hancock album)")_ (1974), _[V.S.O.P.'s Tempest in the Colosseum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VSOP:_Tempest_in_the_Colosseum "VSOP: Tempest in the Colosseum")_ (1977), and _[Direct Step](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_Step "Direct Step")_ (1978). In 1977, after what one critic called due to "perhaps pangs of conscience," he formed VSOP with the Miles Davis classic quintet with Freddie Hubbard in Miles' role. The album _[The Quintet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Quintet_(album) "The Quintet (album)")_ was recorded live and released to critical acclaim. _[VSOP: Live Under the Sky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VSOP:_Live_Under_the_Sky "VSOP: Live Under the Sky")_ was a VSOP album remastered for the US in 2004 and included a second concert from the tour in July 1979. From 1978 to 1982, Hancock recorded many albums of jazz-inflected [disco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disco "Disco") and pop music, beginning with _[Sunlight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunlight_(jazz_album) "Sunlight (jazz album)")_ (featuring guest musicians including Williams and Pastorius on the last track) (1978). Singing through a [vocoder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vocoder "Vocoder"), he earned a British hit,[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-British_Hit_Singles_&_Albums-27) "I Thought It Was You", although critics were unimpressed.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-28) This led to more vocoder on his next album, _[Feets, Don't Fail Me Now](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feets,_Don't_Fail_Me_Now "Feets, Don't Fail Me Now")_ (1979), which gave him another UK hit in "You Bet Your Love".[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-British_Hit_Singles_&_Albums-27) Hancock toured with Williams and Carter in 1981, recording _[Herbie Hancock Trio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock_Trio_(1982_album) "Herbie Hancock Trio (1982 album)")_, a five-track album released only in Japan. A month later, he recorded _[Quartet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quartet_(Herbie_Hancock_album) "Quartet (Herbie Hancock album)")_ with trumpeter [Wynton Marsalis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wynton_Marsalis "Wynton Marsalis"), released in the US the following year. Hancock, Williams, and Carter toured internationally with Wynton Marsalis and his brother, saxophonist [Branford Marsalis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Branford_Marsalis "Branford Marsalis"), in what was known as "VSOP II". This quintet can be heard on Wynton Marsalis's debut album on Columbia (1981). In 1984 VSOP II performed at the Playboy Jazz Festival as a sextet with Hancock, Williams, Carter, the Marsalis Brothers, and [Bobby McFerrin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_McFerrin "Bobby McFerrin"). In 1982, Hancock contributed to the album _[New Gold Dream (81,82,83,84)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Gold_Dream_(81,82,83,84) "New Gold Dream (81,82,83,84)")_ by [Simple Minds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simple_Minds "Simple Minds"), playing a synthesizer solo on the track "Hunter and the Hunted". In 1983, Hancock had a pop hit with the Grammy Award-winning single " [Rockit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockit_(song) "Rockit (song)")" from the album _[Future Shock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Future_Shock_(Herbie_Hancock_album) "Future Shock (Herbie Hancock album)")_. It was the first [jazz hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_rap "Jazz rap") song[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-Koskoff2005-29)[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-Price2006-30)[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-Keyes2002-31) and became a worldwide anthem for [breakdancers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breakdancer "Breakdancer") and for hip-hop in the 1980s.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-32)[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-33) It was the first mainstream single to feature [scratching](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scratching "Scratching"), and also featured an innovative animated music video, which was directed by [Godley and Creme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Godley_and_Creme "Godley and Creme") and showed several robot-like artworks by [Jim Whiting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Whiting "Jim Whiting"). The video was a hit on [MTV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTV "MTV") and reached No.8 in the UK.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-complete-34) The video won in five categories at the inaugural [MTV Video Music Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTV_Video_Music_Awards "MTV Video Music Awards"). This single ushered in a collaboration with noted bassist and producer [Bill Laswell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Laswell "Bill Laswell"). Hancock experimented with electronic music on a string of three LPs produced by Laswell: _Future Shock_ (1983), the Grammy Award-winning _[Sound-System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound-System_(album) "Sound-System (album)")_ (1984), and _[Perfect Machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_Machine_(album) "Perfect Machine (album)")_ (1988). During that period he appeared onstage at the [Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Awards "Grammy Awards") with [Stevie Wonder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stevie_Wonder "Stevie Wonder"), [Howard Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Jones_(British_musician) "Howard Jones (British musician)"), and [Thomas Dolby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Dolby "Thomas Dolby"), in a synthesizer [jam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jam_band "Jam band"). Lesser known works from the 1980s are the live album _[Jazz Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Africa "Jazz Africa")_ (1987) and the studio album _[Village Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Village_Life_(album) "Village Life (album)")_ (1984), which were recorded with [Gambian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gambia "Gambia") [kora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kora_(instrument) "Kora (instrument)") player [Foday Musa Suso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foday_Musa_Suso "Foday Musa Suso"). In 1985, Hancock performed as a guest on the album _[So Red the Rose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/So_Red_the_Rose_(album) "So Red the Rose (album)")_ (1985) by the [Duran Duran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duran_Duran "Duran Duran") spinoff group [Arcadia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arcadia_(band) "Arcadia (band)"). He also provided introductory and closing comments for the [PBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PBS "PBS") rebroadcast in the United States of the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC") educational series from the mid-1980s, _[Rockschool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockschool "Rockschool")_ (not to be confused with the most recent _Gene Simmons' Rock School_ series). In 1986, Hancock performed and acted in the film _[Round Midnight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Round_Midnight_(film) "Round Midnight (film)")_. He also wrote the score/soundtrack, for which he won an [Academy Award for Original Music Score](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Original_Music_Score "Academy Award for Original Music Score"). His film work was prolific during the 1980s, and included the scores to _[A Soldier's Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Soldier's_Story "A Soldier's Story")_ (1984), _[Jo Jo Dancer, Your Life Is Calling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jo_Jo_Dancer,_Your_Life_Is_Calling "Jo Jo Dancer, Your Life Is Calling")_ (1986), _[Action Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_Jackson_(1988_film) "Action Jackson (1988 film)")_ (1988 with [Michael Kamen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Kamen "Michael Kamen")), _[Colors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colors_(1988_film) "Colors (1988 film)")_ (1988), and the [Eddie Murphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Murphy "Eddie Murphy") comedy _[Harlem Nights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlem_Nights "Harlem Nights")_ (1989). He would also write music for television commercials, with "Maiden Voyage" starting out as a cologne advertisement. At the end of the _Perfect Machine_ tour, Hancock decided to leave Columbia Records after a 15-plus-year relationship. ### 1990s to 2000 \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Herbie_Hancock&action=edit§ion=7 "Edit section: 1990s to 2000")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/40/Herbie_Hancock-Chameleon_Live.jpg/250px-Herbie_Hancock-Chameleon_Live.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Herbie_Hancock-Chameleon_Live.jpg) Hancock playing keytar in [La Spezia, Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Province_of_La_Spezia "Province of La Spezia"), July 2008 The departure led to a hiatus from recording and the release of several compilations during the first half of the 1990s.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-:0-35) He returned with Carter, Williams, Shorter, and Davis admirer [Wallace Roney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallace_Roney "Wallace Roney") to record _[A Tribute to Miles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Tribute_to_Miles "A Tribute to Miles")_, which was released in 1994. The album contained two live recordings and studio recording songs, with Roney playing Davis's part as trumpet player. The album won a Grammy for best group album. Hancock also toured with [Jack DeJohnette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_DeJohnette "Jack DeJohnette"), [Dave Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Holland_(bassist) "Dave Holland (bassist)"), and [Pat Metheny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pat_Metheny "Pat Metheny") in 1990 on their _[Parallel Realities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallel_Realities "Parallel Realities")_ tour which included a performance at the [Montreux Jazz Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreux_Jazz_Festival "Montreux Jazz Festival") in July 1990, and scored the 1991 comedy film _[Livin' Large](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Livin'_Large "Livin' Large")_, which starred [Terrence C. Carson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrence_C._Carson "Terrence C. Carson"). Hancock's next album, _[Dis Is da Drum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dis_Is_da_Drum "Dis Is da Drum")_, released in 1994 is a return to [acid jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acid_jazz "Acid jazz"). Also in 1994, he appeared on the [Red Hot Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Hot_Organization "Red Hot Organization")'s compilation album _[Stolen Moments: Red Hot + Cool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stolen_Moments:_Red_Hot_+_Cool "Stolen Moments: Red Hot + Cool")_. The album, meant to raise awareness and funds in support of the AIDS epidemic in relation to the African-American community, was heralded as "Album of the Year" by _[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")_ magazine. In 1995, the release of _[The New Standard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_Standard_(Herbie_Hancock_album) "The New Standard (Herbie Hancock album)")_ had Hancock and an all-star band that included [John Scofield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Scofield "John Scofield"), DeJohnette and [Michael Brecker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Brecker "Michael Brecker"), interpreting pop songs by [Nirvana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nirvana_(band) "Nirvana (band)"), [Stevie Wonder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stevie_Wonder "Stevie Wonder"), [the Beatles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beatles "The Beatles"), [Prince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_(musician) "Prince (musician)"), [Peter Gabriel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel "Peter Gabriel"), and others. A 1997 duet album with Shorter, _[1+1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1+1_(Herbie_Hancock_and_Wayne_Shorter_album) "1+1 (Herbie Hancock and Wayne Shorter album)")_, was successful; the song "Aung San Suu Kyi" winning the Grammy Award for Best Instrumental Composition. Hancock also achieved great success in 1998 with his album _[Gershwin's World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gershwin's_World "Gershwin's World")_, which featured readings of [George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Gershwin "George Gershwin") and [Ira Gershwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ira_Gershwin "Ira Gershwin") standards by Hancock and a plethora of guest stars, including Stevie Wonder, [Joni Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joni_Mitchell "Joni Mitchell") and Shorter. Hancock toured the world in support of _Gershwin's World_ with a sextet featuring [Cyro Baptista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyro_Baptista "Cyro Baptista"), [Terri Lynne Carrington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terri_Lynne_Carrington "Terri Lynne Carrington"), [Ira Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ira_Coleman "Ira Coleman"), [Eli Degibri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eli_Degibri "Eli Degibri"), and [Eddie Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Henderson_(musician) "Eddie Henderson (musician)"). ### 2000 to 2009 \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Herbie_Hancock&action=edit§ion=8 "Edit section: 2000 to 2009")\] In 2001, Hancock recorded _[Future2Future](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Future2Future "Future2Future")_, which reunited Hancock with Laswell and featured doses of [electronica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronica "Electronica") as well as [turntablist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turntablist "Turntablist") [Rob Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rob_Swift "Rob Swift") of [the X-Ecutioners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_X-Ecutioners "The X-Ecutioners"). Hancock later toured with the band, and released a concert DVD with a different lineup, which also included the "Rockit" music video. Also in 2001 Hancock partnered with Brecker and [Roy Hargrove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Hargrove "Roy Hargrove") to record a live concert album saluting Davis and [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane"), _[Directions in Music: Live at Massey Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directions_in_Music:_Live_at_Massey_Hall "Directions in Music: Live at Massey Hall")_, recorded live in [Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto "Toronto"). The threesome toured to support the album, and toured on-and-off through 2005. [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/44/Herbie_Hancock_2006.jpg/250px-Herbie_Hancock_2006.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Herbie_Hancock_2006.jpg) Hancock performing at the [Tollwood Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tollwood_Festival "Tollwood Festival") in [Munich, Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich "Munich"), July 2006 A duet album called _[Possibilities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Possibilities "Possibilities")_ was released in 2005. It featured duets with [Carlos Santana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Santana "Carlos Santana"), [Paul Simon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Simon "Paul Simon"), [Annie Lennox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annie_Lennox "Annie Lennox"), [John Mayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Mayer "John Mayer"), [Christina Aguilera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christina_Aguilera "Christina Aguilera"), [Sting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sting_(musician) "Sting (musician)"), and others. In 2006, _Possibilities_ received nominations for Grammy Awards in two categories: "A Song for You" (featuring Aguilera) was nominated for a [Grammy Award for Best Pop Instrumental Performance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Pop_Instrumental_Performance "Grammy Award for Best Pop Instrumental Performance"), and "Gelo No Montanha" (featuring [Trey Anastasio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trey_Anastasio "Trey Anastasio") on guitar) was nominated for a [Grammy Award for Best Instrumental Performance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Instrumental_Performance "Grammy Award for Best Instrumental Performance"), although neither nomination resulted in an award. Also in 2005, Hancock toured Europe with a new quartet that included [Beninese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benin "Benin") guitarist [Lionel Loueke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionel_Loueke "Lionel Loueke") and explored textures ranging from [ambient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambient_music "Ambient music") to straight jazz to [African music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_music "African music"). During the summer, Hancock re-staffed the Headhunters and went on tour with them, including a performance at the [Bonnaroo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonnaroo "Bonnaroo") Music and Arts Festival. The lineup did not consist of any of the original Headhunters musicians. The group included [Marcus Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Miller "Marcus Miller"), Carrington, Loueke, and Mayer. Hancock also served as the first artist in residence for [Bonnaroo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonnaroo "Bonnaroo") in [Manchester, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester,_Tennessee "Manchester, Tennessee"), that summer. [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/Herbie_Hancock.jpg/250px-Herbie_Hancock.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Herbie_Hancock.jpg) Hancock playing a [Roland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roland_Corporation "Roland Corporation") AX-7 [keytar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keytar "Keytar"), at [The Roundhouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Roundhouse "The Roundhouse") in [Camden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Borough_of_Camden "London Borough of Camden"), London, November 2006 In 2006, [Sony BMG Music Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_BMG_Music_Entertainment "Sony BMG Music Entertainment") (which bought out Hancock's old label, Columbia Records) released the two-disc retrospective _[The Essential Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Essential_Herbie_Hancock "The Essential Herbie Hancock")_. This set was the first compilation of his work at Warner Bros., Blue Note, Columbia and [Verve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verve_Records "Verve Records")/ [Polygram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygram_Records "Polygram Records"). This became Hancock's second major compilation of work since the 2002 Columbia-only _The Herbie Hancock Box_, which was released at first in a plastic 4×4 cube then re-released in 2004 in a long box set. Also in 2006, Hancock recorded a new song with [Josh Groban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josh_Groban "Josh Groban") and Eric Mouquet (co-founder of [Deep Forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_Forest "Deep Forest")), "Machine", which featured on Groban's album _[Awake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Awake_(Josh_Groban_album) "Awake (Josh Groban album)")_. Hancock also recorded and improvised with guitarist Loueke on Loueke's 1996 debut album _Virgin Forest_, on the [ObliqSound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ObliqSound "ObliqSound") label, resulting in two improvisational tracks – "Le Réveil des agneaux (The Awakening of the Lambs)" and "La Poursuite du lion (The Lion's Pursuit)". Hancock, a longtime associate and friend of [Joni Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joni_Mitchell "Joni Mitchell"), released a 2007 album, _[River: The Joni Letters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River:_The_Joni_Letters "River: The Joni Letters")_, that paid tribute to her work, with [Norah Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norah_Jones "Norah Jones"), [Tina Turner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tina_Turner "Tina Turner"), and [Corinne Bailey Rae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corinne_Bailey_Rae "Corinne Bailey Rae") adding vocals to the album.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-36) [Leonard Cohen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Cohen "Leonard Cohen") contributed a spoken piece set to Hancock's piano. Mitchell herself also made an appearance. The album was released on September 25, 2007, simultaneously with the release of Mitchell's album _[Shine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shine_(Joni_Mitchell_album) "Shine (Joni Mitchell album)")_.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-37) _River_ won the 2008 Album of the Year Grammy Award. The album also won a Grammy for Best Contemporary Jazz Album, and the song " [Both Sides Now](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Both_Sides_Now_(song) "Both Sides Now (song)")" was nominated for Best Instrumental Jazz Solo, which made it only the second time in history that a jazz album won those two Grammy Awards. On June 14, 2008, Hancock performed with others at Rhythm on the Vine at the South Coast Winery in [Temecula, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temecula,_California "Temecula, California") for [Shriners Hospitals for Children](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shriners_Hospitals_for_Children "Shriners Hospitals for Children"). The event raised $515,000 for Shriners Hospital.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-aboutrotv-38) On January 18, 2009, Hancock performed at the [We Are One concert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/We_Are_One:_The_Obama_Inaugural_Celebration_at_the_Lincoln_Memorial "We Are One: The Obama Inaugural Celebration at the Lincoln Memorial"), marking the start of [inaugural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_inauguration_of_Barack_Obama "First inauguration of Barack Obama") celebrations for American President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama").[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-39) Hancock also performed _[Rhapsody in Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhapsody_in_Blue "Rhapsody in Blue")_ at the 2009 [Classical BRIT Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_BRIT_Awards "Classical BRIT Awards") with classical pianist [Lang Lang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lang_Lang "Lang Lang"). On February 27, 2025, Hancock was one of the 2025 laureates for the [Polar Music Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polar_Music_Prize "Polar Music Prize"), awarded in [Stockholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm "Stockholm"), [Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweden "Sweden").[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-52) ## Personal life \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Herbie_Hancock&action=edit§ion=10 "Edit section: Personal life")\] Hancock has been married to Gigi Hancock ([née](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_name#Maiden_and_married_names "Birth name") Meixner) since 1968[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-marriage-1) and the couple has a daughter. In a 2019 interview, Herbie said: "Gigi is very compassionate. She really cares about other people. She spends most of her time helping her friends. She has a big heart. At the same time she won't let you get away with anything. If you try to sneak something past her, she'll call you on it in a second. She got me into the pop art scene in New York in the 1960s and I introduced her to my jazz world."[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-53) In 1985, Hancock's sister, Jean, a computer consultant and a lyricist who wrote for him; [Earth, Wind & Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth,_Wind_&_Fire "Earth, Wind & Fire"); [Dianne Reeves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dianne_Reeves "Dianne Reeves"); and [Booker T. & the M.G.'s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Booker_T._&_the_M.G.'s "Booker T. & the M.G.'s"), was killed in the crash of [Delta Air Lines Flight 191](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delta_Air_Lines_Flight_191 "Delta Air Lines Flight 191").[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-54) In his memoir _Possibilities_, written with Lisa Dickey and published in 2014, Hancock revealed that he had previously battled an addiction to [crack cocaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crack_cocaine "Crack cocaine"), in the 1990s, and that his wife and daughter helped him get sober: "This was an intervention, and I was so embarrassed, but there was another feeling creeping in, too: relief. I had been struggling with this habit, and this secret, for so long. I looked at my daughter and sobbed, wondering how I had gotten to this place but thankful that it was finally going to end".[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-55) Since 1972, Hancock has practiced [Nichiren Buddhism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nichiren_Buddhism "Nichiren Buddhism") as a member of the Buddhist association [Soka Gakkai International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soka_Gakkai_International "Soka Gakkai a lecture at Harvard University titled "Buddhism and Creativity" as part of his Norton Lecture series.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock#cite_note-61) ### Cobra automobile ownership \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Herbie_Hancock&action=edit§ion=11 "Edit section: Cobra automobile ownership")\] In 1963, at the age of 23, Hancock purchased a new [1963 AC Shelby Cobra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AC_Cobra "AC Cobra") from a dealership in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") for $6,000.
